en: Now begins the *Śrī Tantrāloka*. First Āhnika.
The Mother is the great new creation resting upon the pure creative power (*vimalakalā*), her body full; and the Father is he whose splendor is hidden within the five faces.
May that Heart of mine— the family of the nectar of the Absolute (anuttara), consisting of the emission of existence vibrating from the union of those two—
throb forth! I bow to the Goddess, the supreme Yoginī Bhairavī, who is the creative intuition of consciousness,
whose abode is the lotus of the trident formed by the portions of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
I bow to the Goddess who resides within the body of the dancing Bhairava,
who sports like a streak of lightning in a sky thick with monsoon clouds; she who,
throbbing, has incinerated the three bonds of duality with her mass of blazing light.
May the spear of knowledge stand forth, capable of cutting through both the true and the false positions.

The sovereign power of freedom, the desire to emit in succession, and the nature of succession—this is the manifestation of the All-pervasive Lord. May that very triad of Goddesses abide within me, expanding my own unsurpassed essential nature.

May Gaṇapati, the son of the Goddess, whose own state is that of the Lord of the Great Wheel of Radiance arising from the manifestation of those deities, and who possesses the luster of the shimmering moon, thoroughly cause the ocean of my consciousness to surge forth.
(6) He whose web-like network, reddened by passion and strewn with the openings of its knots, functions through expansion and contraction; (7a)
May that Lord, the master of my own will, who is well-pleased with me, grant me that which he fashioned on the outer path as a *kalombhita* [a specific type of ritual vessel].

Victorious are the former Gurus, who possess a splendor superior to the clusters of fine pearls from the Tāmraparṇī river of the lineage proclaimed by Tryambaka; they are the pure helmsmen in the playful sport of the waves of the ocean of the great scriptures of the Guru.
Victorious is the Guru alone, the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha, renowned upon the earth;
as well as the Lord Maheśvara and Bhūtirāja, who are his other manifestations.
[The teachings] have issued forth from the venerable Somānanda and the illustrious Utpala.

Victorious are the compositions of the fragrance of consciousness, spreading in all directions! We pay homage to the bee-like intellect of the teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, which is nourished by its immersion in the abundance of that [fragrance] and is enchanted by the primordial sound (nāda).

May that most excellent Guru, the illustrious Cukhulaka— who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures and rests in the bliss of fullness— grant me his instruction. May that unique Śambhunātha, who together with the Goddess is capable of uplifting the world, be victorious!
By the rays of the teaching proclaimed by me, this path of the scripture, though profound, has been made manifest.

(13) There exist many diverse manuals (*paddhati*) in the various streams [of the scriptures], but not even one is seen regarding the sequence of the meaning of the Unsurpassed Trika (*anuttara-ṣaḍardha*). (14)
Thus requested many times by virtuous disciples and fellow students,
I compose this clear exposition, which fulfills its intended purpose.
From the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Bhaṭṭanātha, and likewise from the pair of feet of the venerable Bhaṭṭārikā, there has descended a lineage of gurus.
Abhinavagupta—who blazes with the awakening arising from that very service which dispels the poison of the fetters other than Awakening—composes this work.
(16) There is nothing here that has not been taught by the God of gods in the *Śrīmālinīvijayottara*, either by its own name or through its indicative mark. (17)
The teaching of the Lord is divided into ten, eighteen, and sixty-four [Tantras];
the essence of that is indeed the Trika scripture, and the essence of that is the Mālinīmata.
Therefore, everything contained herein [is established] by the wise who are free from sectarian traditions.
By the command of our Guru-Nātha, we shall reveal that which has not been seen before.
This is the work of Abhinavagupta, whose name was proclaimed by his teachers as one who attained renown through meditating upon the lotus feet of the Three-Eyed Lord (Śiva). 19–20.

O you who seek to worship the Great Lord, pluck this lotus of Abhinavagupta’s heart, its contraction dispelled by the radiance falling from the feet of the sun-like Śrī Śambhunātha. (21) [The Opening Statement]

In this regard, it is proclaimed throughout all the scriptures that ignorance is the cause of transmigratory existence, while knowledge is the sole cause of liberation. They maintain that impurity is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:

"By means of this qualification, having dispelled the possibility that liberation occurs at some time subsequent to transmigratory existence—which might otherwise reside in the intellect—it declares that liberation occurs in the absence of that [intellectual state]. (1.23–24)
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not the mere absence of knowledge, because that would lead to an over-extension of the term;
for such absence exists even in a clod of earth and the like, yet it does not undergo transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*).
Therefore, [ignorance] consists in the non-manifestation of the reality (*tattva*) of the object of knowledge in its entirety.

"That very knowledge is ignorance," so it is stated in the *Śivasūtras*. In the two sūtras, "The Self is consciousness" and "Knowledge is bondage," this meaning is demonstrated through their conjunction and their alternative application.

The word "caitanya" (consciousness), ending in a nominal suffix, denotes nothing but absolute freedom (svātantrya) without implying any specific attributes; thus it is stated in the ancient Sūtra. But by the second Sūtra, [he teaches] either action or the instrument.
By speaking thus, duality is said to belong to that which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
The manifestation of duality is ignorance regarding that [consciousness]; because of its worthlessness, it is called bondage.
For this very reason, it must be completely eradicated—this has been established through repetition.

Whether it be something insubstantial or even something substantial that is distinct from the independent Self, there is no such thing as "liberation" (mokṣa); nor is even a separate name for it ever grasped. However, that which consists of the full and perfect manifestation of the true nature of the object of knowledge— AbhT_1.31a/. svatantrātmātiriktastu tuccho@ tuccho@pi kaścana / AbhT_1.31b/. na mokṣo nāma tannāsya pṛthaṅnāmāpi gṛhyate // 31 AbhT_1.32a/. yattu jñeyasatattvasya pūrṇapūrṇaprathātmakam /
That progressively higher knowledge bestows the pacification of each respective form of transmigratory existence.
"I am untainted by passion and the like; I am inwardly empty; I am devoid of agency"—through such knowledge, both in its concise and detailed forms, one is liberated from that much [of bondage].
Therefore, even one who is liberated remains as if unliberated because, despite being freed from one limitation, he still abides within another;
whereas one who is truly liberated is devoid of all limitations. That knowledge of the true nature of the object of knowledge which is free from [the sense of] a universal self—
Nowhere is that ignorance, which bestows true liberation, [removed] by limitations.

That which has been described as the nature of both knowledge and ignorance is each said to be twofold in the teaching of Śiva, distinguished as being of the person (pauruṣa) and of the intellect (bauddha). 35–36.

In that regard, the ignorance of the person (puṃs) which is called "impurity" (mala), as well as that which arises from it, consists in the veiling of one's own Śiva-nature—which is the form of perfect consciousness and action;
it takes the form of contracted vision and action, and is undifferentiated for the bound soul (paśu). (AbhT 1.37–38a)
That ignorance is not a part of the intellect (*buddhi*), because it lacks determination (*adhyavasāya*) and the like.

When [the intellect] possesses the determination, "I know this in this way," through the reflection arising from the individual soul (*aṇu*) within the opening of the sixfold sheath (*ṣaṭkañcuka*), [then that ignorance is not the intellect].
Then, an intellect is born that is of such a nature as to be designated by the term "ignorance" (ajñāna).
That [intellect] belongs to the Buddha-consciousness (bauddha), and it is both the nourisher and the nourished of the individual soul (pauṃsna).
But when the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the bound soul (paśu) have perished, the person attains the supreme state.
That consciousness which is expanding, belonging to the Person (puruṣa), and free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka) [is the ultimate].

That which concludes through the fitness of knowledge whose nature is expanding and non-conceptual is the "cognitive" (bauddha); its "personal" (pauṃsna) counterpart, as previously described, is both that which is nourished and that which nourishes.
In that case, although the ignorance pertaining to the individual soul (*pauṃsna*) is destroyed by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means,
nevertheless, at the end of that body, that knowledge becomes clearly manifest.
But when the expansion of intellectual ignorance is [removed] by intellectual knowledge (*bauddha-jñāna*), [the same occurs].
When that [doubt] dissolves, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) rests in the palm of one's hand. Even initiation, when preceded by Buddhist gnosis (bauddhavijñāna), truly brings about liberation;
therefore, even in that case, Buddhist gnosis holds primacy.
This duality arising from knowledge and ignorance has been established by the venerable teachers Kheṭapāla and others in the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Ruru*, the *Mataṅga*, and other scriptures,
for the sake of attaining the perfection of the Buddhist consciousness whose nature consists of such a determinative realization.
The scripture alone is primary, for it reveals the reality that is to be known. Even when the internal knowledge consisting of the individual soul has dissolved through initiation,
conceptual thought may still arise, because the [impurity] residing in the intellect has not yet ceased.
Since the sense of self-existence persists within the intellect as long as the body exists,
liberation would not occur even at the end of the body if human ignorance were not destroyed. However,
upon the cessation of intellectual ignorance through the uprooting of conceptual construction, liberation is certain.
"At that very moment, liberation occurs"—thus it was stated by the Creator in the venerable *Niśāṭana*.
"But for one whose consciousness is joined with conceptual thought, he shall go to Śiva upon the fall of the body;
for the other, however, at that very moment"—this is the primary teaching of the scripture in this regard. (AbhT 1.50–51)
For the supreme reality of that which is to be known is Śiva, whose nature is light;
for that which is not of the nature of light can possess neither luminosity nor even substantiality.
Furthermore, the non-substantiality of entities is also solely within the domain of aesthetic wonder (camatkāra).
This cognition is not like a wall; it is also [the realization] that "this is a non-entity.
Furthermore, this which is called "manifestation" shines everywhere;
since it cannot be denied, what is the use of constructing means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it? (53–54)
Even those means of valid cognition which extend life to objects—
their supreme life-force is that very Supreme Lord. For even He whose nature consists of the power to negate everything exists in this manner.
"It appears to me that [the claim] 'knowledge is for the sake of the self' is not so. Whether in the negation or the proof of entities, such is the primary [nature of things];
what, then, is the utility or application of means of knowledge (pramāṇas) therein? (56–57)
[58 missing]
In the Kāmika [Tantra], it is stated for that very reason that [the Lord] is devoid of causal discourse;
for that God of gods, no dependence on another exists.
Since another depends upon Him, He is established as being independent.
For the independent Lord who has mastery over all, the sequences of place, time, and form are not restricted;
thus He is the all-pervasive, eternal Śiva, whose form is the universe.
Because of His omnipresence, He goes everywhere; because of His eternal nature, He is devoid of beginning and end.
Because he possesses the form of the universe, he is the illuminator of the manifold variety of both consciousness and the unconscious;
therefore, his possession of many forms is described in the *Dīkṣottara* and other scriptures:
the world, the body, light, space, sound, and the mantra itself.
Śiva is said to be sixfold, being differentiated by the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and so forth.
Whoever is established in the nature of that [particular aspect] attains its very state.
Through the thorough knowledge of the sounds beginning with *vyoman*, liberation is attained; of this there is no doubt.
In the case of the Lord’s having a universal form, this very [state] serves as an illustration;
it occurs when he has ascended to the state of being undivided and when there is a dissolution of division for him.
And it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "The Lord possesses all forms and is formless."
Like water or a mirror, by him all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded.
And this property of his, such as liberation and so forth, does not differ from one another;
this single property of his exists by encompassing everything.
Therefore, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is endowed with the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone;
even His possession of manifold powers is simply His inseparability from that very power. And what is called "power" is the very nature of an entity as conceived by the subject (*mātṛ*).
Therefore, even when he is conceptualized as possessing power (*śaktimat*), he alone remains non-dual.
For, regarding the various forms of the Lord imagined by the subject (*mātṛ*), what difference is there in reality? It is like the burning and cooking capacities of fire.
In the ultimate sense, this [world] is not nothing, because it does not exist apart from manifestation;

for there is nothing whatsoever, nor is the distinction between the power and its possessor real. Indeed, that which generates the abundance of its own power arises from its identity with the reality itself.

That power is likewise the Goddess herself, appearing even while possessing a different form. And Śiva, whose glory is never diminished, appears as if created within the mirror of his own consciousness— the subject— by virtue of his sovereignty in acts such as creative contemplation.
Therefore, by whichever aspect this [reality] shines forth, even though it is partless, it appears as such;
thus, "power" (śakti) is indeed the reality itself, and the sequence of power and the possessor of power is manifest.
And in the venerable *Kiraṇa-śāstra*, this is presented by way of a question and its answer.
Even the experience of conceptualization belongs to the mind; the mind does not exist in Śiva.

(75ab) And regarding the question, "How can there be initiation without knowing Śiva?", the answer is as follows: (75cd) The experience of hunger and so forth is not a conceptualization, for it is not mental. (76)

Just as a conceptual thought perceives a tree through its form alone even when its taste and other qualities are not perceived, so too does one perceive Śiva through sound, the point (bindu), and so forth. Because this Śiva is said to possess manifold powers, he is therefore "Great" (Mahān).
The extensive expansion of divisions— consisting of *kalā*, *tattva*, *pura*, *varṇa*, *aṇu*, *pada*, and so forth—
as well as creation, maintenance, concealment, withdrawal, grace, and the like, even the "fourth state" (*turya*), is the unfolding of the Lord’s manifold powers.
The states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and those that transcend them—
all these too are the abundance of the waves of sovereignty belonging to this Lord.
The Great Lords of Mantra, the Lords of Mantra, and the Mantras, preceded by Śiva, [are likewise His manifestation].
In the Age of Strife (akalau) and as the manifest (sakala), these are indeed the manifestations of Śiva alone.
The nature of the entire collection of principles (tattva-grāma) must be imperishable;
for it is stated in the venerable *Triśiromata* that the Self itself is the essence of one's own nature.
Abiding in the heart, abiding in the entire body, abiding in its own nature, and exceedingly subtle—
the totality of the principles (tattvas) is proclaimed by the word "group" (grāma). It is said that the Self alone is Dharma, overflowing with the nectar of Śiva.
Knowledge established in luminosity, situated in the midst of existence, non-existence, and so forth,
should be known as abiding in its own place— the state of the seer free from veils,
stainless with the pure consciousness described as the distinct reality.
One who abides in the conduct of worldly life is said to have everything accomplished for him.
Having abandoned the upper [state], he enters below; established in Rāma, he moves within the middle region.
His movement, his station, dreaming, waking, and the opening and closing of the eyes [are all his].
Running, leaping, exertion, and the testing of one's strength;
likewise, various states of intellect, dispositions, designations, and manifold actions—
this pervasive Rāma is Śiva, the supreme cause here.
When the mind is cleansed of impurities through the cessation of mere memory,
one meditates upon the supreme object of meditation, which abides in the state beyond coming and going; indeed,
by means of recitation alone, one attains the supreme Śiva known as Bhairava.
That very nature, free from the states of existence and non-existence, is declared to be *japa*.
Even here, the distinction of being distant or near is fashioned by its own sovereignty, in dependence upon the freedom of consciousness.

Thus, because of His fullness of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), this Supreme Lord manifests by what form indeed would He not appear? He shines forth unobscured, yet He also shines while His own nature is veiled.
He shines as both veiled and unveiled through the manifold convergence of differentiation.
Thus, this triad of powers within the Lord— whose other name is absolute freedom (svātantrya)—
has been made manifest by the teachers under the designations of Will and the rest.
For the God is taught by means of words whose meanings correspond to their etymologies as declared in the scriptures:
this Lord Mahābhairava is the supreme Śiva;
he sustains the universe through the application of filling and supporting, and by that [sustenance], he is honored.
By virtue of being accompanied by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and by its nature as sound (*rava*), it brings about the cessation of fear of saṃsāra.
Even from the sound born of the fear of saṃsāra, when there is reflective awareness in the heart,
the discernment of the fear of existence becomes manifest through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
And it is manifest within those whose minds take delight in the absorption of devouring Time (kālagrāsa), which dries up the reality of time that impels the stars;
and it is the roaring of the goddesses of one's own senses, which strikes fear into the limited, bound souls (paśu).
He is the Lord even of the fourfold host of Khecarīs and others, both internal and external;
he who is most formidable in shattering the cycle of transmigratory existence is praised in the scripture by the teachers as "Bhairava" through these etymological meanings.

In the absence of discourse regarding what is to be abandoned or accepted, there is an overflowing due to being a mass of one's own bliss; play is the desire to exist in a state of supreme excellence, as well as sovereignty.
Discourse is the internal conversation that occurs through differentiation, even though the Self is non-differentiated.
Because it illuminates everything, its radiance is praised as being "all-encompassing" (sakala). From the very moment of attaining its own nature, it is inclined toward every duty to be performed;
consisting of pure consciousness, composed of all actions, and possessing the qualities of vision and action, it is the ultimate goal.
Thus, according to the etymologies in the *Śivatanuśāstra*, the Lord is remembered by the teachers as such;
through the application of teaching (*śāsana*), obstructing (*rodhana*), protecting (*pālana*), and maturing (*pācana*), He benefits all.
Therefore, Śiva is the Lord who consists entirely of supreme bliss (*śreyas*); therein, there is nothing whatsoever that is not auspicious (*aśiva*).
Whatever form of this kind may manifest even slightly among Rudra, Upendra, and others,
it is for the sake of removing that limitation [of theirs] that the qualification "supremely great" (paramamahat) is employed. Thus,
that true nature of the object of knowledge is shown by the command of Śiva.

By me, through my own self-awareness, sound reasoning, the scriptures of the Lord, and the Trika system, these three powers— Parā and the others— manifest as that [Triad]. Because they appear during emission, maintenance, withdrawal, and the fourth state (turya), they are thus declared to be twelve.
To that extent, this supreme Śiva is said to be of a perfectly full nature;
therefore, the worshippers here are directly established in that very state.
Furthermore, there is the application of the various degrees of deficiency or excess regarding the aspects of those [energies].
By the very power of His sovereignty, He is defined in the scriptures as follows:
the Solitary Hero, the Couple, the One with Three Powers,
the Fourfold Self, the Fivefold Form, the Sixfold Self, the Sevenfold, and the one adorned with eight.
The ninefold self, possessing the powers of the ten directions and consisting of eleven kalās,
is Bhairava, the lord of the great twelve-spoked wheel. In this manner, the Lord [resides] even up to the thousand-spoked wheel or the wheel of innumerable spokes.
In the Viśvacakra, Maheśāna, whose power is the universe, unfolds. Furthermore, because those wheels also consist of their own respective groups following [their respective principles],
the differentiation within the wheels has been described here and there through their unity.
In the Traiśirasa doctrine, because of the application of counting four, six, two, and twice two [chakras], the Lord—
who possesses a manifold innate form— is said to be the master of the six chakras. Therein, the names of the goddesses of the chakras are given according to the distinction of their functions.
Because they are conceived according to their literal meaning, these deities are joined with meditations on peaceful or fierce forms.
For the internal body of the one Lord of Consciousness is His intuitive flash (*pratibhā*);
whether peaceful or otherwise, that measured wheel of the waves of consciousness is what is worshipped.
"May there be nourishment for this [soul]"— from such an utterance, from meditation mixed with internal discourse, and even from external activity, this Goddess of Consciousness (saṃvid-devī),
having become manifest, shines forth and bestows a corresponding fruit upon him.
The nourishment of the withered and its becoming moist is therefore white water.
Following that, meditation is extended as being primarily concerned with that;
and just as colors by their very nature flow with flavor.

Those [phonemes] consisting mostly of dentals, labials, and dentals, when combined with certain other letters, enter into the state of being seeds and make that consciousness manifest. [The mantras say:
"Bring about nourishment; cause this to swell exceedingly with rasa."
Even internal discourse, being conceptual in nature, why should it not fulfill that very [intention]?
"This is nectar, this is milk, this is clarified butter which brings strength;
by means of this, I shall nourish his seed"—thus one should fulfill this action.

Therefore, Viśveśvara, who is Bhairava as pure consciousness, is worshipped by people seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation, both through the state of being limited and the state of being unlimited. For this reason, the Guru has instructed that even those who are devotees of other deities [should worship him].
For those who perceive anything distinct from consciousness as being an object of sacrifice,
they too, upon discerning the object of knowledge, conceive of it as non-different from consciousness.
Therefore, [consciousness] consists of the manifestation of the "I" (ahantā), whose nature is the form of uninterrupted reflective awareness.
There is no injunction for that which is self-manifest; moreover, its nature as creation precedes it.
For the manifestation of the deities is an object of knowledge, having arisen from the cause that is power (*śakti*).
Consciousness, however, whose form is "I," is eternal and consists of self-manifestation.
The injunction (*vidhi*) is a command; it consists of three parts and is the creative realization (*bhāvanā*) whose essence is the impulsion (*codanā*).

Indra and the other deities are established solely through that [injunction], for the deities are preceded by the injunction. However, the awakening of the "I" (*ahaṃbodha*) is not like that; they [the deities], on the contrary, possess the nature of being objects of cognition.
Seeing [the Self] as if merely emerged, they do not know It even though they claim to know It.
Thus it is said: "But they do not know Me in truth; therefore they fall.
Falling, indeed, is nothing other than the attainment of a fragmented state of being.

"Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods," and so forth— this was described by him [the Lord]. However, those who, having submerged the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) therein, know the state consisting of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayī sthiti*), even though they are merely devotees of that [lower deity], they go to Me, which is unconditioned.
In all these cases, the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) here denotes solely pure consciousness (*bodhamātra*).
That [consciousness] is expressed by the two terms "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*) and "Lord" (*prabhu*), as well as by the roles of the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛ*) and the object of sacrifice (*yājya*).
It is taught that the consciousness belonging to the sacrificer (*yājamānī saṃvit*) alone is the object of sacrifice, and nothing else.
But there is no other form whatsoever, for no deity has been conceived [therein].
Nor has any ritual procedure been taught here, nor any mantra or the like, nor any locus for its function.
This very [Self], having veiled itself, remains in the state of insentience.
The Self, whether veiled or unveiled, extends from the gods down to the level of stationary objects;
there is a wonderful diversity even within this duality of the insentient and the sentient.
Indeed, what could that independent being not conceive?

This has been stated in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*: "He who knows [the Self] as the perfectly awakened one (*saṃbuddha*)—for the state of being an object of knowledge is a property of consciousness; its shadow cannot obscure that [consciousness].
Therefore, for the non-inert portion designated as the person (*pudgala*), the atom (*aṇu*), and so forth..."
In the portion belonging to the unobstructed state, manifold variety exists in many ways.
Although there is no real division within the eternal nature of consciousness,
nevertheless, that [division] is perceived due to the varying degrees of the removal of veils.
We shall explain that in detail in the determination of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*);
having concluded the discussion on the supreme state, it will be examined in the context of the gross state.
Therefore, the All-pervasive Lord manifests [Himself] toward a certain perceiver.
One's own innate nature is indeed full; through a certain sequence of parts and sub-parts, there is the manifestation of one's true self as the single essence within the state of all things.
That which is the manifestation of the essential nature of the self as the one being of all existents is the supreme knowledge of individual souls; anything other than that is inferior and manifold.
And that [consciousness], manifesting through direct means as well as through the means to those means and so forth,
is divided here by various modalities (bhaṅgī). Even therein, it is distinguished in its entirety and in part according to whether it is mediated by itself or by another.
A vast difference arises through the presence or absence of an intervening medium.
That which is the means for knowledge is not called ignorance;
rather, it is indeed knowledge itself, subtle, and is considered to be supreme, consisting of the nature of will.
The relationship between means and end is merely the resting place of the grossness of cognition;

this very power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is the sole cause of both bondage and liberation. In that regard, within the first self-reflection, which is the singular abode of the non-conceptual, [this occurs].

That which flashes forth manifest and directly is proclaimed as that which is called Will (icchā). Just as an object appears clearly to those with eyes wide open even without mental synthesis, so too does the nature of Śiva appear to some.
Through the repeated contemplation of the process of ascertaining the various portions of conceptual constructions,
that reflective awareness which one attains is known by the wise as the means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*).
However, that [other means] which establishes external objects constructed by such conceptualization—

Then, the means of action (kriyopāya) is taught; there is no difference therein regarding the attainment of liberation. For that which is called "action" is not other than knowledge itself, since it has reached the culmination of yoga through conventional usage—so it is stated in the venerable Gama-śāsana.

Yoga is not one thing and ritual action another; for that intellect which is ascended upon reality is indeed called "action" when it brings about the pacification of the latent impressions of one's own mind.
These latent impressions within one's own mind are born from karma, impurity, and māyā.
The thought directed toward their pacification, which is of the nature of pure consciousness (saṃvit),
presides over the multitude of principles (tattva) that constitute the body and reside externally;
that very [thought] is the action (kriyā) and it is indeed yoga, insofar as it causes the dissolution of the principles into consciousness.
Even in the world, that which is called "I am going" is merely an internal vibration;
when it enters the body, the location, and the senses, it becomes the action of movement.
Therefore, even that which is called action is indeed nothing but knowledge.
Knowledge alone leads to liberation; this has been rightly declared.

For liberation is indeed nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). And the true nature of the Self is consciousness; it is nothing else. Furthermore, as for those [states] which... 156.

Those powers, beginning with action (kriyā), are not superior to the nature of consciousness; for it is impossible for them to possess a non-conscious nature, and because no substratum (dharmin) [for such powers] can be established.
Indeed, in the scripture of the Supreme Lord, it is not as in the system of Kaṇāda.
A certain substratum for the powers, which consist of the nature of attributes (dharma), is taught. Consequently,
if the powers— such as knowledge, action, and will— are likewise distinct,
then this statement that "Śiva is one" becomes devoid of any factual basis.

Therefore, this very state of consciousness is itself that absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); yet, when analyzed in detail, it sufficiently culminates in many powers (*śakti*). Since liberation is the manifestation of the Self, such a doubt need not be entertained here.

An effect does not necessarily follow from its cause; even one who possesses that knowledge is not thereby liberated. Since the relationship of cause and effect that has been described regarding liberation through knowledge is not primary, it is certain that this undesirable consequence does not apply.

Thus, action is indeed of the very nature of knowledge; since it carries a state of grossness within itself, its manifoldness is surely perceived therein. In the method of action (*kriyopāya*), there is a distinction between the internal and external means.

Due to the manifoldness of divisions and subdivisions, there is an incalculability of intermediate [categories]. By this, that which some scholars have suspected—that there might be a difference even in liberation due to the difference in means—is utterly destroyed. (1.164b–165)
Because they consist of the destruction of the impurity, the power [of obscuration], concealment, and descent,

even though there is a difference in their causes, they are not distinct from one another, like the various occurrences of the destruction of a jar and so forth. Indeed, this threefold nature is taught in the scripture named the *Śrīpūrva*.
In the *Samāveśanirṇaya*, it was declared by the Supreme Lord:
"The immersion that arises for one who thinks of nothing at all, through being awakened by the Guru, is proclaimed as the Śāmbhava [immersion]. (1.167b–168)
When one contemplates with the mind alone an object devoid of vocal utterance, the immersion one thereby attains is here designated as the Śākta. [This occurs] through the absence of vocalization,
the instruments of speech, meditation, phonemes, and the mental construction of locations.
That which occurs is the immersion (*samāveśa*) correctly called *āṇava*.
(170) "For one who thinks of nothing" refers to the non-utility of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And by means of that [non-conceptuality], the instantaneous absorption into the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is described. (171)

"How does that [state] come to be? he says: "By means of the exceedingly weighty teacher, through an awakening directed toward the object of knowledge, characterized by its sudden and full development. (1.172) The suffix *-tasi* is explained as having the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), or alternatively, it is explained through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇyataḥ*). (1.173a)
Possession (*āveśa*) occurs for one who is not independent due to the immersion of his own nature into that [higher] nature;
it is the state of being that other nature belonging to Śambhu, who is indivisible from primordial power (*śakti*).
Therefore, the meaning of the statement here is to be understood as follows: that which is to be known unfolds by itself.
Even without conceptual determination, [the reflection] immediately eclipses the Mother (the mirror) while displaying its own majesty, reflected in the mirror of the Mother;
it abides according to the degree of excellence in the purity of the heart.
The object of knowledge is twofold: pure consciousness and the insentient; and of these, the former is imagined.
But the other is likewise real; such is this division.
That immersion which occurs through the insentient has the form of a reflection.
Pervasion by consciousness is indeed identity and nothing else;
therefore, non-conceptual awareness, independent of cultivation and the like,
having attained identity with Śiva, is here the Śāmbhava immersion (samāveśa).
By virtue of that [non-conceptual knowledge],
the subsequent determinations that arise here may indeed attain identity with it, yet they do not possess the status of a means [to it].
One who asserts that non-conceptual [knowledge] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in relation to conceptual [thought]...

It has indeed been answered: for that which is established is followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since there is a very clear manifestation of the certainty [that] "it has been grasped. However, one realizes "I am grasping" through the power of non-conceptual unity.

In the self-awareness of the non-conceptual nature, that which is the very radiance of the object is *siddhi*; it does not arise from conceptual thought, which is devoid of dependence on the actual reality. This is merely the repose of consciousness in either purity or its opposite.

Whether independent of or dependent upon conceptual construction within its own nature, just as one who knows gems at midnight perceives their various specific qualities— even those revealed for only the duration of a flash of lightning—
so too does he discern those very particularities among a multitude of jewels.

This purity of consciousness arises either through the force of prior practice, or from the unrestricted will of the Lord; this will be discussed [later]. Furthermore, the fifty-fold nature of this immersion (*samāveśa*) has been described.
Due to the intention of clearly delineating the distinctions residing within these thirty-six principles (*tattva*),
there exists within this [system] a triad consisting of the individual (*puruṣa*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and power (*śakti*).
This occurs because, in sequence, they possess divisions numbering four oceans (4), eight directions (8), and three fires (3).

That which is designated as the Power (Śakti) of the Puruṣa and Vidyā is all-pervasive; therefore, it is indeed reckoned separately from those things that are not all-pervasive. Furthermore, it is also differentiated from one another according to its states of impurity, being purified, and purity.
The elements (*bhūta*) are established through direct perception, as they are inferable from their effects and causes;
for this very reason, they are designated separately from the group of principles (*tattva*).
Indeed, it is the element alone that constitutes the object of all common experience and existence.
The wise [should understand] the abiding of that [power] here within the fourfold space;
indeed, the immersion into the power of Rudra is discussed as fivefold. What room would there be for the description of the immersion of the elements and so forth therein?

If it is argued that this [objection] arises as a mere incidental consequence (*prasaṅga*), then while such a resolution may indeed be possible, it does not win over our minds; for the world possesses diverse tastes (*bhinnaruci*).
It is stated in the dualistic scriptures (*dvaita-śāstra*) that there is a state of being distinct from the Supreme Lord.

As [the manifestation] of the elements and so forth exists there, it does not exist in the same way in that which is devoid of duality. Whatever constitutes these thirty-six principles, and whatever else there may be—
this is the extent of the Great Goddess, the unimpeded power of Rudra.
For that very reason, in this second chapter, the universal nature (*viśvarūpatva*) of the elements beginning with earth was described according to the divisions of the fifteen-fold set and so forth.
In the same way, let it be understood here as well that there is the realization of the partless nature [of consciousness].
For this very reason, [the Lord] is characterized by non-conceptuality, permanence, sovereignty, and majesty,
or by other attributes inherent within Him, because they are of the nature of His powers (śakti).
Whether in their entirety or in part, those who— due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from what they have heard— worship that all-pervasive Supreme Lord,
[perceive Him] through the intensity of those very attributes flashing within their respective mental constructs (*vikalpa*).
They rest upon the subject, which is the full flood of attributes, without distinction.
For this very reason, the venerable Lord of Vidyās has respectfully declared:
"If the sense-born [cognition] does not take as its object your own nature, which is free from conceptual construction, in the realm of imagination..."
If the manifold cognitions were not internally delineated, experiences would not be manifest.
Thus it has been stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other texts, with such qualifiers as: "Now, the presiding ground of the Lord consists of the rays of His own powers," and so forth.
In that heaven, he is of brilliantly radiant nature, unwavering, and possesses an immovable form.
That very state is the supreme, subtle *kāṣṭhā*, whose essence is the nectar of all directions;
it has destroyed all veils, is peaceful, and is intensely devoted to the pure reality alone.
That virtuous [power], which is devoid of beginning and end, is figuratively treated as having a form (mūrti).
The reason for such a figurative treatment here is purposeful:
through that [form] as a gateway, clarity arises in the substratum, leading swiftly to the state of being absorbed in that [reality].

Those very same dharmas, called powers (*śakti*), are worshipped through various appropriate forms and aspects for the sake of attaining identity with them (*tanmayībhāva*). Among them, moreover, some power may be either infinite or limited.
One should project [the universe] by means of the logic of its existence as a flux, according to its distance and proximity. By that,
one projects the state of being the full nature, luminosity, the essence of consciousness,
the state of Bhairava, and the universal powers, due to their all-pervasive character.
Sadāśiva and the others, however, because they lack upward pervasion and reside below,
would project their powers (śaktis) according to their proximity or distance from that worship.
And in this state, there is the sequence of the path of conceptualization known as the Śākta.
But here, because it has been taught [otherwise], the counter-correlative is non-conceptual.
(1.210b) Established on the path of non-conceptuality, by whichever path one may enter—down to the level of Earth and Sadāśiva—one becomes Śiva through each of those paths. (1.211)
In the stainless heart, which shines with the radiance of the foremost portion of the [highest] plane,
within that light, by means of that very [heart], consciousness attains the nature of Paraśiva.
Thus, they know this to be the authentic means consisting of a portion of the supreme power of will.
The residents of Sumatyanta [attain] the immersion known as Śāmbhava.
Now, the Śākta [immersion] is described: it consists clearly of the intellect (*cetas*), the cognitive faculty (*dhī*), and the ego (*ahaṃkṛti*);
because it is characterized by conceptualization (*savikalpatā*), it is essentially composed of *māyā*, consisting of will (*icchā*) and the other powers.
That which arises through egoity, by way of the sequence of conceptualization and determination, is the Śākta means;

although it employs Māyā as its instrument, at its conclusion it becomes free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka). Indeed, that state of the bound soul (paśu) which is non-conceptual is the supreme Śāmbhava state.
Incomplete due to the mother’s own deficiency, it blossoms when that [deficiency] is removed.

Thus is the stage of thought-constructs (*vaikalpikī bhūmiḥ*) within the Śākta [power], characterized by the sense of agency and perception; though these two are manifest therein, contraction still persists according to the previously stated principle.
Likewise, for one who is intent upon dissolving the accumulation of contractions, that radiant power which produces internal manifestations at will [arises].
But surely, does not that conceptualizing intellect exist there in the individual (āṇava) state? Indeed, it does.
But here [in this system], he has described another means (upāya) as being devoid of utterance (uccāra).
By the word "utterance" (uccāra), many things beginning with that are meant here;
however, these do not exist in the means of power (śakty-upāya), for in the state of power (śaktitā), there is neither difference nor non-difference.
The subtle (*aṇu*) is indeed a manifest division; the means to that [realization] here is the *āṇava* [yoga].
Consisting of conceptual determination, it becomes non-conceptual in the end. But surely, the intellect, the mind, the ego, and the person would pervade Śiva?
"How is it that such a thing was taught by him as being situated below?
It is said in reply: "In reality, for us, Śiva himself is of such a nature;
having performed the concealment of his own essence, he is again self-luminous in that manner."
This has also been well established in the dualistic scriptures, such as the *Mataṅga* and others:
that very light of Śiva, who pervades even the lower levels, is firmly established [therein], by which the supreme state shines even upon the plane of the intellect and the mind. (1.224–225)

Both of these two types of immersion proceed toward the ocean of non-conceptuality; indeed, nothing at all exists without being rooted therein. Therefore, he stated that no distinction in the fruit of consciousness should be imagined here.
And it is precisely here that the primacy of conceptual construction (kalpanā) is indeed indicated. Even in the view of one who asserts validity with respect to conceptual thought (vikalpa),
the status of non-conceptual perception (nirvikalpa-pramāṇatā) is attained through the sequence of those very conceptualizations.
One who previously did not know the reality of the Jewels (*ratnatattva*)— until the deliberation on the means of certain realization—

is called a "knower of the Jewels" upon attaining non-conceptuality through the absence of [other] means. Here, the Śāmbhava [means] is taught as the means of non-differentiation, while the Śākta is said to be [the means of] differentiation.
The means consists of both difference and non-difference; therein, the means of difference is that which pertains to the individual soul (āṇava).
At the end, within this knowledge accompanied by its means, the entire expansion of ritual action will be included in a clearly manifest form.
For that which is called "action" (kriyā) is not a separate entity from consciousness; it is simply consciousness itself assuming a sequential nature.
It has been stated previously that when this is attained through the power of the means (upāya), it is termed "action.
Furthermore, correct knowledge (samyagjñāna), whether residing in oneself or another, is the sole cause of liberation.

For the manifestations of self, other, and so forth are merely conceptual constructions (kalpanāmātra). Since they are equally conceptual, when the Guru consists of the radiance of oneness (aikyasphuraṇātmaka), he is established as the one Self and is said to be liberated.
For as long as his lineage extends, he is proclaimed to be a Guru;
and because it consists of perfect knowledge, one is liberated from it by means of one's own self.
Therefore, it is said that the Knower saves his own lineage from that very [lineage].
Established through both reasoning and scripture is the fact that the Sage is one and the same.
Therefore, as for those who raise this objection here: "Surely liberation comes from knowledge;
how then can these rituals such as initiation lead to liberation? [236–237]

If it is argued that she is the essence of knowledge, then [liberation] would release only that person in whom knowledge resides. Or, even if it were to liberate another, would this not be inconsistent? Thus, what has been established by others here has been refuted by you from its very root. (1.238)
It is said that "impurity" (*mala*) is indeed a substance, like a film on the eye; initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the rite that destroys it, like the application of collyrium and other such treatments.
We shall refute this later, as it is censured by both reason and scripture.
And we shall demonstrate the persistence of impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and karma.
Thus, regarding the knowledge that has the three powers as its means, the last among them is the root;
the one following it is the middle; and the first is the highest of the high.
Even beyond that is the supreme knowledge, devoid of means and the like;
resting in the power of bliss, it is here called the Unsurpassable (Anuttara).
That self-luminous consciousness [is realized] by the Vidyās, the Īśvaras, and the rest.
Even its true existence is difficult to attain; thus it is stated in the *Śrīsiddhātantra*.
This has been clearly indicated in the eighteenth chapter of the *Mālinīvijayottara*, according to the statement:
"And this [is not revealed] by Śaṅkara unless he is pleased. (AbhT 1.243–244)
By this very reading in the *Mālinīvijayottara*,
that fourfold knowledge which is the great arising of both supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and liberation— this I am now expounding here in this teaching named the *Tantrāloka*.
In this regard, whatever is perceived here, whether internally or externally,
that appears even beforehand in its unmanifest form. Likewise, manifestation occurs in an unmanifested manner through an inexpressible nature.

Doubt occurs regarding a certain form only when that form has been ascertained, and not otherwise. When this primary [object] is present in the form "What is this?", the aspect "this" is well-ascertained; doubt, however, consists in the non-revelation of attributes such as existence or non-existence.
Why does no further meaning manifest for this word?
Rather, it denotes the very object itself whose form has not yet been disclosed.
[In the case of] "Is it a post or a person?"—this is not a primary doubt.

Indeed, it is the very arising of certainty regarding the various properties residing in the object; however, because the two forms [of the object] to be reflected upon have not been disclosed, that [certainty] is doubt. Otherwise, when there is a "what" aspect, it is clearly a conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Therefore, that which is the manifestation of the state of one's own nature as yet unrevealed is here first the enunciation (*uddeśa*), the question (*praśna*), and indeed the doubt (*saṃśaya*).
Likewise, by way of the unfolding of the expansion of existence whose form remains unrevealed...
Self-awareness, expanding forth and having assumed the state of the questioner-pupil,
[proceeds] thus; because of the concealment of its nature as internal reflective awareness and certainty,
it also partakes in the emergence of withdrawal that arises immediately after the expansion.
To whatever extent there may be an external expansion that is clearly manifest in nature, to that same extent, she is said to be the questioner whose form has not yet unfolded. In this way,
consciousness itself consists of both the question and the answer.
Even in the roles of teacher and disciple, this distinction of bodies is indeed non-ultimate.
For consciousness, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, projects outwardly the various forms situated within itself—
both in their general and particular aspects— in an instant.
The creation of some property that is capable of desiring the specific aspects yet to be created is the "creation of the general" (*sāmānyasṛṣṭi*), which is of the nature of doubt. However,
when the specific aspect about to be created ceases [to be desired], then...
The definitive conclusion regarding the Mother is as she is pleased; it cannot be otherwise even in ten million aeons.

Then, through the proficiency of that object’s own inherent power (*vīrya*) in its progressive ascent, there occurs its unsealing by means of that very form, resulting in the definitive determination of its characteristics and its transcendence.

Furthermore, by means of falling back upon the already determined portions of the doctrine, there is a repeated examination of the nature of the summary and the definitions through all means, such as perception, inference, analogy, and authoritative testimony. (261–262)

The triad of enunciation (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and examination (*avekṣā*) manifests for living beings. Enunciation is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpita*); definition, moreover, is conceptualization;
and examination is likewise a succession of conceptualizations within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

"This is a mountain" is the *uddeśa* (enunciation); "it possesses fire because it has smoke" is the *lakṣya* (the object to be characterized). Here, the "network of cognitions" such as pervasion (*vyāpti*) constitutes the *parīkṣaṇa* (examination).
"This is an enunciation" is the former; "that which is called a *gavaya* is similar to a cow" [is the latter].

Or rather, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is as follows: "The remainder (*śeṣa*) constitutes the examination (*parīkṣā*) in the case of analogy (*upamiti*). (AbhT 1.265b) "One who desires heaven" is the enunciation (*uddeśa*); "one should sacrifice" is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*);
and "by means of the Agniṣṭoma and other [rites]" is the examination (*parīkṣā*) which functions as the remainder (*śeṣavartinī*). (AbhT 1.266ab)

The creation of a reality as it truly is, by one who is capable of tolerating other portions that may be projected by conceptual thought according to their preference, is designated as *uddeśa* (enumeration).
At that very moment, consciousness discerns as much as is intended to be projected.
For since she is not limited by time, she unites all that pertains to every time.
That which is the emission of what is about to be emitted and the withdrawal of the portion previously emitted—
while a dharma is being restated— that consciousness is said to be its defining characteristic.

The examination (*parīkṣā*)—which consists of the creation, withdrawal, and rest of further portions following that [initial emergence], and which is fashioned according to the preference of the subject (*mātṛ*) with a limited duration—is now described. These [stages] are:
first, *paśyantī*; then, *madhyamā*; and finally, *vaikharī*.
The Goddess is Parā, Parāparā, and the final one is Aparā by nature. This very triad of powers, beginning with Will (icchā), is thus proclaimed;
it is only through being animated by this that worldly activity is extended.

In the teaching of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara-śāsana), which consists of questions and answers, the nature of the supreme relationship exists within the fivefold connection (abhisaṃbandha-pañcaka). As it is stated in the *Ratnamālā*: "Everything consists of the supreme power (parakalā)."
The great, the intermediate, the divine, the mixed, and another which is the fifth;
that which is the identity between the questioner and the speaker who are distinct is called the "connection" (saṃbandha). And its transcendence consists in the manifestation of perfect oneness.
By this very method, there may also be another relationship sufficiently expressed by the scripture, due to the connection with the perfection of the results and so forth. In this way,
this Goddess of Consciousness is at all times, by her very nature, [all things].
She whose life-breath consists of the triad beginning with the *uddeśa* (enumeration) embodies the nature of all scriptures.
Regarding that, the initial enumeration (*uddeśa*) is stated first, possessing the divisions of the "elder" (*pūrva*) and the "younger" (*anuja*);
the means consisting of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the second, and the supreme means (*paropāya*) is the third.
The means of Śākta, the means of Nara, and then the seventh, the means of Kāla;
the arising of the wheels (cakrodaya), the path of space (deśādhvan), the path of principles (tattvādhvan), the differentiation of principles;
the path beginning with Kalā, the application of the paths, the descent of power (śaktipāta), and concealment.
The commencement of initiation, the initiation for the observance (sāmayī), and that for the son-like disciple (pautrika) according to the rule;
the subtle procedure of the objects of knowledge, the initiation of immediate transcendence (sadyaḥsamutkrama);
then the initiation by the scales (tulādīkṣā), the indirect initiation (pārokṣī), the extraction of the mark (liṅgoddhāra), and the consecration (abhiṣecana).
The funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*), the arrangement of the *śrāddha* offerings, the description of the remaining modes of conduct,
the worship of the *liṅga*, the many festivals, the purificatory rites (*pavitra*) and so forth arising from specific occasions;
the secret practice, the flood of mantras, the mandala, and the ritual for the finger-seals (*mudrikā*).
The unification [of all things] within one's own essential nature is the entry [into that state]; it is the integration of the scriptures.
(283) The narration of the lineage and the determination of the worthiness of the scripture to be adopted.
(284ab) The wise person who always [recites] these thirty-seven [verses]... (284cd)
One who practices these daily observances (āhnika) thoroughly shall become Bhairava manifest;
for when one's awakening is complete within the thirty-seven [topics], one becomes Bhairava.
What wonder is there that even ordinary beings (aṇu) attain the state of Bhairava by his very glance?
Thus, this enumeration of the preceding [chapter] has been told; now the subsequent one is being stated.
In the section on the piercing of consciousness (vijñānabheda), the enumeration of Bharga follows in sequence;
in the second section, the differentiation of the state of having transcended the means (gatopāyatva) is presented.
The nature of the reflection of the universal consciousness, the sequence of the arising of reflective awareness,

the non-differentiation from mantras and so forth— these are discerned in the supreme means (paropāya). Furthermore, the purification of conceptual thought, the reality of reasoning (tarka), and the true nature of the Guru are explained.
The uselessness of the limbs of yoga, disregard for imagined images and the like,
the arising of the wheel of consciousness, the potency of mantra, and the reality of recitation and so forth—
the equality of prohibitions and injunctions regarding this Śāktopāya is here discussed.
Intellectual meditation, the utterance of the principle of breath, the nature of the conscious self,
and the utterance characterized as the path for entering into the supreme reality—
these, along with the instrument and the principle of phonemes, are described in the context of the individual means (āṇavopāya).

The movement of days and nights, the conceptualization of transits (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth, the diversity of the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and the arising of the phonemes— this constitutes the construction of the path of time (*kālādhvan*). In the "Arising of the Wheels" (*cakrodaya*), this occurs through the differentiation of the wheels, as well as the distinction between mantras and vidyās.

The measurement of the worlds (*purāṇām*), their compendium, and the application of the principles (*tattva-yojana*): these two [topics] pertain to the instruction on the path of space (*deśādhvan*), while the determination of the causal relationship and the definition of the sequence of the principles (*tattvakrama*) pertain to the ascertainment of the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*). (AbhT 1.294–295)

The nature of objective reality, the rule of the principles (*tattva*), the definition of the waking state and the others, and the differentiation of subjects— these are investigated within the division of the principles; as well as the essential nature of the *kalās*, and the conceptualization of the principles by means of [the numbers] one, three, five, and so forth.
The sequence of the differentiation of the phonemes (*varṇa*), the description of the foundational power (*sarvādhāraśakti*),
and the investigation of the paths (*adhvan*) beginning with *kalā*— all this is now being analyzed in detail.
Furthermore, regarding the application of the paths, there is the trembling and the laughter arising from the contemplation of non-duality (*abheda*).
The plurality of impurities and the like, the nature of the principles (*tattva*), the diversity of power (*śakti*),
the establishment of independence, and the variety of concealment (*tirobhāva*)—
this is the summary of what is to be said in the examination of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
The disappearance of concealment, the attainment of fullness through knowledge,
and the lack of need for the ritual of *utkrānti* (the soul's departure) are established at the commencement of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Furthermore,
there is the examination of the disciple’s suitability and the conceptualization of the locations and sub-locations within the sacred site.
The varieties of the general deposition (sāmānyanyāsa), the vessel for the water of honor (arghapātra), and its purpose;
the suitability of the ritual substances, the worship, and the external worship at the door in due order;
the entry, the nature of the directions, and the purification of the body, vital breath, and so forth.

The variety of specific placements (*viśeṣanyāsa*), the vessel for the special offering (*saviśeṣārghabhājana*), the worship of the body (*dehapūjā*), and the worship consisting of the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*cit*), and the path of sound (*adhvan*);
the excellence over the multitude of other scriptures, and the worship of the wheel (*cakra*) in every respect.

The acquisition of the field, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the worship of the Earth and Gaṇeśa; the worship of the Weapon-mantra, the fire-rite (vahnikārya), and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) pertaining to the fire;
the libation (tarpaṇa), the preparation of the sacrificial pap (caru), and the purificatory rites ending with the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha).

The ritual of the Hand of Śiva, the consideration of the preparation of the bed, the ritual concerning dreams according to the rule, and the rules themselves— this is the summary; in this fifteenth chapter, there shall be [these topics] regarding the procedure for becoming a Samayin.
The contemplation on the identity with the maṇḍala, the detailed offering of the sacrificial victim (paśu),

the satiation of the fire, the illumination of one's own essential nature, the procedure for the deposition of the paths (adhvan) within the body of the disciple, and the manifold variety of the purified, the purifier, and so forth.

In this sixteenth chapter, there shall be the varieties of initiation, the supreme ritual placement (nyāsa), the purpose of the existence of mantra, the various types of conjunction (yojanikā) and so forth,
the arrangement of the aphorisms, the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi), the burning of the fetters (pāśa-dāha), and then the [final] conjunction.
"Likewise, the distinction of the paths has been thus explained in the ritual concerning the *pautrika* [son].
The absence of birth and so forth, as well as the clear distinction of mantras—
this is contained in the eighteenth chapter, known as the 'Brief Initiation'."

The examination of the *kalās*, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sword and other implements, the movement within the body, and the procedure for the knowledge of Brahman— thus has the immediate transference (*sadyaḥsamutkrama*) been described.
[Now follow] the examination of qualification, the internal consecration, and the procedure of the scales (*tulāvidhi*).
Thus, this entire essence of what is to be said is contained in the twentieth chapter.
The procedure for the dead and the living, the instruction on the Net (Jāla), the group of purificatory rites (saṃskāra),
and the investigation of strengths and weaknesses— this is the rule in the twenty-first chapter.

In the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*, it should be clearly stated: hearing [the teaching], granting permission, purification, liberation from transgression, and the removal of doubt (315). Then follows the examination, the appointment as a teacher, the observance of that vow, and the withdrawal of the [limited] intellect (316).
The division of that [empowerment], its efficacy, and the extent of the procedure for the rite of initiation; furthermore, the qualified candidate, the purificatory rite, and its purpose—
this is what is to be discussed and examined in the twenty-fourth chapter, called the "Final Sacrifice" (antyayāga).
The purpose here is the granting of enjoyment and liberation; the ritual procedure is clear.
This is the summary of topics in the twenty-fifth chapter, the *Śrāddhaprakāśa*.
The purpose of the remaining conduct is the supreme daily worship on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

The nature of the *liṅga* in its various forms, the description of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), the different types of worship— all this must be explained in the exposition on the adoration of the *liṅga*. Following that, there is the classification of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and the rule for their purpose.

The divisions of the lunar days (*parvan*) and their specific characteristics; the discussion of the wheels (*cakra*) and their worship; the determination of the purpose of the worship of the Guru and others, as well as the first day of the month and so forth;
the examination of death; and likewise the ritual for the assembly of the Yoginīs and other such matters. (321–322)
The method of exposition, the rule for hearing [the teaching], and the rule for the worship of the Guru—
this much is established in the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Occasional Rites" (Naimittikaprakāśa). Furthermore,
it contains the distinction between those who are qualified [to practice] and the lineage-transmission (kula-krama) of the Siddhas and their consorts.
The ritual of worship (arcāvidhi), the ritual of the messenger (dautavidhi), the sequence of the secret Upaniṣads (rahasyopaniṣatkrama),
initiation (dīkṣā), consecration (abhiṣeka), and awakening (bodha) are treated in the twenty-ninth chapter.
The nature of mantra and its potency (vīrya) are described in the thirtieth chapter.
The distinction between the trident and the lotus, the description of the sky[-like], the svastika, and so forth—
these are to be explained in detail in the thirty-first chapter:
the distinctions between the subordinate and the primary qualities, their essential nature, and the investigation of their potency.

It is said that "the division of parts" (kalābheda) is taught in the exposition of the mudrās, because from the thirty-second principle, known as Īśa, onwards, [the division] becomes manifest. Since there is no further division beyond that, no other separate heading has been mentioned here.

"And because it is to be known as primary, there follows the sequence of the other sections. (AbhT 1.328b) Thus has the method of enumeration been declared for the sake of easy comprehension. Now, its definition and examination shall be determined in their proper order. (AbhT 1.329ab)

The Self is the abiding state of the light of consciousness; it is the indivisible consciousness that has assumed a multitude of powers (*śakti*). Its essential nature is such that, by veiling its own innate splendor, it takes on a bound form. Its liberation occurs through the method of manifesting the nature of the light of the Self. And this liberation of that which possesses manifold forms is itself manifold; this is the meaning briefly revealed here. (330) False knowledge is a cataract that produces unequal defects of vision; because of its presence, even that which is pure appears as an abode of impurity. (331)

But as for that which is to be perceived, once it has entered the range of vision, how could the suspicion of impurity arise there—since it would long since have dispelled the seal of the defect of cataracts?
O Multitude of Beings! Having forcibly seized the hearts of people and making them dance with various graceful gestures, you sport about while concealing your own heart.

That fool who calls you dull-witted—being ill-trained due to his conceit that he possesses a refined heart—I consider his very dullness to be a ground for praise, since it leads him to imagine a likeness with you. In this matter, those gurus whose impurities have dissolved, who know the higher and the lower, and who consist of the true being of Śiva, are the ones authorized to investigate; therefore, any request to remove the stain of hatred [against them] is fruitless.
Thus ends this first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Emission of the Distinctions of the Existence of Consciousness," in the *Tantrāloka* composed by Abhinava.
Now begins the second chapter of the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"That which is there, the first state, consisting of uninterrupted and unsurpassed cognition..."
To determine that [nature], I shall begin this second chapter. For if the nature [of reality] were without means (anupāya), what would be the purpose of teaching it here?
Indeed, the teaching might occur once, after which it is said that [the goal] is beyond means.
"This reality is without means"—how [could it be realized] without a means?
But as for those for whom that reality is already such of its own accord, what indeed can we say to them?
That fourfold form of consciousness which has been described belongs to the All-pervasive Lord.

One should consider that very nature, for it is eternally manifest and all-pervasive. That which shines forth through these countless natures— some enter it by way of parts and sub-parts, while others enter it without parts.
In that regard as well, because of the connection with difference based on dependence upon means (*upāya*) and so forth,
the diversity of the means itself cannot be denied, since it is distinct from that [ultimate reality].
Among those [practitioners], those whose selves are stainless [perceive] their own consciousness as belonging to Bhairava.
The method for those who rely on that which is devoid of means is now proclaimed.
In this regard, ritual action (*kriyāyoga*) does not deserve the status of being a means; for it is rather perceived as having arisen from that [higher reality]. 7–8ab.
If it is argued that there must be a means for cognition itself, then cognition is being described;
yet how could luminosity in that which is self-luminous come from anything else?
Regarding this principle that the essence of consciousness is self-luminous, what indeed is the use of logical arguments?

In the absence of that [consciousness], the universe would be insentient and thus incapable of manifesting. Whatever means there may be, whether external or internal, they all depend upon that [consciousness] for their manifestation; how then could they possess the status of being a means toward it?
Abandon all acts of focused attention; indeed, where could you possibly apply such attention? Discern this for yourself:
attention is certainly not appropriate toward that which is already full, nor does that which is incomplete attain the state of reality.
Therefore, on the supreme path, [there is no room] for meditation and the like, whose very life-breath is focused attention.
In the tradition of Bhairava, how could [the senses] be a direct means?
Even those who seek to discern that form through a direct means are surely dull-witted, like those who wish to perceive the sun by means of fireflies.
Furthermore, whatever exists here—whether external or internal, and whatever is considered a means (upāya)—is nothing but the nature of manifestation alone; it is the innate body of Śiva himself.
Blue, yellow, pleasure, and so forth: these are nothing but the manifestation that is Śiva.

In that supreme non-duality whose nature is light, what else could there be? For that is nothing but light alone; how could there be the relationship of means and end, or even such notions as "this is duality," "this is difference," or "this is non-duality"?
The Supreme Lord shines forth as having the very nature of light.
On this level, pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, consciousness,
and insentience are synonymous terms— like the words "pot" and "jar"— and they all refer to that one single reality alone.
For how indeed could that which is an unmanifest portion shine forth when [the Light] is presiding?
Or, if it were shining forth, its dualities would be dissolved by that [Light]. Alternatively, if it were not shining forth, how can its status as a real entity be asserted?
Therefore, a distinction between various illuminations is not logically tenable.
Thus, since this doctrine that "this [reality] is a single illumination" is well-established,
those who advocate for the existence of distinct cognitions have truly been refuted from afar.
Pure luminosity alone is declared [as the ultimate], because non-luminosity is negated;
however, the meaning of the word "one" (eka) does not consist in numerical unity, for it pertains to the distinction between individual manifestations of consciousness.
This is not the Great Goddess Śakti, since she does not depend upon anything else.

And this God possesses no power, since He is not the support of anything; He is not the object of meditation because there is no meditator, nor is He the meditator because the object of meditation is absent. He is not the one to be worshipped because there is no worshipper, nor is He the worshipper because the object of worship is absent.
There is no mantra, nor is there one to be addressed by the mantra; there is no master who utters the mantra.

There is neither initiation (*dīkṣā*), nor an initiator, nor even Maheśvara as the recipient of initiation. [Likewise,] there is no ritual regarding the place, the posture, the restraint, the water-offering (*argha*), the assembly, the invocation, and so forth.
In this state, which is devoid of agent, object, and action, there is no end to its emission.
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor is it something that is free from both;
for that state is difficult to discern—it is some indescribable, unsurpassed reality.
For that entity which appears as "this," being of a limited nature, is indeed like a jar in the world; however, Bhairava is not such.
Non-existence and lack of luminosity possess no utility whatsoever anywhere.
Truth is the life-force of the universe, and it consists solely of light.
For these two reasons, it is neither dual-natured nor devoid of duality;
for it shines as the self of all—by what specific form could it be described?
In the venerable *Triśirobhairava*, it is taught that the supreme state is the very nature of supreme gnosis;
through the power residing within its womb, it is the supreme plane containing all power.
It is neither existence nor non-existence, nor both, because it is beyond the range of words.
"Established on the path that cannot be described, situated in power yet devoid of power"—
those who are purified by the supreme reality of established consciousness are established on the unsurpassed path, unconditioned by means.

To them, this entire mandala of existence appears on all sides as if standing right before them, dissolved by the fire of the consciousness of Bhairava. For these [beings], there are no conceptual constructions of pleasure, pain, doubt, fear, or anxiety.
They have reached a state in which nothing remains but the supreme immersion beyond conceptual thought (nirvikalpa-parāveśa).
For them, there is no mantra, no meditation, no worship, nor even mental construction;
nor is there any resting place for the stages beginning with the initiate (samayin) and ending with the teacher (ācārya).
For one whose nature is to tear asunder the terror-inducing net of all constraints,

there is no purpose whatsoever in the remaining mode of existence other than [bestowing] grace. This world, perceiving some duty of its own to be performed, does not through effort direct any of its activities toward the welfare of others.

But for him whose impurities of all worldly existence have been destroyed and who is filled with the state of Bhairavī, his manifest duty is merely this much: the task of the world. Those of pure consciousness who perceive him through the process of becoming one with his nature—they too become of that same nature; such is the extent of his gracious nature.
This thorough knowledge of reality is declared by the All-pervasive Lord in the venerable *Siddhayogīśvarīmata* to be the primary form of sacrifice and so forth, ending with initiation.
(41) The cloth is superior to the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), and the [inner] circle (*tūra*) is superior to the cloth. (42a)

From the cloth comes meditation; from that, the object of meditation; from that, the subsequent stage of concentration (dhāraṇā). From that also arises the form born of yoga, and from that, the supreme knowledge.
For by means of knowledge, one becomes a great adept, a lord of yogins.

If he, by means of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantryadhāman*), desires to bestow grace even upon those whose consciousness is impure, he should resort to the procedure appropriate for that [state]. And that [procedure] is said to be manifold, according to the nature of those to be graced.
Due to the distinction arising from the confusion of the floods of means, such as the supreme (parā), the intermediate (aparā), and so forth,
there is likewise a devoted application to hearing and studying the scriptures and other means for that very purpose, even for one who possesses the nature of the Supreme Lord.
For that independent [Lord], there is no contradiction whatsoever anywhere;
nor is there grace for a person whose mind is impure without the means (upāya).
This is stated in the venerable *Ūrmi-mahāśāstra*, which embodies the lineage of the Siddhas.
This has been stated likewise by the venerable teachers beginning with Somānanda:

"When the cloud of doubt has dissolved—whether through the words of the Guru, through the power of cleansing by composing a collection of arguments, or through the confidence inspired by what has been taught regarding the scripture—one should touch the feet of the Lord who conquers darkness, whose splendor shines forth in the sky of the heart like the sun. (Abhinavagupta, *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti*, 2.48b–49)
This daily lesson, which distinguishes the unsurpassed state and has transcended all means (*upāya*), is completed.
This concludes the third chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, the supreme means (*paropāya*)—the very state of the Great Lord—is being proclaimed.
That supreme light of Bhairava which has been described as pure luminosity—
within that, only its absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) is further distinguished. That which is Light bestows the state of being manifest upon everything.

And yet the universe does not exist apart from Him; rather, it appears as real. Therefore, this Supreme Lord, unimpeded within the void of His own Self, is the manifestor of this vast display of emanation and withdrawal.
Just as earth, water, and other elements appear unmixed within a spotless mirror,
so too do the various functions of the universe appear within the single Lord of Consciousness.
That which is similar [to the object] appears in the eye, the mirror, the sky, and in water.
For in this way, within a pure form, only form itself appears.
A woman concealing her passion, though she touches with her jar-like breasts a mirror made beautiful by the reflection of her lover, is not yet satisfied.
