For its touch is not pure, since its form alone is so; and purity is the extremely dense union with that which is of the same kind. It is simply the capacity for the perception of what is distinct within itself as non-different.
The purity of that which has not abandoned its own self-luminosity is what has been taught by the Guru. (8) Purity is primarily the attribute of the one Lord of Consciousness in every respect;
anything else that is pure in some particular part or degree exists only through His will. (9)
That form of entities which is obstructive is indeed composed of *māyā*;
however, those very same entities possess another aspect consisting of true knowledge (*sadvidyā*), which is non-obstructive.
Thus, manifesting an appearance that possesses both these forms, [the Lord acts].

The Giver of Boons shines forth in his entirety through the perception of the image and its reflection. As for the one who says that the rays of light from the eyes are fully reflected back from a clear surface and, having reversed direction, grasp one's own face—he is questioned as follows: [11–12]
The light that exists apart from the body belongs to the Self, who is its presiding subject. If cognition occurs by means of that very light alone, what need would there be for a mirror?
However, when those lights are inverted and have attained the state of being the perceiver, [the reflection appears].
The form would be seen on one's own face and not within a mirror. Moreover, this form would appear as "mine" with the same tactile sensation as one's own mouth;
however, it is not so for that [form] which is distinct from the tangible and whose essential nature consists solely of being an object of cognition.
That object, which is reflected [in consciousness], consists merely of form and configuration, joined with touch, smell, taste, and so forth, all of which remain subordinate.
This subordination occurs because they lack the status of being perceived objects, and that absence of perception results from the lack of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
And because there is no actual contact with the object, that [reflection] also does not persist in the mirror.
For this very reason, qualities such as weight are not perceived in it;
for it does not reside in the mirror, but is merely the means by which it is seen.
Therefore, because this [consciousness] does not appear as something distinct [from itself], it is so described.
In that regard, the lamp, the eye, and consciousness are, respectively, the means (*upāya*) and the support (*ādhāra*).
Beyond the lamp, the eye, and the cognition, there is nothing further due to the absence of solidity.
And because it is pure in every respect, it does not appear as something separate like a mirror. This has been shown by the God of gods for the sake of increasing awakening;
for the deluded, it becomes an object, yet even there it is not truly other than that.
It is not resistant, nor independent, nor is it stable or unstable;
this is the power of some purely transparent [reality], so [the Lord] has declared out of compassion.
(3.22) There is no location, no form, no connection with time, no dimension, no mutual contact, no separation from that, and no density. (3.23)

"It would neither be a non-entity, nor would it possess any inherent essence; thus, delusion will surely subside"—this was the method of the mirror that he taught. (3.23) When the path of reflection has been demonstrated in this manner, that which is the reflection of sound is called an "echo. (3.24)
And this sound is not born from sound, because it is heard as something arriving;
for even by those standing at a distance, the sound is not heard by that same speaker [if he is obstructed].
Furthermore, [sound is perceived] upon contact with a specific aperture characterized by the covering of a vessel or similar object.
And because this sound is variegated, it appears as a reflection, like a face [in a mirror].
It manifests as "this is the form of another object of cognition," just as when one hears someone say, "I am hearing what has been spoken by another. // 26–27 //
Because the reflection is necessarily oriented toward the original object (*bimba*),
perceivers situated between them hear the echo. However,
the perception of a reflection can also occur even without the apprehension of the original object.
One should see one's own beloved body reflected in a mirror as standing behind oneself;
such a state is called "facing toward" because it exists in non-difference from the mirror. Therefore, that which is reflected in the space of a vessel, such as a well, [is likewise so perceived].
The space within the mouth, being accompanied by sound, appears as if it were the mouth of another;
and just as one standing behind a mirror does not perceive one's own face,
so too one standing behind such space does not perceive the sound.

Sound that has not been manifested does not reflect; that is certain. Its manifestation and its hearing occur simultaneously in the second moment, while its state of being a reflection and its hearing are simultaneous in that very same moment.
For at the same time, we have the certain perception of the hand and its shadow-form.
Having thus demonstrated the true nature of the reflection therein, we shall now speak of the subject at hand, which is worthy of being reflected upon.
In the sky, sound is accompanied by bliss; in the abode of touch, it is beautiful.
Even another kind of touch—arising from a firm blow, a piercing pain, cold, and so forth—is experienced as residing elsewhere; yet, because it is a reflection, it causes one's own body to tremble.
And this [perception] is not primary, because the succession of its effects is not manifested.
(37) In the same way, smell is clearly present within the nose, and taste within the saliva.
(38) Just as a form reflected in the eyes cannot be perceived by the eye without another [external] eye, (39a)

Likewise, taste, touch, fragrance, and so forth, are not perceived by a sense organ even when they are present; nor is that which resides within the locus of touch the object of another sense-cognition directed toward something external. Therefore, when [the object] is brought into proximity by the internal organs and the corresponding sense faculties, it serves its purpose.

Then, that reflection thus grasped by the sense organ indeed brings forth its own corresponding activity. However, that activity does not arise from an object of the mind that is merely remembered; rather, it proceeds from what is present.
Therefore, when the most excellent of tangibles is present and comes into contact with that sense organ, it is known as being capable of such action.
In the absence of an external object, such a supreme touch, being reflected within that very self, produces that blissful state even within some particular series of channels; thus,
the universe offers itself as its own reflection in the mirror of consciousness.
He proclaims the stainless, universal form of this Lord:
just as fragrance, form, touch, taste, and so forth, when reflected,
appear through the coloring of their respective substrates, like a face and other features in a sword.
In the same way, this entire universe, reflected within consciousness,
takes on its full range of attributes, such as luminosity and sovereignty.
And just as [an image] appears on all sides in a crystal that is perfectly clear in every respect, so it is here.
In that same way, a reflection appears within consciousness, which possesses transparency in every respect.
That which constitutes its absolute transparency is the non-appearance of its own form;
therefore, consciousness is the most transparent of all, whereas a jewel is not, because it grasps a specific form.
A reflection is presented by means of an external object that serves as its prototype (*bimba*).
If that very [external object] is itself a reflection, what would remain to be the prototype?
Or rather, whatever cause is designated as the prototype—

Even that [object] attains the state of a reflection within consciousness; otherwise, it would be non-existent. Thus, protected by the weapon of the firm logic of self-awareness, the sovereignty of the reflection unfolds everywhere.

"But surely, in the absence of an original object (*bimba*), how can there be a reflection (*pratibimba*)? What can we do? For it is indeed seen; let it then be called the original object. "Not so; because it lacks the defining characteristics [of an original], how indeed can it be called an original object?"

Just as a face appears independently, unmixed with anything else, so they describe the nature of a reflection as being similar to another form without abandoning its own essential nature, like [the image in] the surface of a sword or a mirror. 53–54ab. 54cd.

And it has been stated by the Buddhists: "Even when there is an external object, the intellect—because it perceives both the one and the many—has a form that resembles the many; however, it is not itself multiple. [AbhT 3.55] But if this is so, what is said to be the definition of a reflection? [AbhT 3.56a]
"Because it is impossible for it to be mixed with anything else, its appearance as distinct from that [source] is unattainable;
they call this a 'reflection,' just like a face in a mirror. This [world], mixed with consciousness, is impossible to appear as distinct from consciousness. (AbhT 3.56–57a)
If there is an awakening to the supreme reality (paratattva) and so forth, why is it not called a reflection?
This is the established definition of a characteristic; if [it is] so, let it be called the original object (bimba).
Wise men apply themselves to the actual thing, but not to a conventional term.
But surely, a reflection cannot exist without an original object (*bimba*). What follows from that? For the original object does not reside within the reflection through identity (*tādātmya*).
And therefore, since that [identity] is impossible, this previously stated definition [of the reflection] fails.

There is no loss [of the cause], yet this question concludes only with respect to the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). Moreover, that [instrumental cause] is never in any way the material cause (*upādāna*);
for instrumental causes may occasionally and in some instances come into existence.
Therefore, through the dense cause of recollection and so forth directed toward the light present before one,
let the form of the beloved be transferred [into that light].
Otherwise, the beloved, having ascended into consciousness, would be subject to separation.
Why does consciousness not appear as something that has moved ahead into a state of separation?
For this very reason, let there clearly be some intermediate state known as the intellect (*dhī*),
wherein its appearance occurs through separation, as in the case of volitional thought or the perception of a dream.
"Therefore, let the powers of the Lord exist in such a manner as the cause [of this world];
thus, this entire universe is a reflection within the Lord, the pure sky of Bhairava’s consciousness—indeed, it does not arise through the grace of anything else. (65)

The supreme Goddess, that unsurpassed *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), which is the Lord’s independence regarding His state as the self of the universe— that indeed they call the Absolute (*anuttara*). She is the one who possesses the expansion of *kula* within this God who is *akula*.
She is the supreme Kaulikī Śakti, inseparable from whom the Lord [exists].
That which is the unified form (*yāmala*) of those two is known as *saṃghaṭṭa*.
She is called the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), from which the universe is emitted.
The reality that is higher than the highest is declared to be this very Goddess;
she is the essence, she is the Heart, and she is the supreme Lord Visarga.
In the *Devīyāmala* scripture, she is called Kālakarṣiṇī.
In the Mahāḍāmara sacrifice, as well as at the summit of the venerable Parā,
she is described in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra as the true essence (sadbhāva) of the Mothers. In this conjunction, because of its nature as consciousness, there occurs that reflective awareness.

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the supreme sovereign of the Aghorā powers; she herself, when her form becomes agitated, arises as the Ruler (*īśitrī*). Then the supreme Ghorā goddesses are born, who act as guides upon the Śaiva path.
That self-reflection which previously existed as the solitary hero (ekavīraka),
consisting of the unfolding of the universe to be known, abides as the power of knowledge;
this is the goddess Parāparā, who is the formidable circle of the Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍalī).

When the aspect of the object of knowledge (*jñeyāṃśa*), opening up due to its intensity, undergoes agitation, it incessantly emits that which serves as the sole lamp for both the pure and impure paths; at that time,
the appearance of deficiency arises within the state of pure consciousness alone.
When that has taken root, it is said to be the beginning of the persistence of the category of objects to be known.
This rooting is the ocean of consciousness assuming various forms;
yogis discern this as the seed of the arrangement of all seeds.
The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is said to be twofold: that which is agitated and that which is unagitated.
For she rests within herself upon the object of will in its twofold nature, by means of the power that flashes like a sudden lightning bolt and has the form of a blazing fire.
The attainment of the desired state occurs through stability in the nature of the earth-element.
Although this [attainment] exists predominantly within the power of expansion (*unmeṣa-śakti*), it is nevertheless merely a locus of manifestation;
it is not its original place of birth.

Therefore, they say that the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) possesses a fourfold nature within the Supreme Nectar (*parāmṛta*). Because there is no further agitation (*kṣobha*) within it, this is not the seed (*bīja*) of anything.
Being a cause of agitation is "seed-nature," and being the substratum of agitation is "womb-nature" (*yoni-tā*).
The form of consciousness is the agitator; it is both agitated and it agitates.
Agitation is the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyadharmatva*), while agitation-causation (*kṣobhaṇā*) is its externalization.
It is the desire to emit the single seed-syllable which is non-different from the universe existing within it.
They know that agitation (*kṣobha*) is the desire for that [object], and the manifestation of the desire for reality is what they call "agitating" (*kṣobhaṇā*).
When that desire attains oneness [with its object], it becomes effective.
The disciples of the venerable Somānanda have called this the substratum of agitation.

That which is the mere object of knowledge (*jñeyamātra*), in which the distinctions of consciousness such as desire (*īṣaṇā*) and so forth have not yet emerged—that is the seed (*bīja*). It is by virtue of its connection with that [seed] that the vowels possess the state of being seeds.
The very emergence of that seed, which is its desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*), is said to be [the seed-vowel] itself.

Since this object of perception appears as if distinct from the conscious self (cidātman), this is "agitation" (kṣobha). However, "the act of agitating" (kṣobhaṇā) consists in forcibly displacing consciousness from its state of indifference by its own power, so that it falls into other subjects who have become silent [in their own agency]. (3.86c–87b)

Even though this desire to emit has arisen, because it becomes unified with another reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it becomes fulfilled; this is proclaimed here as the "substratum of agitation" (*kṣobhādhāra*). Therefore, that intermediate state should be known as desiring a state of apparent differentiation.
From the seed of the universe (viśvabīja), the entire external image will evolve.
I have shown the true nature of the relationship between the agitated and the agitator,
as it was spoken by the venerable Maheśvara, my Guru, through whose grace [this has been revealed].

We speak now of the subject at hand: these four phonemes are not the seed (bīja), nor are they the womb (yoni), because this [seed] does not attain the state of being the substratum for agitation. And because it rests within the Self alone, it is said to be of the nature of nectar (amṛta).
Thus, that pentad which was previously described [mutually]— 92—
arises in various forms surging forth through their mutual intermingling.
That which is the supreme, unsurpassed vibration (spanda) and that which is the surging bliss (ānanda)— 93.

Through the friction of the union of those two— the opening and the closing of the will— they attain an extreme variety when the consciousnesses of the Absolute (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda) are joined within the power of Will (Icchā-śakti). They call that the Triangle, beautiful with the fragrance of emission (visarga).
When the powers of the supreme bliss have attained firm establishment there,
they proceed to abide in the six spokes through the conjunction of two triangles;
even when united with the power of unfolding (unmeṣa), they again become identical with that.
When the two powers clearly manifest the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) through their mutual interaction,
that agitation which has been described as residing in will (icchā) and unfolding (unmeṣa) occurs even from that state;
those two powers partake of that very nature and do not exist otherwise.
"But surely, the Absolute (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda) are, by their very nature, devoid of differentiation. How is it that they have taken to themselves such vast variety within their own self?
Listen first: this Lord of Consciousness is of an unlimited nature."
If Maheśvara, the Lord of the time of the emergence and dissolution of the manifold variety of infinite powers,
were to abide in a single form,
he would lose his nature as Maheśvara and his nature as pure consciousness, becoming like a jar or other such objects.

It is said that the defining characteristic of the insentient is its limited luminosity. Since consciousness is distinct from the insentient, it is not measured by limits; therefore, its own powers emerge as waves from the great ocean of consciousness.

Like waves, they assume a variety of forms through their mutual friction with one another; this very mutual diversity of the powers' own friction is said to be the supreme and manifest body of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
In this fourteenth abode, wherein the three powers have become manifest,
the Teacher has declared in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana that it possesses the nature of a trident;
and this has been called the "Stainless" (nirañjana) by the gurus who perceive reality.

Because the possessor of power (śaktimat) is manifested, whereas power itself is never manifested by anything; that very [possessor of power] is clearly manifested through its own respective [powers], such as will (icchā), knowledge (jñāna), and action (kriyā), which are themselves being willed and so forth. (106–107ab)
When these three, however, flash forth as a unity, then nothing can qualify them, because they mutually cancel one another out. Therefore, that trident is the three powers in a state of fusion.
In which, through immediate immersion, the yogi becomes stainless.
(3.108) Thus, beginning from the state of supreme nectar, this group of eight clearly attains the state of eight eights through the differentiation of the forms of Brāhmī and the others. (3.109)
In this state, that unsurpassed power (anuttara-śakti), although manifesting her own form,
assumes the nature of the Bindu due to the impurity of the portions of the knowable (jñeya-kalā).
When the power of action (kriyā-śakti) has arisen in the abode of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, [she manifests].
That light which is undivided is indeed for us the supreme *bindu*.
And this has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*:
"Abiding within the circle of the heart-lotus, it consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva. (3.111–112)
The Bindu, which is the stainless savior, is to be understood through its various modes of dissolution;
it is that very sound whose essence is Nāda, abiding within all living beings,
and which remains inactive through the division of above and below.

The variety [of qualities] such as delight and sharpness, as well as white, red, and so forth—that very [variety], this Light, is itself independent of them; and the Guru has said: "That which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even fire illuminates... (Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka 3.114b–115).
There is no light whatsoever belonging to the sun, moon, or fire that exists independently of their manifestation; rather, it is consciousness itself that shines forth in this manner,
conjoined with various limiting adjuncts arising through the power of its own sovereignty.
Light undergoes various internal diversities such as sharpness and so forth.
Even the sun, though difficult to look upon, becomes a delight to the eyes when fallen upon the path of water; behold the power manifested by limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
This light belonging to the sun and other luminaries is rendered turbid by limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
for that very reason, it depends upon the light of consciousness belonging to the Great Lord (Maheśa).
That which is clearly manifest as pure light alone is explicitly called the "sun."
Showering down the essential portion of the object to be illumined, it is called Soma.
They say that the Sun is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while they declare Soma to be the object of knowledge (*meyam*).
Although both are independent, they remain inseparable from one another.

This [reality], consisting of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, has attained a state of mutual orientation toward one another; therefore, it is proclaimed as Citrabhānu, whose nature is the blazing consciousness. This very thing is the supreme principle of fire, and it is precisely this that belongs to the subject.
Consciousness alone, however, because it is identical with the object of knowledge and requires nothing else,

is called the "knower" due to its autonomy; it is diversified by the variety of objects of knowledge and nourished by the appearance of diversity arising from the objects to be consumed by the lunar rays [of consciousness].
From that very [source], Agni was proclaimed as Citrabhānu by Maheśin.
For consciousness remains independent of the collection of means such as the objects of knowledge;
it is the knower who abides in the realization "I am," just like one learned in the scriptures.
Since the knower is essentially nothing but consciousness (*anubhavātman*) and not [a material] form,
that state of being a knower does not depend upon a pure object of knowledge and so forth; rather,
in that state, it is called "knowership" by virtue of its inherent capacity.
That very state of being an object of measurement is merely imagined by the previous limited subject;
for consciousness, even while surging forth, is devoid of temporal succession.
Being ever-arisen and full, it takes on the form of the knower, the known, and so forth.
The action of cooking and so forth, being delimited by time, is characterized by a sequence;
even if it were devoid of its final moment, it would not attain the state of being "cooked.
In this way, the nature of the principle of Light (prakāśatattva) abides as the moon, the sun, and fire.
Even their primary nature as pure luminosity is not denied;
that which is their first form, the short vowel, is called the Sun (Sūrya). Due to the power of agitation and bliss, through its long rest, it is called the Moon (Soma).
That which is called the supreme *pluta*, situated beyond Somananda,
is said by those learned in the scriptures to be of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and fiery (*āgneya*). Herein, there is that which is pure light, while the three abodes remain present.
It is stated in the scripture that, by virtue of being the *bindu*, this is considered the *śivabindu*;
it is indeed distinct from the letter *m*, merely bearing its shadow, just as [the letters] *ra*, *la*,
and *ha* abide in the form of the neuter vowels and the visarga.
Just as the vowel *i* itself becomes another vowel through the shadow of a portion of the letter *r*,
in the same way, that [vowel] appears as something else due to a trace of *mahā-*, even though it remains non-vocalic (*asvara*) in its twofold nature.
This internal desire to emit, which has been described as the supreme *kaulikī* power, belongs to this [vowel].
By virtue of that very agitation, she certainly attains the nature of emission (*visarga*).
And it is stated in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*, in the discussion concerning the pervasion of the *kalās*:
"Therefore, the seventeenth *kalā* has the form of the nature of nectar."
She has spread forth by means of the movement of the *bindu* which is both supreme and non-supreme, and which is her own essential nature;
yet, when devoid of emission (*visarga*), she is the manifestor of all things.
She is indeed Śaktikuṇḍalikā as well as Prāṇakuṇḍalikā.
At the terminal point of the emission (*visarga*), however, is what is called the Supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
it is called the Sky of Śiva (*śivavyoma*), the supreme Brahman, the station of the Self.
The mere emission of the Lord consists of the manifold movements of creation and withdrawal.

The state of emission (*vaisargikī sthiti*) is the projection of one's own self into one's own self by means of one's own self. Thus emitted, the emission, having reached a state of solidification, is designated as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the consonant, and the contact (*sparśa*).
The unsurpassed, supreme abode is called Akula;
the emission (*visarga*) of that Lord is called the Kaulikī Śakti. And she possesses the state of emission because of the sequence of the arising of bliss.

The state of overflowing [consciousness] extends up to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) becoming manifest; indeed, emission (*visarga*) itself is of such a nature that it projects all this within itself. Such is the form of the ocean: the infinite succession of its waves.
For this very reason, this emission (visarga), consisting of the unmanifested *ha*-kalā,
is called the "principle of desire" (*kāmatattva*) in the venerable *Kulaguhvara*:
"That unmanifested syllable which is situated in the throat of the beloved."
But when one does not desire the form of sound and is devoid of meditation and concentration,
by fixing the mind there, one may simultaneously bring the world under control.
For this very reason, the state of the emission (*visarga*) is as manifest within the *haṃsa* as it is elsewhere.
In the same way, the letters from *ka* to *sa* abide as the sequence of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) and the others;
from the Unsurpassed, the birth of the fivefold *ka*-group occurs clearly.
Just as each one is clearly manifest within itself as having the nature of the five powers (*pañcaśakti*).
From the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which abides in its own essential nature as a single form, the *ca*-group arises,

consisting of five powers and characterized by a gradual manifestation. That [power], however, which was described as being subject to the turbidity of the knowable (*jñeya-kāluṣya*) due to its connection with rapid movement, [is this].
From that [dual form] arises the pair of consonant groups beginning with *ṭa* and *ta*;
from *unmeṣa* (the opening) arises the group beginning with *pa*, since by it the universe is completed.
For this manifest form of the knowable extends clearly up to the twenty-fifth [tattva].
Because it is an object of knowledge and because it is manifest, this much has been declared as the nature of touch (sparśa).
And that power of will (icchā-śakti), which is twofold according to its being agitated or unagitated,
moves toward the state of the self (yātmatā) when it is oriented toward a portion of a power of a different kind.
That very [power], when stained by the turbidity of the objects of knowledge acquired more rapidly,
attains the state of *ra* and *la* by being directed toward heterogeneous [objects].
Likewise, the power of expansion (*unmeṣa-śakti*), possessing two forms, reaches the power of heterogeneity.

It attains the state of the letter *va*, which rains down the essence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Because it has reached the unsurpassed bliss of Will (*icchā*) through its connection with swiftness, it is called Wind (*vāyu*); because of its luminosity, it is Fire (*vahni*); and because of its stability, it is Earth (*dharā*).
This group of four is called "internal" (antaḥstha) for this very reason:
because they are contained within [the powers of] Will and the rest, and because they abide in their own completion;
furthermore, it involves the conjunction of the powers of Will and the rest with their respective homologous powers.

They say that this [universe] is of the nature of agitation (*kṣobha*), even for those whose nature is both agitated and unagitated. Regarding the homogeneity (*sājātya*) with the Absolute (*anuttara*), there are two possible courses: if that which is the one Absolute therein is for the sake of generating bliss (*ānanda*).
Through that union, the yoga consisting of agitation will clearly manifest.
Even here, the second unsurpassed abode is for the sake of procreation;
yet, without agitation, the state of being the unsurpassed is not sufficient.
That desire which is devoid of action, and that which is colored by the object of desire,
has attained a threefold state through the distinction between rapidity and stability; it remains as the unblown, the blowing, and the fully blown.

That which is desired [as the object] exists in this [power] in a threefold way, without falling away from its own nature; that very [power], by means of its own heat— which consists in the impelling of its own self-sovereignty—
having been projected clearly outward, remains as the triad of *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*.
From that very [source], within this letter *sa*, the universe shines forth clearly.
Yogis declare that to be the nectar (*amṛta*) and the supreme abode;
and at the cessation of the beginning and end of agitation, that alone is the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*).
In the states of the whistling sound (*sītkāra*), bliss, the presence of reality (*sadbhāva*), immersion (*samāveśa*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
that very same [reality] is declared to be the supreme, undivided Brahman.
Thus spoke the Blessed One himself in the venerable *Kulaguhvara*.
In this [reality] whose name is true to its meaning, having attained the identity of power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimad),
I have out of affection for you revealed the reality of poison (viṣatattva)— which is called "without phonemes" (anacka) and has the form of a crow’s beak— free from meditation and concentration.
The reality of desire is its fulfillment, which is clearly perceived in union;
and the reality of poison is nectar, once the state of being concealed by the limited individual (aṇu) has fallen away.
For poison is the pervasive power, since it conceals the light of the non-pervasive one.

The stainless supreme abode is the Tattva; its "stained" aspect, however, consists of the power of action (kriyāśakti), which is composed of the universe and from which everything emanates. Will is desire, poison is knowledge, and the Goddess is action—the stainless.

The penetration of these three is called Śiva-Bhairava; our teachers have declared that one should always establish oneself firmly in this state. Having entered the reality of poison, there is neither the elemental spirit, nor the poison, nor [the subject].
Through the contemplation that "I am indeed the planet alone," it should manifest.
(3.174) Now, if it is asked: "In this [system], birth is said to arise from the neuter vowels;
therefore, how could there be a state of being neuter?"—we reply: here, the neuter does not possess the power of procreation. (3.175)

For it is thus: that very power of will (icchā-śakti) which is said to reside there gives birth to its own object of action, which exists within itself in the form of what is desired. However, because that which is to be desired exists as the cause of coloring [the object], it follows from that [desire].
There is no procreation from a mere portion; that which arises therefrom is turbidity, and its body is likewise [turbid].
The wise know it to be of a composite nature, joined with the coloring of the object of knowledge.
It is neuter, due to the absence of the state of being either an agitator or a locus of agitation.

Because these four classes of phonemes are illuminated by their own *ūṣman* (aspirate/fricative), they are called *ūṣman* by Bhairava, whose nature is stainless. The wise declare that this [series] from *ka* to *ha* is the substratum of agitation (*kṣobha*).
Through union with that [state] in the form of the *yoni*, one proceeds to another state of arousal (*kṣobha*).
By means of the yoga of its manifestation, it attains the nature of the fiftieth phoneme;
it is well-established on the plane previously known as the twenty-fifth.
There are two tetrads, pertaining respectively to differentiation and non-differentiation, in sequence.
The first tetrad is skilled in joining differentiation to pure consciousness;
the other tetrad is the sole cause for the ascent of differentiation into non-differentiation.
In this way, whatever collection of phonemes there is, all that was originally composed of vowels (svara).
Because it is joined with manifestation, it is called a consonant (vyañjana), since its life-force is indeed the vowel.
Here, in the continuum of phonemes, the group of six vowels alone constitutes the root.
Those very six deities are the principal rays of the sun; for within the solar rays themselves reside the lunar digits. Therefore, in this context, the triad of long vowels is clearly the lunar body.

The moon is not something other [than the enjoyer], nor is the object of enjoyment anything other than the enjoyer. It is the enjoyer himself who exists in a twofold state by way of being the object of enjoyment. For the pot does not possess its own nature as an object of enjoyment; rather, that status resides in the subject.
Therefore, that which is established in the Mother is said to be its state of being the object of enjoyment;
for, by virtue of the relationship between the one who perceives and the perceived, it is the unsurpassed [Absolute].
Likewise, the Will and the other powers, having attained the nature of union, constitute the object of enjoyment.
When [the principles] beginning with Will (icchā) have attained the state of being objects of enjoyment within the planes of Anuttara and Ānanda,
the emergence of the diphthongs is said to be the nature of the enjoyer. Furthermore,
the deity consisting of Anuttara and Ānanda is said to be the enjoyer alone.
Desire and the rest are merely objects of enjoyment; therefore, their nature as "powers" (śakti) arises from that very fact.
If the object of enjoyment were dissolved into the enjoyer, then the enjoyer would clearly be manifest in reality as that [object].
Thus, the essence of the six is the triad consisting of consciousness, desire, and expansion.
They declare that very triad to be the supreme majesty of Bhairava.

That triad of the Supreme Lord is celebrated as His full power (pūrṇā-śakti). Since the entire universe is projected by that [power], when this [triad] is worshipped, [the universe is thereby worshipped].
Worship arises toward that which possesses universal power and is devoid of limitation;
yet, it is not possible to say, "Its majesty is only this much.
For who could set a limit to the power of one whose power is unlimited?
Therefore, the Lord is unsurpassed because his sovereignty is unsurpassed;

(195) by virtue of being endowed with the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), he is perfected as the one whose form is the universe. Thus, the Great Lord is the one whose power is full of the fifty-fold reflective awareness (*āmarśa*). (196)
The one whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the [supreme] reality; all other powers are established within this very [reality].
Indeed, the Goddess consisting of eighty-one words will be shown to be contained herein.
Since its essential nature is a single act of awareness, that Mass of Sounds (*śabdarāśi*) is Bhairava.
Through the yoga of touching [the object] by means of its reflection, that very power is Mātṛkā (198).

Through the friction of the mass of sounds, she is Mālinī, whose source is differentiated; like before, through the reflective awareness of her ninefold nature, she possesses the form of the individual classes [of letters]. (199)

But when each [phoneme] is established through reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), that very [consciousness] consists of the fifty [phonemes]. Thus, by being permeated with *nāda*, Śiva— whose essential nature is reflective awareness— abides everywhere as the agent in the form of mother and father.
This very emission (visarga) is that of Śakti; yet, by way of the bindu of Śiva,
it again assumes the nature of the Absolute (anuttara), having internalized the infinite universe within itself—
that which is the Lord’s own self, the inner essence of the undivided universe.
That very reflective awareness (parāmarśa), characterized by the perfection of the dyad,
is said to reside within the non-dual nature of Śiva and Śakti, which is the essence of the unsurpassed emission (visarga).
Because of its fullness, this reflective awareness of the All-pervasive Lord is called "I" (aham).
The emanation beginning with Anuttara and ending with Ha is the very nature of Śakti.
Having withdrawn the entire universe, she dissolves into Anuttara;
this entire universe resides within Śakti, and she [resides] within the supreme Anuttara.
"That which is real within her is encapsulated by the All-pervasive One"—
by this [principle], the form of Śakti is encapsulated in the venerable *Trīśikā-śāstra*. Indeed,
the universe that shines within consciousness also [shines] there by means of consciousness.
These three, through their union as a pair, have attained the state of a composite whole. This is the single supreme form of Bhairava, whose essence is the *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness).
That which is the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) of Śambhu thus exists everywhere.
From that very source arises this entire play of the aesthetic flavor of bliss (*ānandarasavibhrama*).
For instance, when neutrality ceases in the case of sweet song or the touch of sandalwood and the like,
there occurs that state of vibration within the heart.
That very [power] is called the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), because through it a person becomes one who possesses a true heart (sahṛdaya).
Having first cast everything that is to be done into the fire of emptiness, this is known as the "resting of the mind" (cittaviśrānti); immediately after that is the individual (āṇava) [means].

The state of being oriented toward an object—whether seen, heard, or otherwise—within one's own consciousness is called the awakening of the mind (*cittasaṃbodha*); it consists essentially of the fullness of the unfolding of power (*śāktollāsa*). In that state, through the union of this orientation with the object within the heart, [the object is realized].

Due to the fullness of the absorption resulting from [the power of] *rūḍhi*, there is a dissolution of the limited mind into Śiva; because of this dissolution of the limited state— which was previously possible through an orientation toward the future— this supreme emission of Śambhu is called the "dissolution of the mind" (*cittapralaya*).
Therefore, in the *Tattvarakṣāvidhāna*, the threefold nature of emission (*visarga*) is taught:
it is held that the union of those two resides in the center of the calyx of the heart-lotus;
and that emission is said to be internal, characterized by the resting of the mind.
The second is that emission (*visarga*), characterized by the awakening of consciousness (*citta*). Here, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings appears as a single unity.
Indeed, when even the slightest distinction between subject and object is perceived here, [it is no longer that state].
Then that [state] is called "with parts" (sakala); through union with Śiva, it becomes "without parts" (niṣkala).

It consists of a complete grasping characterized by the cessation of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper. That third [state] is indeed emission (visarga), characterized by the dissolution of the mind.

Consisting of the nature of unification, subtle, the essence of consciousness, and blissful within the Self— this meaning has been described in the venerable *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*: "In this context, that Kuṇḍalinī is the seed, consisting of consciousness, which has become the individual soul."
From that [emission] arises the triad known as *dhruva*, *icchā*, and *unmeṣa*; from those, in turn, arise the phonemes (*varṇas*).
Starting from the vowel *ā* (the first of the vowels) up to the power of emission (*visargikī kalā*), there are the consonants from *ka* to *sa*. And that emission is fivefold.
Externally, internally, in the heart, in the resonance (nāda), and then in the supreme state;
the drop (bindu) resides in the self, extending from the heart up to the crown of the head, for it is all-pervasive.
However, mantras devoid of the first and the last [letters] are like autumn clouds.
The characteristics of the Guru are as follows: he should make known [the teaching] from the beginning to the end.

Such a knower is to be worshipped like me, for he is Bhairava himself, whose essence is the deity. Therefore, whatever there may be—whether a verse, a song, or anything else—that is joined with the beginning and the end [is authoritative].

Therefore, one who knows [this] perceives everything in that way as being nothing other than mantra. The power of emission (visarga-śakti) has been described by the Supreme Lord at length in the Vedānta known as the Aitareya as the cause of the universe.
That which is red is Fire; that which is virility has the form of the Sun and Moon.
"A" is the supreme Brahman, consisting of the nature of their union. And even beyond that is the supreme virility, which consists of the digits of the five elements.
And it exists in the form of food to be enjoyed, consisting of sound, touch, and taste. Since even sound is sweet when it brings about the accumulation of vitality (*vīrya*),
that vitality is indeed considered supreme, pure, and characterized by the desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*).

That strength, that vigor, those vital breaths, and that loveliness—these arise from that virility; and that virility is said to reside in ritual actions. It is present in sacrifices and the like, then in the rain, and then again in the medicinal herbs.

In *vīrya* it is thus [the state of] progeny, and in emission (*visarga*) it is the form of the universe. That very [state] is called the Mass of Sounds (*śabdarāśi*), and she is celebrated as Mātṛkā.
Due to the immersion in the relationship between the agitated and the agitator, they call her Mālinī.

Mālinī is indeed the supreme Śakti, ascertained to be universal in form, beautiful through the emergence of emission from the union of the seed (bīja) and the womb (yoni). In reality, she is one alone— the supreme attractor of time.
Through the union with the differentiation of the possessor of power (śaktimat), it attains the state of being a couple (yāmala).
That reflective awareness of it, which consists of the perfect "I," may,
by virtue of its own sovereignty within itself, manifest division.
And when its manifestation as differentiation occurs, its body is said to be threefold,
designated as Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and the gross Vaikharī. Even for these, there is a threefold form according to their being gross, subtle, or supreme.

In that regard, she who consists of sound (*nāda*), beautiful through the arrangement of phonemes, is indeed the gross *paśyantī*, because there is no differentiation of letters and so forth. This state of being a single undivided form is called "sweetness" (*mādhurya*) and "power" (*śakti*).
The state of being "rough" (*pāruṣī*) arises from the friction of the winds and other elements within the body; yet,
because consciousness functions in close proximity to this [state], which is essentially of the nature of sound (*nāda*),
its transformation into the internal state of *madyamā* is perceived instantaneously due to their commonality.
For those who have not attained identification with That, there is no submergence of the body and so forth.
Not knowing this, they are called "heartless" because their consciousness and means of knowledge are submerged.
As for that which is covered by skin and the like, whatever sound exists therein—[that is what is meant].
Because it possesses both manifest and unmanifest forms, that Madhyamā is of a gross nature;
and because there exists an undivided portion within the Madhyamā, there is redness. That which consists of the undivided vowels is truly captivating.
For non-differentiation leads to liberation; let this be seen from the recitation of the *tāla* rhythm. Indeed, one is satisfied by that playing when there is an unmanifest sound;
whereas that which serves as the cause for the production of distinct phonemes [is different]. (AbhT 3.243b–244)

That [speech] which has sentences and the like as its primary effect is the gross *vaikharī*. Within this triad of gross forms, that which is the initial contemplation is designated as the "subtle" (*sūkṣma*),
and each of those three is likewise called subtle.
"I produce the *ṣaḍja* note, I play it sweetly, and I utter speech"— indeed,
these three distinct acts of mental synthesis are experienced.
Yet, even within this triad, there exists that which is primordial and free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhimat*).
Beyond that is the triad; therein Śiva exists as the supreme consciousness-nature. And in the manifestation of differentiation, there are three primary powers here:
the Absolute (Anuttarā), the Supreme Will (Parā-icchā), and that which abides as the Intermediate (Parāparā).

The power of unfolding (unmeṣa-śakti), called knowledge (jñāna), is declared to be the lower (apara). Furthermore, from the state of agitation (kṣobha) of these [powers], the six stainless consciousnesses (saṃvid) are said to arise.
Through the immersion (samāveśa) into these very [consciousnesses], which has arisen as the power of action (kriyā-śakti), [the pure consciousnesses are produced].
Twelve consciousnesses are proclaimed, in which everything is fully contained.
This much is the primary wheel of powers (śakticakra) of the God of gods.
By means of this much, that Bhairava, the God of gods, is possessed of full power.
Because they consist of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), through their connection with emission (*visarga*) and projection (*ākṣepa*),
and because of the knowledge that calculates their limited extent (*iyattā*), they are in some places called *kālikās*.
And it is also stated in the venerable *Sāraśāstra* that the supreme single-syllabled [power] resides in the center.
One should worship the one called Bhairavātman, surrounded by twelve Yoginīs;
from them alone proceeds the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) up to sixty-four.
Starting from a single spoke, it extends to a thousand spokes.

And their names are manifold in the scriptures according to the distinction of their functions (kṛtyabheda). Furthermore, the modes of worship (upāsā) arise from the application of dual, non-dual, and mixed forms; this has been explained at great length in the venerable *Traiśirasa*.
These have not been written down here by us out of fear of prolixity and because they are of no practical use.

They alone are proclaimed to be the stainless, pure, and non-terrible (aghorā) [mantras]. Furthermore, because they give birth to the terrible and most terrible [mantras], they are of that same nature.
In creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as upon the transcendence of those three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
the established form of these very [energies] is divided manifoldly.
The teachers have declared that the form which transcends the adjuncts is twofold.
Either because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not expand, or through the application of pacification;

and this pacification is twofold: by way of tranquility (*śānti*) or by the process of forceful digestion (*haṭhapāka*). Enough with this so-called "taste of the morsel" (*grāsarasa*), which is constantly of the nature of blazing.

That which is the third [state], the pacification of forceful maturation (haṭhapāka), is indeed suited for instruction; it burns away the fuel of duality. All objective existents are forcibly offered as oblations into the fire of the belly of innate awakening.

Kindling that [reality] by means of their own power, they abandon the division of duality. When the differentiated forms of all things have been dissolved through the "forcible cooking" (haṭhapāka), the deities of consciousness consume the entire universe, which has been transformed into nectar.
Satiated, they rest in non-dual identity with the god Cidvyomabhairava, who dwells in the absolute solitude of the heart, full of his own self. Thus,
through the immersion in the performance of ritual acts and the multiplicity of names and forms of worship, [the state of liberation is attained].
Although there is no actual division among them, their forms appear in many varieties.
And through the application of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpa-udvāpa*) of these very goddesses,
[they manifest] by increasing one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or more.
The detailed expansion of divisions begins with the armies of the Rudras, the Suns, and other Kalās;
enough of this excessive detail—now we proceed with the subject at hand.
Within the self of consciousness, this entire manifold array of objective phenomena exists.

He in whom the Lord of the Universe shines as a reflection is indeed the Lord of All. He who possesses such a non-conceptual awareness within himself, ever-arising, is that very person sealed with the Śāmbhava means.
This reflective awareness of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) which has been here discerned—
apart from this, there are no other mantras, mudrās, ritual actions, or forms of worship whatsoever.
Having resorted to this non-conceptual immersion again and again, [one attains liberation].
It attains the state of Bhairavī, which is also designated as "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti). From this point onward, this liberation while living is investigated,
wherein this conceptualization of means and ends is presented even by way of aphoristic summary.
In the preceding daily lesson (āhnika), however, there was not even a slight conception of duality;
therefore, in that "no-method" (anupāya), who is liberated, how, or from what?
[This occurs] within the non-conceptual reflective awareness known as the Śāmbhava means.

The wise one should apply the fifty-fold division previously set forth in the sūtras. Perceiving the earth itself, reflected without conceptualization within his own self, as being Bhairava-nature, he attains that state; this same procedure applies to water and the other elements as well.
Up until the end, there is the supreme reality, which transcends all veils,
pervasive, autonomous, omniscient, and that which is conceived as Śiva;
even that is reflected in the mirror of the noble, non-conceptualized consciousness.
Seeing thus, freed from conceptual construction, one becomes Bhairava oneself.
Just as one seeing a red object before them through non-conceptual consciousness remains well-established in the singular, partless perception of that very jar through its respective sensory gateway.
In the same way, by reflecting upon one's own self as the aggregate and collection of each successive element beginning with earth, one shines forth as truly full:
"All this has arisen from me alone; it is reflected within me alone."
"This [universe] is non-different from me"—this threefold means is that of Śambhu (the Śāmbhava-upāya).
This very sūtra has been composed concerning creation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
it explains "that wherein [it] is situated" and "from whence [it arises]" in the Spanda teachings.
By this much alone, the supreme sovereignty of consciousness has been proclaimed;
and since its nature as the self of the universe has also been shown, what other characteristic could possibly be described?
(3.282) "I am manifesting the universe within my own self, the space of consciousness. (3.283)
Through the expansion [of the thought], "I am the creator, the soul of the universe," there arises the nature of Bhairava. The entire collection of the six paths is reflected within me alone;
through the realization, "I am the agent of maintenance," this universal form becomes manifest.
Seeing that "this entire universe dissolves into me, whose self is matted with the flames of the ever-arisen Great Awakening," one attains peace;
[one who sees] the dwelling of the dream of saṃsāra, which contains within it an infinite and variegated reality.
The consuming fire is none other than I, Śiva, shining forth with the realization: "I am indeed the burner.
From me the entire universe originates in manifold ways through differentiation; yet this world remains rooted in me, and when it has dissolved, nothing else exists.
Thus, he who perceives the partless reality by virtue of unifying creation, maintenance, and dissolution, truly vibrates as the Fourth State (turya) beyond the [three] planes of existence.
In this supreme means, which is characterized by the non-duality of Śambhu,
only a few attain conviction, having been purified by the Lord of Paśus.
[For others there remain] bathing, vows, purification of the body, concentration, and the application of mantras.
The arrangement of time, the ritual procedure of sacrifice, fire-offerings, recitations, and meditative absorptions—
no such conceptual distinctions whatsoever are applicable here.
For one established in this state, the capacity to bestow supreme grace upon others is clearly manifest.
If such a person worthy of grace approaches the teacher,
yet he is not of such a nature [as to receive it] but is instead permeated by devotion to Bhava, then—
impelled by a desire for such grace— he propitiates him.
Then the wise one should learn the various procedures for initiation and so forth.
For even those future forms of worship reach their final consummation in this very [state];
having attained the supreme identity with this, it is described as the auspicious Śiva.
Thus has been described in great detail this supreme Śāmbhava realization of the Self.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Next, we shall explain the circle of means (*upāya-maṇḍala*) pertaining to the Śākta [power], for the sake of the realization of the Supreme Self.
In this supreme nature of the Lord described in the preceding chapter,

one who desires to enter [into it] should immediately perform the purification of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Purified conceptual thought gives rise to a conceptual thought that is purified by its own self-nature.
He [the first conceptualization] is similar to itself; that one [the second] is similar to another; and that one [the third] is similar to yet another.
Among these four very conceptualizations, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) proceeds in sequence:
it is indistinct, becoming distinct, becoming clearly manifest, and having the nature of being fully manifest.
Then [the perception] becomes clearer and clearer until it reaches the state of being most clear at the end;
even when the initial conceptualization is unclear, there exists an intermediate distinction.
Therefore, [the cognition] is augmented by that very nature of clarity and magnificence.

Consciousness attains a stainless state whose very nature is free from conceptual construction (avikalpa). Therefore, for those who reflect again and again upon that Bhairavian splendor, which has consciousness as its essential nature, its manifest reality arises.

But surely consciousness is, by its very nature, the grasper and consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); how then could it be an object of grasping? If it were created as such [an object], it would be insentient.
To this it is replied: self-awareness is, by its very essence, full and overflowing.
It was declared of old that in this [reality] there is nothing to be removed and nothing to be added; however,
because of His power to accomplish the impossible and His stainless autonomy,
the Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing His own nature.
Even though His own nature is unobstructed, that which constitutes the self-concealment of the All-pervasive Lord is precisely Māyā; from it arises this entire manifold activity of the universe.
Thus, the manifestation of duality is said to belong to the Great Lord Himself.
By means of removing that duality, this reflective awareness (parāmarśa) is designated;
the wise cut the root of this tree so difficult to split with the axe of sound reasoning (sattarka) raised on its edge— this is the certainty.

The wise call this very cultivation the "cow of plenty" that milks all desires; it makes manifest even that reality which has transcended the sphere of the mind. In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is declared that reasoning (*tarka*) is the supreme limb of yoga.
Therefore, because one must discern what is to be abandoned and so forth, effort in that regard is praised.
Even if the mind has become steady on the path, it may still be drawn by a desire for objects that are to be abandoned;
thus, one should urge it forward by that [desire] until the state free from affliction is reached.

In this context, the path taught in other scriptures as a means to liberation is to be abandoned; for it is that [limited] will, conjoined with necessity (niyati), which "poisons" (viṣiṇoti) and binds. That which is called the principle of attachment (rāga-tattva) is so named because by it one becomes passionately attached to that [object].

Just as a person of evil intellect might become attached to enjoyments— whether having seen the experience of imperial sovereignty or not seeing even the most base— so too might one be attached to liberation out of passion. That very [attachment] is called a "portion" (aṃśaka), and it is clearly known as "nature" (svabhāva).

The wise know that [attachment] is an obstacle to liberation, even though it may be considered a limb of success; for this very reason, even one who knows the greatness of the teaching of Śiva might become attached to the Vaiṣṇava systems, being deluded and colored by passion.
For within that [extent],
His divine power known as Vāmā unfolds for the followers of the Pañcarātra, the Vairiñca, the Saugata, and others.
Some fools have been seen who, while enjoying imperial sovereignty, nevertheless disparage it.
But it is not through contentment with one's own enjoyments, for [the opposite occurs] from the arousal of desire;
thus, those whose minds are intent on censuring the immersion into Bhairava-consciousness (cid-bhairava-āveśa) are struck down by the most terrible powers (śaktis). 23–24a.

Therefore, one who knows the majesty of Śambhu should not, out of complacency, attempt to cross the great ocean of duality by means of another teaching. This has been clearly stated in the *Śrīkāmika* in the section concerning bonds (*pāśaprakaraṇa*).
Those who know the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, and Purāṇas, those devoted to the Pāñcarātra,
whatever wise sages there may be devoted to other scriptures,
and all those such as the Buddhists and Ārhats— they are all colored by attachment to worldly knowledge.
Because one is bound by the noose of *māyā*, one does not obtain initiation into Śiva.

By the word "passion" (*rāga*), the *tattva* of passion is meant, which acts as a regulator; for it is said in that scripture: "That [tattva] shall regulate him within the realm of *māyā*. (AbhT 4.27b–28)
Even that liberation belonging to the Vaiṣṇavas and others, which is imagined through their own conceptualization—
whether it be union with the supreme *prakṛti*,
or the state of being of the nature of bliss, or pure consciousness alone, or the extinction of the continuum like a lamp [going out]— [is not the true goal].

He consists of the state of being a *pralayākala*, characterized by either having experience (*savedya*) or being without experience (*apavedya*). Having attained that state and remained there for a long time, enjoying the expansion of its enjoyments,
at the end of the dissolution of that particular principle (*tattva*), he enters into the creation that follows it.

He attains the status of a mantra through the awakening bestowed by Ananteśa; we shall elaborate on this further ahead, so let us leave it at that for now. Therefore, he who has been mocked by the doctrines fabricated by ignorant people—
One whose consciousness is fixed upon an unworthy teacher is colored by the noose of *māyā*.

Yet even such a person is led toward a true teacher through the application of right reasoning (*sattarka*). Right reasoning is indeed Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and that is the will of the Supreme Lord.
In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated that he who desires to go forth, by the will of Śiva,
is led toward a true guru for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). In that case, this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) proceeds in a gradual manner.
Having remained with a false teacher or having resorted to another path in a different scripture,

[one may still attain grace]. The diversity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) regarding the distinction between what is real and what is unreal within the teacher and the scripture will be analyzed in detail further on.

It is stated in the *Svacchanda-śāstra* that Māyā causes all those who propound doctrines such as Vaiṣṇavism and the like to wander, even though they desire liberation, within that which is not liberation. But he who, though established therein, is skilled in the emergent supreme awareness—
Purified by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) through the majesty of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*),
he indeed ascends the true path, free from all obstacles.
For some, such an inquiry arises spontaneously of its own accord.
And that [knowledge] is declared in the scripture to be innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), consisting of self-conviction; as it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "From the Guru, from the scripture, and from oneself.
Among these, each subsequent one is primary, while each preceding one is a means to the next.
He who possesses this correct reasoning (*sattarka*) by his own nature is qualified in every respect.
He is consecrated and initiated by the goddesses of his own self-awareness;
he alone is proclaimed as the foremost among all teachers.
In his presence, there is no authority for others who are merely imagined;
he understands the entire meaning of the scripture through sound reasoning alone.
For pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) indeed exists as that which nothing can fail to illuminate.
"Knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises for him spontaneously.
Thus, in the aforementioned venerable passage, by the word "spontaneously" (akasmāt),
that cause which is not well-known in the world is designated as "spontaneous."
And this very [state] is the unfolding of the Supreme Lord’s Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). Its manifestations are manifold: those without support (nirbhitti) and those with support (sabhittika).
It is all-pervading and yet partial; it is established both in the primary and secondary parts.

A wall, dependence on others, supreme wisdom, and its application—(48) even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, if he knows this in truth, shall eternally possess accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is initiated. (49)

It is declared in the venerable *Triṃśaka-śāsana* that for one who knows thus according to reality, initiation leading to Nirvāṇa shall occur. The unconstructed Guru is to be known as the one remembered as *sāṃsiddhika*.
But he who, through the cultivation of his own being as sharing in that [divine] form, acts for the sake of others without [the aid of] another,

is declared in the scripture to be a Guru who, though knowing the scriptures, is a "fashioner of the unfashioned. His varieties also arise from the superior, middling, or inferior nature of the means employed.
Through meditative cultivation, or through meditation, recitation, dreams, vows, or fire-offerings,
the one of great intelligence attains the noble, unconstructed consecration.
This is taught in the venerable Vājasanīya, the venerable Vīra, and the venerable Brahmayāmala.
This has been clearly stated by the Creator in the *Śrīsiddhā* and elsewhere:
"Because its activity proceeds from His own will, an infinity of causes is maintained;
[this occurs] sometimes through the yoga of devotion, through ritual action, or even through knowledge. (4.54b–55)
Through the instruction of knowledge and dharma, or by means of mantras, or even through initiation,
and by many such diverse methods, the Supreme Lord,
the master of the entire universe, bestows grace upon those wandering in saṃsāra.
O Dear One, through the awakening to the circle of the Mothers, through purification, austerity, meditation, yoga,
recitation, knowledge, the propitiation of mantras, and vows,
one attains the common knowledge of the Kula, which bestows the *siddhi* of the Kaulas. (AbhT 4.57b–58)

Wherever the goal, which consists of the knowledge of reality, is observed, he alone is the guru there; let a web of reasons be fashioned for that. In the Brahmayāmala, there is no other defining characteristic [of a guru] apart from the knowledge of reality.

And it is stated in that very same [text] regarding service performed without conceptualization: "If the practitioner does not attain success, what should be done? When this is asked, [the answer is]:
"He should perform his own initiation through the sequence of self-recognition. (AbhT 4.60b–61)
For the sake of establishing the state of vibration (*sasphuratva*), the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is then successfully realized.
By this means, the self-knowledge that establishes the state of vibration is attained;
for it has been stated by the Teacher that [this occurs] primarily if one is not devoid of vibration.
And furthermore, by always performing the prescribed rite for the worship of the venerable Raktā in that very [practice], one is called an Ācārya after a month; a Sādhaka after a fortnight;
a Putraka after half of that (seven and a half days); and likewise a Samayin after half of that again (three and three-quarter days).
Since the goddess Raktā initiates [the disciple] through the application of recitation (japa) according to the sequence,
one should perform this prescribed rite in the absence of a Guru. In the Mata,
such a fault is mentioned regarding the study of the Vidyā from a book.
That which has been stated by him [the Lord] does not constitute a prohibition in the absence of such faults.
When it is asked, "What is the fruit of keeping the mantras, substances, and so forth secret?", [the answer is:
those who have learned the vidyās from books and are devoid of initiation and the observance of pledges (samaya) [do not obtain the fruit].
Those dominated by *tamas* engage excessively in harming others, subjugating them, and so forth;
yet they do not know the true reality (*tattva*). Therefore, it is clear that they are the ones who incur the fault.
The first two lines [of the verse] should be understood as being mutually related as cause and effect.
But he who, without the scripture, does not attain the consciousness known as Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā),
should seek the scripture from a guru and practice the sequence taught therein,
having propitiated the guru with devotion by whatever means possible.
Through the application of the sequence of that initiation, he then understands the meaning of the scripture;
however, he who has merely received the consecration (abhiṣeka) is considered "constructed" (kalpita).
Even though he is capable of turning back the entire flood of bonds, [he is not yet fully realized].
Whoever, through the application of sequential practice toward some subject matter in the scriptures,
should attain sudden awakening— he is indeed both the imagined and the unimagined. That portion of his which is unimagined is considered the most excellent.

Since excellence is produced by the degree of the portion of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), just as liberated Śivas are indeed lower than the primordial, eternally perfect Śiva due to their differentiation,
so too those who have acquired knowledge are inferior to those whose knowledge is innate.
In his presence, they have no authority, like those who are liberated and whose nature is Śiva (muktaśivātman).
Rather, their state is one of silence, or else it is the performance of service in accordance with him.
One who has received the consecration from another is a Guru who is Bhairava in person;
for, through the sequence of the scriptures and by cultivating the wisdom of a Guru who knows that [reality],
knowledge becomes self-validated and, due to its fullness, becomes Bhairava-like.

Therefore, that which is stated in the *Śrīkiraṇa*— that this knowledge arises from the guru, from scripture, and from oneself— and that which is stated in the *Niśāṭana*, namely that it possesses three sources of cognition (*tripratyaya*), manifests in that manner through their combination, inversion, or individual separation.
Because the instrument is diverse,
one takes up a plane, a chisel,
and even a saw to perform that very same diverse cutting; yet, from the perspective of the initial intention, the act of cutting remains essentially one and the same.
In this very way, the inherent nature of the instrument [of knowledge] must be stated regarding its measurement:
a means of cognition does not independently produce an apprehension by force of its own accord,
because apprehension is said to culminate in the conviction of the subject.
And this diverse consolation arises likewise through the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).
Therefore, even when [reality] has been measured by the means of knowledge, there remains a clear scope for further [inquiry].
Having seen again and again, having embraced [the beloved] for a long time, and having relished her in the mind;
What indeed can we say regarding those by whom [the Guru] who is dear [to them] is fully satisfied?
(84) And thus, even when there is an overflow of the mind (*mānasa*), there is no attainment of a further state;
nor is there futility, nor infinite regress, nor even mutual dependence. (85)

Thus, reasoning (*tarka*) alone is considered a limb of yoga and nothing else; it serves to produce an ever-increasing proficiency in internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—[these are the other limbs].
Thus, these five restraints (*yamas*) are not directly useful for pure consciousness.
Likewise, those observances (*niyamas*) such as austerity (*tapas*) and so forth, as well as the postures (*āsanas*),
and all those breath-controls (*prāṇāyāmas*)— all this is merely an external manifestation.

And it is stated in the venerable *Vīrāvalī*: "When the moon and the sun have dissolved through the bond of the dissolution of the mind within that which consists of consciousness alone and whose nature is Śiva;
and when the solar life-force (*jīvāditya*), the awakener of itself, has reached the twelfth part. (AbhT 4.89–90a)
That alone is declared to be liberation; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is useless. Breath control should not be practiced if it causes pain to the body.
He who knows the secret therein is liberated, and he is the liberator.

This which is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) is indeed the drawing back of the senses from their objects by means of the intellect; it is said to be the pinning down of that unbound bondage within. The binding of the mind to some particular object is the nature of *dhāraṇā* (concentration).

The continuity of consciousness that resembles that [object] is meditation (*dhyāna*); when it has set, it is the supreme state. But when identity with the object of knowledge arises within consciousness itself, this voidness of the duality of the grasped and the grasper is *samāhiti*.
Therefore, this triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna,
and samādhi serves no purpose whatsoever with respect to supreme consciousness (saṃvid).
However, the status of being limbs of yoga (yogāṅga) is described for the practices beginning with yama and ending with samādhi.
Because each preceding one serves as the means for the next, and because the final stage is the application of reasoning (tarka),
that [reality] which is rooted within consciousness is projected through that door into the vital breath, the body,
or the intellect; however, this method of practice does not apply to consciousness itself.
Alternatively, according to our view, because the vital breath, the intellect, the body,
and so forth are clearly of the nature of all things, even though [the practice] resides therein, the practice consists in the exclusion of the other.
Due to the impulse of the desire to rise up, characterized by the repeated upward leap of the body, [one attains this].
It is uplifted by the removal of the fear of falling into its opposite.
When one's own self-reflection, which resembles the contemplation of the Guru’s words,
has awakened, there is the total exclusion of its opposites through the study and reflection upon the scriptures.
For it is not possible for a teacher to implant his own knowledge or even his words into the disciple's intellect;
therefore, the process of self-awakening is certain.
For this very reason, even when an object is heard about during the state of dreaming, [it is realized through one's own power].
The practice of meditating on identity is not said to be for the sake of no fruit.
When there is disregard for conventional signs, reflective awareness fixed on the word is recitation (*paṭhi*);
when there is regard for them, the meaning thereof is reflection (*cintā*)—let this be thoroughly considered. (4.102b–103)
In that non-dual consciousness, practice is of no use;
it serves solely to uproot the suspicion of the impurity of duality (dvaita).
And it has been described how these suspicions of duality are examined through reasoning (tarka).
"Let the practice of *yama* and the rest serve as a means for the accomplishment of that [realization] through reasoning.
And it is stated by Śambhu in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, beginning with the passage on the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth: "There is neither duality nor non-duality. (4.105–106)
Whatever has been prescribed here, or even what has been prohibited,
since yogas consisting of parts such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like are artificial,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this uncreated [state].
But here, O Mistress of the Gods, this is prescribed as a rule:
the mind must be made firm in the *tattva*, and that [firmness] should be achieved by whichever means possible for each individual.
Thus, the Supreme Lord [ordains this] for the sake of destroying the perception of duality.
Sometimes he remains constantly perceiving his own stainless nature;
that reflective awareness of one's own nature may occur through the means of the senses, objects, and so forth,
or it may be another [form] independent of those, consisting of the conceptualization of them by virtue of one's own freedom.

And that [power] is clearly said to be the "nocturnal" (naiśa) power of one's own self, which unites duality within the flood of objective phenomena that shine forth from the jewel of the pure and independent Self. But that very same power,
when its sole object is the Self filled with all things, [is called the "daytime" power].
"Everything here is indeed of the nature of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), [expressed as] 'I am this'—
this conceptualization, which is of the form of pure knowledge and characterized by clarity,
destroys here the conceptualization of Māyā that consists of the perception of duality. (AbhT 4.113–114a)
That very reflective awareness of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) manifests in manifold ways through the practice of bathing,
purification, worship, fire-offerings, meditation, recitation, and so forth;
out of this aesthetic relish (rasāt), this entire universe is filled with the sap of one's own self-awareness.
Having entered [the body], the pure [practitioner] should satisfy the entire garland of paths;
when the fuel of the universe has been consumed by the blazing fire of radiant consciousness,
immersion in the white ashes of the body is called "bathing."
Having thus performed his bath and offered libations to the infinite deities,
he should then purify the principles (tattvas) that constitute the body.
Even though these [principles] are essentially Śiva, there exists a cognition that regards them as distinct [from him].
That very impurity is called "other" (parā); purity is the crushing of that [impurity] by means of wisdom.
Thus, perceiving one's own body as the sole vessel of consciousness, with all duality dissolved, the Lord abides in the state of independent pure awareness alone.
Whatever brings joy to the mind, wherever the senses may be situated—
that indeed is to be joined within the abode of the reality of Brahman, for that is the equipment for worship.
Worship, indeed, is the unification of even the manifold flood of objective phenomena.
By means of the self-nature of consciousness belonging to Bhairava— which is autonomous, stainless, and infinite—
this very consciousness exists as both internal and external;
for, by virtue of its autonomy, it proceeds while having the nature of reflective awareness.
And that [sun] is twelvefold there, since everything is contained within it.
For the sun itself has the nature of the moon, and it exists as consisting of the universe;
in ultimate reality, its consciousness consists precisely of the twelve digits (kalās).
And that [consciousness] always shines forth in four ways, depending upon the mother, consciousness, the means of knowledge, the sphere of the senses, and the object of cognition.
In the former case, it consists of pure awareness; in the [subsequent] cognition, it takes the form of speech and the person.
Because the forms of perception occur through the instruments [of sense], as stated in the *Śrīyogasañcara*:
"O Supreme Goddess, those two white circles of the eyes which are directly perceived—therein reside the supreme wheels of sixteen spokes and twelve spokes. (AbhT 4.126b–127)

That which is outside those [circles], red like a *prativāraṇa* flower, is said to be the second; those two circles situated in the middle are black and white. Within that [second circle] are situated two pure [circles] with a luster like crushed collyrium.
O Dear One, those two four-petalled wheels, which consist of the nature of Agni and Soma, should be known as such. O Supreme Goddess, these two wheels, abiding in a state of union,
perform the closing and opening of one another.
Just as the female organ and the male organ flow with nectar through their union, so too, through the union of the nectar and the fire, they flow; of this there is no doubt.
