By the pressure of that wheel at night, a light shines that moves between the sun and the moon.
Having seen that supreme moonlight, the knowledge of time proceeds.
Above those two, there exists a thousand-spoked wheel;
from that wheel, the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa) is said to have arisen.
Situated there, Soma, ignited by Agni, releases a stream;
thus he emits the entire infinite universe within each and every self.
[He does so] from the sixteen-spoked and twelve-spoked wheels, and then entirely from the eight-spoked ones.
In this manner, the supreme nectar flows through all the wheels (cakras) in succession as long as the sequence of the five wheels continues;
then, vibrating with the sound "haṃsa, haṃsa," the Haṃsa drinks it again with delight.
But by hearing this even once, one is no longer stained by merit or sin.
Then, having become modified within the five-spoked [wheel], that pervasive Lord runs through the secret wheels whose spokes consist of the three rasas, [driven] by the nectar flowing from the moon.
From which the world is born and wherein it is dissolved by its own play—
therein lies the bliss of all, and there the one devoted to Brahman becomes a true celibate (brahmacārī).
There, both accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti)— this pair— is attained simultaneously.
From here upwards, he goes again as far as the state whose nature is Brahman;
there, fire and moon are emitted equally by the Self within the Self.
Situated there, the heated moon is established in two ways in the shanks.

Fire causes it to fall downward, and in an instant, nectar flows forth. When clearly manifested at the ankles, knees, and other joints, that power, ignited by the curved sun and heated further, brings forth the sequence beginning with the five-spoked [wheel].
In this same way, it should be understood regarding the sense of hearing as well, up to the range of the tips of the feet;
beginning from the big toe up to the vision of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Thus, one who does not know this is no yogi at all, while one who knows it becomes the sovereign of the universe.

That Supreme Lord is seen by Brahmā and the other gods as if blazing. Here, the fourfold sequence has been taught with full intent regarding each individual sense-faculty; therefore, its twelvefold nature is proclaimed.
It has not been explained by breaking it down into parts because it is an extreme secret;
for even within the object of cognition, the Goddess abides in the form of the lunar mansions, zodiac signs, and so forth.
Therefore, she exists as consciousness in the nature of both the internal and the external.

Having manifested herself, she shines as if manifesting something else therein. Therefore, this pure Goddess, previously eager to manifest in such a way, brings about creation; she is called by that name in the Āgama.

In that same way, that [power] which is directed outwardly colors the aspect of the object as it has been manifested; then, by means of its own wheel of functions, it fully brings about [the state of] persistence. This very [state] is the persistence of the entity, which [it achieves] through the savor of inwardness.
Desiring to withdraw [the universe], she is called "Establishment" (*sthiti*) when she brings about its dissolution.
Then, when the impulse for withdrawal is full,
she herself produces, within one portion, the obstacle of doubt characterized by *Yama*, and she also effects the withdrawal.
Having withdrawn doubt, or having abandoned the objects of doubt within the mandala of existence,
he indeed effects their withdrawal by dissolving them into the fire of his own self. And that withdrawal of existence, which consists of dissolution, he [dissolves] into the Self.
By means of that very [act], she touches [the object] and flashes forth the thought, "This has been swallowed by me.
For the true nature of this consciousness is its capacity to withdraw limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
indeed, it dissolves into the pure, unconditioned form of consciousness.
Even when the flood of objective entities has been dissolved, she [the power of consciousness] at that very moment causes some entity to solidify;
whatever remains exists as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of doubt. Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, this very thing will bring forth the attainment of its fruit.
For this doubt persists either before or after the enjoyment [of the fruit].
It dissolves even that which has otherwise solidified at that very moment,
just as the act of killing a Brahmin is dissolved by rites such as expiation.
By means of obstruction and by means of liquefaction, consciousness thus fashions form;
it may likewise cause that very form to liquefy, or else it may cause it to solidify.
In this way, when even the object of enjoyment has been experienced, its instruments [the senses] are also [withdrawn].
Withdrawing [the senses], she manifests the twelve within herself as the "I" (aham).
Indeed, the group consisting of the organs of action and perception, ending with the intellect (buddhi), is twelvefold in nature.
Because it is illuminating, it is solar in essence and unfolds toward objects that appear distinct.

The *ahaṃkāra*, however, is the instrument whose sole function is self-conceit (*abhimāna*). Because it possesses uninterrupted self-reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it dissolves into that [Śakti] by means of that [awareness]. For just as in the case of distinct instruments such as a sword or a noose, [the agent acts through them].

Just as there is absorption into one's own hands and so forth in that which is non-differentiated, such is this procedure. Therefore, by her own sovereignty, the Goddess of Consciousness herself should contemplate the solar orb of the multitude of the senses within the constructed self of the ego.
He alone is the supreme Sun, the thirteenth, who is like the full moon;
because he is the instrument, he clearly undergoes dissolution into the agent.
And the agent is said to be twofold, consisting of the imagined and the unimagined.
It is conceptualized as being defined by the exclusion of the body, the intellect, and so forth;
in the scriptures, it is designated by the name Kālāgnirudra.
Time (kāla) is that which possesses the quality of delimitation, and fire (agni) is traditionally held to be the enjoyer. Thus, [the term] is explained.
The Lord is so called because He obstructs and dissolves [the ego] through the non-construction and construction of saṃsāra;

there, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) of one whose state as a bound soul (*paśu*) has not yet ceased is dissolved. That [ego], too, because its functions are imagined, [is dissolved] into that which possesses the sole non-duality with the universe.
In the Great Time (Mahākāla), which consists of "I" and "this," the blossoming [consciousness] dissolves.
Within this self-awareness, consciousness shines forth in its fully expanded form as: "I am the all-pervasive Lord; all this is I. 168–169ab. 169cd.
Then, consciousness— though already complete and colored by the enjoyment of the state wherein all things reside within it— dissolves into the abode of Akula.
The multitude of subjects, the flood of means of knowledge, and the various established forms of valid cognition [all dissolve therein].

Whatever constitutes the flood of objects of knowledge here is nothing but pure consciousness alone. That absolute freedom of one's own self-awareness, which assumes such a vast variety of forms, is the Supreme Goddess, the Parameśvarī.
These aforementioned operations are said to be its unfolding, occurring in the following order:

projection (*kṣepa*), knowledge (*jñāna*), reckoning (*saṃkhyāna*), movement (*gati*), and resonance (*nāda*). Projection is the differentiation of one's own self; [knowledge] is the non-conceptualization of that which has been differentiated.
Knowledge is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because it involves enumeration through differentiation from others.
Motion is the ascent into one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), which is exactly like a reflection.
Sound (*nāda*) is the state of being reduced to the self-reflection of one's own Self (*svātmaparāmarśa*) through the dissolution of that [motion].
Thus, performing this fivefold calculation,
the Supreme Goddess (Parā) is called Kālī as well as Kālakarṣiṇī;
she is designated as Mātṛsadbhāvā because she resides within the subjects (pramātṛ).
In this much, through the realization of the end, subjectivity becomes manifest.
In the venerable *Niśisañcāra*, she is called by the name Vāmeśvarī.
Thus, consciousness, abiding in twelve ways within all subjects, [pervades] the universe.
"There is only one"—there is no rule whatsoever regarding the sequence of this [process] anywhere.
Because there is no sequence, there is no simultaneity; because that [simultaneity] is absent, there is also no sequence.
The reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), utterly stainless, transcends all talk of sequence and non-sequence.

Wherever this Goddess of Consciousness manifests, there the worship exists in its fullness through the yoga of identity. Because her very nature is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), her own spontaneous resonance (*dhvani*)— AbhT_4.180b/. Wherever this Goddess of Consciousness manifests, // 180 AbhT_4.181a/. there the worship exists in its fullness through the yoga of identity.
AbhT_4.181b/. Because her very nature is reflective awareness, that which is her own resonance // 181
That very [consciousness], ever-arisen, is said to be the supreme, great Heart (*hṛdaya*).
This self-reflection within the Heart has dissolved the entirety of the universe;
it exists throughout everything from the initial grasping of an object to its final cessation, and is designated as "universal" (*sāmānya*).
In the scripture, that vibration (spanda) is described as consisting of an upward surging within one's own self.
It is a slight movement, which is indeed nothing other than a radiance; it is a wave of the ocean of consciousness, for without this, there is no cognition.
For the very nature of the ocean consists in its states such as being waveless or having waves;
this is the essence of everything, since the inert world has consciousness as its essence. Because it is established dependent upon that, the Great Heart (Hṛdaya) is its essence.
For this very reason, that which is called the Egg of Māyā is indeed the root of Being (sat), namely Brahman.
Without the ascent of will, knowledge, and action, it cannot be called "Being.
Through the ascent of that triad of powers within the Bhairavian self, which is consciousness (cidātman), [it is so designated].
For that [emission] is either emitted from within or emitted externally;
thus, the very reality of these existing things consists of the nature of the three powers,
which exists precisely by encompassing emission through supreme consciousness.

That very reality, which exists externally, is dissolved by the fire of primordial awakening; thereafter, it becomes nothing more than an internal, resonant reflective awareness. Then, through the sphere of the three powers, it fully attains the nature of the void itself.
Having attained the nature of sensation, it dissolves into the essence of withdrawal.
This is the primordial heart of withdrawal, which is also considered the heart in emission;
it is the unartificial and stainless reflective awareness of this very form.
"This very [consciousness] which says 'I' is the luminosity of light.
(4.192b) "For this is the vitality (*vīrya*) of all mantras, consisting of their heart-essence (*hṛdaya*).
(4.193a) "Without this, they would be inert, like living beings without a heart. (4.193b)
When one has ascended to this unartificial heart, whatever he may do—whether he breathes or even touches anything—all that is considered his *japa*.
Whatever [he utters] by his own will, whether externally or internally, due to the inherent nature of emanation; 194–195ab.
That very [form] which is emanated by him would be his ultimate meditation (dhyāna).
For while the abode of consciousness is formless and yet consists of the forms of the entire universe,
a certain form remains as an object of meditation for those who seek a specific fruit.
For just as one, although the object is complete and undivided, brings forth water and, out of desire,
seeks a jar by setting aside other forms; even so,
through the unfolding of the Supreme Lord’s power of necessity (niyati), [the individual perceives the world].
A particular form produces a particular conceptualization of fruit.
But for one whose heart is full and who does not desire any fruit at all,
the Goddess is the form of the entire universe, because she is free from all limitations.
In the lineage of yogins, when one has become reeling from the overflowing supreme liquor of Bhairava,
whatever state of stability exists within the body is indeed *mudrā*.
It is eternal, requiring no external supply of fuel whatsoever.
The fire, with its fierce flames issuing from the entire multitude of senses,
blazes intensely. When objects enter that kind of fire of awakening, they proceed as the cause for the rite of oblation (homa), augmenting the great splendor of that [fire].

Whosoever has been purified by the descent of the power (śaktipāta) of the Supreme Lord, having placed that person before him, the teacher himself should remain as previously described; such a person is indeed initiated.
Even though [initiation] occurs through each individual rite, from the recitation of mantras up to the fire-oblation (homa), [the result is achieved].

In this way, the supreme conventional usage arises; thus it has been described. For just as a horse, being led across various places in a painting—whether level, low, or high—moves according to what is imagined by mere intention.
In the same way, consciousness, by means of various modes such as the peaceful, the terrible, and so forth,
causes one to abandon duality on all sides and becomes Bhairava. Just as one perceives one's own face in a mirror placed before oneself, [so does consciousness perceive itself].

Again and again, he perceives that single essence as the face of his own self. Likewise, by beholding himself as Bhairava within the mirror of conceptual thought— which consists of meditation, worship, and ritual adoration— he shall before long become one with Him.
The attainment called "becoming one with that" occurs within the unsurpassed Self;
it is the supreme limit of fullness, and thus there is no further fruit beyond it.
All fruits are merely conceptualized in relation to various states of incompleteness.

When fullness is indeed unconstructed, what other fruit could possibly be spoken of? (210) This particular sacrificial rite resides in the heart of someone for whom the wheel of consciousness becomes gracious, swiftly bringing about his final birth. (211)
One who has attained firm mastery in this sacrifice reaches absolute liberation (kaivalya),
even while remaining in the state of bodily bondage and being observed by the world. Regarding this,
the Lord has set forth the proper conduct in the eighteenth chapter.
In this state, there is neither purity nor impurity, nor any deliberation regarding what is fit to be eaten and so forth;
there is neither duality nor non-duality, nor the worship of ritual emblems and the like,
nor even their abandonment, nor the state of possessing nothing at all.
Possessing possessions, or the gathering of matted hair, ashes, and so forth;

the renunciation of those things, as well as the performance or non-performance of vows and the like; entering sacred fields and the like, and the observance of pledges and the like—[these are not the cause].
The nature, marks, and so forth of another, as well as names, lineages, and the like—
none of these are prescribed here, nor are they prohibited. Indeed, everything is both prescribed and prohibited herein.
But here, O Mistress of the Gods, this is prescribed as a rule:
the yogin, being well-composed, must stabilize his mind upon the *tattva*.
And in whatever manner that [stabilization] may occur for anyone, in that very manner he should practice.
But one whose mind is unwavering in reality, even while enjoying sense objects, is not touched by defects, just as a lotus leaf is not touched by water; he is like one who,
protected by mantras and the like that neutralize poison, remains unharmed even while consuming it.
Poison does not delude him because of that; likewise, the yogi of great intelligence [is not deluded].
For how indeed can the body and so forth, composed of the five elements, be impure? Indeed, apart from the state of manifestation (prakāśatā), what purity or impurity can there be for a real entity?
And can there be purification for an impure entity by means of something of that same [impure] nature?
For in this case, there would be mutual dependence, futility, and an infinite regress;
thus, earth might be purified by water, and likewise water by earth.
This is a case of mutual dependence; this same logic applies even regarding impurity.
If one were purified by impure water, then the [prescription] for earth would be rendered useless.
Or [if purification were achieved] from air, from water, from air, from fire, or from that [fire] from something else...
The mantras beginning with Bahurūpa are purifying; therefore, there is purity in them. (225) If mantras are pure by their very nature, why are they not so [for others] as well?
If their purity consists in being of the nature of Śiva, why is that [nature of Śiva] not present there too? (226)
The lack of realization of the nature of Śiva does not apply to mantras in the same way it does to the elements, such as earth and the rest.

If it is argued that they are pure because of that [realization], then purity is simply the cognition of that [nature]. That cognition exists for the yogi regarding all entities; thus, there is universal purity.
"But surely, the determination of purity, impurity, and so forth, is made by means of scriptural injunction (*codanā*).
Let it be so; nevertheless, this very injunction is that which has been uttered by Śiva.
If one asks, 'Which [injunction] would be the true one?', this has been explained at length elsewhere."
If it is argued that this [Vedic injunction] is sublated by the Vedic one, why should the reverse not be the case?
If you consider the sublation to be correct, it must be due to the [Vedic injunction] having a more specific scope;
for a rule established as a general precept is to be set aside by an exception.
Purity and impurity are established as general rules for one who has awakened to reality;
these two are indeed sublated in the case of the individual soul, and it has been described thus here.
Furthermore, no suspicion of being a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) or the like can arise regarding a statement of the Great Lord (Māheśvara).
For when [the world] has thus come to be established eternally without prior deliberation,
there may arise a doubt regarding the falsity of the Veda concerning the nature of space and so forth;
yet [the Veda remains] perfectly full with the manifold forms of unconditioned consciousness.
The Lord, abiding as the very soul of the scripture, can never be subject to falsehood.
Just as the Lord, possessing the power of will, desires to abide in the form of existing entities,
so He remains established by expressing His own essential nature.

Even where an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) looks toward another injunction or the like, let it be considered non-authoritative there; however, that same [explanatory passage] is indeed prescriptive when it possesses independence,
or when it enters into a state of subsidiarity within another injunctive sentence.
This [word] is not indeed meaningless, because it possesses a presence like that of an elephant or a fool;
and its communication of its own meaning shines forth through self-awareness itself.
It is impossible to deny that [meaning] within the context of injunctions and prohibitions.
There is both logical reasoning within these statements and one's own uncontradicted self-awareness,
which brings about the certain determination of the reality of all things, like a collection of gems.
Furthermore, that impurity which is proclaimed to exist in a dead body or arising from the body [is likewise addressed].
"Let it be understood that anything other than this is impure, fallen from consciousness, and excluded from it.
Therefore, everything that has attained identity with consciousness is established as pure.
This is stated in the venerable *Vīrāvalī* in the investigation of purity and impurity. (4.240–241)
The living soul (*jīva*) is the vehicle for all; there is nothing whatsoever that is devoid of life.
Know that whatever is separated from the living soul is impure. Therefore, that which is not far removed from consciousness brings about purity.
Through a state free of conceptual construction, even the sages became thus.
However, for the sake of protecting the world, that very reality was concealed by them.
Even though external entities exist, purity and impurity do not [inhere in them] as [the quality of] blue does.

This [distinction] is a property of the subject (pramātṛdharma) alone, arising from the perception of identity or non-identity with consciousness; or else, it may also be a property of the object (vastudharma), conditioned by its dependence upon the subject. In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, wine is pure for the sacrificer, while for another it is the opposite.
By this [principle], even injunctions are sublated by one's own statements;
this has been demonstrated in certain cases, such as the injunction and prohibition regarding the killing of a Brahmin.
Furthermore, the injunctions concerning what may be eaten and so forth have also been deliberated upon by relying on this very logic.
And in the *Sarvajñānottara* and other scriptures, Maheśvara declared that what was uttered by humans, sages, gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others,
each subsequent [teaching] being more distinguished, sublates each preceding one.

The Śaiva [teaching] should never be contradicted by Vaiṣṇava statements, nor should the Vaiṣṇava [teaching] be debated with those originating from Brahmā, and so forth. The deluded person who contradicts [these teachings] through such inversion becomes a partaker of sin.
Therefore, O Skanda, one should primarily not practice worldly dharmas;
one should practice what is taught in one's own stream [of tradition], and not that which is pointed out by other scriptures.
For although even the Vedas and so forth were expounded by the Lord, [they are not the primary path].
Nevertheless, it is said that due to the conceptualization of the presence or absence of the state of contraction,
knowledge belonging to the bound (paśu) is described according to the degree of its contraction;
whereas knowledge belonging to the Lord (pati), which sublates [that bondage], is described according to the degree of its expansion.
"This is duality, this is not"— through such mutual negation,

that which is fashioned by the distinctions of Māyā could never exist in that which is beyond conceptualization. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhargaśikhā* that [the categories of] death, time, the kalās, and so forth [are likewise unreal].
"The one of perfected intellect devours that which arises from the conceptual constructions of duality and non-duality.
(AbhT 4.255b) "In the Siddhānta, the worship of the *liṅga* is taught for one who knows that it consists of the entire path of the universe.
In the Kula and other systems, this [external worship] is forbidden for one who knows that the body itself is the universal Self. (AbhT 4.256)
In this [system], which consists of all things, why are there injunctions and prohibitions?
They exist for the sake of attaining identity with that [Reality] by entering into the restrictive rules (niyama).
In the Kaula system, the abandonment of matted hair and such is taught as an easy means (*sukhopāya*).

The practice of vows is for the sake of realizing identity with the meaning of the mantra; however, the renunciation of those [vows] is for the sake of realizing the universal nature of the mantra's meaning. Entry into the sacred fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) is for the pacification of obstacles.
Now, for one who seeks to propitiate mantras and the like, the method for attaining that is taught; likewise,
the rule regarding the non-going to sacred fields and so forth is described for the sake of knowing the fullness of one’s own self through its universal form.
The true nature of the conduct of the *samaya* is taught as that which must be observed.
Because [the world] is animated by duality, the abandonment of each respective [dualistic notion] is for the sake of the purification of reality (*tattva*).
However, the prohibition of the *samaya* and so forth is stated in the philosophical scriptures (*mata-śāstra*).
"One should realize one's own perfect awakening as being beyond all boundaries;
this form belongs to another, but this is my own object of meditation.
The liṅga of flames and so forth belongs to another, but the skull and so forth is my own. (4.263–264)
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), ascetic practice, the proper time for rites, hospitality, and so forth are mentioned. My name ends with the words *Śakti* and *Śiva*, and not otherwise;
and my lineage (*gotra*) is the succession of gurus, designated by the terms *maṭhikā* and *kula*.
The lineage of Śrī, that called Tryambaka, and that known as Ardhamarda—
thus there are three and a half lineages here in the tradition of Śaṅkara.
According to the sequence of the ages, the lineage of the Siddhas begins with Kūrma and ends with Mīna.

By the word "etcetera," [the text refers to] the house (*ghara*), the village (*pallī*), the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), as well as the seals (*mudrā*) and signs (*chummā*); the procedure for these, established both for oneself and others, is intended for the realization of identity with the Divine. Indeed, one should take recourse in one's own continuum (*saṃtāna*) for that very purpose.
One should eat and worship the Cakra; one must certainly not do so with one belonging to another lineage (parasaṃtānin).
For this is forbidden in the Mata scriptures, because it causes fragmentation.
Even though the supreme reality is undivided, through this [act] division arises.

Thus, from the entry into the field (*kṣetra*) up to the final restriction of the lineage (*saṃtānaniyama*), none of that is prescribed here; for in Śiva, that is not directly applicable. Nor is there any prohibition of it, since that would constitute a fragmentation of reality (*tattva*).
For in the case of the Lord, who is the self of the universe, injunction or prohibition, when conceptualized within his own nature, have no power to effect a fracture of that very nature.
However, upon entering the supreme reality, whenever [a state] is near at hand—
One who understands the means should be accepted, or else at times abandoned;
it is stated in the venerable Trika teaching that no restriction should be observed here,
for there is equality among all deities, as well as among the *ovallī*, mantras, and phonemes.
Since all arrivals and departures are permeated by Śiva,
he indeed perceives the reality of Śiva (śivatattva) as being of unbroken existence.
For he who attains the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) as being of unbroken existence [perceives it as Śiva].
Only the bee, not the fly, is truly a connoisseur of the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower;

likewise, only one impelled by Maheśa finds delight in the worship of the supreme non-duality of Bhairavī. And for those who find rest in this yoga, the ostentation of worldly existence (*bhava*) vanishes.
Like a mass of snow in the great heat of summer, it dissolves of its own accord. Enough with this excessive attachment; there is no need for further elaboration.
Only a wise person such as Abhinavagupta is truly fit for this sacrificial rite.
Thus, in this unfolding of the unsurpassed state, the Śākta means has now been clearly distinguished.
(4.279a) Now begins the fifth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
This [means] is now described for those who, by means of the Āṇava method, desire to attain the supreme abode. (5.1b)
When the purification of conceptual thought itself has occurred, free from all opposition,
the attainment of the desired object— whether enjoyment or liberation— is certain. For some, conceptual thought becomes perfectly stable through the very sovereignty of their own self.
It arises precisely through the absence of dependence on any other means.
However, for some, this conceptualization regarding the purification of one's own self depends upon another means; in that case, the previously mentioned rule is prescribed.
Although that which is called conceptual construction (vikalpa) exists as having pure consciousness as its very nature,
nevertheless, it consists of ascertainment and bestows sovereignty upon the individual soul. This ascertainment is manifold, and the means for it are likewise diverse.
These are called "atoms" (*aṇu*) according to the distinction between being distant or near.
Therein— in the intellect, as well as in the vital breath, the body, and the subject—
even though this [subject] is not ultimately real, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) shines forth.

Since from that Light, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the vital breaths and so forth are not distinct, yet due to its absolute sovereignty, its body consists of both the insentient and the sentient— a twofold nature. This was told to the Goddess by the one who bears the crescent moon on his crest in the *Traiśirasa*.
The individual soul (*jīva*) is the power (*śakti*) of Śiva himself; although she is present everywhere,
she is established in the realization of her own nature through the unfolding of knowledge,
becoming supreme (*parā*) by conceiving the splendor of her own freedom within his true conscious nature.
Perceiving the aspect of insentient nature, he conceals it and becomes non-dual;
there, through the vision of his own sovereignty, he determines his own pure consciousness to be distinct from that [insentient matter], like the reflection of a face in a mirror. (AbhT 5.11–12)
Consciousness is established by force as distinct from intellect, vital breath, and so forth.
In reality, however, it would be non-distinct from them due to their mutual differentiation;
its state of non-differentiation from the universal form arises precisely from its purity.
Because all that exists within consciousness would otherwise be in contradiction with the form of the one, throbbing, perfected form [of Śiva],
how could it possibly transfer from the intellect, or from the vital breath, or from the body, by what means, or in what manner? (AbhT 5.14–15a)

Nevertheless, in this state which is free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), no conceptualization exists without it. Even when something is seen, it is as if unseen [without it]; yet, through conceptualization, there is certainty regarding the supreme sovereignty of the Lord within the intellect, the vital breath, and the body.
The object of conceptualization exists within the void-form [of consciousness], but there is no conceptualization within the subject.
In that state, the intellect consists of meditation (*dhyāna*), while the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of utterance (*uccāraṇa*).
And this utterance consists of the five functions of the breath, beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *vyāna*.
The first, however, consists of the supreme utterance known as *prāṇanā*.
The body exists as a compact mass (*piṇḍa*) through its senses and their objects;
therein, the unsurpassed [state] consisting of meditation is now described.
This light, which is independent and whose nature is consciousness, resides in the heart;
it is said to consist of all the *tattvas* in the *Triśiromata*. It has the form of a plantain-blossom, possessing an exterior, interior, and innermost core.
The knower of reality beholds that which resides within the heart like a flower;
there, with undistracted mind, he should meditate upon the union of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
Through the friction of the fire-drill of that meditation, the sacrificial fire of Mahābhairava [is kindled].
Blazing intensely in the great sacrificial pit called the Heart, one should attain full expansion.

One should contemplate the abode known as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge as non-different from that possessor of power, whose power is expanded and whose splendor is Bhairava. (Abhinavagupta, *Tantrāloka* 5.23–24)
That very triad constitutes the powers of Fire, Sun, and Moon.
This [power] is eternally arisen as Parā, Parāparā, and Aparā;
through their respective acts of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal, each is threefold.
And their fourth form is uninterrupted and unconstructed;
thus these twelve goddesses are situated like the solar disc. Each one of them possesses the radiance of fire, sun, moon, and their respective quiescence.
This unsurpassed wheel [of consciousness] issues forth from the heart through the eyes and other senses via the apertures of the voids into the range of their respective objects.
By means of the rays of that wheel, it proceeds toward those objects through the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
The form whose essence is the radiance of the moon, sun, and fire becomes fully established;
in this way, one should contemplate identity with this revolving wheel as it moves through the path of the void—the ears and other senses—toward objects such as sound. (AbhT 5.29–30a)
By this sequential yoga, wherever this wheel— which is the essence of all things— descends, it acts like a sovereign emperor over that entire domain; in this manner,
the entire array of the paths of the universe dissolves effortlessly.
In the great wheel of Bhairava, which is surrounded by consciousness,
one should then contemplate the great, whirling wheel as the surging forth of one's own self, once the entire universe has been dissolved through mere residual impression (saṃskāra).

Then, through the dissolution of that which is to be burned and the complete exhaustion of its latent impressions (saṃskāra), one should meditate upon the wheel as it becomes tranquil, then as peaceful, and finally as total cessation. By means of this yoga of meditation, the entire universe dissolves into the wheel.
Then, within that consciousness, the object appears as if dissolved into consciousness;
because of the inherent nature of consciousness, there is further emanation, for the Great Goddess is consciousness itself.
Thus, at every moment, dissolving the universe into His own consciousness, [He remains].
And emitting [the rays] again from that point, he shall eternally attain the state of Bhairava.
Thus, starting from the trident and proceeding through the sequence of four and five spokes,
the yogi should contemplate the wheel up to fifty spokes.
With one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the wheel [of the heart] as having sixty-four spokes, or a thousand spokes, or even thousands of innumerable spokes—
[the wheel] of the Great God, the Lord of Consciousness, whose consciousness is ever-expanding. (AbhT 5.38–39a)
There is no conceptualization whatsoever for the Great Lord, who is the power of the universe.
His powers are this entire world, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power;
thus did the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha describe it in the Māṅgala-śāstra.
Thus, the venerable Śambhunātha, being pleased with me, described this first form of means, which is meditation; [he did so] for that venerable Lord Sumati.
Following this very direction, one should also rely upon other meditations.
Those [teachings] which arrive at the burden of the unsurpassed means (anuttaropāya) without following a gradual sequence— now,
that activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), beginning with the act of breathing, which has been described,
we shall explain as the unfolding of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara) by means of it as a method.

First, one should contemplate the "joyless" (nirānanda) state, established within the heart at the mere level of the subject in innate bliss, through resting in pure emptiness. But when the object arises with the emergence of the vital breath, one should contemplate "supreme bliss" (parānanda).
There, satisfied by the inhalation that fulfills the infinite portions of the objects of knowledge,
one should remain established in supreme bliss, adorned by the moon of apāna. Then, one is exclusively satisfied by the friction of the infinite, throbbing objects of knowledge.

Having reached the level of the *samāna* breath, one becomes composed of the bliss of Brahman; even from that state, intent upon devouring the conceptualization of the flood of means and objects of knowledge, one rests in the fire of *udāna* and contemplates great bliss.
Having attained rest therein, one becomes tranquil within this great radiance.
Then there is the unconditioned, great pervasiveness, free from the limitation known as vyāna; indeed, that is the bliss of consciousness, which is not augmented by the insentient.
For here there is no established state whatsoever partitioned into inert forms;
wherein there is no distinction at all, as it vibrates everywhere as the universe.
It is the unstruck consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar.
"That alone which possesses no primary connection whatsoever with [the means of] meditation and the like—
Śambhu has declared that to be the bliss of the universe for us. Resting therein should be established through the yoga of the heart's upward utterance."

That which is perfect rest therein is the state consisting of the Absolute (anuttara). This occurs even within one's own abode, which has a single nature such as the heart and so forth. Now, that form arising from the upward movement of the sixfold vital breath (prāṇa) is described by way of its pervasive extension.
By means of the application of the staff of vital breath (*prāṇa-daṇḍa*), once the front and back have been equalized,
one should take refuge in the mansion of the *lambikā* (the uvula) hanging from the lotus of the four-fold junction.
Then, having traversed the ground of the trident where the three channels meet, [one proceeds].

The wise one should enter into the state of equality among the powers of will, knowledge, and action; he should take refuge in that single, expanding, and ever-unfolding power which is free from contraction—
the series of steps consisting of the eyebrows, the point (*bindu*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the end of power (*śakti*).
There, on the level of the upward-coiled Kuṇḍalinī, beautiful with the vibration within its belly,
the Visarga should come to rest in that state which possesses the condition of the "fish-belly" (matsyodara).
Just as a she-donkey or a mare [reaches] her own abode, the temple of bliss.

Having entered that which consists of expansion and contraction within the heart, one rejoices; likewise, one should take refuge in the union of Bhairava and Bhairavī, who are firmly established in expansion and contraction, and who are intensely filled with the multitude of states repeatedly dissolved and emitted. (59–60)

In the heart, which consists of the emission (*vaisargika*) and the great root-piercing spike (*mahāmūlaśūla*) unified as one, [the yogin] attains rest in the Supreme through the yoga of filling all things. Here, by that very state of fullness, he abides in a condition consisting of the immersion into the universe (*viśvāveśa*).
When light rests within itself, let it be seen as "I" alone,
in the supreme reflective awareness (*anuttara-vimarśa*) which is initially devoid of activity and the like; therein,
the supreme egoity consisting of the reflective awareness of consciousness flashes forth as the first emergence.

Then, by means of the Sun, who is intent on exertion and consists of twelve digits, one should illuminate the objective reality, fill it, and then contemplate it. Then there is the Moon, consisting of sixteen digits, slow in swallowing the emission (*visarga*).
The throbbing *saṃjīvanī* nectar pours forth into the fire of awakening;
it passes through the tip of the ladle of the subtle apertures of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
Thus, that divine nectar satisfies the goddesses of consciousness.
This much is the nectar of emission within the fire-eater known as Awakening.
If all this—the maṇḍala of the sixfold path—were emitted, it would be offered as a sacrifice;
for the emission of the Supreme Lord is the Mistress of Kula.
The agitation of that [emission] is the sequence from *ka* to *ha*; its expansion is the series of the *tattvas*.
Indeed, the Lord of Kula, accompanied by the Mistress of Kula (*aṃ aḥ*), is the supreme separation of the emission (*visarga*); the entire universe is said to consist of that.

One should worship, offer oblations into, and meditate upon this *saṃjīvanī* digit (kalā), which consists of intellect, vital breath, qualities, the body, and internal and external objects— remaining thus attentive to the vibration of the pair of channels of bliss (*ānanda-nāḍī*).
One attains this palatial ground, the outflow of emission (visarga),
during the agitation of Śakti, the immersion into Kula, within the range of the tips of all the channels, during pervasion,
and when the contraction of the entire self occurs; at these times, the wise one should enter the Heart.
From the mutual friction of the web of digits of the Moon and the Sun, the bliss of emission (visargānanda) unfolds within the abode whose nature is Fire and Moon.
Enough with this secret discourse; this is hidden by its very nature.
There, the wise and accomplished yogi should find rest within the Heart of the Yoginī (Yoginīhṛdaya). Having attained firm rootedness in the state where rejecting and accepting are transcended,
he should perceive the universe as the wondrous play of consciousness through its non-dual mode of being.
Having abandoned the wretchedness of seeking external objects of purpose within one's own internal and external self,
and having attained repose in one's true nature, one should resort to the blossomed state of *nāda*.
By means of that, one should properly cause the mouth of consciousness to expand within.
The wheel of consciousness, the senses, and the vital breaths becomes non-different from that which is to be known.
That object of knowledge is dissolved by the fire called consciousness;
once dissolved, it merges into this triangle, the fire of Śakti.
There, perfectly tranquil in the existence of the expansive point (*bindu*) of consciousness, the yogi who rests in the seed-syllable of reabsorption (*saṃhāra-bīja*) becomes supreme.
Whether within, without, or in both, he is beautiful in his universality and its opposite.
The vibration of consciousness consists of the three powers and possesses both contraction and expansion;
yet, even when devoid of contraction and expansion, it is likewise so through its manifestation. With the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, one attains the supreme state.

Then, within the creation of autonomy, which takes the form of various purposeful actions, there is the reflective awareness known as "particularity," designated as "orientation. One should attain rest therein; that is the vitality (*vīrya*) which resides in the circle of mantras.
Since the accomplishments of pacification and the rest arise from identity with their respective forms,
that divine collection of senses known as the freedom of consciousness—
remaining ever-unblinking— should make this universe consist of its own self.
When all mental fluctuations have been dissolved through union with the Great Thousandfold World-system,
one remains fully saturated within the massed flood of one's own rays of consciousness.
There, the one who thinks of nothing and possesses clear vision attains pure awareness.
Those sparks are the sole cause for burning away the ashes of saṃsāra.
This was stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Triśirobhairavāgama*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the entry into the ground of mantra. 85–86ab. 86cd.

The upward movement through the central channel is characterized by the attainment of its [supreme] qualities; it transcends the state at the end of emission and is defined as the ultimate limit. This occurs through the cessation of the downward flow and the avoidance of upward projection.
Having experienced that which bestows the manifestation of the arising knowledge of the Great Light within the supreme abode through the function of the measure (*mātrā*), one should enter the city;
that single, waveless descent is of the nature of Śiva.

Blazing with six wheels multiplied by four, six, and two, one should contemplate the void within that [state]. One should enter the void situated in the void by means of what is situated in the void; having abandoned each void, having ascended to the void, one should utter the void situated in the void as "khaṃ khaṃ."
By virtue of presiding over the center of the void, one should contemplate the rays of consciousness situated in the state of the word (pada).
Established in being, free from longing for objects of thought,
one should block the paths of both existence and non-existence, perceiving the obstruction of both existence and non-existence.
The Self, the individual soul, the root of the lineage, Power (Śakti), Prosperity (Bhūti), Consciousness (Citi), and Delight (Rati)—
this triad of powers, both colored by the subject and the object and free from them,
is declared to be the tenfold Void characterized by the utterance of the utterance.
Abiding in the abode, situated in the midst of the abode, enclosed within the belly of the abode—awaken the abode by means of the abode; make the abode reach the end of the abode.
By means of the movement toward that abode, one should pierce the internal end of the abode.
"By means of the division and sub-division [of the breath], the piercing should be performed from the center. Thus has this Āṇava means of entry been proclaimed,
which was taught to me by the venerable Maheśvaranātha residing within my heart.
And it is stated in the venerable Brahmayāmala: "The glorious Sound (Rāva) consists of ten aspects:
the gross, the subtle, the supreme, that which is in the heart, that which is produced in the throat, and that which is produced in the palate;
and that which is all-pervasive, bestowing the state of omnipresence. (5.97–98)
The great yogin who has conquered sound, entering another body, attains the supreme pervasion; therefore, one should practice this every day until that resonant power, through resonance,
dissolves into the soundless state.
In this regard, for one who desires to enter the supreme path through the means residing within the body by means of contemplation (*bhāvanā*),
bliss (*ānanda*) arises prior to the touch of fullness (*pūrṇatā*). Even beyond that, in the bodiless state which is like a flash of lightning, [bliss arises].
Through a momentary immersion in the Abode (dhāman), emergence occurs clearly as a leaping upward;
this happens through the abandonment of the unity of consciousness and body, which are like water and sediment [separated] by practice.
By the onset of one's own power and the loosening of the body, one experiences trembling.
When the certainty of identity with the body has dissolved because it has been internalized,
one first falls into a state like sleep as long as that [certainty] has not yet taken root in the self of consciousness.
Then, having become established in the state of reality, one perceives consciousness as the self-nature of the universe.

When consciousness whirls, that whirling is known as the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti). Indeed, while there is the conceit of the non-self in the Self, and likewise the conceit of the Self in what is not the Self—such as the body and so forth—that is bondage; liberation, however, is the dissolution of that [conceit].

When, at the outset, the sense of self in what is not-self has dissolved and one’s own true self is attained, and when the state of non-self within the self is destroyed, the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti) proceeds;
this consists of a pentad: bliss, rising, trembling, sleep, and whirling.
For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:
"When the yogi enters into this pentad beginning with Ānanda once it has been demonstrated, he then forcibly attains the state of lordship over each respective wheel. (5.108–109)
Just as a body, though pervaded everywhere by all-encompassing consciousness,
is nevertheless capable of performing some specific action through the eye, such as the perception of form; in the very same way, through entry into a particular *cakra*, a certain [power] may arise.
The wheel of bliss has seven corners; the bulb is said to be the source of emergence.
Trembling occurs in the heart, sleep in the palate, and whirling is the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī.
This has been clearly stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara* Tantra.
Thus has been shown the supreme heart, which is the repose of the upward movement (uccāra);
it is that whose sign is unmanifest, wherein man, Śiva, and Śakti are undivided.
Herein this entire universe is dissolved, and herein it is perceived as abiding within.
This is the complete characteristic of the consciousness of Pūrṇaśaktibhairava:
it is that clear immersion (*samāveśa*) which occurs when the paths (*adhvan*) within the body manifest;
and it is that which is joined with the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) arising from the manifestation [of objects] veiled by the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
This manifest and unmanifest *liṅga* is the potency of mantra, both supreme and non-supreme;
it arises from the emergence of the individual (*nara*) and power (*śakti*), yet remains distinct from the nature of Śiva.
It possesses differentiation because it lacks the immersion into the *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness) of Śiva, which has set aside such differentiation.
That manifest *liṅga*, which consists of consciousness, has the nature of a specific vibration.

From the manifest arises the birth of accomplishments (*siddhi*); from both the manifest and the unmanifest arise the two [powers], and from the unmanifest arises the primordial power of the Supreme. However, this discussion does not apply to the Absolute (*anuttara*).

For one who offers the universe into that manifest human liṅga called the Self, both the manifest and the unmanifest dissolve therein; thus, when that has dissolved, it becomes the unmanifest. Therefore, this liṅga of the Self exists within the Supreme, which consists of the nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu).
This discourse does not rest in the unmanifest, nor does it reach the supreme abode.
This threefold arrangement of differentiation belongs to a single vibration.
Here, in this *liṅga*, one should always remain intent upon worship and repose.
This *liṅga*, the Heart of the Yoginīs, beautiful with bliss,
gives birth to an indescribable consciousness through the union of seed-syllable (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*).
Here, because it is free from effort, this entire host of deities [is present].

He dwells in the abode filled with bliss, consisting of eternally emergent consciousness. Herein shines the power of Lord Bhairava— which, though he himself is neither contracted nor expanded— manifests as both contraction and expansion, and is difficult to accomplish.
Sprinkled by this stream of bliss from the emission (*visarga*) of the union with the *liṅga*,
that very same real universe becomes eternally ever-new.
In this [system], the means is described as being "the unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) precisely because of its identity with that [reality].
Does the sun not shine even when lamps are ablaze?

(5.125) Regarding objects, the means of their enjoyment, and the pleasure or pain arising from them, those whose minds are immersed [in the Self] know within themselves the bliss of the cessation of mental fluctuations—even without entering [into formal meditative absorption], free from all doubt. (5.126)

While the Self exists as the splendor of the nature of consciousness, and while the internal organ likewise exerts its influence upon it, and while the group of senses is rendered helpless by the activity of that [consciousness], and while objects such as pleasure and the like exist—may that Reality be gathered, wherein the yogin remains with the full majesty of his rays, arising utterly free from duality.
(5.127) Thus the rule for vocalization has been declared; the instrument is now being analyzed. (5.128)
And this has been declared by the Supreme Lord in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*:

"They say that practice preceded by awakening consists of sevenfold application through the processes of grasping, the grasper, consciousness, pervasion, abandonment, projection, and immersion" (5.128–129).
That instrument [of projection] consists of its own self-abidance, preceded by the pervasion of that [object],
during the act of projection; and although this instrument is clearly to be understood from the mouth of the Guru,
nevertheless, for the sake of preserving the tradition (āgama), it will be described further below.

Regarding this utterance that has been described, that which exists there as a vibrating [reality] is called a *varṇa* (phoneme), being for the most part an indistinct imitation of sound. The wise know its primary form to be the seed of both emanation and withdrawal.
By the power of that practice, the yogi gradually attains the nature of consciousness (cidātmatā).
For in this way, whether it be the vowel-less or the vowel-possessing [mantra], from the letter *ka* to the letter *sa*,
when remembered or even uttered again and again, each respective consciousness is produced.
Even those sounds such as "jar" and so forth, which depend upon external objects and conventions, can produce within oneself a mental realization of the object, like a kingdom of the mind.
Thus it was said by the Supreme Lord: "Bhairava is all-pervasive in everything."
"Thus, by the continuous utterance of the word 'Bhairava,' one becomes Śiva.
This was also stated in the venerable *Traiśirasa* prior to the extraction of the mantra.
Furthermore, memory (*smṛti*) is, in reality, the prior recollection (*smaraṇa*) within all existing things.
The true nature of mantra is that which effects the attainment of the essential nature of the object to be meditated upon. Memory produces its own nature and colors all things,
existing everywhere through manifold forms.
The attainment of one's own true nature is, in the ultimate sense, pure consciousness;
know that it culminates in manifestation, and that existence is proclaimed as the supreme.
Furthermore, what need is there for conventional rules regarding those seed-syllables and clusters of phonemes?
These [phonemes] cause consciousness to vibrate; they should be led to the state of being means for consciousness.

Due to the absence of a denotable object, and from the vibration of indifferent consciousness within its own abode, fullness is attained in the seed-syllables and clusters through the arousal and cessation of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The first consciousness consists of the blissful sound *sīt*, the true, perfect equanimity, and the initial awareness;
for this primary perception is indeed the touch of the unsurpassed consciousness.
Within the three abodes—the heart, the throat, and the lips—it expands most intensely.

The fourteenth entry is that which consists of the unification with that very Self. Then, during the phase of the utterance of the emission (*visarga*), one intent on recitation leads both paths to the end of the twelve along with the heart into a single unity.

From the bulb (kanda), heart, throat, palate, and the tip [of the nose], up to the end of the process of Kuṇḍalinī, one should bring forth the seed-syllable that vibrates within the central channel of bliss. The seed-syllable of withdrawal is *khaṃ*; it resides in the heart, is labial, and is blossomed at the crown of one's own head.
The fire is triangular at the palate and throat; the bindu is situated in the upper station.
By means of this method, the wise and intelligent practitioner, devoted to the recitation of the phonemes, shall enter the supreme, unsurpassed abode before long.
By the word "color" (varṇa), [one means] blue and so forth; or else, as it is stated in the *Dīkṣottara*:
one should meditate upon [the letters] Saṃhāra, Nṛ, Agni, and Marut, joined with Rudra and Bindu. Then, becoming absorbed in that within the heart, one should perceive the target after seven days.
Like sparks from a fire, variegated with blue, yellow, red, and other colors,
it blazes intensely within the lotus of the heart, awakened by the lamp of the seed-syllable.
Blazing like a lamp, the *bindu* shines like the sun free from clouds.
Through this self-luminous Self, one whose mind is focused on nothing else attains identity with Śiva,
just as copper pierced by mercury attains the state of gold.
This should be understood as an illustrative sign to be applied to all mantras.
Whatever collection of phonemes arises from conceptualization is indeed material;
however, by virtue of the predominance of consciousness (*saṃvit*), it exists as if it were non-material. Therefore, one who is established in such a form ascends into pure consciousness.
When one's intellect is serene, within the unconditioned state where form is not veiled,
the nature of consciousness remains undivided amidst the blue, the yellow, pleasure, or pain; therefore,
it has been taught by the Gurus that there is a diversity of means [to reach this].
Through these— articulation, the organs of action, meditation, and the [five] colors—
the sequential method of the means for attaining the unsurpassed state has been demonstrated. Furthermore,
that [means] consists of non-conceptualization and vigor in meditative cultivation.
In meditation, that [recitation] is also in the utterance; that too is in the instrument, and that in the resonance.
That is in the mental construction of the places of articulation—thus one should resort to this external sequence.
The supreme yogi may leap over it, but the one of dull intellect proceeds by stages.
Just as a eunuch lacks virility, yet even he may possess strength;
so too, this conceptualization of the internal and external would be like a dead body.
Thus, the supreme means regarding the individual (āṇava) has been declared by way of the clear path as the external method.

Now, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, the external means, known as the "determination of the locus," is clearly analyzed. (6.1b) Now, the differentiation of the locus is said to be threefold: in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), in the body, and likewise externally. (6.2a)

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is fivefold within the body, and twofold according to its external and internal nature. The mandala, the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), the vessel, the rosary together with the book, the linga, the drum (*tūra*), the cloth painting (*paṭa*), the manuscript (*pusta*), the image (*pratimā*), and the icon (*mūrti*) [are likewise twofold].
Thus, the external [path] is elevenfold, yet it may further become manifold.
In that regard, the procedure based upon the vital breath (prāṇa) is first taught.
This entire path, though sixfold and very extensive, [is now summarized].
That which will be described is established within the single vital breath (prāṇa).
The reckoning of the paths, which exists as both sequential and non-sequential,
consists of the manifold and unitary reckoning of sequential and non-sequential [processes] within the sphere of objective phenomena.
Time, whose nature consists of succession and non-succession, resides within supreme consciousness.
She alone is celebrated as the supreme power of the Lord, known by the name Kālī.
That very consciousness manifests externally as succession and non-succession, which are contained within her own self.
Expanding [the world] through its process of growth, it abides as the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti).
For that which is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is light,
having cast off the object of knowledge from itself, shines forth as the solitary void.
That very state of emptiness of consciousness is celebrated as the supreme stage of yogis, attained through the reflective awareness of "not this, not this" (neti neti). That same void-nature,
when this object of cognition has been dissolved, becomes oriented toward reclaiming it.

By virtue of its falling and surging upward, it is designated as the wave of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa). For this reason, they say that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath;
thus, the wind has become the substratum for the principle of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
This is that power of vital breath (*prāṇana-śakti*) which bestows the longing for internal exertion;
it is considered to be vibration (*spanda*), radiance (*sphurattā*), repose (*viśrānti*), the living soul (*jīva*), and the intuitive flash within the heart (*hṛt-pratibhā*).
That function of the vital breath makes itself one with [the self] through its five forms, beginning with *prāṇa*.

Because consciousness makes the body its own, it shines forth through that very body. Therefore, the deluded perceive the activity born of a body inlaid with consciousness through its identity with the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), and they think, "There is nothing else."

Taking as their authority that very intellect which relies on knowers who are mostly children, fools, and women, the Cārvākas consider themselves seers of reality. If their cultivation of such a view reaches firmness through constant practice, [it becomes established].

Upon the dissolution of that body, they remain as if asleep until such latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are exhausted. However, when those specific impressions are exhausted, another unexhausted impression,
awakened by some cause, brings forth a manifold abundance of fruits.
Because of the suspicion that [the realization] is not firm, because of the persistence of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
because of the slackening of other duties, because of the possibility of future remorse,
and because of the neglect of the duties of other people who have not attained that state; (19–20a)
They say that this latent impression of nihilism is more wicked than wickedness itself due to its sinfulness.
(20) Enough with this irrelevant matter; now the subject at hand is being analyzed:
the entire path, in its full extent, is established within the vital breath. (21)

And that path is divided twofold, by means of action and by means of form. Indeed, it is taught in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* that the life-force (*prāṇa*) itself is the crest-lock (*śikhā*), which,
when bound at the time of sacrifice and other rites, consists of Śiva because of its partless nature.
Since its movement occurs twenty-four times within the course of a day and night,
it bestows manifold fruits through hundreds of openings known as the "projections of the breath" (prāṇavikṣepa).
Night, the moon, the downward breath (apāna), and the resonance (nāda) abide together in one place.
The sun of life does not rise; such is the twilight of half a *tuṭi*.
With the sun facing upward and the moon facing downward, fire is situated between them.
When the sun is positioned in the middle of the sky, this midday [twilight] bestows liberation.
For its essence has not set; it awakens the wheel of living beings. The Bindu, the vital breath, and the sun—day itself—abide as one.
This is the third Great Conjunction (mahāsandhyā), which stands as the perfectly tranquil self.
When the topknot (śikhā) is bound in this manner, it bestows each respective fruit;
therefore, this entire path comes to rest within consciousness.
For consciousness is formless, all-pervading, and inactive.
That which is the manifestation of forms and actions is itself the path (adhvan) of the Great Lord. The path is the cause for reaching the state that is to be traversed by degrees;
it is called "path" because it is devoured (*adyate*) by the awakened, whereas for dualists it is an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*).

Since one should everywhere here investigate the etymological meaning of words, it is stated in the venerable *Niśācāra*: "In this context, technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) is considered to be threefold:
the occasional (*naimittikī*), the conventional (*prasiddhā*), and likewise the technical (*pāribhāṣikī*). (6.31–32a)
Or, if it belongs to the previous [category], it should be included therein as the primary element.

Therefore, even if this etymological derivation of the word *adhvan* has not been explicitly stated, it should be inferred by one's own intellect in some instances; for how much can possibly be written in a book?
In that regard, the manifestation of action is called the path known as Time (kālādhvan);
the three paths—known as phonemes (varṇa), mantras, and words (pada)—are clearly present therein.
As for the aspect consisting of the manifestation of form (mūrti), that is declared to be the path of space (deśādhvan).
The triad known as Kalā, Tattva, and Puruṣa is here included within this [system].
In each of these two triads, there exists a gross, subtle, and supreme form;
therefore, this entire path is said to be sixfold.
Furthermore, that triad which precedes the sixfold path is indeed this very path of time (*kālādhvan*), clearly established within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
This time is said to be distinct from the time situated in the midst of the principles (*tattva*).
For this is the time of the Lord that effects the manifestation of the universe;
it is the power of action (kriyāśakti) and the supreme form of all the principles (tattvas). This is the principle of Īśvara, which is said to be the body of Śiva.

Since this universe is the identity of the Self with its overflowing manifestations and activities, that which is indeed the nature of the Lord within the Supreme Self is called the *kālatattva* (the principle of time) in the subject conditioned by *māyā*. 40–41a.
That which is Śiva’s own body, beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā,
becomes the sheaths (kañcukas) for the individual soul (puruṣa), beginning with Māyā and ending with Rāga.
For Anāśrita is Śiva, Māyā is Sadāśiva, and Kalā and Vidya [are Īśvara and Śuddhavidyā].
Īśvara is called Kāla (Time) and Niyati (Necessity), while Sadvidyā is said to be Rāga (Attachment).

Anāśrita is the subject of the void (śūnyamātṛ), and Sadāśiva is the subject of the intellect (buddhimātṛ). Īśvara is the subject of the vital breath (prāṇamātṛ), and Vidyā is the state of being the subject of the body (dehapramātṛtā).
For emptiness is indeed without support; knowledge itself is the state of being the intellect (buddhi).
It is the nature of the universe, the state of being the vital breath (prāṇa), and within the body, the total absorption in the object of perception.
Therefore, this universal cognition shines forth upon the path of the vital breath.
We shall describe that form by which it exists; let it be attended to by the wise.

Although the vital breath (prāṇa), whose nature is woven like warp and woof, pervades this body everywhere up to the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), it is nevertheless not clearly manifest in this manner.
Effort is considered to be twofold: that which consists merely of sustaining life and that which is directed toward the supreme goal.
Furthermore, it is divided again into two types—the perceptible and the imperceptible.
One should contemplate each of these as being twofold according to whether they are manifest or unmanifest.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), beautiful with its vibration and effort known as the "perceivable life-force," begins from the bulb (*kanda*) itself; nevertheless, it is not clearly manifest here [in that location]. Therefore, the systematic arrangement is said to begin precisely from the support of the bulb.

In the *Svacchanda-śāstra*, it is clearly stated that the channels serve as the support for the vital winds. Even there, however, this effort does not exist as something perceptible; rather, the movement of the breath is differentiated from the heart by means of an effort that is itself an object of perception.
The power of the Lord Śiva— namely Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā, along with any one of the others— is that which constitutes the self and the vital breath for one who applies effort.
In certain cases, the power of the Lord is primary, as in the case of the movement of the vital winds through the limbs.
In some cases, the power of the Self (ātma-śakti) is primary, as in the contraction and vibration of the *kanda*;
in other cases, the power of breath (prāṇa-śakti) is clearly primary, as in the movement of the breath within the heart.
For attentive yogins, either this triad or this dyad may be the principal means.
Due to attention, the unseen portion [of karma], strength,
and the influence of other factors, there is even a reversal regarding the primacy of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the powers of the self.
Vāmā is the sovereign power of the Lord that ordains the state of transmigrating beings.
Jyeṣṭhā belongs to those who are perfectly awakened, while Raudrikā belongs to those who desire to know.
Vāmā is the one who vomits forth the cycle of transmigration; for Jyeṣṭhā consists of Śiva, she is Raudrī because she dissolves afflictions and obstructs all karmas.
Without knowing the reality (tattva) of emanation and the other [phases], one is neither liberated nor can one liberate others.
And it is said in the *Śrīyogacāra*: "Liberation comes from the manifestation of everything.
Those yogins who do not know emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal [are not liberated].
They are not liberated, for they are permeated solely by the bondage of ignorance regarding that [reality]. (59) All those processes, beginning with emanation, are undoubtedly dependent upon Time.
And since that [Time] consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), its clear articulation (*uccāra*) is now explained. (60)
The movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds from the heart to the end of the twelve finger-breadths at the nose;
for every living being, it measures thirty-six finger-breadths according to the measure of one's own fingers.
Whether the body be the smallest or the largest, it remains exactly the same.
From that, valor, vitality, strength, movement, and the circulation of the vital breath proceed equally.

Within the thirty-six-finger movement, the pair consisting of the outgoing and incoming breaths— the nālikā, the lunar day (tithi), the month, and the year— is clearly established here in their aggregate.
A *tuṭi* consists of one and a quarter finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) of breath; sixteen of these constitute an inhalation (*ucchvasana*).

An exhalation (*niḥśvasana*) is likewise measured here by a *caṣaka*, occurring at every finger-breadth plus a fifth part. A *nālī* is said to consist of one inhalation and one exhalation, and this is declared to be one day and night.
Nine finger-breadths correspond to four *tuṭis*, which constitute a *prahara*; four such *praharas* make up a day.
During the outward movement [of the breath] it is the sun, and during the inward movement it is the moon; the two junctions (*saṃdhyā*) of these two occupy half a *tuṭi*.
Ketu resides in the sun, Rāhu in the moon, and Mars and the others occupy their respective portions of the days of the week.

For other planets, the interval between their risings lasts for two watches (prahara). Success (siddhi) is more remote; liberation (mokṣa), malevolent magic (abhicāra), and results pertaining to the next world (pāralaukikī) [occur] within eight watches, while results pertaining to this world (aihikī) vary according to the degree of distance or proximity.
At midday and midnight, Abhijit bestows liberation and enjoyment;
for the other lunar mansions, their rising occurs sequentially from the middle.
From the water-tattva [proceed] the Nāgas, the Lords of the World (Lokapālas), the Mūrtīs, and the Gaṇeśas.
The leaders ending with Pradhāna are the presiding lords of the Vidyā-tattva;
likewise, there are the Bhairavas beginning with Sakala and ending with Kaṇṭhya and Oṣṭhya.
There are also the supreme powers of the Lord, the Vāmeśas, and the leaders of the heroes.
Those eight [groups] of eight which thus possess the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader—
of these, the gross and subtle [energies] arise sequentially during the eight watches (prahara) of the day;
undoubtedly, the actions are cruel during the day and gentle at night.
Cruelty or gentleness is determined by one's intention; liberation occurs at the end of day or night through the yoga of meditation on pervasion (vyāpti).
These have been taught by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Vīrāvalīkula.
White and black, long and short, merit and demerit, day and night—
these are extinguished through initiation, by means of pervasion, meditation, and yoga. The movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) throughout a day and night is said to be a month.

The day is the dark fortnight and the night is the bright; the two fortnights are as in the previous ritual procedures. Among those sixteen lunar days that have been mentioned, those which are the first and the last—of these two, there is rest for half and half; the other lunar days are fifteen.
A day and night is divided into fifteen [units] of two fingers each, plus a quarter.
Indeed, it is by virtue of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and rest (*viśrama*) that these very [units] constitute day and night;
for consciousness at every moment is joined with manifestation and bliss.
Day and night are fashioned by that [consciousness] to exactly the same extent as it exists; for to whatever degree consciousness has arisen with increasing clarity,
to that very extent a moment may be a kalpa, or even a mere blink of an eye.
To the very extent that there is the arising of consciousness intent upon grasping the object of knowledge as one,
to that same extent there is its setting, which is the savoring of the knower’s own self.
This occurs whether the object of knowledge is external, internal, both, or devoid of both.
In every way, becoming one with that [object] is day; abiding as the knower is night.
The knower who rests in the object of knowledge is the state of being turned inward. First he was deliberating, and afterwards he is of the nature of pure existence alone.
The state of being the knower in the waking state is the dream; the ancient state is the knower.
Beyond that is deep sleep at the dissolution of night and day, which is the non-dual fourth state (turya).
Sometimes, through the equilibrium of resting in the reality, there is a savoring within the Self.

The equality of the object of knowledge and the knower is that state where night and day are equal. However, when there is greater repose in the object of knowledge, it leads to the lengthening of the day;
whereas in the opposite case, repose in one's own self becomes diminished, and the reverse occurs.
For when one's own self-interest has awakened, rest in the object of knowledge is indeed minimal.
(6.86b) One should speak of the sequence of the decrease and increase of day and night in this very way;
just as in bodies the decrease and increase of days and nights are not uniform. (6.87)
"In the same way, it is also [taught] regarding the cities; thus, it has not been stated with specific distinction.
Thus did the venerable Śambhu, the sun in the vast sky of the lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka, proclaim to me the sequence of day and night.

The venerable teacher of the *Santāna* lineage, however, has stated that the state of both the awakened and the unawakened begins from the heart; by means of that, there is a division of day and night. That [division] is unreal within the bright fortnight, which partakes in the splendor of the internal entry.
How could this, which is the very state of the unawakened, become a day?
Enough of this; I have no envy for my former doctrine. But when that which is to be abandoned has been shown, disciples will see exclusively the true path.

The dark fortnight has been explained; therein, the moon resides within the vital breath (prāṇa). Due to its nature of nourishing, it sheds one digit (kalā) on each lunar day (tithi). That which is the fifteenth moment (tuṭi) near the limit of the twelve (dvādaśānta)— AbhT_6.92b/. vyākhyātaḥ kṛṣṇapakṣo ya statra prāṇagataḥ śaśī // 92 AbhT_6.93a/. āpyāyanātmanaikaikāṃ kalāṃ pratitithi tyajet / AbhT_6.93b/. dvādaśāntasamīpe tu yāsau pañcadaśī tuṭiḥ // 93
On this occasion of the new moon, that waning moon enters the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
And it is stated in the *Śrīkāmikā*: "The supreme Nature (*prakṛti*) is neither above nor below;
Māyā, which has the form of Śiva, moves through half-and-half [of the path], divided into two segments. (6.94)
One should fill and dissolve the body by means of the nature of the moon and the sun;
the nectar, in the form of the moon, [flows] twofold and again sixteenfold. All the gods drink those fifteen supreme digits (kalās).
The new moon (amā), situated within the cave of the remainder, is the Amāvāsyā that satisfies the universe.
Thus, fifteen digits (kalās) of the moon wane in succession;
however, the sixteenth digit (ṣoḍaśī) does not [wane], due to its identity with the nature of the nourishing nectar-stream.

Therein, that fifteenth *tuṭi* in which the moon has completely waned— half of the *tuṭi* following that is proclaimed as the junction (*saṃdhi*) between the two fortnights. From that half-*tuṭi* of rest, the first half of the new moon (*amāvāsya*) arises.
The junction is conceived as being half of the *prātipada* and the subsequent [day].
In that case, within that *prātipada*, at the point of half of the half-*tuṭi*, the "portion" (*dala*) preceding it—
the new moon (*āmāvāsya*)— enters the solar eclipse due to the cessation of the lunar day (*tithi*).
There, the moon, dissolved within the solar orb, flows with nectar;
because it is heated, Rāhu, who is co-natal with the moon, drinks that [nectar].
The sun is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while the moon is the object of knowledge (*meya*); they consist of the nature of cognition and action.
Rāhu is the subject of illusion (māyā-pramātṛ), skilled in concealing [reality];
for that very reason, being of the nature of darkness (tamas), he is incapable of dissolving it.
Through the non-dual flash of their union, the primary subject is the one who dissolves [that concealment].
Through the conjunction of the Sun, the Moon, and Rāhu, there arises the measure of the object of knowledge and the knower;
because of that non-duality, this is the great eclipse, a source of merit.
Even without the new moon day, if such a conjunction occurs, it is a great eclipse.
When the Sun is in Aries and Rāhu is in Aśvinī on the day of Aśvinī (the first tithi),
and when half of the new moon has dissolved into the portion of the first lunar day, and that first lunar day becomes pure— then liberation occurs when the Moon has moved far away.
Between the absorption (grāsa) and the liberation (mokṣa), bathing, meditation, fire-offerings,
recitation, and so forth— whether worldly or unworldly— yield abundant fruit pertaining to the next world.
