Entering for even a moment into the cessation of the agitation between the object of swallowing and the swallower, [one attains this].
One who performs meditation, worship, and other rites for the sake of liberation during an eclipse of the moon or sun [attains success].
The interruption of the lunar day (*tithi*) is a debt; coughing is a debt; exhalation is wealth; and inhalation is wealth.
These arise effortlessly, but they may also be produced through effort by means of exhalation (*recana*) or retention (*rodhana*).

Thus, as the sun of consciousness enters the breath, one should fill the moon consisting of nectar with the rays of awakening, digit by digit. These [rays] are beautiful like the nectar of the moon, characterized by a gradual fulfillment.

These fifteen *tuṭis* constitute the lunar days (*tithis*) belonging to the bright fortnight. On the final *tuṭi*, which is the full moon, the junction of the fortnight occurs as before. And the lunar eclipse occurs at the junction of the first day (*pratipad*), due to the previous entry.
In this context, for practitioners who grasp [the reality], there is great fruit pertaining to this world;
as before, this other month is said to be a year within the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra).
In each of six finger-breadths from the heart, the Sun [resides] in the signs beginning with Capricorn.

Standing [in the north], one should perform the six [months] beginning with Māgha; that is the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa). When three transits have occurred and eighteen finger-breadths have been traversed, when the sun has reached Aries, there is the meritorious equinox (viṣuvat) pertaining to the world beyond.
But at the entrance [of the breath] when the sun is situated in Libra, that very moment becomes the equinox (*viṣuvat*).
Here, this bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*), and thereafter it belongs to the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Then there are the states of being an embryo (*garbhatā*), the state of being about to emerge (*prodbubhūṣiṣyat-bhāva*), and the state of desiring to emerge (*udbubhūṣutā*).
The state of being about to arise, the commencement of arising,
and the persistence of arising; birth, existence, transformation, growth, decline, and destruction— in this sequence,
the signs beginning with Capricorn (makara) produce corresponding results through their activity.
In rites for the next world, Capricorn and Aquarius are used for the preliminary service (*pūrvasevana*) of mantras and the like;
indeed, the four signs beginning with Pisces are progressively closer [to the goal].
In that very context, during entry, there are the auspicious rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and so forth.

That action will bear fruit in this life, and its results will become increasingly distant in succession. When [the breath] moves out, there is an increase of days; in the opposite case, the reverse occurs.
In this year, the sequence is five lunar days for every finger-breadth.
In that regard also, the rule for day and night is entirely as before. Within this solar year beginning with Kārttika,
the Rudras— twelve in number— are to arise here in the future, starting from the right and ending with Pitāmaha.
The arising of the year within the vital breath has been explained; now follows the arising of the twelve-year cycle.
In each single finger-breadth (aṅgula), there are sixty lunar days (tithi) in succession;
these constitute the arising of the twelve years, which are said to begin with Caitra.

In the month of Caitra, the emergence of the mantra occurs in the palate; now, however, the emergence of Caitra is said to be in the heart, and for that reason, the emergence of the mantra also takes place there. When three hundred lunar days (tithis) are thus distributed across each finger-breadth, [the emergence of the mantra occurs].

In the breath, a year consists of five and a quarter finger-breadths; furthermore, there is a period of sixty years. This division within the breath—twenty-one thousand six hundred—is said to constitute one day and night of the sixty-year cycle.
The divisions of the watch, day and night, month, season, year, and the sixty-year cycle of the sun—
whatever division or junction exists therein is meritorious for meditation and worship.
Thus, this time within the arising of the vital breath (prāṇa) has Śakti as its sole embodiment.
The Universal Self, residing within, has its form described externally [as follows]:
six breaths constitute a *caṣaka*; sixty of those make a *nālī*, and likewise, thirty of those make a lunar day (*tithi*). Thirty of those make a month, and twelve of those make a year.

A year of the ancestors (pitrya) is a day and night [of Brahmā], divided by the northern and southern solstices. That which is a year according to the measure of the ancestors is called a divine (divya) year. Here, three hundred and sixty human years constitute one divine year.
Having multiplied that by twelve, the number of months is obtained here.
Multiplying that again by thirty, one should state the calculation of days and nights.
And having multiplied that by twenty-one thousand six hundred, [the number of breaths is determined].
One should state the number of breaths there, as well as the emergence of the sixty-year cycle and so forth;
and it has been stated by the Gurus in their own commentaries on the venerable Raurava and other scriptures:
"That which is one day and night for the gods is one year for humans."
Three hundred and sixty human years constitute one year of the gods.
This very same view is observed in the venerable *Svacchanda Śāstra*,
which begins by stating that such a period is a day and night of the ancestors (Pitṛs), and subsequently [continues].
Thus, the day and night of the gods is a summary based on their identity.
Therefore, those teachers who— on the basis of the first two statements in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*—
claim that a human year is a divine day, are indeed deluded and speak in vain.

In the four ages, beginning from the first, there are divine years of one thousand; in each subsequent age, there is a decrease of one [thousand], with hundreds corresponding to those [decreases]. Within these, there are eight junctions (*saṃdhi*).
Seventy-one cycles of the four ages constitute a *manvantara*, and there are fourteen such *manvantaras*.
During that day of Brahmā, fourteen Indras pass away in succession.
At the end of Brahmā’s day, the flame of the Fire of Time (Kālavahni), extending for a hundred thousand yojanas,
having burnt the three worlds, puts the other three to sleep with its smoke.

Because the manifestation of the fire of time (*kālavahni*) from the hells occurred from that [source] in the past, the Lord (*īśa*), although situated below, is all-pervasive (*vibhu*); such is the doctrine of the venerable *Raurava*. When the ashes have been blown away by the breath of Brahmā, [the hells are filled] with the water of his sweat.

The entire universe remains submerged by that [power] until the arrival of night. During that period of night, all individuals residing in their subtle bodies, impelled by the force of fire, become "isolates" (layakevalas) within the world of living beings.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakas, and others sport in the Great Abode (mahadālaya).
At the end of the night, he again effects creation, beginning with the quality of darkness (tamas).
At the end of his own hundred years, there is its dissolution; that indeed is one day of Viṣṇu.

The night is of equal duration; thus, those designated as the hundred Viṣṇus and the hundred Rudras perish in succession at the end of their respective hundreds, due to the dissolution of the cosmic egg (aṇḍalopa).
In this manner, there is a sequence of one hundred years for each [cycle] ending with the principles from Water up to the Unmanifest (avyakta-tattva).

The division of day and night occurs according to the measure of one hundred years of their respective lifespans. By six thousand three hundred (3,600) such cycles of Brahmā’s dissolution and manifestation, there is a single day for the Rudras residing in the Unmanifest (avyakta), and their night is of equal duration.
At that time, Śrīkaṇṭha himself becomes the manifest Lord who performs the act of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Likewise, all the Rudras at the root [of the universe] are the presiding authorities within the womb of Māyā. Indeed, from the unmanifest (avyakta) up to Viriñca, they abide together with Śrīkaṇṭha.

For when his lower karma has ceased, Brahmā is situated there at the base of the intellect; he is neither an enjoyer nor a knower. But once his term of office has indeed expired, he becomes Śiva. This is the intermediate dissolution (avāntaralaya); when it is exhausted, emanation is said to occur.

At the dawn of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha emits those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, the Vedas, and other systems; therefore, such liberation is not truly final. A hundred years born from what constitutes a day and night for Pradhāna is a single day for the Lord.
This is the lifespan of Śrīkaṇṭha, and it constitutes one day for those who dwell within the Kañcukas.
In that sequence, Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā—these go into mutual dissolution; their lifespan is one day of Gahana.
At the end of that day, the universe dissolves into Māyā;
when the night of equal duration has ended, Gahaneśa creates it once again.
Thus, one should calculate the time of the unmanifest as ten *parārdhas*.
A night consisting of as many *māyās* as there are hands (twenty-four) constitutes that dissolution (*pralaya*).
Having multiplied the duration of *māyā* by a hundred *parārdhas*, that is the day of Īśvara; there, Nāda, whose nature is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), emits the universe.
The night of Īśvara is of the same duration, during which the vital breath (prāṇa) comes to rest.

Here, even the entire universe situated within the womb of the vital breath [dissolves] by way of the suṣumnā path. When the vital breath has been stilled in the aperture of Brahman (brahmabila), consciousness alone remains.
Even from this [division], there is a dissolution that is increasingly subtle through its successive parts. By multiplying the time of Īśvara by a hundred *parārdhas*,
one obtains a day and night of Sadāśiva, which is indeed the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

At the end of his own time, Sadāśiva, having seized the moving and the unmoving, ascends through the Bindu, the Half-moon, and the Nirodhikā, and dissolves into the Nāda. Then, by means of the function of the End of Sound (Nādānta), the Nāda forcibly pierces the aperture of Brahmā (Brahmabila).
At the exhaustion of its own time, it goes to dissolution within the principle of Power (śaktitattva).
Indeed, this much is to be known regarding the day and night within the principle of Power;
then, when its own time has dissolved, Power dissolves again into the Pervasive One (vyāpinī).
That [time] of Vyāpinī dissolves into Anāśrita during that day and night;
even when the time of Śakti is multiplied by ten million parārdhas, it dissolves into Anāśrita.
In that time of Anāśrita, there is likewise day and night, even when multiplied by a parārdha.

That [dissolution] also goes to rest in the state called Equilibrium (sāmya), which is beyond the mind (sāmanasa). That time known as Equilibrium is eternal, incapable of decay, and composed of parts.
That form which is beyond the mind is that all-pervading Brahman known as Equilibrium.
Therefore, from that very time which is accompanied by the mind, through a mere opening and closing of the eyes,

she alone produces here the sequence beginning with the *tuṭi* and ending with the *parārdha*. Ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand (*ayuta*), hundred-thousand (*lakṣa*), million (*niyuta*), ten-million (*koṭi*), hundred-million (*arbuda*), and billion (*vṛnda*).
From *kharva* to *nikharva*, then *śaṅkha*, *abja*, *jaladhi*, *madhya*, *anta*, and finally *parārdha*;
having calculated tenfold increments in sequence starting from one,
one should state the positions among these eighteen places, beginning with one and ending with *parārdha*.

These four are the primary dissolutions and their corresponding creations; they reside in Bhūmi, Mūla, Aiśa, and Śakti, and constitute the fourfold cosmic egg (aṇḍa). Kālāgni is the destroyer on the level of Earth, while the Lord of the Time-principle (kālatattva) resides at the end of Māyā.
Śrīkaṇṭha is the single root who effects both emanation and withdrawal. His absorption occurs within that [state]; therefore, he alone is the Lord of emanation and withdrawal.
The illustrious Aghora, at the end of Śakti, is both the destroyer and the creator.

Since within its emanation are included countless creations and dissolutions of worlds, the Great Emanation belonging to Śakti is thus proclaimed. At the time of dissolution, Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, and the five groups of eight [Rudras] [are withdrawn].
Thus, they proceed in succession to mutual dissolution on the path ending with Māyā. Upon the dissolution of the principle of Māyā (māyātattva), however, these reach the supreme state;
for those who abide on the white path above Māyā, their dissolution occurs in Paraśiva.
Even there, others recognize a distinction in dissolution due to the difference caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Thus, when the group of Tattvas and Īśvaras has dissolved, those who are established in that state— either as seekers of that [liberation] or as beloved of Śiva— preside over that station once again at the time of creation.

The power called Brāhmī belongs exclusively to another; wherever one might cast it, he becomes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, according to the sequence starting from Vaiṣṇavī and the rest. Does a power ever go to someone other than its possessor? Such a thing does not occur.
Śiva alone is thus the one in whom all powers, whether concealed or manifest, reside;
in this way, emanation and dissolution are established within the single vital breath (prāṇa).
That [breath] also rests in consciousness, and consciousness in pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is devoid of any object of knowledge.

The Goddess is indeed pure consciousness alone; she is the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī). That thirty-eighth principle is the Heart, which is both supreme and non-supreme. By that, this very state of consciousness vibrates by its own nature.
The statement that "dissolution and emergence [occur] within the vital breath" is a description of the emergence of sixty years;
this investigation into the variety of actions is established solely upon the will.
Therefore, time is a power external [to consciousness], and its form is not fixed.
In a dream within a dream, likewise in a dream during sleep, within the sphere of mental construction,
in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and in the discernment of the sequence of the emanation and withdrawal of the universe—
even a limited portion of time indeed appears as something vast.
Whether there is non-difference or difference of the subject, this [time], assuming various forms and attaining expansion,
arises from the power of the diversity of action in the vital breath (prāṇa). Just as time is thus [manifested] in the prāṇa,
so too it is in the apāna, which flows from the heart to the root-seat (mūlapīṭha).

In the contraction and expansion of the great seat (mahāpīṭha) called Mūla, this apāna constantly carries out the creation and withdrawal of all things from Brahmā up to Anāśrita; yet, although it flows in this manner perpetually, it is as follows: [186–187]
That which is beyond objects of knowledge and effort is worshipped with effort by yogins;
reaching from the heart-lotus, the bliss, the contraction and expansion, up to the end of the twelve [fingers],
Brahmā and the others, ending with Anāśrita, are served here by excellent yogins.
And these, because they are the powers of the Supreme Lord, exist throughout the universe;
as stated in the Kāmika [Tantra], even while pervading the body, they are its causes during childhood,
youth, old age, death, and rebirth.
Upon liberation from the body, Brahmā and the others act as the presiding deities over the six locations;
but at its end lies the Supreme Goddess, united with whom one is not born again.
Merely by knowing this, one becomes capable of bestowing initiation and grace.
When the state of the manifestation of all causes is well understood,
one finds Śiva, who is himself causeless yet the cause of the universe;
this indeed is the downward-facing [power], which utterly destroys the stain of duality.
Through the practice of that [state], the ostentation of the upper and lower [breaths] is destroyed.
Here, at the rising of the apāna, one should apply the calculation of the arising of the sixty-year cycle as before,
extending from the *tuṭi* onwards according to the appropriate division of finger-breadths.
Even though the procedure is thus the same, it indeed pertains to the channels within the heart (hārdī-nāḍī).
Moving in all directions, it is perceived as tenfold;
filling the ten principal great channels (mahānāḍī) and those situated therein.
Moving through the channels that rest within other channels, he maintains equilibrium within the body;
traversing the eight petals of the directions in succession,
this [deity] manifests as both fierce and gentle, imitating the activities of the respective lords of those directions.
That very [prāṇa] moves and remains day and night within the three principal channels— situated on the left, right, and middle—
which consist of the moon, sun, and fire;
it stays for two and a half nāḍīs, which consists of nine hundred breaths.
Carrying [the breath] for a day and night, he should move it twenty-four times;
on the day of the equinox (viṣuvat), at dawn, being situated in the middle, he moves through one *nālī* with its parts.
Through the left, the other [right], the north, and the south, he proceeds until the five transits (*saṃkrānti*).
Thus, when thirteen and three-quarter *nāḍīs* have elapsed,

at midday, one should carry the nine hundred breaths of the southern equinox (*dakṣaviṣuvat*). Then, with the southern, northern, other [northern], northern, and southern [flows], there is again a fivefold transit (*saṃkrānti*).
Thereafter, following the equinox, there is one hundred and nine [breaths] for each [period].
When five groups of five have passed outside the equinox,
just as it is so within, that transition consists of nine hundred breaths.

In this same way, it is also during the night; thus, starting from the equinoctial day, this [movement] proceeds through the increase and decrease of day and night, as well as the transits (saṅkrānti). The end of the night and the beginning of the day, as well as midday, mark the waning of the day.
That [moment] when the night has passed and it is midday is such a *viṣuvat*;
for since the root *viṣ* functions in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and equanimity (*sāmya*) is called pervasion,
that time which deserves this is here declared to be the *viṣuvat*.

The decrease and increase of day and night that occur starting from the equinox (viṣuvat) follow that same sequence for the decrease and increase of day and night during the solar transits (saṃkrānti). In this manner,
there is the conceptualization of two years for the equalized breaths (samānamarutaḥ).
In this state, there is no movement, nor is there any consideration of inhalation and exhalation; yet, even within the single *tuṭi*,
from its beginning up to the scope of sixty years,
the calculation of time— residing in that one extremely subtle movement— is reckoned by the wise.

That which occurs at the junctions of dawn, forenoon, midday, and midnight, and so forth, is indeed to be understood as occurring within the internal transition; that is the primary [time], because it is from that that the fruit arises.
The time associated with the *samāna* breath has been described; now the time associated with the *udāna* is being determined.
Whatever was stated regarding the pervasion of *prāṇa* applies here to *udāna* as well;
its locations are at the nose and the end of the power (*śakti*), namely the cranial aperture (*brahmarandhra*) and the space above it.
Therefore, in this context, *udāna* extends from the heart to the head and further to the end of the twelve.
One should contemplate the entire span of time, from a *tuṭi* up to sixty years;
however, within the pervasive *vyāna*, which is the soul of the universe and devoid of succession,
time exists merely as a form that surges forth in an increasingly subtle manner.
Since emanation, dissolution, maintenance, withdrawal,
and grace proceed sequentially from the time of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the other [vital winds], one should therefore rely upon each respective [state] therein.
Within this movement of the vital breath, there exists the emergence of phonemes, words, and mantras.
It is said to be produced with effort and without effort, subtle and supreme, as well as gross. This single phoneme, whose essence is *nāda*, is undivided from all phonemes;
because its form never sets, it is here called the "unstruck" (*anāhata*).
That indeed is the true being of Bhairava; this is the true being of the Mothers.

She is the Supreme Goddess of the single syllable, in whom the moving and the unmoving are dissolved. Each of the three short vowels [occupies] twelve finger-breadths, and the other [long vowels occupy] the remainder.

"Entry" consists of six syllables that proceed respectively through the paths of the Sun and the Moon. In the initial conjunction of the vowels *i* and *u* with *a*, there are two diphthongs; they know that these are *e* and *o* during entry, while *ai* and *au* constitute the other two.
The neuter vowels are situated at the entrance [of the central channel] and at the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) and the forehead;
the nasal bindu and the visarga are located respectively in the throat and the heart.
The five letters beginning with *ka* are eternally arisen within the first letter.
Thus, within those [letters] possessing their respective positions and colors, that sequence of vowels (sā-ṛṇa-santati) resides.

In the heart, this letter *sa* exists in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being the essence of life. The nasal drop (*bindu*) is the letter *ha*, which stands as the nature of illumination through its character of fulfillment (*pūraṇa*).
This supreme emergence of the phonemes has been described; now their subtle emergence is being stated:
during entry there are sixteen [phonemes], and during emergence there are twelve suns (the vowels), excluding the neuter ones.
These alone constitute the moon and the sun here; the other phonemes are this subtle emergence.

The duration of the thirty-three consonants beginning with *ka* is said to be half a measure (*ardhamātra*). There are five short measures (*mātrā*) and eight long ones; the protracted vowel *lṝ* is three times that [i.e., two and a half measures].
Our Guru has stated that this total consists of eighty-one half-measures.
On account of which the Blessed One proclaimed the mantra of eighty-one syllables;

the Goddess, whose nature is Śiva, is declared to be the Power (Śakti) consisting of eighty-one words. For it is stated in the venerable *Mātaṅga* that Śiva is the very essence of the aggregate of the Dharma.
In that very manner, the Lord, the master of the wheel of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-śakti-cakra*),
is manifested through the reflective awarenesses of the eighty-one gross words.
Therefore, reflective awareness is that by which each single [unit] is brought to completion.
Until then, that state is not said to be liberated, for it is not yet constrained by the rules of nouns and verbs;
rather, it is nourished by the expansive contemplation (*vimarśa*) of the eighty-one words.
This dissolution effected through the measures (*mātrā*) is the gross means (*sthūlopāya*), which is indeed the supreme means (*paropāya*).

In each of the four [fingers], there are nine and nine half-measures (*ardhamātrā*); thus, across thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), there is the emergence of eighty-one quarters (*pada*). When the finger-breadth is divided into nine parts, there are nine such ninth-parts (*navamāṃśaka*).
The Veda is half a *mātrā*, while the other three [vowels] are two, four, and six times that respectively.
Thus, the short vowel occupies two sets of four parts of the finger-measure's intervals;
the long and prolated vowels are respectively double and triple that, and after that, the consonant (*hal*) is half of that.
The letter *kṣa* consists of two and a half *mātrās*, and likewise, there is a *mātrā* within it. When that [half-mātrā] is added, there is a rest of half a *mātrā*;
furthermore, previously, at the half-finger-breadth, there was another half-mātrā by means of the part of the *ari*.
The letter *kṣa* is the self that grasps all conjunctions and is all-pervading;
as the Lord, it partakes in the arising at the junctures of the beginning and end of the emergence of all phonemes.
Thus, within the movement of the thirty-six [phonemes], there is the arising of the letters for the sake of the fruit.

In the case of the cruel and the gentle [consonants], it proceeds in reverse order from *ha* down to the final letter *a*. They know this to be the letter *a* at the heart and the letter *ha* at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
This is the non-dual nature of the "I" (*aham*), which is the repose within the essence of Light.
This single measure of eighty-one [units], through the inseparability of Śiva and Śakti,
circulates by doubling within seventy-two finger-breadths (aṅgula). Thus,
the subtle arising has been described as threefold, while the supreme arising is said to be twofold.
Now, the gross emergence of the phonemes (arṇas), as taught by the Guru, is being described.

During the day, the emergence of the eight groups of consonants occurs for one half-watch (ardhaprahara) each; and during the night as well. Regarding this [emergence], some say there is decrease and increase, but others say there is none at all.
This is the arising of the groups (*vargodaya*), occurring both by night and by day, at the interval of half a watch (*ardhayāma*).
That [total] consists of thirteen hundred and fifty breaths;
indeed, there is one and a half transits (*saṃkrānti*) for each group during the day and night.

In that unity, the rising [of breath] consists of twenty-seven hundred movements (cāras). For those who assert nine groups (vargas), their own hundred breaths [are divided such that] a transition (saṃkrānti) of one hundred and thirty-three breaths is said to occur for each individual group.
In the unity of day and night, however, the two eyes of the Veda consist of one hundred [breaths];
this is the gross arising of the classes (varga), which is now called the arising of the phonemes (arṇa).
In each individual phoneme, there are two hundred and sixteen breaths.
Externally, there are thirty-six cups during the day, and likewise at night.

Therein, one hundred and eight [verses] are dedicated to Rudra, and thereafter those to Śakti. In the yoga of the state of union (yāmala), however, there is the non-differentiation of Rudra and Śakti.
When there is no distinction between day and night,
the external emergence of the phonemes (varṇodaya) is said to consist of the movement of four [units]— two, three, four, and five— plus a fifth part of a nāḍī.
Thus has this fifty-fold analysis of the phonemes been discussed.

We shall now explain the doctrine of those who say that it is one less [than the full number]. Each of the Vedas is a *cāra* (movement), and each is reduced by a fifth part, with half of a *cāra* further subtracted for each.
This is added to the phoneme (*varṇa*), and it is doubled when there is no division between day and night.
This gross emergence of the phonemes has been described; now the subtle [emergence] is being declared.
Thus, the reality of Time (kālatattva), established through the scriptures, oral instruction, and personal experience, has been expounded.
Now, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Now, this supreme secret—the arising of the wheels—is being declared. Thus, that which is born without effort has been explained; now, that which is born of effort is being described.
Everything, consisting of seed-syllables and clusters, possesses the nature of the vibration of consciousness.
It has been described as the means (*upāya*) for bringing about the consciousness of another;

just as the movement of a multitude of water-lifting buckets at the front of a waterwheel occurs through the effort of a single continuous connection, so too one should experience the wondrous emergence of the *yantra* through the effort of a single unifying intent.

When the arising of the mantra occurs incessantly through the power of single-pointed concentration, the deity of that mantra becomes pleased through diligent effort by virtue of identity with it. [This occurs] in the sky at the "taste-eye" (26) when it is eternally arisen; half of that [occurs] in the "dual-cluster" (2).
In the case of three syllables, the arising is considered to be seven thousand two hundred;
in the case of four, it is five thousand four hundred;
and in the case of five syllables, it is four thousand three hundred and twenty.
In the group of six, the rising [of breath] consists of three thousand and six hundred;
in the group of seven, it is recorded as three thousand and eighty-six,
along with twenty-seven hundred in the case of the eightfold division of phonemes.
In the case of the nine-syllable mantra, the emergence occurs at twenty-four hundred [breaths];
in the ten-syllable mantra, at one thousand two hundred and sixty-one;
and in the eleven-syllable mantra, at one thousand eight hundred and sixty-four.
In a twelve-syllable mantra, there would be one thousand eight hundred [breaths] for its rising;
in a thirteen-syllable mantra, it is said to be sixteen hundred and sixty-two;
and in a fifteen-syllable mantra, which is the measure of the worlds, it is fifteen hundred and forty-three.
In a fifteen-syllable mantra, there are one thousand four hundred and forty;
in a sixteen-syllable mantra, it is said to be one thousand three hundred and fifty;
and in a seventeen-syllable mantra, it is one thousand two hundred and seventy-one.
In the case of the eighteen-syllable [mantra], twelve hundred [pulses] are to be known by the wise.
In the wheel numbering twenty-four, there are nine hundred;
but when the number is twenty-seven, the arising consists of eight hundred.
In the great wheel of thirty-two [spokes], there are six hundred and seventy-five [breaths];
in the wheels of twenty-four and forty-eight [spokes], there are four hundred and fifty.
One who knows the yoga of the aggregate should observe the emergence [of breath] within the aggregate mantras.
In the wheel of fifty-four [spokes], there are four hundred;
in the one of thirty-eight, there are three hundred and thirty-seven and a half;
and in the one of sixty-six, there are two hundred and sixty-six and a half.
In the wheel of eighty-one squares, the arising occurs through the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
In the wheel known as the ninety-six, there would be two hundred and one and a quarter [breaths].
In the wheel of one hundred and eight, the arising would be two hundred.
When this wheel has been doubled six times in this manner in succession,
and when it is doubled again from that point,
then— by those skilled in the subtle— one may calculate by means of half-parts, half-and-a-half, or single units. (AbhT 7.19b–20)
By remaining in the sixteenth part, the subtle movement [of the breath] becomes perceptible;
thus, for the yogi whose movement of the vital breath has been restrained through effort,
the gradual swallowing of the movement of the breath arises.
Having attained the state of Kālasaṃkarṣaṇa through the process of swallowing the vital breath (prāṇagrāsa),
consciousness alone remains full, as all distinctions of knowledge have been removed;
for it is thus when the new movement of the vital breath has not yet arisen.
A distinction in cognition produced by a distinction in time cannot be postulated;
cognition is not divided merely because of a division in the objects of perception, just as [the sound of] a mountain peak [remains one despite its various aspects].
Time, however, is the differentiator of that [cognition], and it is considered to be subtle, consisting of moments (kṣaṇa).

The limit of subtlety is that moment during which cognition persists; otherwise, it cannot be defined even by the most skillful. To whatever extent cognition exists, to that same extent its absence does not manifest.

And that absence [of perception] lasts for us as long as there is no conjunction or disjunction within the path of the senses, or with respect to the object, or within the region of the self. If that [perception], consisting of vibration, arises, it is certainly inherent in the vital breath.
Therefore, it would indeed exist; however, in the absence of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it would not exist.

Yet, the absence of consciousness does not follow from that [absence of vibration], for that very thing is itself the intellect (*dhī*). And in reality, this [intellect] is not long, because all distinctions of time are excluded.
For this very reason, in reality, this consciousness does not touch time;
therefore, consciousness is one alone, appearing in various forms in such and such ways.
Even though it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), it becomes conceptualization (*vikalpa*) within the sphere of objective existence as it perceives them.
As long as another vibration has not arisen, for that duration alone it exists;
for that long, it constitutes a single conceptual construction (vikalpa) imagining various objects.
However, for those who do not understand it in this way, conceptual construction is not logically possible.
Indeed, there could never be anyone at all in the three worlds who is not [conditioned] by that;
for it is said that cognition colored by words is indeed conceptual construction (vikalpa).
And since that [coloration] would necessarily be sequential, what, how, and who could construct anything?
Even the conceptual construction "this is a jar" would not exist as such; what then can be said of its persistence?
(34) There is no conceptual construction whatsoever that is established upon mere phonemes, nor is there a collection of cognitions, because they do not exist simultaneously. (35)
Therefore, this conventional discourse born of conceptualization has indeed set;
thus, until another vibration arises, one should remain as a single unity.
That consciousness may even touch upon millions of dharmas whose nature is conceptualization.

Therefore, conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), which consists of the reflective awareness of the noble power of the eighty-one words, bestows the state of Śiva; this has already been explained previously. Just as [the thought] "I am making my ears dance" comes to pass through effort, so it is in this case.
Just as the movement of the wheel proceeds effortlessly, so too does the intellect [move] within that wheel;

therefore, the ritual procedure for recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, consists in the equalization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). In the *Siddhāmata*, the power of Kuṇḍalinī is the *unmanā* state, which is identical to the vital breath.
And this has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the Yoginīkaula:

"Having established the division pertaining to the principle of Śakti within the words, mantras, syllables, and the wheel, the knower of mantras shall partake in the fruit when beginning the recitation and other rites. (AbhT 7.40b–41)

One should eliminate the rising of the hundred [syllables] according to the count of two, three, seven, or eight; thus, O Dear One, the mantras or vidyās that abide in Śakti, which are the leaders of the wheels,
should always be applied after knowing them in their form as words and clusters.
When the Great Reality (mahātattva) is eternally risen and Sadāśiva is established in that rising,

those [mantras] which are not joined to the path of power (śaktimārga) and are not recited with that rising do not achieve success, even if they are recited with effort hundreds of millions of times. (43–44)

In all *mālāmantras*, mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*) is prescribed, or else whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*), according to one's capacity; one should not otherwise calculate their [efficacy]. In all *padamantras*, [recitation should continue] as far as the power of that specific word extends.
Practitioners who are constantly disciplined should perform the recitation (japa) for that long;

indeed, the number of those [syllables] is designated as "padas" within those [mantras]. Having produced that many [recitations], one proceeds in sequence from the utterance of three *padas* at the beginning.
In the wheel called the "Twelve," when divided by twelve, there would be one hundred and fifty;
for its emergence is indeed one hundred and forty-four.
In the wheel called the "Sixteen," when divided by twelve, there are one hundred and ninety-two.
It is taught that half the cycle is equal to one hundred and twelve [breaths].
In the [system] called the sixteen-fold, when divided by sixteen, it results in eighty-four;
that sunrise indeed consists of two hundred and fifty-six.
The wise declare that here there are three additional eighth-parts of the movement;
in the case of the twelvefold [cycle] of eight eights, there are twenty-eight quarters and half-quarters,
because that [movement] consists of seven hundred and sixty-eight [units].
This arising of the wheel (cakrodaya), which brings benefit to practitioners, has been declared. Having restrained the mental fluctuations and attained rest within the wheel,
this arising of the movement (cārodaya) lasts as long as one remains active before returning to rest.
When the aggregate is complete, there are three [phases]: entry, identity, and exit; for this very reason, it is said that for the sake of accomplishment, the central emergence is superior.
Those [mantras] which are free from initial and final emergence and joined with the central emergence [attain success].
Indeed, the hosts of mantra-cakras and vidyā-cakras become partakers of accomplishment (siddhi).
One who knows the arising of the mantra-cakra and understands the meaning of the arising of the vidyā-cakra will attain accomplishment quickly; so it is declared in the venerable *Dviṃśatikatrika*.

One should always recite the Vidyā or the Cakra itself, joined with the emergence of the principles (tattvas), either twice, thrice, or four times according to the measures (mātrās), keeping it distinct at all times. One should recite each mantra— whether as a cluster (piṇḍa), a syllable (akṣara), or a word (pada)— as residing within the principle of Śakti.
But for a mantra, a vidyā, or a cycle (cakra) that consists of many syllables, it does not reside within the Śakti; rather, in that case, the division [of the day] is bounded by *oṃ* and *namaḥ*.
Therefore, in this emergence of the principles (tattvas), the day and night are divided thirtyfold each.
It is divided again into groups of thirty-three.
When, having rested during the first emergence, one should rise with the second,
and enter through the union of half-and-half, then that which was taught as the "half-emergence" occurs.
When the time that consists of the full emergence is equalized, it vibrates through the triad [of states].
Then, during the entry, the resting, and the rising, there occurs the emergence of its own three parts.
Thus, this manifestation of time is established in the vital breath alone.

It resides in the drop (bindu), in space (kha), and in that consciousness (citi); therefore, the entire universe is established within it. Consequently, since the dissolution and emergence of the universe both rest upon consciousness, the reality of its countless vibrations exists along the path ending at Śakti.

It is stated in the *Śrīmālinītantra*: "In whichever part of the body a transformation may arise, that is the *tattva*, the supreme *tattva*. Time is established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the body is permeated by it. (7.64b–65)
Therefore, the form of this [Self] established within the body is now described:
that which is the ultimate grossness of the movements of consciousness and the vital breath,
appearing as a cavity, assumes the form of the channels (nāḍīs) and extends throughout this body.
For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable Svacchanda Tantra:
"Just as a leaf is pervaded by its own fibers, so too is the body pervaded by the channels (nāḍīs) through the relationship of gates and gatekeepers;
[this pervasion] extends from the big toe of the foot up to the Brahmakuṇḍalikā situated at the top."
The entire duration of time is contained within eighty-four finger-breadths;
the wise know that the state of extremely subtle time extends up to the *dvādaśānta*.
In the ninety-six [finger-breadths], by moving down six twice, there are one hundred and eight.
Here, within the interval between the emergence and dissolution of the breath moving through the middle [channel],
all these diverse creations and dissolutions occur according to the sequence of the internal movement of the vital air (vāyu).
Thus, I have described this arising of the wheels (cakrodaya), which is to be cultivated through subtle contemplation, according to the perspective of both direct experience and the scriptures.
Now, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, the eighth daily lesson (*āhnika*):

This procedure for the path of space (*deśādhvan*), as seen in the scriptures of Śiva, is proclaimed through both summary and expansion. This path of time (*kālādhvan*), consisting of the Lord’s power of action (*kriyāśakti*), has been investigated.
The path of space (*deśādhvan*), which arises from the diversity of forms and is born therefrom, is now described.
This entire path is established within pure consciousness alone;
for that which does not find rest therein is like a flower in the sky.

Through the gateway of consciousness, the establishment of the paths (adhvan) occurs within that which is emitted [from it]: in the void, in the intellect, in the vital breaths, in the channels, the wheels, and the sub-wheels, as well as outside the body.
In this regard, the path must be investigated in this manner, because its sequence of manifestation follows that [very process].
While thus maintaining this continuity, the yogi swiftly attains the state of Bhairava.
When he remains pervading all objects merely through the desire to see them, then what need is there for much talk? Thus it is stated in the Spanda teachings.
Having known the entire path, one should dissolve it into its respective lords;
those [lords], in turn, one should gradually dissolve into the wheels of the body, breath, and intellect as before.
All that [is dissolved] into one's own self-awareness, and that awareness is of a nature filled with plenitude.
When worshipped, she is the fire of dissolution for the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
In the *Śrīmahīkṣottara*, the Guru spoke of these Lords of the Path:
from Brahmā down to Ananta is the extent of *pradhāna*; Viṣṇu extends from the individual soul (*puruṣa*) down to *kalā*.
Rudra resides in the knot and in Māyā; Īśa resides in the sphere of Sādākhya;
Anāśrita Śiva resides beyond that; and the Supreme is the pervader of all those.
Thinking that [the Self] has thus attained the state of Śiva, it was described in this way.
"In the *Svacchanda-śāsana*, it is said: 'There is no knowledge superior to the creative process (*prakriyā*).
In the *Triśiraḥ-śāsana*, consciousness is conceived as having a root, a middle, and a tip;
the unfolding of the thirty-six principles is memory, which is the conceptualization of duality."
The state of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), whose divisions are unimpeded, is the root that leads to awakening.
This state, which consists of all the *tattvas*, is undivided within its own self.
Within the midst of awakening, there may be something characterized as the relationship between support and supported.
Through the differentiation of the divisions of the principles (tattva), it is characterized by abiding in its own essential nature.
That supreme awakening is indeed pure consciousness, waveless and vast bliss;
it is that in which the past, future, cities, and all else have been brought into the singular essence of pure awareness.
Bhairava, the Supreme Lord, is uninterrupted consciousness.
And it is stated in the venerable *Devīyāmala*, which is beautiful with its thirty-six principles:
"By meditating upon the sixfold path, one becomes identical with Śiva instantly. (8.16–17)
Although for this Lord— who is non-different from pure consciousness and is perfect—
there exists no real distinction of top, middle, or end; nevertheless,
[such a distinction is made] for the sake of those who seek to understand, as well as for the teacher.

The conceptualizations of being "middle," "beginning," and so forth, follow one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, they know the earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*) to be that which, though situated within the interior of all things, is enclosed by all the coverings (*āvaraṇa*), due to the restrictive power of the subject’s volition (*pramātṛ-saṃkalpa*). (AbhT 8.19–20a)
Now, the arrangement of the worlds within this earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) is described.
Ananta is the leader of the Kaṭāha Rudras who indulge in their desires;
mounted upon the boat, he is reeling from drinking wine within the waters.
Meditating upon the god Bhairava and surrounded by serpents,
he beholds the world of Kālāgni above, which rises for ten million *yojanas*;
yet, out of fear that the worlds might be reduced to ashes, he does not look further upward.

And although it pervades the entire universe, because it scorches this earth, it was manifested prior to the hells; therefore, it is considered to be beneath them. The flame of the All-pervasive Lord extends for one hundred million [yojanas], and half of that above is empty space.
Above that are the lords of the hells, who experience exclusively suffering in succession;
situated below, in the middle, and above, they are surrounded by various subdivisions.
Among them, in order, are those known as Avīci, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava.
Eleven, eleven, and ten; thus it ends with five and three (53).

Of each of these, the height is one less than ten million (9,999,999), while the distance between them is one hundred thousand (100,000) yojanas, according to the calculation of zero, sky, Vedas, and mouths (4000).
Kūṣmāṇḍa is situated above, at the level of one hundred thousand lakṣas and ten million koṭis; he is the lord of that place.
Those who perform black deeds by acting in opposition to the scriptures are tormented there by fearsome world-guardians until the exhaustion of their [karmic] experience.

Those who, even once, go for refuge to the Supreme Lord Śiva with a one-pointed mind, do not become joined with hell; for them, Kṛṣṇa bestows only a small measure of suffering. Furthermore, [the hells] increase by nine thousand in height, each separated from the next by a single interval.

In each of the eight netherworlds (pātāla), there is a single lord; in the eighth is Hāṭaka. Śrīkaṇṭha, whose self is appointed over every world, forcibly bestows many supernatural powers (siddhis) in this manner, according to the teaching of the venerable Raurava.
Those who observe vows but remain engaged in improper actions, those who perform forbidden conduct;

those who, though initiated, have violated their commitments (*samaya*) and do not perform the required penances (*prāyaścitta*); and those established therein who revile the Vāmācāra—[these are the ones excluded].
Those who live on the portions of wealth belonging to the gods, fire, or [their] property, and who abide in the highest state,
yet are devoted to the service of other mantras such as those of Gāruḍa and others situated below—
these various types of servants stand before the Lord Hāṭaka.

But if they, even there, worship the Lord of Gods with devotion, they dissolve into the principle of Īśvara and, in due course, into the supreme Śiva. However, those who behave otherwise, whose natures are intent upon the enjoyment of that [world], [remain bound].
Distressed by the torment of the fire of time and intent on piteous lamentation, they dissolve into the principle of Guṇatattva; then, at the beginning of creation,
they are cast down again by the Mātṛs, preceded by a flood of terrible torments.
In bodies that are most base, according to their own past actions,
among those ending with the human state, some there— being knowers of mantra—
are gradually liberated, while others are bound, in accordance with their prior deeds.
Thus, this account of the Gaṇas, beginning with the name Hulahula,
was proclaimed by the Blessed One in the venerable *Ānandādhikaśāsana*.
Above Pātāla, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas], lies the skull-bowl of the earth (*bhūkaṭāhaka*).
But in the Siddhātantra, [the region] on the surface of the netherworld (pātāla) is surrounded by Yakṣīs;
there lies the city of Bhadrakālī, where practitioners sport with them.
Beyond that is the Taptabhūmi, then the Void, and then the Ahi world.
These are the places of torment for those who revile their guru, the mantras, and so forth.

Above that earth, in the middle, is Mount Meru; it is sixteen thousand [yojanas] high. It is submerged [in the water] to that same depth, and its width at the base is twice that, while its width at the top is half of that.
The golden abode of all the immortals rises to a height of one thousand, four, and eight [yojanas].
Its middle, upper, and lower parts are respectively curved like an arrowhead, circular, and square;
that is the Liṅga of Bhairava, and the earth is its pedestal.
Indeed, all the gods are dissolved therein; it is always worshipped there.
In its center is the Meru assembly-hall, and in the direction of its lord is the temple.
It is the Jyotiṣka peak of Śambhu, and that Lord is a portion of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Descending fourteen thousand [yojanas] from Manovatī, there is the Cakravāṭa mountain range on the four sides; here, moreover, are the Meru and the world-protectors (lokapālas).

Atsara, Siddha, and Sādhya—these are the Vināyakas to the north of her. Tejovatī is the city of Agni in his own direction; to its west, however, are the Viśvedevas, Viśvakarman, and those who follow them in succession.
To the south is Saṃyamanī; to its west stand, in sequence, Mātṛnandā, Svasaṃkhyātā, Rudra, and likewise their practitioners (sādhakas);
Kṛṣṇāṅgārā, Nirṛti, and to its east, the Piśācas. (AbhT 8.50b–51)
The *rakṣasas*, *siddhas*, and *gandharvas* are situated one after another to the north of it;
to its south are the *vāruṇī*, the region called *śuddhavatī*, and the host of *bhūtas*. To the north of this [city], the *vasus* and *vidyādharas* are situated in succession.
To the south of that [Vāyu] is Gandhavatī; there, moreover, are the Kinnaras.
The goddess Sarasvatī with her lute, as well as Nārada and Tumburu, and Mahodaya, Indu, and Guhya—these are to be found again and again on its western side.
Kubera, the Karmadevas, and likewise their practitioners;
Yaśasvinī of Maheśa, and to her west is Hari (55). To the south, further south, are Brahmā, the Aśvins, and Dhanvantari in sequence.
In this Mairava Cakravāṭa, there are thus eight principal cities;
furthermore, twenty-six others are recorded as being situated in between.
Men who are devoted to sacrifices and charitable works in the meritorious land of Bhārata [attain these].
Those who go to Meru and worship Śambhu there even once, or in the manner prescribed; and the supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvata) of Meru, which circle it clockwise toward the north—
namely Mandara, Gandhamādana, Vipula, and Supārśvaka— [are likewise situated].
Those foothills of Meru are white, yellow, blue, and red, respectively.
Supported by these, Mount Meru stands immovable.
They say the forests are Caitraratha, Nandana, Vaibhrāja, and Pitṛvana.
The four lakes are Raktoda, Mānasa, Sita, and Bhadra;
and the trees upon them, in order, are the Kadamba, Jambu, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha.
On these four mountains, three [trees] each are traditionally taught in sequence.
Jambudvīpa extends all around Meru down to the salt ocean;
it measures one hundred thousand [yojanas] and is divided into nine parts by boundary mountains.
To the south are three: Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat.
One hundred thousand, ninety thousand, and eighty thousand [yojanas] respectively;
Nīla, Śveta, and Triśṛṅga are likewise on the left side of Meru. These six boundary mountains extend from east to west.
To the east is Mālyavat, and to the west is the one known as Gandhamādana. These two extend from south to north for thirty-four thousand [yojanas].
Beyond these eight, there are two more pairs in the directions starting from the east, in sequence.
Jāṭhara, Kūṭa, Himavat, Yātra, Jārudhi, and Śṛṅgin—
thus is the division established here, described for the sake of determining the regions (varṣas).
Beneath the circular mountain range (cakravāṭa), it is square and devoid of sun and moon.

It is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent and is called Ilāvṛta; the lifespan there is three *mukhas*. To the west of Meru is Gandhamādana; to the west of that is Ketumāla, adorned by seven principal mountain ranges.
To the east of Meru is Mālyavat; to the east of that is Bhadrāśva.
There, the lifespan is ten thousand years, and it contains five principal mountain ranges.
These [ranges] extend respectively from east to west and from south to north.
It is determined that there are thirty-two and thirty-four thousand [yojanas]. To the north of Meru is Śṛṅgavān; beyond that is the region of Kuruvarṣa.
It is shaped like a bow, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, and the lifespan there is thirteen [thousand years].

To the north of Kuruvarṣa, in the northwestern ocean, there are five thousand islands in sequence, and then ten thousand; these are the two islands, Candra and Bhadraka. To the left of Meru are the Śveta and Śṛṅgin mountains, and in the middle is the golden [mountain].
The extent of those two is nine [yojanas], and their lifespan is twelve and a half.
There, indeed, to the left of Śveta and Nīla, is Ramyaka;
its extent is nine thousand [yojanas], and the lifespan there is twelve [thousand years].
To the south of Meru, between the two [mountains] Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha,
lies the region called Hari, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, where the lifespan is one thousand years greater than that.
In that very same southern region, between the pair consisting of Hema and Himavat, [lies the next land].
Kinnara is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, and its lifespan is one thousand years more than that. Right there, to the south of Meru, lies Himavat;
to the south of which is Bhārata, nine thousand [yojanas], shaped like a bow, a land for the experience of the fruits of karma.
Ilāvṛta, Ketumāla, Bhadrāśva, Kuru, Hiraṇmaya, and Ramyaka,
as well as the regions of Hari and Kiṃnara, are lands of enjoyment (bhogabhū) and not lands of action (karmabhū).
Although these are primarily lands of action, even here there exist those who do not perform [ritual] actions.

For animals, there may be a purification through ritual action (*karmasaṃskāra*) because of such firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Indeed, even in Bhārata and elsewhere, there exist those who lack such purification;
yet, due to firm past impressions and by the will of the Lord, there occurs that which is auspicious or inauspicious.
In other locations as well, ritual action (karman) is observed, and this has been seen in ancient times;
there, the Tretā age prevails eternally, whereas in Bhārata there are the four ages (caturyuga). And in Bhārata, it is divided into nine regions by the waters of the ocean.
The land is five hundred [yojanas], and the water is likewise divided [into five hundred]. 83.
From the ocean [inward], there are Indra, Kaśeru, Tāmrābha, Nāgīya, Gabhastimān in the east, Saumya, Gāndharva, Vārāha, and the one called Kanyā. 84.
And in the ninth [continent], Kanyādvīpa, there are six sub-continents situated in the middle of the southern ocean, adorned by the seven mountain ranges:
Aṅga, Yava, Malaya, Śaṅku, Kumuda, and Varāha; and Agastya is located on Malaya.

And on that very Trikūṭa is Laṅkā; these six are indeed the secondary islands (*upadvīpa*). The inhabitants of these islands and sub-islands are for the most part various kinds of Mlecchas, rich in pearls, gold, and jewels—so it is stated in the venerable *Ruru-śāsana*.
Whatever karma has been performed or exhausted in Bhārata, from the Avīci hell up to Śiva, by that [karma] there is liberation; this is especially so in the place called Kanyā.
Here in Bhārata itself, there are ten million Rudras beginning with Mahākāla.

Because five hundred [lives] on the Gaṅgā and other rivers are required for rebirth here, birth in this place is difficult to obtain (89). In other regions, one merely passes through karma by experiencing it like an animal;
however, for those born in Bhārata, even that which transcends the reach of desire is attainable (90).
Because there is a variety of castes, stages of life, conducts, pleasures,
and pains in Kanyādvīpa, it is for that reason the most excellent land of action (*karmabhūmi*);
for men performing white and black deeds here indeed attain success.
In the *Rauravavārtika*, it is said that heaven and hell are both higher and lower.
Thus, below Mount Meru, Jambūdvīpa— which extends all around—
is divided into seventeen regions in detail, but into nine in brief.

Of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu there were ten sons, and from them three [lines] went forth into the religious life. Now, he who was the king named Agnīdhra in the land called Jambūdvīpa had nine sons; from them this [continent] became divided into nine sections.
The ninth [son] was Nābhi; his grandson was Bharata, the son of Ṛṣabha.
He had eight sons, and with a daughter as the ninth, the land was divided into nine parts by them.
From that [original territory], which measured one hundred thousand yojanas, it was enjoyed by them in nine portions.
The salt ocean is one hundred thousand *lakṣas* in measure, and outside of it are its mountains in the east:
Ṛṣabha, Dundubhi, Dhūmra, Kaṅka, Droṇa, and Indu;
in the north are Varāha, Nandana, and Aśoka; and in the west are Sahasrabalāhaka and [the rest].
The southern wheel is Maināka, and the Vāḍava fire is situated between them.
To the south of the ocean, at a distance exceeding two thousand yojanas, lies the mountain Vidyutvat;
it is three thousand [yojanas] in height and breadth, and here dwell those who subsist on fruits.
Stained with filth, with long hair and beards, and possessing the nature of cattle,
they are naked, live for eighty years, and subsist on grass.
For the sake of attaining the subterranean cave (*bila*), the gates there must always be left unfastened.
This very point has been sung by the Gurus in the illustrious Raurava Śāsana.
Thus, this Salt Ocean which has been described—
outside of that are these six islands, each surrounded by its own ocean.

The six continents, each double the size of the preceding one, are presided over by six sons of Manu: Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomeda, and Abja. There are six oceans consisting of milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, wine, and sweet water.
Medhātithi, Vapuṣmat, Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havi, Rājā,

and Saṃvara— these are designated as the Agnīdhras among Śāka and the other continents within Jambudvīpa. Furthermore, the five continents beginning with Śāka are each divided into seven sections by seven mountain ranges.
The one named Puṣkara consists of two petals; here, starting from the east, are Hari, Yama, Varuṇa, and Indu.

Its measurement in yojanas, from the summit of Meru downwards, is fifty-three lakhs, twenty million, and fifty thousand (253,200,000). 105–106ab. This is the measure ending with the sweet-colored [ocean]. 106cd.

Beyond the seventh ocean lies the golden land, ten crores and one hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent; the Lokāloka mountain is said to be ten thousand [yojanas] in height and breadth. Situated in the eight directions of the Lokāloka are the eight Rudras together with the world-protectors (lokeśas).
Some say that the sun exists only within the Lokāloka mountain and not outside it.

They describe the two paths of the ancestors and the gods, which lie to its north and south, as the two tracks belonging to its own nature; they call these very paths the sun’s northern and southern solstices.
"For all [worlds], Meru is to the north and Lokāloka is to the south.
(AbhT 8.110a) One should thus contemplate the rising and setting of the sun:
midnight occurs in Amarāvatī, and sunset in the city of Yama. (AbhT 8.111a)
Midday occurs in Vāruṇī, while sunrise is traditionally held to be in Saumya.
That which is sunrise in Amarāvatī is midnight in Yamālaya;
sunset is in Ke and midday in Saumya—such is the movement of the sun.
Outside the world-mountain, the darkness measures thirty-five crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand [yojanas]. The king of oceans, known as Garbhoda, is equal in extent to the seven seas.
Beyond Lokāloka, within its interior, lies the entire earth.
Here, in the Siddhātantra, on the shore of the ocean of the womb (garbhābdhi), there is a mandala known as Kauśeya; there Garuḍa resides, surrounded by his perfected wings.
They sport upon the mountain peaks, where there are nine principal mountain ranges (*kulādri*).
From there, thirty rivers of hot water flow down into the subterranean realm (*pātāla*).
In the four directions lies the Naimira garden, which is constantly frequented by *yoginīs*.
From that [the wind], Meru; from that, the Nāgas; from that, the clouds; and from that, the golden egg.
With half of Meru's height, the shell of Brahmā’s egg measures fifty million [yojanas] in each of the ten directions; thus, this is known as the Bhūrloka.

This terrestrial world (bhūrloka) is pervaded by six types of beings—domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, trees, humans, and reptiles—as well as by piśācas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and yakṣas; it is also filled with the vidyādharas, and indeed, what need is there to say more? It is filled with the entire creation of living beings.
Through the power of his self-conceit (abhimāna), he obtains whatever place of enjoyment and residence he desires.
Likewise, the Bhuvarloka extends for one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the sun;
within that interval, there are ten paths of the wind, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas].
There, the first path of the wind is described as being spread out;
fifty yojanas above that is the wind named Ṛtarddhi. It nourishes living beings, and beyond that is the Prācetasa wind.
Fifty yojanas above that, and then another hundred yojanas further up,
is the Senānī wind; here dwell the Mūka clouds that release lightning and rain water at a distance of only one krośa from the earth.
Above those, at a distance of one hundred [yojanas], are clouds that rain down living beings such as frogs;
fifty above that, in this region of the Ogha wind, are clouds that rain down poisonous water.
Furthermore, there are other Piśāca clouds arising from the Skanda wind within the Ogha wind.
Beyond that, at a distance of fifty [yojanas], there are clouds known as Mārakas.
In that place dwell those Vināyakas born of Mahādeva,
who carry away the performed karma of men who have not disciplined themselves.
Fifty yojanas above that is Vajrāṅka; here are the winds, stones, and clouds.
It is here, in Vajrāṅka, that the lowest of the Vidyādharas are established—those who are devoted to the power of spells and those who achieve their goals in cremation grounds and similar places.

Those who have died there attain those perfections; established in the wind marked by the vajra, they remain for fifty years above the vajra-mark, raining down lightning and thunderbolts. Here also are the Apsarases and those men who have performed meritorious deeds.
Those who die by falling from a cliff, in fire, or in water, as well as those who do not retreat in battle,
or those killed while recovering stolen cattle or during the release of prisoners— they reside in the Vaidyuta heaven.
From the Vaidyuta heaven to the Āraivata heaven, there are clouds there that carry nourishment and rain.
Above that is Saṃvarta, the cloud that releases disease;
immediately following it is Raivata, where those perfected in the use of yellow pigment, collyrium, ashes, and so forth reside.
Viṣāvarta is the wind-cloud that releases wrathful waters; that is its location.
Fifty years beyond that, in that very place, are the years of stormy weather born of fire;
and there reside the distinguished Vidyādharas who always worship the Supreme Lord with the Gāndharva [song], as well as those situated in the Viṣāvarta.
One hundred *yojanas* above Viṣāvarta is Durjaya, which is the source of the winds;
here reside the clouds that cause the winds at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).
In Parāvaha, there are the Puṣkara clouds, the Vāyuga winds, and the Gandharvas.

The Jīmūtas and Meghas—those known by these names—are the highest among the Vidyādharas; and those worlds who follow the vow of form (rūpavrata) are established in Āvaha. In Mahāvahe, however, are the clouds created by Īśa that bring about the welfare of all beings.
In the Mahāparivaha [wind], the clouds arise from the skull of the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
This path of the winds extends up to the end of the Mahāparivaha, prior to the region of nectar and prosperity (amṛtarddhi).
Therein dwell the daughters of Agni and the Mothers (Mātṛs), presided over by the power of Rudra.
In the second [ring] are the Siddhas and Cāraṇas born of their own karma;
in the third, the eight divine weapons; in the fourth, the elephants of the quarters; and again in the fifth, Garuḍa; in the sixth, the Gaṅgā; and in the other, the all-pervading Bull.
Dakṣa, however, is established by the power of Brahmā in the ninth [sphere].
In the tenth, on the path of the Maruts, are the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas.
The body of the Sun is nine thousand yojanas, as is its orb.

That power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), threefold in nature, blazes as the sun for the Lord. The *svarloka* is defined as extending from the *bhuvarloka* up to the pole star (*dhruva*). At a distance of one hundred thousand leagues from the sun is the moon; that is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of Śiva.

One hundred thousand *yojanas* from the Moon is the Lunar Mansions (*nākṣatra*) circle; from there, at two hundred thousand, they know that each of the five planets—from Mars to Saturn—is situated at an interval of one hundred thousand.
One hundred thousand from Saturn is the group of the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*), and from there, the Pole Star (*dhruva*) is likewise situated at the same distance.
Brahmā himself, in his other form as the immovable Dhruva, resides in the station of Brahmā;
situated above all the celestial chariots, he serves as their central pivot.
All these [chariots], being bound here, are carried along within the sphere of the wind.
There are seven layers of wind, beginning with the clouds and so forth, which constitute the primary [elements].

Furthermore, those devoid of knowledge who perform sacrifices, oblations, and the like, go to heaven; upon the exhaustion of that merit, they return to the human world by virtue of their remaining store of merit.
Thus, from the earth up to the Pole Star (Dhruva), the distance is fifteen lakṣas;
from heaven to Mahāmeru, it is twenty-five crores and eighty-five lakṣas.
There, the sages, seers, and perfected beings, beginning with Mārkaṇḍeya, are established.
The gods, having relinquished their offices, abide in Mahat;
in the intermediate space between that and Mahat, there are other beings who enjoy their respective offices.
From Mahaloka, eight crores [of yojanas] away, lies Janaloka, where Kapila and others reside.

Many who are to be perfected (sādhya) dwell right there, partaking in happiness; here, tens of millions of people such as Sanaka and others of great intelligence reside. Therein lies the authority of the Prajāpatis, those born from the self of Brahmā.

The abode of Brahmā, however, is Satya, which measures sixteen crores [of yojanas]. Residing there, that Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) manifests this universe. In Satya, the Vedas as well as other [scriptures] exist, cultivated through ritual action and meditation.
Above that, where bliss reaches its culmination, is the seat of Brahmā (Vairiñca), the single peak. Two crores [of yojanas] from the seat of Brahmā, the city of Viṣṇu is described;
through meditation, worship, and recitation, the devotees of Viṣṇu go to that station.

From the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], there are seventy million [deities] belonging to the world of the Supreme Lord. On the path of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), those who are intent on the worship of the *liṅga* but are devoid of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) belong to Rudra, the agent of creation and destruction.
They go to the city of Rudra within the Egg, and never below it.
Residing there, all those Rudras who have been initiated by Śrīkaṇṭha proceed to Śiva when their office has expired,
together with the host of Rudra-maidens.
City after city lies above Rudra, increasing progressively higher and higher;
and below the Egg of Brahmā, above Rudra, is the city of Daṇḍapāṇi. By the will of Śiva, he pierces the Egg and creates the path to liberation.
Śarva, Rudra, Bhīma, Bhava, Ugra,
Mahādeva, and Īśāna— these are the seven auspicious lords of the worlds from the world of Bhūr upwards. Furthermore, the seven higher worlds are composed of gross specific elements (sthūla-viśeṣa).
The Guru has correctly explained in the *Ruru-tantra* that these are "subtle.

Those known as the "Great Elements" (*prabhūta*), which were fashioned from his own body by Brahmā at the beginning of creation—these five gross specificities (*viśeṣa*) and the seven worlds composed of them [are what is meant]. (8.162–163)
Beyond that, by means of subtle *tanmātra*-derived great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as supports for the *liṅga*,
and by the obstructions of the worlds through their mutual [interactions] such as smell and the rest, [the space is filled].
From the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) up to Daṇḍapāṇi, there are ninety-eight *koṭis*.
Above this, within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), is the solid crust (kaṭāha) extending for ten million yojanas.
Fifty crores extend upward from the surface of the earth, and likewise fifty crores downward. Thus, the earth consists of one hundred crores; beyond that is the golden grain (sauvarṇastaṇḍula).

Ending with the Śatarudra mantra and the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, one should pierce that which is difficult to subdue. Ten [mantras] for each direction—thus making one hundred Rudras—are placed on the outside.
And that [array], by its own power, supports the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) in every respect.
The nature of the Egg (aṇḍa) has been described by the teachers in the venerable Raurava and other scriptures:
"That which is oriented toward manifestation, having fallen away from its state as pure power,
being a mass of reality that is undivided and possesses internal differentiation— that is called the Egg."

For that which is permeated by a trace of *tamas*, the *kapāla* is the superior *sattva*; when it is polished and permeated by *rajas*, this *sattva* is the inferior *tamas*. This is called the "mass of substance" (*vastupiṇḍa*), which partakes in the union of Śiva and Śakti.
"The term 'egg' (aṇḍa) refers to the state of manifestation when that [power] becomes manifest. Even so, for those powers submerged in Śiva, there would be the state of being an "egg";
therefore, another statement is made, for they have not fallen away from their power.
To prevent the over-extension [of the argument] that the body, the senses, and so forth might be the "staff" (the instrument), another word is used:
"because there exists no sowing of anything whatsoever within the body, the senses, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the body and the senses constitute a collection, how could there be unity? Therefore, [another term is required].

It is said that "undivided" (anirbhakta) indicates a state of belonging to the same genus (*sājātya*). Even without the word "mass of objects" (*vastupiṇḍa*), it would apply to each individual [element] among the principles (*tattva*). But even so, why would the nature of being an egg (*aṇḍasvabhāvatva*) not belong to them as well? 174–175ab.
It is attached to the reality (tattva) consisting of the flood of the qualities (guṇas), the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the gross elements (bhūtas).
It is called by the word "entity" (vastu), comprising the body, the senses, and the worlds.
Since its form has been described, the aggregate thereof is called an "egg" (aṇḍa).
And there may be a state of being a collection [of those powers] for the Lord who bears the body of the universe;
it has been shown that other differentiating factors have been adopted for that purpose within the circle of the paths dependent on Māyā during those respective states. (AbhT 8.177b–178)
Others say that the application of differentiation [is taught] so that there may not be the state of being a mere egg (aṇḍatva).
Thus, when Viriñca’s egg has perished, there are indeed one hundred Rudras;
of those, the eleven Rudras of great radiance are their own lords.
Then Ananta, Kapālin, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala;
Śīghra, Nidhīśa, Vidyeśa, and Śambhu together with Vīrabhadra—
just as bees surround a kadamba tree with their masses of filaments.

In that same manner, Śiva and Rudras, with innumerable retinues, [reside] within the Egg of Brahmā; their arrangement consists of eight hundred million, ten million, and one crore. Presided over by Śrīkaṇṭha, they create and they destroy.
"The lordship over the gods [is attained] thus," according to the *Rauravavārtika*.
But in the *Siddhātantra*, it is said that outside of the golden egg (*hemāṇḍa*) there are one hundred eggs,
each successively double the size of the last, composed of silver and so forth.

Within those [kalpas], the Brahmās shall exist in succession with lifespans doubled at each stage; they perish in due order, and at their conclusion, the principle of water [dissolves]. Here, starting from earth, the elements such as water and so forth arise in successive order from the one following.
The intellect (dhī) extends tenfold beyond the ego (ahaṅkṛta); from that, it becomes a hundredfold.
From that, the manifest (vyakta) is a thousandfold; the principle of the Person (pauṃsna) is ten thousandfold.
Necessity (niyati) is a hundred thousandfold (lakṣadhā) from that, and its [extension] is ten millionfold (daśalakṣadhā).
From that [Kalā], Māyā extends ten-fold up to the end of Kalā;
Īśvara extends one hundred-fold from that; and Sādākhya extends one thousand-fold from that. And Śakti pervades that [Sādākhya] by means of a multitude of numbers.
The pervasive Goddess is established pervading the entire path.
Therefore, the wise know the supreme Śiva-tattva to be immeasurable and pure.
From the element of water up to the end of the Śiva-tattva, nothing has been seen by anyone apart from Śiva.
Apart from that, there is no supreme knowledge of Śiva, which is the cause of liberation.
Thus Mahādeva has said in the venerable Svacchanda-śāsana:
"A bound soul (paśu) does not attain liberation otherwise, even through hundreds of other types of knowledge."
The knowledge of Śiva does not arise without having received the initiation of Śaṅkara. That [initiation] is again threefold: primordial, supreme, and human.
Above the hundred Rudras is Bhadrakālī; [above her is] the blue-radiant Jayā.
The city of Kālī, Jayapura, cannot be attained through sacrifice, charity, or austerity;
those who are devoted to her and are well-initiated into her maṇḍala go there. By means of initiation without seed (*nirbījadīkṣā*), the Supreme Goddess grants liberation.

To whatever extent one performs initiation for men within the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa), to that same extent do they attain their destination when established in this world. Then, Vīrabhadra, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon, [appears] with ten million [attendants].
And those who, while remembering Maheśvara, die in water, in deserts, in fire, or by decapitation, go to the city called Vijaya,
which belongs to him; they attain the awakening of the Lord, Vīrabhadra of great splendor.
Above Vīrabhadra, the peak extends threefold in width;
the egg of Rudra is watery, situated in the shape of a rainbow.
It extends as far as the world of Vīrabhadra and likewise up to the abode of Bhadrakālī.
It is adorned by thirteen other worlds. Then, from the earth together with its mountains, through the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*),
the wise who have died go to that supreme ground beyond the earth.
Then, from the city of the ocean, there is the city of water through the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*).
After that is the city of Śrī, which occurs especially through death at Prayāga and other such sites, as well as at Śrīgiri during the descents of Rudra’s play.
Beyond that is the city of Sarasvatī, the abode of those who know the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman).
Those [cities] are fit for the Rudras because of their preeminence; likewise, others are situated for the [other] Rudras.
Within these cities, the Gaṅgā exists in many forms, as do Śrī and Sarasvatī among the gods and others.
From Lakula to Amareśa, these eight lords of the gods reside in the waters. Beyond that is the principle of fire (*taijasa-tattva*), wherein Śiva’s fire is established.
Those who have taken recourse to the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on fire proceed toward this very fire.
In the Taijasa [world], there is a group of eight leaders beginning with Bhairava and ending with Hari and Indu.
That world of Prāṇa belongs to Vāyu, and it is tenfold, indeed tenfold.
Having meditated upon this, or having released the vital breaths (prāṇas) after performing concentration (dhāraṇā) right there—
Great-souled ones, having become like the wind and taking on the form of space, enter that [state].
The group of eight worlds beginning with Bhīma and ending with Gaya resides within the element of air.
Having reached the world of space within the element of space, that is attained through the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on space.
From Vastrāpada to Sthāṇu and so forth, there is the group of eight gods in the element of space (vyomatattva).
Those who, though uninitiated among the [lower] elements, possess the conceit of belonging to the Śiva-principle—
even if devoid of knowledge— possess mature concentration (dhāraṇā) and reside outside the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
Those who have been initiated and reside in the cities of Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether,

or even those who die in sacred shrines during such descents of the Lord, do so for the sake of attaining the application of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and not to seek the supreme state. (Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka 8.210b–211b)
Having attained that state, they gradually reach the nature of Śiva.
This has been stated again and again in the venerable *Devīyāmala*,
