and the All-pervasive Lord has also spoken thus in the description of Kashmir in the venerable *Kāmika*.
Those who die in the great abode of Sureśvarī and in her city— beings from the highest caste,
the Brāhmaṇas, down to the mixed castes, and including all animals down to the stationary—
these, the Lord Śiva has declared, are indeed of the nature of Rudras.
O Dear One, above the covering of space and below the ego (ahaṅkāra),

in the teaching of Śiva, are the cities of those beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) and ending with the mind (manas). The great mandala of the subtle element of smell is endowed with five colors.
Covering many tens of millions of *yojanas* and situated in the intermediate space,
the mandalas of the subtle elements beginning with taste exist according to their respective colors:
Śarva, Bhava, Paśupati, Īśa, and Bhīma, in that order.

By his will, the Lords of the subtle elements (tanmātreśas) produce sound and the other [objects], as well as ether and the other [gross elements]. From that arises the Great All-pervasive One; among these [principles] are Ugra and the others as lords, and from them come the Sun and Moon, along with the two sacrificers.

Thus, these eight bodies of Śambhu which have been proclaimed as the supreme (parā) abide pervading everything within the egg of Brahmā; they are the lower (aparā). From them alone, however, the earth and the other elements are produced in every aeon.
Then there is the circle of instruments (karaṇamaṇḍala) joined with the organs of action such as speech;
within these, Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Brahmā are the presiding deities.
From that [arises] the circle of light (prakāśamaṇḍala), which is traditionally taught as the pentad of the sense organs of cognition.
The directions, lightning, the sun, Varuṇa, and the earth are the deities of the ear and the other senses.
Above the sphere of light (prakāśamaṇḍala) is situated the sphere of the five objects (pañcārthamaṇḍala).
Beyond this is the sphere of the mind (manomaṇḍala), because it is presided over by the Moon.
The presiding deity over the external gods consists of the nature of equanimity, sovereignty, and bliss;
therefore, the divine Soma, the pervasive lord of the mind-deity, is proclaimed [as superior].
Even beyond that is the source of all the senses, born from the sense of intellect.
The city of the ego (ahaṅkāra) is joined with eight [levels], beginning with Sthūla and ending with Chagala.
Beyond that is the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), which is the sovereign of the cities of the eight classes of divine beings;
it is proclaimed to extend from the Piśācas up to the realm of Brahmā.
These, according to the Purāṇas, are indeed the abodes of those born of the divine race; descending [to earth], they come into existence while meditating upon their own births,
impelled by the command of the Supreme Lord and driven by Māyā.

Restrained by the power of necessity (niyati) belonging to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, they are manifested at the beginning of creation in manifold ways through names and forms. These great-souled ones, by means of their own portions alone, do not abandon their own abode.
And this was stated in the *Śivatanu* by our Guru, who occupies the station of authority:
"These [eight worlds] are indeed the sources for the manifestation of the powers of the eight deities;
furthermore, their bodies and enjoyments are said to consist of the gross elements below. (AbhT 8.230–231)
There are forty worlds that possess equal enjoyments and superior locations.
(231) These are described as being eightfold and fivefold solely due to the difference in their means of attainment (*sādhana*).
They are accessible through devotion (*bhakti*), yoga, the renunciation of life (*prāṇatyāga*), and other such methods. (232)
Among them, Umāpati alone is the Lord, whose senses are independent and whose nature is free from transformation.
Beyond that, by way of degrees of intensity, the eightfold divine womb is to be perceived;
as are the sense organs of the worlds, which serve as the instruments for the discernment of objects.
From the element of smell up to the Great Principle (mahat), sovereignty is born by increasing by one at each stage;
it consists of the powers beginning with *aṇimā* and extends from this [lowest level] up to Paiśāca and ending with Viriñca.
Having understood this, one should purify the intellect together with the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) and the sense organs.
Then they know the eight Krodheśas, beginning with Saṃvarta, as being dark blue; from the group of eight Krodhas beginning with Balādhyakṣa comes the group of eight Tejas;
then, for the intellect (buddhi), the group of eight Yogas beginning with Akṛta is proclaimed.
That [is taught] in the *Svacchandaśāsana*, while in the root *Śrīpūrvaśāsana* it is as follows:
at the stage of the eightfold yoga (*yogāṣṭaka*) there is *Some*, and indeed *Śrīkaṇṭha*; beyond that, the city of *Māyā* is further described as belonging to *Śrīkaṇṭha*.
Therefore, a second world for each of those two is spoken of.
Therein is the City of Māyā belonging to the Goddess, by whom the universe is presided over. That Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī) is addressed by different names in every Kalpa.
After that is the city of Umāpati, surrounded by the Mothers. Śrīkaṇṭha himself is called Umāpati through his supreme form.
[The Mothers are] Brāhmī, Aiśī, Skandajā, Hārī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, and Saviccikā (Carcikā).
Yellow, white, yellow-blue, blue, and white-ruddy are their colors, respectively;
they reside in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Soma, Yama, Varuṇa, Pūrva, and Nairṛta.
Indeed, by a portion of themselves, they were brought down into the world of men by the Creator.
Those [energies] are autonomous, while others are supreme and established in the highest ether.
They enjoy their own freedom, since Umā exists here in a sevenfold manner.
Above the city of the Lord of Umā resides the supreme group of eight forms.
That form of Īśāna from whom proceeds the creation beginning with Śarva and ending with the sacrificer, starting from Earth (dharā) and so forth— that form is established upon Meru.
Śrīkaṇṭha resides on the Crystal Mountain (Sphaṭikādri), and that [form] pervades the world through the eight bodies.
Those who, self-restrained, devotedly practice the yoga with attributes (saguṇa-yoga) of Śambhu,
or merely behold his maṇḍala, become liberated from duality and have the three [impurities] removed.
This is because the qualities (guṇas), established as pure or impure, exist in a state of relative superiority and inferiority.
And due to the gradations of yoga and the resulting diversity of its fruits, this distinction is declared:
from the difference in the attainment of the fruit of enjoyment, this [distinction] arises.
Furthermore, above the eight forms (mūrti), twelve Suśivas are said to have arisen.
Starting from Vāma and ending with Ekaśiva, they are the color of saffron and possess great splendor.
Above them stands the lord of the mandala named Vīrabhadra;
having attained union (sāyujya) with him, one rejoices together with him.
Beyond that, extending down to the size of a thumb, there is the group of eight Mahādevas;
this is declared to be the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), beginning from the eight divine wombs (devayoni).
At the end of the group of eight Mahādevas, the group of eight Yogas is said to be located here.

Therein, that which is called Śraikaṇṭha belongs to him alone; likewise, Umāpati, the Mūrtis, Suśiva, Vīra, and Mahādeva constitute the group of eight, which is his body. Above the intellect (buddhi) and below primordial nature (prakṛti) is that which is designated as the qualities (guṇas).
In that state, the *tattva* (the principle of intellect), with its qualities (*guṇa*) agitated, produces the intellect (*dhi*).
Indeed, a cause that has not reached a state of imbalance cannot give rise to an effect;
therefore, *prakṛti*, whose nature is the equilibrium of the qualities, becomes the cause.

But surely, in that case, how could she [Prakṛti] produce those uneven qualities (*guṇas*) without agitation? If there were agitation in the first place, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).
This is indeed a fault for the Sāṃkhya; or else, by that [agitation], those qualities [would be produced]. (AbhT 8.255b–256)
For [the Sāṃkhyas], the unmanifest (avyakta) is desired as a state of equilibrium, a mere conjunction and nothing else.

For us, however, it is conjoined with the agitation of the independent Lord’s will. The unmanifest is the cause of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), wherein the qualities (guṇas) have been agitated.
But surely, that very agitation of *prakṛti* which occurs prior [to manifestation] by the will of the Lord of the Tattvas—
that itself must be the *buddhitattva*; what is the use of other imagined *guṇas*,
since this [agitation] does not obstruct the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the nature of causality?
Thereafter, a further agitation must be produced, like the swelling of a seed and the emergence of a sprout;
thus, in due order, the lines of Gurus reside within the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva— namely, three,
thirty-two, thirty-one, and twenty-one respectively.

Playing by the power of their own knowledge and yoga, these supreme teachers are three-eyed, liberated from the fetters, and bestowers of grace here in this world. From the intellect (*buddhi*) up to the limit of the qualities (*guṇas*), there are two hundred and seven [levels].
The Rudras and the worlds are primary, while others are situated within them;

furthermore, the eightfold yoga is taught in the Śivatanu [Tantra] as belonging to the aggregate of the qualities (guṇaskandha). Having transcended the matrices (yoni), these bestowers of yoga reside in the aggregate of the qualities.

Akṛta, Kṛta, Vibhu, Viriñca, Hari, Guha, and then the Goddess follow in succession. The instruments, the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, the effects, and the expansion of cognitive objects— all these, as well as the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, have arisen from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
These bestowers of yoga grant to the persons who possess the [eight] qualities (guṇas) various fruits, such as the knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty.
Beyond them lies the world of the Lord whose throne consists of the qualities of sattva and the rest.
[This is] of the Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, the sole mother of the entire universe. By him,
through his power in the form of a planet (*graha*), the elements are presided over by his sovereign majesty within the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣan, Kṛta, Akṛta, and so forth.
He who, desiring to withdraw [the universe] here, enters the lotus-face of the four-faced one,
and having burnt the four worlds including the world of men (janaloka), creates them anew;
by whose will Rudrāṇī emits [the Rudras] whose bodies consist of the qualities such as sattva.
The secondary rite (anukalpa) belongs to Rudrāṇī; there she is worshipped by means of that secondary rite.
Then Paśupati [is worshipped] by Indra, Upendra, and Viriñca, as well as by the gods who perceive him;
likewise, the sacrifices are diversified by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, and Munis.
That supreme equilibrium of the *guṇas* is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), situated above the *guṇas*.
Therein are those eight: Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotiḥpiṅgala, Sūraka, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śikhoda.
The "thicket," the "repository of the Puruṣa," "Prakṛti," "the Root," "Pradhāna," and "the Unmanifest"—
these are synonyms for that which originates from Māyā, as is the "cause of the Guṇas.
As many as there are *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field), their consciousnesses are smeared with innate and adventitious impurities.
All those Rudras, who enjoy the fruits arising from that [state], are stationed here;

some, however, are devoid of organs (vikaraṇaka) due to their organs being deluded, inverted, or dissolved. Those whose organs are "deluded" are incapable of performing their functions because they lack presiding consciousness.
In the Śāstra, these [faculties] are described as having specific, determined objects and being clearly manifest;
they are destroyed during the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), and during creation they are not produced anew but remain latent.
Dependent upon the Will (icchā), they are further designated as "vikaraṇas," and their effects are likewise so.
In the principle of the Person (puṃstattva), there is the group of nine contentments (tuṣṭi) and the eight accomplishments (siddhi) preceding them;

likewise, there are exactly that many worlds of the eight [powers] beginning with atomization (aṇimā). Here, contentment is that satisfaction which arises from perceiving what is not a reality as being a reality.
Success is the realization that even what is to be abandoned is worthy of being accepted; for thus it has been stated by the followers of Kapila:
"There are four internal [sufferings] known as those of nature (prakṛti), material cause (upādāna), time (kāla), and fortune (bhāgya);
and five arising from the cessation of sense objects due to acquisition, preservation, attachment, destruction, and injury."

Reasoning (ūha), oral instruction (śabda), study (adhyayana), the three ways of destroying suffering, the acquisition of a friend, and giving—these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis). That which precedes accomplishment is the threefold goad (aṅkuśa).
Above [the eight], there are three rows beginning with atomization (aṇimā) pertaining to the teacher and the disciple.

Even there, a threefold nature is proclaimed due to the conjunction with the shadow of the three qualities (guṇas). Above that, there is the group of eight channels of knowledge (vidyā), beginning with iḍā and so forth, arranged in rows.
Within the Puruṣa resides the power consisting of sound (nāda), which is called "emanation" (prasara).
For the person is not a non-agent, and the state of being a cause is established for the agent;
or, even if the person were a non-agent, it must be accepted that he exists as a cooperative cause,
otherwise the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) would be abandoned.

Therefore, in such an undertaking, whatever power a person possesses, having assumed as many forms as there are [powers], he attains fullness. Above the eightfold group of channels, what has been described is called the octad of bodies (vigrahāṣṭaka).
Effect, cause, suffering, pleasure, consciousness, the objects to be accomplished,
and the instruments— this group of eight manifestations constitutes the *puṃstattva* (the principle of the individual soul).
From these eight manifestations arise the worlds and the ten attributes of the body.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from guile, absence of anger, service to the guru, purity, contentment, and rectitude— these ten are proclaimed. Furthermore,
the group of sixteen [principles] ending with smell is situated within the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva) alone.
Beginning with that which is called the city of the bond of the body (dehapāśa), there are then the qualities of the intellect (buddhi).
Right there are the eight [qualities], as well as the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) and those beginning with desire (kāma).
These bonds are differentiated by the adventitious (āgantuka), Gāṇeśa, Vaidya, and Īśvara.
These three types of impurities reside within the person (puṃs) and act as obstructions on the path to liberation.
Whatever is other than the Supreme Śiva— whose nature has been described and who is beautiful through the sovereignty of supreme non-dual consciousness— that is called a bond (pāśa).

Thus, even though the Supreme Lord is full, when He has attained this state of "masculinity" (puṃstva), there is a lack of recognition of His true nature; for this reason, the individual souls (puruṣas) are indeed manifold. As for the bonds (pāśas)—whether mentioned or unmentioned—their characteristics have been described according to the teachings of the Paratantra [Tantra].
All of them [reside] in the Puruṣa; by purifying them there, one is liberated from worldly existence.
Above the Puruṣa is Niyati; situated there are the ten Śaṅkaras. In the Kalatattva, however, those ten are the Śivas, golden-hued and very white.
Each of the attendants has a retinue of sixteen thousand times ten million.
In the sphere of Passion (rāga) is the world of Vīreśa, the city of the teachers and disciples. And in the sphere of Impure Knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) is the city resplendent with the nine powers.
And those [energies] beginning with Vāmā, extending up to Manonmanī, have been proclaimed.
Within the Kalā-tattva lies the supreme city of the three Great Deities. Beyond that is Māyā, which is threefold and primarily consists of infinite crores [of worlds].
It is said that in the body of Śivā, she is again pervaded by the openings of the womb;
at night, the eight Great Gods extend as far as the big toe.
Likewise, in the venerable *Mālinīmata*, [this occurs] through the sovereignty of the eight wheels.
Those who were mentioned in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana* as beginning with Vāmā and others among the [emanations] of Puruṣa and so forth,
are said to exist within the *māyātattva* itself, in the body of Śiva, starting from Ananta.
They are practitioners of the skull-vow (*kapālavratinaḥ*), sacrificers of their own limbs, and performers of arduous austerities.
Free from all fear, those who observe the vow of the sword’s edge and know that specific reality (tattva) gradually attain that very reality where the Lord Ananta is said to reside.
And it has been stated that beyond him is the station of that god who is the sovereign of Ananta.
To the guardian of the door of the cave of the womb, the agent of maintenance, dissolution, and creation—

who draws forth and bestows upon men from the cavern of *māyā* the *dharmas*, the qualities such as *aṇimā*, the various forms of knowledge, ascetic powers, pleasures, and yogic attainments— [salutation]. (8.303–304)

Empowered by His power, their own strength consisting of the qualities of darkness presiding over the cave (guhā), all [the Rudras], beginning with Ananta and ending with Śatabhava, blaze forth. Presiding over the Unmanifest (avyakta), he brings forth the universe by the command of Śambhu.
Since Śiva is the cause of authority over the pure and impure currents,
those who are first established in that great state which is conjoined with the qualities of Śiva are the agents of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe beginning with Ananta.
This is called the "cavity of Māyā," but beyond it is the Cave (guhā), the womb of the universe.

When the powers of the Lord (pati-śakti) undergo agitation within these [powers], they give rise to various wombs; because these cavities of the womb abound with manifold desires, they are designated as the "Bhaga."
When the husband desires this goddess, who complies with his wishes,
then from her are born offspring beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta) and the subtle elements (bhaga).
Because these are exceedingly subtle, their full extent is not described in the ritual injunctions.
Just as many inner chambers are constructed within a single wall,
so too are there many vaginal cavities within the single wall that is the head of Māyā.
Covered by subtle layers of the veil of Māyā as their walls, they are invisible to one another.
There, in every single cavity, countless Rudras dwell in happiness.
In that place, some have attained union (*sāyujya*), others proximity (*sāmīpya*), and others reside in the same world (*saloka*).
Thus has this [residence] for the inhabitants been described by the teachers for every world.
Even the words of all the Siddhas, uttered over a long period of time, might be exhausted;
yet the enumerations of the streams [of existence] cannot be fully expressed because of the infinity of wombs.
Therefore, that which was taught as beginning from the hells and ending with the gatekeepers is but a single [part].
Through that channel, other [channels] of similar nature are also to be known.
In the unmanifest *kalā*, by means of the cave (*guhā*) and the *prakṛti-kalā*, one's own transformation is woven lengthwise and crosswise,
pervaded, fashioned, filled, and encompassed.
In its center are three cavities; within them, there are six Rudras in the lower [cavity], one in the middle, and five above—thus these twelve have been described.
These six are Gahana, Asādhya, Hari, Hara, Daśeśvara, and Trikala-gopati.

In the center is Ananta, and [in the petals] Kṣema, Dvijeśa, Vidyeśa, Viśva, and Śiva. Thus, among those five and six [petals] situated in the squares, the state of affairs revolves through their rotation; indeed, the Lord Ananta remains in the center in every respect.
That knot, as described in the *Mataṅgaśāstra*, is pervaded by a pair of sixfold cavities of skull-bowls situated above and below,
and by eight [cavities] from the center located in the cardinal directions;
furthermore, in the *Śrīsāraśāsana*, it is specified as having six cavities.
This principle called Granthi (the Knot) is the effect of Māyā; therefore, it is Māyā itself.

Indeed, the Māyā-principle is all-pervasive, profound, formless, and the locus of the dissolution of everything. Since there is no division of worlds possible therein, that division belongs to the Granthi. Thus, [it is established that] this [Knot] is distinct from Māyā. 321–322ab.

Ananta, the lord of the principle of Māyā, having deliberated upon the individual souls (aṇu) who have arisen, simultaneously agitates the Night (niśā). She gives birth through her own infinite enclosures (saṃpuṭa).
By that [agitation], the entire web of coverings (āvaraṇajāla), beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth, which has been described, comes into being.

Innumerable and diverse, this is indeed nothing but Māyā, which is to be understood as one. And it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that the dyad consisting of Earth and the Unmanifest (avyakta) is innumerable, while that designated as Night (niśā) and Power (śakti) is of a single nature.

The fetters previously mentioned, the *praṇavas*, the pentad, the group of eight, the lineage (*kula*), and the womb (*yoni*) of Vāgīśī— born of which one is not born again. At the time of initiation, during the purification of that which resides on the lower path, whatever belongs to the lower path [is purified].
All of that is fully established in the presence of Ananta.
The five drops are Sādhya, Dātā, Damana, Dhyāna, and Bhasma;
as well as the Pañcārtha, Guhya, Rudrāṅkuśa, and Hṛdaya, together with their respective arrangements (vyūha).

The eight [categories] of these means of knowledge are: [the five senses], the mind, the intellect, and the mirror of attraction (*ākarṣa*). All those who hold authority over the principle of *māyā* possess unimpaired power;
possessing bodies composed of *māyā*, they enjoy their own respective experiences.
For at the end of the dissolution, they are withdrawn by Ananta; yet at the dawn of the day,
by the grace of another Ananta, even the gods—
stunned by the conceit of their own independence— regard that Supreme One as one who has merely awakened from sleep.
Those who dwell within the interval of Māyā perceive their own self as the cause;
beyond that stands the Goddess Māyā, who deludes living beings. She is the power of the God of gods, capable of accomplishing the most difficult tasks.

Those of lowest birth, who lack devotion toward their guru, the gods, the sacred fire, and the scriptures, have their intellects deluded by that [ignorance] which stands as an obstacle without enmity; thus, these disputants here contend, "This is the truth, this is not."
Abandoning them to the true path, it certainly leads them onto a false path—
those who know the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic. For Māyā indeed causes them to wander, desiring liberation in what is not liberation.

Severed by the sword of Śiva-initiation and likewise by the sword of Śiva-knowledge, it shall not sprout again; there is no other cause for its severance. Above Mahāmāyā is the pure Mahāvidyā, which is Mātṛkā.
And Vāgīśvarī resides there within the city of the nine powers beginning with Vāmā. Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī,
Balavikaraṇī, as well as Mathanī, Damanī, and Manonmanī— these three-eyed goddesses are all yellow.
Seventy million principal mantras are established here within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). Each of these consists of ten million billion parts and resides in cities shaped like lotuses.
Here dwell the seven sovereign queens of knowledge, beginning with Triguṇī, who are the mistresses of seventy billion [mantras].

Above the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva) is the principle of Īśvara; therein lies the city that ascends through the sequence, beginning with Śikhaṇḍin and ending with Ananta, consisting of eight cities. These are:
Śikhaṇḍin, Śrīkaṇṭha, Mūrti, Ekanetra, and Ekarudra.
Śivottama, Sūkṣmarudra, and Ananta constitute the group of eight Vidyeśvaras.
These seven are situated progressively higher and higher, with the all-pervasive Lord as their leader.
Ananta alone is to be meditated upon and worshipped, each succeeding one being superior to the last.

That which consists of three and a half crores of the principal Mantreśvaras is governed by these; therefore, they are the Vidyeshas, the universal emperors (cakravartins). And this has been stated by the Gurus in the Shiva-tantra and other scriptures.
The Lord, seated upon the summit of the cave pierced by hundreds of apertures, is joined with eight powers.
He creates [the universe] beginning from the Thicket (Gahana) down to the Hells, and he appoints the Rudras.
By means of Manonmanī, he uplifts men; yet among them, he remains impartial.
With their minds uplifted by that [grace], they apply themselves to the contemplation of the supreme reality (paratattva).

Furthermore, Śiva has appointed him over the individual souls (aṇu) who abide on the lower paths. Having completed his service to the Lord, he departs together with many millions of mantras of manifold nature.
The Lord Ananta enters that abode and becomes the subtle Rudra;
having graced the individual soul (aṇu), the Lord establishes him in a new state in the station of Śikhaṇḍin.
In this manner, the single Guru proceeds through the eight abodes in successive order.
For that long, they bring about the liberation of countless living beings.
Those eight [goddesses], seated upon pure lotus thrones joined with the group of eight powers,
gaze upon the God who resides in the heart, the supreme cause.
Meditating upon that Blessed One, Ananta, the cause who is peaceful within their own hearts,
even seven crores of pure mantras meditate [upon him].
From Māyā down to Avīci is existence (*bhava*), while that which begins with Ananta is called non-existence (*abhava*).
This [state] also, which ends with the authority over the pure qualities of Śiva, is to be abandoned;
for even here, the Śaiva command is seen to apply to those who are to be graced.
Moreover, its cessation is desired, because non-existence (liberation) does not occur at a lower level.

Since the status of being a cause and the status of being an effect recede from the Lord for those who have attained perfection, Śiva remains perfectly neutral toward them, like one wearing a cloak, under the designation of "transmigration" until their final liberation. As for that city consisting of the fourfold qualities of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—

In this Īśvara-tattva, the wise know that which is called the veil of form (rūpāvaraṇa) to be adorned by the three worlds: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. This is declared by the best of gurus to be the subtle veil within the Īśa-tattva.

From Īśa [comes] Sādāśiva, adorned with the pair of knowledge and action; they call this the Pure Enclosure (śuddhāvaraṇa). Beyond the Pure Enclosure, it is said, is the Enclosure of Knowledge (vidyāvṛti), radiant with the two powers of existence and non-existence.
The veil of Śakti, called Pramāṇa (the Means of Knowledge), is described in the scripture after that.
The veil of Śakti is adorned by Tejasvin and Dhruveśa.
After that is the veil of Tejasvin; the four Vedas constitute the veil of Māna (Knowledge).
Adorned with three cities of the veil of Māyā and the perfectly pure veil (suśuddhāvṛti),
above the perfectly pure veil there should be the single city of Śiva.
Above the veil of Śiva, they say, is that which is designated as the veil of liberation (mokṣāvaraṇa).

Within this enclosure of liberation (mokṣāvṛti), eleven Rudras are described. From the perspective of the enclosure of liberation, the enclosure of the Single City (ekapura) is indeed fixed. Above the enclosure of Dhruva is the enclosure of Will (icchāvaraṇa); therein reside those Śivas.

Residing within the abode of the Lord’s will, that city is said to be one. Beyond the enclosure of will is the one called Prabuddha (Awakened), adorned by the eight Rudras of the directions. Above the enclosure of the Awakened is the great enclosure of the Samaya (the Rule).

Enveloped by the five worlds and containing within it the infinite enclosure, there exists in that [state] the great world of Sadāśiva, which is auspiciously Śiva-like by virtue of its conventional nature (sāmāyāt). Within that is the god Sadāśiva; on his left and right [are his attendants].
Knowledge and action are his own, while the power of supreme will (parēcchā) rests upon his lap.
By means of that will, he performs the fivefold cosmic acts, beginning with emanation.
[These consist of] the five Brahmās, the six limbs, the eight [deities] beginning with Sakala, and the Śivas.
The ten and eighteen Rudras surround Suśiva with them;
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna constitute the five Brahmans, while the Heart is the [sixth].
They say there are six limbs: the Head, the Topknot, the Armor, the Eye, and the Weapon.
Along with the Sakala, Akala, and Śūnya, [the deities] adorn the void enriched by Kalā; this is the final dissolution (kṣapaṇa).
It is traditionally taught that these eight constitute the group of the eight Sakalas, beginning with the eighth [deity], the Kaṇṭhya-oṣṭhya.
They are: Oṃkāra and Śiva; Dīpta, Hetvīśa, Daśeśaka, Suśiva, and Kāla.
Sūkṣma, Sutejas, and Śarva— these ten are the Śivas here, starting from the east.
Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, Vahni, Vīra, Raurava, Mukuṭa, Visara, Indu, Bindu, Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, and Rudra.
Santāna, Śiva, Parakiraṇa, and Pārameśa are known as the Rudras.
The wise know that the gnoses (jñānas) of all these bear names identical to their own.
Then there is [the state] surrounded by ten million mantra-sages, together with the pervasive Vāmā and the other Rudras and their powers.
The seat of Suśiva is a most white lotus with countless petals, graced by the powers beginning with Tārā;
and the host of Śaktis and Rudras constitutes the retinue and the pedestal of Suśiva.
Within each of their respective individual retinues, there are countless millions of parārdhas.

Freed from the impurity of *māyā* and established solely in their functional office (*adhikāra*), these Rudras reside in the enclosure of Suśiva; they are omniscient and fully endowed with all powers. Upon the dissolution of the bond of their office, they become peaceful, identical with Śiva, and no longer subject to rebirth.
Above is the radiant enclosure of the Bindu; there, in each place, is a lotus with the luster of the moon.
Therein resides Śiva, who has transcended the state of Peace (Śāntyatīta), adorned by the lap of his Śakti, and surrounded by the retinue of the groups of Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti.
It is surrounded by countless Rudras and tens of millions of their powers. Furthermore,
in the venerable *Mataṅga-śāstra*, the supreme principle called "Dissolution" (*laya*) is here referred to by the technical term "the Point" (*bindu*).
That which consists of the four forms, radiant, and both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala)—in that, enjoyment is declared; and this is described here:
because the [levels] beginning with Nivṛtti are extremely subtle, there is the state of having a body composed of the elements starting with Earth.
Because it is merged within the mother’s throbbing Great Knowledge (*mahājñāna*), it is not perceived [as separate].

Just as the earthly atoms within gold do not appear separately due to the predominance of its fiery nature, so too the [atoms] residing in the body of the vast Rudra, from top to bottom, do not appear as distinct.
Above the *bindu* is the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and its digits (*kalā*) are Jyotsnā, Tadvatī, Kānti, Prabhā, and Vimalā; these five are the obstructors (*rodhikā*).
Following them are Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Roddhṛī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā.
The best of gurus have declared that these five digits (kalās) reside within Nirodhinī.
The Bindu is remembered as having half a mora and consisting of the form of space (vyoman), comprising four digits;
the Ardhacandra is half of that, and Nirodhikā is one-eighth of that.
One should restrain the causes beginning with Brahmā; therefore, one should abandon that obstructive [power].
Having pierced this power of cessation (nirodhikā), one reaches the supreme world called Sādākhya, where the Great Body of the Five Mantras abides in its supreme form.
Above that, the Great One is the obstruction of the half-moon and the bindu;
the Nāda, resembling a lotus filament, is surrounded by great beings.
Herein are four worlds in the cardinal directions and a fifth in the center.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rodhikā, Mocikā, and Ūrdhvagā;
here in the center is the lotus, and there resides the one who moves upward, surrounded by those powers.
Above the Nāda, however, is the Sauṣumna, where the Lord dwells, bearing those powers.
His Lord is surrounded by Piṅgalā and Ilā on his right and left sides. The goddess Suṣumnā, who rests upon the lap of the Lord and possesses the luster of the moon,
threads through all the paths, both those above and those below.
The Nāda, supported by the Suṣumnā, having pierced through this entire universe,

should emerge below by the lower power (adhaḥśakti) and above from the crown of the head by the upper power (ūrdhvaśakti). Merged in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) through that channel, it is the unmanifest, imperishable sound.
Resounding within all beings, he is indeed presided over by the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti).
Above the Suṣumṇā is the enclosure known as the Brahma-aperture (brahmabila), which has three eyes.
Therein resides Brahmā, white in color, holding a trident, five-faced, and adorned with the moon upon his crest.
In his lap is the supreme goddess Brahmāṇī, who follows the path to liberation;
she is both the obstructress and the giver of liberation. Piercing through her is the upward-coiled Śakti, resembling a sleeping serpent, who is called the support of the universe.
Within that [power] are Sūkṣmā and Susūkṣmā, as well as Amṛtā and Amitā;
in the middle is Vyāpinī, and within her resides Vyāpīśa, the sustainer of Vyāpinī.
This is the Śakti-tattva, whose manifestation extends down to the level of the earth.

Beyond that is the Śiva-tattva; there, situated in the four directions, are Vyāpin, Vyomātman, Ananta, and Anātha, who partake in its power. In the center, however, is the Anāśrita [tattva], where the God of gods, Anāśrita, resides.
Bearing that power in her lap, she possesses a radiance equal to hundreds of millions of suns.
Above the Śiva-tattva is that supreme Power (Śakti), called Samanā;
she stands established as the active agent of all causes.
Sustained by Śiva, she bears many cosmic eggs;
mounted upon her, the Lord Śiva performs the fivefold cosmic act. For that Great Lord, who is the causal agent, Samanā is the instrument.
But that which is non-dependent in its activity is called the efficient cause (*nimittahetu*).
By means of that [power], the All-pervasive Lord presides over the pentad of causes. He is non-dependent, without a master, infinite, and eternally of the nature of space.

He impels the Pervasive One (Vyāpin) by means of his own power through the instrument [of the senses]; below that, Māyā exists in the form of karma as the power Kuṇḍalinī. From this arises the effect consisting of Nāda, Bindu, and so forth—the emergence of the entire world.
Whatever exists in this teaching, from the earthly realm up to Sādāśiva,

all that is declared to be *prākṛta* (of the nature of primordial matter), being subject to birth and destruction. Now, I shall describe the measurement of the entire universe as it was told to me by my own gurus.
That shall now be explained in brief, by which [the reality] may quickly enter the intellect:
Within the Egg (aṇḍa) is infinite Time (Kāla), Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, and Hari;
the Rudras are one hundred along with Vīra. Outside [of this], Nivṛtti consists of one hundred and eight worlds.

In each of the seven—the water, fire, wind, ether, ego, intellect, and root—there are eight [worlds], making fifty-six worlds; therefore, this is called the *kalā* known as Pratiṣṭhā. Regarding this, some say that the eight lords of their respective groups of eight are the ones to be purified.
Others, however, describe all the worlds as being subject to purification.
Furthermore, the venerable teachers, the Bhūtirāja-miśras, have stated that there are one hundred Rudras externally;
internally, there are eight along with Śarva—such would be this Nivṛtti-kalā.

The Rudras, Kālī, Vīra, Dharā, Abdhilakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Guhya—this is the group of eight. [These reside] in Water; the two [deities] Fire and Atiguhyā in Fire; those of Vāyu in Wind; his own city and Gayā and so forth in Space; and the pair of worlds consisting of the Vyomavyāpin and the Pavitrāṣṭaka.
In the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), which is characterized by self-conceit, there is the group of eight beginning with the goat and others; then, within that, the void and the ego.

In the group of subtle elements (tanmātra), there is the group of eight cities belonging to the sun, the moon, and the Vedas, as well as those of the deities of the intellect and the organs of action.
Within the aggregate of the ten subtle elements, there is again a world situated in the group of the senses.

In the abhimāna of the mind (manas), there are exactly twenty-two worlds. In the intellect (dhī), there are eight belonging to the divine powers (daivī); then the triad known as Kratu, Tejas, and Yoga; then Umā; then her Lord (Śiva); then the eight Mūrtis, the twelve Suśivas, and Vīrabhadra.
Then there is the group of eight Mahādevas; thus, in the intellect (buddhi), the number is seventeen.
In the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), there are three rows; the wise know these to be fifty-six cities.
Although the group of eight Krodheśvaras resides in the root [nature] which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya), they are nonetheless located in the intellect.
"That which has been purified does not enter the count again within the *pratiṣṭhā* [tattva].
(AbhT 8.417b) "Thus, from the water-tattva up to the root, there are twenty-four tattvas in the *pratiṣṭhā*.
(AbhT 8.418a) "The group beginning with Ambā and ending with Tuṣṭi, the accomplishments beginning with Tārā, and the group of powers beginning with Aṇimā. (AbhT 8.418b)
The gurus and their disciples, the host of sages, and the eightfold body beginning with *iḍā*;
the city of transformations such as smell and so forth, the eight qualities of the intellect, ego-activity, and the qualities of the objects of the senses;
the twenty-seven adventitious factors beginning with desire, as well as those consisting of Gaṇeśa and Vidyeśa.
Thus, within the fetters (pāśas), there are three cities; here, in the principle of the Person (puruṣa), there are sixteen worlds.
In the principle of Necessity (niyati) there is the group of ten Śaṅkaras, and in Time (kāla) the group of ten Śivas—these constitute two cities.
In Attachment (rāga) is the world of Suhr̥ṣṭa, and in the pair of Knowledge (vidyā) and Limited Agency (kalā) is the city of Teacher and Disciple.
Each world [is a city], and at night there are three cities of the *puṭas*, the city of Speech (*vāk*), and the city of Authority (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, the Vidyā consists of twenty-seven cities and is joined with the seven principles (*tattva*) beginning with Puruṣa.
The subtle form of the Lord of the Left (*Vāmeśa*) is pure; then Vidyā, and the measure of the splendor of Śakti.
Suviśuddhi and Śiva are known by the names Mokṣa, Dhruva, Īśa, Saṃbuddha, Samaya, and Sauśiva. The peaceful [state] consists of seventeen cities, joined with the three cities of Vidyeśa and Sadāśiva.
In the Suṣumṇā channel are the Bindu, Ardhendu, Nirodhī, Para, Sauśiva, Indhika, and other cities.
Paranāda, Brahmabila, the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī Śakti endowed with Sūkṣmā and the others,
Vyāpin, Vyoma, Ananta, Anātha, and Anāśrita— these are the five cities;
then the sixth is the supreme Anāśrita, or else the sixteen worlds of Samanā.
The enclosure of the Bindu, the supreme Sauśiva, and the worlds beginning with Pañcendhika;
the Sauṣumna, the Brahmabilā, the Kuṇḍalinī, the five pervasive [principles], and the Samanā—this constitutes the sixteen worlds. This pair of principles belongs to the Śāntyatītā [Kalā].
And in the venerable Mataṅgaśāstra, this sequence consisting of a multitude of cities is as follows:
Kālāgni, the hells, and Maheśvara, who presides over the seven netherworlds and the seven worlds—these constitute one hundred principal [cities] plus four thousand. 428–429a.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, the seven netherworlds, and Maheśvara, the lord of the seven worlds. 429a.
Thus, that which is within the Egg is the center; outside of that, one hundred Rudras are established.
The ground of the locations consists of two hundred and fifty-seven.
From the middle of the five groups of eight, thirty-two [are assigned] to the four elements.
In the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there are five Viśvedevas; from that, an eightfold group [arises].

In the ego (*garva*) together with the senses, there is the fifth [group]; in the intellect (*buddhi*), the eight deities; and in the qualities (*guṇa*), the eight Yogas known as Krodha. At the root [of the tree of manifestation], along with Time (*kāla*), [there is] the group of nine.
Patadrug and the others, as well as those beginning with Aṅguṣṭhamātra, reside within the principle of Rāga (Passion).
There are twelve [deities] beginning with Ekaśiva in the principle of Vidyā; there are ten in the principle of Kalanā.
This triad of principles consists of three hundred [deities], namely Vāmā and the rest, which is joined by four oceans (four hundred) in its three sections.
Some Śaivas here are Anantas, while others are Śrīkaṇṭhas; this is the summary.

Whenever and wherever one desires to enjoy the experiences of another, one should perform the conjunction (*yojana*) there. Then, upon the loss of that [experience], purification (*śodhana*) must be performed; the remainder, however, should be made internal.

This conceptualized [system] was shown by him in order to propagate the traditional scripture (āgama). Other numerous conceptualizations as well should be inferred by teachers through their own intelligence. Furthermore, in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana, one hundred and eighteen [types] are taught.
Therefore, here the principal objects of purification are stated concisely:
Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Narakeśa, Hāṭaka, and Bhūtalapa;
then Brahmā, Munilokeśa, and the Rudras who reside in the five intermediate spaces.
Below is Ananta; in the east are those known as Kapālin, Vahni, Antanirṛti, and Bala.
[Then] Laghu, Nidhipati, Vidyādhipa, Śambhu, and ending with Ūrdhvānta, along with Vīrabhadra and Pati.
The Egg of Brahmā is surrounded by eleven [rulers] on the outside and likewise by five intermediate ones.
Thus, this city of sixteen is to be understood here as belonging to the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
Lakulīśa and Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi and Āṣāḍhi, Puṣkara and Nimeṣa,
and Prabhāsa and Sureśa— these reside in the water, each with their own individual retinue.

Bhairava, Kedāra, Mahākāla, Madhyāmraka, and Jalpa; Śrīśaila and Hariścandra—this is the group of eight secret [shrines] within the Great Splendor (mahasi). Then there are those known as Bhīma, Indrāṭṭahāsa, Vimala, Kanakhala, Nākhalā, Kurusthiti, and Gayā.
This group of eight extremely secret [shrines] consists of Marut, Satanmātraka, Sākṣa, Sthāṇu, Suvarṇākhya, Bhadra, Gokarṇaka, Mahālayaka,
Avimukta, Rudrakoṭi, and Vastrāpada; this is the purifying [set] in the Sky (Kha).
Sthūla, Sthūleśa, Śaṅku, Śrutikālañjara, and Maṇḍalabhṛt;
Mākoṭa, Aṇḍadvitaya, and Chagalāṇḍa—these eight indeed reside in the ego (ahaṅkāra).
Others, however, say that the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the sense organs (indriyas) are also within the ego.
In the intellect (dhi), the eight wombs (yony-aṣṭaka) are said to reside; in primordial nature (prakṛti), indeed, the eight yogas beginning with Akṛta.

Thus, there is the establishment of seven groups of eight worlds, from the waters up to the root (mūla). In the individual (nara), [the lords are] Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśa, Vīra, Pracaṇḍa, and Gaurīśa.
Aja, Ananta, and Ekaśiva belong to the Vidya-tattva; the pair Krodha and Caṇḍa should be in [the same].
Saṃvarta and Jyotiratha are in Kalā and Niyati;
and this triad known as Vīra, Śikhīśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha should be in Kāla.
Samahātejās, Vāma, Bhavodbhava, Ekapiṅgala, Īśāna, Bhuvaneśa, Puraḥsara, and Aṅguṣṭha— these eight reside at night. This Vidyā consists of twenty-eight worlds, extending from Puruṣa down to Niśā.

Hālāhala, Rudra, Krodha, Ambikā, Ghorikā, and Vāmā should be present. In the Vidyā-tattva there are eight Vidyēśvaras; in Īśvara and Sadāśiva there are five: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śakti, and Sakalā, ending with Śāntā.
There are eighteen worlds, while the Śāntyatītā [kalā] is indeed worldless. Thus has been declared the division of the path of space (deśādhvan), as instructed by the venerable Śambhu.
The Ninth Chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, the detailed classification of the principles (*tattva*), which follows in due order, is being described.
That supreme form, dense with light, which shines as the essence inherent within all those various categories previously mentioned, is the one God, Śiva.

Furthermore, when a differentiation arises from that state of Śiva through the savor of His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), that supreme form which subsequently follows along in manifold ways is what is called a "principle" (*tattva*) in the teaching of the All-pervasive Lord.

For instance, because it extends from the abode of Time (Kāla) up to the city of Vīrabhadra, and because it manifests as support, solidity, weight, and so forth, it has the nature of Earth (Dharā). In this same way, [the presence of] the principles of Water and the rest should be stated, up to Sadāśiva.
In its own effect, in the flood of *dharma*, or even in that which possesses qualities similar to itself,
it exists by way of a universal (*sāmānya*), because of its extension and its state of pervasiveness.
That is the respective *tattva*— beginning with Earth, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Śiva, and so forth— in due order.
Consequently, there would be no further attachment to bodies or worlds;
this was stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Mataṅga-śāstra* and other texts. In that regard, their [nature] is shown as it has been perceived in the *Siddhayogīśvarī-mata*.

The relationship of cause and effect, which is fashioned by the will of Śiva, exists only in reality; the supreme Lord Śiva is the creator of all things. For agency can never be possible for that which is not independent.
The Supreme Lord, whose body is pure consciousness, possesses absolute freedom;
yet, absolute freedom and insentience are mutually contradictory.
Insentience implies dependence upon a subject even for the establishment of its own self-nature.
Indeed, no causality other than that of being an agent can be found. For the principle "when this exists, that comes to be" has its very life in dependence;
how could it apply to entities that are independent and established in their own nature?
If it is argued that "it" (the seed) exists both before and after,
and that if the prior and posterior states are not distinct from its own nature, then [the seed] remains identical;
this being the true principle regarding cause and effect in the case of the seed and the sprout—
Why could there not be a relationship of cause and effect between a jar and a cloth?
If it is argued that the seed transforms into the form of the sprout, leaf, and so forth,
then that transformation is not logically possible for something whose nature does not possess that very essence.
If it is argued that "it has that as its intrinsic nature," then the seed and the sprout would rest in nothing more than themselves, because nothing else could ever arise from them. Consequently,
it would follow that this [seed] possesses a manifold form to that extent.
If it is argued that in an insentient thing there cannot be the occurrence of mutually contradictory forms, [we reply:
let the insentient thing possess variegated forms sequentially; what contradiction is there?
Whether sequential or non-sequential, a form does not exist as something additional to the nature of the entity itself.
In the same way, those two are merely perceptions; and is perception likewise [mere perception]?

Even the perceiver, whose nature is consciousness—whatever that may be—is indeed [the same]. If it is argued that he perceives sequentially because his nature consists of sequential perception, [then...]
In that case, what is this sequence [of the phonemes], given that nothing other than them is perceived?
If you say it is their "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), that cannot be something additional to their own form (*svarūpa*).
For even if the sequence were not additional to the intrinsic form, by virtue of its own nature, it would [be nothing more than that].
If manifestation occurs through His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), what else need we say?
In this way, the venerable Śiva alone is defined as the sole agent (*kartṛ*).
And this agency of His is simply the manifestation of the [objective] measures (*mātrā*) in such a manner.
In that same way, there is an appearance [of sequence] which pertains to the relation of cause and effect.
For just as the coexistence of a cloth with a jar appears, so too does its immediate succession; however, that [succession] is devoid of necessity.
Therefore, we declare that when there is an additional continuity of form, that which invariably appears immediately after something else is the cause of that thing;
and such necessity consists essentially in nothing more than the appearance of that specific form.
The manifestation "from seed comes sprout" does not occur at all times,
because a sprout of that very nature arises immediately after the will of the yogin;
for a restriction manifests when such a form is intended.

In a dream, the nature of causes and their effects, such as jars and cloths, appears with strict necessity, provided it remains uncontradicted for that duration. Therefore, to whatever extent and in whatever form a rule is established free from contradiction, [it is valid].

To that extent, it shines forth as having the nature of a firm cause and effect due to its identity with that [object]. And when such a rule exists, which establishes the state of being the cause and the possessor of the cause,
in reality, causality belongs only to that which consists of consciousness, for that is all-pervasive.

For this very reason, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is said to be the cause for the arising of a jar. And if the causal complex is not accepted as having a single nature consisting of its constituent parts, then there would be no difference in the effect despite the difference in the causes; and that is untenable.
If that which conforms to another possesses the nature of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
and if that [concomitance] is its cause— then this dull logic is not pleasing to us.
For example, the staff, the thread, the wheel, the hands, and so forth, when all together [produce a jar].
We consider that things which are distant and yet destined to exist can likewise function as causes;
for if Mount Meru were present there, or if some future entity were to arise,
the jar certainly would not be produced, being obstructed by those impediments.
Just as the wheel [of time] acts as the cause in specific places and times,
so too do Karki, Sumeru, and the others remain fixed within their respective domains;
likewise, it is by means of those causes that there occurs their conjunction and disjunction.
In this process, Śiva alone is determined as the independent agent who assumes the state of being the creator.
For that consciousness which belongs to a potter when he employs the wheel, the staff, and other tools, is indeed Śiva himself;
since it is Śiva, what distinction could there be in consciousness?
But the consciousness of a potter, because it manifests as limited, may be considered distinct in nature;

yet if it were to be cast away from the midst of the staff, the wheel, and other [factors], then Śiva, whose singular body is the universe, is the creator of each single thing. Thus, in the manifestation of every individual object, Śiva is the one whose form is the totality of all things.
The ego-inflation of the individual soul that "I am the agent" is also the creative act of the All-pervasive Lord;
for this very reason, it exists as the ultimate reality of such an appearance.
Thus, the relationship between cause and effect appears diverse in both the world and the scriptures.

In the *Rauravasaṃgraha*, it is said that from Māyā arise both the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) and Kalā; however, in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara), it is stated that the Unmanifest arises from the principle of Kalā. From that very [Kalā], known as Night, once it has become differentiated (*kalībhūta*), the Unmanifested (*aliṅga*) emerges.
Thus, when this reasoning has been stated by us, [your] explanation is utterly fruitless.

In the world, a scorpion arises from cow dung, from a worm, from a mental construction, from a dream, from memory, from the will of a yogi, and from the power of substances and mantras. (AbhT 9.42–43a)
If it is argued that [the subject] is indeed different [in each case] due to some specific internal distinction, then let it be so;

however, that [distinction] is equal everywhere, and there exists a unity in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it. For this very reason, even regarding one's own nature (*svarūpa*), the state [of experience] differs according to the sequence [of moments]. (AbhT 9.43b–44)
In the scriptures, it is joined with various [principles] according to their respective natures:
Puṃs, Rāga, Vidya, Kalā, Kāla, and Māyā, in sequence, in the Jñānottara;
in the Vairiñca [system], Niyati does not exist, while above Kalā, Niyati is taught.

Beyond the triad of the individual (puruṣa), attachment (rāga), and knowledge (vidyā) lies the enclosure of limited agency (kalā) and necessity (niyati). This sequence—Kāla and Māyā—is declared according to the *Kiraṇa-śāstra*.
The individual soul (puruṣa), together with necessity (niyati), time (kāla), and endowed with attachment (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), and limited agency (kalā), [constitutes this order].
Thus has this sequence been taught in the *Mātaṅga-pārameśvara* regarding the relationship between cause and effect once the reality [of the principles] has been established in this manner.
Now we shall explain the conception of the causes as described in the *Śrīpūrva-śāstra*.
Śiva, whose nature is independent vision and who is perfectly replete with the five powers,
is divided fivefold through the differentiation manifested by his own freedom,
due to the full manifestation of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.
The pentad of principles known as Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā— each one of these principles is thoroughly replete with all powers; yet,
through the predominance of this or that [power], each respective differentiation is described.
For thus, the All-pervasive Lord, by virtue of the perfection of His own absolute freedom,
shines forth through countless and manifold forms, being devoid of all limitation. [These forms are] those born of Śambhu, those born of Śakti, the Great Lords of Mantra, and the Leaders of Mantra.
These five groups, in their respective order, are the pure mantras.
Whatever form is consistently present within each respective group is declared to be the *tattva* (reality) among them,
just as the earth and other elements are [the realities] for Kālāgni and the rest.
Therefore, those who are mocked by their resemblance to mere storytellers—
those who have acquired books and hold desired views without serving a Guru—
claim that Brahmā, the presiding deity of Nivṛtti, is not counted as a separate principle.

What is the logic behind counting Sadāśiva and the others separately? Why is this "half-old-woman" approach adopted— treating the sixfold group known as the Causes (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Īśāna, Suśiva, and Anāśrita) as distinct within that very group?
Thus, because it is destroyed at its very root, calculation is not the cause [of liberation].
Just as a king who is the lord of the earth is not a separate principle (tattva), so too, how could each respective Lord of Kala be a separate principle? 59.
Thus, this pentad is defined as the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).
In that regard, it is the will of Śiva itself that acts as the agent, manifesting differentiation.
[It impels] those groups of conscious beings who, by the power of the Lord’s will, are agitated and longing for worldly enjoyment.
In order to distribute [the fruits of action], Aghoreśa creates here that which is other than white (i.e., the impure).
That which is called *lolikā* among individual souls (*aṇu*s) is a desire devoid of [past] action;
it is the ignorance of feeling incomplete, a stain (*mala*) free from [any specific] limitation.
This is merely a state of potentiality when grasped as a limitation of what is yet to be;
therefore, its impurity has no separate ontological status, like passion (rāga).
However, that [impurity] exists only as a limitation by a portion of action that is itself without limitation.
Attachment in the person, the property of the intellect, the diversity of various actions,
this sense of incompleteness, and likewise the manifestation of forms—
these are the will of the independent Śiva, just as a jar is the form of a jar.

The very desire to conceal one's own nature is the reality that constitutes impurity (*mala*). Just as earth and other elements, though non-different [from consciousness], are conceived as having their own distinct identities, so too is this impurity; thus, in the scriptures, it is described as existing as something separate.

But there is nothing whatsoever that is separate or independent, like a cart or similar objects. [If it were so,] would that impurity—which is accompanied by that [separate entity]—not belong to Śiva and the liberated souls? There is some power of impurity that acts as an obstructer, and that [impurity] belongs to those who are not yet liberated.
Thus, this argument is devoid of logic and is fashioned solely out of mere faith;
this obstructing power (*roddhrī śakti*) of the insentient does not operate of its own accord.
If it were to operate spontaneously, the entire universe would [arise in that way], and likewise, the Lord’s sovereignty would be undermined.

If the Lord joins that power which obstructs impurity to each individual soul (*aṇu*), then to the question "In what manner [does He join it]? there is no answer. Furthermore, impurity is an obscuration, and an obscuration does not differentiate that which is already unobstructed.
This [realization] destroys perception, just as a cloth covering obstructs a jar;
for that which is the true nature of atoms whose forms are veiled by impurity,
Śiva alone perceives it, and that [perception] belongs to Him alone as His impurity.

The absence of that [power] constitutes impurity (*mala*) for the pervasive Lord, whose essence consists solely of knowledge and action, as well as for the multitude of individual souls (*aṇu*); it serves only to destroy their true nature. Furthermore, there is a distinction between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*), while their oneness is established through inherence (*samavāya*).
This was not stated by you like the disciples of Kaṇabhuj;
for it is impossible to cover [an object] with something that is either formless or possessed of form. Likewise, even when there is movement, knowledge [proceeds] by means of the rays of the eyes.
And why is that very same impurity, being material, not perceived by knowledge? Therefore, since [the Self] is all-pervading, why would it not possess omniscience with respect to everything?
Furthermore, the obscuration of light by darkness occurs through things that are resistant to it.
For material things, such as atoms of light, there is resistance; however, for that which is immaterial, it cannot be so.
Furthermore, the impurity (mala), being insentient and not independent, is incapable of veiling the conscious Self. Nor can it be said that the example of the veil over mead [is applicable here].
"You yourselves have stated this: an insentient being is not an agent by itself.
Indeed, these powers of the independent Lord are the impellers.
Therefore, [the soul] is impelled by the force of the Lord's power, which knows the ripening of karma. (9.79b–80b)
Wine produces intoxication, which consists of the fruits of pain, pleasure, and delusion;
for if the impurity (mala) were not impelled by the Lord, it would not veil the person (puṃs). Since the person is [then] stainless, such an impelling power of the Lord is not appropriate.
And since their stainless nature is equal, why would they not impel him?
It is logical that with respect to that Lord, there should be a commonality among the many;
therefore, it is merely the freedom of his own essential nature that is manifested as impurity.
This has been determined and explained by me at length elsewhere, so let there be no further elaboration here.

Impurity (*mala*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), nescience (*avidyā*), the manifestation of greed (*lolikā-prathā*), the defect of worldly existence (*bhava-doṣa*), the raft (*anuplava*), exhaustion (*glāni*), withering (*śoṣa*), and delusion (*vimūḍhatā*).
The fear of the notions of "I" and "mine," the power of Māyā, and the veil; the seed of defects, the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), and the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra—
by such etymological designations as these, this [power] is described here and there.
When this exists, existence arises; because its nature is that of differentiation, it is the "defect of existence" (bhavadoṣa).
Since it carries the stream of suffering like a raft on a bed, it is therefore [called *bhava*].
The remaining words are easy to understand; one should infer the appropriate meaning therein.

Karma is the cause of saṃsāra; it is called the sprout of saṃsāra. Since the fourteenfold diversity of beings arises from karma, for this very reason, in the teachings of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and so forth— [88–89]
The renunciation of "I" and "mine" is taught for the sake of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
For one who is actionless, even when the root impurity called ignorance remains,
there is no upward movement nor downward movement due to the absence of a cause for diversity.
Merely due to limitation, not yet touching non-duality with Śiva,
he is called a *vijñānakevalin*, established in pure consciousness alone. He, however, through the will of Śambhu, realizes non-duality with Śiva.
Gradually, assuming the form of the Lord of Mantras and his leaders, he attains the nature of Śiva.
[Objection: But if impurity (*mala*) is the cause of this karma, how is it that it does not produce a continuity of karma even for the *vijñānākala*? 93–94a.

"Not so; for how could that impurity be the cause [of its own destruction] while it is about to be destroyed in the *jñānākala*? The state of being in the process of destruction arises solely from [the Lord's] sovereignty. Now, regarding the three states known as 'about to be destroyed,' 'being destroyed,' and 'destroyed'..."
Within the ten stages, which possess internal subdivisions according to their own sequential order,
there is the conceptualization of the states of Vijñānākala, Mantreśa, Tadīśa,
and so forth. Furthermore, the manifold variety [of these states] will be explained with respect to the sleeping (supta) and the fourth (turya) states.
Therefore, since its own power has become blunted by the tendency toward destruction,
how can it be said that impurity (*mala*) becomes the cause of action (*karman*)? Moreover, even action does not arise from impurity, because action consists essentially of activity (*kriyā*).

And action arises from sovereignty in the form of agency, not from impurity (mala). As for its status as "action" (karman), which consists in its yielding diverse fruits—that is well-known [in the world] and cannot exist without contraction within the self; and that [contraction] is indeed impurity (mala).

For one conceives of the diverse and differentiated fruit as an object of enjoyment; therefore, this establishment in the form of duality resides within the Self, the enjoyer. Thus, it serves as a cooperative cause in the production of its own effects.
Impurity (*mala*) is the cause of action (*karman*) by way of manifesting its capacity. [Objection:
But if this is so, since action exists, impurity must also persist; how then can there be the state of a *vijñānākala*? [Response: For such a contraction indeed exists for him.
"Not so;
even one whose contraction has not been destroyed abandons the latent impression of action by means of firm contemplation, thinking 'I am not the doer.
That firm state within the self which thinks, 'This action will bear fruit'—[it is this that must be overcome]."
That latent impression (*saṃskāra*) leads to a fruit in this world, but it is not the cause of memory.
Even when the contraction [of ignorance] has not been destroyed, because of the cultivation of the thought "I am not the agent," there is no fruit;
nor is there fruit for one who is intoxicated or deluded, or when an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed.
"Whatever austerity has been performed by me today, let that clearly belong to him"—
for one who possesses such an intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), action does not bear fruit according to that intention. Thus, mental action is a refinement (*saṃskriyā*) known as "intention."
One who effects [the ritual] colored by the fruit is fit for the attainment of that fruit; however,
he who, even in that state, relinquishes the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the fruit with firmness,
enjoys a distinguished fruit brought about by that very renunciation of the fruit.

He who, by this sequence, should cast off the entire continuity of karma with a state free from egoism—even if he is still subject to contraction—he becomes partless (akala). [Objection: But in this way, would not some misdeed of one's own persist due to one's underlying intention?
You have not understood the truly authoritative word regarding another:
if that agent were to possess an intention toward another just as he does toward himself,
then that evil deed would necessarily belong to the other as well.
When one's own intention becomes firmly established through the awareness of another's intention, [the result follows].
However, in the absence of such an intention, there is no connection with the fruit for him.
The conviction that "this is not my misdeed" is rooted in that [ignorance], and it leads to no fruit [of the action].
When the intention to deceive another is severed and there is no intention on one's own part,

the fruit would not accrue to either of the two, because the cause for destruction is established [as absent]. This is because his intention is common to both the cause of pleasure and the pleasure itself.

Even from the perspective of being indistinguishable [from other subjects], it is logical that one is the enjoyer of the fruits of dharma and so forth. However, the general intention—"May suffering or the cause of suffering be mine"—does not exist; therefore, there is no acquisition of adharma.

We shall now speak of that which pertains to the *jñānākala*, as previously described: because of his state of being devoid of the sense of "I" (*anahaṃyutā*), all latent impressions of karma (*karmasaṃskriyā*) have dissolved.
Therefore, he possesses no karma whatsoever that could serve as a cooperative cause for anything.

Let impurity act; by that, this [individual] undergoes destruction. But one whose impurity has been cast off, having been brought under the sway of the internal immersion into Śiva—even though intent on the sense of "I"—does not fall into a state of existence dependent on karma.
And this very point was stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"They maintain that impurity (*mala*) is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence;
it consists of merit and demerit in the form of karma, characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth. (9.120–121)
One should discern pleasure, pain, and so forth as one's own effects by virtue of their being causes. For a cause never exists anywhere without its own effect;
this causality is simply a fitness characterized by the state of following immediately upon the fruit.
Furthermore, how is it that the former [action] serves as a cause through a continuous succession?
It is inferred from the fact that, even when the visible causes are identical, pleasure, pain, and so forth appear in diverse ways;
therefore, there must be some other cause, and that is seen here to be karma.
When qualities such as clarity or roughness arise in one's own body through one's own action,
it is observed that this is caused by karma residing in another body;
for even here, the fruit of karma is clearly seen to reside in yet another body.

Agricultural work occurs in the spring, enjoyment in the autumn, and that other [activity] in the body; this is because there exists a single unifying subject. That very person for whom there was past karma experiences its diverse fruit.
Even a drunken king, if he were to command his cook in the morning,
"Feed [him] such [a meal]," would obtain that result even without conscious intent;
in this same way, karma acquired in another birth bears fruit today through the absence of conscious intent.

One enjoys the fruit even without [the immediate presence of] the cause; for in that case, the stability of the prior [cause] is the reason. Therefore, karma already performed may be neutralized by subsequent action, by austerity, or by knowledge, before it is ready to ripen into its fruit.

Furthermore, regarding that karma which has already begun to bear fruit within this body, how can it be dealt with? (9.130) It cannot be obstructed once it has reached its final stage; as for any other karma—whether present or from the past—it remains right there in that very body. (9.131)
That karma can be rendered impotent by means of knowledge, initiation, and so forth;
for the firmness of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) leads to the firmness of the fruit.
Whenever [the fruit] would perish, at that very moment the karma is destroyed.
Therefore, even if one who is under the sway of delusion has done nothing at all, nevertheless, at the time of [attaining] knowledge, all of that is utterly consumed.
And it is said in the venerable *Parā*: "One who possesses the vision of all things is neither a taker nor a giver."
In a mere moment, it would burn away everything—both the unperformed and the performed—that resides within the body.
The phrase "residing in the body" means that [the consciousness] has assumed identity with the body. It is consciousness itself that is said to be independent; when situated there, karma is consumed.

And that [attainment] comes from abandoning the latent impression of identifying with the body, through abiding in the state of being the self of the universe (viśvātmatā). For whatever refinement (*saṃskriyā*) there may be regarding that which is beyond time, all-pervasive, and non-dual, it is in fact only contraction; and by this [refinement], even that [contraction] consists of identification with the body.
This is declared to be the impurity of karma (kārmamala), along with which the *layākalas* remain within the depths of the cave like sleeping serpents. Then,
their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) awakened, they receive their appropriate lot.

Within this [universe], from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects, beings transmigrate again and again. However, those who have begun the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of destroying the latent impressions of karma (*karmasaṃskāra*), yet have met their end before reaching the perfection of that contemplation, [remain in a state of transition].

Through the excellence of the ripening of their internal contemplation of that [reality], they attain the state of being Mantras; from the wondrous, they proceed to even more wondrous ritual actions. Of this *kārmamala* (the impurity of action), which extends throughout the path ending with Māyā, there is this [extent].

Pradhāna is declared to be the primary cause, while the impurity (mala) consisting of ignorance belongs to the individual souls (aṇavaḥ). The agitation of this [impurity] known as *lolikā* clearly exists by virtue of being a cooperative cause; and that [agitation], which is the orientation toward the state of desiring to remain [in bondage], occurs through the power of the Lord’s will.
Since an insentient thing is never capable of anything without being presided over by consciousness,
that which is called an "atom" (aṇu) is not something other than the Great Lord, whose nature is light.
The individual soul (pudgala), the knower of the field (kṣetravid), and the bound beast (paśu) appear as having both conscious and unconscious forms.
Because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it is all-pervasive; therefore, it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and devoid of action (*niṣkriya*).
It is described as eternal, seeking the means of yoga, and free from physical form.
Due to its lack of mind (*acittva*), there arises ignorance, as well as duality from the object of enjoyment and from other subjects.
That impurity of those atoms is awakened intensely by the power of the Lord’s will;
thus it is stated in the scripture named Śrīpūrva:
“By the power of the Lord’s will, the desire for experience arises in him.”
For the sake of bestowing enjoyment and grace upon those who desire it, the primordial Mantramaheśvara,
having agitated *māyā*, fashions the manifold cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
And what is called *māyā* is indeed the power (*śakti*) of the Lord, inseparable from him.
For in that way, He has brought about the sovereignty of the manifestation of duality; indeed,
that which was the primordial manifestation of duality,
not yet having reached division, is the supreme Night, in which the infinite manifestations yet to come are held within.
She is insentient because her nature is one of differentiation, and since her effect is also insentient;
she is all-pervasive because she is the cause of the universe, subtle because she is inferred solely through her effects;
and due to her inseparable connection with Śiva’s power, she is eternal, unitary, and the primordial cause.

Just as every effect, such as a jar, is insentient and manifold in nature, so too is the Pradhāna; therefore, it is an effect and not the sentient Self. For this very reason, it was previously stated that Māyā exists in two ways along the path.
Just as the Māyā-śakti of the Lord assumes a differentiated state,
so too does the other expansion of principles beginning with Kalā;
it consists of the kindling of a limited capacity for action in one whose power has been obstructed.
The power of the Lord, situated below the Person (puruṣa), is called Kalā because it casts [him] down;
in this same way, these principles beginning with Vidyā and ending with Earth are,
in the ultimate sense, composed solely of Śiva’s power, according to the logic already stated.

Nevertheless, that which appears as a separate manifestation of *kalā* and the other categories through the will of the Lord— therefore, because they are insentient, products, and established as distinct principles, Māyā is traditionally held to be their material cause (*upādāna*), and in some cases, it is even considered to be their effect.

In the same way, a form variegated by appearances, though mutually exclusive [in its parts], appears within conceptual thought; indeed, that which shines forth exists externally, like a jar. We assert the existence of things such as sky-flowers for this reason, so there is no deviation [from our principle].
A sky-flower depends upon time, direction, and a subject, yet it does not exist according to the word "non-existent.
In the same way, absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) should be analyzed like the earth and other elements.
Whatever is conceived in that manner, its external form exists as a conscious being.
From Caitra up to Sauśiva, all that possesses a body of such a nature;
as is the body of one, so is the external city of that same kind.
Therefore, the sequence of worlds extends up to Suśiva.

Having reached that city as their own, [the souls] are like other locations because they are spatial entities. (9.163b) Consequently, the status of the souls as travelers and enjoyers of the path is established without effort.
That Māyā, having undergone agitation, gives birth to the universe on all sides. (9.164)
Just as the fruits of an *āmalakī* tree fall when struck by a staff,
even so,
within the multitude of principles (*tattva*) which are the effects of *māyā*, there exists a mutual relationship of cause and effect due to the appearance of such variegated sequences.
Although that [nature] is clearly seen in many ways in other scriptures, nevertheless,
we shall explain it according to the perspective of the *Mālinīśāstra*.
That which they describe as being within *māyā*, from *kalā* down to the earth (*vasudhā*), [is here explained].
This [world] is indeed distinct for each individual soul due to the differentiation of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
even within a single world, which is a collection of the means for experience, how could there be a difference in experience if the manifestation of pleasure and the rest were uniform? (168–169)
Nor does this [unity] occur through a division of karma, because such a division is itself impossible for that [consciousness]. Therefore, the group beginning with *kalā* is indeed distinct at times,
yet it attains unity through the will of the Lord, as in the case of dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Among all these principles (tattvas), beginning with Kalā, which are yet to arise,
there exists purity for those who have been purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta).
For when Kalā is pure, it gives rise to a corresponding state of action (karmatva).
By this [means], even though it is limited, one is quickly liberated from this saṃsāra.
