Having declared, "In this way, [the self] is pure," the omnipresent Guru spoke thus regarding the pride and praise [of the Self] in relation to passion (rāga), ignorance (avidyā), time (kāla), necessity (niyati), primordial nature (prakṛti), the senses (akṣa), and the collection of objects (artha). (AbhT 9.172b–173)
In this way, the emergence of the principles beginning with *kalā* is analyzed:
from the principle of *māyā*, *kalā* is born, characterized by limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*).
For *māyā* effects a separation of the bound soul (*paśu*) from Śiva, who consists of pure consciousness.
For that very reason, [the soul] becomes as if in a state of deep sleep, devoid of vision and action.

For *kalā* gives birth to a limited capacity for agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*) for the atom (*aṇu*) through its embrace; and when there is a mutual coloring (*añjana*) between that *kalā* and the atom, it brings forth [that agency].
For when there is a separation from the male principle arising from the initiation that grants immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), that [female power],
though still clinging, does not produce her own fruit anywhere;
she is like the first stage of swelling or like the subtle state of a sprout.
Just as water, fire, earth, moisture, and husks cause the germination of a seed through their conjunction, so too this *kalā*—

though born from the conjunction of *māyā* and the individual soul (*aṇu*)— does not make the soul itself subject to modification; rather, it makes *māyā*, which is inherently changeable, the material cause for such modification.

Impurity (*mala*) is the concealer; *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of objective existence; and *karman* acts as the auxiliary cause for the arising of pleasure and pain. Therefore, it performs the function of strengthening the consciousness that has been obscured.
Kālī alone, though insentient, is impelled by the power of Anantanātha. Nor does the Lord’s own power itself bestow consciousness upon her;
for that [insentient Kālī], even when strengthened by it, would not attain the state of being an agent.
This *kalā* is not a primary instrument like *vidyā* and the others;
rather, since it acts as the agent through its role as an instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the male subject (*pums*), who is the actual agent, it is so designated.
When there is thus no perceptible interval between the male subject and the *kalā*, [the state of liberation occurs].
When there is internal knowledge of the interior of Māyā, Garbheśa, Śakti, and so forth, then,
through the destruction of all karma, the discrimination between Māyā and the individual soul (puruṣa) occurs;
one attains the state of a Vijñānākala, and the soul does not go further down below Māyā.

Even when the distinction between intellect and the person (puruṣa) is known, and the difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa is realized, one would not necessarily have one's karma exhausted; for that [exhaustion] can only occur within the Kalā-tattva.
Therefore, according to the Sāṃkhya view, one who has attained perfection does not transmigrate below Pradhāna.
But when there is a discernment between the limited power (kalā) and the person (puruṣa), one does not descend below Māyā.
Seeing the Self as distinct from impurity (mala), however, one attains the state of Śiva.
And in all cases here, the descent of the Lord’s power (aiśvara-śaktipāta) is the auxiliary cause.

The one presiding over *māyā* and the *garbhādhikāra* belongs to both [the *kalās*], while at the end [of the series] is the stainless one (*nirmala*). This *kalā* is indeed inferred to be distinct from the others due to the difference in its effects. Otherwise, the entire universe would become a single effect, which would result in the negation of other [distinctive] causes.
Thus, that power (*kalā*) which is proclaimed in the *Mataṅga-śāstra* and other texts,
having projected agency by way of its being "something" (*kiṃcid-rūpa*),
how could that agency be characterized as "something"? (190–191)
From that state of ignorance, it produces the *vidyā* (limited knowledge) whose nature is partial cognition;
that *vidyā* perceives the intellect (*buddhi*) as it moves upon the mirror of the intellect,
[perceiving] cognitions such as pleasure and so forth, as well as delusion and the rest, within the sphere of cause and effect.
And situated therein, it discriminates the web of karma by means of its own self.
But how can the intellect, which is intermingled with the *guṇas*, experience happiness through discrimination?
Or how could it even present an object that consists of suffering or delusion?
How can an object, when transferred into the intellect which is like its own clear reflection, become an object of cognition?
Without that [intellect], it cannot; and that [intellect] too requires another instrument within the agent, the person (puruṣa).
But surely, from the object situated in the intellect—which is like a bright mirror reflecting on both sides—[cognition occurs].
An object shines because of the light of the subject; do not say that it is a reflection of that [light].
For the primary manifestation of this [object] is indeed its being insentient, and the light of the subject is its illumination.
Why then have you made this conceptualization regarding that which exists as if external to the intellect?
This is the ground of non-differentiation, yet differentiation is investigated here.
Therefore, the state residing in the intellect is the domain of the instrument of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the reflection of objects is what is to be known; from that arises the conceptualization of the intellect.
Since it performs some slight action, there must certainly be another principle beyond that;

this is declared to be the *rāga-tattva* (the principle of attachment), which acts as a coloring agent precisely upon that [will]. Nor is it merely the absence of dispassion (*avairāgya*), because even there it functions through the mode of active attachment.
Even for one who is detached and satisfied, because a subtle attachment still persists,
Time (kāla) therefore imposes this agency through measures such as *tuṭi* and the rest.
Agency that is delimited by its effects, Time will necessarily impose [its divisions].
Necessity (niyati) bestows the connection within the distinguished sphere of effects.
This quartet— knowledge (vidyā), attachment (rāga), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla)—
resides in the state of the enjoyer as the effect of limited agency (kalā), fulfilling the nature of being an enjoyer.

Māyā, kalā, rāga, vidyā, kāla, and niyati—these are said to be the six coverings (kañcukas). While consciousness remains within them, one is a bound soul (paśu). Indeed, it is the cognition of objects of knowledge, such as the body and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), that constitutes [the state of bondage].
This contraction of the sixfold group, which is unperceivable, is the individual soul (*aṇu*).
This has been stated in the *Śivatanuśāstra* once more, by way of a different formulation:
"The obscuration, which pervades all souls, is impurity; though it is distinct, it appears as if non-distinct. (9.206)

Since she is to be consumed by the networks of rays from the fire of Śiva, she is indeed of a different nature [from him]; yet, because she colors [the soul] with her own self through a state that has no prior existence, she is therefore non-different [from him]. For the soul (aṇu) who possesses innate impurity, there are three kinds of coverings (kañcuka) provided by Īśvara and Guha.
For that [soul], which is as clear as a second mirror, a subtle *kalā* is assigned.
By means of this, the bound soul (*paśu*) becomes capable of experience.
And for him, *vidyā* arises from *kalā*, like the light of a lamp within a shelter.
That which distinguishes the experience of pleasure and pain for the bound soul (paśu) through differentiation,
and from which passion arises— like a dye on a clean cloth— from the principle of *kalā*,
is that by which one does not wish to abandon the bliss of the experience of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*).
Thus, defiled by ignorance and empowered by the force of the sheath of the three *guṇas*,
the bound soul (*paśu*) falls helplessly headlong into the dense interior of worldly experience.
By this, the impurity (*mala*) of the individual soul is described as being like the husk of a grain, while *kalā* and the other [sheaths] are like the chaff.
Thus, regarding the principle called *kalā*, which is characterized by limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*),
agency has been discussed first in relation to the subject (*bhoktṛ*) within its specific aspect;
that which arises from this [principle] is the "limited portion" (*kiñcidbhāga*) here, acting as a qualifier.
Kalā gives birth to Pradhāna, which is clearly differentiated as the mere object of cognition.
Indeed, Kalā brings forth both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer simultaneously,
for through its intent toward differentiation, it produces them inseparably from one another.
There would be no state of being the enjoyer and the enjoyed due to their mutual separation;
and when that [state] has dissolved, there would be nothing at all for this Māyā either.
But surely, in the venerable Raurava and other scriptures, the dyad consisting of Passion (rāga) and Knowledge (vidyā) is taught?
For Kalā produces [the effects] simultaneously; therefore, the established doctrine is that it is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
It has been stated here that this sequence indeed appears to be true, for it is sufficient:
one who is being colored perceives everything, and even while knowing, one is colored therein.
Nevertheless, we have here established this reality of the thing-in-itself;
and in that [reality], there can be no sequence whatsoever, or even if there were, it would be the reverse.
Therefore, one should not entertain any misconception regarding the procedure taught in the scripture.

Thus, that which is merely the object of cognition, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—because it will be experienced as such, it is said from the outset to be of the nature of equilibrium (*sāmya*). Pleasure is *sattva* because of its luminosity; luminosity is said to be joy.
Passion (*rajas*) is suffering because its nature is activity; for activity is the sequence of that [passion] and its opposite.
Delusion (*moha*) is darkness (*tamas*), which is obstructive due to its association with the absence of light.
When these qualities (*guṇas*) have entered a state of agitation, they extend forth their effects.
For that which is undisturbed, this heterogeneous effect could not have existed previously;

thus it has been stated in this scripture. The wise know the qualities (guṇas) to be a distinct principle (tattva), and here a separate world is shown according to the differentiation of the qualities.
For the sake of making the individual soul (puruṣa)— which is agitated by the power of the Lord’s will and characterized by a longing for experience—
an independent Lord violently stirs up primordial nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, as for that objection raised by the Sāṃkhya— “Why does she [not stir it] with respect to a liberated soul?”— [it is answered as follows].
Because the Spirit (puruṣa) is subject to transformation, it gives birth [to the intellect]; thus, there is no contradiction here.
From the qualities (guṇas) arises that principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), which is entirely stainless;
therefore, the light of the Spirit, being an object of knowledge here, attains the state of being reflected therein.

And the reflection of the object produced externally by the senses within that [intellect], as well as the similar [reflection] in cases such as imagination and intuition— which does not have those [senses] as its door—
is the functioning of the intellect; it is awareness, and it is certainly the objective support (ālambana).

This is the awakening to the light of self-awareness; even though it is insentient, it is fully capable [of this] because the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) of the intellect reflects the person (*pums*) produced therein. It is that state of being characterized by the thought "I" within the light when it is sullied by the object of knowledge.

Impelled by that [power] which consists of intense agitation (*saṃrambha*), this fivefold vital breath (*vāyu*) serves for life; otherwise, however, there is death. Therefore, [this occurs] from the nature of the "I" (*ahaṃ*) of the pure Self’s sovereignty.

"This other [nature], however, is different from the uncreated," so it is said by means of the word "creation" (kṛti). Thus, this aggregate of instruments (karaṇaskandha) of the ego (ahaṃkāra) has been described; its aggregate of natures (prakṛtiskandha) is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic.

From the *ahaṃkāra* dominated by *sattva*, which clearly touches upon the aspect of the enjoyer, the group of six consisting of the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the five senses is born; however, their distinction is now being explained.
Since the mind has all things as its object, it is intended here [to be distinguished] by that very quality.
The capacity to produce all the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) is the defining characteristic of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*).
They say that intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*), and mind (*manas*) function respectively in discernment, exertion, and desire;
they are the instrument which is not performed by the external deities, nor even by those turned inward.
Prāṇa is not the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), because it is insentient and because [the internal organ] is of the nature of impelling;
this is certain, since [the internal organ] is the cause of the factors of effort, desire, and cognition. Furthermore, determination, self-conceit, and conceptualization are not mere activity.

Since [the intellect] is of a single form, its threefold nature is clearly established within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Furthermore, the intellect is not imperceptible because it is an instrument, just like the mind; thus, the doctrine that the intellect is imperceptible like the *pradhāna* is abandoned.

The ego-principle (ahaṃkṛti) which is characterized by having the subtle element of sound as its cause is the instrument (karaṇa) for the sense of hearing; likewise, that which is declared to have the nature of smell as its cause functions up to the sense of smell.
Therefore, let it be established that these senses are elemental (bhautika), because of this restriction regarding their respective objects.
In cognitions such as "I hear," "I see," and "I smell," the nature of being derived from the *ahaṃkāra* (the I-maker) is clearly established because of the persistence of the sense of "I. Therefore,
its status as an instrument is logical, due to its connection with a portion of the agent.
The instrument is distinct from the agent because it is that which is impelled; how, then, could it be an instrument?
If one were to desire another instrument for that [instrument], there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, through the possession of sovereignty, the agent differentiates his own body.
The Self spontaneously makes its own portion, which touches upon the portion of karma, into an instrument.
By virtue of the contemplation (*tanmayībhāvanā*) that identifies with that portion of itself which has been made an instrument,
it makes even that which is entirely distinct— such as an axe— into an instrument.
Therefore, for him, Vidyā was previously the impure common instrument;
however, regarding cognition and action, Kalā is said to be the common instrument.
But surely, in the venerable Mataṅga and other scriptures, agency is attributed to Kalā?
For when that [agency] exists, knowledge and the other faculties possess the fitness for being instruments.
It is said that agency itself is declared to be the motivator for their status as instruments,
because without it, no other instruments can exist.
Therefore, she is set apart from this group of common instruments;
for without *vidyā*, the other instruments have no inherent existence. And since, without *kalā*, there is no agency in her, there can likewise be no subjectivity.

Then, *kalā* and *vidyā* are known by the wise to be the primary instruments (*karaṇa*) of the person (*pums*). For this very reason, even when [the senses] are sometimes deprived of the organs of intellect and action— as in the case of a blind man or a lame man— the manifestation of form and movement does not fail to appear.
However, by the power of the common sense organs (sāmānyakaraṇa), even when the object of knowledge is of such a nature,
the blind person attains a cognition only of the commonality of form (rūpasāmānya). From that very [ego], however, there is a further [cognition] for one who touches the subtle elements (tanmātra).

The organs of action— speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet— were born. That ego-function (*ahaṃkāra*) which is capable of performing actions, thinking "I speak," "I take up," "I quickly abandon," "I emit," and "I walk," is indeed the organ of action.
Therefore, even for one whose hand has been severed, there exists a hand consisting of the organ of action (*karmendriya*).
The supreme basis of that [organ] is the hand with its five fingers.
Furthermore, as for the grasping that occurs even by means of the mouth, that which functions as the instrument therein is likewise present.
If that [agent] were indeed the hand alone, how could action possibly occur without an instrument?
If such were the case, what would be the purpose of the sense organs of cognition?
Furthermore, it is said that perception depends upon an instrument because it is an action.
It is a matter of wonder that others do not accept the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the case of going;
for movement, upward throwing, and so forth, are perceived as the primary action (*karman*).
Furthermore, in the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), this very [action] is a quality (*guṇa*).

"Action is preceded by the instrument"—by this pervasion, knowledge is preceded by an instrument. To claim that it is not so is clearly a manifestation of blindness. Therefore, they say that the organs of action primarily pervade [their objects] like the sense of touch.
"In that regard, my teachers maintain in the *Matanga* that [the senses] possess their functions within those [elements].
[Objection: "But surely there are many other actions for their sake;
likewise, the instruments (karaṇas) must also be mentioned, and thus there would be no finality regarding the sense organs (*akṣa*). [Reply: ...
"But surely this has been refuted by Kheṭapāla and others:
that the means for accomplishing any action whatsoever would be ineffective. This [refutation] does not serve to quench the fever of our thirst for answers. (AbhT 9.262b–263)
For peacocks are not satisfied by waters that are turbid and mostly lifeless;
this is my answer here, as it was spoken by the illustrious Śambhu, who is the source of all instruction. It is [the state] made powerful by the noble conceptualization of pure self-awareness.

In this context, the one [consciousness] is divided according to the distinctions in the continuity of action (karmānusaṃdhāna). Therein, the continuity is fivefold; hence there are five organs of action (karmendriyas):
for relinquishing, for grasping, for the accomplishment of both, and for the two [others] excluding those two.
For the sake of resting in one's own true nature, there is that fourfold external action;
the organs [of action] are fourfold: the anus, the hands, the feet, and the genitals.
As for the internal action which has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its support, the organ here is indeed speech.
Thus, their various functions in relation to their objects have been briefly described.
Indeed, no action whatsoever is observed apart from these;
for what purpose, then, should this indefinite multiplicity of sense organs be postulated?
This wheel of functions is to be performed by them without confusion; however, the dull-witted perceive a confusion because the senses function simultaneously.
This group of senses has been described as arising from the *rājasa* aspect of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
From the *ahaṃkāra* dominated by *tamas*, which has the nature of obscuring the aspect of the enjoyer,
there arises the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) known as the "origin of the elements" (*bhūtādi*), which are the causes of the gross elements.
This consists of the group of the mind, the intellect, the organs of perception, the organs of action, and the group of subtle elements.
In this regard, the connection with the *rājasa* ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the unifier of the two;
others, however, say that the mind is born from the *rājasa* ego,
for it is swift, impetuous, and capable of moving through all the senses.
Others, however, maintain that from the *sāttvika* [aspect of the ego] arise the internal organ (*svānta*), as well as the organs of cognition and action;
they consider these to be the perceivers and the perceived portions of the *rājasa* [aspect].
But the Kheṭapālas clearly maintain that the group of organs of action [arises from the *tāmasa* aspect].
The ego-sense characterized by *rajas* (the passionate) is born from *rajas*, because it is the nature of *rajas* to be action.
However, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, the mind is said to arise from the *sāttvika* [ego], while all the sense organs arise from the *rājasa*. This appears to us as the most logical position.

For instance, while the external functioning of the senses has the power to manifest their respective objects through mere perception (*ālocana*), the mind (*manas*) possesses the power to internally yoke [them] together.
And it has been stated by the Guru: "The mind, being reflective (*anuvyavasāyin*), should perform [this function]. (AbhT 9.277b–278b)
"The activity consisting of the mother's operation has those two as its objective support.
Thus, the group of "mere-that" (tānmātra) belongs to the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) dominated by darkness (dhvānta).
Regarding this, there is no dispute among anyone that the process of the grasped (grāhya) indeed begins here.

On the earth, within the manifold sphere of fragrances such as the scent of jasmine and others, that which is the universal property of "fragrance-ness" (gandhatva) is indeed named the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra). It is said to be all-pervasive for that very reason; however, because it possesses a cause, it is not eternal.
Dissolution (*tirobhūti*) within its own cause is what constitutes destruction (*dhvaṃsa*); therefore, it is not non-eternal.
This same application should be made for the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with taste and ending with sound.
For the state prior to the specific (*viśeṣa*) is necessarily one of non-specificity (*aviśeṣin*).
The subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), when agitated, provides the various forms of hearing.
Space is sound whose nature is vacuity, because it is capable of supporting the superimposition of the signified.
When that very [space] undergoes agitation through conjunction with the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), [it becomes air].
Through that [process], it attains the state of air; therefore, in this case, it possesses the nature of both sound and touch.
Others, however, say that sound is the sole quality of space (*ākāśa*);
that too is logical, since air does not attain its own form without space.
Since each preceding element resides within each succeeding one,
for that very reason the non-separation of wind and space from one another is taught.
However, sound and touch, together with form, have entered into a state of agitation.
They say that the *tejas*-tattva consists of three qualities, just as before;
with those three plus taste comes water, and with those plus smell comes earth—this is the sequence.
Therein, the accumulation of the qualities beginning with earth is established through direct perception.

The earth does not appear as something distinct from the stream of properties such as odor and the rest. Just as for those who maintain the duality of quality and the possessor of quality, this single variegated form appears on a cloth, so too do the properties appear sequentially upon the earth.
Just as variegated colors appear simultaneously on a spread-out cloth,
even so does the earth manifest in its entirety to yogis. Therefore,
the earth possesses a variegated form, ranging from fragrance to sound.
Due to the diversity of means, this [consciousness] appears through the distinction of succession and non-succession.
For that very reason, the differentiation of cognition is said to be produced by the manifestation of succession.
Likewise, the use of the genitive case and the relationship between the differentiated and the differentiator arise from the differentiation of cognition.
Therefore, there is no such thing here as a "substratum" (dharmin) that exists apart from its attributes (dharmas).
In that regard, there may be various types of smell, form, and taste in the earth; likewise, there is touch produced by maturation (pākaja) that is neither hot nor cold, and sound which is manifold.
Whiteness, sweetness, and coolness, as well as various sounds, are found in water. Whiteness, brilliance, heat, and various sounds are found in fire.
Being unproduced by heating, neither cold nor hot, and possessing various sounds, are the characteristics of wind.

Sound consists of phonemes (*varṇa*) and is a reflection of speech within the ether; as for the claim by the followers of Kaṇāda that "sound is not a quality possessing touch" and so forth—who could accept that which contradicts their own perception? (297–298)
In the case of a drum, that which appears as "sound" is indeed uncontradicted;
yet it is not [the sound] itself because it is perceived as being grasped merely by way of its cause.
And in our view, the sense of hearing has the ego (ahaṃkṛt) as its cause in each respective instance.
Thus, participating in the process of perception, it fully grasps the sound from that location.
As for the one who says that the auditory organ is space, differentiated by its connection with the ear-cavity—
that sound born of sound arrives and produces the cognition of sound.

When even a faint sound of a drum is heard, how is there the perception that "this is the hearing of that [sound]" when it is at a distance? For a sound produced by a sound does not arise from a distant or non-distant location.
For that which has reached the space of the ear, there exists the nature of being distant or near;
yet it is not logical that this initial sound should be so pervasive as to reach everywhere.
However, by this [perceiver], it is heard with an intense character along with those situated at that [distance].
How could it be heard while remaining dull, for it would then be dependent on other properties? This has been refuted by others in many ways;
thus, to labor again is in vain—for who is not wise enough to avoid striking at what has already fallen?
Of these [elements], beginning with Earth, as many groups of principles (tattva-gaṇa) as existed previously,
so much does [the subsequent principle] manifest, pervading them by virtue of its superior qualities. Indeed,
this relationship of the pervaded and the pervader among the principles has been shown.
That [success] is established through the predominance of qualities, not because of causality nor because of parsimony.
For passion is clearly pervaded even by non-causes such as knowledge (vidyā) and the like;
since that which cannot exist without another is said to be "pervaded" by it.
In this regard, there is no such thing as "lightness" within our own philosophical system.
Therefore, due to the superiority of qualities, the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is clearly understood.
For that which is superior in qualities to another is said to be "above" it.
In the venerable *Mālinīvijaya*, the state of being upward-pointing and all-pervasive is clearly explained.

Therefore, beginning from the state of Śiva, the Earth (bhū) shines forth intensely by means of the entire collection of attributes belonging to the series of principles, which remain present as its pervader; it does so by firmly assuming the nature of luminosity within itself.
In this way, even for the elements beginning with water up to the abode of the *śakti-tattva*, there exists a corresponding body [of manifestation].
However, the distinction is that the subsequent element exists as *śakti* itself, whereas the preceding one exists as its attribute (*dharma*).
This has been demonstrated in detail within the *Anuttara-prakriyā*.
Therefore, one who seeks detailed knowledge and is discerning should perceive this from that [source].
(313) Thus has the complete elucidation of the nature of reality been accomplished.
(314) Now begins the tenth chapter of the Śrī Tantrāloka.

It is said: "The single secret of the Trika scripture, which pierces through the categories of reality (tattva), is now declared. Furthermore, regarding these very categories that follow along within their own respective groups, another internal division has been proclaimed here in this scripture called the venerable Trika."

Through the division of the possessor of power (śaktimat) and power (śakti), the series beginning with Earth and ending with Mūla-prakṛti is divided fifteenfold, along with its own essential nature (svarūpa) and the individual soul (anara). The Pralayākala is like Rudra, being diminished by two divisions up to the end of Kalā.
In the same way, Māyā is ninefold; furthermore, the Jñānakalās are sevenfold.
The Mantras are fivefold, their Lords (Mantramaheśvaras) are threefold, and the Lords of the Mantreśas are threefold.
Śiva, however, is not divided, being composed of the dense consciousness of His own singular self-luminosity.
Śiva, the Mantramaheshvaras, the Mantras, Akala, and Kalī—these seven are the possessors of power (śaktimant), while their powers (śaktis) are likewise fourteen.
Their own essential nature is the fifteenth; thus, that ground consists of fifteen aspects.

For thus, three powers of the Lord were described previously; these very same [powers] are established here as the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. Herein, the aspect of Parā is the form of the knower (mātṛ), and the aspect of Parāparā is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
The object of measurement is the Supreme, consisting of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān) and Power (Śakti), which is one's own essential nature (svarūpa).
Among these, the essential nature of the earth-element is that which exists separately as insentient matter,
uncolored by limiting adjuncts such as the subject (mātṛ) and the means of knowledge (māna).

The state of being known by this [individual] through the subjects (mātṛkāḥ) beginning with the Sakala and ending with Śiva constitutes its sevenfold divisions; these are formed by the possessors of power whose powers are not yet manifest. When the powers of those beginning with the Sakala and ending with Śiva have become predominant, [these seven distinctions arise].

There are seven divisions produced by the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*); thus, there are fourteen [divisions] in total. That portion of the means of knowledge belonging to the *sakala* (the limited subject), which consists of *vidyā* and *kalā*, is of a general nature; it is reckoned as the power (*śakti*) itself, but not its specific subdivisions.

For the *layākala*, that very same portion of the means of knowledge (*māna*) is supremely manifest. For the *jñānākala*, however, the means of knowledge is one in which the veil of the *kalā* of *vidyā* is dissolving,
and it is joined with the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the destruction of the *kalana* of impure *vidyā*.

When pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is about to awaken, it becomes the instrument for the protection of those who are to be saved. Once fully awakened, pure knowledge is conjoined with that residual impression (*saṃskāra*).
It serves as the means of cognition for the Lords of Mantras; when devoid of that residual impression, it [functions] for others.
The instrument of the Mantra-Maheśvaras is said to be their power (śakti). That divine power of will, which exists as pure sovereignty, is the very instrument of Śiva; through it, he knows and acts.
From Śiva down to the Sakala [level], those seven Mothers are twofold;
because their powers are either latent or predominant, that distinction constitutes the differentiation of the objects of knowledge.
For indeed, what is called "knowability" is the very innate nature of an entity.
In the cognition "I know what is to be known by Caitra," what is it that actually appears here?
[Objection: Is it not the case that here only the consciousness belonging to Caitra is manifest? [Reply:
No; rather, a property called "knowability" (vedyatā) appears as belonging to the object, just like its blueness.
If the property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) were an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity,

then it would be cognizable by everyone, just like the properties of a jar, blue color, and so forth. Or, if it possesses the property of being an object of cognition by virtue of the power of the cognizer’s consciousness (*vedakasamvitti*), [then...]
Even so, this fault remains, like a cloth produced by a weaver.
If that property called "knowability" were itself unknowable, it would be like a flower in the sky;
if it is knowable, then there too must be another "knowability," leading to an infinite regress.
Consequently, nothing would be perceivable, and the entire world would be as if in a swoon. [Objection:
But surely, let it be said that the form [of consciousness] is embellished by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the knower. [Reply: That is not so;
for while the nature of an entity consists in the manifestation of its object—just like cognition—this [embellishment] is unreal.
If it were cognizable by a single knower, it could not be cognizable by other knowers;
if it were cognizable by all knowers, it could not be cognizable by a single knower.
Therefore, there is no such thing as "cognizability" that constitutes an inherent property of an object.
The very emergence of consciousness is the perceptibility of an object;
for in that case where cognition, having the form of grasping an object, inheres within itself,
the object to be manifested is perceptible only in relation to that [cognition].

To this we reply: if knowability were not the inherent property (*dharma*) of objects, then those objects would remain unknowable even when knowledge has been described, just as the broad base and other features of a jar remain [unperceived] despite the existence of the jar itself. (AbhT 10.28b–29b)
A cloth that does not possess the nature of those [qualities] does not attain the form of having a broad base and so forth;
likewise, even though cognition exists as inherent in the cognizer,
how could entities whose nature is unknowable ever attain the state of being known?
Behold this very great disadvantage:
that the object itself is of the nature of light, while its consciousness is not manifest, and its substratum is likewise unmanifest;
the same applies to the mind, the lamp, the eyes, and so forth.
What indeed is this so-called "manifestation" when the entire world is asleep? Is it not the very nature of cognition to manifest objects, just like a lamp?
Therefore, we shall dance for joy at this unprecedented discovery!
Let that nature of cognition which consists in the manifestation of the object be examined:
(34) Is the object the manifestation, or is the manifestation the object, or is it cognition itself? Or is it said that its nature is that which is the manifestation of the object? (35)

If the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is used in the sense of the agent (kartari), the aforementioned fault remains difficult to remove. If, on the other hand, this genitive is used in the sense of the object (karmaṇi), then the meaning of the causative suffix (ṇyartha) is already present in the mind.
To demonstrate this, we ask: does light illuminate itself?
Although it is unmanifest, it is not as if it were nothing at all.

If one asks, "In that case, how is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) explained in the world regarding the state of consciousness?"— the primary domain of the causative suffix is [consciousness], whereas in insentient things it is metaphorical.

For instance, even though Caitra is capable of going, because his movement depends on another, he says, "I have been sent by my master," while fully aware [of the situation]. Likewise, the master, having recognized Caitra's capacity for movement, clearly perceives his own independence.
Perceiving [the agent's intention] and fearing [his own] withdrawal, he says, "I am going.
In this way, there is a fundamental connection with the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) between the one who is impelled and the impeller;
based on that intention, others in the world also conduct their affairs accordingly.
In the expression "he causes the arrow to go," one who considers himself the impeller becomes so only figuratively by imparting a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as momentum (*vega*).
In the expression "the wind causes the mountain to fall," both [the wind and the mountain] are insentient.
By observers, these two are conceptualized as having the nature of the impeller and the impelled.
In such a relationship with an insentient object, the primary sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not applicable.
Let this matter rest; I have already explained it at length elsewhere.
This manifestation with respect to an object would therefore be a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
If it is granted that [the object] shines forth, then it must be that very [object], like a falling mountain.
Indeed, a metaphorical designation occurs only by means of some underlying cause (*nimitta*).

In the case of the statement "the wind causes it to fall," the cause is the action performed by that [wind]. By means of this [action], the object undergoes a fall from the mountain due to the destruction of its conjunction [with the mountain].
But here, in the case of knowledge, that [knowledge] does nothing at all to the object.
How indeed could that metaphorical designation (upacāra) exist, for it too must concern a non-existent thing? For an object that is not actually manifest is metaphorically treated as being manifest.
Is a child of such a nature [as fire] ever burned by the metaphorical application of the term "fire"?
In the case of a child, when one metaphorically attributes "fire" to him, the basis for that—such as sharpness and so forth—is indeed real.
But what is the basis for the metaphorical attribution of "light" (prakāśatva) in which such reality exists?
For such a metaphor is clearly appropriate only when consciousness is established as a reality.
That [superimposition] also consists of mental projection (*adhyāropa*), and its life-force is the act of synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*).
Yet, even now, there exists no consciousness whatsoever; this [synthesis] is not even a cognition.
It is unmanifest to another, and even if it were manifested by that other, the same rule would apply.
"But surely a lamp is the illuminator of form; how can it be so? (52) "In this case as well, why do these logical constructions not apply?
For a lamp illuminates a form according to its own nature. (53)
Such [an object] shines forth by itself, yet our cognition does not shine in that same way.
Furthermore, this lamp sufficiently bestows the state of being manifest upon entities;
otherwise, they would not be manifest. And such a rule applies even in the case of non-difference.
Therefore, this aforementioned supreme Śiva is indeed Light alone.
In whatever way He manifests, that very thing clearly appears as the body of an entity.
And thus, that which is called "blueness" manifests in a certain manner.
In the same way, the state of being an object of cognition (vedyatva) shines forth, and that follows upon the aspect of the objective entity (bhāva).
Therefore, there are two [results]: the manifestation of the object and consciousness (saṃvit).
Furthermore, these two are mutually connected and protected from their opposites.
For instance, a thief who is on guard clearly perceives, "This is known by Caitra";
having understood this, he does not immediately seize it, even though he is overcome by the desire to possess it.
Likewise, [the woman thinks], "She looks at me with a sidelong glance from the corner of her eye" with great affection.
The lover perceives his own body as if sprinkled with nectar;
yet this is not merely a cognition of knowledge following upon a portion of an objective entity.
If that [perception] performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*), what indeed could it be other than a real property (*dharma*)?
As for what was said— that an entity possesses the property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*) in relation to everyone—

this [argument] destroys your own position, like a weapon poorly discharged against oneself. But for us, who maintain that there is only the self-luminous state of Śiva, [this objection does not apply].
The very statement that "it shines toward another" does not exist; and as for the statement,
"that blue is toward all [observers], and it is that jar," that too is for the most part unknown, yet it is grasped by those of deluded intellect.
The blueness perceived in the body of Kālāgnirudra is not [inherently] blue;
how then could yours be blue? Let it not be so, for it is not blue.
This [color] is not blue in relation to anyone, nor is it blue in relation to that which stands before it.
To him alone should that [object] be known, ultimately by means of mental construction (saṃkalpa). Just as you assert that knowledge consists in the manifestation of an object,
so too must the state of being knowable by its knower be declared to be the very nature of the entity.
And there is no fixed knower here in this cognition as there is for you.
When each individual is the knower of an object, let that which is to be known be called its form;
let that state of being known by each respective knower shine forth for everyone.
I think that one who urges this [objection] would reach the height of deafness;
for that state of being an object of knowledge does not appear in that way to anyone other [than the subject].
When it is said that "it is the form of an entity," what is this misplaced distress?
By this method of reasoning, infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has been uprooted. For that [regress] is not like [the regress] involving other things such as blue and so forth;
rather, it is the property of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*), by connection with which [the Self] possesses all properties.

The possessor of attributes (dharmin) attains the state of being perceivable, just as existence (sattā) does through its inherence (samavāya). For you assert that existence acts upon both the existent and the non-existent; likewise, inherence, though itself connected, connects those things that partake of both connection and non-connection.

The final particularity (*viśeṣa*) consists in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); it [serves] to exclude those things that are devoid of exclusion. Just as whiteness [excludes] what is not white, and likewise motion [excludes its opposite], so too does the substratum (*dharmin*) itself abide, endowed with its own constituent properties such as blue and the rest.
That which was previously unknowable attains knowability through the attribute (*dharma*) consisting of the state of being knowable;
and this knowability, while manifesting, becomes luminous by virtue of its own self-luminous attribute, just like the attributes of blue and so forth. (75–76a)
If the universe indeed finds its rest in the Light,
then for that which has accomplished all its purposes, there is no further expectation whatsoever from any quarter.
And just as differentiation is manifested by the Lord Śiva through His absolute freedom (svātantrya), [so too does the universe rest within Him].
Just like blue and other such qualities, this property of being an object of cognition (vedyatā) is likewise said to be a property [of the object].
Thus, since the state of being cognizable is established, let it be a property of the entity; what cause for pity is there?
However, this must be considered by all subjects mentioned up to the level of the Sakala.
The state of being an object of cognition would then be of a single form; how, therefore, could there be a fourteenfold division?
It is said in reply: if this nature of the object is described as being perfectly complete, then that is called the all-pervasive Lord Bhairava, the Blessed One himself.

Now, if that sequence of parts and sub-parts were merely imagined through its own inherent majesty, then why would it be tolerated? What, then, is accomplished by this aforementioned conceptualization?
For this very reason, whenever and in whatever form anything appears as such—
Then, that very form [is realized]—this is the supreme secret teaching (upaniṣad).
One knows what is to be known by Caitra, or by two, or even by many;
[one knows it] through the mantra, or by Maheśa, or by Śiva whose power is overflowing.
In whatever manner an object appears through such-and-such [a means of cognition],
it attains an immeasurable variety of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) and so forth;
for indeed, even an entire assembly of people with one-pointed attention [perceives it in that way].

One regards dance and song as an ocean of the shower of nectar. For this very reason, it is said in the instruction on the observation of wrestlers and actors that there is an identity with all subjects, which brings about the experience of the full form.
If they were each individually satisfied with the mere cognition of their respective objects, what collective benefit would there be for them, and how could there be a unity of the subject? However,
when [the object] is infused with the totality of its various attributes of being cognizable...
Then that object is rightly said to be different from its previous dried state;
even in the scripture, such-and-such a state of being perceivable performs a specific purposeful action (arthakriyā),
and this is likewise stated extensively in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*.
In this way, one should contemplate the sixfold path as presided over by him;
for the presiding of the Lord consists in the manifestation of the universe. When known in this manner as being perceivable by the Lord, it accomplishes the task at hand.

Thus, when [an object] is established, the property called "knowability" (vedyatā) appears as belonging to that entity. However, when there is no appearance of it [as an external object], it is called the "own-nature" (svarūpa), clearly dispelling any suspicion of association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 91–92 ||

That form by which an object shines forth from one's own self is its own true nature; in the cognition "I know the jar," [the Self] is devoid of the coloring of being an object of knowledge. It is designated as "the jar alone shining forth in its own nature."
"But surely, in that case, the state of being self-known depends upon the mantras and so forth. (10.94b) "Moreover, it certainly exists; let it be so. But it does not appear as something existent.
The regions beyond Mount Meru, whose form is the fire of time, are indeed unperceivable. (10.95)
In the consciousness "this is mine," the supreme pure reality shines forth. Although it is an object of knowledge because it shines, it does not shine as an object of knowledge.
For its manifestation is indeed non-objectifiable; thus, whom can we question?

In this way, this earth consists of fifteen aspects; likewise do water and the other elements up to the Unmanifest (avyakta). This is because each of these possesses the quality of being an object of cognition for every limited subject (sakala).

"Sakala" (the embodied) is a designation for those characterized by the predominance of the six sheaths; they possess the coverings (*kañcuka*) consisting of the essence of impure consciousness, passion, limited agency (*kalā*), and so forth. Those termed "sakalālaya" (the abode of the sakalas), however, have all their coverings rendered subordinate.

The conclusion is that the Vijñānākala subjects are those whose coverings (kañcukas) have been destroyed. Therefore, even when the primary object of knowledge is present, the person exists as a Sakala subject with the coverings manifest; thus, the state of fifteen-foldness (pāñcadaśya) is established.

The state of being "fifteenfold" (pāñcadaśya) exists even within the Sakala, who is situated within the earth and the rest; for here too, within the object of knowledge, there is indeed a cognizer (mātṛ).
[This is so] because he possesses both contraction, such as being enveloped by gross matter, and expansion, which is the opposite of that.

Yellow and the other [colors], fourteen in number due to their being stable or mobile, reside within the elements beginning with earth (dharā). Then, on the paths of the vital breath and the body, they become insentient by nature; yet, when they partake in the state of the subject (pramātṛtā), these are declared to be the *dhāraṇās* in the *Vijayottara*.

But when the state of being an object (*meyatā*) is attributed to the person who has reached the end of *kalā*, then that portion of the coverings (*kañcuka*) which has arisen is the object; he possesses no subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*).
Therefore, for one known as *sakala* (the "one-with-all-impurities"), true subjecthood does not exist.
The state of being thirteen arises from the exclusion of the duality between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).
Therein, the subject whose coverings (*kañcuka*) have become latent is the *layākala*;
those situated in *māyā* are the *vijñānākala*s and so forth, just as described previously.

In the *māyā-tattva*, which consists of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), even that concealment (*kañcuka*) which is the state of submergence [of the subject] is itself an object of knowledge; for *māyā* is extremely subtle, being one with the concealments.
Therefore, in this context, the *vijñānākala* alone is the knower whose concealments have been removed.

Even when the Akala is immersed in māyā, it is likewise; thus there is an elevenfold nature. When the Vijñānākala is the object of knowledge and is well-established through the destruction of the coverings (kañcukas), the state of being the subject (mātṛtā) belongs only to those mantras whose awakening is about to arise.

When even those mantras become objects of knowledge (*meyā*), then the knower (*mātā*) is their Lord (*tadīśvara*). For he possesses full awakening (*pūrṇabodha*) due to his emergence; yet when that [awakening] reaches the state of being an object of knowledge, he becomes the Knower, the Great Lord of Mantra (*mantramaheśvara*), whose nature is fully emerged.

When that [object] has attained the state of being known, the supreme Śiva, who is self-luminous, becomes the cognizer (*pramātā*); he is one for whom all objects of knowledge are manifested through identity with his own self. Śiva is the cognizer, not the object of cognition, for the nature of an object is to have its manifestation dependent upon something else.
That state of being an object of knowledge does not exist there, for this Lord is self-luminous. If some self-luminous principle were not admitted here, then,
since what is non-luminous could not become luminous, an insurmountable infinite regress would result.
Consequently, the universe would be as if asleep, yet it does not appear so;
for its manifestation is dependent on another, and that other is Śiva.
Since he is self-luminous, what need is there for other displays of logic?
For it was stated from the very beginning that the supreme life-force (*jīva*) of all measures is indeed that [Śiva] himself.

But is there not such a state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) even in Śiva, who is self-luminous? Otherwise, how could there be the conventional usage of "instruction" and "the instructor"?
That [limited subject] is indeed real, having been thus created by the Supreme Lord;
it is led to the level of the Great Lords of Mantra (Mantramaheśvara) and so forth and is established therein.
And being such, it is an object of cognition for those whose consciousness is not yet undivided. (10.118–119ab)
The state of being an object of knowledge is logically impossible for that which is full, due to their mutual contradiction;
likewise, even if it were of the nature of an object, in reality no entity whatsoever could ever abandon its own nature as Śiva. Thus, the cultivation of that [realization] will indeed bear fruit.
In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated by him that Śiva is not divided in his manifest form (*sākṣāt*). By the word "manifestly" (*sākṣāt*), this entire meaning has been made clear.
[An objection: But if Śiva is endowed with a single uniform nature, he would necessarily become subject to that [state of being divided].
Regarding the Great Lord of Mantras (Mantramahānātha), who possesses the three Vedas— what dispute can there be here? Likewise, for the mantras of Maheśvara and Īśa, as well as for the two Kevalins,
each indeed exists with infinite divisions, just like the Sakala [deities].
Therefore, when the object is the *layākala*, there exists a subject who is a *layākala*.
Thus, there would be thirteen [subjects], and not eleven.
Even when the object is known by a *vijñānākala*, there would be another subject who is a *jñānākala*.
In that case, there would be eleven [deities] including the Mother, and certainly not nine;

for if other Lords of Mantras were to arise within the Mantras and their Lords, then because they are objects of knowledge (*vedyatva*), there would be nine, seven, or even five—how could that be? (10.126–127)

It is said: "True, this conceptualization exists; however, just as differentiation is very clear here in the *sakala* state, it is not so in the *akala* and other states. This is clearly because [in those states] there exist such distinctions of infinite internal species of birth. (AbhT 10.127b–128)
This entire fourteen-fold [manifestation] possesses differentiation;
however, in the case of the *layākala*, although that differentiation exists, it arises solely from residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
It is only for the sake of distinguishing the *sakala* from the *akala* that such differentiation is applied.
Even in that [state], there is indeed no difference for those such as the Vijñānakevalas;
rather, it is solely Śiva’s own freedom (*svācchandyamātra*) that unfolds as their differentiation.
Perceiving this intention, he observes the distinction here among the Sakalas and others.
The All-pervasive Lord did not speak of a thirteenth [state] and so forth regarding the *layākala* and others.
Now, one might object: "Let it be that being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) is a property of entities;
however, the *layākala*s do not perceive anything here at all—how then can there be such dependence upon it?"

Listen: while this reality of the oneness of consciousness (saṃvid-ekātmya-tattva) is thus established, consciousness indeed exists even in the insentient; what then need be said of that which is about to be awakened? At the moment of its own awakening, the one who is isolated in dissolution (layakevalin) will indeed awaken.

And his awakening is of two kinds: for the state of mantra and for worldly existence. This occurs through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and other means taught in the systems of the Vaiṣṇavas and others;
thus, he is refined according to his own particularity through the various gradations of lower and higher levels.

When dormant, one attains the state of a mantra, or else the state of its Lord. But those who are devoid of autonomy and forcibly subjugated by delusion awaken from the state of the *layākala* due to their own residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of worldly existence (*bhava*).
Even the *jñānākala* awakens to the state of a Lord of Mantras (*mantreśa*) or a Great Lord (*maheśa*),
or occasionally to the state of a Mantra and so forth, or even to transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*).
For his descent [into various states] differs according to whether he exists as a possessor of discerning knowledge (*vijñānin*) or a yogi.
And it is said that the Lord of the universe, desiring to emit the world, awakened them;
thus, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana*, it is stated that there are eight *vijñānakevalas*.
Therefore, while these two are about to be awakened, they possess the fitness for awakening.
By the power of that [consciousness], knowability here exists precisely through the state of being fit for knowability. For instance, even when her beloved is in deep sleep,
the woman going to meet him does not fail to perceive her own limbs with the thought, "He will see me."
In this way, Śiva also thinks: "Let this [object] be made known to him;
it shall go [to him]," and "I shall create it. At that time, that very capacity is the state of being knowable for that object, and its state of being an enjoyer is likewise coextensive with that.
For the experience of the *layākala* is indeed manifold; by what could it be conceptualized?
For in whatever manner consciousness occurs, that experience is either manifest or unmanifest (144).
Whether it is capable of being remembered or otherwise, it does not, however, forfeit its status as an object of experience.
Even one who is stupefied by deep sleep, his body embraced by his beloved,
is said to be the enjoyer; he too considers himself an enjoyer as before,
even though he is devoid of any mere mental construction (utprekṣā) regarding some noble lady standing before him.
Upon seeing her about to enjoy [the pleasure], he immediately experiences intense joy;
yet, even though he shares the same underlying disposition (*āśaya*), upon seeing her at that very moment, another does not experience it in the same way. What cause for this do we perceive here?

This is well-established in the world as a perception that occurs even without an external cause. When one says, "I am becoming clear," "I am sinking," or "I am extinguished," this differentiation of reality has thus been described in detail.

Due to the mutual distinction between powers (*śakti*) and the possessors of power (*śaktimant*), as well as among the distinctions created by them, and likewise due to the mutual distinctions among those [distinctions] together with other principles (*tattva*),
there is no end anywhere for one who attempts to calculate the primary and secondary divisions.
From that very [source], this manifold arrangement of worlds and so forth is established.
Even though they share the quality of earthiness (*pārthivatva*), there is no equality between the worlds of Rudra and Viṣṇu;
what then need be said regarding other matters, whether it be their experience (*bhoga*) or their essential nature (*svarūpa*)?
Although that detailed account cannot be fully expressed by us in its entirety,
let it nevertheless be discerned as it is being told by way of a mere outline.
When there is mutual differentiation among the seven Mother-Powers (mātṛśakti), [the following occurs].
The form [of the Sakala] consists of forty-nine [principles], and beyond that is its own essential nature (svarūpa).
Since everything has everything as its essence, therefore, within the Sakala-mātṛkā,
there truly exists, in reality, the manifestation of the powers beginning with the Layākala.
But that [undifferentiated state], while remaining unmanifest, would nonetheless be capable of imparting a portion of differentiation;
and among those very differentiations,
there is a manifoldness of mutual distinctions when the primary divisions and sub-divisions are further split by water and the other elements.
The infinity of ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is declared by way of its primary modes of differentiation.
(157) The innate powers of the eyes and other senses of the *sakala* [individual] arise; and when they are suppressed, they clearly manifest yet another variety of differentiation. (158)

In this way, for the *layākala*s and others, another distinction arises either from the intensity (*pāṭava*) or from the exhaustion (*prakṣaya*) of that which is described as their latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Even while remaining in a state of indifference by relying on a suppressed power (*śakti*), [another distinction emerges].
When one knows something as if not having entered [into it], that is indeed a different kind of knowability.

When one knows as if having entered, as if immersed, as if blossoming, and as if reeling, there is another kind of knowability; here, the distinction consists in its suitability for causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
When one power is concealed and another arises quite clearly,

a further distinction should be understood, like the sight of a lute-player [who perceives both the instrument and its sound]. The concealment and emergence of a power may occur through another of its own powers or through something external.
Whether being perceived or unperceived, they manifest a state of manifold diversity.
(10.163b) Thus, whatever state exists among the principles beginning with Earth, even that which is called a "jar," therein the various divisions have been demonstrated. (10.164)
In this case as well, what is called "knowability" is identity with the knowers.
Therefore, this jar, being knowable by all, is indeed the Sakala [state] itself;
until it is knowable by Śiva alone, it manifests as Śiva himself.
For consciousness indeed shines as a single body for as long as [it persists];
now, here, the totality of the entire principle of earth (dharātattva) is shown. The fifteenfold nature previously mentioned is declared here in its entirety.
That light which shines forth as inseparable from the earth-principle (dharātattva) is indeed Lord Śiva; here, the earth is considered to be Brahman.
[This is said] for those who are striving to bestow the supernatural powers (siddhis) residing within the earth-principle.
Those who, by the will of Śiva, impel [others] are the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvara).
Those being impelled, however, are the Lords of Mantra (mantreśa), while the mantras are clearly their designators.
Having practiced yoga pertaining to the earth-tattva through the knowledge of Śiva, [they attain their respective states].
But those who possess a dualistic vision— such as the Pāśupatas, Sāṃkhyas, Vaiṣṇavas, and others—
who have not yet attained the abode of the Fixed (Dhruva) and who experience the state of the Vijñānākala,
undergo dissolution at the end of a kalpa through the enjoyment of those respective levels of reality (tattva). // 171–172a //
Endowed with the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptāvasthā*), they are here the *pralayakevalas*.
For in deep sleep, the dissolution into the *tattvas* is indeed clearly perceived;
otherwise, from what would a fixed perception of dreams arise?
Even the state of deep sleep appears variegated— clear, unclear,
and so forth— as is seen from the diversity of recollections such as "I slept happily. (174) At the very moment one awakens from that subtle sleep, [the variety of experience is evident].
At that very moment, this is [simply] memory; it is not a memory born from a cognition produced by an object.
Therefore, as for what is said by the deluded—that for one who is awakened, there is here and there a memory of the pleasant touch of a mattress and so forth—whence could that be?

In this world, all individuals who have ascended to the level of the earth (dharā) should be known as those whose impurities are turbid, being thoroughly mixed with the manifestation of great karma (māhākarma).
Regarding the performance of their respective functions within this very group of seven:
That very agitation is clearly said to be the group of seven powers (śaktis). For Śiva is of the nature of imperishable consciousness;
as for those three powers of his, by virtue of assuming the form of the grasper through the power of his own freedom, [they become seven].
The three [powers] ending with the Mantras remain as if indifferent; however,
due to the coloring by the form of the object and by virtue of the form of the subject,
those three— ending with Sakala— are considered to be Will, Knowledge, and Action.
Thus, subjectivity here is sevenfold; likewise, its agitation is the state of the means of knowledge (mānatā).
That which is devoid of contact with consciousness in the form of the grasper is pure and insentient—that is its essential nature. In this way, the universe consists of the three aspects.

In this same way, the one of great intelligence should speak of water and the other elements as well, divided by their various distinctions. Following this direction, such differentiation exists for the most part among all distinct categories. This fifteenfold division extends up to the level of the Great Lords of Mantra (Mantramaheśvara).
Nevertheless, because it lacks clarity, this [state], though existing, has not been discussed.

And this was aphoristically indicated by the Creator in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra), where He speaks of the states of waking and so forth through the passage beginning with "by virtue of being the sovereign possessing activity. (10.184–185)
Although Śiva is undivided within, in accordance with the subtle consciousness residing therein, this division—

beginning with the fifteen-fold [division] and so forth— is now being analyzed as it pertains to the network of principles (tattva-jāla) situated within the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti), just as the illustrious Śambhu has instructed.
When the entire object is to be grasped here, there are sixteen moments (*tuṭi*) in the movement of thirty-six finger-breadths,
each calculated as two finger-breadths with a fractional part.
Among these, the first consists of the essence of indivisible flavor, characterized by supreme non-duality.
The second [moment] is perceived as having the nature of the manifestation of the grasper;

however, the final one, due to its identity with the grasped, has attained the state of being the essential nature itself. Indeed, the penultimate moment of the grasper is not to be perceived separately.

Starting from the third moment, that which remains for six moments is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), consisting in the covering of the emerging conceptualizations. The wise know that very state to be the form of Śiva, whose essence is the supreme power (*paraśakti*).
The second middle hexad consists of the state that is both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).

Even this [state], which is the ascent of conceptual thought (vikalpa), has gradually attained full manifestation. In this first hexad, the three goddesses possess the activity of unfolding (pronmeṣa).
Having quickly attained the state of sixfoldness by touching upon the activity of the winking [of the eyes],

they likewise exist in the second hexad; however, here, having reached the stage of coloring through the path of the perceivable (grāhya), they abide in the state of being both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara).

In this first group of six, those goddesses, by virtue of the mere radiance of their own sovereignty, remain undeviating from their supreme nature even when an objective adjunct (*upādhi*) is desired to be grasped. Furthermore, there exists a certain progressive excellence among them as well.
That which is revealed by the wise, who possess the wealth of discernment, even after they have made it manifest;
some, however, knowing that one *tuṭi* belongs to the object and one to the subject,
assign them through identity and recognize seven groups of seven.
Regarding this subtle consciousness, those who strive to discern its nature experience whatever form it takes; what is the use of verbal boastings therein?
(198) Thus, the process pertaining to the vital breath extends from the earth up to the root. (199a)
In the fifteenfold division, [the divisions] are taught according to the succession of the lineage of gurus (guruparvakrama).
However, as the divisions decrease in sequence, there is also a decrease in the *tuṭis*.
In that [state], there is a diminution of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) and the clarity of the non-conceptual (*avikalpin*).
Just as one who has long been afflicted by suffering, having later attained a state of happiness,
forgets that very suffering through the path of resting in bliss; so too do people remain established in pure consciousness even when conceptualization has ceased.

By the power of the cessation of conceptual construction, they no longer conceive of that [empirical] existence. Through the gradual reduction of conceptual construction, consciousness—which is barren of thought—proceeds toward the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*).
Thus, one of keen intellect should strive for focused attention upon that manifestation of the true nature of consciousness.
In the perception of the grasped and the grasper, there is attentiveness toward their relationship;
this is what has been described here and there as the "cow of plenty" (*sarvakāmadughā*), because it fulfills all desires.
In this way, duality after duality is diminished until it reaches the state beyond differentiation.
During that time, two *tuṭis* clearly undergo a gradual diminution.
For this very reason, in the immersion (*āveśa*) into Śiva, it is proclaimed as "two *tuṭis*";
yet there, that single *tuṭi* is full, pure, and absolute.
The second [power] is indeed the form of Śiva’s Śakti, consisting of all knowledge and action;
what is there that the yogi, absorbed in her, does not know or cannot do? (10.207)
And so it has been stated by the illustrious Kallaṭa:

"The attainment of omniscience and omnipotence occurs at the falling away of a *tuṭi*; the subsequent *tuṭi* is the falling away of the [preceding] *tuṭi*. But in the first *tuṭi*, everything is entirely full of oneness."

Once [the state] has gone there, what object of knowledge, or what effect, could possibly remain subject to designation? Therefore, the wise, for the sake of attaining omniscience and other perfections, contemplate the Goddess Pratibhā— the primordial spark that causes the manifestation of duality.
That very power of Śiva is said to exist during the third and subsequent *tuṭis*; then,
the Lords of Mantras and so forth, along with their powers and the Lords of Mantras, arise in succession.
For one who fixes the mind upon those [powers], making it focused on that single quality,
the immersion into each respective accomplishment arises spontaneously.
For this very reason, just as there is a multiplicity of divisions, so too is there distance.

In consciousness, however, due to the abundance of *tuṭis* (moments), it is like the lack of contact between the sense organs and their objects. For, as there is a decrease in the number of *tuṭis* through the reduction of differentiation, so too does consciousness attain extreme proximity, culminating in Śiva.
Therefore, the Śiva-tattva is said to be near from every side;
for this very reason, no effort is required for entry into it.
For as there is greater distance, so too must there be a greater application of effort.
Because of this, those who possess the wealth of the tradition consider that [practices] such as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and ritual instruments (*karaṇa*) have no scope within Śiva.
Indeed, let the world be observed in this regard: just as it is in the perception of a jar or other objects...
Does it appear as if possessing effort in the same way during the experience of pleasure?

They say that this "internality" consists in being characterized by proximity to consciousness; and they define that [proximity] as the unfolding of the nature of consciousness, while externality is its closing.
For those who are to be liberated, even that which is proximate does not appear as such; thus, there is extreme distance.
For indeed, when something distant has become near, its manifestation occurs; how could that be the case here?
Nor is it like the sequence of seed, sprout, creeper, leaf, flower, fruit, and so forth.
This consciousness would be sequential; in that case, the sprout would indeed arise from the seed.
But here, the creeper does not come from the sprout, nor does it come from the seed alone;
rather, the reality of consciousness, manifesting everywhere, is indeed complete in every respect.
Since it is proclaimed as the cause of all and is said to be present everywhere,
if this activity of the vital breath should flash forth even within a jar,
it will immediately find rest right there and go to dissolution in the seed of Śiva.
But there is never any succession whatsoever within the state of being Śiva-nature;
other causes, such as mantras, lords, and so forth, exist only because of His presence.
Furthermore, [this occurs] either through non-difference from Śiva, or else, in the state of duality, through the perception of proximity. And by this method, discerning everything at all times,
one quickly attains the state of being the Lord of the Wheel of Consciousness, which is indeed the very nature of Bhairava.
Thus, this division pertaining to the vital breath (prāṇa), concealed within the wheel of the Khecarīs,
has been revealed by me, following the command of the venerable Śambhu. On this very path, when the state of being an object of knowledge is attained, whatever consciousness arises—
The inherent variety of that [consciousness] is designated by the term "states" (avasthā);
these are waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), and that which transcends it.
Thus, they speak of five states while there is but a single perceiver.
In that regard, concerning this sequence of principles (tattva-paddhati) beginning from the earth-principle (dharātattva) and ending with Śiva:
if there is but one single cognizer within it, then the states of waking and so forth must necessarily exist.
This is demonstrated by me through the grace of Śambhunātha.
That which is here to be presided over, and never the presider itself,
the object of knowledge residing within consciousness— that is declared to be the waking state (jāgrat).
[This includes] Caitra, Maitra, and other beings, as well as the principles (tattvas) beginning with the earth.

Words have become the instruments of denotation, and what is denoted is the means of valid cognition (pramā). When this entire universe— consisting of the fourfold set of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the resulting cognition— is presided over [by consciousness], that is traditionally known as the waking state.
For that which shines within internal cognition in the form of a mental construction as "blue" is the conscious subject who presides over the external;
however, for that [external object] which appears as blue by virtue of its externality, no such [subject] exists.
In some way, the state of being an agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) is called "waking" (*jāgrat*). In that state, when Caitra appears, that which is the bodily portion is said to be unawakened;
however, that which is the cognitive portion is awakened and acts as the agent of cognition.
The sequence of the awakened (*prabuddha*), the well-awakened (*suprabuddha*),
and the measure of valid cognition (*pramāmātra*) constitutes the fourfold nature proclaimed within the state of waking known as "the abiding in the body" (*piṇḍastha*).
Indeed, each of these four states— waking and so forth— is present here individually.
The waking-within-waking is non-awakened; the waking-dream, however, is the state of awakening.
And so forth. But as for that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta), how could it be separate, given its all-pervasiveness?
It has been stated in the *Piṇḍaga* that waking is both non-awakened and awakened.
This is traditionally held to be fourfold: the awakened (*prabuddha*) and the well-awakened (*suprabuddha*).

This primary ground of the object of knowledge (*meyabhūmi*) is called "waking" (*jāgrat*); the others are intermediate. That portion of the elements, principles (*tattva*), and designations which is said to be the object of presiding power (*adhiṣṭheya*)—this is the waking state.
"They call that state 'residing in the body' (piṇḍastha)," so it is said in the venerable Mālinīmata. This term "waking" is a worldly designation,
while "residing in the body" is a technical term defined for the sake of yogis to achieve success in yoga.

For the yogin who dwells in the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) upon that which is to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*), there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*); for the "lump" (*piṇḍa*) is measured and condensed. This is said to belong to the knowers (*jñānin*) who are firmly established solely in higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*).
The "All-Auspicious" (sarvatobhadra) state is completely filled on all sides by the reality of the sacrificial altar (vedi).
From whatever direction the knower perceives the universe as being completely filled with the reality of all existence,
from that very direction the true nature of his consciousness shines forth.
Indeed, by virtue of the threefold nature of worldly yoga and *prasaṃkhyāna*, three names are proclaimed; this same rule applies even to the states of dream and so forth.
That which exists by presiding over the state of the locus and the instrument [is thus designated].
The object of knowledge previously described as consisting of the expression of the reality of the elements (bhūtatattva) should primarily be understood as a dream;
for it appears as identical to the object of knowledge that has ascended the path of conceptualization. (AbhT 10.247b–248b)

Even this dream is established by worldly convention; and its similarity [to waking] consists in its lack of external form. In perceptions such as imagination, dreaming, volition, memory, and madness, whatever class of objects is clearly manifest is considered primarily to belong to the waking state.
But that which, even there, appears as an indistinct object while having a clear presiding subject,
and which is an object of knowledge contained within another conceptualization— that is called the state of dream.
At that very moment, he himself indeed knows its non-externality.
The state of being unstable in nature arises from the loss of existence common to other subjects;
therein, one should likewise conceive of its fourfold division according to the previously mentioned direction:
gone-and-come, well-distracted, conjoined, and well-composed.
In this case as well, as before, the worldly name for this is "dream" (svapna). For sleep is considered the non-perception of those entities that are regarded as external.
The state of all the paths is the vital breath (prāṇa), which consists of volition (saṃkalpa) and has the nature of comprehension.
Yogins know that state and its meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) to be established in the ground (*padastha*),

entirely without depending on the existence of any object of knowledge (*vedya*) as something external. Knowledge, possessing sovereignty over the object of knowledge, experiences the dream-state through its all-pervasive nature.
