This stage of pride (māna) is the primary one; for dream consists of reflective awareness (āmarśana). Indeed, the manifestation that is the shadow of the object of knowledge is called the "substratum" (adhiṣṭhāna) within the object; it is the stable body of the previously mentioned presiding [subject], such as Bhūta and so forth.
That seed of the universe which has become silent is called the state of deep sleep;
for it is that very same seer who exists within both experience and conceptualization.
Because there is no grasping of objects by him, he is said to be in a state of perfect sleep.
Due to its similarity to that [state], the wise consider ordinary sleep to be *suṣupta* (deep sleep).
Its state as a seed, its non-apprehension, its equilibrium, and its silent nature—
this primary stage of the subject is called by the name *suṣupta*.
Furthermore, because it possesses form (*rūpatva*), that [object] is form; moreover, for the yogin, there is identity with that.

Those who possess form know that the state of indifference resulting from absorption (*samāpatti*) therein is "abiding in form" (*rūpastha*). For one who possesses discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyānavat*), there occurs here a certain contraction of the object of knowledge.
Therefore, there is no "Great Pervasion" (mahāvyāpti) following from that [mere presence]. Even for one who is indifferent, there is an object of knowledge which is fourfold;
this fourfold division here arises from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the elements and so forth.

It is said to be vast, tranquil, and exceedingly serene; furthermore, that form which consists of valid cognition (pramā) stands above the cognizer. It is the state of being oriented toward attaining fullness, and the departure from indifference.
That fourth state is called the immersion into Śakti; indeed, it is so regarded.

However, some have stated that this consciousness is self-luminous and distinct from the object of knowledge (prameya), the means of knowledge (māna), and the knower (mātṛ), because those three exist for its sake.
The object of knowledge rests clearly within the means of knowledge, and that [means] likewise within the knower;
and that [knower] also clearly finds its rest within that very act of knowing. Thus, this Goddess alone is the sole life-force of the universe.
Transcending the three aspects—form, the seeing [eye], and "I"—she exists.

The means (upāya) rests merely upon the door; [the state] "I see" is without means. This subjectivity, whose nature is autonomy, shines forth in this way as the very form of the fourth consciousness (turya); it is itself the essence of light.

Through identity with that immersion, the state of being the subject (*mātṛtva*) becomes manifest; through the coloring of that immersion, the state of being the means of knowledge (*mānatva*) arises, and furthermore, the state of being the object (*meyatā*). Through proximity to that immersion, these three [states] come into being by virtue of their respective grace.
Because the distinctions of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and so forth have dissolved, this [state] is called "the healthy" (*anāmaya*);
because it bestows grace upon the subjects (*mātra*) and others, it is said to be "possessed of activity."
Even the states of waking and so forth are established as the powers (*śakti*) of the Lord.
That [power] is twofold: the lower (*apara*) and the intermediate (*parāpara*); however, this one is the supreme (*parā*).
Because it possesses form and has fallen away from neutrality, it is oriented toward fullness.
In that state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the yogin transcends form;

through the application of intent toward fullness, he perceives the universe as identical with himself. Because it is calculated by way of accumulation, this [state] is considered "Accumulation" (*pracaya*).

In this state, indeed, no other fourth stage (turya-daśā) is possible. Consciousness (saṃvit) is certainly not an object of cognition, for it shines only as the very act of cognizing. This is because the three prior stages—waking and so forth—are possible only in relation to it.

Because it favors the triad, this [state] is described in the Trika teaching as *manonmana*, *ananta*, and *sarvārtha* according to its divisions. That which is full, undivided in form, and overflowing with bliss—
They call that state "Beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta), which is indeed the supreme plane (paramaṃ padam).
Since there is an absence of cultivation (bhāvanā) and so forth here, there is no existence of yoga;
for how could there be an object of cultivation (bhāvyatā) in that which is immeasurable, undivided, and independent?

Because of the absence of yoga and the like, the All-pervasive Lord designated this [state] here by that name; however, through the power of *prasaṃkhyāna* (discriminative discernment) and due to its union with fullness (*pūrṇatva*), this form is proclaimed here as "Anuttara" and known by the designation "Mahāpracaya."
Because she is fullness itself, there is no possibility of differentiation within her (281).
To preclude such [a notion], no qualifying distinction of differentiation has been stated regarding her.
The term "constantly arisen" indicates her all-pervasiveness (282).

Indeed, there is never any differentiation whatsoever that exists as something singular; this notion that "in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) there is one eternally arisen differentiation" is the talk of the deluded. Therefore, its non-differentiated nature is established.
In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, it is stated by him that they know the "stationed in the word" (*padastha*) to be inferior;
the mantras and their lords, together with Īśvara, are proclaimed as the "stationed in form" (*rūpastha*).
The "beyond form" (*rūpātīta*) is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), which, though engaged in activity, is untainted.
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, pure, and established in its own self;
Śiva is to be known as that which transcends all, by knowing which one is liberated. Thus [ends] the *Śrīsumatiprajñācandrikā*, which has stilled the darkness of ignorance.
The venerable Śambhunātha has described the true nature of the waking state and the others.
Others, however, resorting to a different manner of presentation, explain these;
that which is the nature of the waking state and the rest is now being defined.

Therein, that which consists of the grasping of external forms by relying on the activity of the senses is waking, which is manifest, stable, and continuous again and again. Dream is the creation of one's own mental constructs; it is the opposite of waking.
This is the experience of the *layākala*, occurring through the power of impurity (*mala*) and karma, and not otherwise.
(10.290) Because of the absence of night, it becomes stable; sleep consists in the non-perception of pleasure and so forth.
(10.291a) For the *jñānākala*, experience arises solely from impurity (*mala*), which exists in isolation. (10.291b)
Inherently distinct yet non-different from itself, both the insentient and the sentient are intended to be brought forth.

Within that state of the Fourth (turya), there abide the three: the mantra, its lord, and the supreme lord. They remain until they become capable of entering into the interior of Bhairava-consciousness.
Entities, their own inherent essence dissolving, are themselves non-dual;
they become absorbed in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*) within this fifteen-fold [system].
Whatever form appears clearly to anyone, let that be considered waking (*jāgrat*).
That which appears unstable, preceded by such [an experience], is a dream;

that which appears indistinct, whether occurring while asleep or even before one's eyes, is deep sleep. It is by virtue of the synthesis (*anusaṃdhi*) of these three that [the state of waking] arises.
The fourth state, which is like the thread of a garland, should be understood as present in all divisions.

That in which every distinction has been dissolved by the surging intensity of the weight of non-duality is called "Beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta); one should apply this principle everywhere in this manner.

In the state of *layākala*, however, one's own true nature is the waking state, while that which preceded it constitutes the sequence beginning with dream and so forth; the wise person should follow this entire sequence everywhere.
Even when the Lord is fully present in a single instance, He is said to transcend the four states.
Bliss is the Fourth State (turya), while Will alone is the seed-stage (bījabhūmi) and deep sleep (suṣuptatā).

The power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is said to be the dream state, whereas the power of action (kriyāśakti) is the waking state. And this is not merely a metaphorical designation; in reality, everything exists right there.
If that were not so, there would be no primary status anywhere, nor even a metaphorical one;
this has been clearly stated by the Great Lord in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra. In that context, the triad consists of the essential nature (svarūpa), power (śakti), and the manifest (sakala).
Thus, this waking state consists of fifteen divisions.
In the [remaining] two, which are devoid of parts, lie dream and deep sleep; the fourth state partakes of the classes beginning with Mantra;
and the state beyond the fourth consists of Śakti and Śambhu—thus, in another enumeration, there are thirteen.
In the state of *pralayakevala*, one's own nature (*svarūpa*) is waking, while the other states are as before;
in *mantravirakalpa* (the state of the Vijñānākala), one's own nature is waking, while dream and deep sleep are two [other states], and the fourth (*turya*) and beyond are as previously described.
Even within the division of the Vijñānākala, "one's own" refers to the Mantras and the Lords of Mantras.
Thus, in this system, there are five states beginning with waking, consisting of their respective lords, Śakti, and Śambhu. However,
in the sevenfold division known as Mantra, the five states beginning with waking are said to consist of the Mantreśas, the Maheśvaras, Śakti, and Śambhu.

The essential nature [of the Mantreśa] consists of the Mantra, the Great Power (Māheśī Śakti), the Great Lord of Mantras (Mantramaheśvara), the Power (Śakti), and Śambhu; these are the fivefold divisions within the Mantreśa. Here, the fifth is Śambhu, who is one's own self, action, knowledge, and will.
In the threefold division of Maheśa, the states of waking and so forth have been described [as follows]:

through activity, through sovereignty, through the loss thereof, through the state of being an impeller, and through the cessation of desire and abiding in one's own nature; thus, although Śiva is one, he is fivefold. (Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka 10.308b–309)
Thus, this path of the principles (tattvādhvan) has been shown by us in detail; now,
the path of the limited powers (kalādhvan) will be explained in accordance with the command of the illustrious Śambhu, in the eleventh chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Just as within the previously mentioned worlds, that which follows its own respective group and is distinct from what follows it is called a "tattva" (principle); likewise,
even among those principles, that which consists of following its own class [is a principle].
In the teaching of Śiva, it is called *kalā* because it is turned away from the class of others. Furthermore,
some say that which is the extremely subtle power within the principles (*tattvas*) is called *kalā*, just as the earth is called the "supporter" (*dhārikā*).
In these two positions, the object does not appear as something distinct;
therefore, a persisting universal (*sāmānya*) is not accepted here as it is by the Naiyāyikas and others.
Others say that [the term "universal"] is used in initiation and other rites for the sake of easily grasping [the concept].
The category [of letters] beginning with *ka* was fashioned by Śiva as the basis for the *samaya*.
And since the *samaya* established by the God of gods does not fail to reach the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is not untrue, nor does there arise any other *samaya*.
Withdrawal occurs within the principle of earth; *pratiṣṭhā* and *vyakta* constitute its sphere.
*Vidyā* is at the end of *niśā*, and *śāntā* is at the end of *śakti*; this is the fourfold egg (*aṇḍa*).
*Śāntātītā* resides in the principle of *śiva*, while the supreme *Śiva* is beyond even *kalā*.
For here, in the abode where the splendor of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) unfolds in every direction, neither classification, nor convention, nor even mental construction is appropriate.
Yet, by virtue of that very freedom, one's own true nature remains unfallen from the attribute of the cognizer.
In order to establish the state of the ultimate reality through instruction and its penetration,
the Lord is clearly perceived as bringing about that which is to be awakened. Therefore,
even within the Śiva-principle, the association with the *kalās* (limited powers) is taught.
And they call the Egg (aṇḍa) the cause for the maintenance of the division of the worlds;
they say that its enclosure extends as far as the level of Śakti, for indeed,
although the sequence of worlds exists even within the principle (tattva) called Śiva, [it is here that it is fully established].
Even so, it has been stated that since this [Self] is non-obstructive, there is no possibility of obscuration (āvṛti) within it.

But if that is the case, [one might ask: apart from the earth, how could there be the occurrence of an egg (aṇḍa) even in the case of the powers of *prakṛti* and *māyā*, given their non-obstructiveness? How indeed could an egg come into being?
Regarding this, our teachers have said: "This pentad beginning with earth appears as direct perception; there is nothing else whatsoever [besides it].
It exists as the object of knowledge through its grossness and subtlety, and as the means of knowledge through its nature as an instrument. (AbhT 11.15b–16)

Through the radiance of the agent's creative power (*kartṛtollāsa*), the thirty principles (*triṃśattattva*) arise clearly within the state of agency as a manifold nature; their non-differentiation is considered "Night" (*niśā*).
This occurs when the distinctions such as "being the effect" and "being the instrument" have dissolved.
They declare that the pentad ending with Śiva consists of expansion, eagerness, and sovereignty.
This has been stated extensively in the venerable Kālottara and other scriptures:
"These five principles indeed pervade the entire universe."
Therefore, in the body of the five mantras, [the sequence] beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna is spoken of;
in each respective case, it ranges from the earth element up to the ether.
Thus, the Śiva-tattva is the Void beyond the void (śūnyātiśūnya), which is without support.
That which is the undifferentiated self of all, independent and beautiful with consciousness—

(21) they call that the thirty-seventh principle, designated as Paraśiva. When, according to the method already stated, even its state of being an object of knowledge is here imagined, (22) [it becomes the thirty-eighth].
When it remains uninterrupted, that is called the thirty-eighth [tattva].

Indeed, there would be no infinite regress in this way; let it be observed by the great-souled ones. Whatever object of knowledge appears, when that [object] ceases, that which shines forth [remains].
That reality, thus determined as the thirty-sixth principle, shines within the heart.
Its nature remains a state of expectancy— neither "is it something" nor "is it nothing"—
when it is taught that its sole form is consciousness, bliss, and absolute freedom.
The thirty-seventh [tattva] shines forth there, and no further desire remains;
even that state of being an established object of knowledge, wherein it shines, is composed of consciousness (cinmaya).
That too is taught as the thirty-eighth for the purpose of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).

Even if, for the sake of argument, that [subject] were again to become the thirty-seventh [category], its nature—consisting of indivisibility, autonomy, and consciousness—would remain exactly the same; the only difference is that it has been made an object of cognition. 11.28ab–28cd.
On the earth [tattva], at the end of the Guṇas, and at the end of Māyā, they are situated respectively;
smell, taste, and form exist internally according to the sequence of their subtle states.
This being the established principle, even at the end of the Śakti-tattva, there exists that which possesses subtlety.
There is a certain touch for which yogins always long;
at the conclusion of that touch, consciousness takes on the form of the pure sky of consciousness. Established in that state, one attains the supreme reality whose nature is self-luminous.
From this [Bindu] comes the Nāda, from this the Rūpa, and from this the Rasa;
thus it is stated in the Spanda that these function as agitators, whereas the Sparśa does not act in such a way.
And this is the view of the Great Lord, which he proclaimed in the Śrīpūrva [Mālinīvijayottara Tantra].
The Sustainer, the Nourisher, the Awakener, the Purifier,
and the Giver of Space— by employing these terms, the procedure for the five principles (*pañcatattva*) beginning with *nivṛtti* is declared. Now, the three principles (*tritattva*) are described.
The self extends up to the Vijñānākala, ending with the Vidyeśvaras;

in the remaining [levels], Śiva exists within three principles (tattvas), while in the single principle, Śiva is supreme. These two divisions are made solely on the basis of the differentiation of the principles.
And thus, this is indeed the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*); there is no contradiction here with the established state of the sixfold path.

Even in the ritual procedure consisting of nine principles—namely, *prakṛti*, the individual soul (*puruṣa*), *niyati*, *kāla*, *māyā*, the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), *sauśiva*, and Śiva—it possesses the nature of the path of the principles.
In this manner, the wise man should state the same principle even regarding the procedure known as the eighteen-fold one;
for wherever there is a desire for enjoyment,
initiation possesses infinite varieties through the predominance of that [desire] and through the inclusion of other [elements].
By that [means], the procedure for the thirty-six principles up to the single principle (ekatattva) is established.
That very path of principles (tattvādhvan) has been taught by the Lord both in detail and in summary;
and this procedure for the single principle is intended for a teacher who is perfectly awakened.
And because Śambhu, being delighted, has [bestowed grace upon] the disciple whose desire for enjoyment has ceased,
the Lord remains eternally resting within his own undivided self, having repeatedly expanded and then dissolved the sense of duality by means of his power whose nature is absolute freedom.

Thus, the division of the threefold path according to its gross, subtle, and supreme natures has been declared as residing within the objective portion (*meyabhāga*), consisting of worlds (*pura*), principles (*tattva*), and limited powers (*kalā*). Now, the form situated in the subjective portion (*mātṛbhāga*) is described in three ways.
That form which constitutes the measure of the path and belongs to the portion of the subject is called a *pada*, because it consists of the penetration into the nature of comprehension (*avagama*).
And that very *pada* is a *mantra* when it has fallen away from its agitation (*prakṣobha*).
Although the Mother remains silent and established in quietude,
she does not abandon her nature as reflective awareness; therefore,
she possesses the nature of both the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), yet unlike an ordinary person, she does not undergo agitation.

In the Trika teaching, it has been stated that the own-form (*svarūpa*) of both mantras and words is indeed indivisible when [the subject] is neither agitated nor stirred by the supreme [state]. This occurs upon the abandonment of indifference and the non-descent into agitation.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) resides within the portion of the Mothers; it is that same measure which was previously described.

Since that [measure] consists of an undivided nature due to its being the full form, therefore each individual phoneme exists within each respective principle (tattva), beginning with the earth (kṣamā).
Having established [the sequence] within the supreme Śiva, the sixteen syllables are said to extend up to the Visarga.
Therein, the vibration of Śakti has been previously described in its full extent. Now, everything is stated in summary for the sake of the experience of bliss.

The syllable of the mantra of the *pada* is sixteen-fold, and it is called *nivṛtti*. Another *pada* of the weapon-mantra consists of the syllables of the principles (*tattva*), namely fire (three) and eyes (two), making five; it is the city of the flavors (six) and arrows (five).
The next *kalā* consists of the syllables of the sages (seven) and the principles (twenty-five), and its mantra has two *padas*; it is the world of the eight and the eyes (eight), making sixteen.
The fire-syllable, the principle (tattva), the single-word mantra, and the world of the army—this is the fourth [state].
There are sixteen phonemes, one word, one mantra, and one principle; this is the state beyond peace (śāntyatītā).
These three Āryā verses have been spoken by Abhinavagupta for the benefit of his disciples as a summary.
This entire path, existing in a state of non-difference from Bhairava,
appears as possessing autonomy by attaining autonomy through His [Bhairava’s] sovereignty.
For it has been described that the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) resides within the form of the subject (mātṛ).
For when the state of the denotable object is swallowed by the reflective awareness of consciousness (cid-vimarśa),
it becomes intent upon protection through the thought dependent on the knowledge and action of Śiva,
due to its proficiency in the playful eagerness for the entire multitude of powers.
Falling away from the form consisting of the conceit [of the subject], consciousness attains the state of the path of mantra;

having assumed the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the path proceeds to the state of being the word (*pada*). For in this way, the resting of the subject occurs after he has synthesized those many phonemes.
And that successive collision consists precisely of the nature of internal discourse (saṃjalpa).
It is clearly the very form of conceptual thought (vikalpa), consisting of immersion in enjoyment.
Therefore, our Guru declared this state to be the form of valid cognition (pramāṇatā).

Without abandoning its immersion in the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet proceeding toward the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*) through the application of temporal calculation, the path is said to consist of *kalās*. This occurs within the pure sphere of the connection to the object of knowledge, which partakes in both subtle and gross states.

The Guru should follow in sequence the nature of the path of principles (tattva) and the path of worlds (bhuvana). This path, which consists of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower, exists above [the lower levels];
let this path, whose essence is the phonemes (varṇa), be perceived here as being situated within the self of valid cognition (pramātman).
Through the yoga of relishing the repose in pure, surging consciousness,
yogins possess unimpeded powers by virtue of their capacity for all designations;
they are projected toward objects that arise simultaneously with their own selves, extending down to the level of the earth.
Touching those many objects without distinction within the ground of their own consciousness, those floods of phonemes bear a true awareness that is the very form of valid cognition (pramā).
This applies even to children, animals, and other subjects who do not participate in linguistic convention.

Relying upon this self-awareness— which is the essence of unartificial *saṃskāra*— they too attain various states of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) according to their diverse [limitations]. And within this [self-awareness],
they find their rootedness in the consciousness of infinite, unartificial colors (*varṇa*).

If these conventions were to proceed [as independent entities], they would themselves fall into the state of being non-conventional; yet without this [power], all the numerous conventions that have been established would,
due to a lack of rest, lead to an insurmountable infinite regress.

A child is taught by means of that [gesture] through the search for a convention (*saṃketa*). Even when a finger or the like is pointed out to him, his cognition is not free from conceptual construction (*avikalpā*).
Conceptual construction has its root in speech, and speech has its life in convention.
Therefore, that infinite and non-illusory collection of phonemes,
which is accompanied by the reflective awareness of consciousness, indeed perpetually unfolds.
And it is from this very source that the illusory phonemes have extended their manifestation.
And those [phonemes] which are established as having the nature of *vīrya* among the phonemes of *māyā*—
let it be understood that they constitute valid cognition (*pramā*) independently of convention (*saṃketa*).
For, when the words of another are heard, one's own [innate] [cognition] is veiled.
He whose cognition is inert does not attain the status of a knower regarding that object;

like a parrot, he merely recites, participating solely in the sequence of those [sounds]. However, through the attainment of autonomy, when one's own cognition is acquired, there arises the state of being a true cognizer.
For he whose awakening to his own true nature occurs through the suppression of opposing factors,
that cognizer shall attain mastery over the collection of phonemes in his own speech and other expressions.
And in whatever measure that uncreated form transcends [the conditioned], [so much does he attain mastery].

In that same manner, the gradation of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is perceived as each subsequent [level] becomes submerged within the phonemes of the primordial *māyīya* [speech], and as each preceding portion dissolves into the conventional sign (*saṃketa*). This constitutes the differentiation of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*).
Even when the primordial intensity is great,

those who are established in the self of intuitive insight (pratibhā) certainly attain a state endowed with poetic and oratorical power in every respect, as long as they remain within that light which is free from the degradation of conventional designations.
Once one has found rest in that which consists of consciousness, what is there that one does not know, or what is there that one cannot do?
For this very reason, when the perfection of speech is attained, the phonemes (varṇas) are to be worshipped.
Or rather, in the attainment of omniscience and other such powers, what perfection is there that is not composed of that [consciousness]?
This has been stated by the Giver of Boons in the *Śrīsiddhayogīśvarīmata*:
"By that [phoneme] being concealed, the remaining phonemes are clearly concealed.
In the purification of his own body, that path attains purity in six ways;
when the purification is achieved through one form,
the Guru, possessed of continuous contemplation, should perform the purification by internalizing the other modes within that very one.
But when there is no capacity for inclusion, one should purify [the object] more and more subtly. Once purified, it does not produce a subsequent continuity from the state of being a seed.
Purification is manifold; it consists in the single-minded focus on attaining each respective experience.

Its sovereignty, its renunciation, the realization of its nature as Śiva, absorption in it, and its transcendence— all of this occurs both sequentially and non-sequentially. For this very reason, those mantras are purifiers and possess diverse forms.
In the Siddhānta, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other systems, they propagate various forms of purification.
As for those mantras of the Anuttara, Trika, and Krama traditions, they indeed bestow everything; however, each has its primary importance in a particular context.
Therefore, in the scripture known as the Śrīpūrva, by virtue of its nature as a purifier,
the established arrangement of the Parā, Parāparā, and other mantras within the paths (adhvan) is described;
and the state of being a purifier belongs to Mālinī and to the triad of goddesses.

[This applies] to the three deities, the faces, and the eight limbs. Or rather, what need is there for excessive detail? In the sequence of the doors, the site, the support, and the preceptor, with the exception of the mantras for the ritual of the world-protectors, everything else is purificatory.
And as for this state of being purified and the purifier that has been described regarding the path,
it is taught in the scripture that these are joined in non-difference from Śiva by virtue of His absolute freedom;
for all of this indeed shines within the eternal Supreme Lord.
Because it exists in the form of a reflection and not as something external,
such a notion of various bodies and so forth arises within the auspicious void of consciousness alone for transmigrating beings— just like the notions of a snake, a garland, or a wave in a rope.
Since the doctrine of the death of the previous body belongs to the realm of dreams,
what kind of birth of a new body occurs at death?
Even in a dream, [this occurs] by the power of the manifestation of a mere commonality consisting of a mental representation.

Just as particular features appear [in a stone] even though they are not being produced, so too the consciousness (*citi*) possesses a heart variegated by the lines of the levels beginning with *māyā* and ending with *bhūmi*, just as certain *śālagrāma* stones bear diverse forms.
Cities, oceans, mountains, and so forth, conform to His will;
they are neither inherently existent nor non-existent, nor are they characterized by being causes or non-causes,
due to the cessation and the setting into motion of long-established necessity.
For one who has not ascended [to this state], this Bhairava of the space of consciousness remains independent.

For one who partakes in non-difference from Bhairava, who is filled with pure consciousness alone, the lack of self-reflection that "I am thus" acts as a divider within the circle of objective existence.
Just as no other agent is established by any means of valid cognition in a dream,
so too should it be understood everywhere regarding self-awareness, which is self-established. Indeed,
he who knows thus may sport in the variegated city-garden of the mind.
"I alone abide within the cities of the elements, states of being, and principles. Thus,
the various manifestations of birth and death— such as "I am born" or "I have died"—
appear upon the wall of the mind, fashioned by itself, even though there is neither birth nor death.
In reality, for consciousness, there is neither space nor time; the other world and this world consist merely of the consciousness of others.
If this creation were material rather than composed of consciousness, it would not have come into being.

If one were to examine that [universe], who among them could even support a single mountain? In the sequence of the relationship between container and contained starting from the group of elements and subtle essences,
it is ultimately the power consisting of consciousness— whose nature is Śiva alone— that is the supporter.
Therefore, in this context, it is consciousness alone that is both the agent and the sustainer; she is Śiva.
Consequently, all entities exist therein as entities, and from her proceeds the power that serves as their substratum.
Thus, even that which is purely volitional and without a physical support does not fall downward.
Thus, let it be contemplated that the entire universe rests within its own foundational power (*svādhāra-śakti*).

Its very establishment as the earth and so forth consists in the density of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃ*) and other such notions; finally, when the realization "I am consciousness" (*cid asmi*) has arisen, the state of being Bhairava is attained.
Just as colors such as blue appear in a gem or a rainbow within the auspicious [consciousness],
in ultimate reality there is never the arising or the passing away of these anywhere;
nor is it logical to say that their creation occurs in a particular place or time.
For even the creation of space and time is brought about by the Lord, whose nature is consciousness.
Within the scope of three and a half cubits, which is regarded as the waking state,
and within each watch of the day, various dreams arise, perceiving diverse spaces and times.

For this very reason, we do not consider even a "moment" (kṣaṇa) to be anything at all; for within a single moment of action, there would indeed be many rapid actions. Therefore, those who have maintained that the contraction of existence ends with a moment—

They surely rely upon this channel [of the void] as their view of emptiness. Therefore, that Lord Śiva, our Master, is the Sovereign who, by virtue of His absolute freedom, can render existent things empty and manifest non-existent things in such a way.
Thus, the Supreme Lord is celebrated as being of universal form;
however, it is not logical for anything distinct, such as the earth and so forth, to exist [independently].
And this has been stated previously, so it will not be analyzed further here.
And further, one should desist from [the pursuit of] external objects by means of many refutations thereof.
Thus, this detailed exposition of the path beginning with *kalā* has been determined.
Now begins the twelfth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, the application of this path (adhvan) to the subject at hand is revealed:
In this way, this entire path, as it resides within consciousness,
likewise resides through that [consciousness] in the void, the intellect, the vital breath, the network of channels, and the body.
Externally, as well, he exists everywhere—in the form of the *liṅga*, the image, the fire, the sacrificial ground, and so forth;
thus he remains both collectively and individually, through sequential and non-sequential means.
This entire path that is established, beginning from the principle of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*) and extending outward, is external.
In each respective case, one’s own form appropriate to that situation should manifest through its own autonomy.
Indeed, every form manifests everywhere for it as well;
for we cannot tolerate limitation anywhere, even in a dream.

In this way, one should contemplate the body as being filled with all the paths (*adhvan*), variegated by the operations of time, and the abode of the vibration consisting of space and time. When thus contemplated, it is seen to consist of the deities within the universe.

He who is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and gratified— being possessed by Him, one is liberated. Thus, whether one sees a jar, a cloth, a linga, a sacrificial mound, a book, water, or whatever else anywhere, one should attain identity with that.
In that context, the offering (*arpaṇa*) of objects is considered to be worship through non-differentiation.
Likewise, meditation (*dhyāna*) is said to be the contemplation of the state of being complete in form. Bringing about unwavering firmness in the contemplation of that completeness—

Likewise, by means of internal mental discourse, one who is intent on the rite of oblation should offer up the objects of meditation after dissolving their own diversity while reflecting upon them as the vessel for recitation; thus,
he should dissolve the distinctness of the entities projected therein and offer them as being the very essence of its rays.
In that same way, for one who acts thus, perceiving everything with equanimity,

there is unwaveringness, the pure vow, and the equanimity proclaimed by Nandiśikha. Likewise, through the sequence of the rules for worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and vows, [the goal is attained].
The ancient teachers have declared that the state of complete fullness is *samādhi*.
In this regard, whether in external or internal states during worship, recitation, and so forth,
there is no ritual rule whatsoever regarding the multitude of substances, nor is anything prohibited.
In this [state], there is no utility whatsoever for the purification of mental constructs (*kalpanā*), the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), and so forth.
And it is stated at length in the venerable *Trikasūtra* regarding the performance of sacrifice:
"One who does not know the ritual rules and one who knows them," and so on.
When, in whatever manner, by whatever means, and in whatever place one's own self-awareness becomes clarified,
then, in that manner, by that means, and in that place, each respective object of enjoyment and its ritual procedure [is established].
Therefore, one should employ everything here, both worldly and transcendent.
If one is trembling while [the other] is motionless, one should forcibly diminish that trembling by whatever means possible,
whether gradually or all at once;
in such a way that doubt dissolves within, one should apply effort.
One should satisfy the goddesses residing in the intellect, the action, and the senses with precisely those things that are prohibited;
this is the teaching of Bhargaśikha: "One should take delight in the vow of the hero (vīravrata).
For in this way, doubt, impurity, exhaustion, and contraction—these [are overcome]. (AbhT 12.19b–20)

Within the prison-house of saṃsāra, those mantras whose nature consists of phonemes act as the massive pillars, while that which is composed of the five elements acts as the jars. As for the multitude of living beings whose essence is consciousness, what confusion could there be therein, and how?
Since there is no possibility of confusion, what is this doubt? Even regarding that [confusion], it is clearly evident.
One should not entertain such doubt; thus, the doubt dissolves effortlessly in the *Śrīsarvācāra*, the *Vīrālī*, the *Niśācara*, the *Krama*, and other such texts. (AbhT 12.22b–23)
For this is extensively set forth in the scriptures, as it is stated here and there:
"From doubt arises exhaustion; through doubt one becomes a vessel for obstacles.
And the illustrious Utpaladeva, the teacher of our own teacher, has said:
"We bow to that path of Maheśvara, which is a thunderbolt against all doubts.
(AbhT 12.25b) "O wise ones, understand this Āṇava [means]—the method for attaining the unsurpassed state—which has been shown in great detail.
(AbhT 12.26a) Now begins the thirteenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, as for the discussion concerning eligibility—namely, who here [is eligible] and how—it is sufficient to state that the sequence of the various descents of power (*śaktipāta*) will be explained.
Regarding this, some here say that this procedure is the descent of power;
having demonstrated and refuted that, my own view will be shown.

In this regard, that which is perceived as existing and partaking in pleasure, pain, and delusion— though it is inherently unequal— is conceived as an equal cause; that is the Unmanifest (avyakta), which, through its various forms such as *sattva* and the rest, is insentient.
The reason why she is like a jar or other such effects is that this Night is her sole cause.

She is insentient because of her conformity to the nature of an effect, and indeed, within her, the effect already exists. Due to her insentience, she is incapable of bringing forth [the universe] from the level of *kalā* down to the earth (*dharaṇī*).
By that [means], the Lord agitates her; her agitation is the state of being fit for birth (sūti).
And she brings forth for the male various beginningless objects of experience (bhogya) in their distinct forms.
Furthermore, if the male were without distinction, why would that [agency] not apply even to liberated souls (muktāṇu)?
"The cause is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of karma, and that does not exist in them.
If this is argued, then from where indeed do they have the absence of karmic impressions?
For it would follow that there is no other portion of karma [to account for their state], which is an insurmountable difficulty. (7–8)
The simultaneous experience of [the fruits of] actions is not logical, for they indeed ripen in succession.

Why should an action that is destined to bear fruit ever abandon its own nature? If it is argued that the destruction of karma occurs through knowledge, then from what [source does that knowledge arise]? It arises from being impelled by the Lord (Īśvara).
If [knowledge] arises from dharma and the like, from what does that [dharma] itself arise? If it is said to arise from karma, let that be explained.
For there is no such karma by which knowledge is set in motion;
and if that knowledge were born of karma, it would certainly fall into the category of [ordinary] fruits.
How could [the Lord's action] burn away the fruit of other actions and the prior mass of karma?
For how could this ever apply to the Lord, who is devoid of hatred, attachment, and the like?
Furthermore, there is no such intention [on His part] elsewhere, because of the absence of any cause for differentiation.

But [it may be argued]: "In that case, knowledge would burn away the nets of karma, for karma indeed produces results such as heaven when it has ignorance as its auxiliary cause. Ignorance, moreover, is destroyed by knowledge, even from the fruit of other actions. (13–14ab)
Furthermore, other acts such as fasting and the like would become the fruit of evil karma;
it is indeed accepted that they render evil karma fruitless.
As for that which is called "ignorance," if it is merely the absence of knowledge, then what is it?

Is it prior non-existence or destruction? In the first case, does this apply to all cognitions or to some specific cognition? The former position is impossible, for there is no such person whose cognition has ever arisen in that manner [i.e., as a prior non-existent]. (AbhT 13.16b–17)

In this beginningless existence, there is no atom whatsoever; what kind of succession could there be when it is established that even prior to its arising, knowledge has a prior non-existence? That [prior non-existence] certainly exists even for a liberated soul, yet it does not exist prior to birth.
If it is argued that knowledge will arise once this [body] is liberated, then let this be examined:
Why does knowledge not arise here? Is it not because of the birth of the body and so forth?
Why is that [birth]? Because of the exhaustion of karma. Why is that? Because of the destruction of ignorance.
How can there be the destruction of ignorance when consciousness is in a state of prior non-existence?
This ignorance is not a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), because its production as a positive entity (bhāva) is impossible.
Why would that knowledge not be future [and thus a prior non-existence]? Indeed, because the body and so forth have not yet been born.

Thus, this sharp whirling of the wheel destroys all opposing positions. Now, if it is argued that this ignorance exists as mere destruction and is eternally present within liberated souls, then let the manifestation of the effects of *māyā* reside in them.
Now, ignorance is not non-existence; rather, it is considered to be false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
That very [ignorance] is the auxiliary cause for actions in their own respective functions.
[Objection: Then, what must be said regarding the action when it produces its own fruit?

At that very moment, false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), being present, attains the status of a cause. Now, if at the moment when the action is performed, false cognition exists in its own nature, then from such an action the fruit [arises].
In the former view, once dissolution has occurred and the prior creation is being set in motion,
false cognition cannot arise anywhere because of the absence of bodies and other such factors.
In the latter view, however, whenever, by whomsoever, or wherever [it might occur]—
Whatever action is performed at that time is accompanied by ignorance;
thus, for no one whatsoever would there be an exhaustion of karma. This remains necessarily so even if one performs some action having become possessed of knowledge.
If that [knowledge] were fruitless, what would become of the mass of prior karma? Furthermore,
even at the time of dissolution,
since the individual souls (aṇus) possess the nature of consciousness, how could their knowledge possibly be false?

If it is argued that [the manifestation] occurs by its own nature (*svabhāva*), then why does it not occur likewise in the liberated soul (*mukta*) or in Śiva? It is not so. Furthermore, that which is called "non-perception" (*adarśana*) is the cause for transformation in the *pradhāna*; for that [non-perception] exists through the conjunction of both the mixed and the distinct states.
Having begun from the intellect— which is the companion to the soul's unique fitness for perception—
down to the existing earth,
whatever exists therein [is perceived] because the state of being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect occurs through the grace of the soul's exertion.

For the manifestation of the intellect together with its object is called "enjoyment" (bhoga). When there is a consciousness of duality, one thinks: "I am the intellect alone, subject to the nature of transformation; but who is this other, distinct from me, who is a single Self? Thus [is the state of separation]. 34–35ab.
Because the purpose of the person has been accomplished and due to the absence of auxiliary causes,
[Nature] does not produce for that person at all, but indeed for another.
In this regard, the non-perception of both the person and the root [nature] is the property of the two.
Alternatively, let this option remain as it is; rather, let this be discussed:

what is the limit to the claim that "enjoyment culminates in discernment"? If, upon attaining discernment, there is the vision of the entire process of emanation, then what of that [vision] itself? (37–38ab)
In the eastern [tradition], [the result] may arise from a single birth, either through general or specific [means];

in the northern [tradition], it would never occur because of the connection with the future time. If it were to occur for all [practitioners] simultaneously through only certain specific [means], [it would be illogical].
Since there is no separation due to beginningless conjunction, what indeed could be their mutual diversity?
Therefore, even from the perspective of the Sāṃkhya, this ignorance is not tenable;
without ignorance, bondage and liberation cannot be established as distinct states.
That [bondage and liberation] are joined together is not tenable by the arguments already stated;
for even though the existence of the individual soul (aṇu), the Lord (deva), and the will to act (karma) remains,
there can be no connection between bondage and liberation because the cause of their distinction is impossible.

Therefore, by the term "ignorance" (ajñāna), some obscuration of the conscious atoms (cidaṇu)— which possess the attributes of consciousness and agency— must be stated by the wise. Established as having the nature of an obscuration, it is non-different from their own essential nature.
Because there is no evidence for its division, that [consciousness] is one in all selves.
From what, then, could it have arisen? If you say from Māyā, how indeed does she exist?
For she would produce this [consciousness] only in some cases, and not in liberated souls.
If no cause can be found, then the aforementioned objection would apply;
however, because there is no origination, it is eternal and does not perish.
For that very reason, in its state of oneness, it is common to all other selves.
It is not a non-entity because it performs a function, nor is it the mind because it is conventional;
nor is there a connection of the selves with this [body], because such a cause is impossible. Therefore, the single entity is existent and eternal, eternally connected with the selves.
That dull impurity is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
When its obstructing power remains indifferent due to the rays of Śiva, then the individual soul is touched;
once touched, his own powers of knowledge and action become manifest. (AbhT 13.49b–50)
Impelled by this, it enters [the object] just as a sun-crystal is activated by the sun;
and due to the gradual progression of the intensity of the neutrality of the obstructing power (rodhrī-śakti),
they say that there is a variety in the manifestation of one's own consciousness.

This very [process] is designated in the scriptures as "the descent of power" (śaktipāta). Regarding this, it has already been stated in the *Pūrvāhnika* that such a notion of impurity (mala) is not tenable; what, then, is the purpose of repeating it here?

What could this "ripening" (*pāka*) of impurity be? If it were the destruction [of impurity], then since it is stated that there is only one single impurity, it would follow that [the Self] is inherently pure (*nairmalya*).
Alternatively, if it is held that [impurity] is restricted to each individual self and is beginningless, like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
In that way, the impurity would be destroyed; yet, if this destruction were caused by a cause, [one must ask:
is the cause karma or the will of the Lord? First of all, karma is not of such a nature.
And as for the independent will of the Lord, why does it act in that manner only in certain instances?

If its destruction were causeless, it would have perished even earlier. If you argue that it produces a similar subsequent moment, then that is simply permanence. Furthermore, for an eternal entity whose birth is not dependent upon a cause, [destruction is impossible].

The destruction [of a thing] is observed as its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); let it be so, for that [non-existence] is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*). Now, what is called its "ripening" (*pāka*) is simply its being bound by its own power; thus, this [power] would be obstructed for everyone, like poison or fire.
And when its power has arisen again, it would perform its own function like poison or fire;

thus, even those who are liberated would not be liberated, for we do not admit the existence of such a power in Him. If you say it is "obstructive," then of what [is it obstructive] among men, regarding their knowledge and agency?
If [the Lord] were an obstructer by virtue of His mere existence, then there would be no possibility for liberated souls or bound souls;
furthermore, impurity (mala) does nothing beyond its mere presence,
because if it were to transform the Self, the consequence would be that the Self is impermanent.
The mere states of being a knower and an agent do not have the *pudgala* as their substrate;

if that [substrate] were obstructed, alas, the destruction of its very form would follow. Furthermore, this obstruction is invisibility, and it does not constitute a difference in the nature of the entity itself.
Knowledge acts like a jar; it cannot be obstructed.
How can that very knowledge, which is itself the object of obstruction, be the obstruction?
If it were not known in that way, then what is called "obstruction" would be a mere name.
Who can be the restrainer of that obstructive power (*rodhrī śakti*), O Lord?
If [the Lord] were devoid of dependence [on anything else], the answer has already been given there.
Alternatively, his will proceeds by depending upon the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*).
The nature of that [state] must also be explained: for what indeed is the equality of karmas?
Due to the greatness of the sequence of their experiences, at some point in time regarding the fruit, two opposing karmas remain obstructed; such is this state of equality.
And the omniscient Lord, perceiving that impurity as a portion of time (*kālāṃśaka*), obstructs it;
and that time becomes perceptible through the avoidance of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
This does not occur through actions that are sequential, purely pure, mixed, or of various forms.

In the same way, when one's own fruit is to be given, what is this mutual obstruction? If there were such an obstruction between those two, then even birth and lifespan would not exist; consequently, the body would fall away. If it is argued that the obstruction applies only to the bestowal of experience (*bhoga*), [we reply: surely...
If Śaṅkara, when the conditions for [the ripening of] karma that bestows birth and lifespan are present,
obstructs the impurity (mala), why would he fear the karma that grants experience?
Even hundreds of times, he brings about a state devoid of both pleasure and pain.
And yet, an immersion into the flavor of devotion has not been observed in abundance. Nevertheless, the Supreme Lord acts in such a way by taking account of the majesty of time;
one must now explain what kind of time this is.
Furthermore, this experience is beginningless, as is karma along with the person (*pudgala*).
Consequently, the duration of the cycle of experience for everyone is equal.
For if anything had a beginning, it would follow that this [cycle] could arise from outside of this group.
"By this [karma] a variety [of experiences] is enjoyed for one kalpa, and by that [other karma], for two;
from such a sequence of enjoyments, there arises an equilibrium of karmas.
By means of this seed of reasoning, I consider [this] to be the cause of variety. (76–77)

The karma that has been ordained for the world does not hold together in that manner; for all individual souls (aṇavas), though equally covered by beginningless impurity, are diverse in their succession of karma despite being identical in their nature as vision and action. 78–79ab.
How have they come to rely upon such a variegated succession of karma? 79cd.
If it is argued that [the world] is diverse because of a craving for enjoyment, then how indeed is that so?
If it is further argued that it is due to the diversity of beginningless karmic impressions (*saṃskāra*),
then one must explain from where that very diversity of necessity (*niyati*) and attachment (*rāga*) arises.
If this greatness belongs to both of them, why are they not subject to inconsistency?

Furthermore, the will of the Lord, if independent [of anything else], cannot be conceived as the cause of differentiation. Or, if it is established merely by its beginninglessness, that is devoid of logical justification.
If this established order is sufficient, then let this impurity (mala) be useless.
For indeed, as long as Māyā does not operate upon the person (pudgala), there can be no karma;
nor is its operation without a cause, and therefore that impurity is established [as the cause].
And thus, when karma is conceived as the cause for this effect of *māyā*, if karma itself were beginningless, what would be the purpose of postulating a *mala*? [Objection:
Well then, let there be no *mala* at all with respect to the various forms of karma.
When [the states] revolve in a continuous succession, no fixed arrangement is possible;
for, because actions are diverse at the beginning and in the middle,
this particular form of the self would likewise exist as such during the time of its manifestation.
In this way, this entire sequence of bondage, liberation, and so forth, is utterly cut off.
It has been examined that bondage arises from ignorance and liberation from knowledge.
Furthermore, these two types of action, which are mutually contradictory, may at some point produce their respective fruits simultaneously.
If they both remain indifferent, then let this karma be awakened. But what opportunity could there be for the descent of Śiva’s power (śakti) by that much alone?
For it is only when, at some point in time, those two [Śiva and Śakti] are indifferent that this occurs.
Because the conflict between those two remains unremoved even after a lapse of time,
therefore, in the end, neither of them nor other karmas will bear fruit;
for they have been obstructed by those two [opposing forces] which, having reached their own time, have already begun to be experienced.

Thus, liberation occurs always during the course of life and likewise at the fall of the body; let this conceptualization of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and so forth rest for now. Now, [consider] the momentary interval following the conjunction with those two types of indifferent karma.

If an action produces its fruit at another time, why does it not do so even at that very moment? Or if those same two [causes] produce it in a subsequent moment, then by what has the removal of obstacles for those two been effected? What causes the absence of obstruction in them?
The equilibrium of karma exists in its own nature and does not admit of degrees;
nor is it subject to the will of Śiva. Therefore, when the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs as its effect, that [equilibrium] would no longer exist.
Furthermore, this which is called concealment (tirobhāva)—how could it arise again?

Whatever was to be done by way of the equilibrium of karma has, it is said, already been accomplished. Furthermore, if the will of the Lord (Īśvara) were the cause, the same argument as previously stated would apply.
By this, other factors that might be postulated as dependencies for the Lord's will are also refuted.
For even those [other views] are destroyed by the refutation of [theories such as] eternalism, other-causality, causelessness, and so forth.
(97) Dispassion, distaste for enjoyments, a certain degree of virtue, discernment, association with the virtuous, and constancy in the practice of worshiping the Supreme Lord and so forth— (98)
The occurrence of adversity, the observation thereof, certain signs within the body, service to the scriptures, the fullness of the assembly of enjoyments, and divine knowledge—
these are what are required by the Lord; yet these too are to be rejected, as before.
There is also deviation, both in its totality and in its parts, as well as in its essential nature;
furthermore, there is mutual interpenetration and manifold inconsistency.
Therefore, we do not understand what this sequence of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is.

Thus, I shall describe this great medicinal herb of the scriptures, vomited forth from the mouth of the illustrious Śambhu, which grants liberation from the fainting spell caused by the onset of the poison of delusion.
By nature, the Lord is autonomous, of the form of consciousness, and his essence is light.
Through the practice of play that conceals its true form, the atom (aṇu) becomes manifold. It is described that by means of actions consisting of the conceptualization of forms imagined by itself,
it binds itself here through its own sovereignty.
This is indeed the majesty of the Lord's sovereignty,
that he, though consisting of atomicity, again touches his own perfectly pure nature;
yet it cannot be said how or in which person this occurs.
Indeed, there is no person whatsoever who can be questioned regarding this;
for if he is indeed the Lord himself, and his very nature is such,
then what room is there for questioning the nature of one whose essence consists in such manifestation?

Our supreme preceptor, the most excellent of teachers, has stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* that because one possesses the nature of Śiva through the performance of the fivefold cosmic act, for one who is thus engaged in his own duty,
what need is there to seek other external causes? (108–109a)

Whatever fruit arises for the person when his true nature appears as concealed, that belongs to the individual soul (aṇu) who already exists; for that [fruit] proceeds from his own agency. And the Lord’s desire to conceal His own nature serves as the instrumental cause.
Therefore, there exists a beginningless state of karma and impurity;

concealment is the incompleteness of that which is full in nature, and its fulfillment is [the process of completion]. Impurity is the state of craving arising from a sense of separation toward each distinct object.

Without the nature of Śiva, which is pure and self-luminous, nothing whatsoever is possible; therefore, Maheśvara is the cause here. In this way, he depends upon Māyā during the triad of creation, maintenance, and destruction.

It is well established that impurity (mala), as well as action (karman), exist for the sake of [the soul's] tasks; indeed, they exist solely by the will of Śiva. However, in that case where Śiva manifests in his own true form, he has no need for impurity or action, at least so long as he is not subject to the state of an individual soul (aṇu).
If its nature as an atom were abandoned, how could that which resides therein function as a cause?
Therefore, one should establish its independence from *māyā*.
Consequently, it is Śiva alone—pure and self-luminous—who is the cause here.
And that [power] reveals degrees of intensity solely through its own autonomy.
Disregarding the excellence of family, caste, body, action, age, and ritual performance,
devotion to Śiva is the descent of power (śaktipāta) for those who do not seek worldly fruits.
Devotion that arises from a desire for results depends upon ritual action and the like;
therefore, in this case, there may be a distinction regarding the result, but not so in the case of liberation (apavarga).
This is clearly evident even for one who intends both enjoyment and liberation.
In the former stage, one requires past karma because of its diversity, but not so in the latter;
for even that which has not yet manifested its form appears as if it were already manifest.
Having remained [in that state] and having grasped the mantras and so forth, when one abandons them, that constitutes his concealment (tirobhava).
In the Śrīsāraśāstra, the Blessed One spoke of this reality:
"One should oneself envelop one's own self—without doubt—from the Avīci hell up to the end of Śiva—with manifold states consisting of merit and demerit. (AbhT 13.121b–122)
In the same way, he alone envelops [the universe] by means of the multitude of powers;
the Lord of Gods binds himself and releases himself alone.
He is himself the enjoyer, himself the knower, and he alone should perceive [all this].
She herself is both enjoyment and liberation; she herself is the Goddess, she herself is the Lord.
She herself is the single syllable, just as heat is inherent in fire.
Here, by virtue of her sovereignty, the reality that has been described is the manifestation of the nature of one's own Self.
It is also stated in the venerable *Niśākula*: "Those of meager intellect, whose minds are conditioned by falsehood, suffer through their investigation into impurity (*mala*) and *māyā*.
O Dear One, what can dust on a crystal stone do to it? (126–127)
For just as there is no impurity in the sky, one should therefore abandon the suspicion of impurity.
The venerable Vidyāguru has stated this in the *Pramāṇastutidarśana*:
"At the time following the pervasion and destruction of merit and demerit, that descent of power (*śakti*) which is realized by those who have plunged into the depths [of reality]."
Those such as Stavaka and others, asserting that [liberation] occurs according to their own will, would claim that sovereignty is independent of You.
As for the manifestation of degrees— intense, moderate, and mild—
these very [degrees] each abide in a threefold manner within the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

The most intense descent of power (*tīvratīvra-śaktipāta*) bestows liberation by itself through the falling away of the body, either at that very moment or at another time according to the degree of intensity. Furthermore,
from the medium-intense descent, all ignorance is completely removed.
Since one knows the nature of the self as both bondage and liberation by oneself alone,
that great knowledge which is intuitive (*prātibha*) is independent of scriptures and teachers.
The moon-like teacher, having extinguished the darkness through the moonlight of intuition, [is thus described].
It destroys both darkness and heat, expanding the vision that is filled with bliss.

He is designated as "the taught" (śiṣṭa) because of his status as the agent of the action; the other is a disciple (śiṣya) by virtue of being the object of the action. And he is "taught" (śiṣṭa) everywhere—in the Smṛti, in words, in time, in lineage, and so forth.
The Self-born One has declared that there is no living being whatsoever who is not grounded in the intuitive realization of the meaning of the scriptures, which are rooted in Him.
Even therein, there is an infinity arising from degrees of excellence, ranging from firmness to instability.
Reasoning, scripture, the teacher, debate, practice, and so forth are required [for those who lack realization].
For consciousness that is still trembling will indeed return to its own state;
however, for some, stability arises through reasoning and other such means alone, while for others, it does not.

To the extent that there is a diminishing of dependence on others regarding intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), to that same extent is this guru the most excellent, having reached the further shore of consciousness. Even one who has learned infinite knowledge from another [becomes such] through the power of intuition.

Whatever he knows in each respective case, that is his supreme state of Śiva-hood. For him who follows the path of intuitive insight (*prātibha*), there is no sequence beginning with the status of a *samayin*, nor is there initiation;
there is no lineage (*santāna*) and so forth, nor the vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*).

Since he is presided over by that Great God, the Primordial Knower (Ādividvān), his purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are for the sake of achieving that very presiding; yet that [presiding] belongs to him spontaneously. Therefore, he has been initiated by the Goddesses and possesses devotion to the teaching of Śiva.
Furthermore, through the distinctions of firmness, imperturbability, and penetration, he himself should then, by means of his vow,
prepare his own purification through austerity, recitation, and other practices under the guidance of a guru;
for it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka that one should oneself sprinkle [the water] upon one's body.
Beginning with these words and concluding with that final perfection,
one becomes truly consecrated in this manner, and not by means of external jar-water.
That is likewise stated in the *Śrīsarvavīra*, the *Śrībrahmayāmala*, and other such texts.
This has been described by Maheśa; how much more could be written of it?
(145) In this way, what and for whom might intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-vijñāna*) not accomplish? For the great sage Śeṣa declared that through intuition, everything is known. (146)
Others, however, say that for one who is free from desire, such a teacher is one of spontaneous intuition (*prātibha*);
whereas in the case of rites performed with desire, the result arises from a collection of causes (*sāmagrī*), and therefore the teacher is considered a mere instrument of purification (*saṃskṛta*).
The power of destiny (*niyati*) does not cease even when the fruit is yet to be accomplished.
"Once consecrated and having fulfilled the observances of the *vidyā*, he bestows the fruit [of the practice].
To this, the teachers who perceive reality—led by the illustrious Somānanda, Kalyāṇa, and Bhavabhūti—said: "This is incorrect."
For thus those wise ones have declared in their commentary on the *Triśikā-śāstra*:
"That innate knowledge which is spontaneously attained is called the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
In its absence, for that purpose, the knowledge acquired through effort is held in esteem. (150–151ab)

For one who knows this in such a way according to reality, there occurs an initiation leading to Nirvāṇa that is undoubtedly free from the offering of sesame and clarified butter. Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, if anyone knows it thus according to reality, [attains the same].
"He shall always possess success; he is a yogin and he is initiated. One who was ignorant of the rules becomes a knower of the ritual with respect to sacrifice.
By such words spoken in the *Triśikā* and clearly belonging to Maheśvara, [this is established].

Knowledge is described as the true essence of purificatory rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth. However, for those devoid of knowledge, ritual action such as initiation serves as the means to that knowledge. Let this matter rest for now; it will be addressed in its own proper context later on.
The teacher, the scriptures, the means of valid cognition, and so forth, are indeed directly means;
yet this supreme intuition is the true [goal], since it is the cow of plenty that grants all desires.
Through the sequence of the application of means, one then reaches the state beyond means and beyond sequence.

Whatever form [is perceived], that is the supreme reality, firmly established in each respective case. But he who is beautiful through the twofold refinement of both intuitive insight and external [learning], and who is said to require no other assistance, is the Guru who directly bestows boons.
Whether for one's own liberation alone or for the liberation of the entire universe, an intuitive flash of insight arises—
like a firefly, a gem, the stars, the moon, or the sun. Therefore,
this scripture composed by us is intended for that intuitive realization.
He who practices [this] is truly a guru; for those who merely mimic the meaning of reality are not so.
All things do not appear in this way to one who lives by depending on others out of a lack of understanding;
without the instruction of that [guru], one does not know [the truth] due to the dullness of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
And this is clearly demonstrated in those various scriptures;
likewise, it is stated in the *Kiraṇa* that [disciples are classified] according to the teacher, the scripture, and themselves:
some are fit for knowledge, while others are fit for ritual conduct.

In the venerable *Nandiśikhātantra*, this has been set forth in detail; it is now described without interruption by way of questions and answers. Since Śiva is indefinable therein, let the means [to realize him] be described.
When this question was posed by the Goddess, the illustrious Śambhu explained: "In this matter,
O fair-hipped one, the sole means is discernment (*viveka*), for it causes one to abandon that which is to be abandoned and bestows upon him the supreme intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*)."
When one is endowed with intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), then being liberated oneself, one may liberate others.
Through the descent of the supreme power (*para-śakti*), the person’s impurity of *māyā* is destroyed.
But surely, if liberation was previously [attained] through initiation (*dīkṣā*), how can it now be [attained] through intuitive insight? 167.
When the Goddess had thus posed the question, the speech of the All-pervasive Lord proceeded:
"O Dear One, a living being is liberated through initiation (*dīkṣā*) as well as through intuitive insight (*prātibha*).
That initiation, however, depends upon the Guru for the purpose of releasing one from the bondage of that which binds."
But his intuitive nature (*prātibha-svabhāva*) bestows the accomplishment of the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*).
For one who has attained oneness, liberation is indeed certain; is that not [attained] through the Supreme Reality?
Indeed, you have described these three principles as Man, Śakti, and Śiva.
The soul is not bound; it is the power of bondage that touches upon agency as its instrument.
It is taught from the scriptures of the Guru that Śiva is the agent for the individual soul (aṇu);
all this has been stated through further discernment—let it now be explained in greater detail.
"O God of gods, what is this discernment (*viveka*), and how is it discerned?
When this was asked by the Supreme Goddess, Śiva, the primordial teacher, replied:
"The triad of principles beginning with Śiva [is discerned] through the tradition of the Guru. (AbhT 13.172b–173)
Through statements consisting of questions and answers, that which is established attains the state of *prātibha* (intuitive insight).
Indeed, for one whose bonds have been severed by initiation and who is cultivated through meditative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), reality (*tattva*) reaches a state of expansion;
that is declared to be *prātibha*.
Like a fire covered by ashes, the intuitive flash (*prātibha*) becomes manifest through the acquisition of reverence;
just as a seed sown at the proper time and watered grows, so too does the intuitive flash become clear through the yoga, sacrifice, and recitation taught by the Guru. (13.175–13.176)

When this discernment, which transcends the senses, reaches its full realization, then the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), and the Lord (pati) shines forth spontaneously. But when intuitive insight (prātibha) has arrived, that other knowledge associated with the senses [is surpassed].
O fair-faced one, that which is perceivable by speech, sight, and hearing, and which is dependent on other things,
the wise man should abandon by resorting to the intellect, just as one discards a lamp during the day.
For one in whom discernment has arisen, [the truth] appears within the range of the cognitive faculties.
Marveling at wonders such as hearing from afar or piercing through objects,

he becomes indifferent to all phenomena by discerning their true nature and turns his back on all worldly existence. With a soul utterly detached from such playthings, he is permeated solely by the state of Śiva.
O lady of beautiful hips, this is declared to be the majesty of *prātibha* [intuition].

One should perceive Śiva, who is both internal and external, like one's own reflection in a mirror; then, knowing the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, one should meditate upon one’s own consciousness.
Indeed, the "net of accomplishments" (siddhijāla) has been taught as a means for inspiring conviction in others;

through the contemplation that "those who have attained accomplishment here shall be liberated at the end of the body," one is declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) due to the firmness of that supreme contemplation.
This characteristic has been declared for you regarding the division of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*).
In matters of cursing or bestowing grace, as well as through practice and power,
one who maintains equanimity toward these is liberated and may liberate others.
Bound by the conjunction with the elements, the senses, and so forth, the individual soul (*aṇu*) inevitably wanders in transmigratory existence.
That same soul, when endowed with *pratibhā* (intuitive insight), is called the principle of power (*śaktitattva*).
Through the descent and penetration of that [power], one is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and becomes Śiva himself.
"But surely, that knowledge has been said by the Teacher to be both with the senses and beyond the senses;
and since it is born of discernment through the intellect, how could it be without the senses?
Thus questioned, he replied: "Because of the single latent impression of dullness belonging to the mind and the intellect."
Through solitude, there is the state of being the witness; when that [solitude] is severed, Śiva is the illuminator.
The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of all entities is proclaimed as their "otherness" (*paratā*). Mind and intellect, however, are not distinct from one another with respect to any other cause.
For these two, strengthened by the power of the Lord, are indeed the causes for discernment (viveka). O Dear One, the attainment of knowledge does not occur for one devoid of mind and intellect;
because it exists beyond their state, that subtle principle is called Śakti-tattva.
The discernment (*viveka*) of all states of being arises from pure being for one of great resolve;
however, the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is superior, inferior, or middling.
It extends even to the powers such as *aṇimā*, yet it is a binding, insentient sense-organ.

"But surely, if liberation occurs through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), what is the use of initiation in the ritual of Śiva? [To this] he replied: "For children, the ignorant, and women are indeed unawakened during initiation; they are liberated by the severing of their bonds and awakened within the ritual of Śiva."
"Therefore, O beautiful one, initiation (*dīkṣā*) exists among these [beings] as the cause;
through initiation, when there is liberation from bonds, [knowledge] born of discrimination arises from the state of purity.
(AbhT 13.195–196a) This is the text that has been recited for those who are themselves incapable of understanding it.

Through the correspondence with the words of Śiva, their awakening shall attain firmness. And in the venerable *Niśāṭana*, it is said that knowledge is threefold by virtue of oneself, the guru, and the scripture; the primary [knowledge] is one's own realization, which carries one across the ocean of conceptual constructs.

"Since doubt, which has its root in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and concerns the nature of mantras, the self, substances, food, the divine, the principles (*tattva*), and so forth, is indeed pacified by one's own direct realization (*svapratyaya*)," [it is said]. Having grasped this very meaning as it resides within, according to the *Mālinīmata*:
Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of his own fitness,
this soul becomes connected with the peaceful power of Śiva, which bestows the fruit of liberation. Through that connection, someone may then attain liberation in that very instant.
Having said this, he speaks again concerning the domain known as *tīvratīvrā*:
"The unification with ignorance ceases for someone who, permeated by the power of Rudra, desires to go forth by the will of Śiva. (201–202)
For the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, he is led toward a true guru.
Having propitiated him and received the initiation of Śaṅkara from that satisfied master,
he shall go to Śiva either at that very moment, through [further] experience, or upon the fall of the body.

The meaning of this is as follows: that certain reflective awareness (*amarśana*) of one's own nature, which consists of the self’s own activity, is what is here called "time" (*kāla*). Here, "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is said to be the state of being worthy of union with identity with Śiva.
"Why was it not so before? Why did it happen only then?"—this is not a coherent [objection].
For there is no such thing as time apart from the manifestation of things in that way.
However, through [the Lord's] absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), let the power of time unfold within that manifestation.
That [power] described as the glory of Śiva is not for the sake of being questioned;
indeed, the great power of Śiva remains eternally connected with the selves. True, she consists of concealment, yet this tranquil one is the vision of one's own true nature.
