For agitation is indeed duality, while unity is tranquility; therefore, one who is absorbed in that [unity] becomes identical with it.
Bound by that peace, remaining established and partaking in the nature of Śakti, he abandons the state of the individual soul (aṇu) and becomes Śiva through the firm consolidation of that power.

Even there, depending on the degree of intensity and so forth, his fall from the body may occur quickly or after a long time; or else, he may attain a state of being like a piece of wood or similar inert matter,
with his consciousness turned away from all worldly activities.

One who is possessed by the most intense and great power attains success. Thus, the preceding portion of the text concerns this [level]; however, elsewhere, another section of the text clearly indicates the portion concerning the medium-intense descent of power.
The state of ignorance in the person consists in consciousness being contracted within the heart;
however, when that contraction ceases, one's own true nature shines forth.
By the phrase "possessed by the power of Rudra," this [state] is described for him.
Regarding the group of signs mentioned here concerning Rudra: unwavering devotion [is the first];

then, in that sequence, there is the perfection of mantras, mastery over all the *tattvas*, the accomplishment of ritual acts (*kṛtya*), poetic genius, and the capacity to understand the meaning of all scriptures. (AbhT 13.214b–215)
Due to the application of their own relative gradations, there may be a state of these [powers] being either separate or combined.
Even in that regard, the wise one should deliberate upon their predominance in both enjoyment and liberation.
This section of the text, ending with the word *sa*, clearly constitutes the second subject matter.

But another, regarding the procedure for the descent of power (śaktipāta) known as "weak-intense," develops a desire to go [to the teacher] through the force of that weak-intense power; and he too, by virtue of the influence of Śiva’s will, [turns] toward a true guru.
In this very regard, it is characterized in the scripture as stated by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin):
"Furthermore, he who knows all these principles (tattvas) according to their true nature is declared to be a Guru equal to Me, the revealer of the potency of mantra. (219–220a)

Men who are seen, honored, or touched by him with a joyful heart are liberated from sins committed even over seven lifetimes. Furthermore, those living beings who are initiated by him are impelled by Śiva.
Having obtained the fruit according to their desire, they go to the state that is free from ailment.

Through the application of inquiry—asking "What is reality? and "Who is the knower of reality?"—one should, through inspired intuition and the company of friends, become desirous of approaching a guru.
Thus, through the application of the desire to go [toward liberation], that teacher is attained; and he,
being perfected and refined through the application of degrees of excellence and so forth,
though previously subject to differentiation, [attains it] suddenly, gradually, in its entirety, or partially.
For it is taught here that the attainment of a guru is indeed distinguished by such varieties as these;
therefore, he immediately receives initiation which bestows Śiva-hood,
through which he knows everything in its true nature as being essentially knowledge.
He is declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and become Śiva at that very moment;
for even his connection with a body is clearly conducive to his state of Śiva-hood.
Indeed, through instruction, union, or contemplation, there is a dissolution of duality within this [state].
Through the scripture, through transition, through the demonstration of the practice of equanimity by the teacher,

through the majesty of mantra, mudrā, and so forth— whether in their totality or individually— and through ritual action, or by means of the entry of the vital breath into the internal forms, [one attains realization].
And at that time, even while remaining within the body, he is said to be liberated.
This has been stated in the two scriptures known as the *Śrī Ratnamālā* and the *Āgama*:
"At whatever moment the Guru reveals the state free of conceptual construction..."

At that very moment, it is said, he is liberated; the machine (the body) remains alone due to the connection with the karma that has already begun (*prārabdha-karma*), resulting in the body’s experience of pleasure and pain. One should not have any doubt regarding this, for it is set forth in the venerable *Gama-śāstra*.
For the body, which is nurtured by ignorance arising from another birth,
is constrained by that very karma even for those possessed of knowledge while in the physical frame;
it persists as a single continuous unit that bestows birth, lifespan, and experience.
For since the particle *hi* follows the singular form that has been stated, there is a logical connection with the word *tena* (by that).
[This occurs] through repetition (*abhyāsa*), reasoning (*yukti*), transition (*saṃkrānti*), piercing (*vedha*), striking (*ghaṭṭana*), and restraint (*rodha*);
or else through oblation (*huti*), the power of mantra (*mantrasāmarthya*), or the application of the severing of bonds (*pāśacchedaprayoga*).
One should perform [the rite] that bestows immediate liberation and effects the instantaneous separation from life.
However, in this regard, there is this rule: one should perform it when the moment of death is near;
otherwise, it should not be done, because the karma that has already begun would not be purified.
And this was indeed stated previously: because of the application of the power of mantra, even one who has been deprived of his vital breaths still enjoys the remaining fruit;
therefore, having clearly passed through the various [experiences] of that remainder of birth, [he attains liberation].
By the cessation of other karmas, one is swiftly liberated.
Therefore, without knowing the moment of death, one should not perform the initiation that takes away life;
for its sole fruit is the transgression of the Supreme Lord’s command.
This has been determined as the "one-and-three" [classification] regarding the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); now, another case follows:
when initiation is performed during the "intense-middling" (*tīvramadhya*) descent, one does not perceive such firm Śiva-nature within oneself; however, at the end of the body, one becomes Śiva.
And it is stated in the *Niśisañcāra* and the *Yogasañcāra-śāstra*:
"By means of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), having established oneself within the body, one attains the state of Śiva at the end of the burning away [of impurities].
Even while being eager for the attainment of Śiva, this occurs when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) falls upon the very center of the middle. (13.241b–242)

Wherever one who desires worldly enjoyment is joined [in practice], having experienced that [enjoyment] at the dissolution of the body, he becomes Śiva. But if he is joined to the principle (tattva) within the "slow" or "middling" [state],
then at the end of the body, having experienced the enjoyment pertaining to that principle, he shall subsequently go to Śiva.
Even there, due to the possibility of gradations [of intensity], there is a difference in speed— whether slow or quick—
as well as a connection with greater or lesser enjoyment, and a sequence of the smallness of the bodily plane.
[This applies to] those who are intensely dull, moderately dull, or mildly dull in their desire for enjoyment.
"By means of the primary [power] alone, through the prescribed method, one eventually attains Śiva.
Others interpret the passage beginning with "one who desires to go" (*yiyāsu*) as being connected to the preceding text,
[placing it] within the scope of the descent of the power known as "intense-middling" (*madhyatīvra*).
When one who is possessed by *pratibhā* (intuitive inspiration),
even while desiring to establish a correspondence [with reality], becomes intent on departing [from this state], then he should be led to a true guru.
Not everyone who is possessed by *pratibhā* is led to a true guru by that power.
Thus he speaks; one who desires to depart must certainly be addressed in this way, and not otherwise.
Possessed by the power of Rudra, he is led toward a true guru. By that means, his mind becomes completely filled with the knowledge arising from attained discernment.
Through the firm establishment of mutual confirmation and so forth, one clearly becomes desirous of going [to the teacher].
This was stated by the Great Lord in the first hexad of the *Nandiśikhātantra*:
"At that time, a longing for the divine Śiva arises within bound souls."
When the supreme atoms (paramāṇu) are indeed endowed with the conceit of being Śaivas,

at that very moment they are liberated, because they have been initiated by the Guru. And it is understood that merely by attaining [this state], they are "accomplished" (siddha) and "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya).
The textual passage beginning with "Having propitiated him" refers to the domain of those whose intensity [of obscuration] is mild or moderate.

This ninefold descent of power (śaktipāta) has been described by Śambhunātha. Here, the essential point to be known is that [the descent of power] belongs to the one whose nature is the perfectly full consciousness.

The supreme descent of power (śaktipāta) is luminous and devoid of limitation; yet even such [a descent] may be characterized by a limitation consisting of a portion of worldly experience (bhoga). This other descent of power bestows the state of Śiva only at the very end.

Since, in both cases, there is no operation of karma and the like which reside within Māyā, He is thus independent in every respect. Therefore, those Rudras who are within the interval of Māyā and those who are above it—
When their respective offices have come to an end, they are forcibly transformed into Bhairavas.
Those who are indeed not overcome by *māyā* are independent of karma and other such factors;
solely by the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), they attain various supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

"But surely, through worship, recitation, meditation, the service of Śaṅkara, and so forth, those [mantras] have attained the status of being mantras and the like; how then can they be independent of ritual action? "Do not say so. For in such [practices as] meditation and recitation that have transcended [the lower levels], there is no dependence on ritual action."

First of all, let the process of their manifestation be examined: why is it that [the soul's state] is corrupted by karma, its equilibrium, dispassion, the ripening of impurities, and so forth? If the will of the Lord is the cause, then the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) alone must be the singular cause.

Thus, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) consists precisely of activities such as recitation (*japa*) and the like, but it is not "karma" (in the conventional sense). For that which is commonly known in the world as "karma"—which bestows inferior enjoyment and obscures the true nature of the enjoyer—is what we mean by that term; however, we place no emphasis on its mere name. (AbhT 13.262b–263)
If it is asked why they possess such an intensity for enjoyment (*bhoga*), the answer has already been given:
this Supreme Lord is autonomous and manifests in diverse forms.
Due to His autonomy, however, there is the bond of concealment; through that, He assumes the state of an enjoyer within enjoyment.
Nourishing its own very nature, it becomes free from impurity, karma, and the like.

It has been said that this power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of Śiva, as it resides within bound souls (*paśu*), is the binder; therefore, it is called "karma" because it effects the obscuration of one's true nature.
And that power of action (kriyā-śakti), when known, immediately brings about accomplishment;

here, accomplishment (siddhi) is said to be the manifestation of one's own uninterrupted self-consciousness. It is the imperishable Great Fortune (mahālakṣmī), the sovereignty over both enjoyment and liberation.
Whatever form of Viṣṇu or others exists in the Lord, that is [manifested] by his own nature (nijātmanā).
Due to the influence of the conjunction of duality, it remains situated within the sphere of Māyā.
Therefore, because of its connection with that form, even though the descent of power (śaktipāta) is already present, [it appears as such].
It bestows only that much enjoyment, but not Śiva-hood in the end;
just as a king, by his own sovereignty, may favor someone,
so too Viṣṇu and the others are fully capable [of doing so] through the penetration of the power of the Lord (Īśa).
Then, by virtue of the descent of power (śaktipāta) pertaining to the office of the Womb of Māyā,
a certain person becomes a discernor of Pradhāna and Puruṣa who has transcended Prakṛti; or,
from that very same [descent], another quickly attains discernment through awakened wisdom.
In an instant, he becomes a knower of the distinction between the individual soul (pums) and limited agency (kalā), as well as between the soul and māyā;
for he has completely brought about the cessation of karma, which rests upon kalā.
However, the previous state was that of a "knowledge-deprived" (jñānākala) bound by karma, because his existence remained dependent upon that [karma].
He never again undergoes creation at the very base of primordial nature (prakṛti). However, impelled by Ananteśa, he may be created within the realm of Māyā;
having attained the state of a Vijñānākala due solely to his residual office (adhikāra).
From Śiva, the Supreme Lord, the impurity attains the state of mantras, their lords, and so forth;
that which is this descent of power (śaktipāta) from the highest Lord indeed [occurs] because of impurity.
It is called the "separation" from that which is known as ignorance, and it is the illuminator of the state of Śiva.

Indeed, the state of Śiva is not revealed by anything else whatsoever. Therefore, it is stated in the *Svacchanda-śāstra* that there are three hundred and sixty-three deluded disputants, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others, who wander within the night.
The exclusive knowledge of Śiva bestows the attainment of the state of Śiva;
and the descent of power (śaktipāta), which culminates in that attainment of the state of Śiva, is now discussed. Otherwise, what indeed could exist that is not presided over by the power of Śiva?
Therefore, those such as the Vaiṣṇavas have no qualification whatsoever here [in this system].
For they function solely within the realm of duality and are far removed from non-duality.
However, by virtue of the sovereignty of Maheśvara, even they may become oriented toward Śiva-hood.
For these [images], there is a twofold consecration: first by the extraction of the *liṅga* (the core essence), and then by initiation (*dīkṣā*).
When the impure residual impressions (*adhivāsa*) have been removed, the water-pot (*kumbha*) is consecrated with flowers.
This same twofold consecration applies to it; such a procedure is not required for a pot that is already pure.

Thus, this glorious descent of power (śaktipāta) has been described here as independent [of external means]. In this same manner, the Mataṅga, Kiraṇa, and other scriptures are to be understood; however, for fear of excessive length, they have not been transcribed and included here.
In the Purāṇa as well, it is taught that devotion to Him alone is desired through His very grace,
by which those whose minds are absorbed in His being attain supreme perfection. By the use of the particle *eva* ("alone"), dependence on ritual action (*karman*) and other such means is excluded.
Clarity (*prasāda*) is the state of being stainless; by means of that, there is the state of fullness. For by means of that very self, Śiva shines forth as full in himself.
However, in some cases where one is devoid of contact with the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) of the state of Śiva, [this does not occur].
Indeed, that devotion which exists toward Vaiṣṇava and other deities does not arise from Śiva alone;
in that case, Śiva is the cause, but not acting in isolation. For even though he is stainless, he depends upon the limited karma and other factors acquired [by the individual].
By means of this, they attain supreme perfection; indeed, this is its very life.
And our supreme teacher, the illustrious Utpaladeva, said:
"O Lord, at the moment of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), You never engage in deliberation. (AbhT 13.289b–290)
"What has come upon me today that you delay in the process of revealing yourself?
By using the two words 'at some time' (*karhicit prāpta*), you have expressed your independence [from external means].
O Lord, [you have also indicated] the difficulty of attainment and the absence of passion in the process of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)."
With the latter half [of the verse],

the manifold nature of that very descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is described through its distinctions such as being obstructed, slow, or rapid; and by the venerable Aniruddha, the power of the Lord known as *unmīlinī* was also [described].

While explaining [the scriptures], it was described by Mātaṅga that the Lord’s state of non-reliance (*nirapekṣatā*)—which consists in the unfolding of His own essential nature (*svarūponmīlanātmikā*)—persists even until the end of the stationary beings (*sthāvara*).
That power (*śakti*), falling [upon objects], is never dependent on anything else; this has been explained at great length.
Thus, while this manifold descent of power (śaktipāta) remains established,
there arises a variety of states such as that of the initiate (samayin) and others, due to distinctions such as degrees of intensity.
Through his grace, someone may attain the state of being a mere portion of Rudra.
The initiate (*samayin*) who is thus described shall gradually attain the state of Śiva;

some, being bound to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), become a spiritual son (*putraka*) and [attain it] quickly through the non-sequential method (*akrama*); while another, being a practitioner (*sādhaka*), attains it either slowly or quickly depending on the intervention of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*).

Someone who has completed all that was to be done is a teacher (guru) established in the form that partakes in the fivefold set of duties; he too partakes in the distinctions of enjoyment, liberation,
and so forth, through the application of the fourfold [disciples] beginning with the *samayin*, both in brief and in detail.

The diversity of the descent of power (śaktipāta) consists of distinctions such as gradual and non-gradual. In the Siddhānta, the descent of power is gradual; thereafter, it is [also] in Vāmaka, Dakṣa, Mata, Kula, Kaula, Ṣaḍardha, and Hṛdaya.
"Whether by means of leaping over [the levels] or even instantaneously and without sequence,

it has been taught in the Śrī Bhairavakula that a Guru who has been well-consecrated by the five initiations and has indeed transcended the lower currents belongs to the Trika scripture. (AbhT 13.301b–302)
The All-pervasive Lord has shown the hierarchy of higher and lower levels in the scriptures,
such as the *Śrī Sarvācāra* and the *Hṛdaya*, through the distinctions of knowledge, conduct,
and so forth. A teacher who has been consecrated in the Vāma path is a knower of the supreme reality.
Nevertheless, in the Bhairava Tantra, one must undergo purification once again. Those who follow the Śaiva, Vaimala, Siddhānta, Ārhata, and Kāruka systems—
all of them are to be known as bound souls (paśus) within the Bhairava circle of Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍala).
In the *Kulakālī-vidhi*, it is stated specifically regarding Vaiṣṇavas—
and those who have resorted to the practice of remaining in ashes— that they possess no fitness for this at all;
thus it was briefly declared by the venerable Maheśvara in the *Svacchanda-śāstra*.
But he who is devoted to other scriptures does not bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
For a guru is considered one who has received initiation through the sequence beginning with that of a *samayin*;
and since that occurs by the power of [divine] energy (*śakti*), what connection could there be with Vaiṣṇavas and others?

If one were to acquire that knowledge through deceit, eavesdropping, and the like, what kind of expiation would there be for such a person who is qualified [for it]? A disciple who is possessed by a desire for fruits has his success dependent solely upon that [teacher].
He would certainly be cooked in hell even by the performance of penance.
This is the manner of concealment (tirobhāva), namely that he has been directed toward such a teacher by Śiva; his devotion to him is not called a descent of power (śaktipāta).

When, however, by virtue of its diversity one should recognize such a state of perverse engagement on his part, one should withdraw that knowledge from him. One should abandon that person of sinful conduct and remain intent upon knowledge.
Just as a king, having seized wealth from a thief, punishes him, so too the one of noble mind,
having extracted the Śaiva knowledge from that of the Vaiṣṇavas and others—
even though he has heard the knowledge of Śiva— is still fully capable of maintaining a state of exclusive attachment to duality.

One who does not abandon [the path] is firmly presided over by Vāmā; such is the best of bound souls (paśu). Having been concealed by Śiva himself and established there by the force of necessity (niyati), how could he, being dependent on another, ever proceed to the state of the Lord?

And it is stated in the *Svacchanda-śāstra*: "Māyā indeed causes those who are devoted to the Vaiṣṇava and other [sects] to wander, through their desire for liberation in what is not liberation. A follower of the Vaiṣṇava and other [sects], while incorporating the Śaiva scripture into his own teaching..."
One who has fallen into doubt certainly goes to ruin by falling away from both;
for, due to the transgression of the rules regarding both his own vision and the vision of others, he incurs sin. Therefore, one should not follow such a course.
And the Supreme Lord has stated the same in the venerable Gahvara:

"The knowledge of Śiva does not manifest in those devoted to other scriptures. Therefore, a follower of the Siddhānta is not [qualified] for the Vāma, nor is he for the Dakṣiṇa, according to our doctrine. (AbhT 13.319b–320)
In the Kula, Kaula, and Trika traditions, each preceding one is not present in the subsequent;
however, one who is established in the infinite does not perceive [the teachings] as limited or non-limited.
Therefore, the teacher who stands above is the one authorized, while the one standing below is the "all-enduring" (sarvasaha).
The supreme Guru, situated above, brings to fruition those lower activities— such as the vital breaths— which are sustained by the touch of his own lower lip;
he is likewise one who serves a Guru of such a nature, even while remaining below and fixed in his gaze.
One who, ignited by such a descent of power (śakti), should swiftly lead this [soul] upward—
even in a field or sacred seat (pīṭha) partitioned by various mountains and rivers—
the lower level is not qualified for the ever-higher levels of consciousness.
Even one who recognizes a teacher higher than his own, if he is lower and lower [in realization],
becomes a vessel for punishment by transgressing the scriptures while performing his duties.
The diversity of fitness for knowledge arises solely from the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).

Knowledge is threefold: that consisting of hearing (*śrauta*), that consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*), and that consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). Among these, the latter is superior, for it is the sole cause of liberation;
it effects one's extraction from the principles (*tattva*) and joins one to either the manifest (*sakala*) or the unmanifest (*akala*) state.
How can one perform [the practice] without the supreme knowledge consisting of meditative cultivation (bhāvanāmaya)?
Even a yogi who has attained various specific accomplishments (siddhi) in the highest state,
such as that of Sadāśiva and others, becomes a unifier [of the self with Śiva] precisely because of his well-practiced state of possessing knowledge.

Whatever perfection born of yoga he may possess regarding the lower principles is not a means for liberation, even if it remains as stable as wealth or a wife. But he in whom all perfections pertaining to the entire path have arisen— he is indeed Sadāśiva.
How can this [teacher], having attained the status of a Guru, directly liberate mortals?
It was said by him in the *Mālinītantra* after reflecting upon the nature of knowledge and yoga:
"For one who possesses well-practiced knowledge is declared by the wise to be the bestower of liberation."
Therefore, the sole characteristic of a Guru is the state of having thoroughly practiced realized knowledge (*vijñāna*).
This distinction has been declared by me as it was shown by Lord Śambhunātha:
one who is intent on the knowledge of liberation should make his own teacher one whose realization is well-practiced.
One should abandon another [teacher], even if already attained; for that has been stated by Śiva:
"Just as a bee seeking fragrance would go from flower to flower, so a disciple seeking higher knowledge should go from one teacher to another. (AbhT 13.334b–335)
Having encountered a guru devoid of power, how can one rely upon him for the knowledge of liberation?
O Goddess, when the root of a tree is destroyed, from where could flowers, fruits, and the like arise?
Even while observing the ever-increasing splendor of higher and higher stages, [one remains]... [336-337]
Who else could be more cursed by fate than one who occupies such a low station?
But he who desires enjoyment, liberation,
and spiritual knowledge should take refuge in a Guru who is a perfected master of yoga and whose own knowledge is well-practiced.

In the absence of such [a teacher], however, one should resort to a man of knowledge (*jñānin*) for the sake of liberation through discernment (*vijñāna*); or, regarding the portion of enjoyment (*bhukti*), one should resort to a yogin who is capable of bestowing that fruit. [But] when a yogin is incapable of bestowing the fruit and teaches only what leads to ruin...
Better is the man of knowledge who would point out the means and even liberate [the disciple].
For if a single knower is not yet complete, he should take up various forms of knowledge through a sequence of parts and sub-parts,
and thus produce a consciousness that is an unbroken circle.
Therefore, one should accept countless gurus for the sake of fulfilling one's own consciousness;
indeed, the fortunate seeker of knowledge finds a guru who possesses complete realization.
[Such a guru] is one whose teaching is infused with the mere flash of intuition arising from the various streams of gurus and scriptures.
Having created an ocean of knowledge, would one not flood it with one's own droplets?
(343) For me, whose lineage of gurus extends from Ātapa to Moṭaka, there is no poverty of instruction for me, who am a disciple of all. (344)
Thus it was described here by the illustrious teacher Kallaṭa.
For this very reason, out of curiosity regarding the perspectives of the lower scriptures,
I did not serve the logicians, the followers of the Vedas, the Buddhists, the Jains, the Vaiṣṇavas, and others.
Through the prescriptions for the rituals of karma-yoga pertaining to the worlds, the internal self, the higher paths, and so forth,
one should contemplate the progressively superior [levels] due to the abundance of the excellence of awakening;
in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, the sages Nārada and others were the questioners.
First come the Vaiṣṇavas and the Buddhists, and after them those who know the Siddhāntas and other systems;
their eyes are then made eager for the moonlight of the knowledge of the meaning of the Trika, in due order.
Therefore, one should never entertain doubt regarding the multiplicity of gurus.

The transgression that is traditionally taught for one who is attached to another guru, who is deluded, or who serves other scriptures, should be understood as follows: he who is authorized in a particular scripture is called the guru therein.
In that regard, one who is not authorized [to receive initiation from a teacher] is called "another guru.
Just as one seated within a particular mandala, desiring to conquer the sovereign of another mandala, perishes by serving him; 351–352ab. so too does he perish by serving such a person.
Likewise, one who seeks to attain the success of ever-higher knowledge,
yet relies upon a teacher of a lower level, meets with destruction. In this very same way, one who desires success based on a scripture that pertains to a higher [level] [is ruined].

One who is devoted to the teachings of Māyā meets with destruction. And it is said in the venerable *Ānanda*: "Having resorted to ritual action out of worldly inclination, one feels disgust when that proves fruitless, and then resorts to something else. (354) (355a)
Thus diminishing day by day, he is cooked in the Raurava and other hells.
But he who, desiring the ever-higher path, would abandon a lower teacher or scripture through the descent of power (śaktipāta)— he is fortunate, for he has been turned toward the truth.
For this very reason, it is in the Śaiva scriptures alone that this purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka-vidhi*) is prescribed for those who have no confidence in the doctrines of other systems. Therefore,
even one who has fallen into another [tradition] may attain the supreme Śaiva state.
In this world, one who is to be favored should be led higher and higher; he must never be allowed to fall.

For this very reason, nothing such as the extraction of the *liṅga* (or the removal of sectarian marks) has been taught in the scriptures of the omniscient ones, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, regarding their own [respective] doctrines.
In this way, Viṣṇu and the others, who alone know the supreme reality of Śiva,
initiated certain people in such a manner because they were deluded and had resorted to wrong views; indeed,
they bestowed such a mindset as one incapable of touching the truth.
Having seen this, it was likewise declared by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other Buddhas.
(361b) Thus, this descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has been analyzed according to both reasoning and scripture.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Let the nature of concealment (*tirobhāva*) be examined as it is being described:
because the Supreme Lord, by his very nature, manifests while touching upon the sequence of necessity and non-necessity, he is therefore called "Svacchanda" (the Independent One).

Relying upon *niyati* (the principle of necessity) regarding both action and its fruit, this Maheśvara ordains the processes of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as the intermediate states;
and again, during the great emission (*mahāsarga*) which is characterized by an infinity of creations and dissolutions.
That one God, the Lord who is the soul of the universe, has arrived through the power of necessity (niyati).
And whatever creation and maintenance occur in the intermediate state, they too are here not constrained by any external mechanism;
for He does not abandon His body, and He remains here established as that which has cast off necessity.
When, by means of necessity (*niyati*) itself, through the process of veiling its own true nature,
it experiences suffering, delusion, and so forth, then that is the sequence of the fruits of karma.
But when it abandons the constraint of karma, [it is freed] from being enveloped by suffering and delusion.
Desiring to manifest [the world], he remains indifferent toward its concealment; just as one who is enlightened, by virtue of the sovereignty of light, acts like one who is unenlightened,
so too does he, though not yet transcended, act as if he has transcended.

Just as the Buddha, even while performing those deluded actions, remains free from hatred, so too are the activities of the awakened ones pleasing to the heart; for the Lord of the Śrīvidyā spoke thus in the *Mānastotra*.

Those who have received initiation into your path of instruction yet fall into error through the power of delusion—surely they lack the application of your light; for can the rays of the sun ever cause the lotuses to close?
Even those who have known what is to be known and stand in the position of a creator, if they stray from your path onto a false road, they too are not correct.

For the most part, their false awakening— arising from inferential cognition and the like— is comparable to a lamp fueled by snake-fat. For just as copper pierced by the primary essence of mercury does not return again to its own original nature,
so too has that nectar not been drunk by those dwelling on the surface of the earth, since they continue to be afflicted in this world by the pains of thirst and hunger.
Then, his activities—such as the practice of mantra and ritual worship—awakened;
yet, fueled by hatred, they burn him from within, for that burning is indeed nothing but doubt.
Moreover, he does not possess such greatness of karma by which he might remain in this state.
For what indeed is that karma, or why is the rule here the same as the previous one?
Therefore, it is the will of the Supreme Lord by which he, thus deluded,
seeks to become a vessel for suffering to be experienced throughout infinite time.
Even there, due to the variety of desires, suffering is likewise divided into three types— pertaining to this world, the next, or both— and is further distinguished by its duration or its swiftness,
as seen in the cases of Kāla, Kāma, Andhaka, and others who dwell in the city of Paulastya.
Likewise, the concealment of others is indeed painful both here and in the hereafter.
Furthermore, there is another form of concealment consisting of the transgression of the rules (samaya), as stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Ānandagahvara: [17–18]
O Goddess, due to the transgression of the *samaya*, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years.

Even there, the sequence is manifold, depending on the distinctions of mildness, intensity, and so forth. Furthermore, by the sovereign will of Maheśvara, even such a person may become self-manifested.
Or he may enter through another door; moreover, he is fully capable of bestowing further grace.

When further grace is bestowed and the performance of penance and so forth occurs, and when initiation and other rites are carried out according to the proper method, he shall become one whose nature is Śiva.

Even one whose life-force has departed and who has become invisible is favored through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by means of initiation and other rites, after having been brought to mind by kinsmen, friends, and teachers.
Even in that case, there exists a distinction based on the speed or slowness of time.
"So be it"— this is that descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by which one attains the nature of Śiva.
Thus, within these five— creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace—
the agency belonging to the self of consciousness is Śiva-hood.

For the yogi who possesses the conviction that his own self is complete and independent in its fivefold activity, worship, recitation, meditation, and yoga are perpetually manifest. He should never take delight in the accounts of magicians.
Even that enjoyment which belongs to the level of Sadāśiva is a bondage for those whose nature is [otherwise] appropriate.
Śiva-hood is precisely the state of being the knower; that is what is here called sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
Agency, like that of a potter, is not primary, because it is presided over by that [sovereignty].
Knowing this, one should never at any time entertain a sense of fragmentation, thinking:
"If I am Śiva, why does the universe not follow my will?
In this awareness of the "I," there flashes forth the thought: "Let [all things] follow my will."

Is Śiva, or the Supreme Lord, himself created as the body and so forth? First of all, this [body] belongs to Śiva; however, since it was fashioned by you in that manner, what else could its nature as a body be? What ground is there for further censure?
And it is said in the *Siddhasantāna*, the illustrious *Ūrmi-mahākula*:

"Those who have exerted themselves in such things as the whirling of the wind and the projection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and who are deluded by deceptive practices and the like—they are deluded regarding the supreme state. (31–32a)

In all cases, even that upward departure which is performed with great reverence for the sake of liberation is taught in the essential scriptures as a means for worldly enjoyment. [The opponent asks: "If the Lord is omnipresent, tell me, where will He go by departing? 32–33ab. 33cd.
If, on the other hand, it were not all-pervading, then it would be like a jar;

this application of the procedure for the departure [of the soul] is taught as pertaining to that which occupies only one part. But how can there be any connection with the process of departure in the partless reality of Śiva?
Just as [one proceeds] from the earth up to the wind through the elements of ether, water, fire, and fasting,
so too is the process of the soul's departure into the sky;
therefore, one should not cause the individual soul to depart with the desire for the supreme reality.

In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, however, that which was stated regarding the characteristics of the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*) is not intended as a means for liberation; rather, it is for the sake of abandoning worldly experience, since such is the desire [of the practitioner]. One who has attained perfection through recitation, meditation, and so forth, by virtue of his autonomy and the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), [acts thus].
If one is detached from enjoyment, one should thus cast off the body;
for it is heard that even Bhīṣma and others, though possessing the power of voluntary death,
approached the end of their lives only upon attaining a distaste for worldly enjoyment.
The body becomes a recipient of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) through yoga, mantras, the nectar of immortality, excellent substances, and so forth;
otherwise, it cannot be abandoned except by means of the yoga of the aforementioned sequence.
And such [a teaching] was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the *Mālinītantra*.

"Or else, considering even every enjoyment to be deformed"—by speaking thus and so forth, [the Lord] has taught that His own sovereignty over the performance of creation and other acts is such that its internal reality is not perceived by anyone. Thus [ends the teaching]. 42.
That alone shall be the primary initiation for the disciple, bestowing the state of Śiva.
And it is stated in the venerable *Niśicāra* by means of the Bhairavian splendor:
"Those whose minds are free from conceptual construction perceive the entire universe as pervaded [by that light]. (43–44a)

But one whose mind is joined with conceptual thought may attain Śiva through the collection of alms. Through the application of external initiation and so forth, and by means of the mental constructs of conduct and observances, one who is free from conceptual thought becomes liberated while living this very day; of this there is no doubt.

Because the internalized volitions—which are like the root-clusters of the withered tree of saṃsāra—are [consumed] by the fire of the ultimate reality, even if there should remain but a tiny spark, at its end the mass of the fire of pure awakening blazes forth intensely. (46) Thus has this commencement of initiation been shown, in accordance with the scriptures. (47a)
Now, in the fifteenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Next, for the sake of its application, sacrifice (*yāga*) is first described;
therein, initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone serves as the means for both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mukti*).
Whether by its own nature or through the application of refinement (*saṃskāra*), that limb [of the ritual] is demonstrated;
whoever desires enjoyments in a particular place is enjoined to that very place by the power of the mantra, according to the Lord in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva*.
"By the power of [spiritual] fitness, wherever one's latent impression (vāsanā) lies, there he is to be joined;
he does not fall away from that"— thus says our venerable Guru in the *Śrī Mālinīmata*, declaring that initiation is a means for the attainment of enjoyment and other goals.
Without initiation, there is no eligibility for the yoga of Śiva;
nor does this [initiation] result in eligibility for yoga alone.
Through initiation by Śiva, one also gains eligibility for mantra and liberation.

In this statement from the Mālinīvijayottara-tantra, the fact that initiation is the direct means to liberation has been declared; furthermore, by means of the preceding text, it is stated that through the process of purification,
it is also the indirect means to both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
"For those who possess the resolve [to seek liberation] but lack the capacity for [higher] knowledge, this procedure taught by the Guru is declared to be an easy means. Thus,
in the venerable *Mataṅga*, the status of being a means to liberation has been stated."

For knowledge (*vidyā*), whose intrinsic nature is perfect cognition (*samyagjñāna*), is the direct liberator. It has been clearly stated in that very [text], in the section on Knowledge (*vidyāpāda*), while explaining what is to be abandoned and what is to be acquired according to the causal relationship among the principles (*tattva*). (9–10)

But for those who are incapable in that regard, their initiation, ritual practice, and meditative absorption are preceded by [empirical] knowledge; therefore, the possessor of [transcendental] knowledge is the highest of the high. And since that knowledge comes from the scripture, one who has not been initiated should not be made to hear it.
Therefore, for him, initiation has served only as a means of purification (saṃskriyā).
Wherever he may be joined by the Guru, that knower (jñānin) attains a fruit appropriate to his own realization; this was indeed stated previously.
But for one who, by the grace of the Lord, possesses some kind of divine fitness,
as well as for the guru and the disciple— neither of them requires initiation.
At that time, knowledge itself is the initiation, according to the teaching of the venerable *Traiśika*.
And the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises in him spontaneously.

Thus, according to the principle of the *Mālinīvijaya*, he whose consciousness is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) shall be a candidate for the highest office; for a teacher is considered to be one who possesses such knowledge.
"Whether for oneself or for others, one who desires their welfare should practice this.
By stating this in the *Mālinīśāstra*, all of that has been made manifest.
Furthermore, some are fit for knowledge (*jñāna-yogya*), while others are fit for conduct (*caryā-yogya*).
"In the procedure of the venerable Kiraṇa, it is said: 'She is fit for initiation, she is fit for yoga.

In that regard, the Guru is declared to be one who possesses the characteristics described therein, who is proficient in ritual action (karma), yoga, and knowledge (jñāna), and who is superior by virtue of the progressively higher stages."
Having examined or questioned the disciple— who has been purified by the descent of one of the aforementioned powers— he should perform the rite of initiation.
And it is stated in the Svacchanda Śāstra that the Guru himself should question the disciple:
Whatever kind of fruit you desire, such is the means you should undertake. Through the differentiation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the attainment of the goal is impelled by mantra.
Regarding the mantras, mudrās, paths, and substances used in the fire-oblation (*homa*), the rule is common to all.

The fruit for disciples and for the Guru differs according to the distinction of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The practitioner (*sādhaka*) is of two kinds: one who follows the Śiva-dharma and whose state is abandoned by the world; and one who follows worldly dharma, who desires fruits, who abides in the auspicious, and who has abandoned the inauspicious.

The seeker of liberation is of two kinds: the seedless (*nirbīja*), who is devoid of [the observance of] pledges and the like; and the other, the seeded (*sabīja*), who includes children, the simple-minded, the elderly, women, those devoted to worldly enjoyment, the diseased, and so forth. For such [persons], initiation is thus taught in the teaching of Śiva.
For those who are learned and capable of enduring dualities, initiation is "with seed" (*sabījā*) and consists of the *samaya* (vow);
it is a grace-bestowing initiation, and they must observe the specific *samayas*.
One should properly contemplate the non-existence of past karmic actions through ritual practice.
For one who seeks liberation and is indifferent to worldly things, only *prārabdha* karma remains unexhausted.

However, for the sake of the prosperity of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), one should purify [the other karmas] in this very manner. This initiation, which conforms to the nature of Śiva, removes the laws of the world.

This initiation, which belongs to the worldly order (*lokadharmin*), is for those whose nature is unrighteous; it is not a purification for those who are virtuous. It is devoid of the propitiation of mantras.
Upon the dissolution of the body that was begun [in this life], such a person experiences powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest.

Having eaten, he goes upward to that place where he is joined, whether with the *sakala* or the *akala*. However, in the case of the seedless initiation (*nirbījā*), one should purify the bond of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*).
Through initiation alone, liberation occurs, provided there is constant devotion to the God and the Guru.
This [initiation], which bestows immediate liberation, is called "seedless" (nirbījā);

it severs the three bonds of the past, the future, and those currently in operation. At the conclusion of initiation, for one who is purified, the supreme state is attained upon the casting off of the body.
Upon the abandonment of the body, one who possesses the seed-perception (sabījā) perishes due to the absence of [purifying] karma.
However, the initiated disciple must always observe the bond of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra).
Having thus questioned, understood, and deliberated for himself, the Guru [should proceed].

The Guru should resort to such a habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) as is appropriate for one who desires to perform that [initiation], so that he does not show contempt toward one upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred regarding initiation;
this is the command established by Śambhu.

The Guru himself should perform the initiation of one who is poor by means of his own wealth; or else, even with water and *dūrvā* grass, if the disciple begs for the sake of the initiation. First, the disciple [should offer] to the Guru his own wealth acquired through begging.

One should give that by which [the disciple] becomes pure and thus attains fitness for sacrifice. In this regard, first of all, he who possesses the immersion into the sovereignty of the attainment of Śiva-nature— he alone should be made the Guru, for he is capable of performing initiation.
And his immersion into the state of Śiva is shown to have many means (39).
It is gradual and external in form, consisting of bathing, ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth. Through those various rites, he [attains] the state of Śiva within his heart (40).
Establishing himself firmly in this state, he of tranquil intellect attains the nature of Śiva;
having become Śiva, whatever he may desire, that he strives to accomplish. (41) The external means consisting of the conceit of being Śiva is not the cause that bestows liberation. (42a)

"This is Śiva; I am indeed Śiva"—this [conviction] regarding the teacher and the disciple, through the relationship of cause and effect, is the firm conviction that liberates the individual souls (aṇu). There is no external [reality] without the internal, nor is there an internal [reality] devoid of the external.
"That [reality] is manifested as the second [category] through knowledge and action;
it is for this reason that the Lord described it thus in the *Śrībrahmayāmala*.
And in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra*, it is said that there can be no impurity for the wise man."
However, bathing and wearing fine garments serve to produce contentment.
Therein, through the sequence of the purification of the well-known subjects such as the body,
there arises for those who bathe an effortless innermost purity within and within.

And regarding the bath of the God of gods, which is said to consist of his eight forms: therein, while the internal impurities are being consumed by the blaze of the mantra, one should immerse oneself.
Therein, with the heart of the desired mantra [recited], one should walk three steps within the dust raised by cows.
Having gone and returned, one should perform the earthly bath that bestows steadfastness. Then,
having shaken off impurities with earth consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should gradually wash from the head down to the feet with water consecrated by the five-limbed mantra.

Reciting the mantra known as the *sāṅgamūla*, one should immerse oneself until it reaches the navel, becoming absorbed in that state. Then, having risen, one should satisfy with water from the *mālinī* [mantra] the Sun, who is the womb of all deities and the light of all that exists, and who satisfies the entire universe, within the sky.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose essence is vigor, satisfies the gods, the ancestors, the sages, the *yakṣas*, the *rakṣasas*, and all other elemental beings; and that [vital breath] is the Sun. Thereafter, one should recite the supreme, singular [mantra] according to the previously taught method of pronunciation.
This is considered the water-bath (*jalasnāna*) until the realization of identity with That [the Absolute] occurs.

Having consecrated the ashes produced from fire with the Weapon-mantra (*śastra*), which destroys impurities, one should apply the ashes—mantra-empowered by the five limbs—at the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet. (53–54a)
Then, one should throw a handful of ashes—over which the root mantra along with its limbs has been recited—upon the head.

Having washed the hands and feet with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) and so forth, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the recitation (japa). This is indeed the luminous ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
When the wind is pleasant, not excessive, and carries the scent of cow-dust, one should perform the Vāyavya bath while reciting the mantra during the practice of inhaling and exhaling. Or,
with the gaze fixed one-pointedly upon the pure, all-pervading sky, [one should perform it].

If one should sit while recollecting the mantra, what greater purity could there be than that? Or, if one engaged in the recitation of mantras should touch the body with water falling from a cloudless sky, such is the "celestial bath" (*nābhasasnāna*).
Thus, by meditating upon the splendors of the moon and the sun with the nature of Śiva, one immerses oneself;
where then could one not become fit, having washed away all impurities?
The Self alone is the Supreme Lord, the great lake free from all worldly conduct.

Having submerged the universe right there, one should remain as both the pure and the purifier. Thus, these eight types of ablution are progressively superior for the sake of purification; in every case, one should subsequently withdraw that mantra into a state of oneness.
The sage devoted to the eightfold bath attains, in due order, nourishment, satiation, the burning away of impurities, potency, pervasion, radiance, stability, and non-duality;
for these eight forms are essentially Śiva and consist of grace.
Through meditation upon [the deities] both in their own forms and as Śiva, they bestow their respective fruits.

By this procedure, while performing the conjunction of the earth and the other elements starting from the *kanda* and the *ādhāra* during worship— both in detail and in summary— one shall enjoy the fruit thereof.

For thus it is said in the *Yogasaṃcāra*: "On earth, the mantras are of the nature of the Earth; in the element of Water, they are of the nature of Water; and so on, until in Śiva, they consist of the essence of Śiva.
This has also been well established in the *Śrīnirmaryādaśāstra* in this very manner.
There is a specific distinction regarding the elements beginning with earth that is esteemed by heroic practitioners (vīrasādhaka):
the dust of battle, the water of heroes, the ashes of heroes, the great wind,
the cremation ground, the forest, the sky, and the moon and sun as they are situated therein.
The Self, firmly established with all afflictions of conceptual construction entirely shaken off,
is to be worshipped by heroes during bathing, ritual offerings, and so forth; this is the eightfold form taught in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* [Tantra] using wine, rum, liquor, and the like.
With [wine] that is very sweet, clear, thin, and very fragrant—
having performed the fivefold consecration internally and externally using [the wine] contained in a *kandala* vessel or similar,
one should perform inspection, sprinkling, striking, nourishing, and veiling.
In the center of that wheel of mantras, one should perform worship and the libation of drops;
by means of that, there is self-consecration and sprinkling with the jar-mudrā.
This satiation of the deity rests upon both the path of the body and the path of the vital breath.

One enjoys the fruit of all sacred fords, asceticism, sacrifices, gifts, and so forth. By bathing in wine, the supreme adept who seeks liberation becomes absolute (*kevalī*). For wine consists of Śiva, and all mantras originate from Śiva.
There is no difference between Śiva and Śakti; rather, the rays [of consciousness] arise from Śakti. Therefore, wine—which generates bliss for those rays—is composed of Śiva.
When the full form of consciousness is awakened, one becomes a fit vessel for authority.

That bathing which arises from the distinctions of mantra, meditation, and concentration is not [the true] bath; for the appropriate bath is that which brings about fitness for the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth. This eightfold bath possesses a twofold nature, being both external and internal.
The internal [state] is like the overflowing nectar from the stream of the upward moon;
for from the aperture, they remain pervading one and a half finger-breadths as they move upward. All eight forms are said to extend individually to the limit of the twelve fingers (dvādaśānta).
One should perform one of these ablutions, or even two, three, or more.
Thus has the procedure for bathing been proclaimed by Bhairava for the sake of purification;
now, that which is to be done immediately after bathing is taught as follows.
Having observed that one's disposition is serene, one should then proceed to the sacrificial hall.
That which is described as a mountain peak, a riverbank, a solitary *liṅga*, and so forth, is external here; it serves for specific supernatural accomplishments (*siddhi*), not for liberation.

The internal [practice], such as [visualizing] the peak of a mountain and so forth, which joins the vital breath within the body (81), may serve as a means for practitioners to achieve supernatural powers (*siddhi*), but not for liberation. In the scriptures, it is stated that a sacred seat (*pīṭha*) is always fit for sacrifice (82).
And that [power] is clearly manifest both externally and internally, outside and within the body;
for the Supreme Lord has described it in the *Śrīnaiśasañcāra*:
"His will is the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), the support upon which the moving and the unmoving abide."

That supreme form of desire consists of the non-duality of *bindu* and *nāda*. Then there is the seat of *nāda*, Pūrṇagiri on the right, and again on the left, the seat of Uḍḍiyāna, which is *bindu*; these indeed constitute the three principal seats.
Beyond this, the half-pīṭha is to be known as having the form of conceptualization (saṃkalpanā).
Then there is the Śākta [pīṭha], Kuṇḍalinī, and the Vedakala; these constitute the three upapīṭhas.
Furthermore, there are Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī, as well as Kulagiri.
Lālana, Baindava, and Vyāpti—this is the triad of *saṃdohakas*.
Puṇḍravardhana, Vārendra, and likewise Ekāmra are outside;
thus that seat (*pīṭha*) is said to be ninefold according to the internal and external sequence.

For those who know the sacred fields (*kṣetra*), the eight fields are the eight petals of the heart-lotus: Prayāga, Varaṇā, Aṭṭahāsa, Jayantikā, Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and likewise Lāhulā. (89–90a)
They say there are eight secondary fields (*upakṣetra*), which are the eight petals at the tip of the heart-lotus:
Virajā, Airuḍikā, Hālā, Elā, Pūḥ, Kṣīrikā, Purī, and the one called Māyā; these belong to the region of Maru, both externally and internally.
The joints of the petals of the heart-lotus reach the state of the *upasaṃdoha* [sites]:
Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara;
as well as Mlecchadigdvāravṛtti, Kurukṣetra, and Kheṭaka.
A "two-way path" arises from the union of two, and a "three-way path" from the meeting of three.
They consider a "four-way path" to be where the possessor of power (śaktimat) dissolves right there;
this is established within the body as extending from the end of the nose to the cavity at the end of the palate.

The middle [set] is said to consist of the points known as the center of the brows, the throat, and the heart; that triad of Kaula consists of the navel, the kanda, and the abode of great bliss (mahānanda).
That very same [triad] is also the mountain peak, the riverbank, and the solitary linga.
Or rather, what need is there for so much? Everything resides within consciousness, and from that, it enters the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

From that, it is situated in the body; therefore, one should become established in the abode of the body. However, those who are experts in the path of yoga know that such [consciousness] is likewise present externally.
The goddesses are born from their own nature; that which is external is called the *pīṭha*.
Just as by their very nature the Mlecchas abide on the path of unrighteousness, so too, by necessity, knowledge and yoga are established in certain places within that region.
Just as one who is not even composed of that [element] becomes sinful through contact with them,
so too does one established in the sacred seats (pīṭha) become a fit vessel for knowledge,
yoga, and the rest, by perceiving— primarily within the body, in the vital breath (prāṇa), and in consciousness— the [divine reality].
"What need is there for other grand displays of external wandering, since this entire universe [is within]?
Thus, for those seeking the fruits of various wheels (cakras) both internally and externally, the variety of locations is manifold and beyond numbering in the scripture. (AbhT 15.101–102)

In the *Śrīvīrāvalihṛdaya*, there are seven locations: the pair of the lotus of power (*śakti*), the path of the gods, that which is called the crossroads, the cremation ground, the solitary place, the void, and the tree.
Thus, through the perspective of etymological derivation, qualities, states, and metaphorical usage, it is taught that these are nothing but pure consciousness.
When that [deity] presides over the wheel within the body, the sacrifice may then take place externally;
however, for the sake of liberation, no distinction of location for the sacrifice is prescribed.
This is because [liberation] does not depend on the means of place, but rather arises from the clarity of one's inner disposition.
And it is said in the *Śrīniśācāra* regarding those who desire the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*):
"The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) must abandon this [attachment to] place, just like a snake sheds its skin.
For liberation is not produced by a location, once [this truth] has reached the path of one's hearing. (105–106)

The reality of the Guru is liberation; worship is for the sake of its firm consolidation. In whatever external or internal abode the lotus of the heart attains expansion, there alone the splendor of the sacrifice (yāga) is established.

There is no liberation through going elsewhere; it comes from cutting the knot of ignorance. And that occurs through the expansion of consciousness, according to the venerable *Vīrāvalī*. As for the teachers, they maintain that in both liberation and supernatural attainment, the intellect must be stainless.
In both cases, the cause is that which is pleasing to the mind, the abode of sacrifice;
for although accomplishments arise from the causal complex through the conjunction with destiny and the vital breath,
nevertheless, the purity of being is the highest of all.
When the heart has become stainless, whatever one should reflect upon therein—
that object to be accomplished (sādhya)— becomes capable of fruition through its firmness.
And it is stated in the *Śrīsāraśāstra* that "one who is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa) indeed attains success."
"Those who possess conceptual construction suffer, even when that which is taught in the *Kalpa* has been performed.
By overcoming that [conceptualization], mantras exert their power; this alone is the manifest arising.
Through such statements from the *Spanda*, this very point is established.

Therefore, for the sake of accomplishment or liberation, during worship, recitation, and meditative absorption, one should seek that place where the heart becomes beautiful through rest. Having reached the sacrificial abode, the pure-souled one remains established even outside.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in a general manner for the successful accomplishment of the external sacrifice;

one may employ either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī, or both, in sequential or non-sequential order. One should perform it by means of the two—emanation and reabsorption—either individually, collectively, or in pairs.
The sixteen vowels ending with the visarga are located on the forehead, the face, the eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, teeth, and lips—two in each; then on the crest-lock and the tongue.
The two consonants *ka* and *ca* are located on the right and left shoulders, the arms, the hands, the fingers, and the nails.
One should assign the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group in sequence to the hips, thighs, and so forth;
the *pa*-group to the two sides, the back, the belly, and the heart—thus nine [groups].
These correspond to the skin, blood, flesh, sinews, bones, fat, semen, and the rest.

Thus has this placement of the Mātṛkās been described; now that of Mālinī is set forth. The letter *na* is the tuft (*śikhā*); *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḷḷ* are the garland of the head (*śiromālā*); *tha* is the forehead (*mastaka*); *ca* and *dha* are the eyes, with *ca* for the upper eye; *ī* is the nose; *mudrā* is the [forehead-mark]; *ṇu* and *ṇū* are the ears.
The *ba* group, *i*, and *ā* are, in order, the mouth, the teeth, and the tongue;
*va*, *bha*, and *ya* are the throat and the right and left shoulders; *ḍa* and *ḍha* are the two arms;
*ṭha* is the two hands; *jha* and *ña* are the fingers; and *ja*, *ra*, and *ṭa* are the trident and the skull-bowl.
Pa and ha are the two breasts; mā with the visarga is the life-force (jīva). The letter ha is said to be the vital breath (prāṇa); ṣa and kṣa reside in the belly and the navel.
From ma to śa, they reside in the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs; likewise, [the letters] are in the knees.
The letters *e* and *ai* follow those [vowels], while *da* and *pha* reside in the shanks and feet.

Thus is this Goddess Mālinī, since she is agitated by the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*). Therefore, through the penetration of her function (*kṛtyāveśāt*), that body is in the highest sense one of Śakti.

Through the agitation of the mutual seed and womb, and from the arising of emission, what accomplishment would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill? Although the intermingling of the letters of the womb and the seed exists in many ways, [it grants all]. 126–127ab. 127cd.
Nevertheless, this sequence beginning with *na* and ending with *pha* is proclaimed as the primary one.
By pronouncing [the letters] starting from *pha* and ending with *na*, the circle of the paths (*adhvamaṇḍala*) is withdrawn;
how then can that full consciousness be described by words?
Therefore, in the scriptures, this primary Mālinī— consisting of the letters from *na* to *pha*— is indeed sung of in many ways through various divisions such as the *kulaputtalikā* and others;
for she resides within the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) of Bhairava in a state of non-expansion (*anucchūnatā*).
Because she is like a mother due to her nature as that which is yet to be, she is proclaimed as Mātṛkā;

she is Mālinī because she is garlanded by the Rudras, and Dhārikā because she sustains both spiritual attainment (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa). She is in full bloom with fruits, she is worthy of worship, and she is the female bee at the sound of reabsorption (saṃhāra).

"Since the letters *ra* and *la* are endowed with the powers of withdrawal, bestowing, and taking away, Śambhunātha has declared that they should be contemplated as one; for both the Śabdarāśi and Mālinī are essentially composed of Śiva and Śakti. (AbhT 15.132b–133)
Because each one [of these] is complete in itself, it possesses the nature of Śiva and Śakti. Therefore, even when the ritual procedure, the potency, or the essential form has fallen away,
the mantras deposited by means of this [power] are again fulfilled through re-deposition and bestow their fruit.

And it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvatantra*: "In a case where the specific rule is absent, one should install the *Mālinī* of distinct origin for the sake of the body of Śakti. This is a qualification regarding the cause, and the meaning of that cause has been explained.
And for the sake of accomplishing desired fruits, he spoke this very point here:
"Even those mantras such as the Gāruḍa and others which possess seed-syllables (*sāñjana*) are not supreme;
they lead to success when fulfilled by the Mālinī, but to liberation only through power. (137–138)
Therefore, even one desiring fruit, having installed another mantra here, should install Mālinī;
and having installed her, he should recite her, and even without effort he should recite her for the sake of liberation.
Thus, one should install either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī, or both, in their proper sequence.
Or, according to the pursuit of either accomplishment (siddhi) or liberation (mukti), one may place the phonemes of both [the teacher and the disciple] simultaneously.
These two clusters, *akṣahrīṃ* and *naphahrīṃ*, belong to those who have abandoned the communal assembly (*saṃgha*) and worldly existence (*vihāna*).
When the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) has been performed with these two designators, or alternatively, with only one.
This [deity] may be joined with the limbs, the body, and Brahman, or otherwise;
in the collective arrangement, one should place these two as separate masses either sequentially or non-sequentially, or else one should employ them as a single unit.
He who desires success through ritual action should perform that action repeatedly;
even for one who does not desire it, such action leads to his own abundant fruit.
But he who desires success through the practice of meditation and recitation should perform the supreme ritual action.

For the sake of ritual refinement (*saṃskṛti*), one may perform [the rite] according to one's own will, or even more extensively by means of the previous method; or, if one desires liberation, one should perform it for that [disciple] as desired. For the purpose of these rites, such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), is indeed the attainment of the state of Śiva.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should carry out the procedure for the vessel of offering (*arghapātra*). Thereafter, according to the stated method, one should worship it with the mantras that have been placed.
For [all things] arise from Śiva, who consists of accomplishment, and from all existing entities.
Through worship here, the non-distinctness of the causal factors from the Full (the Absolute) is realized.
The entire multitude of causal factors is shown to be non-different from Śiva;
thus, in the example of worship, everything—even going and so forth—is fully encompassed.

Just as a horse that has attained mastery over the movements of the rider’s stirrups does not deviate from that training even when mounted in battle, so too the agent whose faculties have been transformed into Śiva through the practice of the rite of worship does not deviate from it.
Whether walking or standing still, one casts off the duality of the causal agents (150).
Likewise, for one established in the practice of oneness, this entire universe, by force and through gradual stages,
seems to dance as it vibrates within the undisturbed fullness of Śiva-nature (151).
Our supreme Guru spoke in the hymn of praise for worship:
"Oh, what an indescribable festival consisting of the worship of Śiva, whose delicious flavor is such that the agitation of even the thirty-six principles abounds therein! (152–153)

Those who perform such worship for the sake of attaining immersion into the universe as the perfect Śiva—they are indeed Śivas themselves; what further fruit could there be for those who are already perfect? Even without the practice of knowledge and yoga, ritual action such as ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship [is sufficient].
Thus, by bestowing the attainment of oneness, she grants the supreme fruit;
for the practitioner as well, that [mantra] has attained oneness with the true Brahmin and the mantra,
and as the universe proceeds without obstacle, it shall swiftly bring about his own spiritual accomplishment.
And it has been stated by the Supreme Lord that in the Mata and other systems, there is neither a formal rule nor a sequence of worship;
rather, it is held that the desired perfection arises solely from remembrance.
For, in this way, the act of worship bestows the state of becoming one with That (the Divine).
Through that [process], her supreme form is the identity with all the causal factors (kārakas).
By means of the sequence of the rite for the purification of the locus, there is identity between the sacrificer and the substratum.
[The factors are] the sacrificer, the object of sacrifice, its substratum, the instrument, the taking, and the recipient.

Through the process of ritual deposition (nyāsa), they rest in identity with the state of Śiva. The vessel for the offering (arghapātra) is the source from which [the water] is taken; and that water and so forth contained within it serves as the instrument for purification and worship.
"Indeed, everything touched by droplets of water from the *argha* vessel becomes pure;
what other purification could there be than through contact with the rays of the Sun of Śiva?
Thus the Lord spoke in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* regarding the ritual procedure for the *argha* vessel.
One should not employ any object whatsoever that has not been purified.
Therefore, when everything is purified by that [means], even that which was impure becomes pure.
Furthermore, impurity is to be understood as arising from the perspective of the fettered soul (*paśu*) and its teachings.
Whether from its own prior state or from that which has been prepared,
whatever is here proximate to consciousness through the favor of the Intellect (cit),
even if it be of little measure, is utterly fit for this sacrifice, just like a living being.
By this application of the method, when consciousness [perceives] proximity and distance,
one should then designate fitness or unfitness therein;
for this very reason, among heroes here, there is a mutual nectar that is their own reflection.
That which has been prescribed by the gurus who have purified their own selves for various sacrificial rites is truly excellent insofar as it causes submerged consciousness to emerge;
for bliss is what makes consciousness fit for worship, since it constitutes its emergence.
Therefore, that which submerges the predominance of the insentient body and so forth,
which generates bliss, is worthy of worship, and captivates the heart— [it is found] in the Kulakrama, the Uttīrṇa, the Trikasāra, the Mata, and other [traditions]. (15.168b–169b)

The supreme majesty of substances such as wine, *kādambarī*, and *śīdhu* exists for the purpose of maintaining the worldly order; however, in the scriptures for the bound souls (*paśu-śāsana*), impurity is declared regarding wine and the like,
while their purity is mentioned only in certain specific instances.
The purity of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the purification of the vessels for the *soma* and the *caru*,
the ritual procedure for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*), the holding of a black antelope horn in the hand,
the sacrifice not being performed without a wife, and equality with all the deities— [these are the characteristics].
In the *Brahmasatra*, the oblation of wine is offered, as is the oblation of the omentum, intestines, and heart;
even in the scriptures concerning the fettered (*pāśava*), that was seen by Maheśvara.
It is like a sudden flash of light in the midst of a terrible, blinding winter night.

Regarding the conflicting views such as "the *haṃsa* is edible" and "this one is not edible," that single [view] which is purified by its non-difference from Śiva triumphs over the Smārta traditions. For these [objections],
such as ignorance, lack of Vedic insight, passion, hatred, and so forth, [are merely incidental].
Those [arguments] capable of uprooting the authority within the words of the Munis themselves,
as well as in the Veda, teach that even what is inedible is edible.
There is no single locus for both dharma, known as injunction and prohibition.
Now, if that [meat] is not to be eaten there, then by him it must be so for that reason;
thus, because the subject matter differs, the Vedic revelation (śruti) does not contradict the teaching of Śiva.
If, however, there were a relationship of sublation and sublated based on the identity of the subject matter in some instances, [then the contradiction would hold].
It has already been established that scripture itself is what is to be sublated by that [direct perception].
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body and the vessel for the offering water (arghapātra), we shall now discuss the subject at hand:
having sprinkled everything with droplets from the water in the general arghapātra.
Afterwards, one should perform the external sacrifice with the ritual implements for the sacrifice.
On a halo of light, in the sky, or on well-smeared ground,
one should worship the trident, the sun, the bull, the Mothers stationed at the cardinal directions, and the Guardian of the Field.
One should worship the Yoginīs individually with mantras joined by *oṃ*, *namaḥ*, and their names; or else, they may be addressed as the "external retinue" (*bāhyaparivāra*) with a single utterance.
For the act of worship, the mantra consists of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), the name in the dative case, and *namaḥ*.
Having thus performed the external worship, one should sprinkle the door and worship it thoroughly. This procedure, as seen in the Triśiraḥśāsana and other texts, is now described:
Gaṇeśa and Lakṣmī are above the door, and on the right and left of them, respectively.
In the center, one should worship Vāgīśvarī, and likewise the pair Diṇḍi and Mahodara,
situated respectively on her own right and left; and in this same sequence,
one should properly worship Nandi, Kāla, and Trimārgagā, each one by one.
One should worship Kālindī, Chāga, and Meṣāsya on the two branches of the doorposts from one's own right;
below the threshold, one should worship Ananteśa and Dhāraśakti. In the middle of the door, these [deities] should worship the Great Weapon (Mahāstra) along with Sarasvatī.
All [deities] situated upon the lotus-seat are proclaimed to be destroyers of obstacles.
For the worship, the mantra is prepared as before with two lamps,
along with offerings of water for the guest (argha), flowers, garlands, incense, food offerings (naivedya), and prostrations.
One should perform worship here, including the *argha* offering prepared with the finest substances.
Or, one may perform the worship of the deities stationed at the gateway with a single utterance.
If one performs the secret worship (*rahasyapūjā*), that includes the external retinue.

One should worship the door-keepers within, before the deity, according to the sequence of visualization. Having cast a flower consecrated with the Astra-mantra into the blazing chamber, one should enter while dispelling obstacles, and then gaze upon the chamber with a vision kindled by the rays of Śiva.
One should bind the directions with the Weapon-mantra and cover them all with the Armor-mantra.
Therein, one who desires liberation, or one who is of such a [disposition], should enter facing the northern direction;
for in that way, the fire of Aghora consumes the binding fetters.
Even if there were no such thing as a direction called "east," "west," and so forth,
there could be no cognition of it, for a single [direction] cannot exist without being conditioned.
If it is argued that "easternness" and the like are merely conditions (*upādhi*), then the function of direction is already accomplished by those conditions.
But how could a mere limiting adjunct (upādhi) alone produce such diversity?
Therefore, this light of consciousness, through its aspect of manifesting forms,
is intoxicated by the delineation of diversity known as the divisions of directions such as east and so forth.
In that regard, whatever is capable of being perpetually assimilated by means of luminosity is "above" as the nature of light; however, that which is unfit for contact is "below.
That which possesses a degree of luminosity is the "middle"; from these, indeed, the emergence of the directions occurs.
For that which is capable of some degree of manifestation, [the light] spreads forward facing it;
but when it is turned away, [the light] follows behind it—thus two directions are reached.
That light, having grasped the object facing it, becomes possessed of intensified rays.
Wherever one stands, that which is to the right is so called by virtue of its favorability toward the light;
that which is situated in front of the right is taught to be the "left" (vāma).
For that very [left] is indeed gentle, like the touch of the moon, being illumined by that [light].
Thus, by virtue of resting in the center within this group of four directions, there is another group of four;
therefore, the eight directions are presided over by them.
In this way, within this supreme Śiva, the bestower of boons, who is pure light alone...
The division of the directions is established in the world and is likewise described in the scripture;
