for the Lord of Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the five mantras, [presides over them] in sequence. The directions are distinguished as Īśāna, Aghora, Vāma, Sadyojāta, and the one below.
Īśa is above because of his luminosity; that which extends forward is the eastern face. Puruṣa is the southern, Caṇḍa is the northern, and Vāma is the left, being gentle.
Because he faces away, Sadyojāta is designated as the western face.

Because its lower face, which is the netherworld (pātāla), remains unmanifest, its faces are indeed space, wind, fire, water, and earth. For it is space alone that is said to be the primary upper face, consisting of light.
That very [reality] is primarily non-manifest below, because it is clearly so;
but that which is manifest in the middle is neither the object of manifestation nor anything else.
Since it is manifest, this fourfold direction is being indicated here.

The Lord, whose body consists of the five mantras, is thus the sovereign of all directions; from him likewise arise Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. Because Viṣṇu and the Creator (Brahmā) are unfit for manifestation in the upward direction, the fifth [direction] belongs to [the Lord].
Since those two, consisting of differentiation, are the lords of emanation and maintenance, they do not possess a face;
however, from the four faces, there arises the division of the directions.
When the fifth [face] is joined, those two abandon their own individual natures.
Then, even within the Egg of Brahmā, the Sun— the pervasive power of knowledge—
effects the division of the directions, possessing a nature of intense luminosity.
For it is thus that, during the equinox, [the sun] is first seen from the east.
That which is to the east of that [sun] is its shadow, and that is declared to be the west. For one desiring to go there, that which is to his left is the south;
therein he shines with fierce splendors as if blazing intensely.
That which stands before it is the left [side], slightly inlaid with its radiance;
for that very reason it is gentle (*somya*), yet it is not without light.
That where he sets is established as the west.
In that very same [system], for those for whom there was previously an observation of the light in the west,
that very direction is their east, as has been described regarding the path (*adhvan*). And in that manner, each respective direction bestows its fruit even when reversed.
Since the attainment of various fruits depends upon the Light,
the direction associated with the Sun, though diverse, is likewise [of that nature].
It is presided over by Maheśvara, who assumes its various forms.
Or rather, what need is there for so much? For that very sacrificer, starting from his own front, even the directions are divided as east, south, north, and west;
and Śiva always [recognizes] that division of directions as it is established according to him.
Because he possesses a manifold body, he presides over them just as the sun does;
for even the lords of the directions, Indra and the others, who arise from his own self, rest within him.
Indeed, they are portions of his power of manifestation and conform to that manifestation.

That which is the sovereignty of light is Indra; that which is its radiance (*mahaḥ*) is Agni. Its capacity as a restrainer and its terrifying nature is Yama; its deficiency is the Rākṣasa. That which is the object of illumination is Varuṇa, and it is called Vāyu because of its mobility.
Through the conjunction with the accumulation of states, he is the Lord of Wealth (Vaiśravaṇa); upon their exhaustion, he is the All-pervasive One (Vibhu).
Ananta, whose form is unseen, is the Expansive One (Brahman) above, the all-pervasive Increaser.
Therefore, the guardians of the worlds are proclaimed to be mere portions of the power of Light itself.

In this way, although the solar direction (the sun) is inherently self-dependent, it is nevertheless taught [as such]. For therein everything attains a state of unshakable luminosity, just as even the all-pervading wind becomes manifest when fanned by a fan.
Once awakened, one should perform one's own duties, such as the purification of dharma;
in the same way, all the omnipresent powers,
beginning with Aindī, clearly bestow their respective desired fruits upon practitioners who have attained full awakening through the consolation [of the Guru].
In this way, the solar direction is presided over by Īśāna, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Sauśiva;
it bestows its respective fruits through the firmness of consolation. Or, whatever field, mandala, or dwelling a practitioner may resort to—
Stationed according to that [sequence], Śaṅkara becomes the center;
for he is the presiding lord over all through his state of centrality.
That solar light which precedes him constitutes the arrangement of the directions in this manner.
To grasp the southern light of the Lord situated in the center, one should face north;
to grasp the western [light], one should face east.
Having sat down in one's own place, one should perform the purification of the body.

Having meditated on the Weapon-mantra (astra) arising from the tip of the big toe, radiant with the flames of the fire of Time, one should burn the body internally and externally with its crests. Burning is said to be destruction itself; that which destroys is known as the mantra.
Likewise, the energy known as speech is permeated by the essence of one's own mental constructs. By that fire of mantra, burning occurs in the body as well as in the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).
This arises precisely from the destruction of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) within the body and the subtle body.

This body does not exist merely by its presence, like any other body; for its status as a "body" resides in the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā), and when that is destroyed, it certainly burns away. Then, the mass of residual impressions (saṃskāra) belonging to that body remains in the form of ashes.

Having shaken that [thought] away with the wind of the armor-mantra, one should remain in the pure self of consciousness (*śuddhacidātman*). When that [self] is stable and waveless, having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), because consciousness possesses the nature of emanation, it enters its primordial state of being wavy.
That very form is known as consisting of the *tāra*, the *sadbindu*, and the letter *ha*;
from that, the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the deity Navātman, which consists of the emergence of the principles (*tattva*), should be performed.
One should then assign its limbs and faces to their respective locations.
Then, as before, by means of the Mātṛkā,

there is the deposition of the three principles (tritattva) upon it— once it has reached the third enclosure— which consists in the manifestation of each respective reality (tattva). Following that is the deposition of the eight Aghoras, whose nature is that of the head and its feet.

Following that, the deposition of the true being of Śiva (śivasadbhāva) should be performed, conjoined with one's own limbs. When these five [depositions] have been performed in this manner, whatever is the primary object of worship and adoration should be applied, along with its limbs, in the sixth deposition.
Therefore, in this context, the Lord Ratiśekhara is suitable for placement (nyāsa).
He is to be placed above [the ninefold mantra] when the one called "Nine" (navākhya) is primary, because they possess a mutual state of being abodes.
Thus, if Bhairavasadbhāva is primary as the Lord, [then Ratiśekhara is to be placed above].

"Ratiśekhara is to be worshipped; he should first be deposited in those respective locations. Thus did Śambhunātha describe my tradition to me regarding the ritual of deposition (*nyāsa*) in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*; for how else could the Lord [have taught it]?

In this [sixfold deposition], the ritual placement (nyāsa) is excluded; yet it indeed possesses limbs as well. The Form (mūrti), Emanation (sṛṣṭi), and the Three Principles (tritattva)—these eight, joined with the limbs of the Form, along with Śiva and his limbs, should be known as the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa).
Above this, one should then perform the sixfold Śākta deposition (*nyāsa*):
first the Parāparā with her faces, then the Mālinī in the same manner as before;
afterwards, the triad beginning with Parā, located respectively in the crest, the heart, and the feet.

Then, [one should place] Aghora and the others on the face, mouth, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and thighs; then on the knees and feet. After that, one should place the five limbs of the Vidyā.
Then, one should invoke the Śakti, whose nature is the true essence (sadbhāva) of the Mothers.

At the time of the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*), the Guru should meditate upon the supreme Yogīśvarī, who is full, the eternal Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, accompanied by her limbs, faces, retinue, and more than twelve powers (*śakti*s), according to the distinctions of the practice to be accomplished.

Among the triad of goddesses, she who stands as the indivisible one is indeed the Supreme Goddess. She is proclaimed to be the very essence of existence, consisting of uninterrupted pure consciousness.
Therefore, she is celebrated as the "Essence" (Sāra) in the *Yāmala* scripture of the Goddess.
The Form with its faces, the Power, the triad of powers, then the group of eight,

the five limbs, and the Supreme Power— this sixfold deposition (nyāsa) belongs to Śakti. This great Yāmala deposition bestows the fruits of both supernatural accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
Furthermore, one who seeks solely liberation should first perform the Śākta placement (nyāsa).
However, the Gurus have declared that regarding these two placements which have been described,
the seeker of liberation should perform them starting from the feet, following the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhṛti).
However many divisions have been proclaimed that denote Śambhu, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu),
in all those mantras the sixfold deposition (nyāsa) is likewise proclaimed.
Nevertheless, whichever mantra is to be invoked, it should be accompanied there by its ancillary limbs (aṅga).
"The sixth should be present"—thus it is everywhere proclaimed that this [reality] is sixfold.
Afterward, the display of mudrās is performed with body, mind, and speech.
The five states beginning with waking, together with the sixth named the "Unsurpassed" (anuttara), constitute the sixfold nature.

Because it possesses six causes and six natures, there is the conjunction with the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). When this great sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhā-mahānyāsa*) has been performed in this manner, this entire universe forcibly attains identity with the body, and one should manifest the pure creation.

That emanation which has spread forth here, beginning from the deposition of the forms (mūrtinyāsa), has been rendered pure through the power of the sequence of deposition by bringing about non-duality. Therefore, those fools who [object] regarding the shaking off of the bonds by means of the awakening [of the mantra]— [The text continues: ...[they are refuted]. By that [process], the burning of the fetters is accomplished. 262. AbhT_15.284b/. svātantryāttu pṛthagbhūtā mantrāḥ syurjñānakarmabhiḥ// 284 AbhT_1
"Once established in the Kṛta, Śānta, and Śiva [states], why would one descend again?"—
those who ask such things have long since been cast away from the ultimate reality of Śambhu.
Deprived of the essence that is the vibration of self-awareness, they do not know it.

Indeed, this Śiva, who is called "the Peaceful," is not some distinct entity possessing differentiation; nor does he exist anywhere as something like a jar, excluded from all other paths. For it is this consciousness, whose nature is the Great Light, that unfolds [as such].
He is Śiva; his very nature as Śiva is manifested through his universal form (vaiśvarūpya).
Therefore, the yoga of such manifestation unfolds by his own inherent impulse (svarasa).
And here, while being manifested, there is both non-duality with his own self and indeed duality.
When duality unfolds, Māyā unfolds for the subject of Māyā;
when non-duality unfolds, the nature of Śiva unfolds for that very subject of Māyā.
Through proficiency in the practice of conceptualizing that [Śiva-nature], the subject of Māyā [is liberated].
Śiva alone is proclaimed to be the fruit of that practice, such as ritual placement (nyāsa) and the like;
for just as it is for one who contemplates, "I am a doer of evil deeds," so too it is for one who contemplates, "I am Śiva, I am none other."
This very thing is called firmness that penetrates the heart of reflective awareness (vimarśa).
Non-conceptuality is the gateway to the flood of conceptualizations regarding identity with Śiva;
otherwise, how could that pure [reality], which subsists through the life-force of reflective awareness, [be realized]? 270–271ab.
How indeed could the form of that which has the nature of shining forth remain unexamined?
Therefore, by virtue of His independent will, which accomplishes even the most difficult tasks,
this [subject], though appearing as vital breath, intellect, and so forth, does not conceptualize itself in that way.

On the contrary, having ascertained that one's own nature is the opposite of absolute independence— characterized by perishability and dependence on what is powerless— one sinks [into the ocean of existence]. Therefore,
[the scripture] destroys such an ascertainment which belongs to the realm of *saṃsāra*.
One should resort to a state free of conceptual construction by means of the certainty regarding the eternal and so forth; however,
it has been described that those who enjoy the purity of a power intensified by the highest degree of intensity do not require initiation, mantra, or ritual placement.
Thus, being the body of the universe, he has clearly attained the state of being the self of the universe (276).
By the mere act of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should worship the body, which has become such, with flowers and other offerings,
either extensively with individual mantras or concisely with the root mantra (277).
Through incense, food offerings, gratification, and so forth— both extensively and concisely—

the teacher should perform everything with the left hand because it is the "left-handed" (vāma) conduct of saṃsāra; and he should perform the rite of libation (tarpaṇa) with that [hand] which is free from disease (anāmaya).

The word "vāma" (left) is also declared in the venerable *Matanga* and other scriptures to refer to the secret [practice]. It is clearly stated that a practitioner of mantra devoted to the *vāmācāra* (left-hand path) should perform the sacrifice;
this is likewise taught in the venerable *Bhargaśikhāśāstra* and the venerable *Gamaśāsana*.
O Dear One, whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices,
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the libation to the Nameless (anāmā-tarpaṇa) in the venerable Nandiśikhā and the venerable Ānandaśāsana.

Thus it has been said: "In the *pūrṇāhuti* the *sruk* [ladle] is used, and in the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-āhuti*) the *sruva* [spoon] should be employed. All other acts, such as worship, fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and recitation (*japa*), are performed with the left hand alone.
In this way, one becomes completely filled with bliss, free from all outward orientation. (AbhT 15.282b–283)
Having produced the body through sacrifice, one should contemplate it as being of the nature of Śiva.
When the orientation toward sense objects has dissolved and limitation has been liquefied,
what could remain in the body other than the essence of the bliss of Śiva?

Filling his body— which is replete with the thirty-six principles and saturated with the essence of the bliss of Śiva— with the vision of it day and night, he should worship it, becoming one whose very self is Śiva; satisfied by resting in the body that is the soul of the universe, he remains steadfastly fixed upon that Liṅga.

One does not desire external signs, vows, sacred fields, or ritual observances; for when consciousness finds rest in that alone, these rites have been taught. The subsequent rites, ending with the external sacrifice, are to be performed here for the sake of attaining the nature of Śiva.
Then, one should prepare the supreme *argha* vessel, which consists of non-difference from Śiva;

it is filled with the essence of bliss and serves as the satiation for all the deities. Just as [the rites] from the cremation in the body up to the end of worship [are performed], so indeed is it here.
The *arghapātra* (offering vessel) should also be prepared through the application of both concise and detailed methods.
It has not been stated which substances are for the sacrifice, nor what indeed constitutes the *argha*;
for one who desires accomplishment, the means of practice itself is the cause for that success.
For one who desires liberation, nothing is prohibited and nothing is prescribed. Whatever is pleasing to the heart is suitable for the non-differentiation of consciousness from Śiva.
Having prepared the vessel of offering (arghapātra), one should sprinkle flowers and other items with drops from it.
And having done so, one should worship one's own self as the supreme Śiva;
for fear that the flowers offered during the worship of the arghya-vessel might become mixed [with the deity],
one should not place a flower in the arghya-vessel here for the purpose of worshipping the god.
In the *argha* vessel, that very water, having become nectar (*amṛta*),
is worshipped solely for the satisfaction of the mantras and for the purification of the sacrificial substances.
Having thus worshipped the body, one should [worship] the forms of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*dhī*), and the void (*śūnya*).
One should worship those who have become mutually identical with Śiva in such a state.
When the placement (nyāsa) based on the vital breaths has been performed there by means of the intellect,
everything is worshipped with a single effort through the presiding presence of the Void.
One should install the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti) four finger-breadths below the navel.
[Therein reside] Earth, the Subterranean Ocean, and Fire, established as the limit of the measurable;
[and] Wind, which has the nature of the Root-Bulb (kanda) because it threads together the entire universe.
One should place four [fingers] each, beginning with the space-womb (vyomagarbha);
this pure *āmalasāraka* [staff] is slightly [thickened] all around. Then, one should fashion the staff known as Ananta up to the tip of the tongue (*lambikā*).
From the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) up to *kalā*, there is that [level]; above that is the knot (*granthi*) consisting of Night (*niśā*).
Within that knot composed of *māyā* lies the group of eight beginning with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), starting from the southeast (fire) and proceeding clockwise;
for *māyā* is their source, while the intellect (*dhī*) is its manifestation.
Above the knot of Māyā and below the trident, one should meditate upon the Catuṣkikā,
which consists of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) and is joined with two coverings. That reality (tattva) should be contemplated as situated between the uvula and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
For here, the yoga of manifestation consists of sight, hearing, taste, and so forth.
One should install the two groups of nine Śaktis by rotating from right to left within the lotus of Vidyā; although this has already been mentioned, it is shown once again.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Bhūtadamanī, Manonmanī, Śāntā, and Śakracāparuci should be here;
likewise Vibhvī, Jñapti, Kṛti, Icchā, Vāgīśī, Jvālinī, and Vāmā.

Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrī—these [deities] are on the eastern petal and all others like the fire of time (kāladahana). One should meditate upon the triad of the sun, moon, and fire in the middle of the petals and the filaments, presided over by their respective lords: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.

For the form of Brahmā and the others that was previously described as transcending *māyā*, that alone shall be the seat (*āsana*), and not one anointed by the collyrium of *māyā*. Above Rudra is the god Īśvara, and above him is Sadāśiva.

And he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as "the Great Preta" (mahāpreta); thus it is declared in the scriptures. He is called the "Great Preta" because he pervades all the principles (tattvas) and because of his awakening;
furthermore, because he has reached the highest excellence, once dissolved, he does not descend to a lower state.
All those who are lords of knowledge and ignorance have indeed attained higher and higher states;
having become Sadāśiva, they then take refuge in the Supreme Śiva. Therefore, Sadāśiva is eternally characterized by an upward gaze and a radiant nature.

The *preta* is emaciated due to the weakness of being an object of cognition, and is characterized by shrieking laughter and so forth. One should meditate upon that [light] which has arisen from his navel and emerged through the three apertures at the crown of the head, consisting of the end of sound (*nādānta*), radiant with the powers of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
Three spokes ending with the twelve [petals], and there also three [petals] of the Unmanifest (aunmanasa);
this white lotus-seat consists of thirty-seven principles.
Since all the principles here have their life-force in differentiation, [this seat serves as their support].

For the object of consciousness is traditionally held to be differentiated by its status as a seat. These very same principles (tattvas), however, are dissolved within Supreme Bhairava; then they are emitted through identity for the purpose of being worshipped as distinct entities.

But these very principles (tattvas), possessing the sovereignty gained through the attainment of oneness with the glorious consciousness of Bhairava, fully attain the state of being the worshiper. The worshiper is the self of the supreme principle (paratattva), while the object of worship is the intermediate principle (parāpara-tattva).
Because it has been emitted, the further web of principles (*tattva-jāla*) serves as the locus for the seat;
in the Siddhānta, it extends up to Vidyā and Kalā, while in the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa scriptures,
it extends up to Sadāśiva, and in the Mata-yāmala, it extends up to Samanā.
This supreme seat, ending with the *unmanā* state, has been described here. Having worshipped the seat, the lineage of gurus should be honored as previously described.
Upon that seat, one should first [place] the two-fold [mantra] consisting of one and a half syllables, which has become the embodied form.
"It should be deposited as the pervader," so it is stated in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*.

One should worship Sadāśiva, the great *preta*, and the form consisting of one and a half syllables; and above that, as the Supreme, one should worship Parā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (AbhT 15.321b–322)
Then one should imagine a second form, called the Self (Ātman), which consists of the Vidyā;
in the center is Bhairavasadbhāva, on the right is Ratiśekhara,
and on the left is Navātman— thus the triad of Bhairavas is like that of the Goddesses.
In the center is Parā, resembling the full moon; on the right is Parāparā, red in color, slightly forward-facing and not terrifying;
while on the left horn is Aparā, terrifying and dark-brown in hue.
As before, the sixfold deposition (nyāsa) is performed here in two ways upon the body as previously described.
Thereafter, one should contemplate their forms as being produced by mere volition (sāṃkalpika),
possessing two, four, six, or more arms according to the specific requirements of the ritual action.
One should visualize [the deities] holding a skull-bowl, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a jar, and so forth;
this is because they are manifoldly arranged on the left and right,
and because in reality these goddesses are of the nature of awakening and possess all forms.
For the sake of liberation, they should consist of the essence of uninterrupted pure consciousness alone.
Therefore, everything beginning with the limbs and faces and ending with the world-protectors and their weapons [is to be worshipped].
In the center, she who is called the Goddess (Devī) is to be worshipped; thus, the triad becomes worshipped.

Then, from that central mass of consciousness which is eternally divine, the limbs and other [constituents] emerge; they are to be worshipped individually as sparks of light. Indeed, she who dwells in the center is the Goddess herself, whose nature is pure existence.
Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī is fierce, peaceful, and everywhere mixed;
in the Siddhātantra, she is celebrated as the Supreme Goddess (Parā Devī) consisting of a single syllable. The Supreme Goddess Mātṛkā is proclaimed as Mālinī in the center.
In the center, one should place the supreme [deity] who has the luster of the sun and consists of all syllables;
at the tip of her crest, however, is the single-syllable [mantra], and from her proceed the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth.
Then the entire universe emerges, worshipped on the right and the left.
That alone would be truly honored; therefore, one should worship once in the center.
This is stated in the *Śrī Devyāyāmala* in the sacrifice known as the *Ḍāmara*:
"At the tip of the nose, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī is always present throughout the threefold time."

Situated in the mouth, she draws [the breath] into the heart by means of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. Through *pūraka* (inhalation) and *kumbhaka* (retention), she sustains it; but through *recaka* (exhalation), she swallows it.
Rising for a moment with the *recaka*, she devours all of time.
The supreme power of will (icchā-śakti), known by that name, awakens the triad of powers; she is the one to be worshipped who draws forth everything that shatters the support of time.
Indeed, it is said here that vision, action, and will constitute Śiva, yet these [powers] function in the destruction of the object of knowledge.

In the gross and subtle [states], there arise respectively the *sakala* (the embodied) and the *pralayākala* (the one dissolved in dissolution). But those who are pure and asleep have attained the state of *jñānākala* (the one possessing knowledge), while those who are awakened and know a few distinct objects of cognition are called *mantras*.
When the entire range of the knowable has been pierced, the Lords of Mantras and their Great Lords (Maheśas) arise;
and when that [knowable] is both differentiated and non-differentiated, the path ending with Suśiva is said to have emerged for the deceased.
As those very [powers] gradually unfold, they expand as the proliferation of duality dissolves.
The three nights are mutually unmixed, yet thereafter they have their distinctions dissolved. These three lotuses and the state beyond mind (unmanasī) together constitute the seat.
Through the desire to abandon the limitations of mutual differentiation, these very [lotuses] [attain that state].
Indeed, it is said that they attain the status of being worthy of worship through the distinctions of power (*śakti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), and so forth;
for from the very first moment when their differentiation dissolves, they each maintain their own respective forms. Moreover, their state as a triad is clearly perceived.

Due to the conjunction with the impurity of karma that is yet to be experienced, and because of the mutual intermingling [of these factors], the three-fold state of being did not previously manifest clearly; however, in this case, it is not so.
This is because [the Self] possesses the power to swallow up the mental construction that delimits the distinctions between the mutual natures [of the categories].

Consciousness, whose sole essence is absolute freedom, is called Kālakarṣiṇī (the Attractor of Time). Furthermore, she draws time back into herself from within and projects it outward; thus, among these Mothers, she is known as Saṃkarṣiṇī (the Withdrawer), for she is their true being.
Reality is existence; it is attained within the Mothers, and by this means the object of knowledge is also real.

For within the powers that give birth to the universe, the ultimate truth is nothing but absolute freedom. This—which consists of the acts of willing, knowing, and acting—is to be worshipped because it is undivided.

In that [reality] all directions, including every limitation, are completely subsumed. For here, that which is free of conceptual construction does not attain the status of being worshipful, nor does conceptual construction reside in one place alone.
Therefore, there are many attributes; thus, whatever attribute there is, it comprises all those attributes.

"Established therein, he eclipses all; others remain below him as being inferior"—thus was the reality of the supreme worship of Bhairava taught by the illustrious Śambhu himself, being well-pleased, to me in the great sacrifice of the ŚrīḌāmara. (AbhT 15.351–352)

In the external sacrifice, however, one should worship within all three lotuses the entire host of the retinue ending with the Weapon [mantra]; such is the tradition of our teachers. In the directions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and the end [of the sequence], one should place the five limbs of the Vidyā.

In this [mandala], one should likewise assign the limbs of Śakti and the limbs of Śiva; furthermore, in the two [circles], one should place the Weapon (astra) in the four directions and that known as the Eye (locana) in the center.
On the eight petals, one should place the pair of eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora, together with their respective consorts.

Likewise, one should worship the twelve, the six, and the four [deities] mixed in pairs; thus, by doubling them all in this manner as a surrounding enclosure (āvṛti), one should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons in their respective ten directions in due order.

Thus, by abiding in the state of identity with the Goddess who extends as far as the trident, and while offering the entire universe here [within that state], one should satisfy the host of deities. Then,
one should perform the recitation (*japa*) for each mantra two or five times.
Because each [element] consists of three natures and because they are entirely non-different,

one should meditate on the wheel of mantras as being like a blazing fire within the hearth at the navel, heart, throat, palate, and above; there, consuming the universe, one should accomplish the oblation.
When the rite of initiation is to be performed, the Guru,
desiring to carry out the initiation by whichever path [he chooses], should first primarily project that [path] into the body itself.
Recollecting this trident, whose tip reaches the *dvādaśānta* and whose base is at the root, [he should do so].
Having abandoned the sequential order, one who reaches the forefront of the wheel of goddesses attains the state of a sky-farer (khecarī).
This Khecarī consists of the filling of the space at the tip of the void, extending from the Mūlādhāra to the end of the twelve [fingers] above;
she is so called because of her movement and abiding in the void, and because of her consumption of the nectar of the void.
One should shorten that trident of Śambhu by four finger-breadths;
from that [Śāmbhava] comes the Śākta, and then the Āṇava—thus the triad of tridents is established.
Having offered one's self to the circle of goddesses situated higher and higher above those three tridents, [one attains liberation].
What is there that is not born, or what is there that it does not know, or what is there that it does not do?

(364) Alternatively, one should worship each individual goddess or the mantra residing in the lotus, according to the conceptualization of the existence or non-existence of the couple, the unity, the limbs, the faces, and so forth. (365)
In this manner, having rendered one's own consciousness— from the vital breath up to the plane of space—

into the state of Śiva through the yoga of worship, one should then perform the external ritual. This is when the external sacrifice is considered primary for the sake of attaining accomplishments (*siddhi*) and other such goals.

The internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) is for the sake of purification; otherwise, the worshipper is a mere beast. But he who is indifferent to supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and the like worships the Lord externally, in order to attain firm establishment in the great internal sacrifice; by that alone, he has accomplished his purpose.

Having performed the internal sacrifice and taken grains and other materials consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should scatter them in the directions to dispel obstacles; then, withdrawing them, one should lead them toward the northeastern direction (Īśāna). Likewise, one should perform the rites of gazing, sprinkling, striking, and nourishing.
In the *Triśiromata*, the veiling (*viguṇṭhana*) and the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are common [to all].

One should consecrate cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter with the mantras ending with the six limbs, beginning from the top; and one should sprinkle [the materials] with this water infused with *kuśa* grass.
For the sake of the disciple, one should set aside the earth and the remainder as the *pañcagavya*.
That water in which the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are present along with *kuśa* grass is so called. In the scripture, this *pañcagavya* water is the destroyer of external impurity.
When worldly impurity has been rubbed away,
one must then apply the extraordinary means of mantra and so forth in order to burn away internal impurity.
One should meditate on the Goddess, who begins with the letter *pha* and ends with *na*, and who extends from the element earth up to Śiva.
One should cast a handful of flowers into the center, as well as incense, perfumes, wine, and so forth;
in that very manner, one should offer these in the middle of the sacrificial chamber, whereby the entire circle of deities is quickly conceived as presiding over the form.
Upon a lotus with infinite stalks, petals of the Dharma and other qualities,
and a pericarp of the true physician, one should worship Gaṇeśa, who resides in the northeast, with the six offerings, perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having worshipped him who stands there for the sake of pacifying obstacles, one should then dismiss him.
Then, one should fill a jar with highly fragrant liquid substances; having worshipped it and anointed it, one should consecrate it a hundred times with the root mantra.
[One should do this] with a sword if the preliminary weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*) has not been performed.
One should worship that pitcher in the northeast, accompanied by the water-pots situated on the left; then,
taking recourse to the direction of the sun (the east), one should worship the world-protectors along with their weapons according to the prescribed rite,
preceded by mantras, using perfumes, flowers, offerings, and so forth.
Then the disciple, holding a sword and a water-pot in his hands, should pour forth a stream [of water] while being followed by the Guru, who holds a water-pot in his hand and says this:
"O Śakra! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in your own direction..."
By the command of Śiva, one must carry out the ritual action with full attentiveness.
In a name consisting of three syllables that is otherwise devoid of meaning, one should remove the single word "bhoḥ," because this mantra has been declared to be bound by metrical constraints.
Then, that pitcher should be placed upon the scattered offerings (vikiro) in the northeastern direction.
Now, a water-vessel for the weapon-mantra (astravārdhānī) should be placed to the right of the pitcher.
The assembly of mantras is empowered by its union with the water contained within the pitcher.
Meditated upon as consisting of the essence of light, it nourishes the entire ritual procedure.

Therefore, the Guru should worship the entire host of mantras within the jar according to the previous rule; and with the weapon-mantra, he should worship the remover of obstacles in the *karkarī* vessel.
Then, in the center of the house, upon a mandala of fragrant paste, the Guru should perform worship—
either to the triad by means of their union as a pair or as a single deity of the mantra.
Thereafter, he should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the performance of the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
That which arises from the unprecedented conceptualization and verbalization of pure mantras and so forth—
the power of action (kriyā-śakti) of Śiva— is the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); through this contemplation,
it is indeed the supreme consecration, even without other ritual sequences.

Thus, whether in the body, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), in the liṅga, in the vessel, in water, in fire, in flowers and so forth, or in the disciple—who is essentially Śiva—the primary consecration (saṃskāra) takes place. For it has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Yogasañcāra as follows: [390–391]
In the fourteenfold being, in flowers, incense,
and offerings, in lamps, in recitation, and likewise in fire-oblations— everywhere here is Caṇḍikā.
One offers oblations, recites, shines forth, worships, laughs, and moves about.

In eating and in sexual union, that very [power] residing in the body is the performer of action. For those who have not yet ascended to such a state of consciousness, the gradual method is taught for the sake of attaining it without delay.

"I am Śiva, consisting of mantra; my volitions are of that same nature. One should clearly remember that the sacrificial pit, the fire, and so forth, which arise from them, are also of the essence of Śiva.
(395) For this very reason, even in that case, one should observe the degree of firmness or lack thereof [in that realization]. (396a)
Whether it is being performed or already completed, the consecration may be either brief or extensive.
Just as someone poor in innate intuition grasps a sentence through the proficiency gained from practice, so too should one understand this case.

398–399. Scratching, sprinkling, pounding, smearing, the four paths, the arrangement of the sense-protectors, the strewing, the enclosing sticks, the seat, and the placement—these ten purificatory rites for the pit are performed with the weapons-mantras. The center is marked with two *darbha* blades, and the walls are covered with *kuśa* grass.
Three lines facing east and upward-pointing lines, surrounded on the outside by a ring of *kuśa* grass;

auspicious creepers, a square, and the ritual for the seats for worshipping the ten world-protectors; the preparation of the sacrificial hall, the placement of the seat, and the protection of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the fiery splendor of the weapon-mantra.
The purposes [of the ground] are for the maintenance of Śiva’s fire and power, and for the removal of obstacles.
Then, once the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been clearly worshipped as the power of action (kriyāśakti),
one should install either the Mātṛkā or the Mālinī, which consists of the nature of volition (saṃkalpa).

The triangular abode of emanation belonging to the goddess Saṃkalpa is of the nature of action (kriyā). Therein, one should cast the drop of the seed of knowledge (jñāna-śukra) after having agitated it three times.
Knowledge, when agitated by will, [rests] in the state of action whose essence is reflective awareness (vimarśa).
Once it is known to have taken root and is clearly manifest through the five limbs beginning with knowledge (*jñatva*), it blazes forth intensely.
Therefore, one should offer oblations once each with those very five limbs;
by that much, the fire becomes purified through all the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) beginning with birth.
The fivefold limbs themselves, consisting of earth and the other elements,
possessing powers such as solidity and so forth that reside in fire, perform the rites beginning with the impregnation (*garbha*).
Then, one [should contemplate] the goddess Parāparā, who contains within her the entire path and the circle of the true goddesses.
By means of recollection and through the power of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should complete the purificatory rites of the fire.
Thus, blazing with the greatness of the true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*) joined with the Lord of Mantras,
the Fire— through its identity with that resolve of Śiva— becomes essentially Śiva.

Thus Śrī Śambhu has explained to me this reality of consecration (saṃskriyātattva). I have also presented it; let those of pure intellect discern it. Therefore, as for those who object here that "just as there is a consecration for a child," [it is not so].
If [the fire] were to be consecrated by another fire, and that [other] by yet another, there would be an infinite regress regarding consecration;

therefore, those [objections] are refuted by the lack of any such arising in this system, the Guru’s philosophy. Once the Śaiva fire has been produced and consecrated, [one should worship] the Śabdarāśi and the Mālinī.
Having worshipped one's own parents, one should dismiss them to their pure abode. Taking a portion from the pure fire, one should set it aside separately for the sake of the sacrificial pap (caru).
Alternatively, having taken the crest of the fire with the left breath while resting in the heart, [one should proceed].
Having brought about unity with the fire of consciousness, one should cast [the offering] purified by the right hand;
for gazing with the firm conviction "I am Śiva" is indeed the purification of everything, since that reality is stainless for him.
Then one should offer nine oblations with the mantra consisting of the nine [syllables] together with the *ātman* (the tenth).
The consecration (*saṃskriyā*) should take place for the fire of Śiva, preceded by the *tāra* (OM) and ending with *svāhā*.
Then, in that fire which has the nature of the universal space of the consciousness of Śiva...
As before, one should join the substratum (ādhāra) with the superstratum (ādheya) and the circle of goddesses (devīcakra).
The Guru should then visualize the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles facing downwards in sequence;
they are to be worshipped as Śiva and Śakti, and thus is the purification (*saṃskriyā*) of these two performed.
"Other than the manifestation of reality (tattva), there is no life for the conditioned (saṃskāra).
To state this, the Lord did not perform the consecration of the *sruva* ladle and other implements in the *Śrīpūrva* [Tantra].
Therefore, the Guru [performs it] with sesame seeds by means of the middle finger and the thumb, [forming] the *mṛgī* [mudrā].
Having performed the root [mantra], one should satisfy it with a hundred oblations of clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle;
likewise, the limbs and faces with a sixth part, and the remaining [deities] with a tenth part.
Even a thousandfold oblation or more may be performed for the sake of satisfaction, according to one's means.

Even when wealth exists, one who is seized by greed and other passions, and who promotes the primacy of external things while relegating consciousness to a subordinate position, does not experience the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). It is stated in the *Svacchandatantra* that such a person, even if initiated, does not partake in liberation.
"But surely, what is the fruit of the ritual action performed for him during his initiation?
To this, those who know the scriptures of the *Āgama* reply: "At that time, the mantras consisting of the power of Vāmā bind him firmly within the great prison-house of worldly existence. (422–423)
That power of theirs which is gracious is ignited by the Guru.
It purifies the act of transgressing [the rules] performed without desire, as established in one's own scripture.
Then, through the placement [of the deities] above and below, it becomes beautiful through their mutual orientation toward one another.
Taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— which are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti and filled with the nectar of clarified butter—
through the yoga of the rite of identity (*aikātmya*), wherein mind, vital breath, and body are equalized;
[the practitioner places] the left hand upon the handle of the *sruk* and the right hand together with the supporting ring (*upayāma*).
Having cast [the breath] down into the throat and pressing firmly with effort,
one should direct the *prāṇa* upward, upward, while holding the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) below,
until it reaches the fire of awakening at the limit of the twelve [finger-breadths] from the lunar wheel.
When the most supreme, delightful, and excellent nectar falls from the tip of the sacrificial ladle,
one should cast the oblation ending with *vauṣaṭ* into the fire, which is the mouth of the mantra.
That very awakening which exists above is indeed reflected within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Fire is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are the essence of consciousness consisting of volition (*saṃkalpa-cid-rasa*). Having thus understood from the beginning the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *sruk* and *sruva*, the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the mantras, one should restrain them within the fire of awakening at the *dvādaśānta* and cast the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Just as a swan flies up into the sky, its reflection sinks into the water; such is the rule here as well.
[The elements are] natural, stable, liquid, radiant, and mobile, as is space.

Māyā, Bindu, likewise Ātman, Nāda, Śakti, and Śiva— thus, by means of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, one should distinguish them down to the innermost core. Below that are the elements beginning with Earth and ending with Mūla-prakṛti, as well as the individual soul (puruṣa).

Ignorance (avidyā), attachment (rāga), necessity (niyati), time (kāla), illusion (māyā), and limited agency (kalā); likewise the individual soul (aṇu), knowledge (vidyā), its two lords (īśa and īśvara), the state called Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Kuṇḍalinī;
Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā—thereafter, one should join [the self] into the Nameless (anāmaka).
"Abiding in the *recaka* [exhalation], at the junction of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), he is the Guru"—
this was declared in the *Traiśirasa Tantra* in the description of the supreme application (*parayojana*).
Then, by means of the fire consecrated by the mantra previously established and deposited [therein]...

Alternatively, the sacrificial pap (caru) is to be prepared by the disciples simultaneously with the fire-oblation (homa). For the sacrificial pap, one may use heroic substances (vīradravya) or common worldly substances according to one's preference. Upon the successful preparation of the sacrificial pap, all ritual actions are performed through the application of the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
Then, having taken the sacrificial porridge (caru) filled with clarified butter, the Guru,
having prepared either the large ladle (sruk) or the small spoon (sruva) according to the pursuit of enjoyment or liberation,
[should offer] three oblations each for the deities, the Śaktis, and the Yantras.
Reciting the seventh [chapter], the *Mātṛsadbhāva*, one by one in sequence,
and having offered the remainder of the clarified butter into the fire with the syllable "svā" which has the color of nectar,
one should repeatedly offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire, which has the form of the weapon-syllable (*hā*).
Through this single continuous connection between the food, the eater, the sacrificial pap (*caru*), and the fire,
and by means of the reflective awareness of *svāhā* accompanied by the mantra, there arises the supreme non-duality.
This is the consecration of the "pouring together" (*saṃpāta-saṃskāra*), for the eater is indeed established within the sacrificial pap.
The supreme essence of the object of enjoyment is that which dances with effort as the object;
through the equalization of the subject and the object by means of a single continuous contemplation,
and through their mutual falling together and union, it is described in this way.
One should offer a portion each to the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and to the water-jar (*kumbha*) and ewer (*karkarī*).
With one portion, the mantras in the fire are satisfied; with two portions, the satisfaction of the disciple and the self [is achieved].
Having thus performed the prescribed duties and being exhorted by him, one should inform the Lord.
In order to purify his disciples through the sequence of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), he should go outside;
there, for them, he should provide the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the cleansing of the teeth.
The descent of that [power] is auspicious when it occurs in the directions of the east, the north, the northeast, or upwards.
In other cases, it is inauspicious; therefore, there should also be one hundred and eight oblations with weapons (*astra*).
Having bound their eyes with excellent cloths consecrated by the Netra-mantra, they are made motionless;
thus, by force, they are restrained so that their hearts become focused on nothing else.
The Guru, having caused the disciples— whose hands are filled with handfuls of flowers such as pearls and gems—
to enter and sit upon their knees before the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), should cause them,
whose minds are purified, to cast those handfuls [of flowers].

Having again filled his hands in the añjali gesture, he should quickly cover their eyes with the cloth; the disciple then suddenly beholds the place illuminated by the radiance of the mantra as it is suddenly gazed upon.
Then, by the power of that immersion, the disciple attains identity with that [divine state].
Just as one whose heart is filled with passion perceives for himself various qualities of a beloved woman,
so too does one refined by the descent of power (śaktipāta) perceive the presence of the mantra.
For when such auxiliary conditions for the sense organs, beginning with the eyes, exist— even if they have never been seen before— aptitude arises. Indeed,
those of perfected wisdom perceive the body, water, and land as having mantras deposited within them.
And seeing an image or the like, the wise perceive its presence or absence;
for [the deity] is somehow sealed by spirits and other beings made auspicious by the rays of the deposited mantras,
as if trembling due to those various conscious faculties and their auxiliary factors.
Then, with his left hand, he should worship the blazing wheel of mantras— which fills all the paths and burns away the fetters— on his right hand;
he should then place that hand upon the head of the disciple, whose series of paths has been established within his body.

One should deposit [the mantras] upon all the limbs in due order, and with that very [hand], one should touch him. This has been stated in the *Dīkṣottara*: "By means of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), which is bestowed and made beautiful by the falling of flames, he is ordained as a Samayin."

Furthermore, it is stated in the venerable Devyāmala that within the wheel consisting of a trident with eight spokes, whose hub is Bhairava and which consists of the eight [deities] beginning with Aghora— AbhT_15.459b/.
