The outer, the inner, the supreme, and the supreme-non-supreme [wheels], with the middle [wheel] as the trident and the supreme-non-supreme [wheel] as the base—
[this wheel] is filled with flames, ruddy in color, and terrifying with the rotating Mother-syllables (Praṇavas).
When this is meditated upon and the outer hand is beheld, one becomes a Samayin.
But for one who desires to depart immediately due to the paralysis of the fetters (pāśastobha) and so forth,
he should worship that [mantra] which severs him from his vital breaths and cast it upon his head;
by this "Hand of Śiva" (śivahasta), he clearly becomes a Samayin.

When that very person undergoes the separation from the bonds of the principles (tattva-pāśa) according to the procedure for the future [initiate], he attains the status of a *putraka*; and he should be joined to the supreme principle by the teachers (*daiśika*). He alone is the knower of the classes of mantras and the knower of the reality of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.

First, having been consecrated with the Nirvāṇa-vase, and then with that known as the Īśvara-vase, the practitioner becomes a true adept; at the end of his worldly enjoyments, he attains absorption into the Supreme. One who is endowed with these qualities is truly initiated into the teaching of Śiva.
One who is proficient in the four-footed *saṃhitā*, devoted to the eighteen tantras, and who knows the ten tantras and the supreme path— he is ordained as an *ācārya*.
[He should perform] the ritual application of this [mantra], beginning from the earth and ending with *nirvāṇa*.

In the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the supreme guru should perform [the rites] for the teacher (*ācārya*). By these words, this has been stated: the initiate (*samayin*) is like a prince; he shall have authority everywhere within the three stages beginning with that of the "spiritual son" (*putraka*).
But the spiritual son (putraka) is equal to the teacher (daiśika) in his application;

he is an authority, yet not [so] again in the practice involving a different application. In this Tantra, one who has attained the subsequent rites through the sequence beginning with the initiate (samayin) [becomes a teacher].

The preceptor is never one who follows the Buddhist, Vaiṣṇava, or other such traditions. Thus, having been determined as a digression, the primary subject is now described: having performed the rite of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), by which the bonds (pāśas) are incinerated.

Having established the disciple through the yoga of meditation until he reaches a state of rest, he should then cause that child-like disciple to perform a prostration before the ritual jar, the weapon-vessel, the fire, and his own self; thereafter, he should cast the offering to the spirits and the Mothers.
Then, having worshipped Śaṅkara and prepared a bed consecrated with the Astra-mantra,
he should place the disciple upon it and perform the deposition of mantras.
Having caused the disciple’s consciousness to rest within the heart-cakra, he should proceed to the dvādaśānta [of that disciple].
Through the arising of the twelve vowels, he becomes one whose web of lunar digits has been exhausted;
then, radiant with the sixteen digits accumulated through the process of entry,
that full moon of his own self-consciousness should rest in the heart of the disciple.
One should personally proceed from the state of emergence up to the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta);
then one should enter again into the heart-wheel. This is the sequence for the procedure of sleep.
Having thus entered sleep, this disciple perceives the moon and the sun as stainless.
In the heart-cakra, he forcibly unites those [energies] consisting of fullness and thinness;
with the light of the moon and sun rendered pure through forceful practice (*haṭha*), he perceives the truth,
which is skilled in making manifest the nature of dreams and future events, whether auspicious or otherwise.

And it is said: having meditated upon the full and the emaciated [forms] within the sphere of the twelve, and having entered into the heart, one should meditate; thus asleep, one attains autonomy (*svācchandyam*). And when sleep has come to the child, the Guru, having worshipped Śaṅkara...
Having eaten the sacrificial oblation (caru) with his companions, he should then consume the tooth-cleansing stick;

he should sleep with his mind fixed upon the heart-center ignited by the rays of the mantra. In the morning, the Guru, having performed all his daily obligatory rites and having worshipped Śaṅkara, [should proceed].
When the two objects seen in dreams by both the disciple and the teacher are known, their relative strength or weakness is determined by the intensity of their awakening.

That which is seen by oneself is stronger than any other, due to the superior application of one's own awakening. Furthermore, when the awakening is equal, there will be a corresponding equality in the dreams of both the teacher and the disciple.
The gods, fire, and the guru; the causes for their worship, as well as ritual implements and the like;
a beautiful woman, the drinking of wine, and the eating of raw meat;
the drinking of blood, the severing of the head, and being smeared with blood, feces, and urine.

Mounting vehicles drawn by mountains, horses, or elephants, or any other delightful conveyance that generally leads to pleasure— whatever such thing may be, it is declared to be auspicious. One should proclaim that [auspiciousness] for the increase of satisfaction, for joy is the supreme fruit.
Therefore, for any other inauspicious [sign] there, one hundred and eight oblations are to be performed with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
The Guru should tell the disciples, "The inauspicious is not inauspicious.
Indeed, a great effort must be exerted to sever a doubt that has become firmly rooted.
But for those whose doubts have dissolved, nothing auspicious or inauspicious arises by the power of dreams; yet, due to the diversity [of their nature],
the individual soul— being of a *rājasa* temperament— clearly perceives [the dream] through the mere presence of the subtle body (*liṅga*).
For such a person, there is nothing pertaining to *tamas*, nor is there pleasure, pain, auspiciousness, or inauspiciousness.
But how, one might ask, can one who is characterized by *tamas* be fit for this ritual?
Do not say so; let there be no dispute, for the qualities (*guṇas*) of anyone may indeed manifest anywhere.
Even if one’s every action is characterized by *sattva*, if they are *tāmasa* regarding food, what of it? Is such a person base, or is the opposite case superior?
Even for one who has received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and has been initiated, [this depends] on the state of their qualities (*guṇasthiti*).
The disciple may indeed possess a diverse nature, yet he should remain concentrated upon the primary object.
Then the Guru should instruct the disciple in the worship of the deity preceded by mantra;
and the disciple should perform that, whereupon the Guru should consecrate him.
Being well-composed, one should touch the six [deities] beginning with Brahmā, who reside in the six wheels starting from the heart,
of the disciple by means of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti). There are eight purificatory rites for each,
performed from the heart up to the end of the twelve [fingers], purified by the touch of awakened consciousness.

Through the destruction of defects such as the state of being subject to food and seeds, one becomes a twice-born (dvija). Thus established as a twice-born, one is filled with the forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
[These are: conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmanta), and the birth ceremony (jātakarma).
Naming, the rite of emergence [from the womb], the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony—these are the eighth;
then the binding of the vow, the *iṣṭi* rites, the tying of the girdle, the *bhautika*, and the *saumika* rites in sequence;
and finally the *godāna*. These are the purificatory rites (*saṃskriyā*) numbering thirty-two, beginning with the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
The fifteenth is the Pratyudvāha; following that are seven Pākayajñas:
the Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the two rites of Śrāvaṇī and Āgrāyaṇī, as well as Caitrī and Āśvayujī. After these, there are exactly seven Haviryajñas.
The Agnihotra is to be established, as well as the Full Moon sacrifice together with the New Moon; the Cāturmāsya, the Animal Sacrifice, and the Sautrāmaṇī— these, along with the Agniṣṭoma,
the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, and the Vājapeya.
The Āptoryāma and the Atirātra—these seven are the Soma-sacrifices.
The Hiraṇyapāda and other sacrifices are encompassed by a thousand [of these].
The Aśvamedha is the thirty-eighth; by this much, one's status as a householder is fulfilled.
In the stages of the forest-dweller and the wandering mendicant, these forty [qualities] are considered [to be present].

Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, respectfulness, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of craving— this is remembered as the eightfold set of personal qualities (ātma-guṇa).
The girdle, staff, deerskin, the three-fold longevity rite, fire-worship, the twilight prayers, and begging for alms—these are the seven purificatory rites (saṃskāras) and the seven vows.
There are two [systems], Bhauteśa and Pāśupata; then Gāṇeśa and Gāṇapatya.

The Unmattaka, the Asidhārā, and the Ghṛteśāni—these fourteen are known as the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) that constitute the limbs of the vow-binding (*vratabandha*). For one who has entered the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) occurs within the womb; thus is he consecrated.
Then that twice-born one becomes fit for the attainment of the portion of Rudra;
the Guru should apply these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) according to the sequence of the vital breaths,
or else by means of oblations of sesame seeds and other materials preceded by mantras.
"OṂ, the heart, [the name], I purify, O beloved of Agni.
In this manner, one should repeat it again and again with the limbs beginning with the head;
for this state of being twice-born consists of the nature of consciousness itself, characterized by peace and the other [qualities].
Through that, consciousness arises as Rudra by that very sequence,
just as silver and other metals emerge from the smelting of ores like gold through the power of the process; likewise, consciousness reaches the state of the twice-born through purification.
In that regard, the womb is not the cause; he whose self is tranquil is called a twice-born (dvija).
This has been analyzed by the Sage in the *Mokṣadharma* and other sections, and it has also been established by the Lord in the *Mukuṭa* and other scriptures.
Due to the merging of consciousness through the union of bodies, and because like arises from like,

a son born of two twice-born parents is considered "twice-born" (dvijanmā) by virtue of his intention toward the [higher] stages (bhūmi) and his memory [of them]. This occurs despite the birth of the mother from a lineage of those considered low-born (antyajātīya).

The sages possess exalted minds; what need is there for Brahminhood as a vessel? For this very reason, in this secret scripture (*rahasya-śāstra*) which teaches the true reality of the goal within the Śāmbhava tradition, conduct based on caste and the like is not prescribed.
The scriptures pertaining to the bound (pāśava) consist entirely of the power of Vāmā;
they exist for the sake of accomplishing emission and so forth for Śambhu, and for the fabrication of doubt regarding those fruits.
For one who has attained the status of the twice-born through unification with his own self at the *dvādaśānta*, [these serve that purpose].
By descending instantaneously through mere touch, without resting [at intermediate stages],
one attains the state of being a portion of Rudra (*rudrāṃśa*), whereby the initiate (*samayin*) becomes consecrated.
This applies constantly during study, listening, worship, and service to the Guru.
Elsewhere, the Guru, having authorized the initiate as a *samayin*, should worship the Lord;
then the Guru should cause him, who has been made a portion of Rudra, to hear the *samayas* prescribed in the *Yāmala* and other scriptures consisting of sixty-four [verses].
Non-speech, non-action, concealment, worship, satiation,
contemplation, slaying, and deluding— this is the eightfold group of eight pledges (samayas).
It is the essential nature of mantras and tantras, the union of the conduct of the pledges.
One should not speak idle chatter, harsh words, or falsehoods in their eightfold form;
nor should one engage in fruitless exertion, violence, or the violation of another's wife.
One should not practice arrogance, hypocrisy, or the science of spirits, poisons, and diseases.
One should conceal one's own mantra, the rosary, the vidyā, and the nature of gnosis; likewise,
one should hide one's conduct, virtues, afflictions, signs of accomplishment,
the guru, the scriptures, the deity, the fire, those advanced in knowledge, women, and religious vows.

One should worship this group of eight gurus according to one's ability; likewise, one should satisfy the poor, the afflicted, the ancestors, the guardians of the field, the hosts of living beings, the birds,
the spirits of the cremation ground, the throngs of ghosts, and the deities of the body.

One should meditate upon Śiva, Śakti, and likewise the Self, as well as the mudrā whose nature is mantra, and both worldly enjoyment and liberation, from the mouth of the Guru. One should [abandon] passion, hatred, envy, contraction, jealousy, and pride.
One should cause those who break the samaya and those who act contrary to its conduct to be slain; likewise,
one should delude the kings' wicked followers, those who create obstacles, and those who are cruel, hateful, treacherous, or dull-witted while remaining on the path of the *paśus*.
The Śākinīs are to be worshipped, and they are described in the *Śrī-gama* as follows:
"Those whose violence is twofold, whose desire is fourfold, and whose greed is eightfold—they are to be sufficiently regarded as Śākinīs. (AbhT 15.531b–532)

In the Śrīmādhava Kula, it is said: "One should not dwell with those who are bound by the lineage-tradition (kulāmnāya) yet remain outside the substances of the heroes; they are but fettered souls (paśus).
One should always worship the circle of deities, the guru, the fire, and the scripture with equanimity."
One should not consume anything at all without having first offered it to these [deities].
One must not take away this substance; rather, one should worship the group of gurus.
And that [group] consists primarily of his brothers, wives, and sisters-in-law, who are produced by means of the Vidyā.
That [relationship] based on kinship is merely worldly, for such a person is like a beast; however,
that group [of relatives] is to be honored like a guru for the sake of accomplishing the propitiation of the Guru,
but not by virtue of their own greatness.

One should not engage in criticism of the guru, nor should one act as a cause for such [criticism]. One should not listen to it, nor provoke him to anger, nor do anything before him without his permission, except for the service of him.

One should not enjoy any worldly or supramundane activity, nor anger, play, austerity, or recitation; nor should one use anything enjoyed by the Guru, such as his bed, clothing, or seat. One should not touch these with one's feet, but rather pay homage to them.

It is also stated in the venerable *Traiśirasa*: "Even by means of penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, one might stand in the forest like a log, even while observing the vow of the sword’s edge;
yet, though established in observances (*niyama*) and restraints (*yama*), one does not attain that supreme state. (AbhT 15.540b–541)
But one who is devoted to the propitiation of the Guru through mind, deed,
and speech obtains from the satisfied Guru perfect and most wonderful spiritual welfare.
Just as the earth is covered on all sides by falling snow, so [is he covered in grace].
Through the union with the wind and phlegm, it remains forever like a stone. Likewise, when the self is made motionless through *yama* and other [restraints], the single state is grasped;
from a Guru who has been fully propitiated, the overflowing knowledge is obtained.

The discourse concerning that consciousness which is omnipresent and resides within the object of knowledge leads one upward immediately; therefore, one should propitiate the Guru. Even according to the *Śrīsāra*, by conversing with him, sin perishes in an instant.

Therefore, having examined [the teacher] with effort through the scriptural teachings and the characteristics of knowledge, one should conduct oneself according to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures; likewise, establish an association with him. One should never speak of knowledge out of affection, for such a person is not led astray by greed.
When he is satisfied, the gods and the ancestors likewise are satisfied;
having crossed over from hell and other realms, they immediately go to the great city of Śiva.
Whether one eats, stays, or travels while in that house, one goes to the city of Śiva.
Knowing this, one should always worship one's own Guru during the ancestral *śrāddha* rites. That Guru himself should eat, or else he should direct others to do so for his sake.
However, one who has been initiated should perform the ritual independently at the beginning of the *śrāddha* and other ceremonies.
All of that [offering] becomes fruitless for him, and he transgresses the *samaya*.
He should avoid substances offered by followers of the Siddhānta that are fit for Caṇḍī.
He should never utter a word expressive of *śākinī*.

Women are to be honored, even if they are deformed, elderly, or earn their living through crafts; likewise those of low birth, those with disfigured limbs, courtesans, and women who act according to their own will.
Thus it is declared in the *Śrī-gama* that they should be worshipped with great effort.
Devoid of proper conduct, eating all things, and abandoned by both dharma and adharma, they roam at will, gluttonous and lecherous like deities.
Courtesans are to be honored there, and their house is Prayāga; one should perform the ritual sequence here.

One should not do anything toward women by which one might feel disgust for them. Therefore, one should not look at them naked, nor with their breasts exposed; however, one should not feel disgust for the seal-ring (mudrikā) of an old woman or one who is deceased.

In that regard, one should not reveal one's transformation, one's beauty, or one's meeting; one should worship the form of the deity as the body of emptiness at the triple junctions and other such places,
especially on all festival days, both common and specific.

One should perform worship of the guru; there is no suspension of study during a gathering (*melaka*), and one must avoid greed. One should never feel disgust toward wine and other substances used by heroes (*vīradravya*). Furthermore, one should not revile them, but rather always pay homage to those who enjoy such things.
There is no fault in giving instruction provided that the heart does not harbor aversion;
one should strive to eliminate the portions of heterogeneous conceptual constructions.
Furthermore, [one should avoid] the name of the Guru, the scripture, or the goddesses within the mantra from whatever source it may come.

One should not utter [the mantra] other than during worship; therefore, one should satisfy the deity once it has been summoned. For the Blessed One has declared that if one does not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantra that has arrived, it takes away half of one's body.
In the venerable *Ūrmi*, one should certainly not publicize the conduct of the goddesses and the heroes;
one should not feel disgust toward it, nor speak of it unless one has the ritual substance (*dravya*) in hand.
One should utter the name of the Guru preceded by the word "Śrī," while holding the ritual substance in one's hand.

One must not step over the shadow of the guru and others, nor should one engage in debate with followers of other paths (tīrthikas). While conversing, one should speak of the meaning of one's own scriptures, but never reveal [secret doctrines]. Furthermore, one should perform the special worship that is constant, as well as that performed according to occasional rites.
Even from that, one should not have another mantra within the middle of the year, nor even within the *pavitraka* rite; furthermore, other scriptures are not to be practiced.
For unestablished realization would waver through the cultivation of other [doctrines].
Household utensils and weapons, through their connection to the deity and the sacrificial offering, are to be honored;
one should not touch them with one's feet, nor should one step over them.
When the circle of gurus has arrived at the house, one should perform some special act of hospitality.
One should not engage in censure or the like toward those who have been initiated out of a spirit of malice;
there is no fault in providing instruction, for that is not preceded by malice. One should certainly not dwell with those who hold inferior views, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others.
One should not manifest one's association with them through eating together, sleeping together,

and so forth. It is stated in the venerable *Mādhavakula* that one should always avoid the Vedic injunctions and the Vaiṣṇava injunctions maintained by those established in other doctrines, as well as whatever has been spoken by them.
From association with those of no lineage, there is the fear of falling from one's own lineage;

therefore, one should avoid them in the communal tradition (*kulāmnāya*) regarding the single vessel. If, however, friendship is formed through negligence, one should worship the *cakra* in the assembly.

And it is stated in the venerable Ūrmi: "One should never maintain association with one who serves other scriptures, who is devoted to another guru, who is a fool, who subsists on the property of the deity, who harms the Śakti, or who is wicked. (AbhT 15.573b–574)
One should not, out of mere conceptual preference, go to a temple or similar place for initiation and the like;
nor should one perform such acts as a cause for the loosening of the established conviction that has been taught.
One should neither look upon those established in the teaching with the prejudice of former caste, nor address them [with such contempt].
One should not interact with anyone at all except by means of absolute non-difference from Śiva.
One should sit together with those who possess the sixfold knowledge and strive for the illumination of that knowledge.
One should not go to an uninitiated person, nor should one render fruitless the [teaching] arising therefrom.
The practice of the midnight meeting at the center of the mandala should be performed away from people;
indeed, he who is dear to the Goddess should smell the scent of burning meat and other such things.
Observing the command of the Guru, one should renounce everything and become composed of mantra.

One should not perform the three types of ritual action— scriptural study, worship, recitation, meditation, solitude, and their auxiliary practices— if they are fruitless. One should not engage in debate regarding mantras and tantras, nor should one consume poison.

In the event of a violation of the rules (samaya), one should consult the Guru; if the Guru is not present, one should consult a member of his circle or one's own lineage; and if he too is absent, another.
One should then diligently carry out what has been instructed by him, free from doubt.
Because his mind has been made one with that [reality] through the awakening provided by the scriptures and other means, the Guru is indeed Śiva himself; no word of untruth can issue from him.
Furthermore, bowing before the Guru is for the sake of purifying one's own self as Śiva.
With the words "for the sake of refreshment," for the sake of both [the teacher and the disciple], that satisfaction bestows fruit upon the child;
for even one bound by the observances (*samayin*), who possesses only a single accomplishment dependent on the guru, may partake in awakening.
Through great respect for that awakening, one should recognize the Guru as the Supreme Guru.

Therefore, he who, having attained higher knowledge, treats his guru with external contempt, does not truly trust that knowledge; he is not merely untruthful, but is utterly fallen. One whose mind lacks confidence in knowledge is merely a scholar by word alone.

One should never honor with one's heart a devotee who corrupts true knowledge; such a person should not be made one's guru, and even if he has been made so, one should abandon him. One should not regard gurus belonging to the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions with the same primary devotion [reserved for one's own].
And likewise, in the venerable *Ūrmi*, a specific qualification of the Guru has been stated:
"The command of the Guru must not be neglected nor doubted even when there is a threat to one's life;
the Kaula initiation, the Kaula scripture, and the knowledge of reality have been revealed [by him]. (AbhT 15.588b–589)
He by whom [this] has been taught is indeed called a Guru; others are merely bearers of the name. And in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra*, that same qualification is stated:
"He from whom initiation, the scriptures of mantra, and the knowledge of reality [are received], he alone is the Guru."
One should remain with unmanifest signs and never wear any outward emblem (liṅga) whatsoever. One should not engage in social interaction with any who bear such emblems.
Those who bear emblems are simply to be protected; they are not to be loathed, even if they are deformed.
In the illustrious Rātrikula it is said that liberation comes from the removal of doubt;
for one whose dwelling is impure, even the talk of liberation is difficult to obtain. Indeed, one should not write down the heart of the mantra as proclaimed in the Śrīmat Mālā.
Then one should extract the mantra from its constituent parts, but one should not write it down in a script.
One should not form an attachment to what is unreal out of partiality toward birth,
learning, family, conduct, body, country, qualities, or wealth.
One should quickly abandon the eight *grahas*, which are like seizing-grahas, as shown in the *Gahvara*;
likewise, those presented as "horses" (*hayatva*) in the *Śrīniśicāra* and other texts.
[The opponent objects: "I am a Brahmin; how could I do anything other than what is declared in the Vedas and the Śāstras?"
This grasping at caste, consisting of what is to be performed, is an obstruction to the Supreme.
In this way, other [examples] are also to be cited by way of the path of the *Kulagahvara*:
that which shows a thing to have a certain nature even when it does not possess that nature, and which is involuntary.
In this context, that which conceals one's true nature is called a "grasping" (graha), just as it is said to be like a planet (graha).
Within the essential nature of consciousness, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever, such as birth and so forth.
However, that [conceptualization], by means of its own non-nature, thoroughly obscures the true form of that [consciousness].
Whatever conceptualization there may be regarding the reality of consciousness, whose nature is indivisible, all such [concepts] cause contraction; one should abandon that grasping.
And this has been stated by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra*: (600–601)
The Lord Vāma is indifferent; purity is not the cause in that regard.
In the sacrifice, the satisfaction of the Goddess comes from blood and flesh, not from the application of ritual purity.
Even at the conclusion of the ritual, the Marīcis should perform their deliberations together with both the twice-born and the outcastes.
Because of conceptualizing that which is changeless, hell comes to be.
It is clear that the body in all living beings consists of all the gods;
this has been well established even by the venerable Nakuleśa and others.
The body alone is the sanctuary; one should not go to any other sanctuary.
One should remember the single mantra as the sacred ford and avoid all other fords.
Having easily understood this rule, one should abandon the entire web of ritual injunctions.
Samādhi is not perceived by anyone other than through certainty;
knowing this, one who understands the ritual procedure should completely abandon delusion.
Apart from the heart of the mantra, there is nothing else supreme anywhere.
Thinking thus, one who knows the ritual procedure should abandon the web of mantras.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be consumed by those born of the river [who have been previously initiated], and one should cast the remainder into the water.
By eating with them—those born of the river who were previously initiated—no fault shall arise.
Because they must be protected from violation, because they are united with the Supreme,
and because they are the means for attaining knowledge, these are proclaimed as the *samayas*.
Having thus caused [the disciple] to hear the *samayas* and having worshipped the God, the teacher—
One should cause [the disciple] to dissolve into the tranquil space of one's own consciousness by dissolving his physical form;
provided that the initiation of a "spiritual son" (putrakadīkṣā) is not to be performed immediately thereafter,
one should then consecrate that child with the Weapon-mantra using the Śiva-pitcher.

And because Maheśvara, whose form is water, then nourishes the self and all [beings] through the application of mantra, that consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed. Thus has this initiation into the Rule (samayadīkṣā) been revealed both in detail and in brief.
Now, the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the status of a "spiritual son" (*putraka*), the procedure established by Śiva is described here.
This occurs when one who abides in the *samaya* (initiatory observance) is appointed to the state of a spiritual son.
When the teacher desires to act in the capacity of a Guru or as an Accomplisher (sādhaka),
he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and on the second day draw the mandala; then,
in the case of a collective sacrifice (sāmudāyikayāga) or otherwise, he should proceed as previously described.

In the scripture known as the Śrīpūrva, the five wheels are declared to be numbered six, eight, twice that [sixteen], and twenty-four. In the venerable Traiśirasa doctrine, they are thirty-two and twice that [sixty-four].
The connection with innumerable wheels has been described in the *Śrīsiddhā* and other texts.
Therefore, in whatever manner the sacrifice may be performed, as long as it is commensurate with the wheel,
one should draw three tridents here by means of that [same method].

On the three prongs of the trident, the triad of goddesses is worshipped through their successive manifestation; by means of the distinction between the central, the right, and the other [left], they become fully and perfectly worshipped. The procedure for the drawing of the mandala will be taught briefly hereafter.
Having drawn the maṇḍala, its cleansing should be performed with fragrant cloth.
Having bathed, the Guru, as before, should worship the deities located outside at the front of the maṇḍala,
and the deities of the gateway at the entrance.

In front of the mandala, starting from the northeast (īśāna) direction and proceeding in order until the southeast (āgneyī), one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others, ending with Kṣetrapāla. These are:
Gaṇapati, Guru, Paramaguru, Parameṣṭhiguru, Pūrvasiddha, Vāgīśvarī, and Kṣetrapati.

Thus, this group of seven has been declared as that which is to be worshipped in the ritual of the lineage of gurus by our teachers. Then, having received the command, one should thoroughly worship [the deities] beginning from the base of the trident, starting with the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) and so forth, using flowers, incense, and other offerings.
At the end of the white lotus, within the three tridents, ending with Śiva, [the deities] are situated in sequence: Sadbhāva, together with Parā, should be in the middle trident;
Navātmā, together with Aparā, on the left; and Para, on the right.

On the trident on the right, Ratiśekhara resides upon the middle prong; he is accompanied by Parāparā on the right, while Bhairava is on the supreme [prong]. On the left trident, Navātman resides upon the middle prong together with Aparā.
On the other spoke, together with Parā, there is Saṃ and Bhairava.
Thus, when the all-pervasive nature of the venerable goddess Parā is established,
the sacrifice becomes perfectly complete merely through her presiding presence.
Therefore, even in a sacrifice with a single prong, one should contemplate that [deity] presiding over it.
Thus it is stated in the *Triśikā*: "One who does not know the rule is indeed one who knows the rule.
Then, in the center, as well as on the right and left prongs, and everywhere.
One should worship [the deity] as a single self, extending from the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) to the weapons (*astra*);
and one should worship all the deities as being supreme.
[One should worship] the illustrious, healthy Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*), the true nature of the Mothers (*mātṛsadbhāva*).
Then, through the sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), one should worship the eight Bhairavas who are limbs of the Vidyā,
the *Yāmala*, and the goddesses of the wheels in their respective external locations,
along with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) accompanied by their weapons, using perfumes, flowers, wine, and other offerings.

One should worship with supreme devotion, free from stinginess regarding one's wealth. Then, through the contemplation of non-duality, one should perform the unification of the five: the pitcher, the weapon-vessel, the maṇḍala, the locus, and the self.
But those who do not find that non-dual pervasion which is of the nature of Śiva,
they enter the path of non-duality by means of the application of the channels of mantra;
having emerged from their own right side, they enter from the left side of one situated within the mandala.
Having entered by one [nostril] and exited by the other, [the breath moves] sequentially through the pitcher (kumbha), the water-jar (karkarī),
and the fire (vahni) positions, until it reaches its own left side;
this occurs when the thread of the vital breath (prāṇatantu) is woven together through the power of reconnecting with the root [center].
In this way, the light of pervasive consciousness shines forth, whose nature is the vibration of oneness.
Then, one should perform the special worship conceived as non-dual;
for that which is sprinkled with the nectar of the non-dual Śiva is indeed supreme.

Therefore, that vision of non-duality with Śiva regarding the water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, perfumes, and so forth, as well as the wine and the sacrificial animal— that is purification and the act of supreme transcendence.
One should offer the living beings and the elements arising from them before the All-pervasive Lord.
Whether they be accomplished, unaccomplished, or mixed, or whatever else among the moving and the immobile;

the hero’s sacrificial animal (vīrapaśu) is eightfold— consisting of the seen, the sprinkled, the one who witnesses, the seized, the obtained, the joined, and the extinguished— and each subsequent type is superior to the preceding.
It should never be given to those who are unworthy,
for the sacrificial offering (havis) consumed by Śiva is not fit to be eaten by everyone. However, even one who is devoid of initiation, if impelled by the injunction of Śiva’s will, [is permitted].

He who eats with devotion becomes complete; such a person, being well-cultivated, shall be a *samayin*. One is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) or "beheld" (*avalokita*) by the casting of a gaze kindled by rays [of consciousness].
One is "sprinkled" (*prokṣita*) when merely sprinkled with droplets from the vessel of honorific offering (*argha*).
The one who has witnessed it, who has been shown the entire mandala and worshipped it correctly,
who has been initiated and consecrated by the three aforementioned rites— he too may shake;
he may tremble, exude [fluid], become rigid, or dissolve, in ascending order.
Seized in the presence of the sacrifice, he is pacified by the winds of the ritual weapons;
he is joined through the process of abandoning the causal body by means of union with Śiva;
and he is extinguished through the offering of the vital breath and the mind to the Guru, perfected by practice.
By means of the southern fire, through the dissolution of the network of lunar digits,
one should first take recourse in the supreme form through a state of unification.
Therefore, by means of the movement of fire, emitting garlands of flames, one should enter [the center].
With the left [hand] of the sacrificial animal, one should melt the mass of moonbeams with heat;
then, one should rest in the navel-cakra along with the multitude of the rays of the vital breath.
Having become supreme through one's own power, one should envelop the individual soul (jīva) here with the [supreme] life-force.
Having heated it with the sun of one's own consciousness, one should melt each constituent part (kalā) by part.
Then, having brought that melted web of parts into unity within oneself,
[one should contemplate] that which is filled with all the principles (tattvas) and performs the act of nourishment.
One should uproot this [serpent] bound by karma from its essence through intense exertion.
Then, by means of the yoga of uprooting and uncoiling, while rotating to the left,
one possesses the bellows of one's own vital breath, filled with the nectar of Kuṇḍalinī.
Having acquired the nectar of the heart-lotus through the process of counter-clockwise rotation,
and by attaining ascent upon the pericarp of the heart, one liquefies the element of vitality (*ojas*)—
the essence consisting of pure moonlight, slightly reddish-yellow in color.
Having grasped [the breath] within the form of the vital force, which resembles the tip of an elephant’s trunk,
one should quickly emerge and enter through the left path of one's own self,
nourishing it in the heart-lotus of the lunar wheel known as apāna.
One should satisfy that circle of deities established there with that essence;
by this procedure, one should likewise gather all the constituents, such as the fluids and blood,
either collectively or one by one according to the sequence of the assembly.

Or else, one should extract the individual soul (*jīva*), which is purely the form of light situated in the midst of the conjunction of fire, moon, and sun, and is known as the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*). Then, through meditative visualization, one should make that soul of one flavor with the wheel of goddesses (*devīcakra*).
That alone is the primary libation; it is the very nature of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
The Great One consists of the fire-enclosed, blossoming syllable, the triangle, and Time (Kāla).
This is the *piṇḍa* used for the movement and attraction of the flow of the essence of blood and other [substances].
In this way, when the sequence of half-ghatikās has been established through the yoga of rest,
the sacrificial offering of the bound soul (paśu) occurs by means of a hundred repetitions.
Having practiced there for some time with undistracted mind, [the goal is attained].
Just as it is taught in the *Cintāmaṇi*, the knower of yoga, free from doubt, attains accomplishment through that very form; this must clearly be kept secret like one's own life.
Even in the case of an animal, such a procedure should be followed for the purpose of its union [with the deity].
One who has been led into the sacrificial ground, slain right there, and consecrated;
and one who is marked by the wheel (cakra) right there—he is called a *vīrapaśu*. But he who is slain elsewhere, whether in his entirety or even in part, [is also such].
One who should offer [the victim] to the deity is indeed considered an external animal (paśu).
Sovereignty, gain, stability therein, devotion to Śiva, identification with Him, knowledge of Śiva, attainment of the world of Mantras, and being part of His retinue—[these are the fruits]. 54–55a.
Through union with that [Śiva], the bound soul attains equality with the heroic practitioner (vīradharman) by means of external [means] and so forth.
Even flowers and other such offerings participate in that attainment through the worship of Śiva.
By this single means, the Lord of Gods, whose nature is the grace of the universe, [is realized].

By means of sacrifice alone he bestows grace upon everything, whether moving or unmoving; therefore, even one who is not a hero, or one who is compassionate, yet possessed of doubt and other such traits,
should never entertain the notion that there is violence in the ritual act involving the sacrificial victim.
This is a great benefit for the sacrificial animal (paśu), even though it may be unpleasant at that very moment.

The cutting of disease through medicine and the application of austerity serve as illustrations here. It is stated in the venerable *Mṛtyuñjaya* that once the bonds of the animal have been severed, [it attains liberation].
Through the separation from the three impurities, the body does not sprout again;
indeed, through the severance of the flood of merit and demerit, the body falls away.
Therefore, this is not called "killing," for this initiation is of manifold forms.

The separation of the vital breaths from one bound by fetters is indeed "killing" (māraṇa). But this [act] is merely the "joining" (yojanā) of the sacrificial animal (paśu) for the gratification of the deity. Therefore, relying on the word of the Lord, one should offer many animals.

Offered once more, having regained his body, and offered again—thus six times; he who is such is here the supreme sacrificial animal (*paśu*) of six births. Just as gold becomes pure through the process of heating, so too has he been described.
What accomplishment would it not bestow, or what would it not itself liberate?

It is stated in the *Ānandaśāstra* that he who, having undergone the consecration of mantra, should abandon his commitments (*samayas*), revile the goddesses, or give mantras away without following the proper method—[he is lost]. 64–65.
Having received initiation, mantras, and so forth, one who is deluded by sons and other worldly ties may abandon them;
yet, having returned to the state of a human being, he does exactly the same again. In this way, through one to seven births, such a two-footed being is of two kinds.
A four-footed animal is born for the sake of the Goddess’s sacrificial pap (caruka).
Offered by the donor, it attains union with Śiva through that very means.
Thus one should contemplate the wondrous activity of these bound souls (paśus).
One should not perform the rite intended for enjoyment upon any other sacrificial animal (paśu) than the one [designated].
Nor, having realized that "this one is not fit," should one set it aside;
rather, if there is a desire for a specific [animal], one should offer that very animal.

One should offer as many animals as there are [deities]; thus it has been stated by Maheśin. When the omentum and fat of the animal have been melted in the midst of the fire, one should offer them to the circle of Śaktis; this is considered the supreme gratification.
One should offer as the primary oblation the heart, intestines, head, shoulders, and liver;
or alternatively, the pericarp, the earrings, marrow, and ribs are most excellent.
Then the teacher should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the circle of mantras in the fire.
Having offered that to the deity,
he should then address the Lord: "O Supreme Lord, you yourself have recognized me as your Guru,
whether through direct instruction, dreams, and so forth, or through mantras received from the mouth of a Guru."

"Disciples impelled by the power of Śiva are to be favored by you; therefore, these individuals of such a kind have arrived, so bestow your grace upon them. Envelop me with the rays of your own self, so that I may become Śiva."
Then, one should rejoice in the word of Śiva, saying, "So be it. Next,
with the desire to bestow grace, one should meditate upon oneself as non-different from Śiva, performing the fivefold activity (pañcakṛtya),
and [one should contemplate] the mantras as the instruments of one's own self and the [deity] form.

Then, having tied on a white turban, one should worship the two hands in sequence for the purpose of burning away the bonds and for the emission of the pure principles (*tattva*). One should then worship the mantras in the form of radiant energy within the hand of Śiva.
Afterwards, one should meditate upon oneself as solitary, like the moon reflected in water, abandoned by the womb, the enclosure, the limbs, the retinue, and the seat;
though divided sixfold due to the influence of functional adjuncts, it is in reality undivided.

I myself am present here within the mandala as the witness of all ritual acts; for the pure state of being the observer has been established by me within the mandala of Śambhu. I abide in the fire as the locus for the oblation.
When the mantras are kindled by the self, they are fully capable of burning away the fetters (pāśa). When the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśvaras), who consist of a common form of radiant energy,
have been summoned, gratified, and informed [of their purpose], they no longer exercise authority over the individual soul (aṇu).
Until the end of the sacrifice, I remain present within the *kumbha* for the pacification of obstacles,
so that my universal form may bring nourishment to the particular [deities],
and so that the fetters upon the body of the disciple may be rendered loose.

For he exists as if shaking off his bonds by the power of his own will. Abiding directly within my own body, I am the agent of acts of grace; because of my sovereignty over knowledge and action, I am skilled in the rite of initiation.
"One who possesses the synthesis of the various groups of effects, forms, and the circle of the senses, is clearly one like me, appearing in six forms such as fire and the rest.
Having reflected thus, by whichever path he desires to perform initiation, [he should proceed].

For the purpose of synthesis, one should worship that [deity] in the five [limbs], excluding the disciple. At the conclusion of the power of synthesis, one should practice intensely through the divisions of concise and detailed forms, filled with the internal inclusion of others.
Beyond that, through contemplation, one should further integrate [the mind] with the nature of Śiva:
"I alone am the supreme reality, and not like a jar or any other object anywhere.
Therefore, this entire universe exists within me as the Great Light. (AbhT 16.90–91)
And that [object] is not presented by anyone else like an external reflection.

"I am the agent of this; it is not dependent on another, but is presided over by me. Purified by such an awareness of the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti), [the practitioner attains liberation]. 91–92ab. 92cd.
A living being who has attained equality with Me is said to be liberated. Just as an iron ball, through a succession of heating, hammering, and sprinkling, attains the state of fire,
so too does the Guru attain the nature of Śiva.

Then, whether [the disciple] is standing before him, or his form is visualized before him, or in the case of an initiation performed in absentia (*parokṣadīkṣā*), or when a deceased disciple has been represented by means of *darbha* grass and other materials— having gazed upon and worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, the teacher should deposit that path (*adhvan*) within him.

The established rule is that whichever path the teacher primarily intends for the initiation, he should project that [path] into the body; everything else is to be subsumed within it. And when the path to be purified has been projected, the purifier is likewise situated right there.

One should install the mantra as desired, according to the suitability of what is to be purified. In some cases, however, the object to be purified is not installed; by the mere installation of the purifier, the object to be purified becomes pure through the power of the purifier.

According to one's desire for the lower, the intermediate, and the supreme method, the deposition of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) is performed by following their respective arrangements: [the first] ending at the forehead, the second at the four [fingers], and the third at the nine apertures. 99–100a. "Eight, ten, and twelve [fingers] up to the end—this is the threefold procedure.
It is taught in due order as it is seen in the scripture known as the Śrīpūrva.
Therein, the placement among the principles (tattvas) extends four fingers to the end of the ankles."
From the earth element up to the root of water and the others, each should be placed sequentially at two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) each;
thus, from the navel upwards for six finger-breadths, one should place the six principles (tattvas) ending with *rasa* and *śruti* at three finger-breadths each.
For the individual soul (*puṃs*), one should project the six principles ending with *kalā* at three finger-breadths each.
Thus, it measures eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) down to the end of the pit of the throat (kaṇṭhakūpa).

The group of four principles beginning with Māyā extends up to Sadāśiva, each occupying four finger-breadths; thus, from the region of the forehead (ālikadeśa), they number sixteen (the waters and the Vasus).
After that, one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva, which is of the nature of undisturbed radiance,

pervading all things both externally and internally. From the element of water up to the end of the intellect (dhi), there are two and a half [tattvas], and from there, the Root (mūla) extends for three finger-breadths.
Due to an increase of twelve finger-breadths, this procedure is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara).
If [the measurement] from the water up to the earth is three finger-breadths, the unmanifest (avyakta) is four;
that [measurement] with an increase of twenty-four [finger-breadths] is also the supreme procedure within the eight hundred [finger-breadths].
The threefold measure is clearly [determined] from the earth and the directions by the subtraction of twelve;

this is likewise stated in the Mayatantra according to one's desire for their respective fruits. One should perform the deposition of nine, five, four, three, or one principle by means of one's own intellect.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) by contemplating the inclusion of the [lower] principles (tattva) within it.
By this very [method], the placement of the five kalās and the egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa) is characterized.
And it is stated in the Triśirastantra how [the deity] resides situated within one's own support (svādhāra).
The upward extension from the body is twelve finger-breadths, equal and extending beyond it;
seventy-two, ten, and two [finger-breadths] reside within the body, ending at the head.
O fair-hipped one, starting from the feet, it extends up to the station of the Unstruck (anāhata).
Even though consciousness transcends the body, by virtue of resting [within it] and through the power of mental construction,
it is designated as "the body. Therefore, for the sake of this determination, it is stated here that the emergence extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the hundred and eight [fingers].
Now, the deposition of the cities (puranyāsa) extends to the ankles; here, there are sixteen cities. From Lakula onwards, each [city] occupies one finger-breadth (ekāṅgula).
Up to Dviraṇḍa, [the span] is three finger-breadths, while Chagalāṇḍa occupies four finger-breadths.
Indeed, there are two groups of eight divine yogas, each starting from one-quarter of an *aṅgula*.
Thus, up to the level of Pradhāna, the measure is forty-six *aṅgulas*.
In this way, there are fifty-six cities prior to the Earth, while on the Earth itself there are sixteen.
Beyond that, by an extension of half a finger-breadth, there are six cities in three fingers;
four in two [fingers], one in one [finger], and one city in a single finger.
Thus, in six fingers, there are twenty-one cities of the Puruṣa along with Rāga.
In one [of these] is the city of Krodheśa, and in two is this Egg;
thus, in the sequence of the principles (tattva) of Saṃvarta and Jyotis,
there is a single and a pair respectively in the cities of Śūra and Pañcānta, as well as in Niyati.
This has been stated by the Supreme Lord Śambhu in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"In the triad beginning with Vidyā, there are two, one, and one division respectively according to the sequence starting from the North (Uttarā).
Because the sequence is not essential, Niyati comes first, and Kalā follows after it."
Alternatively, the two principles may be designated by their mutual designations.
In the [principle of] Kāla, there are three: Ekavīra, Śikheśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha;
these three are placed before Kāla, and this is called the arrangement of Niyati.
Alternatively, indeed, designation by mutual names is observed;
thus, the six principles beginning with Puruṣa are arranged within eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Beyond that, the group of eight situated in the principle of Māyā extends to the end of the thumb’s measure (aṅguṣṭhamātra).
Each [of these] shall be half a finger-breadth within a span of four fingers.
Thus, there are twenty-eight cities for the two eyes at night, starting from the person;
three cities for the two [eyes], each less by one-third of a finger-breadth, in due order.
In the medical tradition, there are two [puras] for each of the two [elements], making five puras within four finger-breadths.
From that point, there are eight puras of Īśvara in a sequence of half-finger-breadths per four [units].
Then, there are three in two [units], and two in each of the next two; thus it is for the group of four.
The group of five up to Sadāśiva consists of eight, one, twelve, sixteen, five, ten, eight, two, and eighteen;
these are the groups of cities (puravargas).
Therein, the digits (aṅgulas) are respectively four, six, four, two, two, four, and twelve.
One hundred and eighteen cities are established here within the body, which measures eighty-four [finger-breadths];
thus, in what remains, the all-pervasive reality (tattva) of Śiva resides.
This other method, known as the "intermediate" (parāpara), has been described in the place of the "taste-veda" (rasa-śruti).
In the subsequent rite, that enumeration of eight arrows made by the Sage (Kha-muni) is to be known. Here,
one should sequentially add a portion according to the count for each of the two rites, starting from Lakula and ending with the group of eight yogas within this collection of worlds.
Now, following the threefold rule beginning with the "other" (aparā) and so forth, comes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the path of words (*padādhvan*).
When the previously mentioned *daśapadī* is placed independently,
if initiation is to be performed by that alone, then this is the prescribed method of placement.
In initiation, however, the sequence of words is [arranged] according to the primary importance of the principles (tattva) and so forth;
thus, it is included therein in accordance with each respective principle.
But when there is a connection with its own predominance in initiation, [one should employ] the series of words.
One should deposit [the mantras] in sequence, not looking toward the faces of the principles (tattvas) and so forth,
in four, eight, eight, ten, ten,
then ten, fifteen, and forty-five [locations].
One should join the nine-fold *mātṛkā* and *mālinī*, which reside within the word *dharā*, with the tenth word known as *Śiva*, which is the pervader. Then,
excluding the word *dharā*, there are five words.
Having set aside twelve finger-breadths [at a time], there should be two procedures;
this same rule applies to the placement and application of the path of mantras (mantrādhvan).
For it has already been stated previously that only the pervasion (vyāpti) would differ, and that is so.
Now, the deposition (vinyāsa) of the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is described here according to the three procedures:
one [phoneme] for each of the four [fingers], two by two on the two [other fingers] in sequence;
there should be twenty-three phonemes [in total], with six phonemes assigned to each of the three [remaining fingers].

Then, in reverse order, there are four [syllables] for each of the four [groups]; these are the letters of the *mālinī* and the *mātṛkā*. The pervader is the Śaiva [seed-syllable], consisting of six syllables (*rasendu*).
Excluding the first letter, it should consist of twelve [syllables], like the *tattvas*.
Among those twenty-three castes, there may also be another two-fold procedure.
Therefore, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, three procedures were first taught regarding the *tattvas*;
however, that [procedure] is extended equally to the two groups of castes—those that are distinct and those that are non-distinct [from the *tattvas*].
Indeed, although the phonemes are of two kinds, a sixfold division is taught;
this should be understood according to the ultimate truth through the prescription of the path of reality (tattvamārga).
That which was stated regarding the words and so forth by means of both direct instruction (upadeśa) and extended application (atideśa), [is as follows]:
Furthermore, it is taught in that very scripture, the Lord of our Heart:

"In accordance with the previous sūtras, one should apply the state of being a triad to the words, mantras, kalās, and so forth, by way of the path described for the principles (tattvas) and phonemes."

That state has been described in relation to the mantras; now it is being defined in relation to the *kalās*. Among the four, six, twenty-two, and twelve [mantras], there are the four beginning with *nivṛtti*; the pervading one is *śāntyatītā*.

In the second digit (*kalā*), however, having sequentially cast twelve [fingers] at a time for twelve [digits], one should perform the dual procedure consisting of the higher-lower (*parāpara*) and the supreme (*parā*) nature. Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the procedure for the four eggs (*caturaṇḍavidhi*) is included.
In that [rite], the threefold procedure should be recited according to the sequence of the four *kalās*.
Having first purified the sixfold path within the body of the disciple,
one should then install the [mantra] considered the purifier, because it is the most eminent among the single [group].
In the path, the flood of mantras for the seats is indeed one purifier from the beginning.
Śabdarāśi and Mālinī are twofold, both collectively and individually;
or else, they exist as a group of six through the union of pairs, each acting as a single hero.

The five-faced [deity] is sixfold through the division of the power (śakti) and its possessor (tadvat); furthermore, it is twofold by virtue of being solitary and stainless. Thus, she consists of twelve aspects.
Furthermore, the six-limbed [deity] is twofold due to the distinction between the manifest (sakala) and the other; moreover, it is twofold like the faces.
Multiplied by twelve, it is divided into twenty-four parts.
There are two groups of eight beginning with Aghora, and the third arises from the *Yāmala*.
Furthermore, there is the *Mātṛsadbhāva* mantra, which exists solely within the Wheel of Revelation (*Śruticakra*).
Through the divisions of one, two, three, and four, it consists of thirteen types;
by virtue of being a single hero, it exists as fourteenfold.
The wheel of emanation, stability, withdrawal, and the nameless is fourfold.
[This group] is augmented by its own deities and by the true being of the Mothers (mātṛsadbhāva).
Thus, this group of purifiers is known as the seventy mantras;
it is taught in the Trika scriptures (ṣaḍardhaśāstra) and in the venerable Sāraśāstra.
In this case, the wise one should perform purification by means of the eight mantras beginning with Aghora;
or else by means of single-syllable mantras, or according to the sequence of the Mātṛkā;
or even by the Heart-mantra of Bhairavī, or by the Heart-mantra of Khecarī.

O Great Goddess, [one should initiate] with Bhairava, or else with the five [deities of the] faces and limbs. For by whichever mantra the manifestation [of the disciple] has been brought about in this Tantra, by that very [mantra] the mantrin should perform the initiation; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus, seventy varieties [of initiation] have been proclaimed according to the different types of purifiers (*śodhaka*).
When initiation is performed by means of these mantras without the placement of the objects to be purified (*śodhya-nyāsa*),
it should be known as being of seventy kinds, devoid of [the rites of] birth and so forth.
Now the classification of that which is to be purified must be stated; it is also described here in brief.
The [purification] pertaining to the principles (tattva) is fourfold, due to the divisions of one, three, five, and thirty-six;
likewise, the paths (adhvan) and the four cosmic eggs (aṇḍa) are each divided into five and one respectively.
Thus, the tenfold object of purification becomes thirtyfold through the three methods;
by distinguishing between the purified and the purifier, there are twenty-one hundred [divisions].
Here too, because the same process is applied to the path (adhvan) as the object of purification through the yoga of ritual placement (nyāsa).
The [number] one hundred and twenty-one would be devoid of birth and so forth.
Such a scripture regarding the hundredfold vision consists of that many [units] composed of birth and so forth;
that too would be increased by seventy due to the distinction between substance and cognition.
Thus, it is twofold; there are one hundred eighty-five [verses].
It is proclaimed as being of two kinds because of its connection to both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
This is due to the complete purification of the impure and the purification of the pure.

Experience is twofold; in the auspicious [state], there is purification within the differentiation of the three times. According to the power of being single, double, or collective, enjoyment is sevenfold, and thus eightfold.
Furthermore, that too is divided into two according to the sequence of teacher and disciple. Thus it is differentiated.

Because in a direct initiation (*pratyakṣadīkṣaṇa*), there is a single continuous connection between the two [the disciple and the teacher], the fruit of such an initiation is complete; however, in the case of a discrepancy, there is ruin. In initiations for those who are absent or deceased, the teacher alone possesses the continuous connection.
By the greatness of his ritual action and knowledge, he should lead that disciple to his desired abode.

When ritual action and knowledge are undivided, as is the case when there is purity of action, their connection remains so; however, it becomes divided again because action is essentially of that nature.

And in the venerable Svacchanda Śāstra, it is stated that the fruit [of initiation] for disciples and for the Guru differs according to the distinction of their latent impressions (vāsanā), even when the ritual actions and so forth are identical;
this is due to the nature of the enjoyment, the purifier, the object to be purified, and the corresponding reflective awareness.

There is a diversity of differentiation, since differentiation has diversity as its very life-force. For instance, when a path has been purified by certain [deities] acting as speakers, and one desires to experience a particular level of reality (*tattva*), that experiencer becomes endowed with their power.
In this world, when auspicious karmas are present, there is a variety of enjoyments;
likewise, when karma is purified, there is yet another kind of variety. Furthermore, enjoyment may occur through immediate departure [from the body] or while still joined with the physical body.
Whether through practice at that very moment or at the end of the body, this [liberation] is fourfold.
When combined with the previously mentioned eight divisions, it is said to have thirty-two varieties. Although liberation is one, such is the case for the seed known as *samaya*.
Whether it concerns a child whose death is known to be imminent and who is devoid of power,

or an elder— whether capable or incapable— the rite is twofold, depending on whether purification has been performed or not. Furthermore, it is threefold based on immediate departure [from the body], and that [immediate departure] pertains to the Guru when death is near.
"This must be done" is the command of Maheśa as spoken in the venerable Gahvara:
having seen a disciple seized by old age and tormented by disease,
one should cause him to ascend and then unite him with the Supreme Reality.
These thirty-five divisions pertain either to the Guru alone or to both the Guru and the disciple. By calculating these two types mentioned above, seventy [divisions] are proclaimed.
Through these divisions, the Guru [should apply] those previously mentioned divisions pertaining to initiation.
Having performed the destruction, one should state the enumeration for the sake of attaining the perfection of well-practiced knowledge:
"The one hundred and eighty-four [units] which have been taught—having divided that by seventy, one should oneself determine the varieties of initiation. (AbhT 16.184b–185)
In this *Mālinītantra*, there are five hundred and ninety-seven thousand,
eight hundred different types of initiation (*dīkṣā*);
the group of those who purify is sevenfold, while that which is to be purified consists of thirty [levels], beginning with the single *tattva*.

The *sāṇḍa* consists of the sixfold sacrifice (*ṣaḍadhvara*) as well as the fourfold procedure (*itikartavyatā*). It consists of substance (*dravya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), and is both devoid of birth and the like, and yet endowed with them. Furthermore, it is thirty-five-fold due to the union of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
Since enjoyment is thirty-two-fold due to the distinctions of the auspicious, the pure, the impure, and time;
liberation is threefold; and the varieties of the object to be accomplished are seventy-two;
this [classification] arises from the distinctions between the purifier and the purified, and from the distinctions in the manner of performance.

Initiation (dīkṣā) is divided in many ways; however, when devoid of the objects to be purified (śodhya), it is seventyfold. This is due to the combination of the various divisions of mantras—such as those with parts (sakala), others [without parts], and those with or without limbs—as well as the enumeration of the fifteen and other divisions of the principles (tattva) and so forth that constitute the objects of purification.
It is impossible to enumerate all the divisions; thus, they are "unmixed.
Furthermore, other mixed divisions exist in great numbers and in many ways (AbhT_16.192).
This is because there exists a manifold variety of divisions, such as the purifier, the object to be purified, and so forth, consisting of pairs, triads, and more. (AbhT_16.193)
When worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) is the goal to be accomplished, the wise man should resort to whatever extensive ritual procedures are required;
for it is said that an abundance of causes leads to an abundance of results—what is surprising in this?
However, there is no such distinction regarding liberation (*apavarga*); therefore, in this regard, one should possess firmness of latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Even a minimal practice is to be resorted to, or else [practice] in mere consciousness; however,
the teacher Abhinavagupta has said that when wealth, place, time, and so forth are available,
even for the sake of liberation, a comprehensive collection of extensive ritual actions and knowledge must be performed.

Even though there is instability due to the manifoldness and flickering of the fluctuations of consciousness, through gradual integration, a firm rooting in each respective object necessarily becomes one whose essence is Śiva.
"This is the reality; it is of this nature; from this, the disciple has been uplifted by me. (AbhT 16.196b–197)
In this way, through the realization of the sequence, even one who is deluded becomes identical with Śiva,

provided he beholds the Guru who is graced by such a sequential grace of Śiva-nature. Even a child, by virtue of the power of devotion and through the vision of non-difference from Him, attains the state of Śiva.

Although the Lord has declared in the scripture that even for one whose mental activity consists of conceptual construction, liberation occurs at the end of the body through initiation alone, nevertheless, one should possess firm latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For even regarding liberation, there exists a distinction— such as being born in the same world [as the deity] and so forth— arising from the smallness or greatness of ritual action.
Some say this, but that is incorrect; for that would merely be described as a diverse experience (*bhoga*).

Within his life, which proceeds from the remainder of past impressions (*saṃskāra*), any violation of the rules (*samaya-lopa*) and so forth—[if it occurs] while he is desirous of liberation—does not result in a web of obstacles due to the abundance of ritual actions.

Because for a person purified by initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*), liberation does not occur if there is a violation of the rules (*samayalopa*) while experiencing worldly enjoyments; it is not so in the case of initiation without seed (*nirbījadīkṣā*).
Thus some believe, and that which is recorded in the scripture is also logical. (AbhT 16.202b–203)

O Goddess, by transgressing the *samaya*, one becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years. Therefore, for the sake of a disciple of great intellect, the sequential rites such as the extraction of the *tattvas*— which are capable of bestowing the firm establishment of the nature of Śiva— are appropriate even for liberation, being exceedingly extensive.
But that Guru who possesses knowledge well-practiced through constant meditation may,
for the sake of the disciple’s liberation, employ whatever means he desires. Thus, having projected the path to be purified upon the body of the disciple as desired, [he should proceed].

One should place the purifying mantra above, in accordance with the sequence of the principles (tattvas). Previously, the sequence of phonemes for the two Mātṛkās was taught according to the arrangement of the principles; one should place it in that same way for the purification of each respective principle.
Although the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has been declared as that which is to be purified, it consists of bonds (pāśātmaka).
The purifier, however, is other: it is of the nature of Māyā, yet essentially Śiva and composed of supreme speech (paravāṅmaya).
Sadyojyotis stated this in his commentary on the *Svāyambhuva*.

"Indeed, one sound has the nature of a fetter, while another has the nature of Śiva. Therefore, it is logical that a single phoneme can possess both the quality of being the purifier and the purified. And it is stated in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra: 'They are embraced by those [phonemes].'"
Having performed the placement six times for the faces beginning with Sadyojāta and the five limbs beginning with the heart,
one should perform the thirty-six-fold placement starting from the Earth element (dhara).
For Parāparā, there should be three steps on the Earth element by way of reversal.
Then, from that water, within the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), based upon the five groups of eight, there are five steps:
three in the triad known as Intellect (*dhī*), Root-nature (*mūla*), and the Person (*puruṣa*);
one in the pair of Impure Intellect (*aśuddhavid*) and Time (*kāla*); and one in the Restrainer (*niyāmaka*).
In this system, one state is said to be progressively assigned to *kalā*, *māyā*, and the non-dual (*advaya*);
then there are five states among *vidyeśvara*, *sadāśiva*, *śakti*, and *śiva*.
Thus, this sequence of states constitutes the "supreme-non-supreme" (*parāpara*) consisting of nineteen.
One and a half, one, one, two and a half, two, the moon (one), the eye (two), then a pair (two);
three, the eye (two), the ocean (four), the moon (one), the ear (four), the moon (one), five, the moon (one), the sun (twelve), and the moon (one).
This is the number of syllables in the nineteen feet of the Goddess.
The number of its own phonemes is calculated as eight (vasu), six (ṣaṭ), four (catur), and three (tri) combined with two *hal* consonants;
from the root [mantra] to the end, there shall be one and a half phonemes, and from [the root] to the end of *māyā*, one phoneme.
This is the rule declared for the placement of the *aparā* [mantra], ending with *śakti*.

The vowels are said to end with *māyā* (the letter *ha*), and then the consonants (*hal*) extend up to the end of *śakti*. Indeed, the supreme deposition (*nyāsa*) is declared for the partless reality (*niṣkala*) of Śiva; for the words "supreme" (*parā*) and "intermediate" (*parāparā*) belong to the two groups of eight beginning with Aghora.
Following that sequence, one should cast these two [groups] into the principles (tattvas) according to the mantras;

this is done by dividing all the syllables of the *piṇḍas* according to their number of phonemes (*varṇa*). Having assigned [the vowels] up to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) within the vowels, one should apply the remainder to the remaining [principles].

One should conceive of the seed-syllables as pervading all the principles (tattvas). Others, however, maintain that the placement (nyāsa) of the clusters (piṇḍas) should be performed like that of the seed-syllables.
Or else, even if the placement of what is to be purified has not been performed, it remains established by the inherent power of the object itself.
By the mere performance of the purification-nyāsa, everything that is to be purified becomes completely cleansed;
this was taught by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīmanmṛtyuñjaya* and other scriptures.
Now, through the mere performance of the nyāsa, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is brought about.
This [practice] for the sake of purifying the body is in fact equal to that [other practice].
Whatever has been stated in one section is appropriate in another section;
whether by way of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*) or directly, why should that not be accepted elsewhere? (AbhT 16.225b–226)

The placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of the Mālinī-mātṛkā which was previously taught in the ritual of worship is indeed the same as that for the placement of the mantras purified solely [by the preliminary rites]. There should be three steps for each pair [of the two hands], and then four steps for each of the eight [fingers].
In the calculation of ten, one, one, six, twelve, five, five, two, two, and one [fingers], this is the measurement in finger-breadths for the Goddess;
by virtue of its eighteen-fold power, it is another, distinct step. This other measurement is intended for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra that effects total purification.
From the fourth state (turya) across six steps, there are two measures known as Parāpara and Parā;
each group consists of twelve, and above the principles (tattva), the rest is as before.
This is according to the intention of Mahādeva regarding the placement of the purely purificatory mantras.

He has stated again the deposition (nyāsa) taught in the sequence of the principles (tattva), even though it is contrary to that [previous] one. By the passage beginning with, "In the partless [state] there is one syllable, up to three in the earthly [element]," the deposition according to the sequence of the principles has been proclaimed. (AbhT 16.231b–232)

Furthermore, in the Mālinītantra, having stated that the words are twofold according to the distinction between the groups (varga) and the vidyās, the All-pervasive Lord taught another kind of ritual placement (nyāsa): "In that [placement],
each [unit] should be known as two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula), and there, the first three words [are so measured]."
Eight finger-breadths, four [and] ten finger-breadths beyond that;
two finger-breadths, two other feet, and six finger-breadths beyond that;
another twelve finger-breadths, and two others, each five finger-breadths apart.
The two feet have four joints, and likewise the other two [hands] have two joints each;
thus is the independent ritual deposition (nyāsa) of the goddess Parāparā described.
One should apply the two Vidyās to the body of the disciple precisely as pervaders.
To demonstrate this, he did not describe a separate ritual placement (nyāsa) for it. Thus,
when the purificatory mantra is placed in this manner, through its connection with its rays and by the power of the Guru’s meditation, the entire web of bonds (pāśajāla) shall dissolve.
When all the wombs within the reality to be purified have been traversed simultaneously,
liberation occurs through the exhaustion of karma via birth and experience. For this individual soul, who is clearly a diverse enjoyer, [this occurs] by means of as many bodies as are required.
The mental synthesis [of experience] does not exist for one who is like the conjunctions and disjunctions of the universe.
Because of necessity (niyati), the activity of the mind is restricted to the body alone;
beyond that, there is no synthesis, since such synthesis is constructed by the senses joined with a single internal organ (svānta).

The knowledge of the self functions only in specific locations; thus, that knowledge which consists of objects of experience cannot maintain a continuous connection across different bodies. However, when that mind—which, though functioning within the body, is certainly [of a higher nature]—[is liberated... 242–243ab.
Then, for one who knows that [reality], there arises a stainlessness resulting from yoga, mantras, ritual actions, and so forth.
Just as a pure mind perceives even what is situated at a distance,
so too, in the initiation by conviction (*pratyayadīkṣā*), there occurs the vision of each respective world-realm.
When one desires to perform an initiation that is devoid of birth and the like, then the appropriate mental construction is the thought, "I am extracting [the soul] from this.
Even when there is the deposition of the purifier without an object to be purified, it is done by means of the mantra.
One should perform the sequence beginning with *janana* while remaining free from the integration of the *tattvas*.
In the case of the solitary extraction-rite (*uddhṛti*) and when devoid of *janana* and the others,
one should conceive of it solely as the "encasement" (*sampuṭa*) of that which is to be extracted.
In an initiation involving material substances, one should offer sesame, clarified butter, unbroken rice,
