and rice grains with their respective mantras during the conjunction and separation of births.
When, however, one should perform the initiation of gnosis (*vijñānadīkṣā*), then the disciple [should be prepared] thoroughly.

By the power of the internal discourse of that mantra, one should perceive [the reality] up until the state free from conceptual construction (avikalpaka). For conceptual construction indeed consists of internal discourse, since it is reflective awareness (vimarśaka);
and this reflective awareness, whose essence is the mantra, is pure and devoid of the nature of bondage.

Eternal and conceived as non-different from Śiva, the bestower of boons who is without beginning, the conceptual thought of the teacher also attains the state of Śiva through union with that [Śiva]. This very point was spoken by the Supreme Lord in the venerable Sāraśāstra.
The apprehension of an object that takes the form of the grasped and the grasper is itself the power of mantra, extended throughout the continuum of mantras. Thus,
the power of mantra is declared to have the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
Appropriation (parāmarśa) is twofold— pure and impure— and it is the differentiator of mantras.
It is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara and other [scriptures] that Brahmā, Viṣṇu,

and the others who reside within the cosmic egg are products of primordial matter (prādhānika), possessed of limiting adjuncts (sāñjana), and characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Because he clings to those [lower paths] as pure, the Guru who has become identified with them is declared to be a *paśu*— such as a Vaiṣṇava or similar— and is unfit for the teaching of the Lord (*pati*). Those mantras situated on the pure path, such as the venerable Śiva (*Śivabhaṭṭāraka*) and others, [are different].
According to the view of the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, the Guru is indeed Śiva, for he is identical with Him.
[Objection: Surely, the state of being a reflective awareness (*vimarśitā*) arises from the connection with independent internal discourse (*saṃjalpa*).
[Reply: If that [discourse] is asked from where it comes prior to that reflection, then from what does that [reflection] itself arise when investigated?

The first [teacher] bestows the state of non-conceptuality by virtue of being an instructor. Whatever discursive speech has been transmitted from that [first teacher] also comes from another instructor.
In this way, through the succession of each preceding one, it is that very [speech] which originally belonged to the primordial Guru.
Let it be understood that this internal discourse (saṃjalpa), having been transmitted, still exists even today;
for by the power of such discourse,
whatever independent reflective awareness (vimarśa) is postulated, that too is certainly of the same nature as that [discourse].

If a distinction is defined in such terms as "jar" or "pot," that too brings about further conceptual constructions and must therefore be diligently disregarded. It is clearly appropriate for the conceptual thought [to employ terms] such as "he bargains" or "he acts."
How indeed could those two—the hand and the verbal expression—be conflated? Therefore, the acquisition of proficiency [in language] proceeds from one word to another through mediation.
Yet, that proficiency arises directly from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), which reflects upon various designations.
The arising of that reflective awareness (vimarśa) flashes forth as consisting of one's own primordial self-reflection;
this continues as long as the consciousness of a child remains within unartificial reflection.
Therefore, conceptualization arises from the specific meanings of the words of those mantras.
The mantra is honored by one who perceives it as distinct from what arises from other sounds.
Furthermore, as for that which was previously described as the nature of consciousness in the case of seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so forth—that belongs to that [mantra] alone;
how could it belong to anything else? Why, then, should there be the conceptualization of it as something else?

For this purpose, the characteristics of a guru have been described with effort in various places; for he is one who is proficient in the mantras and tantras. Therefore, for the sake of awakening to the meaning of the mantras, one should respectfully study the *Mantravārtika*.
Or rather, the Guru should in every way practice the application of reasoning and refutation (ūhāpoha).
However, in the absence of one who knows the meaning of the mantra, he should in every way make the Guru consist of the mantra itself;
for through that practice, the Guru becomes composed of that very intention.
When, through the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra, there arises a mental discourse identical to that [of the deity],
then, since everything is equal, what difference can be said to exist?
If there were even a slight inequality in part, then that causal efficacy would not arise from it.

When, according to the maxim that "a worm [arises] from cow-dung or from another worm," one perceives that very same causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) even through a different mental discourse (*saṃjalpa*),
then this person, whose discourse has become true, is said to be Śiva himself.
Whatever he speaks, that alone shall be the mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This is not the position of Abhinavagupta, whose self is offered to the mantra;
for he maintains that even two such similar insects possess distinct causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
One whose mind is offered to the mantra may remove poison by saying even a few words;
that sound is the mantra itself, for in that regard it is like a jar or other such object. A lover is always beautiful through his constant discourse regarding the enjoyment of his beloved.
Even when performing another [action], one who has been refined by that [previous practice] finds satisfaction within oneself.
Likewise, one who is permeated by the internal discourse of those mantras, even while speaking something else,
will certainly produce that same effect— even without desire— in accordance with their nature.
Even while conceptualizing a single object, one perceives something else as well;
this has been stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana regarding mantras and the like that remove poison. Or rather, even in the destruction of poison, there is variety due to the difference in causes.
It will arise from the infinite variety of effects, such as the nourishment of the elements and so forth.
Thus, through the yoga of practicing the conceptualization of mantra-discourse,
the manifestation of the object to be cultivated occurs by means of the gradual diminution of that discourse.
He cultivates only the object itself, and not this internal discourse again;
he adopts the means of its manifestation, but once it has manifested there, what is the use of that [discourse]?
Thus, as internal discourse diminishes, [the object] possesses the nature of perfect clarity.
Through the nature of innate discernment (*akṛttrima-vimarśa*), the object shines forth free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*).
And that non-conceptual consciousness perceives clearly whatever it sees; for the external object, being of the same nature as that consciousness, exists exactly in that way.

Especially for one who possesses non-difference from the Śiva-nature of Māyā, discursive thought (*saṃjalpa*) is the means to liberation; indeed, bondage and liberation arise from that. Even in the case of conceptualization, this applies when the Guru fully partakes in non-differentiated Śiva-hood.
Waiting for the ultimate state of non-conceptuality is not required;
for that mantra-deity is said to be of the nature of its own reflective awareness,
closely approximating the Great Consciousness (mahāsaṃvit), as stated in the Śrīgama scripture.
Just as those standing near kings can effectively accomplish for others the success associated with royalty, so too do mantras and the like swiftly bring about supreme accomplishment.
This was stated in the venerable *Mālinīmata* with the aforementioned intention.
When it was asked by the sages, "What is the definition of mantras?", they replied:
"Yoga is desired as the oneness of one entity with another entity;
that entity is said to be 'knowable' (jñeya) for the sake of establishing what is to be abandoned and so forth. (288–289)

For the sake of its accomplishment, Śiva has taught that knowledge which has been described; it is also sufficient for the complete perfection of yoga with seed (*sabījayoga*) as well as for the characteristics of mantra. Furthermore, there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śaṅkara without initiation (*dīkṣā*).
And that [initiation] is declared to be twofold, through the distinction between action and knowledge.
It should be performed in two ways; therefore, this has been illustrated. Furthermore, eligibility for yoga does not arise from this alone.
"Even the authority over mantras and liberation are attained through Śiva-initiation.

By this it is also declared that for the sake of achieving oneness with reality, the yogi, being diligent, should take recourse in the root mantra until the state beyond conceptual thought is reached. (AbhT 16.293–294)
Whether seeking to accomplish worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) or liberation (*mokṣa*) through the practice of mantra,

one should receive initiation from a teacher in order to obtain the requisite qualification (*adhikāritā*). By means of that [initiation], whatever one may accomplish through the power of mantra, knowledge, and yoga— [294–295]
That [result] would belong even to this disciple who is joined to another reality (tattva) by means of the Guru;
for initiation is indeed applicable to him, and once he has been consecrated,
the wise one attains either worldly enjoyment or liberation through his own power alone.

Therefore, one who possesses strength through the power of consciousness (*vijñāna*), yoga, and so forth, having first become a *samayin* or a *putraka*, would not remain merely at that level; rather, he becomes suited to his own inherent power. But he who is barren of consciousness, yoga, and the like, is like a blind man on a path.
In every respect, both in regard to enjoyment and liberation, [the disciple] must be entirely dependent upon the teacher.
It was previously stated, through both reasoning and scripture, that initiation alone— even without one's own internal knowledge— is indeed the means of liberation.
But the disciple who, having relied solely on the *yojanikā* performed at initiation,
resorts to the appropriate knowledge or yoga for the sake of its full manifestation—
he too attains identity with that very thing with which he is joined.
Therefore, since his entire existence is dependent upon the guru, initiation, mantras, and the scriptures,

he must perform the purification of all the evil deeds of everyone— past, present, and future; however, for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), there is no need to purify those actions that are of a virtuous nature.
Furthermore, for that child who, having renounced worldly enjoyments such as sovereignty and heaven,
desires supramundane enjoyment,
one should perform for him an initiation consisting of material substances, using clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth, even amidst auspicious rites.
"Thinking, 'I shall purify his karma,' the supreme teacher should offer oblations;
however, in the initiation consisting of knowledge (*jñānamayī dīkṣā*), that [karma] is purified through the union [with consciousness].
Through the power of the Guru, who is firmly established in his own self-awareness, there occurs the destruction of that [karma]. (AbhT 16.305–306)

When his impure karmas have been purified, then [his karma] becomes auspicious. By resorting to its own internal gradations, it yields birth within the course of the worlds; this continues until the completion of the experience of the fruits obtained through the sequence of the ripening of auspicious [karma].
When this [soul] has been joined [to a body], it remains situated therein until the exhaustion of its destined karma is accomplished. Furthermore,
regarding future [bodies]— which are distinguished from one another as being either in the present body or in subsequent bodies—
there would be no cessation of experience once the impure portions have been purified.
For one who constantly enjoys enjoyments until the end of the dissolution of Māyā,
there is nothing whatsoever within the body or along the path that yields the fruit of suffering. Therefore,
having experienced all pleasant enjoyments at the dissolution of Māyā, [he proceeds further].
"By the power of the *yojanikā* [unification], one attains dissolution into either the partless (*niṣkala*) or the with-parts (*sakala*).
Thus has the object of knowledge been described, just as it occurs at the time of initiation by the Guru.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.

Now I shall describe the procedure that bestows identity with Bhairava. Having thus grasped the pervasion through oneness within these five— the mandala, the jar, the fire, the disciple, and one’s own self— one should project the paths residing in the disciple.

The instructor should place the triad of karma, māyā, and the impurity of the individual soul (aṇu) upon the arm, the neck, and likewise the crest-lock by means of knots in the thread. That which appears as not being its true nature is called the "impurity" (mala), and that is designated as the "knot" (granthi).
The external knotting is devised for the sake of strengthening conviction:

Viṣṇu, whose nature is *māyā*, resides at the throat—the seat of action (*karman*)—and his arms [are the hands]. The downward-flowing channel is the *śikhā*; thus, by means of that, this conceptualization is established.
In order to explain the manifold divisions of the triad known as Nara, Śakti, and Śiva,
one should prepare a thread consisting of three times three strands for the purpose of tying it.
This triad of fire, water, and food is likewise threefold in each of its components.
Therefore, some [teachers] in the Vedānta have accepted [the fire] as white, black, or red. Then,
in the fire— which consists solely of the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) and in which all mantras have been satiated—
one should perform the purification of the principles (tattvas) in their general form according to the sequence.
There, first, one should invoke the Earth through the yoga of one's own mantra.
Having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, one should then satisfy her with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and so forth.
Afterwards, one should [invoke] the presiding deity of the *māyā*-tattva, who pervades those respective principles.

Having invoked the power of Māyā with her own mantra and worshipped her, one should satisfy her with libations. Regarding the invocation, the Guru has declared that one should employ the phonemes of the Mātṛkā, and for worship, the phonemes of the Mālinī; this is because of the two purposes of restoring her essential nature and providing nourishment.
The syllable *tāra* (OM), then the color (*varṇa*), then the word for perfect awakening (*saṃbuddhi*), and after that the word "you" (*tvām*).
Following this is the object of the action (*karmapada*) joined with the singular case-ending of the highest person, and then the illuminator (*dīpaka*).
Then the name [of the deity] in the dative case, and after that the appropriate illuminator.

Thus, one should carry out each respective rite by means of the application of the modified mantras (*ūhamantra*). Indeed, all rites are declared to follow immediately after the invocation (*āvāhana*).
And invocation is the awakening [of the deity] from its abiding in its own inherent nature.

The state of being fully immersed in the identity with one's own self, which consists of the "I" (ahaṃmaya) of existence, is called the stage of Śakti; it is in this stage that worship is primarily performed. This is because there is no distinction between the human self and the self of Śiva, owing to their non-manifestation [as separate] and their non-duality. 14–15.
Then, for the sake of establishing consciousness within the principles (tattvas) that appear as insentient, the Guru—
having first performed the invocation with the fourth case ending—
should fashion a state of full existence by means of its connection with the ending of the salutation.

Then, through the union with the abundance of that form, there arises the state of being full by nature; for the abundance of the object of meditation occurs by virtue of the meditator’s state of total surrender. This has been described in the *Śrī-Svacchanda* as: "Having invoked, worshipped, and gratified [the deity]."
"Our teachers have declared that she is to be led by this very path;
however, that which is to be worshipped as the Supreme is of the nature of autonomous consciousness.
Because it is an undivided light, it is not an object of illumination anywhere. (AbhT 17.19–20)

For it is because this [world] shines forth as his object of worship, his object of meditation, and so forth, that he possesses this very sovereignty—the power to accomplish what is otherwise most difficult to achieve.
Since he is of the nature of pure awakening (*saṃbodha*), how could there be any need for him to be awakened? (AbhT 17.20b–21)
In the act of illumination, there would be no luminosity for the light itself,
were it not for the vocative case-ending, which— without the status of being an object (*karman*) or other grammatical powers—
reveals its sovereignty; therefore, one should employ this *ūha* (mental substitution) therein.

Saying "I invoke the deity," one then offers a lamp to the deity. (23) According to the previously mentioned method, there should be the offering of fullness (*pūrṇatā*) accompanied by *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth.
Praise, the state of fullness, and the supreme nourishment arising from the union of fire and moon [are also included]. (24)
One should cause the nourishing *procchāla* oblation, beginning with *vauṣaṭ*, to blaze forth;
therein, even externally, the ritual action is enjoined as established through identity (*tādātmya*).
If there is a word for the ritual action, the Guru should never alter it.
The mantra is employed for the purpose of making manifest that object which has not yet been manifested. What need would there be for it where that object is already clearly manifest?
Therefore, in rites such as sprinkling, consecration, and recitation, [the mantra's function] is certain.

One should perform the mental projection of that rite; otherwise, it would result in an obstacle. Likewise, when the state of being the Self is absent externally, the performance of the ritual action should be carried out [mentally].
[This applies] during the satisfaction [of the deity], the offering of oblations, the burning of the fetters by the fire of the oblation, the severing [of bonds], and so forth.
When a procedure has been prescribed and must subsequently be accomplished through its infinite constituent parts consisting of ritual actions—
as in the case of the rites of initiation and so forth— there is no modification (ūha) of the mantra in that context.
Therefore, [the teacher] strikes the disciple with the Astra-mantra at the location of each respective principle (tattva).

Then, having performed [the rite] with the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), one should touch the heart. Thereafter, having reached the heart of the disciple through the path of one's own channel (nāḍī) and having attained oneness with the disciple’s self, one should take him up with the Heart-mantra.
There, by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should perform the so-called "swan-form" (*haṃsarūpa*) folding;
this causes [the deity] residing in one's own heart to become manifest through the splendors of the disciple's body, due to the non-separation from the mere rays [of light].
By moving from its own place of bondage, by attaining the state of independence, and by no longer being dependent on its own karma, it is fit for birth everywhere.
(34) Therefore, having first brought the individual (pudgala) into the heart of one's own self, [one should proceed]. (35a)
In the realm of Māyā, he should project for him bodies composed of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth.

Therein, one should perform for him a single purificatory rite (saṃskriyā), beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) along with the rites of the male-child-conception (puṃsavana) and so forth, up to the emergence from the womb (garbhaniṣkrāma).
Birth, the state of being an enjoyer of experiences, and their union constitute a single purification;
thereafter, one should effect the dissolution of the self into identity with those very experiences.
Then, one should perform the severance of the bonds belonging to each respective level of reality (tattva).

In this group of four formative forces (saṃskāra), one should sequentially apply the lower, the intermediate, and the higher [energies]; likewise, one should apply the fifteen mantras, or the higher [energy],
as well as the eight beginning with Pivani and the six beginning with the Weapon (śastra), which is the higher.

Thus, these fifteen [syllables] should be used in sequence for the consecration of dissolution (*līnatva*). Then, having first uttered the *aparā* mantra as before, one says "I perform the *garbhādhāna*," and again that same mantra.

Uttering [the mantra] ending with *svāhā*, the Guru should offer three oblations. Then, [reciting] the mantra of Parāparā: "I [perform] the state of being an enjoyer of experiences for the one born as such-and-such," he then [offers] the Parāparā [oblation]. (AbhT 17.41b–42)
At the end, having uttered "svāhā," one should offer three oblations; then,
having uttered the *pibanī* mantra as "of such-and-such a self," and again that same mantra with the words "I effect dissolution into enjoyment."

One should offer three oblations ending with *svāhā*, using clarified butter, sesame seeds, and other materials. This very same procedure applies from the *vama* [mantra] up to the end of the fifteenth.
First, one should employ the mantra consisting of the Supreme Self (*parātmaka*), followed by the words "of such-and-such a soul" (*amukātmanaḥ*).
Then, reciting the supreme mantra "I perform the severing of the bonds," followed by "HŪṂ SVĀHĀ PHAṬ," one should offer three oblations.
These are the mantras I have taught for this set of four purificatory rites.

In those [mantras], one should utter the word for the *dharātattva* (earth-principle) before the word for the ritual action (*karmapada*). Then, having addressed the Lord of the *dharātattva*, worshipped him, and gratified him, the Guru—aroused by the sense of identity with Śiva—should give this instruction: 47–48.
O Lord of the Tattvas, by the command of Śiva, you must not place any obstacle in the way of this son as he proceeds to the state free from affliction;
for if he should desire to go into the space between the earth-tattva and the others, [you must not hinder him].

The mantra-practitioner, with a tranquil mind, should separately purify the fivefold path beginning with the worlds (bhuvana) using the *aparā* mantra as before, offering three oblations for each while employing the modification: "I purify the city" (*puraṃ śodhayāmi*).

In this same way, the wise practitioner should offer three oblations each for the *kalās*, mantras, words, and phonemes, either individually or collectively. Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the supreme mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having extracted the disciple by means of another mantra, one should lead him to one's own heart.
However, when [the disciple] is purified by a single [mantra], because one contemplates his inclusion within that,
one should not purify him separately after the instruction from the Lord of the Tattvas.
Then, having offered the full oblation, one should lift the individual soul (aṇu) and unite it with oneself;
for the sake of the yoga of abiding in that [state] and abiding in the self, one should offer further oblations with that same [mantra],
according to some who maintain that it should be accompanied by the words denoting the ritual action.
But other teachers have declared that such [initiation] consists of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
In this case, no external oblation should be offered separately for the instructor;
or, if one should offer it, there is no fault, for that is a means within contemplative practice.

In this way, the Guru should unite [the disciple] with his former state of abiding in the Self; then that Self, purified from the entire path, should be led into the heart of the disciple. To achieve firmness in that, there should again be a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Supreme [mantra].

First, for the purification of that which is contrary [to the natural order], one should offer the Mahāpāśupata [oblation] with the Astra-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. One should cast it again; then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship Māyā and subsequently dismiss her.

One should contemplate the earth-principle (*dharātattva*) as purified when mixed with water that possesses a pure form; thereby, the water becomes fit for purification. Likewise, through the successive mixing of each respective city-principle (*purātattva*), [the subsequent elements become purified].

The entire series of principles (tattvas) becomes Śiva when purified; otherwise, they remain separate. Separateness is the impurity known as Māyā; as long as that exists, even upon the exhaustion of karma, there is no liberation, as in the case of the Vidyeśvaras and others.
Then, from that [water-tattva] as well, [one proceeds] through fire and into the sky which is of the nature of consciousness;
[this continues] from the entire rite of invocation onwards until its dissolution into light.
Thus, when the *kalā*-tattva has been purified in due order, the fetter residing in the arms [is removed].

For that *kalā*, whose nature is the unfolding of limited agency, should be severed. And one should burn that knot, which consists of the manifestation of the impurity called *karma-mala* and is situated at the tip of the sacrificial ladle,
together with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering into the fiery splendor of the mantra.

For the mantra, being of universal form, assumes such a state by virtue of its support; thus, manifesting in the fire, it effects the burning away of the bonds. Once the bond is burnt, its nature is dissolved, and with respect to that [liberated soul], it is like Śambhu himself.

One attains the state of being nothing but the residual great splendor of the Supreme Lord. Here, when the bond of karma is to be offered as an oblation, one should offer with the *pūrṇāhuti* all of his karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious, whether past, present, or future.

One should cast the full oblation with the mantra "I burn, phaṭ, phaṭ, vauṣaṭ. In this way, when purification up to the level of Māyā is complete, one should offer the noose of the throat (*kaṇṭhapāśa*) into the fire.
This full oblation effects the breaking of the bond known as Māyā, which consists of the manifestation of duality.

The Guru should cast the full oblation with the mantra: *dahāmi phaṭ trayaṃ vauṣaṭ*. If, however, it is to be performed without seeds (*nirbījā*), then he should cast another full oblation right here, accompanied by the words for burning the seed known as the fetter of the observance (*samayapāśa*).

Devotion toward the Guru, the Deity, and likewise the Scripture must be practiced by him; for this is not a separate rule, but rather the very nature of the descent of power (śaktipāta). When purification has been attained at the end of Māyā, that which was previously Vāgīśī [becomes Śakti].

That very Māyā, consisting of power (śaktimayī), attains the state of the power of knowledge (vidyāśakti). Having summoned that Śuddhavidyā, one should employ the power of knowledge. In this manner, when [the path] has been thoroughly purified up to the level of Sadāśiva, it is complete.
Having cut the topknot (śikhā) together with its knot, one should burn the impurity of the individual soul (mala-māṇavaka).
Since the two bonds known as "qualification" (adhikāra) and "enjoyment" (bhoga) reside in Sadāśiva,
by this statement it is shown that the bond of the individual soul (āṇava-pāśa) [is severed here], while the bond of Māyā (māyīya-pāśa) lasts until the end of the night.

The disciple should bathe as is appropriate, and the teacher himself should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). When the impurity of the downward-flowing crest (śikhā), known as the individual (āṇava) level, has been thoroughly burnt away,
he should then contemplate all the objects of knowledge previously described.
Having united the body, breath, and so forth of the disciple with one's own body, breath, and so forth,

one should contemplate the entire universe within one's own body, breath, and so forth. Thus, by means of the aforementioned procedure, one whose intellect is firm and whose mind is focused on nothing else [should proceed].

The pair of space, time, and the path resides within the vital breath (prāṇa), and that vital breath resides within power (śakti). That pure power, which has entered into consciousness and is of the nature of Śiva,
is non-different from the consciousness of the disciple and non-different from the fire of the mantra and other [principles].

Meditating, as before, upon Śiva— whether as possessing parts (*sakala*), as partless (*niṣkala*), or as both— he should cast the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with his senses completely stilled. This [rite], which consists of the fulfillment of all things, has been taught in the *Traiśirasa Tantra*.
By rising from the root, it is completely flooded by the moon of Śiva;
having arisen from the stream at the root of the cavity in the middle of the end of birth,
that nectar of knowledge is stirred by the intense rays of the sun of Śiva.
With that, having fully stilled the senses, one should properly satisfy [the deity],
radiant with rays of light situated in the center of the lotus of the abode of emptiness;
[this is] the grasping of the scripture of consciousness, which is motionless regarding both the supported and the support.
It is that which shatters the friction of the single *sphoṭa*—the manifold expansion of birth and its substratum.
Beginning from the root station and reaching as far as Someśa, it remains like the sky; so long as it is utterly tranquil, it is so described.
And it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*: "Having filled the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*),
and having likewise established the disciple within oneself while recollecting the root mantra—
[one should contemplate] Śiva, Śakti, oneself, the disciple, the clarified butter, and likewise the fire."
Unifying [the breath] and with undistracted mind, one should gradually proceed to the *dvādaśānta*.
Having established the *kumbhaka* there, meditating upon the Lord who is both with and without parts (*sakala-niṣkala*),
one should remain unperturbed until the exhaustion of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Thus united with the supreme reality by the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva,

one whose bonds of *māyā* have been burnt no longer falls into the state of a bound soul (*paśutā*). However, if upon the fall of the body one should desire to attain [residence] in any of the *tattvas*, [one may do so].

One should bestow enjoyments through various distinctions, both collectively and individually, and finally, the supreme state. Then, on the plane of each respective principle (*tattva*), with a mind focused on nothing else, one should perform the re-union (*yojanikā*) by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

The initiation (dīkṣā) which is proclaimed as bestowing liberation, or as bestowing both enjoyment and liberation, is twofold by virtue of being "with seed" (sabīja) or "seedless" (nirbīja). [It is performed] for a child, for one whose death is known to be imminent, or for one who is incapable due to old age and the like.
When the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) has arisen, the seedless initiation (*nirbījikā dīkṣā*) should be performed.
In the seedless initiation, one should also purify the bonds (*pāśas*) pertaining to the rules (*sāmāyas*).
One who has received the seedless initiation, however, remains devoted to the gods, the fire, and the guru.
By this much alone, one may attain Śiva immediately, or else after having enjoyed worldly enjoyments;
and it is stated in the venerable *Dīkṣottara* that within the movement of thirty-six finger-breadths,
one should abandon the principles (*tattva*) and the worlds (*bhuvana*) in succession from the soles of the feet to the top of the head.
That which lasts for only a *tuṭi* is partless, bodiless, and supreme as the "I.
Meditating thus, "By means of my power, I cast him into that," one should perform initiation.
However, in initiation with seed (*sabījā*), one should not purify the observances (*samaya*).

However, this is the distinction regarding her: for as long as the child lives, the Guru should perform the emission of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) by means of a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), so that the child may have the means for his remaining life. This [emission] flashes forth simultaneously from the undivided ocean of Śiva’s awakening.
While casting the full [oblation], one should meditate upon the emitted web of principles as consisting of the nature of light.
Alternatively, one may effect the emission of the pure principles through the consecration of the water-pot;
likewise, it may be accomplished by the power of meditation alone, or else by means of full consecrations.
The earth, when meditated upon as the form of Śiva, becomes stable for him;
it stabilizes that very meditation, and thus he becomes purified. Water nourishes this [earth], and fire brings it to luminosity.
The void, through contact with the joy of the winds, brings about expansion.
In this way, even the group of subtle elements (tanmātras) is held to consist of the nature of Śiva—
the great pervasion of supreme bliss and the falling away of all impurities.

Going toward Śiva, taking hold [of Him], praising Śiva as that which is to be accepted, and fully [engaging in] the tasting, seeing, and touching of the abundance of Śiva’s fragrance—likewise, listening to Him:
such is the purification of the senses. (106–107)

Volition, determination, and resolve; illumination, attachment, and persistence—this is that purity within the mental and other faculties by virtue of their being of the nature of Śiva. Restriction, coloring, and the state of being an agent, along with the power of differentiation (kalanā), [constitute this].
Sensation is like a state of sleep regarding the objects that are to be abandoned;
thus, for one who has ascended to unity with Śiva, even this group of six coverings (kañcukas) is purified. The person, having attained the state of Śiva, becomes pure indeed.
In the principles beginning with Vidyeśvara and the rest, there is no impurity whatsoever.
Thus, through the emanation of these pure principles, the disciple also becomes identical with them;
for this has been indicated in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara.
The wise have declared that both bondage and liberation depend upon the senses:
when restrained, they lead to bondage; when liberated, they lead to liberation.
When these [senses], together with the mind, abide in the pervasive state, [they lead to liberation].

"Released in some object, they lead to bondage because of their obstruction. Thus, in the doctrine of the Siddhayogīśvarī, the nature of the senses is declared to be twofold, according to the distinction between the pure and the impure.
The illustrious Vidyāguru, however, has stated in the *Pramāṇastutidarśana* that this rule applies to initiation with all mantras:
"In the purification up to the level of Māyā, all rites should always be performed with the Aparā [mantra]."
At the end of the Sakala [state], one should perform [the rite] with the Dvyātmikā [mantra]; at the Niṣkala [state], however, with the Parā alone.
At the end of Īśa, [one performs] Pibanī and so forth; at the end of the Sakala, the five limbs (pañcāṅga).
Having considered this procedure, the best of gurus should perform the ritual action.
The number of oblations for the path of the principles (*tattva*) and the phonemes (*varṇa*) which was previously stated for the path of the city,

one should double that very number for the path of the words (*pada*), and quadruple it for the path of the mantra-fragments (*mantrakalā*). On the path of the sequence (*krama*), they are doubled again and again in successive order.

Up until the purification of the three principles (tattvas), there should then be twentyfold [the previous number]. For each ritual action within the triad of principles, there should be sixty oblations;
however, for a single principle, they say there should be one hundred and eight oblations.
Regarding those full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) prescribed along with the reverse ritual (vilomakarman),
there is no difference whatsoever in their number for the complete purification of all the paths (adhvan).
Thus has been described this initiation (dīkṣā), accompanied by the rites of birth and the rest.
Now, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, the eighteenth chapter:
Now, this abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣiptadīkṣā*) which leads to the attainment of the state of Śiva is taught.
Here, there is no [preparation of] colored powders (*rajas*), no preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), and no formal appropriation of the ground or the sacrificial site (*bhūkṣetraparigraha*).
Having worshipped Śiva in whatever place it may be, the Guru who has reached the further shore of reality should meditate upon the path with his mind and initiate [the disciple].
By whichever path the Guru [performs the initiation], [the disciple becomes] free from birth and the other [stages of existence].

Pervaded solely by the state of Śiva, he should perform [the rite] ending with the single principle (ekatattva). Then, for him, the supreme mantra is: "I now purify this principle, svāhā. This should be done for each principle; once it is purified, he should cast the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] with other mantras, either individually or collectively as previously stated.
The name [of the disciple], ending in the nominative case and encapsulated by the *parā* mantra, followed by *svāhā*, should be used;
with that, one should offer oblations a hundred, a thousand, or eight times, according to one's capacity.
Then, having purified [the soul] as "Full" (pūrṇā), such a supreme state free from defects is attained;
this rite of initiation has been proclaimed there and there by the Great Lord in various scriptures.
One should purify the principles (tattvas) individually by means of the letters of the two *mātṛkā*s.

Or else, this procedure applies to all mantras by means of the *piṇḍa* mantra. To whatever extent the Guru is one whose nature consists of thoroughly practiced knowledge and absorption in that [mantra], to that same extent he should perform the rite in an abbreviated manner, and not otherwise.
And it is said in the *Śrībrahmayāmala*:
"One should indeed contemplate the pervasion common to all the paths even in a concise [rite], but there is no elaboration in the sacrifice.
One who performs a scattered rite, not having become absorbed in that [deity], merely joins the ritual acts together."
"One should perform the rite for the distracted [practitioner] so that he may gradually attain identity with That.
This concise rite has been declared out of compassion by Śiva in the *Dīkṣottara*, in the *Kiraṇa*, and in various other parts of the teaching."
Now, the nineteenth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Next, initiation that bestows immediate departure (*sadyaḥ-samutkrānti*) is described.
By means of that [initiation], one shall go to Śiva either at that very moment, through the exhaustion of experience, or upon the fall of the body.
Thus, in the Mālinīśāstra, this was indicated by the Great Lord:
"When the fall of the body is imminent, because of the manifestation of the descent of power (śaktipāta), one attains the initiation of Śaṅkara; therefore, after that moment of initiation..."
The meaning here— that one shall go to Śiva—

is explained by our illustrious Guru, who is the very embodiment of Śambhu, through a discernment of what precedes and follows. For when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) occurs in one whose death is imminent, [one attains liberation].
In that case, if [the disciple] is dull-witted, his life may come to an end through service to the Guru and others;
or else, through the mediation of kinsmen, friends, and so forth, that [initiation] of his might fall away from the Lord.
Or perhaps he was previously a *samayin* who had not at all obtained the supreme initiation.

Or, even for one who has already received initiation and is desiring to cast off his life-breaths, the final preceptor should then perform the initiation of immediate departure (*sadya-utkrānti-dīkṣā*), provided he is free from afflictions;
but not for one whose impurities are unripened, nor for one whose body still possesses residual karma.
One should perform the upward departure (utkramaṇa), as described in the venerable Gahvara:
having seen a disciple seized by old age and tormented by disease,
one should cause him to depart upward and then unite him with the Supreme Reality.
Regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified,
the venerable Śambhu has here set forth the previously mentioned collection of topics according to the rule of optional application.
Having performed the entire previously stated ritual procedure for the purification of the observance (samaya), [one proceeds].
One should place the flaming *kṣurikā* (knife), which cuts the vital points (*marmans*), upon this [mantra].
Having performed the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*),
together with the pair of the tongue and the cutting instrument, according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*).
Having performed the fire-concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā), which inflames all the vital points (marmans),
one should fill the body with air from the big toes up to the top of the head.
Then, having drawn that [air] upward from the big toes to the end of the head by means of the method to be described, [one should perform the extraction].
One should sever the vital points from the end of the apertures and dismiss [the deity] with the Kālarātrī mantra.
By this sequential yoga, even an initiate who has been joined [to the practice] without the performance of oblations attains that initiation; thus it is stated in the venerable Mālinīmata.
From the sixteen supports, the six wheels, the three targets, and the five voids—
having entered into any one of these, or else as previously described for the bound soul (paśu),
one cuts through the root of the bulb (kanda) and so forth by means of the contemplation of oneness.

By means of the application of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should unite [the soul] with its own desired abode. Having visualized the blazing trident of knowledge, radiant with the three flaming wheels, one should perform for it piercing, awakening, and whirling by means of this [mantra].
One should repeatedly perform kindling, striking, piercing,
and shaking within the wheels beginning with the *kanda*, especially in the heart-lotus; then,
having brought [the breath] to the *dvādaśānta*, one should cast it into the pair of *bindus*.
"In the markless supreme abode, he is united with the Supreme Lord.

One should not perform any ritual consecration for him," so the Lord has declared in the Gahvara. "What need has this perfect one for funeral rites (*śrāddha*) and the like?"—thus it was contemplated.
In the venerable *Dīkṣottara*, this procedure is encapsulated by fire:
the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) is the male principle, placed below which is Rudra accompanied by the *bindu*.
Having applied this to the body of the disciple, one should recite it a hundred times without agitation.
Having ascended in a single upward blink of an eye, the disciple thus proceeds to the Supreme.
This very procedure is prescribed in the venerable Siddhayogīśvarīmata;
this initiation of transcendence (utkrāmaṇī-dīkṣā) must be performed by a Guru who is a yogin.

How can one who has not practiced the movement of the vital breath perform this Brahma-vidyā which is about to be described— both in its manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala) forms intertwined? Alternatively,
one should recite it into his ear repeatedly, or indeed cause him to recite it.

The Guru himself should perform the rite for the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) and so forth; by the power of the mantra-ritual, through the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should thus unite [the disciple] with the Supreme. Even without the practice of yoga, the Guru bestows immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti).
By the power of knowledge, mantra, ritual action, and meditation, one becomes capable of acting [thus].
By this [method], the disciple is made to transcend [time] by force in a single moment alone.
Since his experience transcends time, let it be merely momentary; what does that matter?

There is another [rite] which bestows immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti), in which one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) when his vital breaths are certainly desirous of exiting. Even without ritual action, by the power of the future Brahma-knowledge, the Guru [effects this].
By means of the practice of whispering into the ear, drawing [the soul] out from the web of the sheaths of reality (tattva-kañcuka),
one should gradually unite the individual (pudgala) with whatever is desired— whether in the manifest, the unmanifest, both,
or in any reality whatsoever.
Likewise, both the initiate (*samayin*) and the spiritual son (*putraka*) may recite this vidyā.
By reciting it, the initiate attains the state of being a portion of Rudra,
for both of these are authorized for its chanting and study.
Neither through teaching nor through instruction does this [attainment] occur for him, except through study;
yet, when these two recite, that state arises for him by the very nature of the reality itself.
Just as one who has been forbidden from performing rites such as those involving spirits may, by himself, remember the mantra.
Even when possessed, [the adept] does not incur any lapse anywhere because he has abandoned the sense of agency;
just as an initiate (samayin) reciting scripture in an empty house incurs no lapse because he benefits the multitude of living beings dwelling within it.

Likewise, while reciting this vidyā himself according to the true nature of things, he would not be deprived of it once [the disciple] is liberated, since he has performed no action here [for that purpose]. But surely, one should not utter the sequence of the scriptures in the presence of one who is uninitiated? 37.
Well then, the prohibition regarding even one who stands before a wall is now being stated:
it is only he who is capable of hearing and comprehending [the teaching] who is excluded here;
not walls, insects, or birds.
In that case, he would be like a stone, with the functions of his senses dissolved.
How could there be a transgression of a prohibition for one who recites before him?
Yet, by the very nature of reality, even one whose senses have failed perceives.
Without depending on the senses at all, by means of his own self-luminous power of consciousness, the individual soul—
though desiring to leave the previous body and not yet having entered the subsequent one—
awakens in the interim through the force of an awakener.

Mantras consist of sound; by their very nature as pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), they manifest themselves as the essence of meaning and thus awaken one to that meaning. Therefore, for this person whose senses have dissolved, awakening arises spontaneously.
Due to the proximity of the contemplation (*amarśana*) of mantras that are of the same nature as one's own consciousness,
just as a wind of little speed becomes swift when mixed with [wind] of its own kind,
so too the Self, though its contemplation was dormant, awakens in this way.
He has become awakened, yet he is not said to be uninitiated. For initiation is indeed a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), and it is this that he possesses; it is nothing else.
Therefore, he may read his own scripture at some occasion of the observance (*sāmāyika*).

If some fortunate person hears this and is liberated, there is no harm for him. "Let him not revile the scriptures, which cause the downfall of both [the speaker and the listener]"—this is the intended meaning; one should not recite this in the presence of those who have not been initiated.
Just as a practitioner of the observance (*samayin*), while performing the application of mantras to a piece of wood or a clod of earth,
does not incur a transgression even if it moves away from that spot, so too is it here;
for such is the case for this practitioner of the observance who desires to attain the state of realization.

When that which has proceeded by its own nature is liberated, there is indeed no harm; however, the practitioner is always subject to the constraint of destiny regarding the fruit to be accomplished. Even one who has overheard a mantra like a fly must perform the appropriate expiation.
Thus has been described the immediate departure [of the soul] (sadyaḥ-samutkrānti); by the command of the Guru,

even one who is a *samayin* or of lower status may perform this himself at the prescribed time for the sake of accomplishing the stated goal, provided he has mastered the movement of the breath’s course and its return.

Or even a Guru who has not yet performed his formal duties may [perform this] for the sake of purifying his commitments (samaya), provided he remains in a lower state; however, one whose consciousness is ignited by knowledge [should not do so]. Thus, this immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti) has been indicated in the Mālinīmata.
Whether by himself, by the Guru, or by the Great Lord (Maheśin) as a necessary task—
if, considering all enjoyment to be deformed, he should abandon the body,
then at that moment the initiate (samayī), joined by that very process, becomes Śiva.

This immediate departure (sadya-utkrānti) has been described; it should be guarded by the wise like their own life-breath. Now begins the twentieth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, which provides consolation to ignorant people; herein I shall speak of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
In the triangle, the abode of fire,
blazing on all sides with the color of fire and fanned by the city of wind, [place it] in the right hand, shining brightly;
having grasped some seed-syllable therein, [place it] in the same way within the heart.
And while engaged solely in that recitation, one should intensely contemplate the seed-syllable being burned in the hand;
scorched by the stream of *phaṭ* syllables ignited by fire,
the seed-syllable reaches a state of seedlessness, becoming incapable of producing its own offspring.

This [impurity] has been scorched and will not sprout again; by that very conviction, the impurities known as *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman* are burnt away through the power of mantra, meditation, and ritual action.
Thus, they are no longer capable of producing their own effects, and this [state] is the conviction of the seedless (*nirbīja*).
That illustrious and most gracious Śambhunātha explained this to me:
"In this context, the application of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) must also be performed through the grace of the Guru;
for initiation, being intensely radiant, can liberate even immobile beings."
When a guru, having realized within himself the perfection of recitation, fire-oblation, worship, and meditation, performs initiation,
that initiation is known as "with conviction" (sapratyayā).
This rule does not apply to one who is in the *avadhūta* state, who is beyond conventional conduct, and who knows reality (*tattva*).
Initiation accompanied by ritual conduct is that which is endowed with visible signs of realization.
However, in initiation performed without ritual conduct, no such sign is declared;
for knowledge that is self-evident does not require any further fruit.
"However, it has been stated in the Siddhāmata that meditation and the like are to be accomplished through their fruits;
or one should perform the examination of the purity of the scales,
which serves as a means of conviction, just as it was taught by the Supreme Lord in the Śrītantrasadbhāva."
In the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* as well, this was indicated by the Supreme Lord:
"Bliss, emergence, trembling, sleep, and the fifth is whirling"—
thus spoke he who describes the gradations of power (*śakti*).
Arising through lightness due to the disappearance of the grasping of the body,

the body— which is primarily composed of earth— then abandons its primary nature. Having visualized the disciple as having leaped up by means of the mantra that brings about future lightness, [the teacher should proceed].
In that [rite], the Guru should perform all the previously mentioned rituals without exception.
Thus has been described this initiation of the purification of the scales (*tulāśuddhidīkṣā*), which bestows conviction.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now, the ritual of initiation for one who remains out of sight is being described.
"For the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, he is led toward a true Guru"—
in this statement from the *Mālinīvijaya*, the word *prati* denotes "facing" or "directed toward."
The "presence" (sāṃmukhya) of this disciple consists in his being a fit recipient for that [teacher's] compassion.
The statement "having propitiated him" is an indication of the cause for that compassion.
Through that connection, someone may be liberated at that very moment.
This is indeed the meaning of this excellent jewel of a statement from the *Mālinīvijaya*:
"At that very moment" means that for him there is no other interval of time, such as the moment of desiring to go [to another state];
rather, the Guru, overcome by compassion, should uplift him in this very way.
For one whose body has been worn away by service to the Guru, who meets death before receiving initiation;
or for one who, at the moment of death, spontaneously develops such a longing [for it];
or for one who has received the purificatory rites of initiation according to the lower tantras and so forth.
Furthermore, for one who has attained the conventional [initiation] but has not yet obtained the supreme initiation;
or for one killed in a riot, or devoured by a Yoginī, or killed through malevolent magic (*abhicāra*);
or for one who has died at the hands of a Guru, or been destroyed by means of *yantras*, *tantras*, and so forth—[these are the cases].
Furthermore, even for one who has fallen from his own observance (samaya) or has already received initiation,
[the teacher may act] due to the force of intense entreaty from relatives, wife, friends, or sons,
or else by the power of compassion arising spontaneously toward that object.

The Guru should perform the initiation that rescues the deceased and bestows Śiva-hood upon one whose nature is characterized by a portion of the descent of power (śaktipāta) that has reached him through the medium of [the deceased’s] consciousness. This was stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Śrīmṛtyuñjayasiddha* and other scriptures.
In the case of an uninitiated king or similar person, one who is indolent, one who has fallen from grace, or one who is dead;
and in the case of a child, the sick, women, or the elderly—one should perform the rite for the extraction of the deceased.
The entire procedure has been previously described, but it is here intended in an abbreviated form.

Since that [external ritual] is for the sake of enjoyment in the external world and is devoid of the worship of the Guru and others; (13) Therefore, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), the sacrificial pap (*caru*), the site (*kṣetra*), the bed, and the preparation of the mandala are not useful here for the purification of the disciple and for the vision in dreams. (14)
However, for the sake of the mantra’s presence, satisfaction, and yoga, there is the mandala here;
and on the following day, the worship of the deity—directly, that is not of benefit to him [who has already attained realization].
[This is] by means of ritual action, implements, location, the form of the mandala, and mantras.
Through meditation, yoga, single-minded devotion, knowledge, and the state of being absorbed in that [deity],
for anyone who has entered into that [state]— whether they be disciples or the Guru—
these eleven are said to be the causes for the presence [of the deity]. (16–17)
Each successive stage is more excellent than the last, depending on the degree of their combination.
The ritual action should be most extensive, using flowers and other offerings that are of the highest quality and endowed with auspicious characteristics.
Furthermore, the place of worship should be a site such as a solitary liṅga where the self attains complete serenity.
The mandala consisting of three tridents, a lotus, and a wheel— which exists within the mantra-mandala—
is seen even when not formally invoked to be the means for accomplishing the state of a Samayin. This perfected Samaya-mandala has been taught in the Mālinītantra.

By the two words "merely seen" (*saṃdṛṣṭamātra*) and "merely accomplished" (*siddhamātra*), the form is that which has a blazing nature; likewise, the mantra is intensely radiant. The remainder is clear, and therefore it is not explained here again in detail.

Having constructed a maṇḍala and worshipped the deity therein with *kuśa* grass, one should then fashion a figure out of cow dung and have the disciple lie down upon it. Then, within that figure, one should purify a single path through the contemplation of its pervasive presence (*vyāpti*).
Having cast [the consciousness] as far as the end of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), one should again perform this rite:
by means of the application of the Great Net (*mahājāla*), having drawn the mind from the midst of the entire path, one should cause it to abide there; that is called the procedure.

Rising from the *mūlādhāra*, having forcefully ascended the staff-like path of the infinitely expanded and well-distributed network of channels, and having reached the space of the nose, it is able to cast itself forth to pervade everything.
As long as it covers the wheel of the paths with a mass of flame-tips as beautiful as smoke, this practice called the "Great Net" (*mahājāla*) brings about the summoning of the desired soul.

(25) By means of this, that which is to be covered first comes under one's control and appears face-to-face; thereafter, if one so desires, all of it may be brought forth from the midst of the paths as wished. (26ab)

Whether for the purpose of attracting or extracting a deceased person, or for drawing back a living one, I have declared this method called the "Net" (jāla), as mastered through the tradition of the venerable Śambhunātha.
Just as when two armies that have been separated for a long time meet again, the horses, elephants, and men instinctively rush toward their own respective kind out of natural affinity;

in the same way, the channels (nāḍī) and the wheels [of the body] come together through the vital winds (pavana) and the senses (karaṇa), and by means of their own inherent affinities, they are to be unified once they have been brought under control by one's own net.

Drawn forth by the Great Net by one endowed with discernment (*vijñāna*), the living soul (*jīva*) is released at that very moment from the realms of gods, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell. And this person, having attained that knowledge, mantra, and yoga, [renders] the artificial [reality]...

Just as a yogi abandons identification with the heart of the one to be mastered, so too he abandons the various states beginning with the immobile, such as being in the same world or its vicinity; it is no wonder that he who does so even through ritual action [attains this]. 29–30ab.

Because he possesses a body fit for authority, though residing in a human body, he is not liberated from that body at that time; rather, at the end of the body's life, he shall go to Śiva. Within that very body, however, there arises in him a certain supreme power belonging to Śaṅkara.
Through wisdom born of devotion, or even from a teacher who has not been personally served,
this individual soul (jīva), though residing within its own body,
pervades this body made of darbha grass and the like by the power of the net, even without conscious awareness, through its own presiding authority.
Furthermore, by virtue of the superior power of yoga, mantra, ritual action, and knowledge,
he quickly abandons even the human body at that very moment. Even that individual soul which is bodiless and as if asleep [within the subtle body] is [liberated] from the net.
Drawn forth, he comes with a body made of darbha grass or one consisting of fruit (35). Or, the construction of the body may be done with whatever is available, such as nutmeg;
because it is appropriate for both the internal and external [aspects], that is said here to be the most excellent. (36)
Then, led by the sequence of the network [of channels], that living soul remains as if asleep;
because of the absence of obtaining the totality of conditions such as the body distinguished by the mind,
it does not throb, does not perceive, does not speak, and indeed has no desire.

For such a person, one should perform all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as previously described. Having performed everything previously mentioned through the method of seedless initiation (nirbījā-dīkṣā),
one should cast that [disciple] into the fire along with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) during the rite of union (yojanikā-vidhi).
When the body made of darbha grass and other materials has been offered into the fire of the mantra along with the *pūrṇāhuti*,
one whose bonds are released goes to Śiva, free from rebirth.
This [rite] is considered "with conviction" (*sapratyayā*) when the body born of darbha grass vibrates.

In that regard, through the yoga of offering the vital breath, the mind, and the mantra, it becomes so; this has been stated for one who practices with effort. However, that [result] does not occur by force alone, but rather through the causes as they arise, just as those taught in the *Mṛtoddhāra* [chapter].

Even the initiation for one who is alive but absent (parokṣa) should be performed; however, that is "seedless" (nirbījikā). In that rite, when the ritual construction consists primarily of darbha grass figures, the soul is drawn forth by means of the "net" (jāla) through mere mental resolve, out of fear of death.
The remainder is as before, excluding the burning away of forms arising from *kuśa* grass and other materials.

(44) Because of limitation, lack of sovereignty, and the constraint of destiny regarding the object to be accomplished, the drawing-in by the net does not occur without practice, nor without freedom from passion and hatred. (45)

If one has been initiated by incomparable initiations while [the teacher] was absent, then the higher initiation would be more powerful; however, the lower one serves for the sake of purification. But in the case of the initiation for the purpose of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti-yojanikā*), it is likewise performed by many teachers.
When [initiation] has been performed, there is a variety of enjoyments resulting from the connection with a variety of causes.
In the case of initiation by proxy (*parokṣadīkṣaṇa*), one who has transcended *māyā* should be joined to enjoyment.
Indeed, a lack of desire for enjoyment is rare; even if it exists, it serves to eliminate enjoyment.

For it has been said: "Between one's own consciousness and the consciousness of another, one's own consciousness is more powerful; it is the sublater when there is a conflict, and likewise when there is equality or indifference. The illustrious Dharmaśiva also stated this in his *Karmapaddhati* concerning indirect perception.
If, during the performance of the *pūrṇāhuti* in the rite of initiation for one who is absent,
the fire emits a crackling sound along with smoke, assumes the hue of a dark blue cloud, and repeatedly flares up and subsides; 50–51.
When it is extensive, of a terrible form, and runs toward the earth below,
or when there is an unhearable sound such as that of a crow and the like, then the Guru should observe that [sign].
[This occurs] due to sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as through association with those [sins] and minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
At that time, initiation should not be performed for him until this rite has been completed.
The Navātman mantra, situated within the *phaṭ*-enclosure and further accompanied by five *phaṭ*s, is followed by "the sins of [Name]," then "I burn," and finally eight *phaṭ*s. (53–54)
Thus, a thousandfold oblation should be performed with sesame seeds and rice;
at the end, a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) must be offered, and then the Guru should initiate him.
He should effect the purification of the principles (tattva-viśodhana) up to the ultimate goal of the Supreme (parayojana).
Even for a sinful individual who remains within direct perception,
once he has attained the Jyeṣṭhā power which consists of the Lord, one should perform the rite in this very same way;
or else, if the teacher was not properly radiant for him previously, [one should do so].
Having performed purification through penances, gifts, and breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
and having also carried out this ritual procedure, one may perform initiation without hesitation.
In every circumstance, the knower of reality may liberate bound souls (paśu).
Śiva himself is present there by his own will; therefore, one should always worship him.
One should not practice deceit in that regard, for by doing so, the disciple would go downwards.
Furthermore, one must not proclaim his faults; the one who proclaims them shall go to perdition.
"Therefore, one should avoid hell"—this is the rule stated in the *Dīkṣottara*.
This initiation in absentia (*parokṣadīkṣā*) is declared to be twofold, distinguished by whether the recipient is living or otherwise [deceased].
Now begins the twenty-second chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now we shall explain the practice known as *liṅgoddhāra* (the extraction of the sign), which is uniquely taught in the Śiva-scriptures.
Indeed, it is stated in the venerable *Mālinītantra*: "Having taught the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the earthly element, [it is said]:
'Whosoever is joined to whatever [element], he does not return from that.'"
Whosoever possesses whatever teaching has arisen through the power of his own aptitude,
he should be appointed to that very task at the time of initiation; then,
having attained all fruits, being united with Śiva, he is liberated.
Even one who is unyoked [from the lower levels], having attained purification of the higher realms from the Lord of the Worlds,
becomes pure and attains the state of Śiva, with the bonds of transmigratory existence burnt away.
Having spoken of the *puṃdhāraṇā*, this Vedic conclusion (*vaidāntika*) has been declared by me.
This was previously taught to Kapila in the first chapter;
by means of this sequential yoga, one attains the supreme state.
No longer subject to the condition of a bound soul (paśu), one abides in one's own pure Self.
For this reason, this meaning is indeed intimated even regarding those principles situated below the Śiva-principle (śivatattva).

For one who has been joined to these principles, there remains the possibility of being raised up again [to a higher state] by that which bestows the discernment of the reality taught in all the scriptures.
The Śiva-āgama is superior to all other āgamas;
and without the knowledge of Śiva, the state of being a bound soul (paśu) arises once again. [The stages are:
the descent of power, the removal of impurity, and the desire to go forth.
Initiation, awakening, the abandonment of what is to be discarded, absorption into that which is to be accepted,
the relinquishing of the state of being an object of enjoyment and of bondage, the dissolution of the agency belonging to the Lord [as subject],
and abiding in one's own self— this indeed is the nature of those established in other philosophical systems. (AbhT 22.10b–11)
For it has been declared that [the soul] is to be uplifted when impelled by the power (śakti) of Śiva.
Now, for those situated in lower systems, such as the Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist tantras and so forth,
when the lotus of the heart has blossomed by the masses of rays from the sun of Śiva, [it is then liberated].
First, the extraction of the *liṅga* (the removal of the sectarian mark) is performed, and after that, the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Even one who previously resided within another [sectarian] mark shall attain the state of Śiva through initiation.
Having made him fast there, on another day, he should [proceed] with the mantra together with its support (*sādhāra*).
Having worshipped the Lord upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should cause him to hear his own way of life:
"Previously he was a bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin); now he has been impelled by you.
Therefore, being well-pleased, grant him full grace."
"May there be no penance for him arising from the fear of abandoning his own characteristic [liṅga];
may he, becoming one with Me without delay, attain both enjoyment and liberation. Then the householder accepted that vow of his, saying, "So be it."
Having removed [the impurities] and cast them into water, one should bathe [the disciple] in the appropriate manner.
Immediately after he has bathed, one should sprinkle him with the waters from the *argha* vessel.
Then, one should offer him the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and a tooth-stick.
Then, having led him in with his eyes bound, one should cause him to prostrate.
The Praṇava, Mātṛkā, Māyā, Vyomavyāpin, the six-syllabled mantra, Bahurūpa, and the one called Netra— these seven are common [to all].
From among those [mantras], he should impart one mantra to him;

he too should recite it for a day and night, eating little or even fasting. Having thus imparted the mantra to him, [the teacher should act] according to the ritual procedure for the common [initiation].
When the fire has been gratified with that mantra, one should perform the purification of the vow (vratashuddhi).
Having encapsulated the disciple's name with the worshipped mantra itself, one should apply the modification:
"I purify the expiation, Phaṭ Svāhā. (22–23)

Having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations, and likewise a final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with *vauṣaṭ* according to the ritual application, one should summon the Lord of Vows (*Vrateśvara*) and worship him with the mantra: "Oṃ,
obeisance to the Lord of Vows."
And by your command, you must not cause him to hear anything whatsoever by the order of Śiva. Then Vrateśvara is to be satiated with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*;
having asked for forgiveness, he should be dismissed, and thereafter follows the dismissal of Agni.
The announcement of that [initiation] to the deity and the dismissal with the words "forgive me" should be performed.
Then, on the third day, the entire ritual procedure is prescribed as before,
beginning with the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and ending with the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one's desired goal.
First, for those who bear the marks [of other orders], there is the initiation for liberation which is devoid of authority;
such reborn ones (punarbhuvaḥ) are not fit for the path of the *sādhaka* or the *ācārya*. Yet even reborn ones, when kindled by knowledge, become a locus for the status of a guru.
"It is for liberation alone, not for enjoyment; yet it may also serve for enjoyment by means of a specific method.
Thus spoke the teacher Īśānaśiva in his own manual (*paddhati*), correctly elucidating the reality taught in the *Yāmala* of the venerable Goddess.
Even for one who has served his guru until the end, who looks downward and remains in a state of humility, one should perform this consecration;
however, according to the *Kāmika*, one must not reveal the secret otherwise.
Even if someone has been consecrated in another tantra, one should not disclose the secret to them.
Even if one is established in independence, if one has relied upon an ignorant guru until the end,
and subsequently loses faith therein, one should perform the rite even for that [ignorant guru].
This is because the mantra that has come from the mouth of an ignorant teacher is devoid of potency.
Having recited [the mantra], that Guru here is no longer qualified due to the aforementioned defect.

Therefore, having first performed purification for him, one should then perform initiation. He who was previously initiated by a Guru established in the lower revelation (adhodarśana) [is the subject].
When, subsequently, by the power of an intense [divine] energy, he goes to a true guru,
then that true guru, having likewise performed the purification for this disciple,
should carry out the entire ritual action beginning with initiation according to the prescribed injunctions.
Even if a true Guru has been found, if he does not recognize the disciple’s state of readiness,
then that disciple must demonstrate his own fitness for the bestowal of higher knowledge (vijñāna). For,
in every respect, one who remains silent or speaks erroneously [regarding this] is not a Guru.
Thinking "the ignorant one is [thus] by his very nature," he should abandon that [view] and perform the rite in this manner.
A person of intelligence should not entertain any doubt here regarding concealment (*tirobhāva*).
Concealment consists in being touched by what is below; it is not the discernment of the means belonging to the higher levels.
Those who have been initiated into the Siddhānta, into the Tantra consisting of ten and eighteen divisions,
into the sixty-four Bhairava Tantras, or into the Trika— these bound souls (paśus) one should initiate into the Bhairavīya Kula, which is the essence of the *Siddhavīrāvalī*.
The initiation obtained through the sequence of the five initiations is known as the "supreme" (anuttara) initiation.
By means of it, even one who stands at a lower level is graced through the extraction of the *liṅga*.
This applies even to him who, through the impulsion of the Great Lord residing in the heart, has [performed] the most extensive [rite].
One should seek the knowledge of the scriptures, and for that purpose, one should approach many gurus. One should also receive from them initiations ending with consecration (*abhiṣeka*),
for these strengthen one's knowledge when they are performed by those who possess the respective knowledge.
And it has been stated extensively in various places in the Śrīmata scripture:
"Just as a bee seeking fragrance moves from flower to flower, so too a disciple seeking higher knowledge [moves] from one teacher to another teacher. (45–46a)

Among many gurus, he from whom the highest knowledge is obtained is his guru; for in this regard, initiation is not primary when it comes to consciousness. Having approached a guru who is a treasury of all knowledge, one becomes firmly established.
The wise man, intent on desiring to know each of those [levels], should worship that very [teacher].
Thus has been declared the procedure for initiation, concluding with the extraction of the *liṅga*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter in the venerable *Tantrāloka*.
Now, the procedure for consecration according to the Supreme Lord is being told.
That very initiation which was described for the spiritual sons (putraka) is also applicable, in due order, for the teacher (guru) and the practitioner (sādhaka),
provided it is joined with the principles (tattva) that are to be experienced.

Having recognized that one who possesses well-practiced knowledge is fit— whether he is currently desirous of becoming [an adept] or is destined to be so— the Guru should entrust him with his own office. He who does not know this is not a teacher, even if he has been consecrated.
"In the sequence beginning with the Samayin and so forth," it is stated in the venerable *Kāmika*.
"He who does not know the sixfold junction of the paths (vedādhvasandhāna) situated externally and internally—
such a guru cannot liberate [others]," according to the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*.
"Even one devoid of all [external] characteristics is accepted as a Guru if he possesses knowledge;
it is in the *Śrī Kacabhārgava* that the primacy of knowledge alone has been declared.
One who knows the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition, and is solely intent upon devotion to Śiva..."
The compassionate Guru is one who understands the meaning of the entire Śiva-scripture;
he is not self-appointed, for his characteristics have been declared by the Supreme Lord.
One who is not a devotee, yet acts with the intent to gain a livelihood, is presided over by Īśāna.
One who is self-originated through the Western Self (paścātman) has no authority anywhere;
likewise, the son of one who wears ashes as sprouts, the son of one who neglects his vows, the son of an immoral woman,
the *kuṇḍa*, and the *gola*— these are declared to be corrupt in the *Devyākhyayāmala*.
Furthermore, one who was previously of another sect and has been re-established in the Śaiva tradition is a *punarbhū*.

However, no such restrictive rule at all is enjoined in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara). Rather, [the teacher] is one who reveals [the truth] to the disciple, being a knower of the collection of principles (*tattva*) exactly as they are.
Furthermore, the characteristic [of a teacher] is that he knows all the principles (tattvas), and so forth;
and whatever has been enjoined in this Tantra regarding the practice of yoga, one should perform it exactly as prescribed for the sake of attainment— this, indeed, is described as the Command (ājñā).

But as for the teacher who acts as a ritual officiant (*karmin*), there is the exclusion of those who are one-eyed and so forth; for nowhere is there anything superior to the totality of causal factors (*kārakasāmagrī*) for the rite. And in the *Yāmala* scripture of the Goddess, there is likewise the exclusion of those from Kāñcī and other such places.
Since that [anger] and so forth arise from the defects perceived therein, how could they exist in one who possesses perfect knowledge?
As for the fact that the *Yāmala* and other texts exclude self-manifested (*svayambhū*) and other gurus,
they explained that all of this was intended for those engaged in ritual action (*karmī*).
Therefore, disregarding considerations of place, family, custom, body, and characteristics,
the Guru should make [the disciple] a Guru endowed with complete knowledge;
having worshipped and offered oblations as before, he should announce what he intends to do.
