Then the Guru should consecrate that disciple sixty-four times, and then once more with the water whose essence is those mantras, according to the previously mentioned procedure. Then,
with great abundance, he should speak his own [teaching] to him in full detail.
All that is the essence of what must be done, the supreme secret of the scriptures. (19) Disciples who are impelled by the power of Śiva should be favored by you.
This has been stated in the *Jñānottara*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas... (20)

Eunuchs, women, Śūdras, and whoever else seeks that [initiation] should not be scrutinized at the time of initiation; one should examine them at the time of [bestowing] knowledge. The Guru is said to have knowledge as his root; he should carry out the sevenfold sacrificial session (saptasatrī).
Initiation, exposition, compassion, friendliness, reflection on the scriptures, oneness with Śiva,
and the giving of food and so forth— one should maintain this sevenfold sacrificial session (*saptasatra*).
Furthermore, during the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should provide him with tools such as a chisel and chalk.
The entire collection of ritual implements should be offered to the wise one.
Having been consecrated, he should thereafter honor the Guru with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
A Guru who is a mere ritualist devoid of knowledge should not, after having handed over his own office, [remain as such].
Furthermore, one should not exercise authority over initiation and the like without his permission.
Thus he should be informed, and he too, having offered salutation, should express his approval.
From that time forward, the former teacher has relinquished his authority.
One may wander at will, free from constraints, in the exposition [of scriptures], initiation, and so forth;
for by performing these, one is not obstructed, being like a lamp lit from another lamp.
Such is the lineage; there is no lapse of authority, and one who does not perform [these acts] is not obstructed.
If one performs [the initiation] prematurely, one will be thwarted; this is stated in the Siddhātantra.
One who gives instruction according to the truth is called an Ācārya; and at the time of the ritual, there must be no contempt regarding the liberation from saṃsāra.

A guru who is possessed of the principles [of reality] should not, out of pride, fail to initiate a disciple; for he who does so shall dwell in hell and be afflicted by disease in this world. That guru who has received consecration [should study] the manual of mantras for six months.
One should meditate upon everything taught in the Tantra and recite it until one becomes non-different from it.
When one has indeed become identical with that, then having attained its potency, one may sever the fetters; therefore, one should exert effort in remaining established in that state of identity.
Rising from the heart-cakra, subtle, resembling the moon or crystal, in the form of a line, consisting of sound, and tranquil, it proceeds through the series of cakras;
established at the "end of the twelve" within the Suṣumṇā, in the midst of the three paths.
There, having filled the heart-cakra, one should recite the mantra which possesses a blazing radiance;
resembling the submarine fire (aurva), it flows through the multitude of openings such as the eyes and pores,
until it is strewn with peaceful flames that dissolve the clarified butter of the universe.
Then, with the interior of the cavity of the navel thoroughly satiated by the stream of clarified butter (*ājya*),
the mantras become bestowers of liberation— blazing, awakened, and perfectly pure. [The mantra] reaches the root,
the bulb, the ether, the navel, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the palate.
It reaches the Half-moon, the Obstructress, the Nāda, the End of Sound, and the all-pervading Śakti;
it rests upon the wheels of Samana, Unmanā, Śuddhātman, and Para.
In whichever wheel one should perform recitation, by means of the differentiation of the whole and its parts, [one attains the goal].
"In that very context, it is called 'the Great Mantra' in the *Devīyāmala*;
this is declared to be the Vidyā-vow for the sake of accomplishing the potency of mantra.
And that [potency] is indeed identity (*tādātmya*), as has been stated in the *Spanda-śāsana*. (AbhT 23.39–40a)

Then, having taken hold of that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One, proceed toward their respective functions, just as the sense organs of embodied beings do. After one has performed the vidyā-vow, [the teacher may perform] initiation, exposition, and so forth in every respect.
One should bestow [the teaching] upon worthy disciples, never upon those who are unworthy.
O Brahmin, one should engage a person in the secret [doctrine] only after testing them for the opposite qualities;
even regarding spiritual power (*śakti*), it arises from right conduct and not otherwise—so it is stated in the *Ūrmiśāsana*.
One should perform [the rites] daily and so forth, even if very briefly, as stated in the Brahmayāmala.
O Dear One, one who has completed the observance of the Vidyā-vow may even mentally recollect everything;
for one whose omniscience is obscured by attachment to the body is merely a vessel for hypocrisy.
Even if he does not initiate [the disciple], the teacher is never at fault anywhere;
however, having recognized the disciple's unfitness, he should not initiate him, lest he incur sin.
But once he has understood that [the disciple] possesses knowledge, mastery of the scriptures, supernatural powers, and the status of a guru, he may initiate him again.
One should examine him further to see if he possesses the appropriate fitness for each [task], and appoint him to each respective position, but never otherwise.
[Objection: But how could a desire for that task arise in one who is unfit for it? 46–47ab. 47cd.
The very will presided over by its Lord alone indicates his fitness;
it is true that some awakened will does not reach full manifestation,
just as in the case of one of sinful character, there is no removal of sin [until the will changes], like a flash of lightning.
The establishment or non-establishment of that [desire] depends upon one's own will, which itself arises from the grace of Śambhu.
For this very reason, one whose such desire is not firmly established is not a fit vessel;
likewise, one who, having received perfect knowledge, is devoid of faith in the Guru.
One should not transmit the higher knowledge (vijñāna) to one who has not realized this [truth], lest he cause the world to fall into ruin;
yet, even if he was previously unacquainted with it, once he has realized it, one may proceed to take back the knowledge.
When, however, he has been known again and again to be devoid of trust, [the transmission must be withheld].

Then one should meditate upon him in front, throbbing like the moon and the sun. Then, one should meditate on the deluding power (śakti) Vāmā, who has arisen from the sky of consciousness in the lotus of one’s own heart and is as dark as Rāhu.
Having visualized her as having emerged according to the sequence of the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) and proceeding toward the object to be accomplished (sādhya),
one should contemplate that [object] as its light being swallowed by her.
By means of this sequential yoga, [one overcomes] the evil-minded person of deluded intellect.
Consciousness, mantras, vidyās, and the like may cause harm.
[Objection: But how could consciousness, which resides within the self, be capable of being taken away?
Therefore, how is it stated in the *Śrīpūrva* that there is a "seizure of consciousness"? 55–56ab.
It is said that this disciple’s realization has not yet attained firm stability;
for if it were so, why would there be a seizing away [of his powers] from one who possesses full competence? Rather, he has been rendered utterly deluded by the Lord through the power of Vāmā.
Therefore, by its very nature, this [initiation] is detrimental to knowledge and the rest. However, if the Guru— who is non-different from Śiva— performs the fivefold ritual action,
then his authority becomes complete.

Therefore, just as the Guru is authorized in the fourfold task— namely, the emission, maintenance, and purification of the pure principles (śuddhatattva), as well as the bestowal of union (yojanā) and grace—
he should perform even this fifth [task] through non-difference from Śiva.
Thus, he who is essentially Śiva performs the activity known as concealment (tirobhāva).
For this very reason, in the Śiva-scripture and in knowledge, one becomes a vessel for confidence;
even one who is a locus of anger due to the guru’s own delusion is not concealed [from grace].

For he with whom the Guru is angry is said to be "withdrawn" (tirohita). He remains a transmigrating being, whereas the Guru is indeed a god; this is not a falsehood. For that very reason, even if one is a reviler of the scriptures and so forth out of anger, [the Guru does not abandon him].
Even though he is not burned by the Guru, he is nevertheless concealed. However, when the disciple has himself become concealed, this is our Guru’s tradition:
the wise one should neither be angry nor cast a curse, for he is always one who bestows grace.
If, impelled by the will of the Lord (Īśa), someone were to press a noose against one's throat,
what role would the teacher play as a collaborator in that act? For even though the Guru is non-different from Śiva, he is [merely] the instrument of the All-pervasive One’s grace.
Worshipping the primary power, he should by all means bestow grace.
Such a teaching as this has been declared in the scripture solely for the sake of making known absolute freedom;
it is not a task [to be undertaken lightly], for one must support those who are falling, rather than allowing them to fall.
Precisely because of the autonomy of his will,
the Guru should compassionately initiate that person after purifying him through penances,
once he has turned his face upward again; for even one who has resorted to the higher vision may subsequently lose his confidence.

Even if one resorts to a lower scripture, one does not become a vessel for the highest good (śreyas). However, one who has resorted to a lower perspective but whose mind lacks conviction in it, may instead partake of the higher teaching; he shall cast off that sin and become Śiva.
For even one who is a constituent part of the king's body is destroyed if he acts treacherously toward him;
the opposite, however, does not lead to such a result—thus one should rely upon the higher vision.
This has been stated by him in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*: "As long as [the disciple] has not been extracted by that very [teacher]..."
For here, this meaning is as follows: this much [is taught], augmented by the knowledge previously mentioned. In this context, the word "he" (sa) refers to the Guru;
[he is] one who possesses such well-practiced higher consciousness and abides in the supreme state.
For one who has not been extracted [by a teacher], there is no higher good than being extracted by another guru;
for this very reason, the analogy of the lotus and the sun has been set forth here.
Indeed, the light of the sun, which illuminates the three worlds, is one thing, and the light of the moon is another.
The knowledge of one who belongs to the three higher lineages is different from that of those who abide in the lower ones.
Therefore, when there is an absence of a Guru who has previously appeared,
one who is intent on liberation should again take refuge in another who possesses the required characteristics.
If, while that [state] exists, one were to clearly abandon it by looking upward,
then there would arise a fault pertaining to one or the other which destroys one's qualification (adhikāra).
And the fault in this case is not defined as a fault insofar as it pertains to the worldly realm.
This [teacher] is considered to be characterized by the proclamation of ignorance and the proclamation of what is improper.
Likewise, for the disciple, the primary defect is a state of lack of confidence in such knowledge; for all other defects arise from that.
Who indeed, when their disease has been destroyed, would hold a physician in high esteem?
It is surely one whose disease is not yet destroyed who, being envious, forcibly pretends to be healthy.
Likewise, what would one who is consoled by such knowledge not do for the Guru?
"If it were not so, he would surely remain distrustful while appearing as if he were trusting.
"These defects, such as ignorance and the like, belong to the teacher [himself] and are not worldly ones";
this was stated in the *Mālinīvijayottara* in order to make this known.
One should not investigate his conduct, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
he alone knows what is appropriate or indeed inappropriate.
When he is addicted to improper acts that deprive one of life or wealth...
Then he should be restrained by the wise one with a humble salutation. Since the specific prohibition against improper acts has already been stated according to the intended meaning,
if he does not desist even while being thus strongly restrained, [the following should be done].
Then, having gone elsewhere, he should contemplate Śiva alone;
for there would be no fault in his being a guru [for that person], just as one might perform agriculture on saline soil.
Or he may go at night, for such a person is a thief of wealth and life.
But one who fears what is unpleasant to him should act toward another in such a way that he does not hear that unpleasantness; this has been stated [in the scriptures].
And it is said in the venerable *Mātaṅga*, but it was not studied out of fear of its vastness.
And that which has been stated thus far as "this much must be done" will certainly manifest of its own accord in the hearts of those seized by the intense power [of Śiva]. However,
this instruction is for those of dull or middling capacity, [to be practiced] gradually according to their own [nature].

It is taught that this is for the purpose of inflaming the *śakti*, for in this way she indeed blazes forth intensely. For one who partakes in the expansive intensity of a beautiful and firm passion, the entire essence of love, shining forth spontaneously, is seen elsewhere for the sake of firmness.
"But why is this example given? What inauspicious act has been committed by this [example]?

The vibration of consciousness (citspanda) is all-pervading; it appears in such and such ways due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Someone who had become concealed may, even while remaining so, once again turn toward [manifestation]."

Even without a teacher, as before, one is liberated by oneself. This method, however, has not been described here, as it proceeds through the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), and because it is inconceivable in this context, like [the effects of] intense anger or favor.

Thus, this procedure which has been proclaimed for the Guru, that Guru should observe; otherwise he would not attain Śiva, as described in the *Śrīmatsāra*. Those who act unjustly completely disregard the meaning of the scripture.
Those gurus who have fallen from their commitments (samaya) go to the city of Ardhanārīśa.
Even elsewhere, they would not attain authority; rather, they would reach the state of a Vidyeśa.
Otherwise, due to the abandonment of their commitments, they become eaters of raw flesh (kravyāda) for a hundred years.
The essential meaning here is this: the teacher of the Siddhānta is Unnaya;
the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) is Piśāca, while the Tantrika is indeed Śuddha. The teacher of the Trika (Ṣaḍardha) resides in the world of Ardhanārīśvara.
This is said to be the destiny of gurus for whom ritual action is primary.
And it is described everywhere that for the possessors of knowledge (jñānins), this [bondage] does not exist. This entire procedure is also taught regarding the initiation of an adept (sādhaka).

In this [rite], there is indeed no formal assignment of authority (*adhikārārpaṇa*), nor is there a vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*); rather, there is the assignment of the mantra to be accomplished within the sequence of rites for one's own use. Furthermore, even when [the rite] is performed in its entirety, there should be the instruction and the assignment of one's own ritual implements.
The procedure for initiation has been described by the Supreme Lord exactly as it was described.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Now, listen to the final sacrament, together with its secret, as proclaimed in the teaching of Śambhu."

For all those situated in lower stations, even down to the gurus, one should clearly perform the initiation of the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā*) following the previously mentioned descent of power (*śaktipāta*). This applies also to those belonging to the higher teachings whose souls have violated their commitments (*samaya*).

The initiation of the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā) must be performed by a Guru who knows the reality of the principles (tattva). For it is taught in the venerable *Dīkṣottara-śāsana* that the initiation of the funeral rite should be performed for one who has stumbled due to negligence regarding the faults of the rules of conduct (samaya-ācāra).
Whatever was previously described in the ritual procedure titled "The Extraction of the Dead" (mṛtoddhāra),
all of that should be performed here upon the corpse in place of the [consecrated] image.
This procedure, as taught in the *Śrīsiddhātantra*, is now set forth.
Having made that which was last first and that which was first last,
and having withdrawn each one individually, that sacrifice which is performed is considered the "final sacrifice" (antyeṣṭi) of two kinds;
it is for one whose observance has been consumed by worship, meditation, and recitation, and not for the practitioner (sādhaka).
O Dear One, one who is liberated through alms-food and so forth may become a sky-walker (*khecara*). When a teacher who is perfected in reality (*tattva*) dies anywhere,
no funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) should be performed for that pure-minded one.
Those who have been killed by means of mantras, yogas, and so forth, go instead to hell;
therefore, a compassionate Guru should perform their funeral rites here.
However, in this rite for those who died by lightning, there should be no mandala or similar ceremonies.
Some have declared that even in the abode of the deceased (the cremation ground),
one should perform that [rite]; having worshipped the All-pervasive Lord, one should perform the entire ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before,
by means of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), starting from the feet and ending at the head.
In that very manner, one should awaken him through ritual action (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
One should obstruct the reality-principle (*tattva*) with the *bindu*, pierce it with the seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*),
stir it in the region of the *nāda*, and strike it with the trident (*triśūla*).

By means of the emission (*visarga*) moving within the *suṣumnā* again and again, one should strike all the *kalās*; then that bound soul (*paśu*) trembles. Or he may raise his left hand; then one should unite him with the Supreme.
"Without the means (pratyaya), liberation is indeed unbelievable to those who are deluded.
For that purpose this has been declared; it is not, however, suitable for liberation itself.
Thus spoke the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Kulagahvara* teaching.
Liberation and so forth are the goal to be accomplished and inferred, since they transcend the senses;
and in the *Dīkṣottara*, the offering of the group of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) is taught here.
Regarding that procedure: on a lotus with leaves of scripture, one should place the god Sadāśiva in the center.

Having worshipped the quartet of Īśa, Rudra, Hari, and Brahmā starting from the eastern direction [and proceeding clockwise], one should offer hearing, touch, taste, smell, the two bodies (form and color),
speech, intellect, ego, and mind to Brahmā and the others in sequence.
Having performed the libation for these with a hundred oblations,
the teacher [performs] this initiation of renunciation (*sāṃnyāsikī dīkṣā*), which purifies the *puryaṣṭaka*.
In the absence of the *puryaṣṭaka*, there are no such things as heaven, hell, and so forth.

Having done so, one must not perform any worldly rite whatsoever. Thus it is stated in the Śrī Mādhavakula: "Even when [the teacher] has passed away, one who stands by the teaching should avoid worldly acts such as the offering of funeral cakes, water libations, and tears."
Having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the worship of the wheel (cakrārcā) according to one's capacity,
on the thirteenth, thirtieth, or thirtieth day of the year in due order. Thus has been described this sacrifice of the funeral rite (antyeṣṭiyāga), spoken by the Supreme Lord.
Now, the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.

Next, the procedure for the *śrāddha* rite as taught in the venerable *Ṣaḍardha* is being declared. It was indicated in the *Siddhātantra* during the exposition of the ritual of the [divine] forms (*mūrtiyāga*).
The ritual procedure for those who are perfectly pure and for those who are impure is performed through the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi).
On the third day, the fourth day, the tenth day, every month, at the first anniversary,
every year, and at all times, that rite should be performed by their own kin as previously described.
There, as before, one should worship the deity and likewise perform oblations in the fire.
Then, having first taken the food offering (naivedya) within the reach of his hand,
the Guru [should offer] the power consisting of food, which is nourishing and of the nature of vital energy (vīrya).
Having meditated thus, the wise one should contemplate that disciple as being entered by her [the goddess].

Then, he should offer that portion of his which is bound (pāśava) and consists of the nature of the object of enjoyment, into the Enjoyer (bhoktṛ) by means of the state of oneness. In this way, the disciple becomes Śiva.

The state of being an object of enjoyment, the other body, and the physical body are considered to be of the nature of bonds (*pāśa*). Their transformation into Śiva occurs through the *śrāddha*, the *mṛtoddhāra*, and the final sacrifice (*antayāga*).
Although the purpose may be accomplished by a single procedure alone, [the others are performed for specific reasons].
Nevertheless, one should perform every rite for the sake of achieving identification with that [deity].
For one who desires enjoyment (bubhukṣu), the abundance of results depends upon the abundance of ritual action and practice;
therefore, one should perform for him the rites of the "extraction from death" (mṛtoddhāra) and the ancestral offerings (śrāddha).

But for one whose darkness has been destroyed by the sun of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), no such thing as the ritual for the last rites, the *śrāddha* offering, and so forth, is ever of any use. However, for those [who have not attained this], their teacher, those belonging to his group, his fellow initiates, and his students— AbhT_25.10a/. For one whose darkness has been destroyed by the sun of the knowledge of reality, there is never any need for this [ritual] of funeral rites, *śrāddha*, injunctions, and so forth. AbhT_25.10b–11a/. But for them—their teacher, those in his group, his fellow initiates, and his students—[there is a need]. AbhT_25.11a/. [For them, however... (text continues)

The day on which there is unity for those who partake in that same continuum shall be a festival day (parva). For when there is an overflow of awakening, then it is a festival because of its fulfillment; therefore, the days of birth and of [spiritual] union are festivals by virtue of the perfection of awakening.
When even a spiritual son (putraka) should be of service to someone,
then one should cause the channels (nāḍīs) located between the left, right, and middle [of the mother, father, and power] to flow, and offer what has been presented to the deity.
And in the illustrious Bharuṇatantra, that has been set forth by Śiva:

"One must observe the requirement of the time for its conveyance in order to achieve that state; or else, one may bring about its accomplishment through one's own autonomy according to the prescribed rule. (AbhT 25.14b–15)

In the *Śrāddha* rite of anyone whatsoever, the satiation of the Guru, the Devas, and the Fire, accompanied by the *Cakra-iṣṭi*, is the scriptural (*śrauta*) practice; it is not the rule of the bound (*pāśava*).
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mukuṭa*: "Even one who stands within the Śiva-śāstra..."
In the Vedic tradition, he understands nothing at all, like a broken bell;
however, by performing the rites beginning with the worship of the deity as described above and ending with the *cakrayāga*,
that living being attains the state of Rudra and enjoys divine pleasures.

Now we shall clearly explain the movement of the channels for the sake of glorious accomplishment: whichever channel one desires to cause to flow, that very channel one should contemplate. When one becomes absorbed in that contemplation, that channel clearly begins to flow.

Alternatively, whichever [channel] one desires to cause to flow, one should press that limb with that hand and bend the abdomen; that channel will flow in an instant. In this way, even through the mouth of a faithful disciple, one establishes the state of both enjoyment and liberation.

"Whatever means the compassionate Śiva has declared in various places that the teacher should employ when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) arises in a living being— by that very means he effects their deliverance, which conduces to their liberation. (AbhT 25.22–23)
For he is the God of gods, the deliverer, and his power is inconceivable.
One should resort to the means merely through the gateway of initiation from a guru and so forth;
this was stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* immediately following the question of the sage.

"If liberation comes from the discernment of the principles (*tattva*), from initiation, or from yoga, how could it come from mere conduct (*caryā*) alone? To this, the Lord replied with an equal answer:
"Why do you have this delusion regarding the Supreme Lord? (AbhT 25.25–26).
Indeed, let it be seen that his capacity for universal grace is fully established.
For one whose death has arrived, poison, disease, weapons, and the like are indeed the causes;
likewise, whether small or great, meditative recollection (*anudhyā*) is the cause of liberation.
"However, these external signs are employed for the sake of liberation;
having understood this, a wise person should not entertain doubt in this manner.
'How can liberation come by this much alone?'—thinking thus, one should take refuge in supreme devotion. (AbhT 25.28–29)
The ritual for the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*), which crushes the terror caused by the poison of delusion, has been explained.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Next, the remaining mode of conduct useful for those who live is being described.
This initiation, which has been proclaimed to extend up to the *śrāddha* rite, is of many kinds;
it is for the sake of purification, liberation, enjoyment, or both.
Among these, that initiation which is for the accomplishment of purification does not directly effect liberation.
And that which, by virtue of its connection [to the disciple], directly liberates and possesses seeds—
those who have been initiated by both of these [methods],
for them the way of life must be told, beginning with the "spiritual sons" (putraka), in order to achieve identification with That (Tanmayatva).

Whether for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) has indeed been performed by the Guru— based on his own consciousness, the Guru, and the scriptures— for the sake of purifying the means of valid cognition and the rest. Then, having recognized himself as purified and fit within his own teaching, [he proceeds].
One should practice the performance of those things taught for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation. Furthermore,
even for one who possesses enjoyment and liberation solely through faith in the Teacher,
one should explain the proper conduct to him as well, in order to destroy the arising of obstacles to that [faith].

Even one who possesses an identical realization regarding both his own self-awareness and the awareness of the Guru should be instructed through the "remaining mode of conduct" (śeṣavṛtti) for the sake of pacifying obstacles and other such hindrances.
But he who remains established in his own [nature], having entirely abandoned dependence on others—
Even those who [attain realization] through a sign (pratyaya) do so solely from the sign of the Guru.
Who could say that these two—the one with innate realization (sāṃsiddhika) and the one without seed (nirbīja)—are intent on the remaining practice?
Yet, they both remain devoted to the means of becoming absorbed in That (tanmayatā) and to the worship of the Guru, respectively.
In that regard, for the sake of their remaining livelihood, there are the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties which are constant;

these must be performed excluding those for specific desires (*kāmya*), since desires are manifold and require diverse means. Among these, the obligatory rule consists of the performance of the twilight rites (*sandhyā*) toward the assembly of deities.

Worship performed in the presence of the Guru, the fire, and the scriptures, as well as compassion for all beings— this constitutes the occasional (naimittika) rite. Furthermore, for all [occasions], there is worship and recitation on festival days (parvan),
and, by virtue of specific requirements, the sequence of the Pavitraka ritual.
This initiation of the teacher has been analyzed in its many varieties;
furthermore, the exposition and so forth constitute his specific, constant occasional duty.
In that regard, at the outset, the Guru should clearly explain the daily ritual to the disciple.

Having observed the fitness of those whose natures are either expanded or unexpanded, and having seen the disciple’s suitability for the potency, pervasiveness, and other qualities of the primary and secondary mantras, one should bestow that very root-mantra upon him.
For one who has been initiated into that scripture is apprehensive regarding conduct that is unrestrained;
thus, such a person is not fit for the primary [practice], but fitness arises from the service of another.
This applies to the seeker (sādhaka) who desires enjoyment (bubhukṣu), as well as to one who is becoming a practitioner (sādhakībhāvin).

Once the mantra has been mastered by virtue of the falling of the flower, it should be imparted for the sake of accomplishing what is to be achieved. Alternatively, when a rite has been prescribed— whether extensive or consisting of secondary elements— the Guru, having ascertained the disciple's fitness, should perform the essential, concise procedure for him.

In this regard, there is this rule: whatever is the form of the mantra, that the Guru should not write out and reveal to the disciple—especially in the case of the Upper Teaching (ūrdhvaśāsana). Mantras consist of phonemes, and those phonemes consist of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), which is itself [the essence].

If [the mantra] is non-different from the consciousness of the Guru, then it may be transmitted to the disciple from him. However, a mantra that remains merely as written letters is considered here to be devoid of potency;
its majesty does not manifest from a book through the power of mere convention.
"Therefore, it is stated in the *Siddhāmata* that [there are those] who have learned the vidyās from books;

however, those who recognize the potency (*vīrya*) even in a mantra obtained from a book are said to be purified by Bhairava and are called *sāṃsiddhika*s (those perfected by their own nature). (AbhT 26.23–24a)
Having understood this correctly, the Guru, reeling with supreme bliss,
should perform the ritual after worshipping in such and such a sacred abode,
so that the practice of one disciple is not perceived by another disciple.
The Guru should act accordingly, since a lapse in secrecy is fraught with fault.
He may speak of a pure triad of goddesses, or according to the principle of union (*yāmala*),
he may speak of a single pure goddess, or one whose nature is that of a couple.

There, having attentively grasped the mantra clearly uttered by the Guru from his mouth, either aloud or in a whisper, one should practice it mentally oneself until proficiency is attained. Then, one should master the threefold purification of the locations, the body, and the interior.
One should diligently perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), recitation (japa), mudrās, and worship.
Having awakened there at dawn, one should first remember one's own chosen deity.
Then, having performed the necessary duties and becoming pure, one should go to the house.

Facing the northern direction, having performed the purification of the mantras within the triad of the site, the body, and the internal [self], one should effect their placement in their respective locations,
followed by the display of mudrās and meditation according to their differentiated and non-differentiated natures.
One should perform worship there with the mind in the body, the vital breath, the intellect, the void, and the earth;
likewise, one should perform recitation here according to one's capacity and offer this to the God at every junction of the day for the sake of attaining the state of identity with Him. (32–33a)

Others, however, say that there is a fourfold set of *sandhyās* in the east, north, west, and [south], in the ten directions; but this is the Tantric view, not our own. As for that fourfold *sandhyā* previously mentioned in the section on Time (*kālādhikāra*), [it refers to that].
Having fixed that very [consciousness] within, one should perform the ritual of the twilight (sandhyā);
or else, the initiate may perform the duties of the four twilights at a single time, being intent upon his private study, spiritual knowledge, service to the guru, and so forth. (35–36a)
Through the practice of becoming one with that infinite [reality] arising from meditation on the junctions (sandhyā),
he indeed becomes absorbed in that at all times by virtue of its latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Therefore, at whatever time he desires, he should perform worship with flowers, wine, and other offerings.
On a sacrificial mound or similar site,
the initiate, being thoroughly purified, should perform the entire ritual according to his means, up to the conclusion of the internal recitation (antarjapa).
Having first prepared the vessel for the offering (arghapātra) with his own chosen mantra, as previously described, [he should proceed].

With that [mantra], the wise one should sprinkle everything— the sacrificial ground, the flowers, and so forth. Then, having mentally resolved (saṃkalpya) right there upon the sequence of the door, the seat, and the lineage of gurus, one who is permeated by the state of Śiva should perform worship, preceded by the worship of his own body.
Then, having perceived that sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) to be as pure as the clear sky or crystal,
consisting of the nature of awakening, one should behold one's own host of deities there as a reflection, and through that awakening,
as the original object (bimba).
This is the primary method of invocation, like the wind [invoked] by means of a fan. Just as the wind, though omnipresent, becomes effective when stimulated by a fan,
so too the omnipresent wheel of mantras becomes effective through such established practice.
This very reality is stated by means of the *Catuṣkapañcāśikā*, and it was also proclaimed by the All-pervasive Lord in the *Śrīnirmaryādaśāstra*:
"O God, how can Śiva, who is all-pervading, be without limits? (44)
When asked, "Is [the deity] invoked or is he dismissed?", the All-pervasive Lord replied:

"O Goddess, it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that is invoked, and the latent impression that is dismissed. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), for the God, there is neither invocation nor dismissal."
"The deity has been invoked by me and established upon the sacrificial ground;
having worshipped and praised him thus, and being delighted, one should dismiss the deity—for the sake of generating satisfaction in living beings who are not yet awakened. (47–48a)
How else could their activity, beginning with invocation and so forth, proceed?
By means of time, however, those engaged in the teaching of the Lord come to understand the attainment of the God, preceded by the [attainment of] the worlds, in due order. (AbhT 26.48b–49)
For those whose entire accumulation of ignorance has been destroyed by the radiance of the lamp of knowledge,
from where could that God be brought, or to where could He be led?
For He abides everywhere, through the distinctions of gross, subtle, and so forth.
When the assembly of mantras has been invoked, one should perform a libation with offerings of flowers,
drinks, and incense, as befits the strength of one's faith and devotion;
for the radiant mantras beginning with Śakti and Nāda, this is done with spirits and meat.
First with red [substances] for the libation (tarpaṇa), and afterwards with an abundance of flowers, incense, and so forth;
if one does not perform the libation for the mantra that has arrived,
it is said by Śambhu that it will take away half of one's body.
Whatever indeed brings expansion to his mind,
with that very thing he should perform worship— this is the firm resolve of Śambhu.
For practitioners who desire worldly enjoyment, the rule is constrained by necessity.
For those seeking liberation who know reality, that very [state] is indeed unimpeded; however,
one who desires to produce a specific effect must employ a specific cause,
just as one desiring red cotton-wool requires a corresponding heap of seeds.
There exist various and diverse distinctions in enjoyments, impelled by their causes (57).
Through the conjunction of place and time, and by means of qualities, substances, actions, and so forth—
whether the action be slight or extensive— it bestows delight upon the heart (58).

Whether constructed by external factors or by those born of mental conception, such distinctions do not serve the seeker of liberation regarding the path to the supreme good. Indeed, they do not proclaim variations of magnitude or deficiency within Brahman.
Because the accumulated [consciousness] has autonomy as its essence and consists of a mass of bliss,
there should be an action that brings about identification with it through those things that bestow joy to the heart;
for from the weight of non-difference from Śiva, the entire range of objective phenomena distills that [supreme] rasa.
The wise one should offer that very [consciousness] for worship within the supreme abode;
this has been declared by me in various ways in the hymns and in my own daily ritual manual (nijāhnika).
Resting upon it, the radiance of the unfolding of ultimate reality shines forth.
Those who know the secret worship you with that vision which perceives the supreme nectar.

Having washed the ground of the support (the *ādhāra*) with the sprinkling of the essence of wonder, I worship you day and night within the temple of the body along with the Goddess, using the flowers of my own nature gathered from the mind— flowers rich with their own fragrance— and by means of the priceless vessel of libation (*arghapātra*), my own heart, which is overflowing with the nectar of bliss.

Having squeezed this triple world—possessing various tastes and flavors—placed upon the machine of the heart-center, [I extract] that which flows forth from the weight of the discernment established above and below;
that supreme nectar of consciousness which expands, removing death, old age, and birth—with that supreme oblation, I satiate you, O Supreme One, day and night.
(65) Thus, contemplating within himself the meaning conveyed by these three verses, [he should proceed].
One should satisfy the host of deities by whatever means possible.
Afterwards, one should display the mudrās, either mentally through yoga,
or verbally through the application of mantra, or physically through bodily posture.
Having performed the entire recitation, one should then offer it all to the deity;
this was previously stated in the rule for determining the reality of the agent.
Thereafter, the dismissal (visarjana) should be performed through the practice of identity with pure consciousness.
Or, having performed the satisfaction of the mantra by means of the fire according to the prescribed rule, one should eat the remaining *naivedya*—
which has been offered to the door-deities, the pedestal-deities, and the assembly of gurus—
or else throw it into deep water.
Aquatic creatures were previously initiated by Śambhu himself, according to the glorious Mīnanātha who descended [in that form] through the future ritual procedure;
yet they were devoured by cats, mice, and others who had not been initiated. (71–72)
By causing the torment of doubt regarding that [reality], one brings about disease and rebirth in hell.
Therefore, even a wise knower of reality who has destroyed the torment of doubt should not manifest such [doubt] openly, out of a desire to favor the world.
In the illustrious *Matamahāśāstra*, the All-pervasive Lord himself has stated this:
he should personally be intent on extracting the contraction caused by doubt in such a way that no doubt arises in the minds of others. (74–75ab)

Having wiped [the altar], one should then perform the ritual bath and worship with a flower. One should cast all that [offering], including the flowers and so forth, which remained upon it, into deep water. This sacrifice on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) has been taught by Śambhu for the daily rites.
Now, the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Next, the worship of the *liṅga*, as indicated in the *Mālinīmata*, is described.
For these mantras taught in the higher scriptures, there is no [need for] formal installation (*pratiṣṭhita*).
Therefore, one should exclude these [others], for it is through their secrecy that they bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*).

For those who grant accomplishment by virtue of possessing mastery over the entry into the majesty of the bliss of one's own vital energy (*vīrya*), to treat them as external is a falling away from their true nature.
Furthermore, it has been said: Śiva, when filled with immersion (*samāveśa*), consists of the nature of the enjoyer;
when there is a cessation of enjoyment, he partakes in a craving for enjoyment and consists of restraint (*nigraha*).
His form is intensified by a hunger that arises from the suppression of his state of tranquility (*śāntatva*).
He by whom [the deity] is self-installed perishes when there is no enjoyment [of the ritual].
And this very point was stated by the Supreme Lord in the *Jñānottara*:
"Since Śiva is fond of sacrifice, he especially [delights] when situated in the midst of the Mothers."
Therefore, a wise person should never install outside those mantras which exist in the secret scriptures, especially those that have manifest forms.
For this very reason, the installation for the sake of the deceased that is prescribed elsewhere [is not to be performed there].
In these scriptures, that [practice] should not be performed; rather, the common one should be performed.

Until the perfection of identification with That (tanmayatva) and until the arising of the desired fruit, the spiritual son (putraka) or the adept (sādhaka) should resort to either the manifest or the unmanifest.
The preceptor should be requested by the sons [of the lineage], but the practitioner, knowing for himself, may install it himself;
if he does not, then he too must request the preceptor.
And here, at the time known as *nirodha*, the preceptor should speak thus to the All-pervasive Lord:
"Remain here until this [liṅga] bears fruit, or remain for the duration of its life.
And the liṅga may be made of stone, or of precious gems, or of pearl;
it may be made of flowers, food, cloth, or of fragrant substances.
One should not fashion a linga made of stone produced by an artisan;
one should avoid any [linga] made of metal other than that produced from gold.
Furthermore, in this case, the measurement of the linga and so forth is of no use whatsoever.
Whatever is spoken by mantras of noble power is indeed fruit-bearing.

For that [mantra] as well, one should perform purification according to the prescribed rule for the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth. The entrustment of the mantra should likewise take place, while its cessation occurs according to the stated method.
There should be abundant libations into the fire and a special sacrificial fee for the Guru;
the satisfaction of the poor and others according to one's means constitutes the sacrifice—this is the additional rule.
In all cases where the signs are unmanifest, the primary principle should be that which is non-conceptualized.
And so it has been stated in various places in the *Pārameśvara-lakṣaṇa*:

"In the case of a thread, a vessel, a banner, a cloth, or one consecrated by the self-manifested Bāṇa, as well as that which arises from a river or a spring, there is neither invocation nor ritual construction. (27.17–18)
There is no restriction regarding the pedestal, the temple, the mantras, the time, and so forth;
nor is it necessary that the image be clearly fashioned from variegated materials, cloth, or the like, or made of deodar wood or gold.
Alternatively, the Guru installs an image crafted by a consecrated and skilled artisan.
Alternatively, one should take recourse in a skull that possesses the [proper] characteristics, resting upon its cranium;
one should rely on it according to the procedure for the row, the wheel, the trident, and the lotus.
I shall describe those characteristics as they are set forth in the venerable Picuśāstra.
Yoga performed on a *tūra* that is free from defects is always praised as bestowing accomplishment;
however, if the *tūra* is joined with networks, worn-out holes, or teeth that are deficient or excessive, there will be ruin. When free from these, the sacrifice is supreme.

"Some maintain that the *tūra* [drum] should be used only for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). However, the teachers explain that while one should diligently avoid faults in the case of a rite for desire, this statement from the *Picu* does not apply to obligatory daily rites (*nitya-karman*)."
And in the *Śrīsiddhātantra*, the supreme characteristics of the *tūra* are stated:
[it may have] one to four sections, be shaped like a cow’s face (*gomukha*), or resemble a full moon;
it should be like a lotus, yellow orpiment, pearl, water, or crystal.
In an auspicious [diagram] endowed with one to five lines of vidyā-threads and provided with six openings,
which is free from being rough, crooked, fragmented, long, depressed,
or marked by dots; there, with a smooth vajra-needle, one should clearly [draw] the assembly of goddesses.
One should draw everything that is worthy of worship, beautiful in all its limbs;
this very same characteristic should also be followed for the argha-vessel.
It is also stated in the venerable Brahmayāmala that the best vessel is the "cow-mouthed" (gomukha) one.
The surface of the rosary should have the shape of an elephant’s back or a tortoise’s shell, or the form of a water-pot, a circle, a spear, or a lotus stalk.
One should then fashion a rosary from these, and thereupon worship the sequence [of deities] within it.
It may be made of heroic minerals, water-born substances, pearls, gems, or gold.
One should prepare a rosary of beads that is progressively superior, especially one made of rudrākṣa seeds;
it should consist of one hundred and fifteen, or one hundred and eight, or half of that,
or half of that again, or fifty.
The five faces [of Śiva] arise from the conjunction of consciousness, vibration, knowledge, will, and action.
(32) The rule regarding the penultimate letter is that there is a fivefold unity extending from the beginning to the end;
therein, a twofold nature is declared through the distinction between the power (*śakti*) and its possessor (*śaktimān*). (33)
Then, on a surface of double that measure, one should perform the twofold deposition (*nyāsa*).
On a surface twice as large again, one should deposit either the *Mātṛkā* or the *Mālinī* by means of the two sequences of emanation and withdrawal, on a space measuring fifty [units].
In the highest [initiation], however, the teacher should first deposit the previously mentioned [deities] and then deposit the two [groups].
Primarily, during the initiation, the instructor should [deposit] those fifteen mantras;
or alternatively, [he may do so] by means of [the mantras] arising from the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), limited powers (kalā), mantras, words (pada), and phonemes (arṇa).
When the thread has been prepared according to the various numerical divisions, the Guru should perform the respective ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon it.
Having fashioned a rosary from that [thread], everything for it should be performed just as for the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).
And with that very [rosary] once it has been worshipped, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) without sloth.
This procedure has been taught by you in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:

whatever one speaks while causing this [mantra] to revolve like a wheel becomes *japa*; and whatever one beholds or offers as an oblation, that occurs through its entry into the fire of consciousness.
Alternatively, one should prepare a great vessel for the *argha* offering; that is the supreme and most excellent.
It may be made of coconut, or of bilva wood, or of gold, or even of silver.
For this as well, the entire procedure proclaimed for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites applies.
Having filled it with the essence of that unwavering [state], one should perform the sequence of worship within it.
Once worshipped, it should always be kept face-down;
however, during the act of worship, that vessel should be turned face-up and made empty, not remaining as it was before.
At the conclusion of the worship, having filled himself with that [liquid] essence and having worshipped it while turned face-down, the wise practitioner should place there a sword,
a small dagger, a knife, or a mirror.
One should perform that pure rite as proclaimed from the mouth of the glorious Kālī.
It is also stated in the Śrī Bhairavakula regarding worship on the Kula festival days:
[one may worship] on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in fire, on a cloth (paṭa), in a linga, in a vessel, in a lotus, or in a mandala.
One should worship [the deity] in an image, a jar, a collection of weapons, a balance, or a thread, using their respective ritual offerings; one must avoid any confusion between them.
Just as mantras are used in water for the purpose of pacification, so too they are certainly used in the case of weapons and the other supports.

Therefore, for one who desires [specific results], he brings about the destruction of enemies and so forth; thus, he must be free from the confusion of mixed intentions. But for one who is without desire, those [mantras] certainly bring about the severing of bonds, the purification of the principles (tattvas), and their nourishment, by virtue of the specific adjuncts of their respective locations.
Alternatively, for a book that is similarly composed according to the sequence of the scriptures on the planets,

which is perfectly pure and prepared by one who has been initiated— the same procedure is prescribed there as well. In this manner, [this applies] to those [images] established by themselves, for as long as their stability lasts.
Satisfaction through one's wealth is purification, provided that there is no interruption [of the practice].
(50) Therefore, when the construction of the mandala lasts for many days, one should perform abundant satisfaction with one's wealth day after day. (51)

And in every case of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the Guru, having contemplated the supreme reality as previously described along with its essential nature (*satattva*), should clearly effect its presence (*saṃnidhi*). Once the fruit of becoming one with that [reality] has been accomplished by the *putraka* initiates and the practitioners (*sādhakas*), [the rite is complete].

That [initiation] is handed over to one of the other two [categories]. This entire procedure applies to him as well; however, if neither of those is available, it should in every way be cast into deep water after having been propitiated and released.
Thus, this procedure for self-installation has been described by Śiva.
In the case of a *liṅga* installed by another, one made of stone (*bāṇīya*), or one that is self-manifested (*svayaṃbhū*),
one should first perform the sequential placement (*nyāsa*) upon the entire seat and then perform the worship.
All mantras belonging to the paths of the pure and the impure culminate in Śiva.
This path is said to reside within the seat; therefore, one should worship it everywhere. As for the invocation and dismissal, one should perform them there as previously described.
This has been stated likewise by the All-pervasive Lord in the *Svacchanda-tantra* of Aghoreśa:
"Alternatively, having performed the desired mandala, one should worship the entire sequence there according to the application of half of half the prescribed measure for each day. (58–59a)

The worship of the *liṅga*, which is divided into many varieties, has been described. [Abhinavagupta’s *Tantrāloka*, Chapter 28] Thus, the daily ritual (*nityavidhi*) has been proclaimed; now the occasional ritual (*naimittika*) is being told.
When this principle is established— that whatever is necessarily destined to occur is "eternal"—

then becoming one with that [destiny] constitutes its primary state, and everything else is merely occasional (*naimittika*). However, when necessity arises from the conceptualization of days and so forth, then everything is considered eternal.

Because it is determined by days, months, lunar mansions, years, and so forth, it is then described as follows: the wise call this "occasional" (naimittika), which occurs at some specific time, whose existence is necessarily certain and beyond doubt, yet which is not restricted to any particular subject.
The worship at the junctions (sandhyā) and other festival days (parvan), as well as this Pavitraka rite, is always performed;
because it is of a constant and fixed nature, it applies to everyone who has taken refuge in the teaching.
Likewise, there is the attainment of knowledge, the scriptures, the guru, brothers, and their respective groups.
The distinctions regarding the sacraments of that birth, the gathering for the festival of one's own birth,

the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the averting of calamities, joy, the sight of wonders, the assembly of Yoginīs, and the meeting with one’s own spiritual descendants and so forth— these are the occasions.
The beginning, middle, and end of the commentary on the scripture, the arising of the sequence (kramodaya),
the vision of the deity, dreams, the command (ājñā), and the atonement for transgressions of the observance (samaya)—
thus has the occasional (naimittika) ritual been described in the illustrious Tantrasāra.
The basis for specific worship consists of twenty-three varieties.
Regarding that, we shall explain the rule for the festival (parvan); the festival is twofold: *kula* and *akula*.
The former, performed by means of the eight *kulas*, was previously taught in the *Śrīyogasañcara*.
"Ocean, moon, sage"—this is for the lineage of Brahmā associated with Māheśī;
for Kaumārī, it is the first and fifteenth lunar days joined with the [tastes] and fires (63);
for Vaiṣṇavī, it is ocean, eyes, and moon (122); and for Aindrī, it is the weapon (astra) and the thirteenth day (13).
For Vārāhī, there are two [days] corresponding to the nine openings (randhra) and Rudra (eleven); for Caṇḍī, the eight, the eyes (two), and the pair (two).
For all [the others], there are two lunar days (tithis) each; however, for Yogeśī, it is the tenth.
Furthermore, because the eighth day belongs to her as well, she is proclaimed to have two lunar days.
Other [days] are also characterized as non-family parvas (akulaparva) by way of their reversal; we call those family parvas (kulaparva), as it is taught in the Bhairava-kula,
in the Haiḍara, the Trikasadbhāva, the Trikakālīkula, and so forth.
That time which was previously explained in great detail as being based on the vital breath (prāṇa),
when it moves through the piercing of the cakras, generates a certain self-awareness (svasaṃvid). The moment of attaining the fullness of that self-awareness is called a *parvan*.

The word *parvan* is derived from the root *pṛ*, which signifies "filling" (*pūraṇa*). Thus, through etymological analysis (*nirukta*), *parvan* is so called because it "fills. Furthermore, in this context of the *haiḍara* [Tantra], this word is heard in two forms: one ending in *-n* and the other otherwise.
Those who are skilled in the movement of that wheel and possess complete consciousness,
being joined with that *melaka*, are always intent upon its worship.
Even one who is not yet identical with it, by worshipping according to his own sequence at that time, [attains the same].
Through the gathering of the assembly of those yoginīs and siddhas, one becomes identical with them;
just as in a theatrical performance, by entering into that [assembly], one immediately attains the non-differentiation of consciousness with each respective spectator as it unfolds in succession.
Through the immediate entry into the unity of this consciousness, they obtain their own full self-awareness, which has been acquired through the sequence of yogic practice;
and at that very moment, because of the fullness of consciousness, it becomes a cow of plenty that milks all desires.
Therefore, by worshipping [the deity] there at that time, one quickly obtains those respective fruits,
just as one who possesses long-accumulated wealth joyfully performs a festival and favors a guest who has arrived with knowledge of that specific occasion. (23–24a)

Likewise, for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of excellent fruits, the leaders of the Yoginīs and Siddhas, though they themselves exert effort, bestow their grace upon that one who knows the [proper] time. And it has been stated there by him that this is common to all in this Kula; enough [of further elaboration].

O Goddess, whatever mantra, yoga, or *krama* exists within one's heart by the command of the Guru, that shall grant success through worship. O Mistress of the Gods, one should worship according to the *Kulācāra* for the sake of both spiritual power (*siddhi*) and liberation.
O Goddess of the gods, those who, out of negligence, do not perform the special libations (tarpaṇa) on the festival days for their gurus and deities—
those wicked ones of evil conduct, O fair-faced one, are equal to beasts.
Because of the absence of regular daily worship, one must certainly perform worship during these [occasions].
That which is proclaimed as "wandering" (aṭana) is for the sake of attaining the power of knowledge and other such qualities;
and that which is called the "sacrifice to Śakti" (śaktiyāga) involves subjugation, attraction, and killing.
All that is accomplished without effort on the days of the festival (parva).
That festival is defined as sixfold, by way of both general and specific types.
The first and the fifth day of the month are designated as the "Auspicious Day" (śrīdina).

Because of its excellence, the day of the festival (parvadina) is spoken of as being preceded by the word "Śrī. For this is the convention: that which is secret should not be stated without its prefix.
[The worlds] of the fourth, eighth, and the final one belong to both [the upward and downward sequences].

In this context, the commonality between the two fortnights is proclaimed as the *parvan*. On these very days, there occurs that which consists of the nature of the future planets; it is a dual-natured particularity, and that constitutes the state of being both general and particular.
And that [power], though one, is declared by the All-pervasive Lord to be elevenfold in each [of the five breaths].
Śambhu has thus delineated it as being of the same kind yet superior.
The positions are: black-and-black, fire-and-white, Veda-and-black, and fire-and-white.

The Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Moon; Mercury, Jupiter, and Moon; the Sun, Venus, Jupiter, and Moon—these are the lords [of the months]. The constellations are Parva-phalgunī, Caitra, Maghā, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Pūrva-phalgunī, Śravaṇa, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, Rohiṇī, Viśākhā, and the one known as Śravaṇa.
In the eighth, the fifteenth, and the twelfth; in the eighth, the first, the sixth, and the ninth;
in the first night and the middle of the night; at midday and the five [hours];
at sunrise and midday—these are the times for the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, starting from the first night.
A maiden, an outcaste, or a courtesan who is full of passion and a knower of reality serves as the messenger (dūtī).
These are to be worshipped, respectively, both in detail and in brief, in the wheel known as the *anuyāga*.
Furthermore, on every festival day (parva), one should perform the *anuyāga* wheel with particular excellence.
The secondary sacrifice (*anuyāga*) is indeed complete through the sequence of the ritual conduct of yoga, including both secret and non-secret procedures;
it is said to be primary in every application of ritual action. Therefore, one who is intent on that supreme goal should strive to obtain the proper time for the secondary sacrifice.
There is no specific conjunction of asterisms and planets in the month of Āśvayuja; therefore, that month is excluded.

The calculation of time, asterisms, and planets has been taught for the eleven months. As for the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna, it is declared to be a sacred festival (parvan).
The conjunction of piercing at the first lunar day is the most primary distinction here;

for this purpose, one should divide both day and night into three parts, consisting of the first, middle, and latter divisions. Among these three divisions, the time for worship is the most primary period.

If the time, the most eminent [deity], the planets, and likewise the *cakra* should coincide, that sacrifice is the primordial sacrifice (*ādiyāga*). Through worship alone on such festival days (*parvan*), one's desired goal shall be accomplished.
Therein, even by means of the calculation of the day, the time, the planets, and the *kalās*, there exists both the gentle (*saumya*) and the fierce (*raudra*) nature.

Having understood this, the preeminent practitioner should perform each respective rite at its proper time. Some maintain that if the lunar mansion, planet, or lunar day occurs after the stated time for worship has been exceeded, one should disregard that specific [astral] factor and prioritize the conventional (sāmaya) time.
"No," say our teachers, "for here it is the lunar day (*tithi*) in its specific form that is the factor, not the time of day.

The portion of the moon, which is the object of perception, is filled to whatever extent by the mass of rays from the sun, which is the perceiver; that lunar day becomes manifest through the planets and constellations.

Therefore, in this context, the lunar day (tithi) is primary, and it is to be distinguished by its conjunction with planets and asterisms. Time (velā) is not the principal factor here; this is appropriate, for thus the Supreme Lord has declared in the venerable Trika, Bhairava, and Kula scriptures regarding the days of festival (parva): [50]
Indeed, there is a certain conjunction of time (*velā-yoga*) distinct from the conjunctions of lunar days, asterisms, and planets.
(51) The lunar day (*tithi*), however, is to be honored because it is the primary form. They indeed prescribe the sacrifice of a black goat in the absence of a white one. (52)
Furthermore, although the time [of practice] is mentioned in scriptures such as the *Ūrmi*, it is intended for those desiring specific results (*kāmya*);
for the primary injunction refers to that [time], namely the day of the full moon in the month of Pauṣa.
Having performed worship at midnight and having meditated and recited [mantras], just as for one who has gone outside...
Likewise, a command bears fruit in Māgha, and from the wheel, speech bears fruit.
(54) In the five [months], there is the swift attainment of one's desired goal, friendship, wealth, and meeting.
In the place of the wheel, through wrath and the shattering of stones, there is the destruction of the enemy. (55)
The attainment of the prophetic instructions of the Siddhas up to the end of the path is described by the Lord.
In the absence of the conjunction of lunar mansions and planets, one must certainly observe the time of the lunar day (*tithi*);
for that [time], being of such a clear form, will grant the natural arising of the *tithi*.
If a day be obtained that is auspicious in its asterism, planet, lunar day, time, and degree, and beautiful in all its parts,

then one should perform a most special worship on it. For this is not merely for the sake of attaining specific desires, since it has been taught that [the rite] must be performed even when these [desirable factors] are absent.
In the venerable Bhairavakula and in the Ūrmiśāstra, it is stated that there is a violation of the observance (*samayavilopa*) for those who are wicked,
of evil conduct, like bound souls (*paśu*), and who do not know the sacred festivals (*parvan*).
Furthermore, there can never be any transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the non-performance of an optional rite (*kāmya*).
Therein, for the sake of accomplishing the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga), the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga) is described.
That which is called the "form-sacrifice" (mūrtiyāga) in the venerable Yogīśvarīmata— the daily and occasional rites taught here by the Great Lord— [is now explained].

In all cases, the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga) is primary here, especially in rites for specific desires. Whether he be a man or a woman, a man of knowledge or a yogi, one should diligently engage them in this yoga known as the "Form" (mūrti); for such a person is the unsurpassed vessel.
"Through contact with that [offering], fullness arises"—thus it is stated in the *Traiśirasa* and other scriptures.
Therefore, whoever gives or performs [an act] for a man of knowledge (*jñānin*) or a yogi has offered everything desired, including the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving. (63–64)
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Dīkṣottara*: "Food is Brahmā, its essence is Hari, and the eater is Śiva. Thus, the man of knowledge may uplift even outcastes;
for if that practitioner eats while becoming composed of all the *tattvas*, [he attains liberation].
By feeding him alone, it is as if ten million have been fed at once.
Now, O Dear One, if one who knows reality should eat from this [offering], there would be no limit to the number; so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.

"All that is to be enjoyed is of the nature of *māyā*, and Śiva—and he is also I—is the enjoyer. He who truly knows this is a teacher who has reached the further shore of reality (*tattva*). Seeing him approaching like a god, the medicinal herbs play within his house.

"Today we have indeed turned back from the dense ocean of saṃsāra; since we have reached his mouth, we shall go to the supreme state. For others subsist on the downward breath (apāna), whereas the upward breath (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna) here are directed downwards. (AbhT 28.69b–70b)
O Goddess of the gods, when that [deity] is the enjoyer, even hundreds of lineages of the giver are swiftly liberated from the ocean of torments such as hell.
This is also stated in the venerable Niśāṭana: "Even from the mere seeking of the teaching..."
When [the mantra] has issued from the mouth of the Guru and reached within the ears, at that very moment one is liberated; the machine remains alone.
Even a drinker of liquor, a thief, a killer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the Guru’s bed [is freed].
Whether he be an outcaste or a twice-born, a child, an old man, or even a youth—
any wise man who dwells on the borders of the land is a purifier of that very region. There, the Lord is present together with his Goddess and his attendants.
Therefore, having made the Guru— who is proficient in knowledge— the primary focus,
one should perform the Mūrtiyāga for him according to the ritual prescribed in the Yogīśvarīmata,
especially during the Pavitrārohaṇa, at Śrāddha ceremonies, and on festival days.
During solar and lunar eclipses and other such worldly festival days,
at celebrations such as weddings, during the sacrificial rites of Brahmins,
during initiation (dīkṣā), during consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and for the purification of the rules (samaya).
And for the sake of fulfilling desires, the image-sacrifice (mūrtiyāga) should be performed; it is fivefold:
the solitary, the paired, the mixed, the wheel-joined, and the hero-conjunction.
The solitary is performed with teachers alone, while the mixed is combined with others.
That [sacrifice] is again twofold, being either with a consort for the practitioner and others,
or else through union with a wife, or through association with a courtesan purchased for the purpose. Furthermore,
the Cakriṇīs and other [powers] appropriate for union with Śaktis will be described.
Through union with that, the sacrifice joined with the *cakra* bestows all fruits.
A sacrifice performed together with all [the initiates] is called a "heroic gathering" (*vīrasaṅkara*).
The Guru should be in their midst, and the group of Gurus forms its enclosure.
There are three outer layers ending with the *samayin*s in their respective order;
or else, all of them may be arranged in rows. Among them, the Guru is always in the center.
Then, with that [substance], incense, garlands, ointments, and garments—
One should worship each respective wheel according to its sequence, thinking, "This is that very wheel.

(84) Just as one should contemplate the ritual of the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*) in a wheel with a single spoke, one should contemplate the Couple (*yāmala*) in a two-spoked wheel, and likewise the Triad (*trika*) in a six-spoked wheel. (85)

In that wheel which possesses such a nature, one may worship six Yoginīs, or seven, or seven in each of the eight [spokes], or eight in each of the eight, or some other similar arrangement. Then, when the vessel is filled with wine, the wise practitioner should first worship the wheel.
The libation must always be joined with a support; never is there a libation devoid of a support.

Without a support, there is a fall [of the offering], and the rays [of consciousness] are not satisfied. The vessel takes the form of a *preta*, while the nectar of power (*śāktāmṛta*) is the liquor (*āsava*).
The power that is the enjoyer therein is Śambhu, the Supreme Lord;
having thus meditated upon the triad as merged— the individual soul (aṇu), power (śakti), and the self of Śiva—
one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for each successive enclosure in order.

By means of the process of re-absorption (*pratisaṃcara*), one should cause [the breath] to enter back inside again. That which reaches as far as the presence of the Guru is called a "complete rotation" (*pūrṇabhramaṇa*).
In that regard, the sequence is as follows: first the deities are to be gratified, and then the heroes (*vīra*).
"The Vīra and the Vīra-Śakti—such is the lineage of our gurus.
Then, the best of practitioners should scatter various appetizers, including meat, fish, and so forth, before them there until they are satisfied. (AbhT 28.92–93a)
Furthermore, in the absence of a vessel, the wise one should employ the *bhadra* and the *vellitāśukti*;
this is the sequence according to the *Siddhāmata*.
With the right hand, it should be the *bhadra*, while the *vellitāśukti* is so called [when performed with the left].
One should place the little finger of the right hand over the left;
with the joining of the index finger and thumb, the fingers of the left hand are placed below the right.
When both hands are thus joined without gaps, it is called the *vellitā-śukti* (the curling shell).

At that time, during the drinking, those drops which fall upon the earth—by them the Vetālas, Guhyakas, and others, as well as the rays of light, are indeed satisfied. Bhairava is satisfied by the stream; after that, the supreme *karapāna* [hand-drinking] follows.
In this case, no one should be granted entry beforehand;
however, if someone has entered through negligence, one should not subject them to investigation.
Having done so in this manner, [one should proceed] in due order until the end of the scripture, accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

The wise one should offer unguents, betel, clothing, and so forth. A person of sound intellect should not give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) inferior to half a rūpaka. For those who have taken the pledges (samayins), the fee should be double for each successive stage, up to that of the Guru.
This is the Mūrtiyāga, which is the foremost of all sacrifices. In the performance of rites for specific desires (kāmya), such a procedure should be performed seven times.
First they recognize his house, and then his capability.
After that, the Mothers marvel at his strength and weakness;
then they draw near, and thereafter, being granters of boons, they are well-pleased with the Goddesses and their Lord, along with their retinues.
Therefore, this sacrifice of the forms (mūrtiyāga), which is dear [to the Lord],

should be performed by the wise man in a passionate and secret house; there, the heroes and the Śaktis, even if they do not know each other's signs, may be joined together by the recitation of the names of the deities.
In the absence of the wheel of images (mūrticakra), one should worship only young maidens.
However, for the sake of attaining desired objects, one should not worship a maiden who is deformed, nor one who has breasts or menstruation.
[The appropriate times are] on the first lunar day known as Śruti, and on the fourth day and the three Uttarās.
The fifth [tithi] is in Hasta, the sixth in the first two Punarvasus;
the seventh is in Ārdrā, and likewise the ninth in Rohiṇī.
The twelfth is in Mūla, and the full moon (fifteenth) is in Jyeṣṭhā and Aśvinī.
When the new moon falls on Dhaniṣṭhā, this [day] consists of eleven [units].
Even if the group of days (ahargaṇa) is joined with any one of the three starting from the Sun or with Venus,
it is renowned as a "Yoga-parvan," whether by night or by day.
On the occasion of a yoga-parvan, the worship of the Form (mūrtiyāga) must by all means be performed.
That wise man who would worship all the days known as yoga-parvans—
even he becomes a Samayin through the worship of the Form, even without the mandala.
Thus concludes this rite of the offering to the forms (mūrtiyāga) according to the venerable Siddhayogīśvarīmata.
Now, the clear procedure for the sacred thread (pavitraka), as taught by Śiva, is being described;
it has been further indicated in the venerable Ratnamālā and the Triśiraḥśāstra.
In the *Śrīsiddhāṭana-sadbhāva-mālinīsāra-śāsana*,
the procedure taught by the venerable Māla is stated there primarily as follows:
[The Lord] was rendered unconscious by the stupor of poison arising from the churning of the ocean of milk.
The Naga king did not dwell in his own abode during the rainy season;
rather, for a hundred years, remaining pure and subsisting only on air,
he worshipped the divine Lord Bhairava with tenfold intensity.
And he requested that pleased Lord: "I am unable to remain in my own Pātāla during the rainy season. The Supreme Lord likewise appointed a Nāga to reside upon the seat of his own matted locks.
Then he was borne upon his own head by the entire multitude of gods.
For it is no wonder that those who are great and honored possess universal worshipfulness;
therefore, [he is placed] upon the head of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) and of all the deities in every respect.

One should perform that purification for oneself preceded by sacrifice; ten crores of other worship-rites are not equal to the offering of the *pavitra*. Initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, and even the propitiation of the Guru is in vain [without it].
Without the purificatory thread (*pavitra*) and other such items, a Nāga may take this away by the command of Śiva.
Therefore, it must be performed with every effort by those who know the Kula.
The ritual procedure begins from the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha when the sun is situated in Gemini or Cancer.
That [practice] should be performed without cessation until the full moon of Tulā;
the final day of Kārtika is considered the conclusion of that which is marked by Tulā.
Others, reading the word *kula* instead, provide a different interpretation.

For those who know the *Nityātantra*, Kṛṣṇa is the final day of the month of Kārttika. That is considered to be where the fullness of the *Kula* and the *Nityācakra* resides. The final day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is considered the *Kulaparvan*.
The state of fullness of the moon therein is that lunar day known as the Kula-pūrṇimā (Kula Full Moon).
Time, moving southward and northward, is declared to be of the nature of Kula and Akula.
On the final day of that Kula, its state of fullness is proclaimed.

Therefore, in the injunction, the performance [of the rite] during the six months of the sun's southern course is prescribed for the sake of establishing the luminosity of the dark path within the *pavitraka* ritual. The Lord has thus delineated this form as it is taught in many scriptures.
In the *Śrīratnamālākulāgama*, it is stated by a single verse:

"In this context, during this [auspicious] time, the rite of the sacred thread (*pavitraka*)—which consists of the fulfillment of all ritual procedures—must be performed in every respect during the bright fortnight. (28.128–129a)
The filling [of the petals] occurs through the union with Śakti, and the white petal is of the nature of Śakti.
Because it shares the same origin as the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), its ritual procedure is described accordingly.
One, two, three, four, five, six, or seven large cords [are used].
One should make a purifier (*pavitraka*) of pearls with knots marked by gold and jewels;
for the Guru, it should be a golden thread tripled [in thickness] with one hundred and one knots.
For the *para-guru*, however, there should be three more [knots], and for the *parameṣṭhin*, four more.
In the case of a pre-established teacher who is a Lord of Yoga, [the number] is six (rasa) more;
for Śiva, it is said to be eight more, filled with various jewels.
Furthermore, regarding the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), the rosary, and so forth, they are like the teacher and like Śiva.
In the absence of gold for the *vaṭuka*, one should fashion it from silver;
