likewise, one may use silk thread, linen, or cotton, each tripled three times.
From that ninefold thread, one should proceed by multiplying it threefold and so forth.
Up to a limit of twelve strands (the number of the sun's rays), or even three times that;
by this, that which arises from eighteen threads is considered inferior,
while the middle is one hundred and eight, and the superior is held to be three times that.
The knots are equal in number to the principles (tattvas) by virtue of the reckoning of the six paths;
alternatively, they are diverse through expansion and contraction, filled with excellent fragrance. Having first worshipped them according to the specific rule, one should then offer them.
The *pavitraka* [offering] is performed through the contemplation of the complete fulfillment of all the paths (adhvan).
It extends from the knees to the navel, the throat, and up to the crown of the head for both the Guru and oneself.
Thereafter, a great festival should be celebrated, preceded by the worship of the Guru.
All those who follow the teaching should be gratified with sacrificial fees, garments,
and food. A great festival consisting of song and dance should be performed for four months, or for seven days, or even for three days if that is not possible.
At the end of that, one should ask the deity for forgiveness and dismiss the mandala and other elements.
Then, the fire ritual and the previously described wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga) should be performed.
The rite of the sacred thread (pavitraka) should be performed every month, every four months, or once a year.
It should be performed in every way according to the extent of one's wealth;
however, in the absence of wealth, it may even be done with *kāśa* grass woven together with *kuśa*.
But if wealth exists, deceit leads to disease and to hell.
In daily worship, completeness is achieved through the fulfillment of the festival (parvan) worship;

therein, even further completeness is attained through the veneration of the *pavitraka*. However, if the *pavitraka* is omitted, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"Being thoroughly purified, one should perform [the rite] once again; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Now, the procedure for that as proclaimed in the *Triśiras* is clearly written down.
[It concerns] the Śaiva [system] of the three objects of knowledge, or that which consists of five times five."
Herein is described the sixfold stream of the [tantras] divided into ten and eighteen parts.

Those men who have fallen from their commitments (samaya), who revile the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth, and who are devoid of the daily, occasional, and other rites, as well as the junctions of the sacred festival days (parvan)— [for them this is taught].
Whether committed unintentionally or intentionally, for those who engage in subtle misdeeds,
O Śivā, this purifying rite is performed for their pacification during the auspicious bright fortnight from the beginning of Śrāvaṇa until the end of Kārtika.
But it is not [auspicious] when Kṛṣṇā brings suffering to the agent, the kingdom, the king, and so forth.
As for the silk thread— whether made of wild silk, cotton, or linen—
it should be spun and dyed by a woman belonging to one of the four stages of life (cāturāśramika), O fair-browed one.
Having tripled the measurement in three ways, one should determine the number of threads;
it should be one hundred and eight, or half of that, or half of that again.
The reduction from the previous count proceeds by tens in succession.
With nine, five, or twenty-seven [threads], starting from Śiva,
one should make as many knots as there is a corresponding arrangement of threads;
these should be smeared with the four unguents or else with saffron.
In the manifest form, [the worship] should extend to the edge of the knees; in the *liṅga*, it should end at the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
In the images (*arcā*), it is auspicious when performed upon the head through the conceptualization of the three principles (*tritattva*).
This applies also to the powers of the twelve knots and to the flames of the faces of Brahmā.
In the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), in a mobile liṅga, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), and in the assembly of the Guru;
in the bell, in the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva), in the disciples and the initiates (liṅgin), and on the gateway arch (toraṇa);
as well as in one’s own body and in the fire-seat (vahnipīṭha)—that [installation] is desired according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
One should cause it to be made with nine colors in a palace and in a sacrificial hall;
however, in a Vidyāpīṭha, there are fifty (khaśarāḥ) for an image, a liṅga, or a pedestal. There are eighty-four (vasuveda) on a bell, and eighteen (śarākṣi) on a *sruva* ladle.

In the Veda (four), the eye (two), and the *sruc* (six), there are thirty-six; in the temple (*prāsāda*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), there are twelve (the sun). In the bath-house, there are sixteen (rasa and indu); in the meditation-chamber and for the Guru, there are four (abdhinetra). Seven belong to the practitioner (*sādhaka*), five to the spiritual son (*putraka*), and seven to the initiate bound by the rule (*sāmaya*).

Furthermore, for a disciple who adheres to another scripture, four knots are prescribed; for those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgin), five are said to be used. One should fashion ten knots on the archway (toraṇa).
There should be eight knots at the doors; having thus prepared the purificatory thread (pavitraka), [one proceeds].

Having worshipped the network of mantras, and having [realized] their abiding within oneself, one should then prepare the sacred threads (*pavitraka*) and perform the consecration by pouring together the remnants of the oblations (*saṃpāta*). Thereafter,
for one year, one should meditate upon Bhairava as the witness of one's lapses.
O Goddess, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should bow to Mantrabhairava:
"Oṃ! O Lord who fulfills all defects in ritual action, regarding this vow—whatever has been left undone or done wrongly, O Delighter of the Mothers! (164–165).
"O Lord of Gods, may all that [evil] perish through your grace.
In every way, O Lord of the Wheel of Rays, homage to you; be gracious to me.
With this [mantra], one should offer the invitation-pavitra to the deity.
Then the Guru should offer the bali-oblation to the Yoginīs, the Kṣetras, and the Mātṛs;
meanwhile, the disciples should everywhere partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-stick.
The Teacher should go to sleep, and having risen in the morning, he should perform his daily rites.
Then, having performed the ritual worship, one should collect the purifying substances (pavitrāṇi):
a tooth-stick, clay, an emblic myrobalan (dhātrī), and an abundant myrobalan together with water;
and one should apply ashes along with these four equal parts to the five [substances].

One should place these five purifying substances in order upon the faces located in the east, south, west, and above, within the sphere of Īśa; one should also arrange *kuśa* grass, fuel, and the five products of the cow before Śarva.
Then, one should offer the threefold food offering (*naivedya*) combined with the nectar of the left (*vāmāmṛta*) and other substances (verse 171).
Likewise, one should offer blood, wine, and various drinks.
After that, there is the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the flesh of great beasts and with sesame seeds (verse 172).
With sesame seeds mixed with ghee, or else with rice grains or *dhānyaka* seeds,
saturated with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and pieces of sugar-candy;
one should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times for the face of Brahmā within the triple power (*triśakti*).
Then, one should cast a hundred and eight oblations of light;
thereafter, one should take the purifier (pavitra) in the hollowed palms and recite this:
"O All-pervasive Lord, whether through lack of desire or through desire, whatever has not been performed by me..."
"O Lord, by your command, may this [observance] be flawless for me through your purifying power. Then, with the root mantra, one should say "fill it," and thus conclude the ritual rule.
One should then offer the purifying thread (*pavitra*) ending with *vauṣaṭ* and terminating with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
The three [levels] ending with Nāda, ending with Samanā, and ending with Unmanā, respectively; in this way,
one who is still a worldly being (bhautika) should offer the fourfold set in direct order (anuloma),
whereas one who has reached the final goal (naiṣṭhika) offers the fourfold set of purifiers (pavitraka) in reverse order (viloma).
Whatever various items there may be— clothing, umbrellas, ornaments, and so forth—
these should be offered, as well as rows of lamps and a vessel of sesame seeds made of gold,
accompanied by a pair of garments, for the purpose of fulfilling all requirements.

The devotees of Śiva should be fed and honored according to one's ability. One should hold a great festival for four, three, two, or one month, down to a single day; thereafter, they should never go to another place.
Then the teacher should be honored, and he should give him a fresh, milch cow adorned with gold, jewels, silver, and garments.
And the Guru should say: "May the ritual for you be complete."
One should speak to the God of gods regarding his return;
then the dismissal should be performed, and the ornaments and other items should be kept secret.
The Guru, having taken the food offering (naivedya), should employ it for the purpose of sacrifice.
The *pavitraka* is traditionally held to be common to all four [classes];
there is no vow superior to this—what further praise could be said of it?
As for the remainder, one should cast it into a deep torrent of water and not leave it to remain fixed.
Now, that procedure for portents which was previously outlined by me is being described. In that regard, a special worship of the Lord must be performed,
and the Wheel-sacrifice (cakrayāga) should be carried out by the wise according to the previously stated rule.
In that regard, whatever— whether consisting of consciousness or the unconscious— is conducive to one’s own desired enjoyment or liberation, whether mediately or directly,
that is to be worshipped; and the means for that [attainment] are also to be worshipped in order to achieve identification with it.

The means (upāya) as well—consisting of the form, time, ritual action, and so forth—should be fully honored. Being a means consists in the capacity to give birth to the goal (upeya); by worshipping that [means], and through becoming one with its nature, one shall swiftly attain the goal.
To the extent that one draws near to the means [of practice],
to that same extent the necessity of accomplishing the goal arises, especially through worship and other such acts;
thus, there is the attainment of a certain knowledge that assists both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

When that very primary day is declared by the wise to be the "occasioned" (naimittika) day, then the scripture is the means (*upāya*) therein, and the teacher (*guru*) is the one who employs that means. Likewise, a brother of the teacher who possesses that same knowledge is also a giver of wisdom through their dialogue.

The wife of the guru, as well as the brother, the son, and so forth—this group [of kinsmen] does not exist by virtue of a connection through the womb; rather, it arises from a connection through knowledge (vidyā).
Those whose sense of ego (ahantā) is not established in the body, which is a transformation of the vital energy (vīrya) and the dawn of consciousness (aruṇa), [are truly related].
The continuity that provides benefit to the body is established as kinship;
likewise, in the Smṛti scriptures,
the inheritance of the lineage is logical, for it is said to extend to that degree according to the distinction of distance or proximity.

But those who have abandoned attachment to the body and partake in the state of "I am consciousness" (bodhāhaṃbhāva) possess kinship [with the Lord] because of the two-fold continuum that assists consciousness. In this regard,
when one whose vision and action have been opened by power first perceives in this manner:
This body, for its part, is constructed from successive prior material causes.
The Self, however, is devoid of transformation because of its eternity and is without cause;
yet, due to its sovereignty, it remains as if concealed by things belonging to itself.
And again, having become manifest, he becomes a vessel for the state of Bhairava. Regarding his manifestation therein— which consists essentially of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*)—
the appropriate means is this very continuum of knowledge (*jñānasantāna*).
By means of a continuous stream of such similar cognitions that gradually become manifest, and through the exclusion of heterogeneous elements,
the goal is indeed attained swiftly;
and this occurs in the same way for the continuum of consciousness that has been accustomed to beginningless saṃsāra.
Upon the dissolution [of the ordinary state], supramundane gnosis would take recourse in another continuum—
that of the vast stream of consciousness appropriate for non-saṃsāric existence.
The primary and primordial cause of that is the gnosis of the Guru, which has entered into one's own self.
Because one's own particular qualities are clearly deposited therein to an extreme degree,

that [consciousness] is rightly considered the material cause (upādāna), even though there is a difference in bodies. For difference and non-difference belong to the continuum of consciousness, not to the continuum of the body.
Just as the body of a child is not [transformed] into its true state by being possessed by a yogi’s will,
why is it that for a yogi who does not abandon his own body, there is no assumption of various forms of knowledge when bringing about the animation of another's body and so forth? 206–207ab.

Therefore, because the lineage of consciousness is primary over the biological lineage, that lineage of teachers which is established in the knowledge of Śiva [is what matters]. This being the case, the triad is both the principal cause and the auxiliary cause.
The group of Gurus constitutes a single entity consisting of both cause and effect;
here, the Guru is said to be the cause, and his wife is the auxiliary cause (sahakāriṇī). For one who is devoid of power (niḥśaktika), there can be no entitlement to the sacrifice.
Just as a yogin possesses the capacity to produce an effect even without an external auxiliary cause due to his internal, noble power of consciousness,
so too those born of the same source are brothers; however, anyone who merely resembles them is someone else entirely.
Furthermore, due to the connection of the lineage, the group of gurus is also mentioned;
however, this primary lineage is always to be worshipped and honored.
This applies both at the birth of the gurus and others, as well as during initiation and even at the time of their departure.
That which is not the hand is indeed the cause of consciousness, the means, the body, and so forth.
(213) Thus, one's own birthday is said to be the means of consciousness;
it is the cause of the body, which is the basis for such experiences as worldly enjoyment and liberation. (214)

The day on which the purificatory rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth are performed for one's own self shall be the primary "day of birth," because it is the birth of the continuum of knowledge. As for the day of one's own death, that will become [the primary day of birth] for others.
Because one who dies due to a specific cause (naimittika) becomes non-different from Śiva at that time. In this context, we shall clearly explain the nature of death as it arises incidentally:
although Śiva is all-pervasive, due to being sealed by the contraction fashioned by His own will, [He appears otherwise].
By the power of a flood of various fruits of karma, one assumes this or that body;

and the state of possessing a body consists simply in being situated within the body while still in the womb. This is the first emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇana*) for consciousness established in the void.

Furthermore, his sovereignty lies precisely in the fashioning of the body while it remains in the womb. Because he is the creator of the body and its other components without contraction, he is called the Lord (Īśa).
That self of wind, together with the conscious self (cidātman), [resides] within that firm bodily machine.
Driven like the air from a bellows by a mechanical device, it moves about;
therefore, it awakens just as one who has been in deep sleep wakes up. Gradually, the vital breath becomes stronger along with the body.

Even there, by the power of the necessity of karma, she grasps the state of vital breath (*prāṇana*) and the senses due to the predominance of the sensations of void, hollow space, consciousness, and touch. Thus, in this sequence, the strength of his body and vital breath becomes fully nourished.
Residing in bodies born from a womb or not born from a womb, one experiences the enjoyments produced by karma.
And it has been stated by the Moon-crested Lord in the scripture known as the Gahvara:
"Just as a householder, having constructed a house, dwells within it..."
Likewise, having assumed a body while being devoid of qualities such as action (kriyā) and the rest,
that embodied soul (dehin), though previously partless (niṣkala), is designated as "merely a slight vibration" (kiñcitsphuraṇamātra).
But when the principles (tattva) beginning with the sense organs become manifest, he is called the "soul with parts" (sakalātman).
One should read extensively from that very source what has been stated in the venerable Gahvara, beginning with these words:
"But when those karmas are exhausted and the mechanism of the body undergoes a change, the mechanism of the vital breath falls apart, and consequently the body becomes like a wall. (AbhT 28.227–228)
In the wheels of the channels (nāḍīcakra), there occurs contraction and expansion in reverse order;
likewise, breaking, drying, or moistening through the decrease or increase of wind, phlegm, and fire—
whatever such things may be that destroy the prior configuration.

The wise have declared that the disintegration of the bodily machine occurs precisely at that point. When that machine has disintegrated, that consciousness assumes the nature of the vital breath within another body born of a womb, or elsewhere, variegated by karma.
Then that body awakens like one who has risen from sleep; for it too, there are experiences, their loss, and deaths, exactly as before,
since these processes of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal proceed by the power of karma.

Therefore, since [the soul] conforms to the diversity of necessity, time, and so forth, how could that grace— which consists in the expansion of one's own essential nature as the very essence of consciousness—
depend upon karma, necessity, and the like? (233–234)
Since karma, time, necessity, and so forth, have their life in contraction,
how can there be a cause for grace within this [reality] whose nature is the abandonment of contraction? Furthermore,
grace is distinguished as being either gradual or intense.

Since this has already been explained at length previously, what is the use of further repetitions? Therefore, one whose bonds of contraction have been burnt away by initiation and the knowledge of Śiva becomes Śiva himself at the end of the body; for him, there is no remaining in another body.
Even those who have entered the reality and follow the command of Śaṅkara,
having died in the abodes of self-born beings, sages, celestial seers, humans, and so forth, reach that city and are initiated by the lords of the cities in due order.
Whether descending into the mortal world or not, they attain Śiva and are free from rebirth.
Among them, the self-born (Svayambhūs) are of two kinds:
some are intent upon bestowing grace, while others merely occupy the station of their own manifested portions (aṃśa) for the sake of their specific task.
If a man dies among those who have been commanded for the sake of bestowing grace,
he clearly attains that grace even without a descent into the mortal world; however,
one who is performing his own duty should not abandon that station even in the slightest degree.
Just as Gaurī, performing austerities, entered a cave in Kaśmīra,
or as the all-pervading Lord Narahari arose there at Dhyānoḍḍāra,
proud and terrifying the Daityas as he led them toward the Vitastā; || 242–243 ||
Just as Viṣṇu or Śiva reside in the Śāligrāma for their own enjoyment,
and likewise Nara and Nārāyaṇa perform penance at Badarī,
so too do these and other deities abide in their respective portions of activity.
When propitiated, they swiftly bestow the fruit appropriate to them;
and those who reach their end while remaining within the domain of their own specific duties,
having enjoyed such enjoyments there, descend again among mortals.
Those who have descended among mortals are portions of those [deities] and are composed of their essence;
through the sequence of initiation, knowledge, conduct, and so forth, they attain the nature of Śiva.
Even bound souls (paśus), from the immobile to the animal realm, who die within these two [categories], [attain the same].
Due to the piercing (*vedha*) by the refinement of their own karma, men who experience variety in that world—
though they are merely bound souls (*paśu*)— attain residence in the same realm (*sālokya*) because of their lack of discernment (*aviveka*).
This lack of discernment arises from the non-emergence of specific distinctions and likewise from delusion.
Immobile beings and the rest attain that state or a progressively higher one;
yet they do not directly reach that state of Rudra, but rather do so again through a gradual sequence.
[This occurs] in a place crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and filled with various families of trees.

This has been stated in the Āgamas; therefore, I shall now describe the measurement of the sacred field (kṣetra) as proclaimed in the venerable Sarvajñāna-tantra and other scriptures. When a Linga is installed by a preceptor (ācārya), the sacred field extends one hundred cubits from the Linga.
In the case of a self-manifested (*svayambhūta*) [liṅga], the merit is a thousandfold; half of that is for one established by a seer (*ṛṣi*).
When a knower of reality (*tattvavit*) installs a liṅga, the fruit is equal to that of a self-manifested one.
However, when an ācārya who does not know reality installs a liṅga, [the result is different].
Otherwise, it would be a fault, for such a rule would corrupt both;
if one holds the view that "I am one, the Supreme Self is another,
and Śiva is yet another," then he would neither liberate nor be liberated, since everything is composed of the Self.
Therefore, whatever supreme *liṅga* has been established by one who knows reality,
that alone one should resort to as a sacred abode for the sake of enjoyment and liberation;
this was stated in the *Śrīratnamālā* once [the practitioner] has recognized that the time [for such action] has arrived.
One who seeks liberation should not experience fear; he should cast off the body without hesitation.
Or, O beloved, one may bide one's time at sacred fords, shrines, and holy places.
This is the path for those who are not yogins; a yogin, however, should transcend [death] through yoga.
But being incapable of deception, he should go to a sacred field or a sanctuary;
by taking refuge in such a holy place (tīrtha), his deception is indeed accomplished.
And by this means, through the yoga of practice upon the principles (tattva) beginning with Earth, [he attains success].
Even for those who enjoy supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the utility of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) for the sake of liberation has been stated;
however, the account regarding one possessed of perfect knowledge will be taught further on.
This is the account concerning bound souls (*paśu*); as for those who have been initiated into the various levels of reality (*tattva*), [the following applies]:
They attain proximity to their respective lords through the application of their own fitness. Whosoever possesses an impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the force of their particular capacity,
they should be appointed to that very [station], provided they possess the higher purification from the Lord of the City (*pureśa*).
Thus it was previously stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* as well:
"Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular [world], he is joined to that very place;
he becomes a possessor of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) through the efficacy of mantra," and so forth, as described elsewhere.
But those wise ones who abide in the knowledge of the various principles (tattvas), mantras, and ritual conduct,
upon death, attain union with the respective Rudra there. Even for those who have attained such union, [the state continues] due to their own residual impressions (saṃskāra).

In whatever manner [the descent occurs], the manifestation from that portion may be diverse; for this is heard extensively in the Siddhāntas, the Purāṇas, and other texts. Although the status of being an incarnation of Rudra is equal, there is diversity in their actions and experiences.

Since the body of an entity is inlaid with manifold powers, it is not something other than those powers; it could not exist apart from their aggregate. Therefore, from that which is called the aggregate of powers, [the world arises] from a portion of Rudra and the others.
That appropriate rite shall succeed, for that portion [of the deity] clearly descends.
And those who have received initiation in a lower level but have not abandoned their attachment to it,
if they die in a higher reality (tattva), they partake in excellence even within the lower [level], like wood [carried upward].
But those who have abandoned that [lower] excellence partake in what lies beyond it.
Even those who have received initiation into higher principles, even if they have not yet attained discernment (*viveka*),
are fortunate recipients of the fruit of that initiation, provided they have reached the limit of the lower levels.
For you still maintain an attachment there, even regarding initiation as prescribed by the scriptures;
without discernment, you have resorted to that attachment based on worldly renown.
Sālokya belongs to one who is merely a bound soul (paśu), while sāmīpya belongs to one who has been initiated.
"But for one devoted to that [other path], union (*sāyujya*) is attained; so it has been declared by the Supreme Lord.

(273) "However, he who has studied the higher scriptures but has abandoned his commitment to them due to doubt—such a person, even while proceeding toward a sacred site (*āyatana*), does not obtain any fruit whatsoever. (274)
The God of gods has explained at length how initiation, knowledge, and likewise pilgrimage sites are in vain for such a person; yet even one who is thus unfit remains in the abode of Śiva.
Afterwards, by means of the binding of the *āsthāna*, one shall enjoy the fruit for that long.
That merit which consists mostly of rivers, mountains, and lakes does not [lead to liberation] at death;
however, for those who die there, it is excellent, resulting in the enjoyment of celestial pleasures in heaven.
Furthermore, those who have attained discernment through higher knowledge, yet at the time of death resort to a lower abode, remain hidden here; for indeed,
they incur the sin that has been described as the defilement of that knowledge.

It is the established rule that [these impurities] are destroyed through the sequence beginning with initiation (dīkṣā) by the respective lords of those cities. However, those who mentally defile the knowledge of the seats of initiation and practice [forbidden acts] therein, they all go to hell.

The loss of the bond of commitment (*āsthābandha*) regarding the initiation into the abodes of knowledge (*jñānāyatana*) and so forth is to be known by one's activities and speech; these too are of two kinds:
those which never again arise within one's state of composure (*svāsthya*).

In the state of ill-health, those [experiences] arising from the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are merely the experiencing of that [state]. And due to the imbalance of the constituents, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of saṃsāra are awakened; yet even when they emerge through the gaps [of consciousness], they do not take root, being mostly burnt away by knowledge.

But those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to isolation (*kaivalya*), which are always unmanifest during a state of well-being, become manifest during a state of ill-being through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). This is because worldly impressions are refined by intense prior habituation.
Thus spoke the Lord of Serpents, according to the Sūtra:
"In those [states] which are the intervals [between experiences], those cognitions that partake of isolation (kaivalya) are never cultivated for the sake of worldly existence;
therefore, these arise through the descent of power (śaktipāta). (285–286ab)
By those whose actions are expressed through the provocation of the humors of the elements,
who have not attained certainty or discernment, who are like those who are asleep or intoxicated,
and even by those who are perverted and who revile the knowledge, initiation, and the Guru; (287–288a)

Concealment (tirobhāva) is not to be understood [as occurring] in the heart due to the absence of firm rooting there. For this very reason, even one who is awakened, while remaining within the body, may experience perceptions such as those of Yama’s messengers or serpents, which consist of the nature of experiences arising from karma.
It is not by this much alone that he is not liberated, for death is an experience just like birth;
and like [the state of] persistence, death is therefore twofold, consisting of suffering and pleasure.
Thus, just as for one who is awakened there is a variety of pleasures and pains, [so too is the nature of death].

While remaining [in this world], they do not destroy their state of liberation; likewise, even at the time of death, they remain so. Furthermore, those who are yogis, in whichever reality (tattva) they have well-cultivated their practice, they fix their minds precisely upon that reality and, free from doubt, attain it.

In the Śrī Svacchanda, it is stated: "By means of the concentration on fragrance (gandha-dhāraṇā), those who have died [attain liberation]," and so forth; likewise, the fruit of the concentrations is described in the Mālinīśāstra. However, for those who [possess] a body, there is no experience known as death associated with these [concentrations].

By means of the *dhāraṇās*, they quickly abandon [the body], like entering another's body. For this experience of death consists of the piercing of the vital points (*marmans*), delusion residing in the senses, and the turbidity of darkness in the mind; and none of these exist in them.
For in this way, one applies mental effort through the sense of "I" in another's body until the transition of consciousness occurs;
then the wheel of vital breaths, which is dependent upon that [consciousness], also moves along its path.
Therefore, by that very means, one should awaken the wheel of the senses within the body of another;
just as flies rise up following the king of flies when he has risen,
and settle down following him when he stands still, so too do all the functions of the senses follow the mind.
Therefore, when he moves into another body and so forth, there is no mingling [of his senses].
This subtle [state], situated in the midst of the senses, becomes like a body once again.
Thus it is for yogins who move into the bodies of others and so forth.
For those who move within the body of each respective reality-level (*tattva*), there is no delusion.
They should be known to be of two kinds: the worldly and the initiated.
The former gradually become Śivas, while the latter [become so] merely through the experience of those [worldly] enjoyments.
Initiation (dīkṣā) also, through its application to various higher and lower divisions, becomes manifold;
when differentiated by yogins, it bestows diverse fruits.
As for those who possess realized knowledge (vijñānin), they are here of two kinds, according to whether they are "trembling" (kampretara) or otherwise.
Among them, those whose consciousness is trembling become clearly Śivas at the end of the body (303).
For their consciousness has arisen, yet it is not very clear;
nor is its nature uprooted through the engagement with other conceptual constructions (304).
Therefore, the conceptual construction arising from negligence regarding the body will necessarily perish upon the fall of the body; and that supreme knowledge is also awakened,
having been established within while the mental impressions and their conceptualizations have been obliterated.
When its ripening has been reached, that [consciousness] indeed shines forth for one who restrains it from falling into a state of misfortune.
But those whose nature is always composed of well-practiced consciousness and is identical with Śiva are truly liberated while living; for them, there is no further deliberation regarding death.
Just as there is no deliberation regarding the state of those liberated while living—
whether they experience pleasure, pain, or delusion—
even so there is none at the time of death.
The Supreme Lord spoke this in the *Śrīratnamālā-śāstra*, and the Lord of Serpents, who bears the burden of supporting the universe, also said it in his own scripture:
"In the midst of a street, amidst urine and excrement, in the house of a Caṇḍāla, in hell, or in a cremation ground..."

Whether he possesses thought or is free from thought, the man of knowledge attains liberation even at the end. (28.310) The word "even" (*api ca*) expresses his state of being liberated while alive (*jīvanmuktatā*).
The mention of both "possessing thought" and "being free from thought" indicates the extent of his possible states of existence. (28.311)
Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even one whose memory has failed may cast off the body;
liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge, he attains absolute isolation (kaivalya), his sorrow destroyed.
This *Anantakārikā* indeed declares this to be the cause of bondage.
One might suspect that his good and evil deeds [could affect him], yet they do not belong to him. By the force of the word "api" (even), it is indeed possible that he possesses unimpaired memory;
however, death belongs only to one whose memory has perished—since he is already dead, what is the use of such memory prior to death?

The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility; indeed, it is possible that this [liberation] might occur. Furthermore, the word "time" (*kāla*) declares that death is not the cause of liberation. And as for the doubt regarding whether isolation (*kaivalya*) is the goal—even though the body has ceased to exist—[it is still possible].
Because it bestows a sense of duality, even this [identification with the body] is destroyed by him; thus, he attains freedom from sorrow.
Just as connection with another's body and so forth does not create division for him, so too is his connection with his own body, even though he is liberated while living.
And for this reason, there is no distinction between one who possesses a universal form and one who is devoid of it—
namely, one who is non-different from Śiva— whether he exists within a body or even in its absence. Nevertheless,
because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that previous duality still persist, [one must proceed as follows].

The state of being "alone" (kevalatva) has just been described, whether it arises from the absence of other factors or from the support of other measures; those [factors] do not perceive him as distinct, and by them he is said to be liberated. This is also stated in the venerable Traiśirasa: "In that which is devoid of the cavities of the sun and the moon..."
When [the mind] stands free from the state of aversion, remains everywhere as if paralyzed,
is devoid of all calamity, and transcends the means of valid cognition and their objects—
merged within that inner consciousness, the agent of action is likewise untainted.
Primal matter, a jar, space, and the self: even when the jar is destroyed, the space [remains]. In that very same way, this self does not perish; it becomes one with Śiva.
Established as independent, the man of knowledge may expand into all things.
Its state is neither existence nor non-existence; it is neither a formal structure nor a mental construction.
Having taken this very point into account, the Guru spoke in the *Gītā*:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end... (AbhT_28.324–325a).
"To that very state he goes, O son of Kuntī, being constantly permeated by the nature of that [state]. Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight.
When you are dissolved while sattva has increased, then you shall go upward."
Gradually merged into rajas and tamas, one enters the womb of karma as a deluded being;
therein occurs the confusion of the senses and the state of being overwhelmed by labored breathing. This is the experience of death, not the actual abandonment of the body.

That single final moment, consisting of the last breath, immediately after which this body becomes like wood or a wall— that infinitesimal fraction of time at the moment of abandoning the body is what separates one from the physical frame.
For that very reason, she is indeed freed from the pleasure, pain, and so forth of that body;
whatever she remembers therein due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (saṃskāra)—
caused by the abundance of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), repeated practice, or the descent of power (śaktipāta)— [she experiences that].

That very form attains the states of being happy, suffering, or deluded (331). Whether it be devoid of pleasure and pain or of the nature of bliss, why does this [consciousness] attain that? Because it remembers it within its own awareness (saṃvidi) (332).
That which first manifests as something additional is this body, due to its being presided over by consciousness (cit).
That very prior presiding by consciousness occurs through the mode of identity;
that is what is here called "dissolution" within the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).

Since consciousness, having first assumed a conceptualized body [as its substrate], fully effects its presiding over objects of knowledge such as blue, yellow, and so forth, it acts as the presiding ground (adhiṣṭhāna). Therefore,
even though a wall is merely something to be presided over (adhiṣṭheya), it can function as a "body" [for that consciousness].
There is a distinction regarding the body, namely that it is the primary substratum for all [objects of perception].

While other [objects] possess a mode of existence consisting in identity [with the subject], this [identity] is not perceived even though it exists. However, in the case of the objects of perception, [this is so] because the body is eternal and never-failing [as their locus].
And that [memory] belongs to that very body through its previous death and subsequent birth;
it is joined with memory, variegated by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience.
By this reasoning, our lineage-guru Kallaṭa [established this].
It has been stated that, despite there being no difference between bodies, the cause [of the stability of consciousness] is the firmness of what is called the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

That is logical; otherwise, if the body were the sole factor, what would be the reason for the stability of the breath in one case and not another? Even though the state of being a body is indistinguishable, this question remains unresolved.
"Remembering"—this form [of the verb] indicates the cause; he attains that state.
Since the body was previously remembered as being presided over by consciousness and vibrating [with life], therefore that final memory which occurs among non-omniscient subjects [is the cause].
Since the determination of another body is never within the range of perception,
that which is the clear recollection of kinsmen, beloved ones, sons, drinks, and so forth,
does not pertain to another body; for that [recollection] would not be final.
However, when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of anyone whatsoever awakens at the end of the body, then,
due to the fitness of that embodied being, a clear experience arises.
As it is told in the Purāṇa regarding the thirst for a young deer.
A certain sage, being thoroughly permeated [by latent impressions], assumed the state of a doe;
in that case, the experience there is not the cause for the production of another birth.
Rather, his latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the cause, occurring by chance like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence.
"Now, why does he remember that very thing? To this he says: "Because [the mind] is always permeated by that; therefore, being thoroughly imbued with its state (*tadbhāva*), he remembers that alone.
'I am thus' and 'I shall become thus'—this is called its state (*tadbhāva*). (AbhT 28.346b–347)
For the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that which is yet to be is performed, never of that which already exists. Cultivation is proclaimed to be the process of gradually making [the object] manifest.
And the experience of what is already manifest is not this cultivation; this is clear.
Even in the case of an infant born that very day, or a beast, an insect, or a tree,
although they are then in a state of delusion, their prior cultivation (bhāvanā) was indeed manifest at that time;
for, upon the end of that deluded body, [that cultivation arises] again through the awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra).
By means of memory, that [latent impression] yields its fruit in the form of diversity within the body;

for it has been stated that even when there is a separation by place and other factors, latent impressions (vāsanās) arise because memory and mental traces (saṃskāra) possess an identical nature of immediate succession. Thus, [memory arises].
In the same way, even though it is clearly ascended upon through experience,
why does that which is being cultivated not produce a body similar to its own continuum?
[It does so] together with such kinsmen, sons, friends, and others.
It appears even in another world through the sequence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like a dream. [Objection:
But why is it that it is not perceived in that same way by other subjects, such as kinsmen, sons, and so forth?
[Response: Who said this? Let him first understand the nature of what is being perceived.
Regarding the multitude of other objects perceivable through a mass of activities and verbal expressions,
the statement "that [dream-object] does not exist" is devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For those very things which are seen while awake are perceived by me as such.
"Let it be that this [dream] is false because of the strength of the words of its cognizer:
'I saw these cognizers in a dream, yet they are none at all;
they do not grieve, nor do they look at me'—what proof is there for this? (AbhT 28.357–358)
Since all inferences are established in self-awareness (svasaṃvedana),
the existence of another cognizer is grounded in consciousness and does not reside in that [other cognizer].
The existence of a jar or similar object is grounded in consciousness, but it does not reside in that [object].

In the same way, even when there is a change of the subtle body (*mātrantara*), this consciousness remains grounded in [the Self] and does not belong to that [new body]. Therefore, it is established that whatever is meditated upon, that very thing indeed [is realized]; if it were not so, one would not awaken at the end of the body, or if one did, it would be with a different kind of awakening.
For it has been stated that a living being is liberated at the final moment because of the power of prior impressions (*saṃskāra*), having been refined by hearing the knowledge of Brahman;
this is established by the two particles [tathāhi], the word "end" (*anta*), the act of remembering, and the mention of the four ends.
From the entire quarter-verse and from the half-verse immediately following it,
as well as from the word *līna*, all that has been stated regarding the true nature of reality (*arthasatattvaka*) is derived.
Without knowing this, everyone is merely clutching at straws like grass and reeds.

Some [commentators] propose an inversion of "yat" and "tat," while others suggest a different sequence; they also treat the two particles as having a broken order and interpret the word "tyajati" as being in the seventh case (locative). However, all of that is not useful for the application of the stated reasoning.
And that which has been shown by him is not false, nor does it cause delusion within one's own mind; thus,
having learned this reality regarding the time of death from the venerable Śambhunātha,
he declared it, and through that, fear of death is destroyed.

O gods, you who have realized the true nature of death— if you now swallow this Kālakūṭa poison, which arises from the churning and extraction of the potency of the Heart of the Immovable (Śiva) from the ocean of consciousness, and drink it as "nectar," then your state of Śiva-hood will be certain. For even any worldly festival brings about a sense of joy.
That [state], which resembles a wave in the ocean of consciousness, gives birth [to experience] just like a mountain.
By this, the mountains [of experience] in cases such as joy at the destruction of misfortune are explained; therefore, in those instances as well, there is specifically the worship of the deity.

Whatever wonder occurs, such as the agitation of the city and so forth, that arises from the sovereignty of one's own consciousness bestows firmness; therefore, on the day of its attainment, there is a special worship (vaiśeṣikārcana).
The gathering of Yoginīs is twofold: by force and likewise through affection.
One should guard against vulnerabilities in the east, while in the north there is freedom of action.
Both of these will be demonstrated in the context of the extraction of mantras.
Furthermore, through the gathering of yoginīs, one necessarily attains knowledge.
Therefore, that festival is likewise the meeting of one's own lineage and so forth.
Consciousness, which is the self of all things, may become contracted due to the differentiation of bodies and the like;
yet in the *melaka*, it expands through the mutual friction of reflections.
The surging flood of one's own rays, reflected within the consciousnesses,
shines forth effortlessly like [an image] in many mirrors, even while extending toward all things. For this very reason, in the case of singing, music, and so forth, before a large assembly...

The joy that arises when one becomes identified with everything as a whole does not belong to a single individual alone; rather, consciousness, filled with bliss, attains such oneness with each [individual] object,
such as a dance performance, and thereby experiences fullness of bliss.
Because here there is no cause for contraction such as envy or malice, that [consciousness] is blossoming,
unimpeded, and joined with the bliss of pure awareness. However,
it is obstructed when some object other than itself (atanmaya) stands in its way.
When consciousness stands as something heterogeneous, like the sensation of a rough surface,

then in rites such as the worship of the *cakra*, one must never admit that which is heterogeneous and not composed of that [consciousness], for it is the cause of the contraction of consciousness. (379–380a)
As many bodies as there may be, one should worship them all as if they were one's own limbs, having entered into that single, perfectly full consciousness;
once entered, one should not fall into contraction through negligence.
One should perform one's own prescribed conduct together with him;

if he is pierced by the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*), he will become absorbed in that [state]. But one who is pierced by the *vāmā* [power] will revile it, and subsequently, he may even kill him.
And it is stated in the venerable Picumata: "At the outset, one should protect [the initiate] with effort;
once he has entered, one should not subject him to further deliberation. But if such a person remains established in worldly conduct, then [the same applies] when he has entered. (AbhT 28.383b–384)
Without having performed that ritual conduct, one should worship the wheel once again.
Now I shall describe the method for the exposition of the scriptures by the Guru,
as it was proclaimed by the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) in the Devyāyāmala Śāstra and other texts.

One who knows the ritual manual (kalpa), knows its collection, knows the treatise (śāstra), knows the meaning of the compendium (saṃhitā), and knows the meaning of all treatises— such a person is designated as a distinct kind of Guru. Furthermore,
whoever has thoroughly practiced knowledge in a particular treatise, he alone should conduct the exposition therein.
It cannot be otherwise; for if that [knowledge] were absent, he would not act in such a way at all.

And in the Śrī Bhairavakula, such mastery of the ritual procedures (kalpa) and so forth is described as the defining characteristic of a Guru, which is simply the state of possessing complete knowledge.
Even there, that [activity] which consists of the movements of consciousness and the actions of the ritualists is also intermediate.
This was stated in the fifty-second chapter of the *Devīyāmala*:
"The Lord himself, desiring to abide in the form of a Guru, becomes tenfold."
Ucchuṣma, Śavara, Caṇḍagu, Mataṅga, Ghorāntaka, Ugra, Halahalaka,
Krodhin, Huluhulu— these ten gurus of the east are composed of the essence of Śiva. Having assumed human bodies according to the sequence of their own mental dispositions, [they act].
Although their cognitions and actions differ from one another, they are all completely filled with knowledge.
They are all devoted to meat, wine, sexual union, initiation, worship, and the study of the scriptures;
yet there is an internal distinction based on pride, its pacification, anger, forbearance, and so forth.
Having understood this, the wise disciple, desiring an explanation, should always request a teacher who has mastered the complete scriptures, preceded by ritual worship.
He [the teacher], moreover, [should teach] such a scripture even to his own disciple or to the disciple of another.
One should provide an exposition for those worthy of hearing it, such as Vaiṣṇavas and others who are on lower paths.

Furthermore, the Guru, filled with the essence of compassion, should explain [the teachings] even to an inferior person— avoiding, however, the most vital points— considering indeed the variety in the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*).
On ground smeared with [unbroken rice] and on a square pedestal, one should fashion three lotuses arising from the mud;
this constitutes the Vidyāpīṭha, which measures thirty-six finger-breadths.
In the center is Vāgīśānī, and in the south and north are the Gurus and Gaṇeśa.
Having worshipped Kalpeśvara with offerings of water, flowers, and libations for the sake of the lower rite and the ritual manual (kalpa),

the wise one should then properly satisfy the maṇḍala using the vessel of general offering prescribed by the rules; thereafter, he should deliver the exposition preceded by an account of its connections.
By means of connecting the sequence of the chapters, sentences, and words of the Sūtra through their mutual relationship,
one should lead the statements forward, ensuring that what precedes and follows is uncontradicted and augmented;
this should be done according to the appropriate principles, such as the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluta*) and the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*).

One who knows the nature of sentences should apply the meaning of the scripture without confusion, ensuring that the preceding and succeeding parts are not contradicted; and by means of sound reasoning— such as the repetition of a system, refutation, and the application of logical consequences— he should state the subject matter while establishing its distinction from other entities.

Whatever point comes within the scope of the *vyāhṛti* formulas, that very thing one should strengthen with more robust arguments, even if it is something that is yet to be established later; for the subject matter to be stated must follow the path of uprooting the previously firmly constructed prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Then, the disciple’s mind quickly ascends, becoming free from doubt and error.
Whatever the disciple approaches— be it language, logic, debate, absorption, or the sequential stages—
the teacher should likewise employ that very thing as a means for awakening through exposition.
Having completed the subject matter to be explained, there should be a libation and worship within the maṇḍala.
One may speak of another subject thereafter, but one must not speak beyond the chapter.
At the end of the commentary, having asked for forgiveness and dismissed [the deities], one should cast everything into deep water.
One should perform special worship at the beginning, middle, and end of the scripture, and so forth.
One should perform special worship for the sake of expiation from the violations of the *samayas*;
however, for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpamati*), there may be no need for such penances.

"Even so, one should act in that manner for the sake of favoring those groups who do not know reality. "O Lord, if even the mere remembrance [of the deity] destroys sin according to the *Śrīpicu*, why then has the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) been taught?"— thus was the Goddess prompted.

Truth alone— mere remembrance— is what liberates here when recited even once from the entire web of karma for one who knows the subtle essence of the reality of remembrance. Nevertheless, the prescribed ritual must be performed for the sake of maintaining stability.
For those who do not know reality and are solely intent upon mere conduct,
when their minds waver, the loss of knowledge arises. Therefore, if one is free from conceptual construction and has ceased from conventional activity, [one attains stability].
Those who are always dependent on the practice of the scriptures should avoid such confusion; or,
if they should seek out confusion, they should perform expiation so that their minds do not become wavering regarding the meaning of the scriptures.

Whatever was previously enjoined in the ritual known as the Śivahasta, by reciting the Astra-mantra one hundred times, one is liberated from [all] sins— with the exception of killing a woman. O Dear One, the destruction of a Śakti results in a great fault and leads to eternal hell.

Thus, in the *Śrīratnamālā*, when a transgression of the *samaya* has been committed, this "Evil Cutter" (*duṣṭakartarī*) is declared as the expiation for those born of the *kula*. Just as it was taught in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara) for the purification of the *samayas*: 416–417.

Either the Mālinī or the Mātṛkā [mantra] should be recited up to three hundred thousand times by one who lacks the qualification to behold established [shrines] such as Pūrā. Thus it is stated in the venerable Brahmayāmala that an expiation must be performed.

The killer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the stealer of a hero’s property, the stealer of divine property, the destroyer of forms, the breaker of lingas, the one who neglects daily rites and so forth, and the one who has fallen away from his own measure and retinue—[these are purified]. 419–420ab.
