One who causes the impairment of a Śakti, kills a yogin or a man of knowledge, or is a destroyer [of the teachings], should perform twice as many recitations as the number of hundreds of thousands prescribed for those who commit occasional transgressions. Endowed with some specific vow, eating moderately, and observing celibacy, he should practice.

If, while engaged with a messenger (dūtī), one goes elsewhere deluded by passion, one should then perform a hundred thousand recitations; thus it is stated in the Brahmayāmala. At the conclusion of the rites for initiation, consecration, and occasional ceremonies, there is the worship of the Guru.
On the following day, it should always be performed according to the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*.
That teacher who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, who is a poet (*kavi*), and who knows the true nature of the Trika,
must always be accepted as the Guru, even if one must set aside another who is established in that [tradition].
Having drawn a svastika in the mandala, one should prepare a seat made of gold or other precious materials there;
having done so, one should worship the Path (adhvan) situated therein, which brings about the end of all things.
Then, with devotion, one should request the Guru for his empowerment (adhiṣṭhiti).

There, he should be worshipped with his own mantras using an abundance of flowers, incense, and water offerings (argha), followed by unguents, fine garments, food offerings (naivedya), and libations in due order.
Having worshipped him until he is pacified, the disciple should honor him with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

One who is purified should bestow his entire wealth upon him, even his own self. But if one does not satisfy the Guru completely with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), then even a knower of reality remains bound by that debt and falls into a state of subordination.
"One who fails to perform worship of the Guru is born for a hundred lifetimes [in lower states];
thereafter, becoming qualified, he attains liberation—thus it is stated in the *Skandayāmala*.
Therefore, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must certainly be given again to the Guru."

For that which was previously prescribed as a constituent part of the sacrifice is for the sake of his satisfaction; then, having been enjoyed by him and having received his command, the initiate himself should eat. Thereafter, he should worship the *cakra* according to the extent of his available means.
Since that which has been performed without performing the sacrifice to the Guru is as if unperformed,
therefore the sacrifice to the Guru must be performed with effort according to one's capacity.
For even if the Guru is not present there, he is to be worshipped by forming a mental resolve as before.
That substance should then be used for the rites of the deity or among the devotees.
This occasional (naimittika) rite is divided into [festivals] such as the Parvan and the Pavitra.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter of the Śrī Tantrāloka.
Now, the secret ritual procedure is taught here with reference to the qualified practitioner;
furthermore, this entire system of worship is explained according to the Kula method,
which is appropriate for those gurus and disciples who have ascended the stream [of realization].
And it has been stated by the Supreme Lord regarding the essential nature of the sequential worship (kramapūjana):
"That which occurs for one who is engaged in the Siddhakrama in a single month would not occur even in thousands of years through various multitudes of mantras."
The family (*kula*) of the Supreme Lord consists of power, capacity, loftiness, sovereignty, vigor, and vitality; it is the aggregate, consciousness itself as the body.
For one who perceives all classes of beings as being thus [identical with that], [all things are seen as such].

For one whose entire mass of doubts has been destroyed, the sacrifice is of that very nature. Whatever a hero may perform by way of mind, speech, and body for the sake of establishing that form, that is remembered as the *kulayāga*.

"Externally in the Śakti, in the couple (yāmala), in the body, on the path of the vital breath (prāṇa), and in the intellect— thus the worship of Kula is sixfold, distinct for each division. That which consists of bathing, the maṇḍala, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and so forth, as well as the sixteen-fold deposition (nyāsa) and the like, is not that [true worship]."
Nothing here would be of use, nor would anything that has been done serve to refute us.
In the *Traiśirasa* doctrine, the Kaula is said to be free from the six mandalas, devoid of all obscurations, and consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.

In this sacrifice, whatever substance is prohibited in the continuous tradition of the scriptures, that very thing the wise man should employ, saturated with the nectar of the Left (vāmāmṛta). It is also stated in the venerable Brahmayāmala: "Externally, wine is the essence of Śiva."
Without her, there is neither enjoyment nor liberation; yet that [liberation] cannot be achieved by means of flour, honey, or molasses.
She, appearing in the forms of woman, neuter, and man, bestows both prior and subsequent enjoyment.
But the supreme splendor arising from the grape is Bhairava himself, free from all conceptual construction.

This very essence is pure, consisting of light, bliss, and consciousness; it is eternally dear to the deities, therefore one should always drink this. And in the *Śrīmatkramarahasya*, it was described by the Supreme Lord:
The vessel of honor (arghapātra), the sacrificial abode, and the lamp—these three are so called.
In the Kaulika sacrifice, this is the secret: therein, the honor-offering arises from union with Śakti;
and the abode, known as Earth, Cloth, Body, and Seat, possesses excellence in successive order.
"Lamps arise from ghee, for cows are known as deities dwelling upon the earth;
knowing this triad, the Kaulika should be diligent in these three.
Thus, having understood the preeminence of the arghya vessel, [Śambhu taught] the ritual substances.
Regarding those things which have been stated, one should be free from doubt here, for doubt is indeed a defiler.
Having entered the sacrificial chamber, rich with perfumes and incense, facing either east or north,
one should [proceed] with the Parā or the Mālinī, both in reverse and in direct order.
One should perform the purification consisting of burning and nourishing, according to the distinction between the radiant and the gentle,
either sequentially or by means of the Mātṛsadbhāva mantra.
If one intends to perform initiation, one should then carry out the conceptual placement of the paths to be purified.

Then, by means of power alone, one should lead the objects to be purified to the state of immortality (amṛtatva). Alternatively, [the mantras] may be enclosed within the *parā* [mantra], or enclosed within the *mātṛkā*, or simply the *mālinī*; these are used in all ritual acts.
One should fill the vessel for the honor-offering (arghapātra) with substances that are the causes and fruits of bliss;

through identification with the mantra taught therein, one should bring it to the state of being Bhairava himself. By means of that, one should make oneself completely full, both internally and externally, extending to the primary and secondary wheels (cakras).
One should satisfy [the deities] with drops [of nectar] above and below, and by drinking from within.
Likewise, because of the force of the surging state of one's own mental activity, whose mass of rays is full,
one who desires to see such a self externally should perform external worship.
Then, on an auspicious red cloth twelve finger-breadths wide— or twice or thrice that size—
on a sky-blue cloth beautiful with vermilion,
or one bearing lapis lazuli; or else in a vessel made of coconut or other materials, filled with wine.
Or else, when the form has arisen and the mandala is established, the wise one should perform the sacrifice; the sequence for this is stated as follows:
in the northern direction, from the northeast corner to the northwest, [one worships] Gaṇeśvara.
One should worship Vaṭuka, the three Gurus, the Siddhas, the Yoginīs, and the Pīṭha. Then, starting from beneath Gaṇeśa in the eastern direction,
one should worship the circle of Siddhas (Siddhacakra) in the four directions, ending at the spot below Gaṇeśa.
Khagendra, together with Vijjāmbā and Illāīambā;
Vaktṛṣṭi, pure and joined by Anantamekhalāmbā, [is worshipped] first;
Kūrma, with the Śakti Maṅgalā and Illāīambā.
In the south are Jaitra, Avijita, and Sānandamekhala;
Kāmamaṅgala with Meṣa and Kullāīmbā;
and on the other side, Vindhya, Ajita, and Mekhalā along with Ajarā.
Macchanda, Kuṅkuṇāmbā, and the six pairs [of deities] who hold authority;
in the north, from Marutta to the end of Īśāna, such is the second row.
These six are, in order: Amaravara, Devacitra, Ali, Vindhya, and Guḍikā.
Śillā, Eruṇā, Kumārī, Bodhā,
Samahālacchī, and Aparamekhalā— these are the six Śaktis. Indeed, these are the authorized ones who are to be worshipped, for whom this [tradition] has many divisions.
The lineage is uninterrupted, diverse, and consisting of disciples and grand-disciples;
it ends with Ānandāvalibodhiprabhu-pāda and then with Yogīśa. These are the *ovallis*, and these six constitute the sequence of the six mudrās.
From the right thumb to the little finger, and then from the left little finger;
[the sequence] ending at the twelve [petals], the upward-moving [Kuṇḍalinī], the Bindu, the Heart, the Navel, and the Kanda—these are the *chummās*.
Śavarāḍa, Billapaṭṭilla, Karabilla, Ambiśarabilla.
Aḍa, Bīḍa, Ombī, Dakṣiṇabilla, Kumbhārikā, and the one called Akṣara;
Devīkoṭṭa, Kulādri, Tripurī, Kāmākhya, and Aṭṭahāsa—
this is the group of six belonging to the Southern Seat (Dakṣiṇapīṭha), situated respectively in the Gharapallī seats.
Thus, if one who knows the secret signs wanders among the sacred seats (pīṭhas) desiring accomplishment,
he will before long obtain from the mouth of the Yoginī whatever is to be attained.
Bhaṭṭa, Indravalkala, Ahīndra, Gajendra, and Mahīdhara—

These six are those whose vital energy (retas) flows upwards, having abandoned the six stages of office (adhikāra). For office is the expansion of virility along the path of the Kula; because they lack that expansion, they are called "those whose retas flows upwards" (ūrdhvaretas).
And other wives of the Gurus, arisen from the lineage of the venerable Kālī,
who have not assumed a physical body, sport without hesitation through various bodies.
When their will is awakened in such a manner, the Kaula reality shines forth within that which is born therefrom.
In that state, such a nature is defined as "heaviness" (gurutva).
Because of those specific qualities, they are not to be worshipped, but should merely be remembered.
Then, from within that, [one should contemplate] Vāyu and Agni together with the Mātṛkā.

Mālinī is to be worshipped in sequence; then follows the internal wheel of mantras (mantracakra). That which resides within Kula—consisting of mantra, the perfected ones (siddhas), vital breath, consciousness, and the senses—is the sovereign Consciousness whose nature is the wheel; she is declared here to be the Mistress of Kula (Kuleśvarī).

In the center is the venerable goddess Śrīparā, whose nature is the true essence of the Mothers (mātṛsadbhāva). She is to be worshipped; then, through the superimposition of that [essence], she is Aparā and Parāparā.
She may be worshipped as the Solitary Heroine (ekavīrā), or else as the Mistress of the Kula (sakuleśvarā).
The power (śakti) should expand as it swells, while Bhairava is again full of radiant joy;
thus one should worship the couple through resting in the bliss of their union.
Like sparks from consciousness whose nature is great light, [the emission proceeds].
One should worship that very mass of rays here as the host of deities.
Having worshipped the inner group of twelve, then the group of eight times eight (sixty-four),
or the group of four, or as one desires— what limit indeed can there be to the number of rays?
Māheśī, Vairiñcī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī are in the four cardinal directions;
Aindrī, Yāmyā, Muṇḍā, and Yogeśī are in the corners starting from the northeast.
Then, in this group of eight, the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora and ending with Pavana are assigned respectively.
Having worshipped that which has become a couple (yāmali) with a vision of the bliss of their union,
this very same rite is prescribed even in the ritual of the sixty-four [deities] (aṣṭāṣṭaka), though it is elaborated in many ways under various names; there,
the garland of lamps should be of that same number.
In the *Śrīratnamālāśāstra*,
however, the wise one should count the number of syllables of the Vidyā that is primarily to be worshipped as illuminating lamps;
or else, one should perform the worship of the Kula together with the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), fields (*kṣetra*), and so forth.
Just as it was taught by the Supreme Lord in the illustrious Mādhavakula:

"One should worship the fourfold sequence of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the Nameless, together with the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and cremation grounds (śmaśānas), for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation. (56–57)
One should then remember this supreme rite of the Lord pertaining to the body known as the *pīṭha*, as a placement (*nyāsa*) for oneself, or for the Power (*śakti*), or for the Wheel (*cakra*).
[Specifically: Aṭṭahāsa at the location of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and Caritra in the aperture of the head (*karandhra*).
In the two ears is Kaulagiri, and in the two nostrils is Jayantikā;
in the eyebrows is Ujjayinī, in the mouth is Prayāga, and again in the heart is Vārāṇasī; on the pair of shoulders is the Śrīpīṭha, and in the throat is Viraja.
Eḍābhī is in the stomach, Hālā in the navel, and Gośruti in the *kanda*; Marukośa is in the genitals,
and Nagara and Pauṇḍravardhana are in the thighs and the right and left hips respectively.
Kuḍyākeśī is at the staircase, as is Māyāpūkṣīrakā;
likewise, Jānujaṅghā is at the pair of ankles, and Āmrātā is at the pair of shanks.
Vairiñcī is at the support of the feet, extending down to Kālāgnidārikā.
"I am not this, nor does another exist; I am solely the powers.
One should cultivate this impression at all times through mere remembrance.
No lunar day, no asterism, and no fasting is prescribed [for this].

One who delights in worldly pleasures shall indeed achieve success through constant recollection. In this ninefold sacrifice, the beloved wives of the outcaste, the blacksmith, the butcher, the bow-maker, the leather-worker, the sword-smith, the miner, the fisherman, and the oil-presser constitute the nine [offerings].

Saṅgama, Varuṇā, Kula, Giri, Aṭṭahāsa, Jayantī, Caritra, Āmraka, Koṭṭa, and Haimapura shall be the ninth; among these, Cakriṇī is the principal. In their midst, Kuṇḍalinī crushes the seed by means of the division of juice and husk.
The leader of the three-and-a-half seats, residing in the *kanda*, revolves everywhere.
Having thus worshipped the emergence of the wheels, the Mistress of the Kula is to be worshipped in the center;
at the very end of that is Saṅkarṣiṇī, who effects both withdrawal and nourishment.
The Solitary Heroine (Ekavīrā), joined with the Wheel (Cakra), or even situated in union with the Wheel— these one should worship in groups of three,
starting from the directions of Īśāna, Indra, Agni, Yama, Kravyād, Kubera, Vāyu, and Varuṇa,
conjoined with the three future deities of their respective triads.
The heart, Kuṇḍalinī, and the space between the eyebrows— these three in sequence are the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*). They are the field-born (*kṣetrabhava*) assembly of Sadyoginīs,
elevated by eight finger-breadths, circular at the top, and slender in the middle.
One should prepare lamps with red wicks and clarified butter for the ears and eyes;
or else, one should worship whatever practice is performed in the center. "Non-duality alone, not duality"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, the mantras taught in the Siddhānta, Vaiṣṇava, and other systems are possessed of impurity.
Because they cannot endure that [supreme] splendor, they become lifeless here in this non-dual reality.
[The ritual involves] the jar, the binding of the eyes, and so forth, as well as the mandala, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the fire.
Having abandoned [other rites] here, success is found in the midst of the vessel of fine liquor; one should worship Kṛśā in the center.
For one performing this sacrifice day and night, on the following day, once the feast of heroes (vīrabhojya) has been provided, the mantras necessarily succeed without effort.
In this sacrifice called "Bringer of Fortune," one should recite the *Pīṭhastotra* here. Alternatively,
the wise practitioner should worship in due order the deities in the form of couples, who are heroic in nature, free from worldly conventions, and beyond all formal conduct.
Then, the Lord of Kula, though being himself one alone,
may satisfy as many powers as there are through the union of the couple (*yāmala-yoga*), like the one who possesses universal form.
In the consciousness consisting of light, there can be no such thing as succession.
For the non-existence of consciousness does not exist at all; therefore, there is no [fixed] time for its satiation.
In this sequence, because the tree of duality has been uprooted along with its roots, any discussion regarding the seat (āsana) is not appropriate as something separate;
for the Supreme Lord rests within the very domain of His own powers.
Then, the recitation (japa) should be performed according to the divisions of three hundred thousand and so forth;
this has been stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra*, and it is of a manifold nature.
At the time of emergence, union, and subsidence, the recitation is said to consist of three hundred thousand [utterances].

In the *āsya*, *gamāgama*, the *sūtra* called *haṃsa*, and the pair of *śaiva*—these five are said to consist of five hundred thousand [recitations]; one should perform a fire oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that amount.
In the *netra*, *gamāgama*, *vaktra*, *haṃsa*, and the *akṣasūtraka*—[the same applies].

In the union of Śiva and Śakti, the recitation (japa) is said to consist of six hundred thousand [units]. O beautiful lady, the sevenfold recitation is traditionally taught as being performed in the eyes, in the coming and going [of breath], in the ears, in the *haṃsa*, in the mouth, in the hands, and in the pair [of arms].
The eyes are at the two entrances and exits, the ears, the mouth, the secret place, and the private organ;
O beautiful lady, these are situated in the hundred-spoked and thousand-spoked wheels.
This is the recitation consisting of one hundred thousand repetitions of Rudra, and the fire-oblation here is one-tenth of that amount.

One should practice twice over the eyes, the path of coming and going, the ears, the mouth, the interior of the *brahmabila*, the breasts, the hands, the feet, and the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*). Wherever the eye has gone, and wherever the mind has gone— 88–89a.
There, the *haṃsa* is to be practiced twice, consisting of expansion and contraction.
That is the Self, the Goddess Mātṛkā, Śiva established within the body;
therefore, one should not entertain the conceptual construction that "He is one and I am another."
For one who wavers, both spiritual accomplishment and liberation are very far away.
Now, when the movement of the vital breath has reached sixteen hundred thousand [breaths] as previously described,
the abandonment of pure and impure conceptual constructions is called "solitude" (ekānta).
Abiding there, he himself performs both the oblation and the recitation.
Recitation is the activity of internal discourse, whose nature is the reflective awareness of the primordial sound (*nāda*).
The dissolution of that which is thus reflected upon into the fire of consciousness is proclaimed as the oblation (*homa*).

The "contemplation" (āmarśa) previously mentioned consists of twelve goddesses; among them, the two final consciousnesses constitute the act of offering (āhuti) in the form of dissolution. The other ten serve as the means for that [dissolution], and thus they constitute the "tenfold portion" (daśāṃśatā) in the fire-sacrifice (homa).
The illustrious Śambhunātha, the moon for the ocean of the meaning of the Trika,
gave this instruction: when he performs worship together with an external Śakti,
then this secret procedure taught by the Supreme Lord is said to be [the one to be followed].
It is stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra*: "One should maintain steadfastness in celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
bliss is the supreme Brahman, and that resides within the body in three ways.
Among these, two are auxiliary, while the other is the fruit consisting of that [bliss] itself. (97–98a)
One who practices with the three [consonants] ending in the labial is called a celibate (brahmacārī).
Those who avoid that are like cattle, devoid of bliss;
those who perform the wheel-sacrifice (cakrayājaka) while avoiding that [practice] have artificial bliss as their food.
"Both go to the terrifying Raurava hell;

such is the characteristic of power (śakti), for it is non-different from that which possesses it (tadvat). Therefore, one should perform that [initiation] in such a manner, without regard for caste and so forth. (AbhT 29.100–101)
Due to the union with both the worldly and the trans-worldly natures, and because of the superior identity [between them],
that [power] is said in the teaching of the Guru to be threefold— arising as effect, cause, or simultaneously—
and it is further threefold as being direct, indirect, or equal to those.
In the *Śrīsarvācārahṛdaya*, this very point is summarized:
"These six powers have been declared to bestow the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.
Through two of them, however, come emanation and withdrawal; therefore, their union is supreme. (103–104a)
Having brought her [the Śakti] and having worshipped each other mutually, they should satisfy one another.
Through the very sequence of the inner limbs (antaraṅga), there is the worship of the primary wheel (mukhyacakra);
for that which is a mass of bliss is indeed the inner limb of consciousness.
That [wheel] is the primary one; the others are subordinate wheels (anucakra).

It is called *cakra* because of its expansion (*vikāsa*), its satisfaction (*tṛpti*), its severing of bonds (*pāśotkartana*), and its power of action (*kṛti-śakti*). Indeed, it is said that the word *cakra* is derived from the roots *kas* (to shine), *cak* (to move), *kṛt* (to cut), and *kṛ* (to do).
Sacrifice and libation are said to be external; that is proclaimed as "expansion" (vikāsa).

[This occurs] from what is conceived by the possessor of power (śaktimat) within the primary wheels (cakra) and subordinate wheels (anucakra), or from the consumption of that which flows with bliss through the vital breath (prāṇa). // 107–108 //
Through the external offering of perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth, there occurs an overflowing of consciousness;
in this manner, with portions of objects appropriate to themselves,
the two [the teacher and the disciple] should perform mutual satiation within the secondary wheels for the sake of achieving oneness with the primary wheel.

And it is said in the *Triśirastantra*: "The sphere of the pure seat (*vimalāsana*) is situated in the midst of the six senses; one should enter the station of Rudra within that very place, while contemplating one's own essential nature as it unfolds through the full expansion of its respective enjoyments. (AbhT 29.110b–111b)
Gradually, the goddesses of the subordinate wheels (anucakra) enter the central wheel of consciousness;
for they abandon the body of another who is established in his own self, since [the central consciousness] remains there. Thus, that egoistic subject is neither full nor does it overflow.
Having attained vigor through the filling of the rays whose nature is the deities of the secondary wheels,
that pair of Power (Śakti) and the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān) becomes mutually oriented toward one another;
that pair experiences an agitation born from the contact of entering the upper abode.
It agitates even the subordinate wheels (*anucakra*), which at that time are identical with it and not separate. Thus,
when this couple (*yāmala*) exists as one in which all talk of duality has dissolved,
that very consciousness— through its union with the gradations of the sequence— is indeed the friction of emission (*visarga*).

That supreme abode of the Pole Star, which is both the world and the noble bliss of the Self, is neither quiescent nor arisen; it is the Supreme Kaula, the cause that gives birth to both the quiescent and the arisen. One who desires the unconditioned state should always make that consciousness one's own.
For the form of the Goddess of Consciousness is, in the ultimate sense, indeed uninterrupted;
by means of discourse concerning the dissolution of states arising from such and such tranquility, the fortunate one enters the uninterrupted, naturally emitted (vaisargika) abode. 118–119a.

The pair consisting of the quiescent and the emergent arises simultaneously as the power and the possessor of power. The emergent form resides in the abode of the other, while the quiescent resides in its own self.
In reality, both together constitute the couple (*yāmala*); thus, what is called "emergent" is also quiescent.
In the same way, Śakti nourishes the appropriate creation, but not its possessor (tadvān),
even though there is an equilibrium in the union of the reflective awareness of both forms— namely, the quiescent and the emergent.
Therefore, in the scripture, Śakti is described as having a central state that is fully radiant.
In that very [lineage], the Guru should properly transmit the Kula-essence;
by means of that, he should transmit it among men according to the stated sequence. Then he said: "[transmitting it] as one who is permeated by a state of being superior to his own body."
The venerable Lord Kallaṭa has spoken this statement for the sake of attaining all goals:
"That primary wheel, which is the mouth of the Yoginīs, was taught by Maheśvara.
From that [wheel] comes this tradition; from it, knowledge is obtained.
This very [reality] is said to be unwritable, because it resides within the mouth [of the teacher] and is transmitted from mouth to mouth through the logic of liberation.
How can one's own consciousness—the primary wheel—be written down?
Now, those who contemplate this twofold creation within the abode of the quiescent and the emergent, [attain the goal]. (AbhT 29.125b–126b)
Those who, established in that unconditioned state where the existence of emission resides in the East,
desire to attain perfection, should then take up the form that has arisen;
they should worship with that very form, which is the most pure essence due to its proximity to consciousness.
And that [Kula] is indeed mutual, for it is said to reside in the mouth by virtue of the primary speaker;
it is the supreme Kula, intent on bestowing the state of being ageless and immortal.
Even those who have not yet attained full awakening are firmly established in the sacrifice that has blossomed forth.
The deities situated upon the wheel imagined therein attain consciousness.

Within that wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), by means of that very essence consisting of the flavor of bliss, [they pervade] externally in the four directions, beginning with Gaṇanātha, according to the prescribed order. All of this—

Having worshipped the pair of Kuleśas in the central position, [he should worship] the goddesses in the three circles. Then, on the outside, at each spoke, he should indeed worship the wheel of rays (*raśmicakra*) consisting of four,
eight, and sixty-four [spokes], worshipping them in sequence in various ways, O Sage.
In the very same way, one should practice worship within the abode located in one's own body;
by practicing that tranquil form through the realization of the heart,
one indeed attains the tranquil state of Śiva, which resembles an ocean whose waves have subsided.
Due to their abiding in that state of peace, the entire host of deities situated within the wheel remains with its functions ceased,
resting upon the void and devoid of bliss;
even those who possess the nature of the subordinate wheels, such as sight and the rest, are likewise dependent upon that [state].
Therefore, immersed in bliss, he remains longing for bliss;
for this multitude of rays of the senses remains devoid of its own nature until it encounters the supreme essence,
and thus it is turned toward the attainment of its true nature.
Through the process of chewing upon external objects which are filled with one's own essence by means of the relish of longing,
one attains a certain abode of rest within oneself and then offers that [rest] back to one's own self;
through this offering of one's own object, there arises a downpour of fully surging consciousness.

With his vigor stirred by the fulfillment of the hosts of deities of the subordinate wheels, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara) also surges forth with impetuosity according to the previously stated reasoning. Thus, the emission is threefold; likewise, the friction is described as emergent and quiescent.
"From which the manifold creation issues forth, and wherein creation ceases—
this has been declared in the *Śrītattvarakṣaṇa*, the *Śrīnigama*, and the *Triśiromata*:
the sacrificial pit is Śakti, Śiva is the liṅga, and their union is the supreme state."
In the *Gama*, emanation and withdrawal occur through two [channels], while their emission is threefold.
It consists of the awakening of the wheels above and below until the end of the two currents,
as well as rest, immersion, and likewise the vital breaths within the channels.

Śiva eternally brings about the union of the movements and arrivals within the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍīs*), the joints, and even the vital points (*marmans*) of the body, which has transcended all divisions, as well as within the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*).
Through that effort, one should always abide in the union within the state of Bhairava;
that is characterized by the attainment of the formless state of both.
It is devoid of the division of measures (mātrā) and clearly illuminates the manifest reality.
One should practice the realization of pure being by turning away from all objective phenomena.
Having restrained both the sun and the moon through the path of dissolution and distraction,
that which arises in the abode of the attainment of immersion into the threefold reflective awareness— [that is the true state].
Sound, whose essence is the touch of consciousness, is itself the potency (*vīrya*) of mantra here.
One who is eager to obtain such a fruit as has arisen therein,
if he remains constantly contemplating his own mantra, truly knows the arising of mantra.

In this very state, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) upon the arrival of the consciousness of oneness within the subordinate wheels (*anucakra*). Through the very function of *nāda*, the manifold expansion of a hundred thousand divisions occurs simultaneously. Furthermore, in the *Śrīyogasañcara*, it is said that this supreme mudrā is beloved by the Yoginīs.
In the lotus that covers the mandala which is eternally oriented toward the interior of the three corners,
there is a stalk never separated [from it], its excellent root joined with a sixteen-petaled lotus.
By means of the friction produced by the pair of lotuses strung upon the central stalk, [the fire arises] in the southeast.
From the friction of the mass of digits of the full, beautiful moon situated in the center with the sun, and from the contact of the red,

three-petaled vitality-digit (vīrya-kalā) in the center, there is the sprout, which is emanation (sṛṣṭi). Thus, by the mudrā of the friction of the moon, the lord of the day, and Citragu, [emanation arises] instantaneously.
Bringing the sequence beginning with emission (sṛṣṭi) to an end within, one attains stability in the Fourth state (turya) during the immersion into the Khecarīmudrā of the mutual Śakti and Śaktimat.
This occurs in drinking, enjoyment, play, laughter, and so forth, that which consists of reflective awareness (vimarśamaya).
Through the unmanifest sound, resonance, *sphoṭa*, audible sound, resonance, and the end of resonance—
[these] being of the nature of the uninterrupted *anāhata*— there arises the potency (*vīrya*) of that mantra. Thus,
established upon the eight wheels and performing the innate recitation (*sahajajapa*) in the supreme abode, [one attains the goal].
One attains that state of the eight Bhairavas, which is differentiated by the eight kalās,
during the going and coming [of breath], at the conclusion [of the process], in the ears, in the eyes,
and in the union of the two genders; likewise in the yoga of their conjunction, in what is called the end of the body, and in the yāmala-cakra.
That which is indistinct, moving from the region of the breasts, the middle of the chest, and the heart up to the lips and reaching the throat,
and which is heard between those two wheels at the moment when agitation ceases— therein they find rest; and thus is the supreme eightfold Nāda-Bhairava.
That supreme pervasion consisting of mantra is said to be produced by light, sound, and breath.
It is free from all parts and even the slightest impurity; likewise, it is the void enriched with its digits (*kalā*) and the destroyer (*kṣapaṇaka*).
This pervasion, situated within the gutturals and labials, extends from the Moon up to the Transmental (*unmanā*).
Thus, remembering the all-pervasive nature in every single action, wherever it may be,
one who is eternally unstained and liberated while living becomes the Supreme Bhairava.
Such a person is someone whose body is fashioned from the bud of the *melaka* (union) even within the womb.
He has been declared to be a Yoginī-born Rudra, himself a vessel of gnosis;
for even as a child still in the womb, he is of the nature of Śiva according to the venerable Vīrāvaliśāstra.
This is because the essence is extracted from him, and he is that which is primary.
And because it is the primary sacrifice, this is remembered as the "First Sacrifice" (Ādiyāga).
In various scriptures, the All-pervasive Lord has praised its essential nature in the *Śrīvīrāvali*, the *Hārdeśa*, the *Khamata*, and the *Arṇava*.
By the grace of this couple, even one who is devoid of vows and yoga— whether in the Śrīsiddha, Utphulla, Maryādā, Hīna, Caryā, Kula,
and other [traditions]— should always maintain mindfulness and remain solely intent upon the primordial sacrifice (ādiyāga).

One should project the Vidyā and the Kūṭas in their proper sequence into one's own body, which is the embodiment of power (śakti). Having meditated upon the lotus as resembling the moon and oneself as having the radiance of the sun,
one should then unite the two seats, consisting of the Vidyā and the Mantra, right here.
It is not recited by me again in explicit words because of its secret nature;
however, one who is curious should discern it from the very thorough study of the taught scriptures. That which all always resort to, and that which the God and the Goddess possess—[that is this].
That supreme wheel brings about the presence [of the deity] at the beginning of the sacrifice to the Goddess and other rites.
(170) The body itself is the supreme *liṅga*, auspicious and consisting of all the *tattvas*;
it is the abode of worship, most excellent, as it is graced by the circle of deities. (171)
That very mandala is primary, consisting of three tridents, lotuses, wheels, and voids;
therein one should always worship the circle of deities, both externally and internally,
preceded by the reflective awareness of their respective mantras, with the fluids born from that [practice].
One should touch [the deity] with abundant bliss through the procedure of emanation and withdrawal.
By that touch, the Lord of the wheel of consciousness, awakened by its intensity,
attains the supreme abode once all the deities have been satisfied.

According to the procedure prescribed for the secondary sacrifice (*anuyāga*), one should satisfy [the deities] within by means of substances that captivate the heart, through the application of their respective reflective awareness (*kāmarśa*). Having made the ground of the support (*ādhāra-dharā*) washed by the sprinkling of the essence of wonder (*camatkṛti-rasa*), one should offer mentally gathered flowers of one's own nature, which abound with their own fragrance.
Day and night, in the temple of the body, I worship you, O God, together with the Goddess, by means of the priceless vessel of my own heart, which is overflowing with the nectar of bliss.
This very supreme sacrifice has been praised by the Moon-crested Lord in the collection of scriptures beginning with the *Śrīvīrāvalī* and the *Amayādā*.

Alternatively, by means of the very method previously described, the Guru should perceive the entire host of deities residing within the functions of the vital breath (prāṇa) and worship them right there. [He should worship] the goddesses supported by the vital breath through the various [channels] beginning with the Brahma-nāḍī.
The satisfaction [of the deities] occurs through the lunar wheel of the apāna entering via the apertures of the ears.
In this way, by means of the sequence of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, one should satisfy the host of deities;
then, through their grace, one soon attains the accomplishments of knowledge (jñānasiddhi).

The circle of goddesses, established in pure consciousness alone, should be gratified by the wise man through the offering of consciousness and by means of the enjoyment of the universe, because of its reflection within that consciousness.
In that [state], all things go to dissolution and the accumulations of the principles (tattvas) are consumed.
Behold that funeral pyre situated within the body, blazing with a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction, in this cremation ground of the nature of emptiness frequented by yoginīs and siddhas—
a place of play, most terrible, where all formal structures have set.
