"Who, having entered the support of all the deities, would not attain perfection?
Thus spoke Bhairavī in the venerable *Vīrāvalīśāstra*.
Having first performed the sacrifice in this manner, one who possesses such fitness [should proceed].
In such a sequence, he should initiate that disciple who has completed one hundred thousand [recitations].
Having sprinkled him with the power of Rudra (rudraśakti), he should place him near the deity. Beholding his two arms, he should inflame them with the power of Rudra.

With that very [flower], he should place a flower upon his two hands, which have been smeared with perfume. Having placed those two hands of his so that they are without support, he should contemplate them being drawn upward by the power of Rudra, which has the form of a blazing hook.

Then, having himself taken a cloth, he should have his eyes bound; and he himself should cast a flower, and from its falling, one should discern his *kula*. Then, having uncovered his face, one should cause him to prostrate at the feet [of the teacher].
One should worship the circle of goddesses on his hands and also upon his head.
By means of the relationship of the attractor and the attracted, and that of the impeller and the impelled,
it is stated in the *Śrīratnamālā* that the navel is enclosed within the staff.
Adorned with ornaments on the left arm and leg, and likewise decorated by the hip,
one should apply the weapon-mantra of exhortation (*codanāstra*) into the hand of the disciple who holds flowers;
until he reaches a state of trembling, it will fall of its own accord upon his head.
This very Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) produces immediate conviction.
By this very procedure, the Guru should have the disciple take the sacrificial pap (caruka) and the tooth-stick; their falling is exactly as previously described.

One should observe therein the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of such a kind— distinguished as intense, mild, and so forth— from the moment the blindfold is placed on the eyes until the taking up of the tooth-stick. (196–197)
Thus, this person is declared a *samayin* (one bound by the pledges) in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra) by means of the trembling of the hand.
However, in the *Śrībhogahastaka*, it is said that one becomes a *samayin* through the paralysis of the hand (*karastobha*).
Or rather, the Guru should give [the sacrament] like a sacrificial oblation (*caru*), drenched with the nectar of the left (*vāmāmṛta*).
By receiving [the teaching] without hesitation, one becomes a member of the Śakti-lineage (śaktigotra) who is freed from illusion (māyā). However,
one who receives it while trembling becomes a Samayin, [fit for] recitation and so forth,
provided that after some time he purifies the paths (adhvan) through the observance of his established commitments (samaya).
The venerable Ānandeśvara says that such a person is a "vessel for accomplishment" (siddhipātra). When one is to make someone a spiritual son (putraka), then one should perform initiation.
It is stated in the Śrī Ratnamālā: [one should contemplate] the letters from *na* to *pha*, possessing blazing luster.

One should perform the deposition up to the topknot; by that, [the disciple] falls down, and such is the sequence here. For the consecrated child, upon whom the path of the elements to be purified has been deposited as prescribed, and who stands with a straight body, one should contemplate the Power (Śakti) having arrived from the feet to the top of the head.
The Guru, becoming absorbed in that [state], should contemplate [the goddess] as blazing and burning away the fetters (pāśas).
Then, having sat down, he should contemplate her burning in sequence, starting from the root to be purified and ending at the limit of the internal purification.
In this manner, all the principles (tattvas) and so forth are to be purified as previously described.
Having burned them away, the yogi should meditate upon them as dissolved either in the Niṣkala or the Sakala Śiva.
When joined to the path by the yogi, there is the nourishment of that which is of the same nature.
It acts and utterly consumes the entire multitude of distinct classes [of impurities].
For the disciple being purified by this [initiation],
through the various intensities of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), the bodies— whether internal, external, vital breath, consciousness, or space— are [transformed].
Entering [the body], the power of Rudra gradually produces this fruit:
bliss, arousal, trembling, sleep, and a whirling sensation within the body.
Thus, for the self whose bonds have been stunned and who has been united with Śiva, [these signs arise].

One should perform the emission (*sṛṣṭi*) directed toward the remaining enjoyments, which has reached the completely purified reality (*tattva*). Alternatively, if someone does not undergo such an immersion (*āveśa*), [the teacher] should burn him with the aforementioned power both externally and internally; thus he shall fall to the ground.
But one whose [doubt] persists even in this way should not be abandoned here, like a corrupted [text].
Now, I shall describe the initiation with conviction (sapratyayā dīkṣā),
taught by the Lord Śambhunātha and seen in the *Sadbhāvaśāsana* by the wise one who is satisfied.

Sudhā, agni, marut; manda, para, kāla, agni, vāyu; vahnī, saudhā, asu, kūṭa, agni, vāyu—all these, together with their respective sixth letters, are said to be three clusters that effect *stobha* (arrest or paralysis) individually.
That which is known as the seed-syllable of Śakti should be placed upon all the limbs.
The mantra, adorned with the twelve vowels, is to be placed in the heart-cakra.
In its center is consciousness, resembling the hibiscus flower.
One should meditate upon that wheel impelled by the wind and illuminated by fire,
and recite the mantra through the method of interspersing it with the [disciple's] name;
within half a blink of an eye, the disciple will undoubtedly experience a state of paralysis (stobha).
O Goddess, when he is joined to each reality (tattva), he beholds the Self;
but when he has reached the supreme reality, then he does not see it.
By this sequential yoga, he perceives the entire path.

Alternatively, he may cause [the disciple] to grasp all the scriptures at that very moment. For one who is subject to the power of fitness, the yogi who has attained perfection should perform initiation according to the specific rule for each principle (tattva) by means of the prescribed practice of those principles.
Thus, for this seeker of liberation who has been duly initiated,
the Kula-krama-iṣṭi, endowed with five states, should be prescribed for his remaining conduct,
so that consciousness may remain unfailing throughout the states of waking and the rest.

Likewise, the Kula-sacrifice (kulayāga), which resides in the mouth of the Yoginī, should be taught. Everything that is to be performed while awake should be done in the dream state individually for each mantra.
Having withdrawn [the mantras] during sleep, there is that which is called the Root (mūla), augmented by its own power.
In the fourth state, there is only one called the Messenger (Dūtī), while in that which transcends it, there is the Mistress of the Kula.
Thus proceeds the worship for those who are fully perfected by their own power.
And the [states] beginning with "Established in the Body" (Piṇḍasthā) and ending with "Transcending All" (Sarvātītā), as previously described, [are also included].
One should explain to him the five states, distinguished as previously described. For the seeker who desires worldly enjoyment, there is the formal consecration for yoga;
having worshipped the Lord there with riches, [one should fashion] a flawless image made of gold or other materials.
One should kindle eight lamps, filling them with ghee and red wicks;
they should be worshipped by means of the eight families (kulāṣṭaka), as well as the two Lords of the Families (kuleśvarau) within the conch,
which is filled with the nectar of bliss, according to the path taught in the *Śivahasta*.
With that [substance], he should subsequently consecrate him; he [the disciple] should then perform the practice for the realization of the mantra.
This is the consecration of the teacher, which carries with it authority;
he should prepare sixty-four lamps made of flour and other materials for him.
They should be worshipped with eight times eight [offerings], and in the center, as before, the two Lords of the Kula;
by the very method taught for the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), one should also consecrate the Guru.
Thus, these two are consecrated by the entire host of yogis.

Once these two have been recognized there, the Guru shall be the bestower of liberation. This is the essential meaning of this quarter-verse: he who was previously the practitioner becomes the Guru, and he fully grants the supernatural powers (*siddhis*); another [Guru] grants liberation.

To these two, one should fully explain all three kinds of knowledge and bestow one's own command regarding the performance of their respective duties. That which is known as the hexad of causes, as well as he who is Supreme Śiva—
Together with Bhairavanātha, that group of eight has been proclaimed.
Perceiving the universal nature of each one of them as residing within its own function,
the Guru should transfer that [consciousness] into whichever sense organ it may be— be it the eye or any other.
That very [initiation] is considered the supreme consecration by means of full jars;
it is stated in the *Śrīvīrāvalibhairava* that this occurs even without external [implements].
However, for one who desires immediate enjoyment, the most accomplished Guru [bestows it] through yoga.
One should perform the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣaṇa), which immediately bestows the desired fruit. This initiation by piercing has been described in various ways in different places;
it must be performed by one who possesses mastery through practice, so that [the soul] enters higher and higher [levels].
A firm realization of the piercing of the wheels (*cakrasaṃbheda*) arises in the disciple,

by which the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and others are proclaimed in the *Śrīmālā*. When the state of the upper wheel is not attained, that [realization] is merely a possession by a *piśāca*.
The piercing initiation (*vedhadīkṣā*) is taught by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Gahvara* as being sixfold, consisting of Mantra, Nāda, Bindu, Śakti, Bhujaṅgama, and Parā.
[One should visualize] the wheel of eight spokes and so forth, filled with flames, as described in one's own scripture.
Having meditated thus, by means of piercing his heart-center with that [mantra], there occurs the piercing of the mantra. Then, having projected the form in nine ways upon the body,
one should transfer it to the disciple through the yoga of projection as a blazing, great radiance.
"Then, through the paralysis of the bonds (pāśastobha), there is his union with the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
Thus, the procedure taught by Śambhu has been seen by me in the Dīkṣottara.
By means of the utterance of Nāda, that which is called Nāda [is established] through the application of the sequence of emanation."

One should pierce the mind with the *nāda*; this is declared to be the piercing by *nāda*. O Great Goddess, the mind, situated in the place of the *bindu* and established on the path between the eyebrows, or else at the target of the heart, [should perceive] the *bindu* whose radiance is filled with flames.
By means of that, one should awaken the sādhya; this is proclaimed as the one called Bindu (the Point).

O beautiful one, through the upward movement of the empowered (śaktimat) from the empowered (śākta), by means of the upward movement of the scent (gandha), [one perceives] the crooked one (kuṭila) in the form of a coil, seated upon the throne of the Śṛṅgāṭaka.
Having uttered it without utterance, one should pierce the entire universe;
thus, by means of the "bee-piercing" (bhramaravedha), the piercing of power (śāktavedha) is described.
And that very supreme power is the one that causes bliss to blossom.
Adorned with five hoods, she departs from the place of birth;

she consists of the fivefold nature of the *kalās*, the *tattvas*, the [faces] beginning with Nanda, the voids (*vyoma*), the *kulas*, the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, and the sense organs. 248–249ab. 249cd.

Thus, that [power], having emerged from the station of Brahmā in fivefold form, shines forth as it dissolves like lightning while entering the station of Brahmā. Having entered, it pierces the body and penetrates the self.
Thus has the piercing by the serpent (*bhujaṅgavedha*) been described in the Bhairava-āgama.
One should contemplate the mind until the mind has reached its dissolution.
O Goddess of the gods, when the mind is dissolved, that which is called supreme bliss (*parānanda*) arises.
It is neither the senses, nor the vital breaths, nor the domain of the internal organ;
it is not the mind, nor that which is to be thought, nor the thinker, nor the act of thinking.
That in which all states of being have utterly perished is declared to be the supreme piercing (paravedha).

Other gurus, who know the secrets, divide this Veda into nine parts according to the distinctions of human power, the world-form, the knower, the aggregate, the locus, the channel, and the supreme. [This occurs] within a triangular mandala joined with the mass of fire-syllables containing the womb of Māyā.
Having meditated upon that [flame] which is terrifying with its blazing form, one should pierce the knots;

one should strike with flowers and unite [the self] with the Supreme—this is the procedure known as Mantra. Having entered through either of the two channels, one should [place] consciousness in the abode of the *kanda*.
Having condensed [the breath] and whirled it about with force by means of the five- or eight-pointed crest,
one should forcibly direct it, having brought it to the tip of the spear of power (śaktiśūla), into some wheel.
This is the piercing by power (śākto vedhaḥ), which produces immediate conviction.
With the crest of flame, white as moonlight, issuing impetuously from the *ādhāra* and dissolving into the sky by way of the seat at the base of the disciple’s big toe, [the teacher],
having rendered the body translucent while recollecting the previously mentioned series of cities beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *na*, [should proceed].
Through the intense meditation on one's own maṇḍala, the piercing of the worlds is reflected.

Having meditated with identification upon some beautiful form within the abode of the Bindu arisen between the eyebrows, the teacher should subsequently make the disciple consist of that very essence.
Thus has the piercing of form (*rūpavedha*) been described; and here, that very form attains visibility. At the end, the disciple, having become one with it, attains union (*sāyujya*) with it.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is eightfold, consisting of the instruments known as the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*).

One should cause that [power] to circulate within the disciple by means of the sequence of the threads of their respective channels. This piercing known as "consciousness" (vijñāna-vedha), through the process of binding with firm conviction,
instantly brings about the rising of the sun of divine knowledge in the sky of the heart.
The *piṇḍa* is the supreme [self] consisting of *kalā*, subtle; the *puryaṣṭaka* is external and gross;
the *chāyātman* is known to be turned away, yet facing forward in a mirror and the like.
Thus, one should forcefully pacify this differentiation of the *piṇḍa* in each successive stage.

Through the piercing of the *piṇḍa*, by means of the gradual burning away of each respective [impurity], one reaches the supreme state. Whichever *cakra* exists within the body, having reached it and rested there in due order, one should cause that *cakra* to blaze; this is the piercing known as "of the place" (*sthānākhya*), which bestows its specific fruit.
There are three principal channels (nāḍīs), while others connected to them are innumerable.

Here, the piercing of the channels consists in unifying with those [others]; this produces its specific fruit. The flow of the desired channel occurs through the primary ones, which terminate in the eyes and other sense organs.
Through the piercing of the channels (*nāḍīvedha*), there occurs the attainment of a diverse and manifold awakening.
Like one possessing the strength of a tail’s form, the great yogi, having struck another channel enveloped by his own, forcibly brings down even a perfected being to the earth. (AbhT 29.269b–270)
Perceiving non-duality within all the wheels (*cakras*),
the Guru— who bestows the attainment of the state of Śiva— should effect the supreme Śiva through the supreme piercing (*paravedha*).
This has been described in this way in the venerable *Vīrāvalikula*.
One should know that which is entirely indivisible; having known the middle, one is not stained.
One who is perfected in the sequence of its division is a Guru and may liberate the bound souls (paśus). The disciple should enter before the Guru; he should pierce mouth with mouth.
When form [is merged] with form through the sense objects until they become of one flavor (*samarasībhavet*),
and when the mind has become of one flavor, there is the state of the Transmental (*aunmanasī*) for both. Through the movement of the Transmental in both, at that moment one becomes initiated.
When the moon and sun are conjoined, the individual soul (jīva) attains identity with that [reality].
Here, the gods beginning with Brahmā, desiring liberation,
restrain their own wheel of rays for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

If that [power] devours [the breath], it is proclaimed as the initiation of Śarva; this very state is declared to be liberation, motionless within all living beings. One should remove the vibration by means of the striking together of the digits of Agni and Soma.
The external breath, having gone outside through the connection with the form of darkness,
emerges through the pores of the skin and wanders by means of all the causal factors;
having established oneself in the middle which is beyond characteristics, one should cause it to wander and then release it.
By means of the yoga of friction and upward extraction, one should pierce the five knots;
one should contemplate the pair of functions of friction within the central abode. One should not practice the conjunction of the self, the void, the external mantra, and the body.
This initiation bestows the state of Śiva upon all living beings.
At the conclusion of the initiation, having cooked lamps together with all the practitioners,
the *caru*— which destroys even the greatest sins— should be consumed by the Kula teachers.
Thus, in the *Śrīratnamālā*, whatever procedure regarding deficiency or excess may occur, that itself constitutes a transgression; this [following] method for its pacification has been proclaimed.
On the following day, a sacrifice must be performed for the Guru, for [the rite] cannot proceed without it.
The ritual procedure does not reach completion; therefore, one should perform it with effort.
Whatever may please the Guru, that one should offer to him.
Within this practice of the wheel (cakracaryā), its procedure is called "wandering" (saṃcāra).
Having beheld the vessel of wine, perfectly full and held in the hand of the lord of heroes, one should drink it as the supreme Brahman by the command of the guru.
Having gratified the spirits, one should then offer it to the guru.

Having prostrated on the ground to the Guru and taken [the substance], one should satisfy the sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs); then, having honored one's own mantra, as well as the messenger (dūtī), Gaṇapati, the Gurus, the Guardian of the Field (kṣetrapa), and the assembly of heroes (vīrasaṅghāta) in the proper sequence beginning with the Guru; then—
One should drink the substance touched by a hero oneself, and never otherwise under any circumstances.
Those who do not know the Supreme Brahman, who are devoid of the knowledge of coming and going,
and who indulge in greed, delusion, pride, anger, passion, and deceit— [they are not fit].

One who desires his own welfare should not perform this together with them. At the beginning of a sacrifice, during the sacrifice, at the end of the sacrifice, during the worship of the Guru, and in the prescribed occasional rites, the disciple should carry out this procedure.
Thus has the secret procedure been thoroughly discussed, made perfectly clear through the experience of the teacher’s oral instructions.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Next, the collection of mantras appropriate for the practice is described, as it pertains to the sequence of the three lineages (*trikakula*).
For those whose intellects have not yet ascended to such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), this is taught in sequence for the sake of attaining that state.
For these awakened mantras possess reflective awareness as their sole essential nature;
by virtue of the sovereignty of the independent abode of consciousness, they consist of the power of agency.

The [deities] enter the teacher and, through the firm establishment of identity with him, they make him independent; even the instruments attain the status of the agent. In the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and in the fourfold beginning with Earth, [the seed-syllable is] *hrīṃ*.
They say that the four syllables are *kṣlāṃ*, *kṣvīṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *kṣam* in sequence.
*Haṃ* is in the stalk; likewise, *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *laṃ*, and *vaṃ* are in the four [petals] beginning with Dharma.
And *ṛṃ*, *ṝṃ*, *ḷṃ*, and *ḷḷṃ* occur in the [other] group of four in reverse order.
OṂ AUṂ HA—these three constitute the triad of Vidyā, Māyā, and Kalā;
the Anusvāra and Visarga belong to the two principles (tattva) of Vidyeśvara and Īśvara.
The letters from KA to BHA are in the filaments, and the Vital Breath (Prāṇa), conjoined with the eight vowels, is in the pericarp.
With the bindu, one's own name is illuminated upon the eight petals. For the nine powers, there should be *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* within the three mandalas.
One should arrange *kṣma* with the bindu for the Pretas, and *jra* upon the prongs of the trident.
In the worship of separate seats, these mantras are prescribed in sequence; however,
in the abbreviated worship,
one should take the first and the final seed-syllables and worship [the deities] starting from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) up to the prongs of the trident.

The mantra Ratiśekhara consists of fire (Ra), wind (Ya), earth (La), water (Va), with the sixth vowel (Ū) and the bindu (M). Its faces and limbs are formed by the short and long vowels. [The sequence is:
fire (Ra), breath (Ha), fire (Ra), withdrawal (Sa), time (Ma), Indra (La), water (Va), and wind (Ya).
The Navātman [mantra] consists of the six vowels together with the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and the crescent moon (*ardhacandra*), and so forth;
such is the pervasive expansion (*vyāpti*) according to the venerable Traiśirasa doctrine.
Then there are: casting away (*kṣepa*), seizing (*ākramaṇa*), awakening consciousness (*cidudbodha*), inflaming (*dīpana*), and establishing (*sthāpana*).
The realization of that [reality] and the attainment of it are designated by these names.
This much is proclaimed here as the "Great Pervasion" (*mahāvyāpti*) in its formal aspect;
its transformation and dissolution are called "salutation" (*namaskāra*).
This [mantra], deprived of the three syllables at the bottom and joined with the six long vowels,
should be used to fashion its six limbs, beginning with the heart, as well as its faces;
[these are formed] by the seeds *kṣaya*, *rava*, and *la*, which are radiant and adorned with the bindu.
The letter *jha*, with the withdrawal of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), accompanied by the sixth vowel and the bindu—
this is the abode of Bhairava, adorned with the half-moon and other ornaments.
The two mantras, Mātṛkā and Mālinī, have already been fully described.

The mantra for Gaṇeśa and the others consists of the syllable *oṃ*, followed by their names in the dative case, and then the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*) in that order; however, for those in whose case a seed-syllable (*bīja*) has not been prescribed,
it is the first letter of their name, illuminated by the vowel *ā*, the bindu, the crescent moon, and so forth.
That [syllable] is the fourteenth [letter] joined with the sixteenth for all the seed-syllables (bīja).
It is the invocation for the triad beginning with Aghorī, arranged in sequence;
it consists of the seed-syllables with the visarga, Māyā, Huṃ, the letter Ha, and the visarga.

Furthermore, there are three successive vocatives for the triad of goddesses; in the second word, the letter *e* is traditionally taught here as the substitute for the letter *ā*. Then follows the mantra of the two powers (*śakti*), wherein the final syllable is elided.

Both [the letters] *ha* and *agni* (ra) are joined with the five vowels, each separately. Joined with the vowel *a*, they form *astra* (phaṭ). Then *huṃ* and *ha* with the visarga (*haḥ*) are the *śara*.
Together with the *tāra* (oṃ), it consists of eight, three, and two and a half syllables.
This is the Vidyā of the goddess Parāparā in the Śrī Trika teaching;
it consists of syllables numbering five, six, five, four, two, three, and two. In the group of seven beginning with Aghorī, there is the remainder of Pivani.

In the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*, it is taught that the arrangement of the circle of deities (devatācakravinyāsa) is also prescribed for each individual phoneme; however, because of its great multiplicity, it is not recorded here. The mantra consisting of *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), the *visarga*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ* is of the nature of Aparā.
The supreme [power] has been described as the perfect pervasion; the individual soul (jīva), together with it, constitutes the fourteenth.
That [power], though diverse in its own nature and crowded with many arrangements, has been declared by the Great Lord in the *Triśiraḥśāstra* to possess manifold divisions. (27–28a)
In this context, the individual soul (jīva) resides within the vital breath (prāṇa), or the vital breath is situated within the individual soul;
they exist through the relationship of container and contained, by virtue of their inseparable connection.
One should contemplate the *Haṃsa* situated in the midst of nectar, differentiated by Kālarudra.
Joined with the head of Bhuvaneśa and conjoined with two Anaṅgas,
it should be known as more radiant than radiant when applied according to the sequence of the six cakras.
One should place the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the seat of the staff (daṇḍāsana), conjoined with the will of the secret power (guhyaśakti).
This other [mantra] has been declared as oral, by virtue of its nature as Great Knowledge (mahājñāna).
This supreme single-syllable knowledge, however, is clearly the Heart of Bhairava;
it is the pure nectar abiding in the void, or else it is joined with the Sāvitrī.

Endowed with the two voids, this supreme heart of Parā is well-known in the rite of the Couple; it should be performed by those who know reality. Furthermore, whatever other single-syllable [mantras] there may be, they should be used according to the procedure for the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra).
They are protected and most highly protected, yet they are devoid of limbs and noble lineage.
O lords of practitioners, those who abide in the *kula* should be worshipped by the masters of accomplishment,
for they bestow success through the ritual procedure of the *kulakrama* and the yoga of subtle discernment.
O Goddess, these [mantras] should always be practiced by either a woman or a man.

The letter *sa* joined with the six long vowels constitutes the limbs (*aṅga*s), while the same [letter] joined with the five short vowels and the letter *kha* constitutes the faces (*ānana*). 36–37a.
The mantra consisting of five *oṃ*s becomes the heart-mantra of the limbs of the Vidyā.
(37) The *praṇava* (*oṃ*), followed by *amṛte tejomālini* together with *svāhā*, is the eleven-syllable Brahma-śiras according to the Mālinīmata. (38)
"Vedavedani hūṃ phaṭ," joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning, is the *śikhā*;
"vajriṇe vajradharāya svāhā," preceded by the syllable oṃ, is the eleven-syllable *varma*, which is remembered as being highly praised. (39–40a)
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*) (kṣa), joined with the void (*kha*), the arrow (*śara*) [pha], and the vowel-sound (*svarayuk*) [u], as well as *jīva* (sa) itself—
this is the Eye, whose nature is luminosity, and is remembered as common to all.
*Tāra* (oṃ), *ślīṃ*, *paśu*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*— that is the Weapon-mantra, consisting of six syllables.

By means of the long vowels *la*, *ra*, *ṭa*, *kṣa*, *va*, and *ya*, joined with the nasal bindu, [the weapons] of Indra and the others are formed; by the short vowels, those of Viṣṇu and Prajāpati. It is taught that the lotus and the discus are formed from the fourth and second short vowels respectively.

*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, likewise *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are the [six] seed-syllables (*jāti*). They are applied respectively to the six limbs and to the rituals whose nature they embody: recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), nourishment (*apyāya*), eradication (*samuccāṭa*), and pacification (*śāntika*).
In the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the classes of mantras begin with *namaḥ* and so forth; for the Mothers,
they consist of the second letters from the groups of vowels, eyes, and sages, together with the nasal drop (*bindu*),
and the syllable of the Yoni, which is the abode of the Mothers— *Kālakarṣiṇī*.
Whether abandoned by the first [vowel] or excluded by the last,
it is thus considered the Jīva, situated within the sheath of the vital breath (prāṇa), possessing a luster equal to the fire of time (kālānala).
It is exceedingly radiant, the left foot, adorned on its head with the Bindu.
This one, situated on the right knee and worshipped by the entire host of Mothers,
animates all beings and bestows the desired fruit.
For this is the supreme true nature of both the Mothers and Bhairava.

Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should recite this if he desires supreme accomplishment. The immersion (*samāveśa*) into the power of Rudra is eternally established herein, because this is the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), though she is celebrated under another name through differentiation.
Whatever accomplishments (siddhis) exist in the Tantra, she indeed brings them all about;
her limbs and faces are also as before, through the application of the vowels.
The staff, the living soul (jīva), and the trident are located in the right finger and the other breast.
The navel and throat are Marut and Rudra; the Visarga is accompanied by the trident.
This is declared to be the sovereign of all the circles of Yoginīs.
Merely by its utterance, the consciousness previously described shall arise.
The eight-syllable mantra "Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī" and this nine-syllable one, "Sadbhāvakālakarṣiṇī," which is most secret,
were proclaimed in the Śrīḍāmara Mahāyāga as being higher than the highest.

The seed-syllable *chedaka* (the cutter), which lacks vowels, is formed from *sudhā*, *acchedaka*, *kaṣa*, *ṭha*, and so forth. According to the *Mālinīmata*, the *kṣurikā* (razor) consists of one and a half syllables and is known as *Kālarātri*.
By reciting this one hundred times, a piercing pain arises in the head.
Having thus observed these signs, one should resort to the meditation that conquers death;
O Goddess, he who desires long life should not utter this [mantra] otherwise.
Twice the staff and fire, the trident and space, the vital breaths, the cutter and fire likewise.

"These five, together with the peak-syllable (kūṭa), the fire (agnī), and the visarga, are [to be placed] in the five voids," so it was taught by Śiva in the *Tantrasadbhāva-śāsana*. "This is the 'Cutter' (*chedinī*) and the 'Razor' (*kṣurikā*), by which one is joined to the Supreme."

One should meditate upon this blazing weapon-mantra, joined with the *bindu*, the *indu*, the fire-pile (*nalakūṭa*), fire, wind, and the sixth vowel, extending from the soles of the feet to the top of the head.
Then, the contraction of the fingers should be performed, followed by the impelling gesture.
One should contract each successive wheel from the knees up to the outer wheels;
this supreme secret, which bestows immediate liberation, has been taught.
Now, the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is described, which grants immediate realization.
Śiva, the illustrious Bhūtirāja, bestowed upon us this [mantra],
by which, when death has arrived for all living beings,
the soul departs to the stainless state once it has ascended through the recitation of this [text].
When heard even by a man of knowledge who has fulfilled all his duties,
it immediately dispels the agony of death born from the severance of the vital breaths and other functions;
having heard it, even one who was helpless under the sway of great delusion gradually attains [liberation].
Awakening comes to him spontaneously and with impetuosity through the presence of the speaker.
You have come here from the supreme state; you are eternal—cast off this end of the body!
O All-pervading Lord, [the attachment] beginning with the big toe is indeed a fierce bondage.
This noble statement was previously composed with words numbering [sixty] seven.
"Abandon the supreme city situated at the ankles, reaching the knees, located at the collarbone, and likewise at the groin; arise from the heart-lotus! (67–68)
With these many words, this is the second Āryā verse:
"O Haṃsa, O Hayagrīva, O All-pervasive One, you are Sadāśiva; you are the Supreme, known as the individual soul (jīva).
You whose body consists of the point (bindu) produced by the union of sun, moon, and fire—ha ha ha! Depart! (AbhT 30.69–70a).
The third noble statement consists of eleven words as previously enumerated:

"You are the eternal one, composed of the great mantra of the Haṃsa, the observer of the auspicious and inauspicious, seated in the center of the maṇḍala, the great purpose that is the cause of the great bridge of Śakti. (AbhT 30.70b–71)
"O deity-body, come forth into awakening, seated upon both lotuses!
This is the Āryā verse, uttered in eleven words (the number of Rudras).
In the Niḥśvāsa, however, there is the sound "upa" in place of the word "apa."
"Bound by ignorance, you have been awakened; arise, O primordial god!
(73) This is the fifth half-verse of the Āryā, consisting of seven words. Go indeed to the great door, struck by the *auḍumbara* [fruit], which ends at that which is called the palate. (74)
"Having reached it, go, O Haṃho! Or else, go to the state of Vāmadeva!
This is the sixth noble statement (āryāvākya), consisting of fourteen words:
"O Lord of the Knots, Supreme Self, Peaceful One, having reached the great cavity of the palate..."
"Ascend, O Lord of the Body! Go quickly to the stainless state of Śiva! (AbhT 30.76b).
This seventh statement in Āryā meter consists of fourteen words.
In the Niḥśvāsa-śāsana, the reading is "prabhañjanas tvam" (you are the shatterer). (AbhT 30.77a–b).

Having ascended the middle path and having withdrawn the prāṇa and apāna breaths, O Nārāyaṇa, abandon both merit and demerit and go to the limit of peace. This eighth noble statement has been proclaimed with nine words.
"O Brahman! O Viṣṇu! O Rudra! You are Śiva; you are Vāsudeva.
O Great Space, cast off this eternal lump of clay consisting of Agni and Soma!
This is proclaimed as the noble statement reckoned by the worlds.

"The eternal Self, the triple aggregate," "the great sheath"— these three terms appear in the *Niḥśvāsa*, *Mukuṭottara*, and other scriptures. O most subtle one, abandon the stainless covering that is only a thumb's breadth in size!
This tenth noble statement is said to consist of six words:
"Enough, enough," and "the subtle"—thus it is stated in the *Śrīmukuṭottara*.
"O Puruṣa, you are bound by the bonds consisting of *prakṛti* through the thread of *ahaṅkāra*."
"O Non-existence, O Existence, O Ever-Arisen Supreme Self, abandon the path of passion! This is the thirteenth word, the supreme Āryā verse.
Hrīṃ Hūṃ—come quickly, without delay, to the end of the body, you whose essence is the mantra!"
This would be the twelfth Āryā half-verse, consisting of six feet.
"Abandon this body of yours, composed of the qualities (guṇas) and consisting of the six sheaths"—
this would be such a thirteenth Āryā half-verse, consisting of seven feet.
"Do not grasp at this body composed of the elements; instead, take up the eternal Great Body.
This noble half-verse consists of fourteen syllables.
Having pierced through this, go to the stainless, infinite mandala that exists in three ways."
This fifteenth [verse] consists of eight words and is an Āryā half-verse (ardhavākya).
This entire Brahmavidyā is clearly composed of fifteen sentences;
however, its Niṣkalā form is proclaimed by means of five-syllable [sentences].

That which is recited with a response joined at its beginning and end consists of these five syllables, according to the declared pervasion: *Tāra* (Oṃ), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Vedakala* (Svā), *Mātṛtāra* (Hūṃ), and *Navātmaka* (Phreṃ). // 90–91a //

The drop (bindu), the vital breath, the nectar-water, conjoined with the wind and the sixth vowel— by means of this seed-syllable situated in the utterance of Śakti, the bound soul (paśu) is consecrated;
even one who has previously committed the murder of a Brahmin is purified once the rite of initiation has been performed.
Through lightness, the purification by the balance brings immediate conviction.
*Tāra* (the syllable Om), *śama*, *ra*, and *ya* form the *piṇḍa*; with *nati* (namas), it consists of four syllables.
This is the paralyzing [mantra] of the Śākinīs, the vital point, the heart, and indeed the life-force.

Adorned with the sixth [vowel], the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the three peaks (*trikūṭa*), the raised arms, the trident (*śūla*), and the points (*bindu*); and further embellished by the vowel-less [consonant], the nose, the downward-facing face, and the crescent moon—
this is the Heart known as Bhairava, the cause of universal dissolution.
Heated by the fire of Bhairava situated in the center of a circle of fire,
the Śākinīs come under control; if one should burn this place,
one should first dismiss them, otherwise they will cause harm.
With these syllables— *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vleṃ*, *kleṃ*— adorned with the twelve vowels,

one should recite the heart-mantra named *Priyamelāpana* (The Union of the Beloved) in an encapsulated (*sampuṭa*) form. Furthermore, this supreme procedure may be performed using each syllable individually, two at a time, or all together.
The yoga of the conjunction of the scales (*tulāmelakayoga*), which was taught by Śambhunātha in the *Śrītantrasadbhāvaśāsana*, has been shown by me in due order. Now,
[I shall speak] for those who are destitute of wealth and have truly sought refuge.
Due to defects such as place and time, initiation should not be performed in that manner for those who lack firm resolve;
rather, it should be performed as proclaimed in the *Śrīsantatyāgama*.
This [initiation] is now being described as urged by Hāṭakeśāna, the Lord of Pātāla.

O Śrīnātha, O Noble One, O Blessed One, these three—Varuṇa, Macchanda, and Bhagavatta—are indeed located in the *kanda* at the *ādhāra*. These three are in the heart. The four known as the group beginning with Dharma are to be worshipped in the region of the throat.
Preceded by *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*, all [the mantras] ending with the word *pāda* are endowed with perfect awakening (sambodha).
One should then meditate upon the triad of Vidyās on the surface of the head through mental application,
either with flowers, with joys, or even through pure contemplation alone.
If a disciple whose heart is set solely on liberation is [initiated] by a Guru who knows reality,
this initiation— which is skilled in bestowing liberation alone— is called the *paropaniṣad*. One initiated by this initiation, remembering these three Vidyās in his heart, [attains the goal].
Indeed, even without external worship and the like, one goes to the supreme abode at the end of the body.
One should first place the three syllables— the *praṇava*, *māyā*, and the *bindu*—
followed by the beloved of Agni (*svāhā*) at the end of the five words joined with their vocatives.
First, [the mantra] *siddhasādhani*, which has the nature of the Śabdabrahman;
then *nikṛntani* together with the word *samastabandha*;
and that is addressed as *bodhani*, the mother of the true being of Śiva (*śivasadbhāva*). 108–109a.
The five words follow the sequence of five, eight, nine, three, and eight syllables.

This auspicious knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, consisting of fifty syllables, bestows liberation. [The seed-syllable] is formed by the vowels *a*, *u*, and *ī*; the consonant *gha* at the end; and the thirteenth vowel (*au*) with the *s* (*ṣa*).

At the end of these three phonemes, there are the four semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*). Then follows the first of the consonant groups (*ka*), the letter *śva* (the letter *śa*), joined with the triangle (*e*) and the bindu (*m*), and ending with the letter *pa*. After these three phonemes, there is the seven-syllable sequence beginning with the word "mahāhāṭaka" and followed by "īśvarī."
The addressed [mantra] is "kṣamasva," consisting of three syllables, followed by "pāpāntakāriṇi.
Then follows the six-syllable phrase beginning with the word "pāpa" which causes delusion;
such is the ten-syllable phrase: "pāpaṃ hana dhuna" repeated twice. (AbhT 30.112b–113b)
The six-syllable mantra ending in the fifth case [should be recited] by virtue of Rudra’s power;
thereafter, that which is the single syllable is proclaimed as the Brahman of the Visarga. One should recite it through its unification with the vowel-less letter *ka*.
This Vidyā, consisting of forty-nine syllables, is proclaimed as the Dīkṣā-vidyā.
Then there is the Māyā-syllable, the supreme Brahman, and the three words of the fourfold Vidyā;
furthermore, there is the eight-syllable and the five-syllable mantra known as Yogadhāriṇī.
The triad of words consisting of the forms of the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and the Supreme Self (paramātman),
ending with the letter *e* and situated in the state of awakening, is proclaimed as the ten-syllable mantra.
Then, for me, O beloved of Rudra, there is the four-syllable mantra "Rudra-śakti."
"O, burn, burn the evil!"—this is the twelve-syllable mantra consisting of four lines.
In the auspicious Sadāśiva, there is a pair; the six [syllables] carry the Bindu and the Iṣu (the five arrows).
That group of four and a half syllables is the one that destroys the *samaya*.
That Vidyā of the Supreme Lord consists of fifty-one syllables;
the illustrious Bhūtirāja has described these three Vidyās,
he who was Śrīkaṇṭha himself assuming a human body.

In this regard, vigor has already been described; the Guru should follow it everywhere. According to the sequence of the entry of the seed-syllable of the object, the internal [recitation], the utterance, and so forth—there is indeed nothing whatsoever that was not previously explained.
"Furthermore, fruitless repetition never pleases us.
Thus has the essential nature of mantra, vidyā, and so forth been described. 123.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter of the Śrī Tantrāloka.
Now, the true nature of the mandala is briefly described.
Having established the eastern direction, one should draw a cord straight across.
Having halved that, one should again mark the center and the east and west.
From that point as well, one should mark the eastern and western [lines] by measures of half, then half of that, and again half of that;
with that same measure, one should apply a pair of circles using a cord.
In this way, there will be two "fish" junctions in the south and north.
In the middle of that, one should drop a thread for the sake of establishing the south and north;

or else, by means of a thread equal to the east-west line, [one establishes] the north and south. One should mark from the western mark toward the east, and likewise from the eastern [mark] toward the west.
One should cast a long thread through the middle of the fish, from south to north. Then, measuring half the size of the intended field, one should mark the cardinal directions from the center.
By means of two threads arising from two directions, there shall be a fish at each corner.
In the Matsya [Tantra], it is said that there are four Vedas and Sūtras; thus,
the square [maṇḍala] consists of one up to a hundred,
since the maṇḍalas are declared to number one hundred in the Siddhātantra, and that is called its seat (pīṭha).

That which is situated in the center and is considered the primary among the three mandalas is clearly known as the Middle Trident (madhyaśūla), the Triple Trident (tritriśūla), and the Nine-Pronged Trident (navaśūla). Regarding that, the procedure for the trident has been taught through infinite varieties.
We shall describe that maṇḍala which has that as its source, as revealed in the sequence of the True Being (Sadbhāvakrama).
On a square of four cubits based on the Vedas, one should discard a third part from all sides.
One should divide that entire field into sixteen parts.
Then, having clearly established the midpoint between the two Brahma-threads as the "Brahma-position" (brahmapada) and making that the limit, one should first lay down the fourth thread. Then,
immediately following that, one should proceed with the fourth thread drawn transversely.
One should draw two moons within the square, starting from half a part outside [the central area];
their meeting point, situated at the third vital point (marman) from the Brahma-thread,
and another at half the square, thus forming a pair facing inward.
Having fixed it immovably upon the vital point in the second hand from the Brahma-thread,
the wise practitioner should rotate the pair of full moons;
[he should do so] at the third transverse division from the sixth [division] along the Brahma-thread.
Having placed a thread in the middle of the half-cell, suspended from the tip of the full moon,
one should rotate it upwards until it reaches the two fire-divisions at the pair of half-moons.
Then, having bypassed two horizontal divisions from the western side of the half-moon, [one proceeds].
One should likewise proceed as far as the corner and perform two circular rotations to form a section;
from that, a single horn arises with an extremely sharp and curved tip.
This same clear procedure for forming a horn is prescribed for the second [section] as well.
Then, when the middle prong is to be made in the third upper cell and in the fourth half-cell,
there should be two inward-facing crescent moons;
and this should reach toward the single full moon previously drawn.
Through the application of mutual knots, a state of being bound is produced.
(20) Thus, on its second side, by the formation of two crescent moons, the *gaṇḍikā* is joined by the two middle [ends], while one should lead it forward by the other two. (21)
By means of which the thread on both sides reaches the middle peak so that it may be sharp; afterwards,
the second Brahma-thread below those two sides must be taken up with careful attention by the preceptor who understands the inference.

The mantra-practitioner should face westward upon that Brahma-thread; having omitted the middle prong, the entire procedure previously described applies. Then, as for the pair of upward-facing crescent moons mentioned before:
Then, by means of two [units], a *gaṇḍikā* should be made, well-joined within;
by means of two [units] from the two leading threads, there shall be the pair of middle *śṛṅgas*.
By increasing the lower portion of this, there is a lotus consisting of four circles.
Then, that wheel is of two kinds: sixteen-spoked and twelve-spoked.
In its center is the station of Kuleśvarī, which may be a void, a tilaka, a lotus, a six-spoked [wheel], or a twelve-fold void.
In this [mandala] with three tridents and seven spokes, by merely joining them together at the center,
there may be a group of seven lotuses, wheels,
or voids; or they may be mixed or combined through the distinctions of contraction and expansion.
Then, one should add an additional area there, measuring half the size of the field.
In that place, the staff (daṇḍa) is prescribed as a portion consisting of six spokes and an *amalasāraka* [central hub];
it has an extremely sharp point, a beautiful red luster, and brings about possession in an instant.
That goddess Kuṇḍalinī, known as the Wave and possessing great surges,
resides within the center called the Kanda in the form of six deities.
She is eight parts in width and half that in length.

Then, the gates should be constructed in sequence by means of variegated painting; they may have the form of a triangle or a square, or simply be circular. Furthermore, one should make the horns clearly defined, or else in the reverse manner.
Alternatively, having divided the upward-facing pair of moons, one should form a quartet. It may be curved in the middle,
clearly visible, downward-facing, situated on the side,
standing upright, face-up, half-full, uneven, full, joined together, or likewise positioned at a knot.
Thus, the twelvefold movement of the moon destroys delusion.
That [movement] is further considered to be of two kinds, by virtue of being inward-facing or outward-facing.
From its divisions, there arises an incalculable expansion of varieties of mandalas.
From the pedestal, the pathways, the outer ground, the throat, the ears, and the cheeks;
through the differentiation of primary and secondary ornaments (*śobhā* and *upaśobhā*), and by the various arrangements of lines representing the qualities (*guṇa*);
and through the distinctions beginning with a pair of svastikas up to a group of eight.
Through the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, the maṇḍalas are infinite.
Therefore, powders should be applied according to their aesthetic beauty:
vermilion, lapis lazuli, and the finest white chalk.
In this world, the supreme dust-particles arise from the union with the triad of deities:
Parā, who resembles the moon; the goddess Parāparā, who is red;
and Aparā, who is that very Parā Kālī, the terrifying and fierce Yoginī.
Having seen this maṇḍala, all the goddesses dance at all times.
(41) Even if it is not worshipped, one who is uninitiated becomes initiated by the Mothers upon seeing it.
What is the use of saying too much? [The maṇḍalas consist of] three, three, and seven spokes with tridents. (42)
There are six thousand and two hundred and fifty Śūla-sacrifices;
that Goddess who is the supreme power (parā-śakti), established as the flow of the vital breath,
exists here in visible form, coiled within the universe like a serpent.
The principles (tattvas) and the deities of the principles—upon these the universe is established.
Here, above, by means of a mere thread, three spokes of the trident are situated;
they serve as the seat for Icchā and the others, and are the accomplishers of enjoyment and liberation.
But for one whose sole desire is liberation, these [sacrificial threads] have their centers pierced by the spokes of the trident.
Therefore, whether desiring worldly prosperity or desiring liberation, the wise man should worship this great sacrifice with extensive displays of great wealth.

Merely by the sight of this, spirits, vetālas, and guhyakas flee in the ten directions, and Śiva himself becomes manifest and gracious. Even one who is pierced by only a weak power of energy [becomes empowered] through the worship of this maṇḍala.
By constantly practicing for six months, he attains the triple knowledge;
having attained this, he himself discerns what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
At the end of the body, he becomes the very self of Bhairava; or, if desiring supernatural powers (*siddhi*), he achieves them.

He who understands the pervasion of this mandala, as well as the placement of the deities and its construction, is a guru in the Trika teaching; the dust of his feet should be borne upon the head by one who seeks Śiva.
In this regard, one should worship all three—emanation, maintenance, and dissolution—in their proper sequence;
however, the fourth [state] is either in the center or is the fulfiller of them all.
Or else, one should perform the sacrifice with a four-spoked trident and a concealed staff.
There, one should properly worship that clearly manifest fourfold sequence.
Thus has this been declared in the secret *Ṣaḍardhahṛdaya*, the supreme [text];
it is proclaimed and indicated in the *Ṣaṭka* and in the venerable *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*.
Having first laid out the mandala that grants all desires,
equipped with a great trident and adorned with lotuses, wheels, and so forth—
one should draw a trident at each door, excluding the western one.
Furthermore, in the corners, one should fashion a great trident (mahāśūla) provided with trees.
At the tips of the tridents, there should be three [triads] each of the waters born of nectar and the waters of destruction.
In this manner, the trident should be made eightfold or even threefold.
Thus has the divine city of the Khecarīs been indicated;
it is also described in another place within the teaching of the venerable Siddhātantra:
"In the center is a lotus, and its trident-prongs are half that size."
A mandala marked with tridents should be fashioned, and one marked with lotuses for the filling [of the squares]. Now,
the arrangement of tridents and lotuses is taught in the *Śrīpūrva*,
the *Triśiromata*, the *Siddhātantra*, the *Trikakula*, and the *Devīyāmala*.
As it has been stated in the *Sāraśāstra*, the *Tantrasadbhāva*, and the *Guhyatantra*,
so shall it be clearly demonstrated here, even though it follows the sequence already mentioned:
In a square of three cubits based on the Vedas, one should first divide the eastern half.
Having set aside half a cubit on all sides toward the east, north, and south,
[one should divide the space] into squares of three finger-breadths each, arranged eight by eight vertically and horizontally. Then,
having again set aside two parts each toward the south and north, [the remaining central portion is prepared].

On both sides of Brahmā, from the fourth *jīva* line, and likewise on the east, there are two pairs of crescent moons, each measuring half a *bhāga*. Between those two, on the third line, on the southern and northern sides, [there are further ornaments].
In the *jīva* [square], the wise practitioner should create a pair of half-moons through internal rotation.
With the tips of those two half-moons reaching the other vital points (*marman*),
he should perform an outward-facing rotation to form two pairs of half-moons.

In the same manner, one should draw lines in the Brahmā-square measuring one and a half parts. Then, at the end of the second part, two lines should be drawn by the wise on both sides of the Brahmā-square, extending toward the east and measuring one-third of a part.

One should draw two threads, positioned at the upper tip of the single half-moon and meeting at the apex of the Brahma-thread, for the purpose of establishing the central prong. From the *jīva*-thread, one should hold a thread at an interval of one unit on both sides of its tip.
One should lead a thread from the corner of the first and second half-moon segments to the opposite corner;
likewise, one should lead a thread from the other life-line (jīva) of those two, starting from the corner of the first half-moon,
for the sake of establishing the pair of horns.
And in the other half of the field, the staff is two cubits long and five fingers wide;
it is six fingers wide and four fingers long at its base, which consists of pure metal.
Below that, the root is four fingers wide and is intended to have a sharp point.
One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions of the primary field;
they should be one cubit in length, or half of that, and their width should be equal to that as well.
One should make them double [the size] on the outside; now listen to how the lotus is to be made.
One should draw circles according to the measure of each single part, like a Veda-diagram.
Furthermore, there are sixteen life-lines (jīvasūtra): eight in the cardinal directions and another eight;
one should then drop lines equal in number to those [segments] between each pair of them.

One should perform the rotation equal to the side-life (pārśvajīva), situated in the third revolution of these [revolutions], ending at this point; then one should bring forth the tip of the life-line (jīvāgra).
Wherever there is a junction, once that connection is made firm—
Having done that there, the mantra-practitioner should proceed for the successful completion of the tips of the petals. On each petal, one should fashion three filaments.
Likewise, the three horn-like buds should be made with double the eight finger-breadths [of the petals].
The pericarp is yellow, distinguished by its base, middle, and tip;
the network of filaments should be made white, red, and yellow.
The petals are white, together with the protective rim.
Likewise, the pedestal (pīṭha) is four-cornered, with its outer edge equal to half the pericarp.
Its legs are white, red, yellow, and black, starting from the southeast in due order.
It is held that there are four prongs on each side, and three circles [of lines].
The staff should be blue-red; the *āmalasāraka* [seat] should be yellow;
one should make the trident red, which was previously described.
After leaving four finger-breadths to the east of the western door, [one should proceed].
The entrance may be four-cornered, circular, or variegated;
it may consist of one, two, or three stories, being symmetrical, with a central pinnacle, or both;
and it is highly adorned with features such as the cheeks, the neck, the primary ornaments, and the secondary embellishments.
