The Guru should cause one part to descend from above onto his own side;
he should then rotate both [hands] at the end of that middle third.
Having set aside one part, he should rotate them again in the middle of that.
Rotating the third part upward as far as the end of the upper portion,
one should then join it again from above to below starting from the fourth part.
Having rotated upward by that same measure, one should join it with the fourth part.
One should join the thread from above down to the Brahma-thread in sequence.
Having established it in sequence according to its width, one should then reduce the portion again.
The staff is desired to be half a part in measure, while the [other] is twice that.

Having taken a portion from each of the two [sides] from the field of activity, one should rotate it like a leaf of the *pippala* tree; this turning should proceed downwards. One should draw a lotus in the sixteenth part by omitting twelve finger-breadths.
Above that, in the middle portion, one should draw a lotus;
then, at the end of the central prong, one should draw a third [lotus].
Likewise, one should draw two lotuses situated at the hips on the right and left sides.
The pericarp is yellow; the filaments are red, yellow, and white;
the petals are situated outside the lotus and are white; the protective rim (prativāraṇī) is also white.
The trident is with black powder, and the Brahma-line is white again.
The tip of the trident is joined with flame, while the shaft of the trident is yellow.
One should always worship Īśa in the lotus located in the middle of the trident;
above him, the wise man should worship Parā on the right, and Aparā on the left.
That goddess who is Kālāntakā, established as transcending even the Supreme (parātītā), always devours the wheel of tridents by her mere will.
This [goddess] is indeed the digit (kalā) whose form is Peace (śānti); she becomes the supreme one whose form is Knowledge (vidyā).
The other, however, is *pratiṣṭhā*, while *nivṛtti* is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāparā*).
Bhairava is the staff standing upright, whose form consists of the nature of Sadāśiva;
his four powers are gross, while his subtle forms are manifold.

This sacrifice, known as the Ḍāmara and characterized by the three powers (triśaktika), has been fully described. Now, the ritual for the trident-lotus (śūlābja) as seen in the Traiśirasa is being written down.
It is performed with the primary purifiers, such as the nectar of the left (vāmāmṛta) and others, which are most beautiful.
One should worship the ground, the dust, the instrument, and the chalk from the very beginning.
In a square measuring four cubits, there is a trident in the center with three arms;
Caṇḍa is two cubits high, broad, and possesses a pair of pedestals above and below.
It should be made eight finger-breadths wide and provided with three lines;
at the base of the staff, there is a pedestal measuring twelve finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in height above.
Above, it is four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in height and ten finger-breadths in length.
Having made the pedestal at the base of the trident four finger-breadths wide,
one should fashion the staff of the trident with three equal parts on all sides.
It should be eight finger-breadths in measure, making one cubit in circumference all around;
that shall be the tip of the trident, its middle, and its base.
An altar should be constructed in the center, with six finger-breadths on both sides.
It should be twelve finger-breadths long on both sides;
one should fashion an altar at the base with a height of four finger-breadths,
and likewise on both sides, it should have the shape of a half-moon.
One should rotate the chalk-line and form the waistband (*kaṭi*) at a distance of two finger-breadths;
O Goddess, it should measure four finger-breadths in both width and length. Just as it is on the right side, one should arrange it likewise on the left.
In the middle, due to the width of the tip of the trident, it is one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in height;
[the base] is four finger-breadths in width, while the gaṇḍikā should be made six finger-breadths in height according to its proper form.
O virtuous lady, the base of the trident should be fashioned above the pedestal;
the tip of the trident should be made one finger-breadth wide, very sharp, and six finger-breadths long.
The middle of the spokes should be fashioned such that the space between the spokes is six finger-breadths.
One should fashion the center with a depth of four finger-breadths;
that very [line] runs from east to west here, and outside of that,
one should cause a trident to be made by means of three threads, winding each one individually.
The trident-tip consists of three lotuses, twelve finger-breadths in length and divided into four parts;
it has three, eight, and twelve petals respectively on the right, the other [left], and the middle.
There are three wheels, a city of wind, and a lotus with eight finger-breadth spokes.
One should subsequently cast red powder at the base of the trident known as Vidyā.
One should fill the trident up to the end of its staff with lapis lazuli (rājavarta). Behind the three threads, there should be three white spokes.
With white *rajas*, there should be a lotus of knowledge at the base of the trident.
The three upward-facing lotuses are, in sequence, red, reddish-black, and white.
With white [rajas], there should be a line for the void; it extends outward by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) due to its thickness.
Having abandoned that [altar], a sacrificial platform (vedikā) should be constructed measuring one cubit in height;
its width should be three times its length, and it should be square. Furthermore, there should be doors on all sides in the cardinal directions, each measuring one cubit.
Having divided [the space] into three parts sequentially according to a measurement of twelve finger-breadths,
one should fashion the neck, the cheek, the primary ornament (*śobhā*), and the secondary ornament (*upaśobhā*) at its end;
then the enclosure wall (*prākāra*), which is square and provided with the earth-line (*bhūrekhā*).
Then, one should cause [the mandala] to be made with white, red, yellow, and black powders (rajas).
One should fill the center with red powders according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Regarding its pervasion (vyāpti), that which was previously stated should be followed in that very context.
The division of the three spokes consists of entry, exit, and rotation;
it is the pervasion of the plane of the Unstruck (anāhata) and the supreme arising of Kuṇḍalī. The goddesses have gone to the heart-center, at the beautiful middle of the trident.
The staff of the trident is situated at the navel, while the base of the trident resides in the heart.
One should contemplate the tip located in the station of the Śakti, and at that tip, the three wheels;
repeatedly lifting [the consciousness] by means of the *kalā* from its essential nature within the center of the body.

One should enter the root, the middle, and the end, which are the spheres of the trident situated at the end, the middle, and the center of the staff; finally, at the very end of the extremity, one enters the abode of Śakti.
Having rendered the senses motionless, one should once more engage in movement.

Having pressed upon the root-bliss, one should enter the state of the three powers (śaktitraya). There, by worshipping with effort, all perfections (siddhis) arise through the conjunction of all the paths (adhvan) and the contemplation of the pervasion of the sixfold path.
Through such efforts as these, beginning with the entire circle of mantras,
one should contemplate the trident composed of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
The placement of the mantras in the supreme mandala is performed by means of the equinoxal state.
When this [mandala] is worshipped, one attains the state of the Lord of All; therefore, it should be fashioned as a *svastika*. Now, the procedure for that is being stated:
first, one should establish the channels (*nāḍikā*) according to their measure, which is one *muhūrta*.
Situated in the directions of Indra and Varuṇa, as well as those extending toward the south and north,
there are twenty-nine channels (vaṃśas) that run straight and transversely;
thus, eight hundred and forty-one vital points (marma) arise.
With bamboos numbering the objects of the senses (five), there is a lotus with a circle of two moons (two);
with those numbering the tastes (six), there should be a pedestal, a svastika that grants all desires.
With those numbering the Vasus (eight), the doors and the pathways are formed; such is the sequence of the divisions.
One should erase nine, five, five, and three [units] from the outside and the inside in sequence;
likewise, O beautiful one, the vital points (marmāṇi) in the four directions, starting from the center, at the gates, in the cities,
and in the outer and inner wombs of fire, earth, sages, and space.
And one should indeed eliminate the vital points (marmans) that are devoid of internal channels (nāḍīs).
At the gates, walls, and corners, there are [the positions of] the eyes, fire, arrows, and seasons.
The channels of the Brahma-lineage are to be eliminated, situated at the eyes and the tastes (rasas).

From the fire [element], the eye and the fires are to be deleted; from the Vedas, the pair of eyes; and from the flavors (rasa), the eye situated in the north is to be deleted. From the east, the Vedas and the fires [are deleted] from the flavors. Having omitted the channels (nāḍikā) situated in the worlds, the eyes, the Vedas, and the fires follow in sequence.
With arrows, fire, and the pair [of eyes], and from the tastes (six), there is the eye;
from the eye situated in the east, Sumeru is designated as the gate.
And the beautiful city of Svastika—both are situated in the four directions.
Two hundred vital points (marman) multiplied by the directions [ten] by the sages [seven],
and having cleared away the eyes and so forth from the middle of the path, O beautiful one,
the pericarp (karṇikā) shall be formed in the center by the three sages and the sense objects [five].
The *netrī* (two) multiplied by the *vasus* (eight) makes the petals; the *netra* (two) is divided once.
Having placed the *vahni* (three) in the *vasu-gata* (eighth position), one should erase those situated upon the moon (*śaśāṅka*).
From the midst of the *vahnī*, *iṣu*, and *ṛṣi* (3, 5, and 7), one should erase [the numbers] up to the *pīṭha-induka*.
From the eyes of Brahmā, one should take the Vedas and the fires from the eyes;
having erased the "eye" (2) from the ocean, there are the channels situated in the eastern direction.
From the head located at the "element-eyes" (25), and from the eye, [one takes] the two, the three fires, and the three eyes.
From the north, one should erase [the lines] at all four corners of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The petals should be made white, the filaments red and yellow,
the pericarp (karṇikā) resembling gold, and the tips of the sprouts red.
The sky-line is very white, while the interior of the circle of lotuses is blue;
the pedestal is provided with three lines of white, red, and yellow.
And there are four-colored svastikas located in the directions of Agni and Īśāna.
The path resembles coral; outside, in its own directions, are the weapons:
the thunderbolt (vajra) resembling sapphire, the spear (śakti) with the luster of a lotus-gem, the staff (daṇḍa) resembling gold, and its face is exceedingly red.
A sword with the luster of blue light, a noose with the brilliance of a *vatsaka* flower, a banner endowed with flowers and fruits and adorned with five colors,
and a mace resembling gold, exceedingly fierce and embellished with various jewels.
The trident is like a blue lotus, with a crest fierce with blazing fire.
Upon it is a white lotus, with a slight yellowish-red luster;
a wheel resembling gold, radiant, with spokes like lapis lazuli.
The center of the spokes should be a beautiful yellow, and the exterior should be reddish like a flame;
this is the temple of the God of gods, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
In the *Śrīsiddhā*, the procedure for the trident was previously described within a square field.

One should divide [the space] by the hand-span into three parts so that there may be nine sections like those of the sun; in the center, there is a trident, and therein one should likewise divide the central portion into three. Thus, it is joined with nine compartments, and then this procedure is stated: 155–156. One should divide [the space] by the hand-span into three parts so that there may be nine sections like those of the sun; in the center, there is a trident, and therein one should likewise divide the central portion into three. Thus, it is joined with nine compartments, and then this procedure is stated.
Having set aside three middle sections, one should rotate the thread from below between two middle sections so that it takes the form of a crescent moon; there,
one should rotate it on both sides so that it forms the shape of the letter *hā* at the tip.
Having drawn a thread from that corner, one should lead it to the previous line. Leaving four finger-breadths to the east of the western door,
the wise one should erase the line so that it takes the form of a trident.
At the tip of the trident, having left a space of half a cubit, one should fashion lotuses;
below, at the center of the three prongs, there should be a lotus with its pericarp measuring one cubit.
One should hold the cord at the front of the mouth and let it fall for a distance of three cubits.
Then, one should draw two lines in the middle, upwards from there,
and downwards for two finger-breadths, so that they form a trident; thus,
from the lower parts and so forth, a line extends upwards.
Having leveled the two upper threads in this very same way,
O illustrious one, the central lotus should be established beneath the trident.
Thus has this procedure for the mandala been taught by the great gurus in a concise manner.
Now, the thirty-second chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*.
Now I shall describe here the procedure for the mudrās as sung in the tradition of the Guru; and in the venerable *Devyākhyayāmala*, a mudrā is said to be essentially a reflection.
By analyzing the two meanings of the term *bimbodaya* (the arising from the original image), it has been stated:

"That which has its arising (*samudaya*) from the original image (*bimba*)" defines the state of being a reflection (*pratibimbatā*); "that which is the arising (*udaya*) of the original image" defines the state of being its means (*tadupāyatā*).
Because it bestows— that is, offers— to the selves, through the medium of the body, the joy known as the attainment of one's true nature (*svarūpa*),
it is described as *mudrā* in the scriptures.
Among these, the venerable Khecarī is the primary one, being of the very essence of the deity.
She is renowned as Niṣkalā (the Partless) by virtue of her indivisibility, and as Triśūlinī (the Trident-Bearer) by virtue of her totality.
She is Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānikā,
Mahāpretā, Yogamudrā, Jvālinī, Kṣobhiṇī, and Dhruvā.
Thus, this venerable Khecarī alone is celebrated in her many such divisions;
however, in the Mālinīmata, others such as Padmā and so forth are considered her limbs.
Because of their great number and because they are secondary, they are not described here.

Whatever place one who is possessed by the illustrious Khecarī may resort to, that becomes a site for the presence of the Goddess; what need is there for vain displays? And in rites for specific desires, they may at times be the primary means for anyone.

Mudrā is fourfold, distinguished by body, hand, speech, and mind. Among these, I shall describe Khecarī alone in its complete form: having assumed the lotus posture, the yogi should cast the lord of the eye into the navel.
One should lead that [breath], which has the form of a staff, as far as the three voids;
having restrained it there, one should swiftly impel it by means of the three voids.
By binding this [mudrā], there is movement in the sky; thus it is stated in the venerable *Pūrvaśāsana*.
Having caused the mind, joined with sound, light, and wind, to rest above, one should,
through this yoga of practice, pierce through Śiva and go to the Supreme.
Placing the hands below the collarbones and the left foot upon the right—
Having opened the mouth with the two little fingers and the nose with the two middle fingers, the wise practitioner should contract the ring fingers, knit the brows with the two index fingers,
move the tongue, and utter the sound "hā hā."
Having reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by means of the practice of the trident,
and having abandoned that very state, he instantly leaves the earth behind.
Having merged the wind and fire into the single staff within the dissolution of the void and the non-void, [he attains liberation].
One should recognize that trident as being connected with the three powers and presided over by the three deities, by means of which the wise man may fly up into the sky;
having abandoned the state of space, he becomes established in pure existence alone.
Having made the trident of equal flavor, he remains like one essence within another essence.
O Dear One, having recognized that triple trident as a single staff moving through the sky,
and having bound the khecarī mudrā, he should meditate upon himself as Bhairava.
One who is endowed with the wheel of the *khecarī* immediately abandons the earth.
Having abandoned all parts [of worldly existence], free from conventional conduct (*nirācāra*), devoid of doubt, and shunned by the world,
such an *avadhūta* is without conduct and contemplates, "I am not."
Devoted solely to the mantra, he perceives all the deities residing within the body:
in joy, agitation, egoism, anger, sleep, sexual union, and envy;
or in form and the rest, and in every way within the agent, the object, and the instrument.
Thinking "I am not [this]," and contemplating the unified state,
one clearly attains success through the Khecarī [mudrā] by constantly perceiving the host of deities situated in the wheels of the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and so forth, as the grasper.
One who doubts the Vidyā, doubts the impurities, or doubts the scriptures does not attain success.
Śiva is the sun; Śiva is the fire, for as the digester he is the domestic priest (purohita). All the deities reside therein, illuminating the entire universe.
Having opened the mouth with the little fingers and likewise the eyebrows with the two index fingers, one should touch the tongue to the palate with the ring and middle fingers in the mouth.
This is the goddess Karaṅkiṇī; now hear of Jvālinī.
Extending the hands from the jaw and forehead with the fingers clearly displayed,
the wise one should move them with the force of the wind while knitting the brows; having opened the mouth wide along with the tongue, he should utter the sound "hā hā."
This is Jvālinī in the fire-wheel (agnicakra); if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with her, then the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, shall be mastered.
Furthermore, one perceives oneself within the bodies of others, and others within one's own body.
One should perceive it moving, established in the states of going and coming through the process of abandonment and acquisition;
it is singular, situated within the nine apertures, roaring, all-pervasive, and eternal.
Indeed, by means of this, the one who moves in the void is called the "Illustrious One Moving in Yoga" (Śrī-yogasañcāra).
Having bound the *kulakuṇḍalikā*, which perceives the interior of the atom,
she is intent upon the withdrawal of that which is left-handed (*vāma*) in this world. Having attained repose in her own place, she consists of the essence of the nectar of gnosis.
One should proceed to the state of the *kanda* in the center, having indeed rendered soundless that which was sounding.
As long as one lives, [one should practice] the four-cornered [mandala], the support of the *piṇḍa*, and that which is desired.
Having awakened her there, and having understood the destiny that has come down through the sequence; 34.
O Goddess, just as one should tear apart the knot of darkness at the root-place by means of the branch fixed on both sides of the wheel and hanging from the tips of its branches,
so too, by means of that which is born of knowledge, should one [tear apart] the one called Vajra from both ends of the branches.
One should pierce the base of the *liṅga* emerging from the center of the corners. There, the pair of wheels, joined together, shines as a unity;
however, by reversing that [process] and casting them apart, they then proceed to a state of duality.
She should cast [the breath] from the thighs down to the big toe and the fire of time;
she, the possessor of the mark, should move in the coming and going of her movement.
There, through union with that state, she brings about the unfolding [of consciousness].
He who understands this attains success in the taking up and emission of the vital essence (rasa).
This supreme state, characterized by waves and the unfolding of the light, is accompanied by attachment;
yet there is another sequence beyond this, the transcendent Khecarī which proceeds even through inversion.
Renowned as the "support of the womb," it is called the "root of the trident.
Therein, the phonemes (varṇas) reach dissolution into that which is without phonemes (avarṇa), yet possesses the form of all phonemes.
Having uttered the sequence from *na* to *pha*, one should contemplate the Lord of Kula (kauleśa), who is identical with the body.
Having first ascended the wheel, [the practitioner] is pressed by the foot upon the machine in the sky.
Indeed, the Nāda contains the womb of Śakti; from that womb comes the state of Kaulinī.
This occurs through the movement of the five seed-syllables, according to the sequence of piercing the trident.
By piercing the knots of the heart-piercing trident, one should awaken the power of Rudra-consciousness (*cidrudraśakti*).
[This power] reaches the center of the navel, known as the *bindu*, which resides within the wheel of the vital breath (*vāyucakra*);
from there, it emerges through the twelve channels and arrives at the station of the uvula (*lambikā*).
By reversing the sequence of the lunar wheel, one should enter the cage of the elements (bhūtapañjara). Furthermore, one performs the play residing within the cage of illusion;
again, emission and withdrawal are performed by the wise through the Khecarī.
In the glorious Vīrāvalīyoga, this is the procedure for the Khecarī:
that supreme reality which is heard through the mouth in the form of a kiss,
swallowing this entire universe within the cavity formed by the union of the moon and the sun.
"By that very [means], one becomes a traveler through the sky; thus it is stated in the venerable Kāmika.
For mudrās are indeed powers (śaktis) that, having liberated one from existence, dissolve the bonds.
Among these, Khecarī is the primary one, and she is threefold according to the vocal utterance."
O Goddess, the *triśiromudgara* is taught as belonging to the body; having reached the nose, the two eyes, the heart, the two breasts,
the two testicles, and the penis, it is thus situated within the body.
One should determine the state of existence and the state of non-existence through the upward breath (*uccāra*).
This [state] is mental; other than this, there are eight seals (*mudrā*) beginning with Padmā. These belong to the family of the Mother-array (*mātṛvyūha*) and are her attendants.
The entire body, which has the form of the peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara),
is this Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Bhairava, according to the Gahvara.
Seated comfortably upon a lotus, with the rays from the fingertips [of the hands],...
With rays suddenly rising while turned away and positioned behind [the body],
this is the internal state of Khecarī, known as Saṃkocā (Contraction), who possesses the moon.
Therefore, having raised both arms and bent them inward...
Because it is correctly situated within the voids, the Khecarī mudrā is considered to be named "the Void.

Through the clashing of two fists at the heart, that same mudrā is called "the Heart" (Hṛdayā). When the pair of hands is raised and positioned one above the other, it is known as "the Peaceful" (Śāntā).
And it is to be looked upon with an even gaze, with the hands joined externally. This very same [mudrā] is the Śakti-mudrā if the hands are moved downward;
immediately after the closing of the fist of the ten fingers.
By a swift upward throw, she is the goddess Khecarī, considered to be the fivefold Kuṇḍalinī;
this very same gesture is the Saṃhāra-mudrā if it is indeed thrown upwards.
She is the Utkrāmaṇī, who instantly severs the fetters of bound souls (paśus).
As if suddenly throwing oneself into a very deep abyss,
with a forceful entry, the pair of hands are drawn back,
the gaze is directed downward, and one is endowed with perfect vision.
This Khecarī, known as Vīrabhairava, increases awakening;
thus has she been described in eight ways here in the Śrī Bhargāṣṭaka-śikhākula.
In this manner, though she remains as one, she abides by resorting to various kinds of divisions.
One possessed by that Śrī Khecarī attains the supreme seed-syllable (bīja).
That single seed-syllable consists of emanation; it is the potency present in all mantras. Khecarī is the one mudrā, and by her the entire multitude of mudrās is animated.

Thus, whatever form may manifest when one has ascended to the wheel of the Khecarī, that alone should be considered the Mudrā; everything else is merely a physical transformation of the body. [This applies] at the beginning of the sacrifice, in its midst, at its conclusion, and during the contemplation of the yoga of knowledge.
The rule for the ritual procedure of mudrās consists of the pacification of obstacles and the severing of bonds.

The sequence of their functions is as follows: the penetration of awakening, presence through oneness, dismissal, returning to one's own nature, the shattering of doubt, and the radiance of the arising of the wheels (cakras). // 66–67 //
Thus has been declared the procedure for the mudrās, which is well-guarded and bestows fruit.
Now, in the thirty-third chapter of the Śrī Tantrāloka,
the unification [of all things] is being expounded as it has reached its proper occasion.
Regarding that which was stated— that the triad is to be worshipped together with the division of the wheels—
this is the method for the unification of those divisions of the wheels:
Viśvā, her Lord [Viśveśa], Hāraudrī, Vīranetrī, and likewise Ambikā.
In the six-spoked [wheel], the goddesses are shown as heavy (gurvī) by the venerable Siddhāvīra:
Māheśī, Brāhmaṇī, Skāndī, Vaiṣṇavī, Aindrī, Yamātmikā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Yogīśī; or else, there are the eight beginning with Aghorī.
Together with Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśa, and the Mothers, they are twelve in number:
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Kālī, Karālī, Vikṛtānanā, Kroṣṭukī,
Bhīmamudrā, Vāyuvegā, and Hayānanā.
Gambhīrā, Ghoṣaṇī, and [the others]— this is the procedure for the twenty-four spokes.
Siddhi, Vṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti,
Sudhā, Dhṛti, Dīpti, Puṣṭi, Mati, Kīrti, Susthiti, Sugati, and Smṛti.
Suprabhā and Ṣoḍaśī are the powers (śaktis) beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha; Bali, Balinanda, Daśagrīva, Hara, Haya,
and Mādhava are remembered as being in the six-spoked wheel, while these [others] are in the twelve-spoked wheel.
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Śauṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, Manmatha, Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, Pitāmaha, Śrīkaṇṭha,
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Śaṃbareśvara. (8–9)
Arghīśa, Bhārabhūti, Sthiti, Sthāṇu, Hara, Jhaṇṭhi, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraha, and Krūra-sainika— these sixteen,
joined with that which is immortal, are full of its radiant essence.
The Flood, the Wave, the Flow, the Limbs, the Body, the Eructation, and the Mouth; the Lord of the Form of Sprinkling the Body, and another who holds all nectar—
these sixteen powers are proclaimed through the venerable recitation.
Saṃvarta, Kulika, Bhṛgu, Sita, Baka, Khaṅgin, Pinākin, Bhujaga, Bali, Kāla;
Dvija, Chagala, Aṇḍa; Śikhin, Śoṇa, Meṣa, Mīna, Tridaṇḍin, and Āṣāḍhin;
Devīkānta, Tadardha, Dāruka, Halin, Somanātha, and Śarman.
Jayavijaya, Jayanta, Ajita, Sujaya, Jaya, Rudra, Kīrtana, and Āvaha; Tanmūrti, Utsāha, Dava, and Vardhana; Bala, Subala, Bhadra, and Āvaha; Tadvān, Dātā, Īśa, Nandana, Sama, Bhadra, and Tanmūrti.
Śivada, Sumanas, Spṛhaṇaka, Durga, Bhadra, Kāla,
Ceto'nuga, Kauśika, Kālaviśva, Suśiva, and another, Kopa— these are the [deities] in the thirty-seven [year-cycle];
however, by reading them as feminine, they are these Śaktis.
The syllable *juṃ* and the consort of Agni (*svāhā*) are on the six-spoked [wheel], excluding the neuter vowels.
On the twelve-spoked [wheel], they are included; on the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the vowels appear in sequence.
On the double of that (the thirty-two-spoked), the consonants (*ha* to *la*); and on the eight-spoked, those beginning with *ya* and ending with *ha* in groups of three.
In the thirty-second spoke, the final letter is the nasal *m* (sānta), with the *bindu* above all [the letters] at the head.
In this manner, one should conceive many other varieties of wheels from this [system].
This very Self of Consciousness alone has the essential nature of the awareness of the universe.
Therefore, Śakti and her Possessor (tadvān) are proclaimed as Mātṛkā and Śabdarāśi. When these two are divided and conceived as Śakti and her Possessor,
they take on such a form through agitation (*kṣobha*) as Śabdarāśi and Mālinī.

Likewise, when the internal reflective awareness is differentiated, there are in reality three [powers] called Anuttara (the Unsurpassed), Icchā (Will), and Unmeṣa (Expansion), from which the entire universe arises as reflective awareness.
When these are joined with Ānanda (Bliss) and Īśa (Lordship), they are declared to be six.
Through the conjunction with the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*), that [group] is declared to be eightfold.
When the four squares of nectar (*amṛta*) are absent, it becomes twelvefold;
through their conjunction, it is known as sixteenfold, and so on until it reaches an incalculable number.
Since the universe is clearly capable of being grasped as a single unity from the very beginning,
and since it ultimately endures even the various perceptions of its constituent parts and sub-parts,
therefore there is a state of identity with the fifty [phonemes], which consists in the diversity of vowels and manifestations.
The eight groups consist of a division of phonemes, arising from eighty-one kalās.
This has been previously demonstrated on account of their capacity to endure the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*);
for even within a vowel there is a half [of a mora], since the circumflex (*svarita*) possesses a half-mora.
The knower of words has stated that its first syllable is acute;
thus, this consciousness consists of the reflective awareness of the nature of the object of sacrifice. And this circle of wheels is non-different from consciousness.
One should employ that [power] in many ways according to the distinctions of the Lord and the veils (āvaraṇa).
The other, the supreme, and another [state] correspond to emanation, maintenance, and concealment;
however, the fourth, which is the true nature of the Mothers, is called rest (viśrānti).
And that light, residing within the mouth [of the teacher], has been indicated at every step;
one should establish rest in the Fourth state, which flows from the true being of the Mother.
In this way, the entire universe appears to him as having attained identity with his own self.

Thus has been stated this unification of the meaning of the scripture as taught by the Guru. That which has been described in many ways as the individual (āṇava) means for attaining the state of Śiva— having entered into that repeatedly, one should rest in the proximate state. Then,
by abandoning even that individual means, one should take recourse in the empowered (śākta) stage.
Even beyond that, one clearly attains the state of Śāmbhavī through this same sequence of gradations.
Thus, one who partakes in the state of Bhairava— the expansion of which is completely filled by the great rays of awakening arising in due order—
finally enters his own eternal Self, which contains the form of the entire universe, precisely by means of independence from all external expedients.
This entry into one's own true nature has been taught by the Supreme Lord.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*,
wherein the synthesis of all scriptures is here set forth.
In this world, first of all, this ancient worldly convention is uniform;
following upon established consensus, that very consensus is called "scripture" (āgama).
For positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are dependent upon established consensus.
If those two were dependent solely on themselves, what would be the status of their manifestation within a multitude of individual instances?
Even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which arises from specific conditions such as the eyes, the self, lamps, and objects,
requires at its root that very kind of established [prior] cognition.

Born in a place completely enclosed on all sides, the infant is alone and hungry. What can he do? What can he grasp? With what can he see? Where can he go? For even in a place strewn with hundreds of objects, whatever indeed [is within his reach]— [The rest of the verse is: ...that alone he perceives; the rest remains as if it were not there. Thus, by the power of the Lord, this [infant] is made to experience the fruits of karma through the body born of past actions. And since the body is composed of the elements, how could it perceive anything else? Therefore, it is established that the soul (*ātman*) is distinct from the body. Furthermore, because the body is subject to growth and decay, while the soul is eternal, the two are different. Moreover, the body is insentient, whereas the soul is conscious; thus, they are distinct. And because the body is perishable and the soul is imperishable, they are not one and the same. Consequently, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Furthermore, since the body is an object of perception and the soul is the perceiver, they are different. Also, because the body is the instrument of action and the soul is the agent, they are distinct. And since the body is the locus of suffering and the soul is the sufferer, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Additionally, because the body is produced by parents and the soul is beginningless, they are different. Moreover, the body is a composite of parts, while the soul is partless; therefore, they are distinct. And since the body is limited and the soul is all-pervading, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Furthermore, because the body is subject to change and the soul is unchanging, they are different. Also, the body is visible, while the soul is invisible; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the field of experience and the soul is the experiencer, they are not one. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the result of material causes and the soul is the witness, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the vehicle of movement, while the soul is the mover; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the support of the senses and the soul is the knower of the senses, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the product of the three qualities (*guṇas*) and the soul is beyond the qualities, they are different. Moreover, the body is the object of desire, while the soul is the desirer; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of enjoyment and the soul is the enjoyer, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Furthermore, because the body is the cause of bondage and the soul is the bound one, they are different. Moreover, the body is the instrument of liberation, while the soul is the liberated one; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the path of transmigration and the soul is the transmigrator, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the vessel for merit and demerit and the soul is the possessor of merit and demerit, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the field of action, while the soul is the doer of action; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the locus of the results of action and the soul is the experiencer of those results, they are not one. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the source of pain and the soul is the feeler of pain, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the instrument of pleasure, while the soul is the enjoyer of pleasure; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of attaining heaven and the soul is the one who attains heaven, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of worldly existence and the soul is the one who exists in the world, they are different. Moreover, the body is the support of the mind, while the soul is the master of the mind; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the field of the intellect and the soul is the knower of the intellect, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Furthermore, because the body is the product of ignorance and the soul is beyond ignorance, they are different. Moreover, the body is the object of meditation, while the soul is the meditator; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of knowledge and the soul is the knower, they are not one. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of death and the soul is immortal, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the vessel of birth, while the soul is unborn; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the locus of old age and the soul is ageless, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the cause of disease and the soul is free from disease, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of treatment, while the soul is the patient; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of healing and the soul is the one healed, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of exhaustion and the soul is tireless, they are different. Moreover, the body is the object of fatigue, while the soul is the one fatigued; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of recovery and the soul is the one recovered, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Furthermore, because the body is the cause of hunger and the soul is hungry, they are different. Moreover, the body is the object of nourishment, while the soul is the one nourished; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of satiety and the soul is the one satisfied, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of thirst and the soul is thirsty, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of drinking, while the soul is the drinker; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of quenching thirst and the soul is the one whose thirst is quenched, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the cause of sleep and the soul is the sleeper, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of waking, while the soul is the one who wakes; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of dreaming and the soul is the dreamer, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of wakefulness and the soul is the one who is awake, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of consciousness, while the soul is consciousness itself; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of cognition and the soul is the cognizer, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the cause of memory and the soul is the rememberer, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of recollection, while the soul is the one who remembers; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of mindfulness and the soul is the mindful one, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of desire and the soul is the desirer, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of longing, while the soul is the one who longs; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of fulfillment and the soul is the one fulfilled, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the cause of aversion and the soul is the one who feels aversion, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of repulsion, while the soul is the one who is repelled; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of detachment and the soul is the detached one, they are not identical. Thus, the soul is proven to be other than the body. Additionally, because the body is the cause of effort and the soul is the one who exerts effort, they are different. Furthermore, the body is the object of exertion, while the soul is the one who exerts; thus, they are distinct. And since the body is the means of achievement and the soul is the achiever, they are not the same. Thus, the soul is established as separate from the body. Moreover, because the body is the cause of speech and the soul is the speaker, they are different. Whether seeing, smelling, or touching, the mind becomes serene; having immediately grasped that very object, it partakes in positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Indeed, even this serenity of the mind which pertains to a particular object—
That [object] too is constructed by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the form of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
it is not born from the clarity of external means of knowledge such as perception, inference, and so forth.
Since this depends upon prior latent impressions, it is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).
A man does not develop a desire to consume clay as food;

if reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) subsists upon prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then that [desire] is indeed such an impression. If it has come from the past, this is established as belonging to a previous time.
Nor is the entire course of worldly transaction based solely on the clarity of consciousness.
Let it be understood that in every case, established convention (*prasiddhi*) is the root and the authority for that;
when one seeks the basis by relying on each preceding stage, that [convention] itself is found somewhere.
For previously, all worldly transaction shone forth without doubt within that single one whose nature is omniscient;
indeed, no complete worldly transaction whatsoever exists in any other cognizer.
Therefore, this [omniscience] is not established merely by the fact that [the opponent's source] was preceded by one who is not omniscient.
There is no proof whatsoever for the existence of many previous omniscient beings.
Adorned by hundreds of established instances of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and their causes,
this Supreme Lord Bhairava has the nature of that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Then, through the connection of parts and sub-parts, that established tradition—

whether relying upon a lineage or a scripture— is extended and causes the worlds to engage in worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*). By means of that very [tradition], everyone from childhood onwards partakes in the laws of worldly transaction.
The virtuous rely solely upon the primordial scripture of Śiva (the Śaiva Āgama).
However, others who are incomplete do not partake in the fruit of liberation;
they partake in its fruits only to the extent that they rely upon it.
Even when childhood has passed, the fact that this person proceeds to eat food is established by common experience alone;
it is not known through direct perception, nor through inference, because [the latter] is impossible.
Furthermore, there is no suspicion of any defect here, since all such doubts have been removed.
Established consensus is a cognition arising from non-discrepancy, consisting of verbal expression.
Since this is the very nature of the Mother [of Speech], one never doubts her;
for Śaṅkara is omniscient precisely by virtue of his own self-origination.

As long as he has not attained the state of Śiva, for that long he does not doubt that very well-known [notion] which follows his own self. He would be suspicious of another [notion], and he highly values that [well-known one].
Thus, one who is destined for the state of Śiva considers this [attainment] to be certain success. This is the single scripture revealed by the all-seeing Lord,
which stands upon both the path of worldly engagement and the path of withdrawal.
Regarding the various fruits— whether complete or incomplete— in the realms of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, the Śāmbhava Āgama is the sole means.
For it bestows diverse fruits through its distinctness from other objects.
Even the instruction on diverse means (upāyas) would not entail contradiction [with our system]:
the worldly, the Vedic, Sāṅkhya, Yoga and the like, Pāñcarātra, the Buddhist and Jaina systems of logic, and the arrangement of the categories (padārtha) according to their sequence. // 25–26 //
Since all systems— the Siddhānta, Tantra, Śākta, and so forth— originate from Brahman,
they are taught in the *Śrī Svacchanda* and other scriptures through the divisions of Sadyojāta and the rest;
just as even within a single system such as the Veda, there are those who follow various stages of life (*āśrama*).

In this case as well, there is another preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), such as the extraction of the *liṅga* and so forth. Just as in that previous stage one does not attain the fruit of the subsequent stage, so too in the Pāñcarātra and other systems, one does not attain the nature of Śiva.

Therefore, there is but one single scripture; for everything therein—from the worldly treatises up to the Vaiṣṇava, Bauddha, and Śaiva traditions—is firmly established. That supreme goal which is to be attained by that [scripture] is designated as Trika.

Because it is entirely undivided and indestructible, that alone is called the *kula*. Just as there is a single life-force within the various limbs of the body, which possess a hierarchy of upper and lower parts, so too, according to the scriptures, is the *trika* one and the same in all things.
In the illustrious Kālīkula, it is taught that which is free from the five currents;
this is proclaimed to be the essence of the eighteen-fold division [of the Tantras].
As fragrance is in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, the soul in the body, and nectar in water, so is this [essence] found within.

Just as it is, so too the family of scriptures is established within [the body]. This single scripture is manifold according to the diversity of its qualified recipients; for that very same tradition extends to both those of one's own school and those of other schools.

One should not disparage Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, or the Vedas; for, as stated in the Svacchanda-śāsana, all of these originate from Śiva. Furthermore, these have been extracted as various fragments from a single, unified scripture.
In the world there are scriptures, and by them people wander, deluded.
Even when there are many scriptural positions, a distinction of their respective domains must be stated;
for the sake of establishing their validity, there must necessarily be a hierarchy of higher and lower levels.
Otherwise, the validity of anything whatsoever would certainly not be established. For us, neither eternality nor non-contradiction constitutes the ground for validity;
rather, even in this respect, the validity of that very [scripture] would exist because it has been taught in such a manner.

Otherwise, if [the scripture] were assumed to be indeterminate, untrue, or intended merely for persuasion, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of subverting all scriptures. Therefore, one must necessarily accept this means of knowledge called "scripture" (āgama). 35.40b–41b.
This determination of the culmination of the scripture must necessarily be undertaken;
for, in reality, effort expended upon the primary limb [of the teaching] is what bears fruit. Therefore, someone impelled by Śambhu should apply themselves with effort to this.
In various scriptures, this was described by Maheśin:
"One who is qualified for such [a practice] is clearly difficult to find.
Thus has the *Śāstramelana* been told to me by the venerable Śambhunātha.
Now, in the thirty-sixth chapter of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*,
the origin of the scripture is described as it has come down in due course;
it is that which was pointed out by the venerable *Siddha* and other [scriptures] and elucidated by the Gurus.

Bhairava, the goddess Bhairavī, Svacchanda, Lākula, Aṇurāṭ, Gahaneśa, the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Śakra, and Guru [each] studied it in succession from ten million verses down by ten million, until it was reduced by nine [to one million]. Thus, it was studied in nine stages, its extent being ninety million verses.
Thereupon, from those [ten million verses], the Guru bestowed one quarter upon Dakṣa and the others,
and two quarters upon Saṃvarta and the others;
he gave one quarter to Vāmana and the others, and half a quarter to Bhārgava.
One-quarter of the foot is for Bali;
and that other quarter of the foot is for Siṃha. From what remains, two parts are for Vinatā’s son (Garuḍa), one quarter for the serpent Vāsuki—these, then, are the seventeen portions.
Then Rāvaṇa took half from heaven, and Rāma likewise took half from that [remaining portion].
He obtained [the rest] through Vibhīṣaṇa, by way of the traditional succession from teacher to disciple. Thereafter, it became divided into nineteen parts.
It is divided into sections and sub-sections, and into eight parts according to the distinctions of the previously mentioned quarters and so forth.
These are: the Quarter (Pāda), the Root (Mūla), the Extraction (Uddhāra), the Subsequent (Uttara), the Great Subsequent (Vṛhaduttara), and likewise the Ritual Manual (Kalpa).
Then there are the Saṃhitā-kalpa and the Skanda; the Unsurpassed (Anuttara) is all-pervasive, being threefold and consisting of three [sections].
In this [chapter], the goddesses are described in their progressively expanding forms;
however, in the ninth stage, which is devoid of any further division, no enumeration is mentioned.
From Rāma comes Lakṣmaṇa, from him the Siddhas, and from them the Dānavas.

From them [came] the Guhyakas, and from them the yogins, the best of men. When, in the course of time, that [tradition] had been lost among them after some interval, then, by the power of the command of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the Siddhas descended.
Tryambaka, Āmardaka, and the venerable Śrīnātha— renowned as such— are experts, respectively, in the non-dual, the dual,
and the dual-non-dual teachings of Śiva.
And from the lineage of the first [Tryambaka] was born the second [Āmardaka] through the transmission of his daughter.
And that lineage known as Ardhatryambaka is well-established. From this,
there are three and a half monastic centers (maṭhikās) here,
expanded through disciples and grand-disciples established in hundreds of branches according to the sequence of the lineages.
Having extracted the essential sap from the stream of the three and a half lineages, this *Tantrāloka* now flows forth, distilling all aesthetic flavors (*rasas*).
The transmission has been described; now its status as that which is to be adopted is being determined.
Now, the thirty-seventh chapter in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:

When all worldly transactions proceed precisely according to the method already described, and since common consensus (*prasiddhi*) is that upon which one must depend, the scripture (*āgama*) necessarily must be accepted. (1)

Just as one who engages in correct worldly conduct partakes of other fruits through the consensus of the world, so too one who acts correctly [in this system] partakes of Śiva through that same consensus. Therefore,
since a scripture that teaches its own specific portion must necessarily be accepted, [one should follow it].
That which is most worthy of being adopted yields even a slight fruit, while the opposite is its contrary.

Just as poison goes to destruction through the state of fearlessness regarding one's identity as the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), so too does the persistence of karma reach its end through the fearlessness that arises from the state of Bhairava.

That which is declared in the Ārṣa [tradition] to be a cause for downfall, that very thing leads to swift accomplishment in this Left-hand teaching (vāmaśāsana), because everything belonging to the Ārṣa is situated within the belly of Māyā.
Furthermore, what could that be which has been seen by every omniscient one?
When the unsurpassed fruit is brought forth through instruction that leaves nothing remaining, then—

just as each higher [teaching] is proclaimed by way of restating the reality of the objects taught in each successive lower one— that [higher teaching], being established by direct experience (*saṃvit*), truly becomes so.
Because of the determination of the reality established through the higher consciousness that has been described,

it is understood that the declarations regarding the "non-omniscient" found in the lower teachings [are made] even after one has seen and yet abandoned a portion of the reality belonging to the higher teaching.
In the lower scriptures, the nature of Māyā is observed through the creation and preservation [of the world].
And it has been declared by the Supreme Lord in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra* and other works:
"The word of the sages involves much affliction, yields unstable and meager fruits, and is limited. (AbhT 37.10)
The wise man should not hold other scriptures as authoritative; he should take refuge in the Śaiva Āgama alone.
That which is declared in the [other] Ṛṣi-scriptures to be a cause for downfall is not so in this Vāma teaching.
This is because all that belongs to the Ṛṣis resides within the belly of Māyā, whereas [in this system] everything leads to swift accomplishment.

Just as poison is destroyed through the state of fearlessness regarding one's identity as Khageśvarī, so too does the persistence of karma perish through the fearlessness that arises from the state of Bhairava. This occurs when one has been bitten by the lower teaching, which is characterized by ignorance and a lack of authentic instruction.
By the reversal of this [false teaching], the doctrine of Śiva must necessarily be grasped;
therein, the two authoritative ones are the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha and Lakuleśvara. This scripture, which bestows the supreme good when properly understood, possesses two streams.
Furthermore, it is established that the Eastern [tradition] bestows enjoyments according to one's desire.
And that is said to be fivefold, variegated by the diversity of powers;
it is proclaimed as the "Five Streams" (Pañcasrotas), the teaching of the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha.
The fivefold stream, which consists of eighteen and ten [channels],
is further expanded into sixty-four divisions known as Bhairava;
this was indeed proclaimed by the Lord in the venerable *Ānandaśāstra* and other works.
This assembly is the *pīṭha*, and it is twofold: from the right and from the left.
Therefore, there is the pair consisting of mantra and vidyā, which reside within the mudrās and the maṇḍala.
That which bestows reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*) is called "mantra," and therein [it functions] through the vidyā.
For that [mudrā] is the reinforcement and the nourishment which illuminates the object of knowledge;
the mudrā is the counterpart of the mantra, and it is that which effects its nourishment.
Indeed, the maṇḍala is said to be the essence (*sāra*); by the term *maṇḍa*, that which is called Śiva is intended.
Thus, the four seats (pīṭha) function through mutual interpenetration. Therefore, in reality, everything exists within each and every seat;
yet, due to the predominance of this or that particular entity, there is again a sense of differentiation.

This has been declared for the sake of the accomplishment of their respective goals by the foremost of practitioners. Each of these is fourfold: the mandala, likewise the mudrā, the mantra, and the vidyā; and the pīṭha is the most excellent, higher than the highest.
The Siddhayogīśvarīmata is the preeminent authority among the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
The Mālinīvijayottara is its supreme essence. And this very point was stated by the Supreme Lord in the Śrīratnamālā: 24–25.
The essence of all Tantras without exception, which rests upon both the Left and the Right,
has converged as one in the Kaula tradition within the teaching of the venerable Trika (the Six-and-a-Half).
In the Siddhānta, ritual action (*karma*) predominates, being defiled by impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and the like.

Abandon from afar that discipline which is rich in fierce deeds on the right, crowded with supernatural powers on the left, possesses little merit, abounds in afflictions, is devoid of personal realization, and is lacking in the knowledge of liberation. (27–28)

And at the very moment when the Guru has revealed the state free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), one is liberated by that very moment; the machine remains alone. This form of the currents [of scripture] has been [revealed] by me from the stable, unsurpassed state.
This has been explained at length, beginning from [the start], in the *Mālinīślokavārttika*.
One who desires to know may therefore be capable of ascertaining this from that very source.
We, however, do not favor the fruitless task of merely repeating what has already been said.
Thus, bestowing effortlessly the great fruit of liberation while living,
this true scripture— the essence of the Trika— stands established as the giver of all desired great enjoyments; it is clearly to be accepted.

Although this infinite series of worlds was produced by the power of the thirty-six principles, the Egg of Brahmā is exceedingly captivating; for there is no state of beauty devoid of variety. Even though that [universe] is filled with the seven cities beginning with Bhūḥ, I consider the second world to be the true abode of happiness.
Where else is there such a place, adorned by the divisions of enjoyment throughout the expansion of day and night, shining with the sun and moon that move through various paths?
Even there, the land called Kumārikā is indeed superior to the other continents and islands, which are highly prized for the enjoyments of the three heavens;
for it is there that the fortunate possess the priceless authority to ascend from the lowest of low states all the way to the supreme state of Śiva.

What is the use of a birth that partakes only in enjoyments suited for a bound soul (paśu) experiencing the fruits of past karma, even if it be in a realm consisting solely of happiness? For everyone finds supreme satisfaction in a future state that is highly esteemed, but not in the present which is subject to fleeting moments.
Even in this world called Kanyā, there is a most exalted region where, they say, the supreme scriptures serve as one's eyes.
Who would not censure birth in a house blind from birth, when there is the light of the sun appearing as if through applied collyrium?

Indeed, Madhyadeśa is the abode of all scriptures; in that land was born a twice-born man of preeminent qualities, known by the name Atrigupta—a name whose lineage is etymologically explained as being like the Agastya clan, ever-rising for the purpose of consuming the ocean of the scriptures.
Then King Lalitāditya, out of the intensity of his affection, led him to his own city called Kaśmīra, situated upon the summit of the Himalayas;
for there the beloved of Gaurī dwells with his hands—Vijaya and the others—to simultaneously and with delight savor the entire essence of all enjoyments.
It is in every place that all the sages have made their dwellings, and it is there that the Moon-crested Lord himself resides at every step.
Therefore, I consider that for the attainment of all desired perfections, there is no city superior to Kashmir; nor for the satisfaction of one whose conduct is complete.
(40) There, the goddess renowned among people as Śrī Śāradā—white as the autumnal moon, well-pleased by the essence of Śāṇḍilya’s service—endows all people with her own splendors. (41)

In that [liṅga] resides the Great Bhairava liquor, brilliant with its four powers, possessing a luster as ruddy as an orange, a complexion as pale-white as a blooming *vallī* flower, and a radiance as beautiful as the golden hue of a freshly opened, pure *mātuluṅga* fruit; it shines with a dark splendor resembling the mass of hair on the head of a young girl.
Here, the multitude of Cupid’s arrows, melted by the flames of the Great Three-Eyed One’s wrath, manifests itself under the guise of this liquor.

Otherwise, how could it incessantly subjugate the world with the afflictions of desire, instilling passion, delusion, pride, and the fever of love? (43) That grape-wine (*mārdvīka*) bestows maturity upon the amorous words of beloved women; it shakes off all trepidation during the act of love without obstacle; in it, all the goddesses who move in circles find delight; and it instantly provides both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (44)

Where the earth is strewn at every step with saffron flowers—dark red petals blooming like rising pale sprouts, variegated by rows of filaments shining with a deep, intense crimson—it reveals itself as a garden for the perfect worship of the triad of goddesses.
(45) Where every person is a poet, a scholar, or a hero, and even eloquent; where the women of the city possess the radiance of the moon and move with graceful gait. (46)
There, where the infinite path of the *suṣumnā* blazes with glowing coals, swallowing the sun and moon, and where the host of yoginīs is as pure as the sky;

there stands the glorious city named Para, which the lord of the earth Pravarasena constructed. It is said that at the conclusion of his worship of Maheśvara installed by himself, he flew up into the air and released a bell of incense.
With charming and heroic cries arising from her swaying, she proclaimed his virtuous conduct;
for those whose forms possess the brilliance of the essence of noble character resound even more powerfully with their master’s virtues, even when they have been cast away.
She possessed a beauty tawny with the thick saffron of a lover’s body-paste, which was like the pure luster of the full moon.
She incessantly bestows upon Smara the royal consecration with floods of white chowries from the swaying cane-creepers;

she is worthy of being saluted by sages, Siddhas, and men whose sins have been destroyed by the mass of immersions in her gently rolling waves, through the perfumes, flowers, and unguents used for the worship of the self-manifested *liṅga* of Maheśvara established upon her banks.

In that place, where the Vitastā river—acting as a wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpavallī*) that fulfills both worldly enjoyment and liberation; surpassing the celestial river of the gods and *siddhas* which delights solely in granting enjoyments; and having descended from a portion of Hara’s Pināka bow—constantly adorns the land, there exists a state of sanctity born from the sight of the moon-crested Lord Śiva facing him directly, as he wanders through the city of Kubera.
The king, having provided him with abundant wealth, established a dwelling for that twice-born man on a riverbank measuring a *vitasti* in width.
In his great lineage there arose a certain person named Varāhagupta, upon whom the Blessed One himself, at the time of his final end,
bestowed supreme grace with insistence— He whose crest was embraced by the waves of the celestial river.
His son was Narasiṃhagupta, renowned among the people as Cukhalaka, whose intellect was as pure as the moon;
he, whose mind was brightened by immersion in the essence of all the scriptures, was supremely adorned by devotion to Maheśvara.
Casting aside the surging waves of the ocean of youth, he firmly boarded the boat of dispassion with resolute effort.

He who, having attained the mountain of devotion, completely shattered those calamities of worldly existence with the wish-fulfilling gems of meditation upon Maheśvara—his son is the renowned Abhinavagupta, purified by the pollen of the lotus feet of the illustrious Moon-crested Lord (Śiva). His mother, it is said, was separated from him while he was still in infancy; for destiny prepares one for the tasks yet to come.
"There is a common saying that the mother is the ultimate kinsman; for affection makes the bonds exceedingly tight.

When the root-bond has dissolved, I believe that liberation exists for him even while he is still alive. Having been introduced by his father into the dense thicket of grammar, his mind was purified by the spray from the waves of the ocean of logic.

Devoted to the enjoyment of the intense aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of literary works, he was seized by a devotion to Maheśvara that was headstrong in its spontaneous grasping. Having become one with that [devotion], he no longer reckoned with any worldly path whatsoever;
rather, in order to increase his enjoyment of that [divinity], he himself formerly performed service in the houses of his gurus.
Vāmanātha, son of the excellent teacher Erakavara, is the helmsman of the great ocean of the lineage of Ānanda;
he is the sun in the vast sky of the lineage of Śrīnātha, the son of the illustrious Bhūtirāja, who received grace from his own father.
Lord Lakṣmaṇagupta, son of Utpala and born of Somānanda, who rested upon the ocean of the expansion of the Traiyambaka lineage.

Śambhunātha, the knower of all things, was indeed the full moon for the great ocean of the lineage known as the Fourth (turya), having received it from the venerable Soma. [His disciples were] the venerable Candraśarman, Bhavabhaktivilāsa, Yogānanda, Abhinanda, Śivaśakti, Vicitranātha,
and other great masters such as Dharmaśiva, Vāmanaka, Udbhaṭa, the venerable Bhūteśa, and Bhāskara.

These [teachings], which bestow grace through the essence of service and are made beautiful by the manifest instructions on the firm core of the scriptures, were indeed bestowed upon him as his own domain;
and because he did not look upon people who were not fit vessels, he remained day and night delighting in his own Self, finding his pleasure in the essence of serving the ultimate reality.
Then, in order to favor his own brother—who was devoted to Śambhu and filled with the discernment of all the scriptures—[he acted].
As long as he directed his mind toward that which is called the "fulfillment of desires," so many people approached him.

(64) The son of Śrī Śauri, known by the name Karṇa—who, in his youth, had realized the essence of the truth of Śambhu—by casting off his body, demonstrated to the people the truth of the Great Sage Kṛṣṇa’s words regarding one who has fallen from yoga. (65)
Then there was his childhood friend, the renowned son of a minister named Śrī Mandra, who was delightful with all the essence of virtuous qualities;

the illustrious power of his fortune eclipsed even the rivalry between Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī as they adorned him together. Others were the nephews of his paternal uncle—Śivaśakti, Śubhra, Kṣema, Utpala, Abhinavacakraka, and Padmagupta—who were radiant with the energy of Śiva.
Those who considered even worldly prosperity as mere straw, contemplating within their hearts their own inner self fulfilled by the service of Śambhu;
he by whom the entire ritual system, beginning with the maṇḍala,
was mastered in the Trika scriptures— he was Rāmagupta, whose complete path was intent upon the practice of serving the Guru and the Śiva-scriptures.

Even any other person, whose own collection of powers has been brought under the sway of the impulse of Śiva’s descent of power (śaktipāta), has made this group an object of grace by means of that untrained [teacher], despite his being averse to requests. He earnestly entreated the teacher for the complete and correct mastery of the Tantra.
For one whose intellect is graced by destiny, prosperity arises as a continuous flow of success, a single essence of well-being.
(70) He too accepted what was desired by him; for indeed, that which had descended was his own instrument for dancing.
For the true gurus are inclined toward grace through the great sprout of the birth of auspiciousness, by the power of their command. (71)

Then, desiring to abandon his state of distraction, the gentle [prince] chose to remain in his own excellent city, where even down to the children and cowherds, the people practiced service to Maheśvara as if they were dwelling in a sacred seat (pīṭha). It is said that he had a paternal aunt for whom the Creator had fashioned away all the diverse anxieties of worldly existence.
Her sole ornament was the pollen from the lotus-feet of the Moon-crested Lord; she bore a name appropriate to her nature as a compassionate mother.
She was like forgiveness incarnate, like compassion embodied, and like the very upholder of auspicious character taken into physical form.
She was the full state of ripening for the essence of dispassion, and the mountain soil where the jewels of the true meaning of reality shine forth.

Even his brother Śauri, whose mental disposition was supremely purified by devotion to the one who wears the moon-bright crown, abandoned his position as a minister to the king after having attained the status of a minister to the Lord. His daughter-in-law, the wife of Karṇa, having shaken off the ways of worldly existence, [gave birth] to only one son.
She gave birth to the one named Yogeśvaridatta, whose essential nature shone forth in accordance with his name.
When she was in her early youth, the Three-Eyed Lord himself, out of devotion, favored her who was distressed by separation from her husband.
Truly, misfortune draws in a succession of future benefits for those people who are filled with the intensity of their own future power.
Having obtained the horripilation arising from devotion as her manifest bodily ornament, the prostration before the venerable Śambhunātha as her forehead-ornament,
and the Śaiva scripture as her ear-ornament, she bore an exceeding inner auspiciousness. Indeed, she who was named Ambā beheld that Guru, her own brother, with the very eye of Śambhu.
His intellect, radiant with the power of his future destiny, did not disregard the virtuous out of a sense of kinship;
for he was his brother, both by name and indeed by his own noble conduct.
Having drunk the essence of realized knowledge, his thirst for that very [truth] increased intensely.
He and the other [disciples] possessed a radiant splendor, born from the heart-lotus whose contraction was dissolving away by the mass of rays of Śiva;
Lumpinga attended upon him during his exertions—for indeed, a virtuous person provides a helping hand.
Thus, staying in the house bestowed by Vatsalikā, he composed his mind for many [years].

Reflecting with his own intellect upon the scriptures he had previously heard, he extracted their essence from them. He composed that highly significant work, which sets forth the reality of the Tantras through both reasoning and scriptural authority;
having obtained this illumination, the world shall proceed happily in its ritual activities.
O virtuous ones, favor this work of his; first, accept it—for such is the rule.
Then may that [work] also grasp your minds, and may it immediately favor you with the vision of reality.
O Śiva, You whose ears extend everywhere, please listen for a moment to this essence of the scriptures woven by Abhinavagupta.
"This is indeed your praise; for it is an exposition upon your own nature. Being thus newly gratified, make the world your own. 85.
